title: A Review of Robotic Surgery: Engineering Considerations and Future Directions From Surgeons' Perspectives
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Since its initial inception, robotic-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS) is continually being applied to a wider array of procedures. However, there are significant limitations in current surgical subsystems, including a large learning curve, lack of effective haptic feedback, decreased surgical intuition, and decreased dexterity. METHODS: A narrative review of the literature was conducted to provide an overview of key developments in the field. Relevant articles were identified through searches of PubMed, IEEE, Google Scholar, and EMBASE, along with manual screening of references. RESULTS: A selection of representative articles covering topics including teleoperation, kinematics, dynamics, and haptic feedback is discussed to highlight major themes and recent advances. CONCLUSIONS: Despite recent advances, limitations to operator experience remain. Numerous strategies and approaches are currently being proposed and explored to further advance surgical subsystems, improving dexterity, haptic feedback, movement time delay, and learning curve.
authors: Noah Shaikh; Walter Fitschen; Abhinaba Bhattacharjee; Dimitrios Stefanidis; Michael W. Sim; Meghan Turner; Sohel Anwar; Muhammad Ashraful Alam
venue: International Journal of Medical Robotics and Computer Assisted Surgery

title: Occupancy Network-Guided Autonomous Robotic Partial Nephrectomy
abstract: Autonomous soft-tissue cancer surgery has been limited to interventions on organ surfaces, because current systems cannot perceive and adapt to anatomy once it deforms or is cut. We introduce the first vision-guided autonomous system capable of performing complete tumor resections for partial nephrectomy. Our system integrates conditional occupancy networks, trained entirely in a physics-based simulation, that infer full 3-D anatomy (tumor, margin tissue, and kidney) from single-view partial point clouds. These occupancy networks maintain intraoperative tracking even as tissue is cut and deformed, enabling adaptive planning and execution. The surgical platform combines a depth camera for capturing surface point clouds, dual robotic arms for electrosurgical cutting and vacuum-based tissue manipulation, and an autonomous control strategy for tumor resection. In patient-derived hydrogel phantoms under an open partial nephrectomy setting, the robot performed eight consecutive autonomous tumor resections comprising 77 electrosurgical cuts, with all cuts achieving negative surgical margins and 1.61 $\pm$ 0.48 mm mean absolute margin error. This work demonstrates, for the first time, a foundation for supervised autonomous closed-loop, imaging-driven, margin-negative tumor removal in phantoms.
authors: Ethan Kilmer; Pit Henrich; Jiawei Ge; Paul Maria Scheikl; Laura Connolly; Soum D. Lokeshwar; Joseph Chen; Justin David Opfermann; Kaitlyn Kumar; Lauren M. Shepard; Ahmed Ghazi; Nirmish Singla; Richard Cha; Kevin Cleary; Franziska Mathis-Ullrich; Axel Krieger

title: Multimodal data-driven intelligent diagnosis in traditional Chinese medicine: Current status and future perspectives
abstract: With advances in artificial intelligence, traditional Chinese medicine diagnosis is gradually becoming more intelligent. This review departs from the conventional framework that categorizes the four diagnostic methods in isolation. Instead, it starts from five heterogeneous data modalities, namely vision, audition, olfaction, textual, and tactile, and systematically reconstructs the digital mapping relationships of traditional Chinese medicine diagnostic information, thereby directly aligning traditional Chinese medicine diagnostic problems with the input paradigms of artificial intelligence. This study comprehensively examines the current state of research on multimodal acquisition technologies, fusion methods, and clinical applications, and analyzes the core challenges and future directions in this field. This study aims to provide a theoretical foundation for achieving truly intelligent integration of the four diagnostic methods.
authors: Jiaqi Sun; Zheng Yu; 高俊虹

title: Robotic technologies relevant to brain tumor surgery: a bibliometric and knowledge-mapping analysis of global trends and translational frontiers.
abstract: To map the global development, collaboration structure, intellectual foundations, thematic evolution, and translational fronts of robotic technologies relevant to brain tumor surgery and cranial neuro-oncology. The Web of Science Core Collection was searched on August 25, 2026. English-language records were manually screened to include both clinically deployed robotic applications and engineering/preclinical systems with an explicit cranial tumor-related use case. Bibliometric and science-mapping analyses were performed with R/Bibliometrix-Biblioshiny and CiteSpace 6.4.R1. Of 329 records identified, 106 publications were included (98 article-type records and 8 reviews). The corpus spanned 1997-2026, 47 sources, and 620 authors, and accumulated 2,195 citations. The USA led country production (30 records) and citations (748). Universite Paris Cite was the most frequent affiliation (12 records), Sutherland GR the most prolific author (5 publications), and the International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery the leading source (9 publications). Keyword clustering identified ten communities spanning image-guided targeting, robotic biopsy, force feedback, continuum/concentric-tube systems, frameless navigation, sensing, pediatric brainstem biopsy, and robot-guided local therapy. Recent bursts centered on diagnostic yield, efficacy, safety, and brain tumors. The mapped literature represents a translational continuum from clinically integrated stereotactic biopsy and tumor-directed intervention to emerging sensing, continuum robotics, and data-driven control. Bibliometric prominence does not establish clinical effectiveness. Further translation will require reliable sensing, compensation for tissue deformation, workflow integration, standardized reporting, and multicenter validation.
authors: Guolong Zhang; Yan Dong

title: Retrospective Evaluation of Safety of Using a Semi-automatic Robotic System for Transthoracic Biopsy of Lung Mass Under Positron Emission Tomography-computed Tomography Guidance.
abstract: Lung cancer poses unique challenges due to heterogeneity in tumor and metastatic cellular composition. The use of 18F-fluorodeoxy glucose positron emission tomography-computed tomography (18F-FDG PET-CT) integrates functional and anatomical imaging. This study assessed the safety and diagnostic yield of PET-CT-guided transthoracic needle biopsy for intrathoracic mass lesions using a semi-automatic robotic system. Forty consecutive patients underwent whole-body PET-CT imaging following which they underwent transthoracic biopsy, using a semi-automatic robotic biopsy system (MaxioTM III; Perfint Healthcare Pvt Ltd., Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India), consisting of docking system, digital screen and a stereotactic arm. Clinicodemographic profile, PET-CT and biopsy findings, histopathology reports, and complications were retrieved from patient records. The mean age of the patients was 57.08±12.39 years, and the mean maximum standardized uptake value was 16.71±8.61. PET-CT revealed a unilateral lung mass in 92.5% (n = 37) and bilateral lesions in 7.5% (n = 3) of patients. Heterogeneous 18F-FDG uptake was noted in 97.5% (n = 39). The average target lesion distance was 40±12.7 mm. At least four biopsy cores were obtained in all patients except one. Core length was 2 cm in 90% of cases. The most common complication was local pain, followed by pneumothorax in 12.5% (n = 5). Tissue was adequate for analysis in all cases. None of the patients had to undergo repeat PET-CT or biopsy. The diagnostic yield was 100%, with malignancy in 82.5% (n = 33), acute inflammation in 10% (n = 4), and tuberculosis in 7.5% (n = 3). 50% (n = 20) underwent next-generation sequencing for targeted mutation testing. Semiautomatic robotic assistance can be a safe option for diagnosing intrathoracic mass lesions, with an acceptable diagnostic yield.

title: Paradigm shifts in prostate biopsy strategies in the era of precision medicine
abstract: The escalating global burden of prostate cancer necessitates continuous refinement of diagnostic strategies. Although prostate biopsy remains the gold standard for diagnosis, key procedural aspects, including biopsy template, guidance methods, and biopsy route, remain subjects of ongoing debate. Current approaches have yet to achieve the dual goals of high sensitivity and high specificity in diagnostic performance. In recent years, ongoing advancements in related fields have generated substantial clinical evidence, offering further insights into optimizing biopsy strategies. This review provides a synthesized framework for navigating the paradigm shift from traditional, standardized biopsy toward personalized, precision-based approaches. We not only trace the evolution of biopsy techniques but also offer a comprehensive, in-depth exploration of how patient-specific factors, such as prostate volume, prostate-specific antigen density, and Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System scores, can inform individualized biopsy decisions, thereby providing practical clinical guidance. In addition to critically evaluating conventional biopsy paradigms, we systematically examine emerging biopsy strategies and synthesize high-quality studies at the forefront of this field. Finally, against the backdrop of the artificial intelligence era, we highlight the transformative potential of artificial intelligence and robotic platforms across the diagnosis. By integrating current development and future directions, this review offers a structured framework for personalized biopsy decision-making, ultimately aiming to achieve both high sensitivity and high specificity in individualized prostate cancer diagnosis.

title: Clinical validation of an AI-based computer-aided detection system for risk classification of radiologist-identified prostate MRI lesions
abstract: AI-based tools for MRI demonstrate high sensitivity for clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) detection, yet performance varies across cohorts. We evaluated a commercial AI-based computer-aided detection (AI-CAD) system for csPCa classification in radiologist-identified suspicious lesions in a real-world setting. This retrospective, single-centre study included 113 men with a PI-RADS ≥ 3 index lesion undergoing 3T in-bore MRI-targeted robotic biopsy. Cases were analysed using QP-Prostate ® . Lesion-level diagnostic performance was assessed for csPCa (Gleason ≥ 7) and overall PCa (Gleason ≥ 6) under two positivity thresholds (Moderate + High and High-only). Analyses were stratified by prostate zone; exploratory analyses included PI-RADS 3 lesions and a theoretical simulation of biopsy-sparing. Mean age was 70.1 (SD 7.9) years; csPCa prevalence was 58.4%, and 15.9% of lesions were PI-RADS 3. For csPCa classification, sensitivity and specificity were 0.92 and 0.32 (Moderate + High), and 0.79 and 0.43 (High-only), respectively. Performance was higher in the peripheral zone (PZ) than in the transitional/central zones (TZ + CZ) across both thresholds. For overall PCa, sensitivity and specificity were 0.91 and 0.43 (Moderate + High), and 0.80 and 0.61 (High-only), respectively. In PI-RADS 3 lesions, csPCa sensitivity was 0.33 across thresholds, with specificity improving from 0.60 (Moderate + High) to 0.67 (High-only). In the theoretical biopsy-sparing simulation, 20/113 biopsies (17.7%) would have been withheld with Moderate + High and 34/113 (30.1%) with High-only, with 5/66 (7.6%) and 14/66 (21.2%) csPCa cases missed, respectively. Among patients without csPCa, 15/47 (31.9%) and 20/47 (42.6%) biopsies would have been avoided, respectively. In a challenging cohort of radiologist-identified PI-RADS ≥ 3 lesions, the AI-CAD system maintained high sensitivity for csPCa classification particularly in the PZ, with lower performance in the PI-RADS 3 exploratory subgroup. The theoretical biopsy-sparing simulation showed a threshold-dependent trade-off between potential biopsy withholding and missed csPCa. Prospective validation is required before AI-CAD-informed biopsy avoidance can be considered clinically safe and effective.
authors: Joan Carles Vilanova; Rubén Martínez-Granados; David Bazaga; Encarna Sanchez Bernabe; Almudena Fuster-Matanzo; Claudia Llinares-Monllor; Andrea Lorenzo Polo; Ana Jiménez-Pastor; Ángel Alberich‐Bayarri

title: Perilesional biopsy in – systematic out? Comparative analysis of targeted, perilesional and systematic core yield by needle tracking with robotic-assisted transperineal MRI/US fusion prostate biopsy
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To characterize prostate cancer (Pca) detection rates by Gleason Grade Group (GG) in targeted, perilesional, and systematic cores sampling the remaining prostate using robotic-assisted transperineal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) /ultrasound fusion biopsy (RA-TP-FBx), enabling precise spatial documentation of every core relative to MRI-lesions and the prostate. METHODS: We analyzed prospectively collected RA-TP-FBx cases between 2020 and 2024. Biopsies were performed with the iSR'obot Mona Lisa (Biobot). Sampling included a traditional targeted + systematic strategy and a Trizonal approach: targeted + perilesional + systematic. Perilesional cores were defined at biopsy as samples within 10 mm of the MRI-lesion margin and systematic cores as samples outside the targeted-perilesional areas. Individualized 3D prostate maps were correlated with per-core histopathology. Clinically significant PCa (csPCa) was defined as GG ≥ 2. RESULTS: The full cohort included 566 RA-TP-FBx cases. Diagnosis of csPCa (n=131 in the Trizonal cohort) was exclusively due to perilesional sampling in 6.1% (8/131). Systematic biopsy detected csPCa not captured by targeted or perilesional cores in 3.8% (5/131), but only 1.5% (2/131) originated from MRI-negative lobes. Overdetection of GG 1 (n = 58 in the Trizonal cohort) would be reduced by 24.1% (14/58) by omitting systematic cores when targeted and perilesional cores were negative. CONCLUSIONS: Robotic-assisted mapping demonstrated that perilesional sampling effectively complemented targeted biopsy, while systematic cores yielded minimal additional csPCa detection but increased GG 1 overdetection. These data support adopting targeted + perilesional sampling and omitting or deintensifying the routine addition of systematic cores in the remaining prostate.
authors: Viktor Alargkof; Manuel Walter; Christian Engesser; Hans‐Helge Seifert; M. Henkel; Hanns‐Christian Breit; David Jean Winkel; Keller Nicola; Pawel Trotsenko; Christian Wetterauer

title: Frameless VarioGuide biopsy for pediatric brainstem lesions in the molecular era: diagnostic performance and workflow characteristics in a comparative single-center series
abstract: BACKGROUND: Molecular characterization has become essential for the diagnosis and treatment of pediatric brainstem lesions. While frame-based stereotactic and robotic-assisted biopsies are well established, comparative data on frameless VarioGuide biopsy for pediatric brainstem lesions remain scarce. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance, safety, and workflow characteristics of frameless VarioGuide biopsy compared with frame-based stereotactic and ROSA-assisted techniques. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed all pediatric patients (≤ 18 years) who underwent stereotactic biopsy of a brainstem lesion at a single tertiary neurosurgical center between 2016 and 2026. Patients were grouped according to biopsy technique (frameless VarioGuide, frame-based stereotaxy, or ROSA-assisted biopsy). Diagnostic yield, molecular diagnostic yield, complications, operative times, and workflow parameters were analyzed. RESULTS: Twenty-two pediatric patients met inclusion criteria. Six underwent frameless VarioGuide biopsy, nine frame-based stereotactic biopsy, and seven ROSA-assisted biopsy. Overall diagnostic and molecular diagnostic yields were 95%. Diagnostic and molecular diagnostic yields were 100% with VarioGuide, 89% with frame-based stereotactic biopsy, and 100% with ROSA-assisted biopsy, without statistically significant differences between groups (p = 0.62). Median operative times were similar among groups (32, 36, and 25 min, respectively; p = 0.28). However, preoperative setup time differed significantly, with the shortest duration observed in the VarioGuide cohort (40.5 min) compared with ROSA-assisted biopsy (64 min) and frame-based stereotaxy (112 min; p = 0.002). Despite the absence of intraoperative neuropathological assessment, all VarioGuide procedures yielded diagnostically and molecular-pathologically informative tissue. No procedure-related hemorrhage, infection, permanent neurological deficit, or procedure-related mortality were observed. CONCLUSIONS: In this exploratory single-center cohort, frameless VarioGuide biopsy achieved high diagnostic and molecular diagnostic yields without permanent procedure-related morbidity and was associated with shorter preoperative setup time. These findings support further evaluation of frameless VarioGuide biopsy as a workflow-efficient approach for tissue acquisition in pediatric brainstem lesions.
authors: Sepide Kashefiolasl; Karsten Lachner; Christian Joerg Braun; Katharina Johanna Weber; Luciana Porto; Marcus Czabanka; Tobias Finger

title: Robotic systems in cranial surgery: a systematic review of accuracy, clinical outcomes, and adverse events
abstract: Robotic-assisted surgery is becoming more prevalent in neurosurgery. Many studies have classified the advantages and disadvantages, particularly in spinal robotic surgeries. However, the use of robotics in cranial procedures has been limited to individual studies without large-scale review of the different modalities. This study is a comprehensive systematic review of the major robotics utilized in cranial neurosurgical procedures and their respective outcomes. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, a systematic review was conducted over PubMed, Cochrane, and Embase for articles published between January 2000 to February 2025. EndNote and Rayyan were utilized to organize the 1,409 identified studies and conduct a blinded multiphase process for including and excluding studies. Originally, studies were intended to be run as a meta-analysis to compare robotic modalities, but the existing data was too heterogeneous to statistically contrast outcomes. Overall, 51 studies were included, with six robots being discussed in more than one study. The use of robotics in cranial neurosurgery stretches mostly across functional neurosurgery, with different applications in brain tumor biopsies and resection, hemorrhage drainage, and endoscopic surgeries. Cranial neurosurgical procedures primarily apply robotics in the world of functional neurosurgery. Outside of this subspecialty, robotic-assisted cranial surgery remains sparse in the literature. As technology evolves, more use cases may be realized.
authors: Alison E. Burgess; Bailey D. Lupo; Luke P. Landry; Ben V. Peco; Nadia V Haik; Zack Karzoun; Norris C Talbot; James R. Bridges; Michael S. Folse; Ryan Diaz; Jamie Toms

title: From imaging enhancement to surgical autonomy: the evolutionary role of nanotechnology in AI-driven robotic surgery
abstract: Robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery provides stable visualisation and manipulation, but direct access to local tissue state remains limited. Lesion boundaries, mechanics, molecular activity and microenvironmental changes are often inferred from conventional feedback. This review evaluates how nano-enabled imaging, flexible and local sensing, and micro/nanorobotic intervention may extend signals and localised actions in robot-assisted procedures. We organise the evidence along an information-flow framework: signal acquisition, processing or computational interpretation, task-relevant state estimation, conversion into a decision variable or control-relevant input, and feedback-guided robotic action. Processing may involve calibration, signal processing, computational modelling, conventional machine learning, deep learning or artificial intelligence (AI)-based methods. The evidence reviewed is strongest for localised signal acquisition and supervised intervention. Selected forms of computational interpretation have been demonstrated, and localisation- or motion-derived geometric states enter feedback controllers in some systems. By contrast, biochemical, spectral, tactile and physiological states are usually displayed, analysed offline or returned through human-facing feedback; they rarely modify an online surgical controller. Closed-loop navigation in phantoms, surrogate-device studies and constrained navigation autonomy therefore represent partial control capabilities, not clinically relevant surgical autonomy. The principal missing transitions are robust validation of task-relevant tissue states, uncertainty-aware conversion of those states into control inputs, and safe action within realistic surgical workflows. Near-term clinical use is more likely to centre on bounded nano-enabled sensing or intervention modules embedded within supervised procedures. Progress towards bounded task autonomy will require reproducibility, material safety, workflow compatibility, explicit human supervision and prospective evidence of patient and task benefits.
authors: Jiahao Zhu; Shengcheng Tai; Zhihang Zhang; Ruicheng Wu; Dengxiong Li; Xiaodong Jin

title: Self-Powered Triboelectric Biofluid Sensors for Early Disease Screening and Diagnosis: A Review.
abstract: With the growing demand for continuous health assessment and early disease screening, biofluids have attracted increasing attention because they provide molecular information that cannot be obtained from conventional physical signals alone. However, practical biofluid analysis remains constrained by limited sample volumes, unstable wet interfaces, complex fluid transport, and dependence on external power sources. Triboelectric nanogenerators and triboelectric nanosensors offer a promising solution by combining mechanical energy harvesting with direct signal transduction. This review provides a critical overview of the theoretical basis of triboelectric biofluid sensing, including working modes, figures of merit, charge-transfer mechanisms, and the differences between solid-solid and solid-liquid electrification. Material selection, interfacial functionalization, fluid collection, wearable configurations, and multimodal integration are further discussed. Recent applications involving sweat, tears, saliva, urine, interstitial fluid, blood, and wound exudate are summarized to clarify how triboelectric devices function as either power sources or active sensing interfaces. Particular attention is given to their potential in early screening, risk assessment, and auxiliary diagnosis. Current limitations associated with biofouling, charge dissipation, individual variability, biosafety, durability, calibration, and clinical validation are also evaluated. Finally, future directions are proposed to improve analytical reliability and accelerate the translation of self-powered biofluid sensors from laboratory prototypes to clinically meaningful healthcare platforms.

title: Research on UWB radar human posture recognition in complex disaster environments based on active sensing closed-loop feedback
abstract: Complex disaster rescue scenarios—such as mine accidents, earthquakes, fire sites, and explosion scenes—are often characterized by severe challenges, including multipath reflections, strong background noise, and nonlinear signal interference. These factors significantly compromise the accuracy and stability of traditional Ultra-Wideband (UWB) radar posture recognition systems, making them inadequate for practical rescue requirements. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a UWB radar anti-interference posture recognition method based on active perception theory. We construct a mathematical model for an active perception closed-loop feedback system. By calculating the energy entropy of echo signals and recognition confidence in real time, the system estimates the interference level of the current environment and the uncertainty of posture estimation. Simulation and experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method exhibits significant robustness against interference in complex scenarios involving multipath reflections, noise, and nonlinear disturbances. This study provides effective technical support for the rapid localization and posture determination of trapped victims in disaster rescue operations.
authors: Lei Han; Xin Li; Zhen Yang; jun bo zhang; Si yang Qiao; Qi Cheng

title: Beyond static perception: Animals, neurons and synapses move to compute efficiently
abstract: Neurons are often modelled as immobile systems that transmit information through chemical and electrical signals constrained by noise and bandwidth. However, this static view contrasts with biological reality, in which dynamical processes operate across scales, from whole-animal movements to motion at the subcellular level. Here, we combine recent experimental observations with biophysically realistic modelling to show that neural information processing, beyond electrochemical signalling, is dynamically shaped by motion, from morphodynamic ultrastructural changes to whole-body movements. In this framework, ultrafast mechanical adjustments in cellular and synaptic structures interact with retinal, eye, head, and body movements to accelerate encoding and enhance precision. Movement across scales dynamically alters the waveforms, latencies, refractoriness and ultrastructural organisation of quantal sampling events. These changes improve signal fidelity and extend spatiotemporal resolution, enabling neurons to generate reliable, high-speed representations with minimal delay. Through active sensing and morphodynamic sampling, animals can therefore enhance the speed and reliability of sensory representations. This perspective, in which self-generated movements across multiple scales enhance encoding and perception, offers new insight into how the brain achieves efficient, predictive and noise-resistant computation while providing a foundation for future experimental tests and biologically inspired AI designs. We first explain how motion-coupled encoding improves neural performance, focusing on edge computing in early sensory systems. We then extend these ideas more speculatively, proposing how motion-coupled sampling may have influenced the evolution of neural architectures at multiple levels, potentially contributing to efficient predictive cognition.
authors: Mikko Juusola; Jouni Takalo; Joni Kemppainen; HaDi MaBouDi; Bruce Yi Bu; Shashwat Shukla; Yiyin Zhou; Aurel A. Lazar; Gonzalo G. de Polavieja

title: Active Visual Perception: Opportunities and Challenges
abstract: Active visual perception enables an intelligent system to improve perception by controlling how visual evidence is acquired. However, differences in how studies define active perception and evaluate its benefits make approaches difficult to compare across tasks. This review first clarifies the field’s functional scope by examining whether an action is selected for its expected effect on subsequent visual evidence and whether the resulting observation informs a later decision. This definition distinguishes active observation acquisition from processing fixed inputs and guides the selection of representative literature. Within this scope, this review develops an analytical framework organized around four questions. It begins with what evidence the task requires, examines which actions can obtain that evidence and how a candidate observation should be valued, and considers how the next sensing action should be selected and executed. New observations then update the perceptual state and guide subsequent decisions, forming a closed loop that provides a common basis for comparing methods across applications. To examine how their benefits can be demonstrated, this review assesses whether existing datasets support observation selection, how interactive environments enable controlled comparisons, and what physical platforms reveal about execution feasibility. It further examines how baseline comparisons can establish whether adapting observations is necessary and whether informed selection offers benefits beyond simpler sensing strategies. These considerations underpin an evaluation framework that links improvements in visual evidence to downstream task outcomes while accounting for acquisition costs and risks. Its core value is to help isolate the contribution of sensing decisions and determine whether their benefits justify the resources required. The analysis concludes that predicted observation value does not guarantee that useful evidence can be acquired through feasible actions, while task success alone cannot establish the benefit of active observation selection. Further progress requires reliable value estimation and planning over longer decision sequences under physical and resource constraints. It also requires grounding semantic reasoning in acquired evidence and maintaining effective collaboration under imperfect communication, with these capabilities verified through reproducible evaluation of the complete perception and action loop.
authors: Yian Li; Xiaoyu Guo; Hao Zhang; Jiayu Chen; Shuiwang Li; Xiaowei Dai

title: Artificial Intelligence Models for Early Disease Detection Using Clinical Data
abstract: In a variety of chronic and acute diseases, earlier detection of disease is a major determinant of better patient outcomes, better treatment costs savings and reduced mortality.The current diagnostic process, mostly manual, manual interpretation of clinical data, is limited by the capacity of the human mind, by inter-observer variability and by the amount of data produced by modern healthcare systems.Artificial Intelligence (AI) that leverages machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) capabilities has become a rapidly evolving technology that can help uncover patterns within very large, heterogeneous and high-dimensional clinical datasets, well in advance of what traditional methods could accomplish.In this research paper, a thorough investigation of AI models for early disease detection from medical data, such as laboratory results, electronic health records (EHR), vital signs, and medical image metadata is conducted.We examine the theoretical underpinnings of important classifiers like Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, Gradient Boosting methods, Artificial Neural Networks, Convolutional Neural Networks and Long Short-Term Memory networks and compare their performances using the metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC).A systematic procedure of data acquisition, data preprocessing, feature engineering, model training, model validation and interpretability is suggested and illustrated using simulated experiments.The results show that ensemble and deep learning algorithms (especially XGBoost and CNN) are more accurate at forecasting than traditional statistical models, but they are less interpretable and more demanding in terms of resources.The paper also highlights these issues of data privacy, class imbalance, explainability of AI models, and clinical integration, and proposes directions for future research such as federated learning, explainable AI, multimodal data fusion for early disease detection, among others.

title: Advanced Drug Delivery Systems: Barriers and Emerging Strategies for Clinical Translation
abstract: Advanced drug delivery systems, including nanoparticles, liposomes, hydrogels, and hybrid composites, promise substantial improvements in targeted therapy and reduced systemic toxicity, yet their clinical translation remains limited. We conducted a systematic literature review covering publications from 2016 to 2025, employing a structured extraction framework across nine domains to evaluate platform design, biological barrier penetration, and translational outcomes. Our analysis reveals that hybrid composite systems consistently face greater manufacturing scalability constraints and regulatory ambiguity compared to single component platforms such as liposomes and lipid nanoparticles, which have achieved Phase III trials and market approval. Smart stimuli responsive hydrogels in chronic inflammatory diseases demonstrate improved therapeutic indices through reduced systemic exposure and enhanced local efficacy, although formal ED50 or TD50 values were not reported in primary studies. Living drug delivery systems pose higher immunogenicity risks than biomimetic alternatives, with standardized testing protocols existing for synthetic coatings but lacking quantitative acceptable ranges. Multi scale computational modeling, including a physiologically based pharmacokinetic model for blood brain barrier penetration, achieved strong validation with a correlation coefficient of 0.848, indicating improved translational feasibility. Chemical modification of natural polymers, particularly hyaluronic acid, yields route dependent improvements for example, thiolation produced a twenty fold increase in mucosal deposition, while sulfation enhanced transdermal bioavailability ten fold. The primary contribution of this work is a comprehensive synthesis identifying cross cutting translational barriers manufacturing complexity, regulatory uncertainty, and incomplete immunogenicity validation that inform future development priorities. These findings underscore the necessity for standardized characterization protocols, advanced computational modeling to bridge in vitro and in vivo performance, and strategic chemical modification approaches tailored to specific administration routes.
authors: Nucky Indra Praja; Callista Putri Nabila

title: Cardiac mechanomedicine: Putting evidence into practice
abstract: Cardiovascular diseases constitute a leading global health burden, contributing significantly to morbidity and mortality worldwide. Traditional diagnostic and therapeutic strategies primarily focus on biochemical markers and imaging findings, often neglecting the fundamental mechanical mechanisms that govern cardiac physiology and pathophysiology. The heart, as a highly dynamic mechanical organ, depends on a precisely regulated biomechanical microenvironment, and alterations in this microenvironment can contribute to disease initiation and progression. This review summarizes the concept of cardiac mechanomedicine and its major research domains, including the biomechanical properties of the heart under physiological and pathological conditions. It also details how cardiac cells and tissues respond to mechanical stimuli. Finally, the review highlights recent advances in measuring mechanical biomarkers, alongside new diagnostic tools and therapeutic interventions targeting mechanical pathways, underscoring the clinical potential of this field.
authors: Guoliang Li; Tao Shi; Changying Zhao; Yingjin Kong; Shengpeng Wang; Yang Yan

title: Wearable sweat sensors for arthritis monitoring
abstract: Arthritis, including rheumatoid arthritis and gout, imposes increasing clinical and economic burdens. Current diagnostic tools such as serology, imaging, and clinical assessments are episodic, resource-intensive, and insufficient for capturing the daily dynamics of disease activity. Epidermal sweat sensing has emerged as a promising non-invasive technique for at-home physiological tracking. This review presents a comprehensive analysis and proof-of-concept for the application of wearable sweat sensors in arthritis management. The current state of detecting arthritis-related biomarkers in sweat, including specific metabolites, proteins, and markers of oxidative stress, is examined. The review surveys critical components of existing sensor architectures, ranging from substrates to transduction modalities. Methodologies for establishing sweat-blood correlations are discussed, emphasizing the physiological partitioning of biomarkers from blood to sweat. Finally, current challenges and the potential of integrated sweat-sensing systems to transform early detection are addressed.
authors: Appurva Tiwari; Ben Bin Xu; Xuehua Zhang

title: Synergistic Li + -functionalized Mo 2 CT X MXene and polyaniline composite for rapid and stable moisture sensing in wearable wound monitoring application
abstract: Abstract Managing optimal moisture balance is essential for chronic wound healing, yet current clinical assessments are often subjective and intermittent. This study reports the development of a high-performance, flexible resistive moisture sensor designed for real-time, quantitative wound monitoring. The active sensing layer consists of a lithium-ion (Li + ) functionalized Mo 2 CT X MXene and polyaniline (PANI) composite. Li + intercalation was utilized to expand the MXene interlayer spacing, enhancing water adsorption and ion transport. Simultaneously, in situ polymerized PANI was introduced to provide stable proton-conductive pathways. Current–voltage characterization verified that the Li + –Mo 2 CT X /PANI composite forms robust Ohmic contacts with the electrodes, exhibiting over a 40-fold enhancement in baseline electrical conductance compared to pristine Mo 2 CT X . The composite was integrated onto screen-printed circular interdigitated electrodes on a flexible PET substrate and encapsulated with poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) (PDAC). This protective PDAC layer acts as a semi-permeable moisture-diffusion barrier that regulates water molecule transport, prevents surface fouling and uncontrolled hydration saturation, and ensures environmental stability without compromising response speed. The sensor demonstrates a linear response across a wide relative humidity (RH) range of 20%–80%, featuring sensitivity of approximately 2.0 Δ R /%ΔRH, with a rapid response time of ∼1 s and a recovery time of ∼11 s. The device demonstrates high mechanical flexibility, and stable operation over a 15 d period. Real-time assessments using finger-touch tests and PVA-hydrogel wound models successfully distinguished between dry, normal, and wet clinical states. The superior performance is attributed to the synergistic effects of Li + -assisted interlayer hydration, Grotthuss-type proton hopping, and moisture-induced PANI protonation. These findings position the Li + –Mo 2 CT X /PANI composite as a promising candidate for next-generation smart dressings in digital wound management.
authors: Syahirah Umairah Mahadi; Siti Nabila Aidit; Norazriena Yusoff; Sharifah Fatmadiana Wan Muhamad Hatta; Yasmin Abdul Wahab; Fazliyatul Azwa Md Rezali

title: SurgGraph: Quantitative Laparoscopic Video Understanding via Geometry-Grounded Scene Graphs
abstract: Surgical videos are a primary resource for teaching trainees anatomy, tool usage, and procedural skills. Yet learning from them at scale requires systems that understand surgical scenes. Existing approaches fall short: vision-language models lack fine-grained domain reasoning, task-specific models do not generalize, and prior scene graphs omit clinically meaningful detail. We present SurgGraph, a training-free pipeline that generates quantitative scene graphs from surgical videos. Operating on segmentation masks and depth maps, SurgGraph encodes each clinically meaningful relation (attachment, occlusion, separation, tool actions) as a tuple whose numeric value quantifies the relation's extent over time. Technical evaluations show more precise scene understanding than state-of-the-art surgical VLM baselines. We then build SurgGraphQA, a proof-of-concept learning application that retrieves meaningful and boundary-case exemplars and generates visual explanations and feedback. A study with 17 medical students and 2 resident surgeons shows significant learning gains, demonstrating its educational value.

title: Real-time environmental understanding through active classification using tactile sensing in robotic disassembly
abstract: This paper proposes a generalized active classification framework designed to classify the environment of a robot through controlled tactile interaction, with direct application to robotic disassembly of Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE). In this domain, purely vision-based systems frequently fail due to occlusions, dust, and reflective surfaces, making haptic identification an operational necessity. By formulating environment identification as an active sensing problem, we utilize the entropy of learned interaction models and a receding-horizon optimization to select control inputs that maximize information gain from force–torque feedback. Our approach transitions from a passive classifier to an active framework that dynamically probes the environment to resolve belief uncertainty across six distinct tactile classes, demonstrated through the high-precision detection and unfastening of screws using an industrial 6-DOF robotic arm. Experimental results on a consumer microwave demonstrate that the active framework achieves a 51% reduction in detection latency for screws compared to passive baselines and consistently outperforms expert-designed heuristics. Furthermore, the system exhibits robust zero-shot generalization to novel industrial objects, indicating that learned tactile signatures are invariant to the global object context. These results provide a scalable foundation for autonomous disassembly in high-variance environments like electronic waste recycling, while offering a broader methodology for any robotic classification task where control can be leveraged to accelerate information gain.
authors: Annalena Daniels; Théo Karst; Samuel Tovey; Dirk Wollherr

title: Wireless Brain‐Computer Interface With MagnetoElectric NanoParticles: Recording of Neural Activity
abstract: ABSTRACT Non‐invasive recording of neural activity from deep brain regions with high spatial and temporal resolution remains an unsolved challenge. Here we investigate the feasibility of exploiting the converse magnetoelectric effect of magnetoelectric nanoparticles (MENPs) to enable wireless non‐invasive recording of electric fields due to local neural activity deep in the brain. To validate the proposed mechanism, we developed a physics‐based simulation of MENP‐assisted neural recordings. The model incorporates nonlinear magnetization dynamics, multistage filtering, and realistic noise sources to stimulate MENPs‐assisted neural recording. The results demonstrate extractable neural activity with positive signal‐to‐noise ratios (SNRs), confirming the theoretical feasibility of wireless MENP‐based brain recording, with a simulated peak‐based SNR of 24.4 dB. These findings validate the physics of the approach. Importantly, the mechanism favors membrane‐local electric fields, suggesting sensitivity to highly localized neuronal activity, while the detectable bandwidth overlaps with canonical neural oscillations. The system further enables dynamic control of nanoparticle behavior through frequency‐dependent switching of the superparamagnetic state, allowing separation between stable delivery and active sensing. Together, these results establish a physically grounded pathway toward non‐invasive, real‐time mapping of neural activity in deep brain regions.
authors: Max Shotbolt; Elric Zhang; Shawnus Chen; Jieyuan Tian; Mostafa Abdel‐Mottaleb; Zeinab Ramezani; Marta Pardo; Ping Liang; Sakhrat Khizroev

title: VibraGlot: Contactless Vocal Disorder Screening via mmWave Neck-Surface Vibration Sensing
abstract: Vocal disorders often begin as subtle mechanical irregularities in vocal-fold vibration before speech quality noticeably degrades. Early identification of such abnormalities is valuable because timely intervention may prevent progression to more advanced stages. However, detecting these weak early cues outside clinical settings remains challenging: microphone-based analysis observes an acoustically shaped signal that may only weakly express source-level irregularity, while contact-based vibration sensors suffer from low user compliance. We present VibraGlot, a contactless screening system that leverages millimeter-wave radar to sense neck-surface micro-vibrations during a short, non-linguistic sustained phonation (3-5 s). Rather than adopting generic end-to-end learning, VibraGlot uses a kinematics-first design. It first isolates the laryngeal region through observability-aware locking to suppress static clutter, then performs cycle-synchronous reconstruction in a canonical phase domain. Crucially, this pipeline explicitly preserves template-violating motion as structured residuals, transforming irregular mechanical behavior into diagnostic features rather than smoothing it away as noise. We evaluate VibraGlot on a clinical cohort of 74 subjects spanning five common vocal pathologies and healthy controls, collected in both hospital and home environments. Under a strict minimal-input protocol, the system achieves a macro-F1 score exceeding 0.91. These results demonstrate that radar-based neck-surface kinematics provide a robust, interpretable, and contactless pathway for scalable early vocal disorder screening, particularly when pathology is still expressed as subtle mechanical irregularity.
authors: Yuanhao Feng; Zhi Liu; Takuya Fujihashi; Shunsuke Saruwatari
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive Mobile Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies

title: Biosensors for viral and bacterial pathogen detection: From biological recognition elements to small-molecule engineering of electrochemical interfaces
abstract: Infectious diseases pose a serious threat to global public health, and the COVID-19 pandemic has clearly demonstrated the critical need for rapid, accurate, and accessible diagnostic tools. Portable point-of-care analytical systems provide an alternative to conventional laboratory methods such as ELISA and PCR, enabling rapid pathogen identification outside centralized facilities, which is essential for timely diagnosis and treatment decisions. Beyond initial detection, such systems also hold potential for quantitative monitoring of viral or bacterial load, relevant for assessing disease stage and therapy effectiveness. Electrochemical biosensing platforms most favorably combine the required analytical performance with broad possibilities for miniaturization, automation, and scaling. However, despite the exponential growth in publications, clinical translation and commercialization of such devices remain limited by insufficient stability and reproducibility of the bioreceptor layer, uncontrolled interfacial orientation, and matrix effects in complex biological samples. This review provides a critical analysis of current approaches to the directed structuring of the bioreceptor layer in electrochemical sensors, comparing biological recognition elements (antibodies, DNA/RNA probes) with synthetic and biomimetic alternatives (aptamers, engineered peptides, and molecularly imprinted polymers). Particular attention is given to the multifaceted roles of small organic molecules as structural elements — cross-linkers for oriented immobilization, redox mediators and electrocatalysts for signal transduction, and independent low-molecular-weight recognition ligands — for the design of next-generation electrochemical test platforms with operational characteristics tunable at the molecular level.
authors: Tatiana S. Svalova; Andrei V. Okhokhonin; Anna A. Saigushkina; Margarita V. Medvedeva; Elizaveta V. Galiautdunova; Elizaveta V. Tiupa; Р. Ф. Муктасибова; Козицина Алиса Николаевна

title: A Multi‐Axis Plantar Load Measurement Platform for the Assessment of Foot Disorders: Comparison of Patients With Psoriatic Arthritis to a Healthy Control Cohort
abstract: BACKGROUND: Accurate assessment of plantar loading, including shear forces, is crucial for understanding foot pathologies such as dactylitis in psoriatic arthritis (PsA). Existing devices predominantly measure plantar pressures, neglecting important shear stresses which may initiate dactylitis. This study presents a novel multi-axis plantar load measurement platform to address this gap. METHODS: The study utilised a newly developed plantar load measurement system, comprising a Hall-effect-based magnetic sensing array, custom data logging electronics, and tailored data processing software. The system's efficacy was evaluated in a pilot feasibility study involving patients with PsA with no, current, or previous dactylitis, and healthy controls. Participants walked barefoot on the platform, capturing plantar shear and pressure data. FINDINGS: Shear stresses were notably higher in the second to fourth rays compared to other regions, particularly in the left foot, aligning with the hypothesis that repetitive local trauma might initiate dactylitis in PsA. However, no consistent differences in stresses were observed between diagnostic groups, likely due to small sample sizes and gait alterations associated with pain. A marked asymmetry was observed between the right and left feet, suggesting dominant-foot placement effects. INTERPRETATION: The new platform demonstrates potential clinical utility in capturing comprehensive foot-loading profiles, including critical shear stresses previously under-assessed. Although the current pilot study was limited in number, the results support the theory that local mechanical stresses may contribute to PsA-related dactylitis. Future larger-scale studies are needed to clarify these findings and overcome limitations related to altered gait patterns due to foot pain.
authors: D. A. Jones; Lefan Wang; Max Houghton; Jennifer Jones; Richard A. Wilkins; Heidi J. Siddle; Graham Chapman; Ali Alazmani; Peter Culmer; Philip Helliwell

title: MATE-Hard and the count-invariance problem in multi-agent active perception
