title: Contact-Aware Impedance Controller for Robot-Assisted Ultrasound Imaging
abstract: Safe robot-assisted ultrasound imaging requires a reliable controller able to detect and localize probe--tissue interaction. In this paper, we present a B-mode ultrasound image-based contact perception method and a contact-aware impedance controller for robotic ultrasound imaging. The proposed method detects acoustic contact independently of force measurements, enabling contact-conditioned force/torque taring to reduce residual wrench bias. During contact, the method continuously estimates the effective contact location along the curved probe surface and uses it to update the controller interaction frame, enabling visual servoing of the physical probe--tissue contact point during imaging. Experiments on an agar phantom demonstrated a contact-localization RMSE of $\mathbf{1.46 \pm 0.14}$~mm over probe roll angles from $\mathbf{-15^\circ}$ to $\mathbf{15^\circ}$. During static rolling, the proposed controller maintained task-space tracking accuracy comparable to a conventional fixed-frame impedance controller while reducing the maximum compressive interaction force from $\mathbf{31.56}$~N to $\mathbf{20.09}$~N, corresponding to a $\mathbf{36.3\%}$ reduction. These results demonstrate the potential of ultrasound images as direct contact feedback for safe and accurate robot-assisted ultrasound imaging.
authors: Md Miraj Arefin; M Efe Tiryaki

title: Wearable plasmonic SERS patch for quantitative sweat metabolite profiling via dual-track spectral inference
abstract: Abstract Wearable sweat sensing offers a non-invasive route to monitor human metabolism, but quantitative analysis is limited by strong endogenous backgrounds, spectral overlap, and mechanical instability of the skin. Here, we present a wearable plasmonic surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) patch that enables robust, multiplex sweat analysis under realistic physiological conditions. Gold nanoparticles are generated in situ within a hydrated agarose matrix, forming a diffusion-accessible and mechanically stable plasmonic network compatible with on-skin wear. To resolve low-abundance, intake-related metabolites masked by dominant endogenous signals, we introduce a dual-track deep-learning framework. High-abundance sweat components are quantified directly from mixed spectra, while trace targets are recovered through an unmixing-assisted residual pathway. Using paraxanthine, a primary metabolite of caffeine, we demonstrate quantitative detection across large concentration disparities despite severe spectral congestion. A controlled on-body study combining caffeine intake with exercise-induced sweating reveals subject-specific paraxanthine trajectories with delayed peaks consistent with known pharmacokinetics, while endogenous metabolites show broader exercise-driven trends. Together, this platform advances wearable optical sensing from qualitative detection toward quantitative, personalized metabolic monitoring in complex biofluids.
authors: Rowoon Park; Bo You Heo; Se Jin Choi; Seungki Lee; Jaewon Kim; Mi Jeong Kim; Jihwan Kim; Jinah Jang; Oh Seok Kwon; Hyun Ju Yoo; Jahyun Koo; Yong‐Sang Ryu; Ho Sang Jung

title: MoS2 Biosensing: Technologies Insight into Photo and Electrical Detection
abstract: The semiconductor industry has foreseen a replacement for the old-fashioned Si-based technology. For quite some time, since the International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors (ITRS) predicted it back in 2007, the floating-gate MOS structure cannot be scaled-down due to the tunneling layer reaching an impasse point where the leaking current is a major issue. The ITRS directives focused on the search for a replacement for Si. In 2007, graphene appeared to be the holy-grail material to replace it and to develop the whole brand new electronic-devices for the semiconductor market. Sadly, it did not deliver but shed some light on which sort of material might be the right one. The transition metal dichalcogenides feature key characteristics that might work as the replacement for Si and push forward the semiconductor industry. From those materials, there are a few that can be used in a straight forward manner, such as MoS2 that shows elemental characteristics to be implemented by continuing with the path started by graphene to be the key material for the up-coming semiconductor devices. In this chapter, we show how MoS2 can be the backbone for the semiconductor industry, that is, photo/electrical biosensors.
authors: Andrea Carolina Villalvazo-Hidalgo; Orfil González‐Reynoso; Martha Angélica Hidalgo-Ríos; Gregorio Guadalupe Carbajal Carbajal Arízaga; María Esther Macías-Rodríguez; Everardo Vargas-Rodríguez; ANA DINORA GUZMAN CHAVEZ; Mario Alberto García Ramírez

title: Design and optimization of an Ag/Cu–black phosphorus/Franckeite heterostructure for high-sensitivity surface plasmon resonance biosensing
abstract: Introduction Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) biosensors enable label-free, real-time detection, but simultaneously achieving strong field confinement, near-critical coupling, and a high figure of merit (FoM) remains challenging, particularly when low-loss silver must be protected from aqueous media. Methods A CaF 2 /Ag/Cu/black phosphorus (BP)/Franckeite Kretschmann heterostructure was modeled at λ = 633 nm using the frequency-domain Maxwell wave equation and the transfer matrix method under TM-polarized angular and phase interrogation. The Ag and Cu thicknesses were optimized individually and jointly, size-dependent Drude damping corrections were applied, and performance was benchmarked against a Cu-only reference with identical BP/Franckeite overlayers. Fabrication tolerance to BP layer number and Franckeite thickness was also evaluated. Results Joint optimization identified a near-critical-coupling configuration at approximately 31 nm Ag and 7 nm Cu, with a minimum reflectance of 1.1 × 10 −3 within the sensing window. Over 1.328–1.336 RIU, the sensor reached a peak angular sensitivity of 372°/RIU and a FoM of 47.0 RIU −1 at n s = 1.332, approximately 62% and 78% higher than the Cu-only reference. Phase interrogation reached 29,200°/RIU, corresponding to a minimum detectable refractive-index change of approximately 3.4 × 10 −7 RIU. The 1/e evanescent-field penetration depth was 178–201 nm. Size-dependent damping reduced the FoM by approximately 5%, and realistic 2D-layer thickness variations reduced it by no more than approximately 10%. Discussion The Ag/Cu/BP/Franckeite architecture is a promising platform for label-free biosensing, including carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) detection, subject to experimental validation of long-term stability, surface functionalization, and thermally compensated phase readout.
authors: Jacob Wekalao; Tobias Otieno

title: Design and Simulation of Multilayer SPR Biosensor Based on BK7/Ag/BN/BlueP/WSe 2 /BP for Label‐Free Detection of A549 Lung Cancer Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT A label‐free surface plasmon resonance (SPR) biosensor was explored for the detection of A549 lung cancer cells. The proposed sensing platform uses a multi‐layer platform consisting of a BK7 prism, Ag, BN, BlueP/WSe 2 heterostructure, and BP layers. To excite the surface plasmons, a silver coating was applied to the BK7 prism using the Kretschmann arrangement. These BN, BlueP/WSe 2 , and BP layers increase the confinement of the electromagnetic field and light–matter interaction and reduce the dissipation of plasmonic energy. The transfer matrix method (TMM), which uses angular interrogation at an operating wavelength of 633 nm, was used for the numerical analysis. The optimized multilayer architecture exhibited excellent sensing capability, with a sensitivity of 366.589°/RIU, quality factor of 100.054 RIU − 1 , detection accuracy of 1.8010 deg − 1 , and full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 3.6639°. The results show the efficiency of the proposed design for A549 lung cancer detection.
authors: Gundala Vasanthi; Ramachandran Balaji; Yesudasu Vasimalla; Santosh Kumar

title: Printable Inks for Flexible Healthcare Sensors: From Materials to Device Insights
abstract: Printable inks have been widely used in wearable healthcare sensors, and their functions go beyond simply creating conductive or sensing layers. Ink formulation controls printability, film formation, electrical path creation, adhesion to flexible substrates and stability of the process under mechanical strain such as bending and stretching. This review highlights recent advances in printable inks used in wearable healthcare sensing devices including metal-based, carbon-based, polymeric, and biofunctional ink systems. Their merits as well as limitations including high curing temperature, poor dispersion stability, limited conductivity, poor substrate adhesion, and difficulty of biological functionalization will be discussed. This review focuses mostly on the relationship between ink formulation, rheology, printing, printed microstructure, and sensor performance. The existing research usually studies them separately, therefore, making it difficult for comparison between different ink systems and prediction of the performance of devices in real-life situations. Rheology has been studied usually only as a limitation in printing process although it affects pattern resolution, film homogeneity, formation of conductive paths, and repeatability. The commonly used printing methods, particularly inkjet, screen printing, and flexographic printing, are also compared in terms of resolution, material compatibility, throughput, and scalability. Although wearable healthcare sensors have developed considerably, several challenges still limit their use beyond laboratory demonstrations. These include material-related limitations, poor long-term stability, mechanical degradation, biofouling, and reduction in sensor performance over time. Overall, this review highlights the importance of understanding the process-structure-performance relationships of printable inks for developing reliable, scalable, and real-time wearable sensors.
authors: Naveen Bokka; Ankammarao Padamurthy; Tata Rao Lanka; Abhishesh Pal; Prasanth Kumar Enaganti
venue: Journal of Science Advanced Materials and Devices

title: A wearable closed-loop insulin micropump toward a miniaturized artificial pancreas for diabetes
abstract: The application of a fully autonomous artificial pancreas faces fundamental constraints from the bulky mechanical drives of conventional insulin pumps and the spatially separated glucose sensing unit. Herein, we report a wearable closed-loop insulin micropump that enables a miniaturized artificial pancreas for diabetes treatment. It seamlessly integrates an electrochemical micropump with an optical glucose-responsive microneedle (MN) sensor. The core actuation module features a novel semi-dry sandwich electrode configuration combined with a highly elastic latex membrane and a groove-type epoxy sealing architecture. This structural paradigm shift effectively eliminates bulk fluid flow and ensures robust hermeticity for precise, electrolysis-gas-driven, microliter-scale dosing with a precision of 0.5 μL. For continuous glucose monitoring, a polyvinylpyrrolidone/polyvinyl alcohol (PVP/PVA) hydrogel MN array functionalized with 9-anthracene boronic acid (9-ANB) is employed. The specific binding of interstitial glucose triggers measurable fluorescence quenching, which is precisely digitized by an integrated XYZ true-color sensor (detection range: 0-600 mg/dL). Comprehensive in vitro and in vivo evaluations demonstrate the platform's predictable, programmable delivery kinetics and excellent biocompatibility. In type 1 diabetic mouse models, a smartphone-controlled system by autonomously and effectively suppressed postprandial glycemic spikes, maintaining glycemic fluctuations within 25 mg/dL. This highly integrated, miniaturized design offers a compelling paradigm shift for next-generation, patient-friendly diabetes management systems.
authors: Ziyu Kuang; Xiangbin Kong; Tan Cao; Rui Lin; Zhihe Long; Tianyou Jiang; Xianchun Jin; Xinyu Xue; Zhangzhi Zhao; Meihua Chen

title: Gate-Tunable Single Ag–rGO FET Platform for Room-Temperature Trigas Detection with a CMOS-Compatible PWM Readout Interface
abstract: Abstract Room-temperature gas sensing requires high sensitivity and selectivity, which FET-based architectures achieve through gate-controlled modulation of surface potential and carrier transport, enabling tunable and efficient chemical transduction. In this work, we introduce a smart trigas sensor capable of selectively detecting three target gases─acetone, formaldehyde, and ammonia at room temperature using a single FET by simply tuning the gate voltage. By leveraging gate-induced modulation, this study demonstrates dynamic control over the interaction between gas molecules and the silver-decorated Reduced Graphene Oxide (Ag-rGO) channel-based gas FET sensor, enabling the individual and selective detection of three distinct gases using the single device. Furthermore, the proposed platform demonstrates distinct cross-sensitivity characteristics, wherein gate-bias modulation enables selective discrimination between formaldehyde, acetone, and ammonia under mixed-gas environments. The device exhibits high detection capability with experimentally estimated limits of detection (LOD) of 158 ppb for acetone, 31 ppb for formaldehyde, and 36 ppb for ammonia, highlighting its potential for low-concentration, room-temperature multigas sensing applications. Beyond material and device-level innovation, a TSMC 180 nm 3.3 V CMOS readout circuit is designed and simulated in Cadence Virtuoso, featuring analogue front-end design for interfacing the proposed gas sensor with a low-power embedded system via PWM signals. The proposed multigas sensor platform and the designed and simulated readout circuit establish a compact and low-power sensing framework, providing a foundation for future studies on breath biomarker analysis and disease-detection applications.
authors: Mayank Kohli; Nimisha; Swapnil Sharma; Santanab Majumder; Gourab Dutta; Tarun Kanti Bhattacharyya

title: Tail-Risk-Aware Information Guidance for Angles-Only Spacecraft Rendezvous Under Markovian Measurement Outages
abstract: Angles-only spacecraft rendezvous couples guidance and navigation because trajectory geometry changes both observability and measurement availability. This paper develops tail-risk-aware guidance for geometry-dependent, burst-correlated optical outages. A planar benchmark uses explicit Markov measurement-arrival scenarios and conditional value at risk to shape terminal navigation uncertainty, followed by independent 10,000-run validation. Relative to expected availability guidance, the selected trajectory reduces 95% conditional value at risk by 39.2% and 99% conditional value at risk by 15.7%, at 35.8% higher maneuver expenditure. A separate 200-run nonlinear three-dimensional holdout uses two-body-plus-oblateness truth dynamics, azimuth/elevation sensing, maneuver errors, unscented Kalman filtering, and covariance-weighted terminal feedback. The risk-aware trajectory increases realized measurement availability from 20.7% to 56.1%, reduces mean longest outage from 14.39 to 6.80 epochs, and reduces median and 95th-percentile terminal estimation error from 49.64m to 0.89m and 223.24m to 21.93m, respectively, while mission success remains statistically comparable. This demonstrates that the operational payoff is navigation robustness rather than consistent superior terminal accuracy. Because approach-corridor constraints are monitored but not enforced, the study does not establish safety-compliant proximity operations.
authors: Archit Das

title: Amortized Feedback Planning: Turning Model-Based Rollouts into Executable Policies
abstract: Closed-loop planning accounts for future observation-dependent actions but can be expensive to repeat at deployment. Bellman-gradient (BG) refinement differentiates conditional rollouts through an existing actor, corrects the current action, and stores the result in an executable policy. A backward sweep reuses deployed future feedback; full-horizon rollouts in an identified Gaussian belief model need no learned value critic. A nonlinear error recursion links quadratic continuation error, local correction, and policy storage. A controlled non-LQG example exhibits second-order policy accuracy with consistent storage, while ideal affine LQG admits exact backward recovery. In nonquadratic thrust, BG reduces actor cost by 2.47-3.20% and remains within 0.13-0.53% of the tested feedback MPC; original policies execute in 5-6 microseconds in a seed-0 native audit. With matched storage, BG attains competitive plant costs at about one ninth (arm) and one sixtieth (docking) of feedback-teacher-plus-student construction time on one GPU, excluding shared learning and node preparation. Richer common maps substantially narrow some student-BG gaps. These results expose the roles of learned feedback, local correction, and storage in executable control.
authors: Jeonggyu Huh

title: Usability of graphic medicine as an educational tool among psychology students: quasi-experimental study
authors: Jessica Marian Goodman‐Casanova; Ángela del Carmen Escorza Aguilar; Isabel Prieto-Torrero; Elena R. Serrano‐Ibáñez; José Guzman-Parra; Estela Castilla‐Ortega

title: Remote sensing of hydrothermal alteration in active volcanic environments: A critical review and integrated analysis of Lastarria volcano
abstract: Hydrothermal alteration is a key process in active volcanic systems, influencing edifice stability, fluid circulation, degassing pathways, and volcanic hazards. Remote sensing is widely used to map hydrothermal alteration; however, many approaches treat alteration-related surfaces as static targets, so their reliability, transferability, and process significance in active volcanic environments remain insufficiently evaluated. This study synthesizes commonly used remote sensing approaches and examines the behavior and interpretive implications of representative outputs at Lastarria volcano, which is an arid, high-altitude, vegetation-free system with active fumarolic fields. We compare visual interpretation, VNIR-SWIR reflectance products, pixel-based and sub-pixel mapping outputs, UAV thermal infrared observations, and LiDAR-derived surface-state information. The results show that visual interpretation, reflectance-based products, and pixel-based or sub-pixel outputs delineate broad alteration-related patterns, but their extent, internal structure, and interpretive meaning vary with methodological choices, surface mixing, and environmental surface states. Thermal infrared observations constrain apparent surface-temperature anomalies and fumarole-proximal activity, whereas LiDAR-derived products provide complementary information on surface state, morphology, and roughness. These observations do not converge on a single alteration representation; instead, they capture different aspects of the volcanic-hydrothermal system. Environmental, climatic, and surface controls, including exposure state, moisture, surface reworking, and seasonality, further limit direct transferability among volcanic settings. We suggest that remote sensing of hydrothermal alteration in active volcanic environments should move from deterministic mapping toward process-oriented and uncertainty-aware interpretation, with temporal persistence, spatial coherence, process plausibility, and independent support providing a basis for future multi-temporal analysis and monitoring.
authors: Ge Gao; Thomas R. Walter; Samuel T. Thiele

title: Total-field atomic magnetometry using an elliptically-polarized frequency-modulated light beam for geomagnetic-field applications
abstract: We investigate an all-optical scheme for high-sensitivity measurements of the Earth's scale magnetic field ($B$). The scheme is based on the Bell-Bloom technique with frequency-modulated light. A single elliptically polarized light beam is used both for pumping the alkali-metal atoms and probing Larmor precession of their spins under the external magnetic field. In contrast to many other high-sensitivity magnetometry schemes based on nonlinear polarization rotation of the light, the proposed approach enables the observation of magnetic resonance via changes in the light-beam ellipticity parameter. The approach has been validated in experiments with a vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser, irradiating a $0.125$ cm$^3$ cesium vapor cell filled with a buffer gas. In the current experimental conditions, the achieved sensitivity is estimated at $220$ fT/$\surd$Hz under $B$$\,\approx\,$$50$ $μ$T, while the shot-noise floor corresponds to $\approx\,$$20$ fT/$\surd$Hz. The bandwidth is estimated at $\approx\,$$1$ kHz. The proposed simple and robust single-beam scheme is well suited for miniaturization and is therefore particularly promising for the development of compact, highly sensitive, low-power-consumption atomic magnetometers for a wide range of applications in the geomagnetic field.
authors: Denis V. Brazhnikov; A. O. Makarov; K. S. Kozlova; M. A. Rusina; A. M. Mikhailov; V. A. Vasiliev; E. V. Tanakov; Andrei Goncharov; M. A. Bobrov; Ya.N. Kovach; A. A. Blokhin; N. A. Maleev; S. A. Blokhin

title: Wheat Nitrogen Fertilizer Management Using GreenSeeker Handheld Crop Canopy Sensor
abstract: One of the essential factors in increasing agricultural yields of cereal crops is increasing the grain yield without increasing production costs. Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) is the main crop in the food basket of the entire world. Therefore, it is necessary to determine the appropriate nitrogen (N) requirements to obtain the optimal production of wheat crops by investigating the impact of different N levels on the wheat crop yield in the Al-Muthanna region, as well as determining the possibility of predicting grain yield using the GreenSeeker handheld proximal crop canopy sensorbased differences vegetative difference index (NDVI). Thus, there is a need to re-evaluate the previous recommendations using remote sensing techniques. The experimental treatments were five levels of N fertilizer including (0 Kg N ha-1 , 50 kg N ha-1 , 100 kg N ha-1 ,150 kg N ha-1, and 200 kg N ha-1, and each N level was divided into 100%, 70%, 50% percentages, respectively. This study was conducted at the Experiment Station and Agriculture Research of the College of AgricultureAl-Muthanna University. The NDVI measurements were obtained at FK5, FK7, and FK9 according to the Feekes scale growth stage. The results indicated significant differences in grain yield between different levels of N fertilizer and a 70% percentage outperformed on the 100% and 50% treatments for each of the two N levels of 200 and 150 kg ha-1 . The results also show significant differences between NDVI values for different N fertilizer levels. The NDVI readings and wheat yield values increased and followed a similar pattern with increasing N fertilizer levels. This suggests that NDVI can predict wheat grain yield when the NDVI is not saturated. This study showed the potential of using GreenSeeker proximal crop canopy sensor-based NDVI readings as a useful tool to predict wheat grain yield.
authors: Mohammed A. Naser
venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF AGRICULTURE AND EARTH SCIENCE

title: Engineering quantum dot-based nanosensors for practical detection of pesticide residues in food and water systems
abstract: Pesticide contamination in food and water systems poses significant risks to human health and environmental sustainability, necessitating the development of rapid, sensitive, and on-site detection technologies. This review explores recent advances in quantum dot (QD)-based nanosensors for ultra-sensitive pesticide detection. Owing to their unique optical properties, high surface-to-volume ratio, and tunable fluorescence, QDs enable detection at trace levels ranging from femtomolar to nanomolar concentrations, outperforming many conventional analytical techniques. Various sensing strategies, including fluorescence, electrochemical, photoelectrochemical, and Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET)-based mechanisms, are discussed alongside biorecognition elements such as aptamers, enzymes, and antibodies. Additionally, hybrid systems integrating QDs with metal–organic frameworks, polymers, and nanocomposites demonstrate enhanced sensitivity and selectivity. Despite challenges related to toxicity and matrix interference, QD-based nanosensors offer promising solutions for real-time monitoring, food safety assurance, and environmental protection.
authors: Farhang Hameed Awlqadr; Mohammed N. Saeed; Ammar B. Altemimi; Muhammad Waqar; Ahmad F. Hama Sdiq; Tablo H. Salih; Mohammed Yasir; Anubhav Pratap Singh

title: Whole-Blood Boundary Analysis of BioFET-Based ctDNA Detection for Intravascular Sensing in Intrabody Nanonetworks
abstract: Liquid biopsy can detect tumor-derived biomarkers such as circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), but ultra-low-fraction assays remain costly, slow, and difficult to scale. This motivates interest in intravascular in vivo sensing in the context of intrabody nanonetworks, where nanosensors could support local biomarker monitoring. BioFET-based nanosensors are relevant here because they are label-free, highly miniaturizable, and have shown strong ctDNA sensitivity in controlled media. We examine whether this sensitivity still yields reliable ctDNA detection in whole blood using a reduced-order stochastic simulation model that links operating-point selection, Debye-screened charge transduction, stochastic finite-capacity binding, nonspecific adsorption, background fluctuations, and intrinsic electronic noise to blank-threshold detection. Monte Carlo evaluation under the stated physiological screening and lumped interface assumptions shows that short Debye length and interface attenuation reduce the current shift, while low-frequency noise and background fluctuations reduce the margin between target-present and blank responses. Across the tested quasi-static charge-gating regimes, sensitivity ranges from low values under short Debye length and thicker interfaces to near 100% for higher target concentrations under stronger coupling conditions. Specificity ranges from approximately 85% to 91% across the evaluated oxide thicknesses. The model therefore provides an exploratory whole-blood boundary analysis that identifies how screening, interface geometry, target concentration, and electronic noise shape BioFET-based intravascular ctDNA detection.
authors: Ida Kleger-Rudomin; Filip Lemić; Sergi Abadal; Eduard Alarcón; Ethungshan Shitiri
venue: ACM International Conference on Nanoscale Computing and Communication (NANOCOM)

title: Advanced Piezoelectric Nanogenerators for Next-Generation Self-Powered Nano-Bio Sensors
abstract: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) material-based piezoelectric nanogenerators (PENGs) are emerging as efficient energy-harvesting devices that convert mechanical stimuli into electrical energy. Owing to their tunable electronic, mechanical, and structural characteristics, 2D materials, including TMDs, MXenes, h-BN, etc., offer significant advantages in flexibility, durability, and low-power operation, making them highly suitable for next-generation self-powered systems. This review systematically highlights recent advances in 2D material-based PENGs, emphasizing fabrication strategies, performance optimization, electromechanical coupling enhancement, and their applications in self-powered nano-biosensors. The interdependence between material properties, device architecture, and measurement conditions is comprehensively analyzed to establish robust structure-performance relationships. Furthermore, critical challenges, including low output power, signal instability, integration complexity, and the lack of standardized evaluation protocols, are systematically analyzed. Emerging strategies to enhance energy-harvesting efficiency, signal reliability, and device scalability are also highlighted. Overall, this review establishes a unified framework for the rational design and advancement of high-performance 2D PENGs, providing key insights for their practical implementation in portable, wearable, and autonomous self-powered systems.
authors: Abhay Singh; Manish Sharma; Rajesh K. Gangwar; Ajeet Kumar Kaushik; Sanjeev Kumar K. Sharma

title: Multi-Channel Shielding Induced Trap Robust Plasma Wave Rectification in AlGaN/GaN HEMT THz Detectors
abstract: Abstract This work investigates trap-induced degradation in multi-channel (MC) GaN high electron mobility transistor (HEMT) terahertz (THz) detectors operating in the non-resonant plasma-wave rectification regime. The THz detection characteristics of MC-HEMTs are systematically compared with conventional single-channel (SC) architectures to evaluate responsivity, transient response, and stability under surface and buffer trap conditions. The results demonstrate that the MC-HEMT achieves enhanced responsivity of 12,500 V/W compared with 10,000 V/W for the SC-HEMT under trap-free conditions due to improved carrier transport and stronger nonlinear rectification behavior. Systematic trap analysis further reveals that surface donor traps have minimal influence on the THz response after saturation of the two-dimensional electron gas density, whereas buffer acceptor traps strongly suppress plasma-wave rectification in SC devices. In contrast, the MC-HEMT exhibits significantly improved robustness against buffertrap-induced degradation even at high trap densities ranging from 5 × 10¹⁶ to 1 × 10 19 cm⁻³. Numerical physics-based simulations further shows that trap activation is primarily confined to the lower channel while the upper conducting channel remains electrostatically shielded from trap-induced carrier modulation. The results identify a channel-shielding mechanism intrinsic to MC configurations that preserves stable plasma-wave rectification under trap-loaded operating conditions.
authors: Shivansh Awasthi; Vikas Kumar; Ankur Gupta

title: Beyond Sensitivity: A Perspective on Transitioning Photonic Sensors into Real-Life Applications
abstract: Photonic sensing encompasses technologies at markedly different levels of maturity. Fiber-optic sensing systems are already widely deployed in infrastructure, energy, transportation, and industrial monitoring, whereas many integrated biosensors and plasmonic, metasurface, and wearable platforms remain at laboratory or early translational stages. This review critically examines the factors that have enabled some photonic sensing technologies to achieve sustained deployment while continuing to constrain others. Practical performance is considered not only in terms of the optical transducer but also through molecular recognition, sample composition, environmental cross-sensitivity, fabrication variability, optical interrogation, microfluidics, packaging, calibration, electronics, and data processing. Established, transitional, and emerging platforms are comparatively assessed across healthcare, environmental monitoring, industrial process control, structural monitoring, and security applications. Real-life readiness is evaluated through analytical validity, selectivity, reproducibility, stability, dynamic range, response time, manufacturability, usability, and total system value. An application-driven framework is proposed in which sensing architecture, recognition chemistry, sample handling, interrogation, packaging, and validation are co-designed according to the intended operating environment. The analysis shows that successful deployment depends on robust system integration, reproducible manufacturing, application-specific validation, and a clear practical advantage rather than record sensitivity or nominal detection limits alone. Future evaluations should therefore use representative samples, independently manufactured devices, realistic operating conditions, standardized reporting protocols, and comparisons with established analytical methods.
authors: Muhammad Ali Butt

title: INDIY ASOSIDAGI NANOZARRALAR: SINTEZ STRATEGIYALARI, TUZILISH VA XOSSALAR O‘RTASIDAGI BOG‘LIQLIK HAMDA BIOTIBBIYOT, SENSOR TEXNOLOGIYALARI VA KATALIZDA ISTIQBOLLI QO‘LLANILISH SOHALARI
abstract: Indium-based nanoparticles - metallic indium, indium oxide (In₂O₃), indium tin oxide (ITO), indium-doped oxides, indium chalcogenides and indium-containing quantum dots - combine tunable band gaps, oxygen-vacancy-controlled conductivity and luminescence, and plasmonic responses extending from the ultraviolet to the infrared. Although In₂O₃ nanoparticles have received far less attention than ZnO or TiO₂, they are emerging as promising materials for biomedicine, chemical sensing, photocatalysis and optoelectronics. This review compares physical (solvated metal atom dispersion, pulsed laser ablation, laser/electron irradiation), solution-chemical (thermolysis, hydrothermal, solvothermal, sol– gel auto-combustion, hot injection), electrochemical (ionic-liquid and aqueous electroreduction) and plant-mediated synthesis routes, with emphasis on green synthesis using Aloe vera, Aerva javanica, Artemisia vulgaris, Vitis vinifera and green tea extracts. The roles of oxygen vacancies, dopants and composition in determining optical and electronic properties are discussed. Applications are surveyed, including antibacterial and anticancer activity, photothermal and photoacoustic theragnostic, drug delivery with SPECT imaging, quantum- dot-based biomarker detection, ethanol and humidity sensing, ITO-based electrochemical sensing, dye photodegradation and heterogeneous organic catalysis.
authors: Nigora Qutlimurotova; GULORO RAXIMOVA
venue: Zamonaviy jamiyat va innovatsiyalar ilmiy-nazariy jurnali

title: From Prototype to Sustainable Food Production: Translational Barriers and Design Priorities for Agricultural Biosensing Systems
abstract: ABSTRACT Agricultural biosensors could advance sustainable food production by enabling timely detection of crop stress, pathogens, nutrient imbalances, and environmental contaminants. Despite decades of research, however, robust commercial biosensing platforms remain uncommon because analytical performance under controlled conditions does not necessarily translate into dependable field operation or measurable sustainability benefits. Sensors affected by fouling, calibration drift, unstable biorecognition elements, ambiguous biological signals, or frequent replacement may increase cost and material consumption without improving management decisions or reducing agricultural inputs. This perspective article examines the technical, biological, operational, and socioeconomic barriers that limit the transition of agricultural biosensors from laboratory prototypes to resource‐efficient decision‐support systems. It considers performance standards, recognition‐element durability, plant–device biocompatibility, validation practices, user education, and uncertainty communication across open fields, controlled‐environment agriculture, plant wearables, and in vivo platforms. A sustainability‐oriented framework is proposed that connects analytical validity and operational reliability with decision relevance, maintainability, lifecycle considerations, and responsible resource use. Future progress will require biological co‐design, realistic multiscale validation, multimodal data integration, modular and repairable devices, actionable user interfaces, and transparent communication of uncertainty. Agricultural biosensors should ultimately be evaluated not only by their ability to detect target analytes but also by whether they enable reliable interventions that reduce resource consumption, environmental burdens, production risks, and avoidable waste.
authors: Frank Efe Erukainure; David B. Langston; Zachary M. Easton; Blake N. Johnson; Abhilash Kumar Chandel
venue: Journal of Sustainable Agriculture and Environment

title: Hints Towards the Formation of a More Comprehensive Theory of Life
authors: Samuel Taylor Coleridge

title: Semiconducting zirconium–cerium oxide nanocomposite derived from Ficus religiosa bark extract for high-performance electrochemical sensing of dopamine
abstract: Despite significant progress in electrochemical dopamine sensing, the development of eco-friendly, low-cost, and highly sensitive platforms based on green-synthesized ZrO₂ nanocomposites remains challenging. This study synthesized a zirconia-ceria (ZC) nanocomposite using Ficus religiosa bark extract and evaluated whether CeO₂ incorporation could improve the physicochemical properties and electrochemical performance for dopamine detection in real samples. ZrO₂ nanoparticles and the ZC nanocomposite were green synthesized using F. religiosa bark extract as a natural reducing and stabilizing agent and characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), UV-visible spectroscopy, particle size analysis (PSA), zeta potential analysis, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Characterization confirmed a tetragonal crystalline ZC nanocomposite with the successful incorporation of CeO₂ into the ZrO₂ lattice. The ZC nanocomposite exhibited a mean particle size of 64.8 nm, porous interconnected granular morphology with quasi-spherical nanostructures, optical band gap of 2.0 eV, and zeta potential of −79.4 mV, indicating semiconducting behavior and excellent colloidal stability. The synthesized materials were used to modify screen-printed carbon electrodes (SPCEs) for dopamine sensing using cyclic and differential pulse voltammetry. The ZC@SPCE exhibited a linear range of 0.5–100 µM, sensitivity of 642.14 µA mM⁻¹ cm⁻², and limit of detection of 0.009 µM (S/N = 3), whereas the ZrO₂@SPCE showed a sensitivity of 70.38 µA mM⁻¹ cm⁻² and limit of detection of 0.024 µM (S/N = 3) within −0.2–1.0 V. The ZC@SPCE also exhibited strong selectivity against relevant interferents. In goat, sheep, and fetal bovine serum, recoveries of 98–101% with RSD values below 3.22% demonstrated g​ood accuracy and precision. Overall, CeO₂ incorporation markedly enhanced ZrO₂ electrochemical performance of ZrO₂, establishing ZC@SPCE as a sustainable and highly sensitive platform for selective dopamine detection in physiological applications and supporting future development of miniaturized electrochemical devices for rapid real-sample dopamine analysis and monitoring.
authors: Lasina Jarajana; Saraswathi Kailasa; Venkateswara Rao Kalagadda; Naveen Kumar Kalagatur; Vinay Viswanath Konduri; Usha Kiranmayi Mangamuri; Akshay Arabindi; Gulli Palli Veeraswamy Sri Durga Sai Kiran; P. Sudhakar

title: Pathwise Information Certificates for Decentralized Adaptive Sensing
abstract: We study decentralized adaptive sensing, where multiple agents choose measurements from evolving local beliefs while exchanging information over a communication graph. We ask whether the measurements actually selected by an adaptive policy have collected enough evidence to distinguish the true target from every plausible alternative. We develop a pathwise certificate based on the Rényi--Chernoff information accumulated along the realized sensing trajectory. It yields nonasymptotic MAP-error bounds and an anytime, network-wide stopping rule for arbitrary history-dependent sensing policies, while separating accumulated statistical information from a bounded network-mixing transient. Linear growth of the information against the least-resolved competitor implies exponential decay of MAP and squared-localization error. A classical pairwise KL converse, specialized to the adaptive decentralized transcript, shows that insufficient information on any pair prevents a positive uniform error exponent, confirming the hardest competitor as a fundamental bottleneck. Across policies, graph topologies, sensor profiles, and seeds, the worst-competitor score correlates more strongly with localization speed than an average-pair proxy in both 1D ($r=0.89$ versus $0.40$) and structured 2D sensing ($r=0.77$ versus $0.48$). Our results provide a practical way to certify and diagnose adaptive multi-agent sensing systems using the evidence they actually collect.
authors: Theodoros Tsiligkaridis

title: Rendered-Egocentric Vision for Short-Horizon Body-Risk Prediction in Quadruped Command Selection
