title: Blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome as an uncommon cause of gastrointestinal overt bleeding: a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge.
abstract: A 76-year-old woman on anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation presented with melaena. Her medical history included previous jejunal resection, aortic aneurysm repair, and cervical cancer in remission. Initial upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and complete colonoscopy showed no source of bleeding. Despite discontinuation of anticoagulation, she developed recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding with severe transfusion-dependent anaemia. Capsule endoscopy demonstrated bluish submucosal vascular lesions in the jejunum, suggestive of Blue Rubber Bleb Nevus Syndrome (BRBNS), a diagnosis further supported by dermatological findings. Single-balloon enteroscopy revealed multiple jejunal venous blebs, with no active bleeding, throughout the first 240 cm of examined small bowel. Treatment with somatostatin and sirolimus was started; however, ongoing bleeding and clinical instability prompted an enteroscopy-guided surgical strategy. At laparotomy, multiple subserosal jejunal lesions were identified, corresponding to the endoscopic findings. A 20-cm bleeding jejunal segment was resected, followed by end-to-end anastomosis, with preservation of 250 cm of jejunum. BRBNS, also known as Bean syndrome, is a rare vascular malformation disorder characterised by multiple venous malformations, most commonly affecting the skin and gastrointestinal tract. Gastrointestinal involvement may lead to chronic occult bleeding, recurrent overt haemorrhage, iron-deficiency anaemia, and transfusion dependence. Current evidence is largely limited to case reports and small series, making management challenging. Endoscopic therapy is generally preferred when lesions are accessible, but extensive or multifocal small-bowel disease may limit its effectiveness. Sirolimus has shown promising results as systemic therapy, although its delayed onset of action may be unsuitable in patients with severe ongoing haemorrhage or clinical instability. This case highlights the value of capsule endoscopy and device-assisted enteroscopy not only for diagnosing small-bowel BRBNS, but also for guiding bowel-sparing surgery when endoscopic treatment is insufficient and systemic therapy cannot provide timely haemorrhage control.
authors: López-Picazo García M, Alajarín Cervera M, Ono Ono A, Argumánez Tello V, García Vázquez A, Fernández Nievas R, Egea Valenzuela J.

title: Wearable 3D Transmitter for Omnidirectional Wireless Energy Delivery for Microrobot.
abstract: Capsule robot has emerged as a non-invasive and painless diagnostic tool for gastrointestinal examination. However, the growing demand for high-definition video and advanced functionalities significantly increases power consumption, while the capsule's compact size imposes stringent battery constraints. Wireless power transfer (WPT) offers a promising solution to overcome this energy bottleneck. This paper presents a wearable three-dimensional transmitting coil (3DTC) and a one dimensional receiving coil (1DRC) to enable omnidirectional and uninterrupted wireless charging for capsule robots. By acquiring attitude data from the capsule, the magnetic field of the wearable 3DTC is adaptively controlled to maximise receiving efficiency despite changes in the capsule's position and orientation. The capsule's built-in thermal and charging management circuits monitor the device's temperature, battery voltage, and stop charging when necessary to ensure safety. Beyond demonstrating a maximum received power of 1690 mW and a peak efficiency of 16.09%, this work further examines a range of practical challenges including, the effects upon the flexible coil bending in garment, charging robustness under various capsule motions, and thermal safety. These evaluations contribute to safer, more efficient, and more sustainable ingestible biomedical devices.
authors: Zhang H, Lee CK.

title: Advances in the Diagnosis of Barrett's Esophagus.
abstract: Barrett's esophagus (BE), the intestinal metaplasia arising from chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease, is the principal identifiable precursor of esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC), whose incidence rose from 0.4 to 2.8/100,000 person-years between 1975 and 2017 and whose prognosis, once symptomatic, remains poor. Because outcomes depend on intercepting the metaplasia-dysplasia-carcinoma sequence, diagnostic accuracy is decisive. White-light endoscopy with Seattle-protocol biopsy remains the reference standard, yet it is constrained by the following three interrelated weaknesses: sampling error, as random forceps biopsies interrogate only about 3.5% of the Barrett's mucosa; poor reproducibility of dysplasia grading, with interobserver agreement of only κ 0.24-0.27 for the pivotal distinction of low-grade dysplasia; and a substantial burden of missed disease, with roughly one-quarter of EACs diagnosed within a year of an index endoscopy reported as nondysplastic. This review synthesizes the technologies converging to address these gaps. Advanced imaging, encompassing high-definition endoscopy, narrow-band imaging, acetic acid chromoendoscopy, and the optical-biopsy platforms confocal laser and volumetric laser endomicroscopy, raises dysplasia yield by approximately 34% over standard white-light examination. Image-enhanced endoscopy improves targeted detection while remaining complementary to structured biopsy sampling. Molecular, genetic, and epigenetic biomarkers, notably DNA-content abnormalities, p53 immunohistochemistry, and multi-gene methylation panels, add an objective read on progression risk. Their pairing with non-endoscopic sampling, including Cytosponge-TFF3, capsule endoscopy, exhaled volatile organic compounds, and circulating microRNA liquid biopsy, is reshaping screening at population scale, while artificial intelligence standardizes interpretation and narrows the expert-nonexpert gap. Together these advances point toward a risk-stratified, multimodal paradigm, though prospective validation and cost-effectiveness evidence remain prerequisites for guideline adoption.
authors: Patel R, Ghazanfar A, Fatima R, Shah R, Patel A, Karmani VK, Bhatt D, Bilal M, Khan ZH, Ghazanfar H.

title: Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome
abstract:
Clinical characteristics

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is characterized by the association of gastrointestinal (GI) polyposis including distinctive arborized smooth muscle polyps, mucocutaneous pigmentation, and cancer predisposition. PJS-type hamartomatous polyps are most common in the small intestine (in order of prevalence: jejunum, ileum, and duodenum), but can also occur in the stomach, large bowel, and extraintestinal sites including the renal pelvis, bronchi, gall bladder, nasal passages, bladder, and ureters. GI polyps can result in chronic bleeding, anemia, recurrent obstruction, and intussusception requiring repeated laparotomy and bowel resection. Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation presents in childhood as dark blue to dark brown macules around the mouth, eyes, and nostrils, in the perianal area, and on the buccal intestinal mucosa. Hyperpigmented macules on the fingers and toes are common. The macules may fade in puberty and adulthood. Recognition of the distinctive skin manifestations is important, especially in individuals who have PJS as the result of a de novo pathogenic variant, as these skin findings often predate GI signs and symptoms. Individuals with PJS are at increased risk for a wide variety of epithelial malignancies (colorectal, gastric, pancreatic). Females are at risk for breast cancer, sex cord tumors with annular tubules (SCTATs), a benign neoplasm of the ovaries, and a gastric-type adenocarcinoma (adenoma malignum) of the cervix, a rare aggressive cancer. Males occasionally develop large-cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumors of the testes, which secrete estrogen and can lead to gynecomastia, advanced skeletal age, and, ultimately, short stature if untreated.

Diagnosis/testing

The diagnosis of PJS is based on clinical findings. Identification of a heterozygous pathogenic variant in STK11 by molecular genetic testing confirms the diagnosis and allows for testing of at-risk relatives and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing.

Management

Treatment of manifestations: Routine endoscopic surveillance with polypectomy decreases the frequency of emergency laparotomy and bowel loss resulting from intussusception. Small bowel imaging includes video capsule endoscopy (VCE) and/or MRI enteroclysis. Magnetic resonance enterography (MRE) may be used if MRI is not tolerated, but MRE is less sensitive than MRI for polyps smaller than 1 cm. Balloon-assisted enteroscopy allows for removal of distal small bowel polyps. Occasionally intraoperative enteroscopy and enterotomy is needed for removal of large distal small bowel polyps. It is advised to remove polyps >15-20 mm or smaller if causing symptoms. Intussusception and malignancies should be treated in the standard manner. Surveillance: Surveillance in people with PJS is preferably done in a center of expertise. Children and adolescents – colonoscopy and upper endoscopy at age eight years; if normal, resume GI surveillance at age 18 years and continue every one to three years. If polyps are detected at initial examination, repeat every one to three years based on size, number, and histopathology of polyps. Small bowel surveillance by VCE or MRI enteroclysis (or MRE if not tolerated) every one to three years based on findings beginning at age eight years. Examination for precocious puberty in females annually beginning at diagnosis or at least by age eight years. Testicular examination and examination for feminizing changes in males annually beginning at diagnosis or at least by age eight years through adulthood. Adults – colonoscopy, upper endoscopy, and small bowel examination by VCE or MRI enteroclysis (or MRE if not tolerated) every one to three years. Clinical breast examination in women every six to 12 months beginning at age 25 years; breast MRI with contrast in women annually from age 25 to 50 years (or if breast MRI with contrast is contraindicated or unavailable, breast ultrasound from age 25 to 30 years and mammography from age 30 to 50 years); consider tomosynthesis and ultrasound for those with dense breast tissue annually from age 30 to 50 years; mammography with consideration of annual breast contrast MRI for dense breasts every one to two years from age 50 to 75 years. Pelvic examination with pap smear and cytology (including those with negative HPV testing) in women annually beginning at age 25 years. Pancreatic imaging with endoscopic ultrasound or MRI is suggested annually beginning at age 40 years in a framework of a study or registry. For lung cancer, provide education regarding signs/symptoms of lung cancer and importance of smoking cessation. Testicular examination and examination for feminizing changes in males annually; testicular ultrasound for those with abnormal findings on examination. Agents/circumstances to avoid: Due to the increased risk for cervical, lung, and pancreatic cancer, smoking should be avoided. Evaluation of relatives at risk: Evaluate apparently asymptomatic older and younger at-risk relatives (including parents, sibs, and children) of an affected individual in order to identify as early as possible those who would benefit from initiation of surveillance, treatment, and preventative measures. If the pathogenic variant in the family is known, offer molecular genetic testing to at-risk relatives. If the pathogenic variant in the family is not known, offer clinical diagnostic evaluations.

Genetic counseling

PJS is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Most individuals diagnosed with PJS have an affected parent; some individuals represent apparently simplex cases and may have the disorder as the result of a de novo pathogenic variant. If a parent of the proband is affected and/or is known to have the pathogenic variant identified in the proband, the risk to the sibs is 50%. To date, all reported individuals with pathogenic variants in STK11 have shown clinical manifestations; however, variable expressivity is common among affected family members. If the STK11 pathogenic variant has been identified in an affected family member, predictive testing for at-risk family members and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing are possible.
authors: Amos CI, Wagner A.

title: A Preclinical Multifunctional Capsule Robot with Unified Diagnosis and Targeted Thermal Therapy for Gastrointestinal Diseases
abstract: ABSTRACT Capsule endoscopes play an essential role in visualizing the gastrointestinal tract and identifying pathological lesions, but existing systems are still largely limited to passive visualization without therapeutic capability. Here, we present a proof‐of‐concept multifunctional capsule robot (MCR) integrating diagnostic imaging, magnetic navigation, wireless power transfer, and targeted thermotherapy. In the ex vivo environment, the MCR relies on magnetic navigation and control to position itself at the target site. This enables site‐specific thermal ablation, where controlled high temperatures are applied within the tissue to achieve substantial cellular destruction. These results support the feasibility of the prototype's intended functions. Through a series of in vitro cellular experiments, the MCR further demonstrated controllable temperature regulation, achieving up to 89% cell mortality under 70 heating for 120 s. The findings demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed approach at a proof‐of‐principle level. The experiments validate the system‐level feasibility of integrating diagnostic imaging, targeted treatment, and wireless charging within one capsule. At this stage, the platform remains a preclinical prototype and is not ready for clinical translation; further engineering and preclinical validation are required. Nonetheless, this MCR architecture provides a preliminary framework that may support future improvements in minimally invasive gastrointestinal therapeutic systems.

title: ARCGym: Benchmarking Deep Reinforcement Learning in Autonomous Robotic Colonoscopy
abstract: Simulations for learning-based autonomous colonoscopic navigation focus mainly on fully actuated capsule robots, failing to capture the contact-rich navigation of long and flexible clinical colonoscopes. We present the Autonomous Robotic Colonoscopy Gym (ARCGym), an open-source reinforcement learning environment and benchmark for image-based navigation in clinically derived deformable colon anatomies. ARCGym supports multiple types of colonoscope robots, spanning capsule robots and flexible endoscopes, with this work focusing on flexible endoscopes including magnetic-driven tip actuation and clinically used proximally translational actuation. This work includes five CT-reconstructed colons representing typical clinical scenarios, a set of clinically meaningful navigation subtasks, and unified success metrics. We introduce a reward combining depth-based lumen alignment with a lumen-visibility score to improve learning under occlusions. Experiments across tasks, robots, and anatomies show that autonomous navigation remains challenging for both magnetic-driven and proximal-insertion flexible robots, with proximal-insertion actuation remaining an open problem.
authors: Guanglin Ji; Martina Finocchiaro; Kenny Erleben; Hang Yin

title: Capsule endoscopy: Emerging technologies and future clinical applications
abstract: Capsule endoscopy has evolved from a diagnostic tool for small bowel evaluation into a complex platform with expanding diagnostic and prognostic potential.This mini review aims to summarize recent advances in capsule endoscopy and explore potential clinical applications and future directions of this technology.The introduction of pan-enteric capsule endoscopy has enabled comprehensive evaluation of the entire gastrointestinal tract in a single, minimally invasive examination, supporting treat-to-target approaches and improving disease phenotyping in inflammatory bowel disease.Artificial intelligence (AI) represents one of the most important recent developments in capsule endoscopy.Deep learning algorithms have demonstrated high accuracy in lesion detection while reducing reading times.More recently, AI has been applied to automated inflammatory activity scoring, bowel cleansing assessment, and computer-assisted reporting, facilitating standardized interpretation and improving report quality.Magnetically controlled capsule endoscopy has further expanded the role of capsule technology by enabling active navigation within the upper gastrointestinal tract.Recent innovations include detachable-string systems for esophageal examination, remote 5Gassisted capsule navigation, and integration with AI-assisted image analysis, opening new perspectives for noninvasive evaluation from mouth to anus.Experimental robotic capsule prototypes have explored the feasibility of interventional functions, including tissue sampling and targeted drug delivery.These technologies remain at the preclinical stage, and their potential clinical applicability requires further investigation.
authors: Clelia Marmo; Maria Elena Riccioni

title: Rare Disease Classification in Video Capsule Endoscopy
abstract: Video capsule endoscopy offers a non-invasive way to examine the small bowel, however, the rare but clinically important findings that appear only in less than 1\% of labelled frames, provide very less signal for detection. As a result, while models can achieve high overall performance, they almost completely miss these rare findings. We condition each frame's decision on evidence from the rest of that patient's video, not on the frame's own posterior alone, supplying information a single frozen frame can never contain. Building upon Expected Gain Arbitration, a per-frame, macro-F1-optimal correction over the confusion matrix, we further compose it with video-disease-presence conditional resulting in our decoding method Hierarchical Conditional-Expected-gain (HCE). We evaluate HCE on two independent VCE datasets, Kvasir-Capsule and GALAR, against a static temporal-smoothing baseline and an optimal-transport (OT) frame-level correction. HCE significantly improves rare-class recall over a temporal-smoothing baseline on GALAR (2.7--3.1x; 95\% CI excludes zero in both scopes) and shows a similar, though not statistically confirmed, gain on Kvasir-Capsule (up to 3.4x). Against OT, HCE still improves rare-class recall in all four evaluation settings (+0.016 to +0.029), and additionally improves macro-F1 and MCC.

title: Complementary Roles of Intestinal Ultrasound and Capsule Endoscopy in Crohn’s Disease: A Prospective Blinded Comparative Study
abstract: Background and Aims: Precise and longitudinal assessment of small-bowel inflammatory activity is essential in Crohn’s disease (CD). Capsule endoscopy (CE) provides comprehensive mucosal evaluation but is limited for routine use by cost and availability. Intestinal ultrasound (IUS) has emerged as a non-invasive, accessible, and complementary imaging modality. This study compared the diagnostic performance of IUS with CE for detecting terminal ileum inflammation. Methods: In this prospective blinded study, adult patients with suspected or established CD referred for CE underwent same-day IUS. Inflammatory activity was quantified by the International Bowel Ultrasound Segmental Activity Score (IBUS-SAS) for IUS and the Lewis score for CE. Results: Ninety-eight patients were included with a mean age of 42±14 years, 42% male. IBUS-SAS showed a significant association with the 3rd tertile Lewis score (ρ=0.515, p<0.001). This association differed according to inflammatory burden, as among patients with a Lewis score <350, the correlation was weak and non-significant (ρ=0.149, p=0.198), whereas a stronger correlation was observed in those with a Lewis score ≥350. IBUS-SAS demonstrated excellent discrimination for a Lewis Score ≥350 (AUROC 0.889; 95% CI 0.807–0.972), and an IBUS-SAS cut-off of ≥13.7 yielded 90.5% sensitivity, 76.3% specificity, and 96.7% negative predictive value. Discriminative performance remained high across suspected and established CD. IBUS-SAS was the only predictor of capsule-derived inflammation, when adjusted for clinical and laboratorial biomarkers (OR 1.149 per point increase; 95% CI, 1.070–1.234; p<0.001). Conclusions: IUS accurately detects clinically significant ileal inflammation (Lewis score ≥350) and performs best in patients with higher inflammatory burden. In contrast, its performance was lower in patients with absent or low-grade inflammation, in whom the correlation between IBUS-SAS and Lewis score was weak. These findings support a complementary approach, with CE remaining the reference standard for detailed mucosal assessment and IUS serving as a practical, non-invasive tool for the assessment of clinically significant ileal inflammation.
authors: Joao Goncalves; Francisca Dias de Castro; Leite Sílvia; Joana Magalhães; Bruno Joel Ferreira Rosa; José Cotter

title: Zero-shot classification of bleeding, angiectasia, and normal mucosa in video capsule endoscopy by general-purpose multimodal models
abstract: A diagnostic accuracy study measuring how well current general-purpose multimodal models, given no task-specific training and no worked examples, assign video capsule endoscopy frames to one of three categories: fresh blood, angiectasia, and normal clean mucosa. Frames are drawn from the publicly available Kvasir-Capsule dataset by two-stage stratified sampling at the level of the source recording. The primary outcome is macro-averaged F1. Predictive values are recalculated across the range of frame-level lesion prevalence met in clinical reading; calibration of stated confidence and the rate of declining to answer are treated as outcomes; and a prespecified probe tests whether the models recognize the provenance of the images they are shown. This project holds the protocol and the analysis code, registered before any model was queried.
authors: Ahmed Salman

title: WCE-SECUREAI: A LIGHTWEIGHT HYBRID CRYPTOGRAPHIC FRAMEWORK FOR SECURE DATA TRANSMISSION IN IOMT USING WIRELESS CAPSULE ENDOSCOPY
abstract: Wireless Capsule Endoscopy (WCE) is a diagnostic tool used for the detection of gastrointestinal (GI) diseases due to its non-invasive approach to visualizing the digestive tract. Nonetheless, the application of DPA in Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) is limited due to twofold difficulties, including secure medical data transmission and high computational complexity, as well as the poor applicability of current cryptographic schemes to resource-constrained devices. Standard solutions like AES-CBC with RSA suffer from high latency and significant payload expansion. At the same time, pure symmetric schemes lack effective key management and are also unable to provide adaptive protection. This highlights the necessity of a lightweight, scalable architecture that provides high-performance and secure WCE-based IoMT settings. In this work, we present WCE-Secure AI, a holistic framework architecture with a newly proposed hybrid encryption module (LightHybridCrypt) that utilizes AES-GCM for authenticated encryption and elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) for efficient key exchange. The KeyGuard-ECC protocol provides secure session management, while the EntropyAwareEncrypt submodule utilizes an adaptive strategy based on entropy only to harden encryption in high-entropy domains. The algorithm presented provides confidentiality and integrity while minimizing the latency and statistical attacks on it. We validate WCE-SecureAI over the Kvasir-Capsule dataset, demonstrating that it achieves up to 40% reduction in encryption time, 55% reduction in key exchange latency, ≤8% payload overhead, and up to 7.99/8 bits of entropy, with 99.1% integrity verification accuracy. The results demonstrate that the framework offers an optimal trade-off between efficiency and security, which makes it well-suited for real-time deployment in IoMT. Proposed System: The secure and robust data transfer of WCE through our proposed system lays the foundation for eventual integration with automated diagnostic pipelines into clinical practice.
authors: P.ANITHA SHRAVANI AMAR
venue: Journal of Theoretical and Applied Information Technology

title: A Two-Element Capsule Antenna for Near-Field Polarization MIMO in Wireless Capsule Endoscopy
abstract: Multiple-Input-Multiple-Output (MIMO) technology is considered to be a viable method for spectral efficiency and data rate enhancement in wireless communications. This article presents a two-element capsule antenna with orthogonal current distributions for polarization multiplexing in a wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) application at 915 MHz. The proposed antenna was evaluated in a MIMO link where it served as the transmitter and an existing on-body antenna was the receiver. The performance was assessed in two distinct environments: an anatomically accurate human body model using full-wave (FW) simulations, and a homogeneous liquid tissue phantom, using both FW simulations and measurements. The former was used to evaluate the performance in a realistic environment and to demonstrate the superiority of the proposed capsule antenna against existing two-element antennas in the literature, while the latter aimed at verifying the antenna design by comparison of simulated and measured MIMO links. We studied channel capacity and eigenvalues for the comparisons. The MIMO link with the proposed antenna provided nearly doubled median channel capacity relative to a baseline single-input-single-output link, consistently in the simulations and measurements. Our results prove the suitability of the proposed antenna for polarization multiplexing and, in terms of channel capacity, establish it as the best conformal two-element capsule antenna design at 915 MHz.

title: An Accurate and Efficient 3D Reconstruction Method for Wireless Capsule Endoscopy Based on Harris Corner Detection and Fixed Template Matching
abstract: To overcome the limitation of wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) in providing only two‑dimensional intestinal images—which constrains accurate diagnosis of intestinal lesions—this study proposes an accurate and efficient three‑dimensional detection method. The approach applies 3D reconstruction to WCE images by computing corresponding points across successive frames and estimating the capsule’s position and orientation. A critical step involves the selection of highly specific feature points and the determination of their correspondences. Accordingly, this paper combines a Harris corner‑based feature extraction algorithm with a fixed matching template algorithm to achieve robust feature point matching in WCE intestinal images, substantially improving both matching efficiency and robustness. Using the obtained feature matching points, an intestinal model is reconstructed via 3D reconstruction. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method offers advantages in efficiency and reconstruction quality compared with conventional 3D reconstruction approaches, indicating its potential to enhance WCE‑based lesion localization and diagnostic accuracy.

title: Long-Term Outcomes According to a Device-Assisted Enteroscopy Strategy after Capsule Endoscopy in Patients with Small Bowel Bleeding: A Nationwide Population-Based Cohort Study
abstract: Background/Aims: Although the use of device-assisted enteroscopy (DAE) has increased, few large-scale studies have examined long-term outcomes focused on small bowel (SB) bleeding. We analyzed National Health Insurance Service data to evaluate the clinical utility of DAE in patients with SB bleeding who underwent capsule endoscopy. Methods: We included a cohort of 11,690 patients who underwent capsule endoscopy for SB bleeding (identified using ICD-10 codes) between 2014 and 2022. Patients were categorized into three groups: no DAE, diagnostic DAE, and therapeutic DAE. We assessed four major outcomes, including the probability and factors associated with SB rebleeding, severe SB rebleeding, rebleeding-related mortality, and all-cause mortality. Results: Of 11,690 patients, 5,211 were included in the analysis (no DAE, n=4,960; diagnostic DAE, n=173; therapeutic DAE, n=78). The probability of SB rebleeding and severe SB rebleeding was highest in the therapeutic DAE group, followed by the diagnostic DAE and no DAE groups (p<0.001), with 7-year rebleeding probabilities of 19.8%, 15.8%, and 5.0%, respectively. Rebleeding-related and all-cause mortality were also highest in the therapeutic DAE group, followed by the diagnostic DAE and no DAE groups (p<0.001 for both), with 7-year rebleeding-related mortality probabilities of 9.3%, 5.9%, and 2.7%, respectively. Risk factors for both rebleeding-related and all-cause mortality included age, male sex, liver cirrhosis, and malignancy. Conclusions: Patients who require therapeutic DAE for SB bleeding remain at increased long-term risk of rebleeding and mortality. These findings likely reflect their greater underlying disease burden and highlight the need for individualized long-term surveillance and careful management of comorbidities, even after therapeutic intervention.
authors: Joo Hye Song; Jung Rock Moon; Jin Oh Kim; Jin Oh Kim; Jung-Bin Park; Seong Ran Jeon; Ji Sung Lee

title: Design and Comparative Evaluation of Two Low-Cost Analog RF Transmission Approaches for a Wireless Capsule Endoscopy Prototype

title: Concordancia diagnóstica entre la cápsula endoscópica y la enteroscopía de doble balón en la hemorragia digestiva de intestino medio en un hospital de referencia en Perú
abstract: Introduction: The diagnostic approach to mid-gut gastrointestinal bleeding requires several examinations, primarily video capsule endoscopy followed by double-balloon enteroscopy) at tertiary care centers. Objective: To evaluate the level of diagnostic agreement between video capsule endoscopy and double-balloon enteroscopy in patients treated with mid-gut gastrointestinal bleeding at a referral hospital in Lima, Peru, during the 2020-2025 period. Methods: This was an observational, retrospective, and comparative study. Diagnostic agreement between the two procedures was calculated using the Kappa coefficient. Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics v.20.0 and R software version 4.1.2, with a significant p-value < 0.05. Results: In fifty-one patients with mid-gut gastrointestinal bleeding (28 women; median age: 65 years [IQR: 55-71]), video capsule endoscopy and subsequent double-balloon enteroscopy (39 antegrade and 12 retrograde) were performed. Most patients (34/51; 66.7%) presented with overt mid-gut gastrointestinal bleeding, while the rest had occult bleeding, with a mean hemoglobin level of 7.3 ± 2.24 g/dL. The median time interval between the two procedures was 13 days (IQR 5-29). In 10 (19.6%) patients where video capsule endoscopy showed positive findings, no lesions were identified during double-balloon enteroscopy , whereas in one case (2%) with a negative video capsule endoscopy , double-balloon enteroscopy was positive. Overall diagnostic agreement was low (κ = 0.37; [95% CI: 0.10-0.64]; p = 0.002). Moderate agreement was observed regarding lesion type (κ = 0.58; [95% CI: 0.42-0.74]; p < 0.001) and lesion location (κ = 0.50; [95% CI: 0.31-0.69]; p < 0.001), with moderate agreement for vascular (κ = 0.60) and tumoral (κ = 0.60) lesions. Conclusion: Video capsule endoscopy and double-balloon enteroscopy showed low overall diagnostic agreement in patients with mid-gut gastrointestinal bleeding, and moderate agreement regarding the type and location of the lesion.
authors: Ofelia Brisaida Castillo Contreras; Jairo Asencios-Cusihuallpa; Elizabeth Ayala-Quintanilla

title: ARISE: Adaptive Agentic Reasoning with Image-grounded Self-Evaluation for Interpretable IBD Assessment
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) requires frequent imaging-based assessment, yet interpretation of modalities such as wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) and intestinal ultrasound remains heavily dependent on specialist expertise. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate significant potential in multimodal medical image analysis, but their clinical adoption is hindered by their insufficient domain-specific reasoning, susceptibility to hallucination, scarcity of high quality training data in fine-grained diagnostics and limited interpretability. We introduce ARISE (Adaptive Agentic Reasoning with Image-grounded Self-Evaluation), an autonomous planning framework that models few-shot medical image understanding as a sequential agentic workflow. ARISE structures agent execution into a transparent 5-stage workflow: hypothesis generation, image-grounded evidence summarization, evidence-conditioned refinement, symbolic verification, and final diagnosis. We apply ARISE to IBD assessment across two independent patient cohorts: wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) images for Crohn's disease and B-mode ultrasound data for ulcerative colitis. ARISE consistently improves diagnostic performance over baseline VLMs while exposing where reasoning succeeds or fails, providing a more interpretable basis for clinical decision support and realistic deployment.
authors: Pronoma Banerjee; Anuva Shah; Jason Wu; Md. Masudur Rahman; Sanjay Mohanty; Satya V. Kurada; Juan Pablo Wachs

title: Swallowable Electronics: A Review on Digital Pills from Adherence to Diagnostic
abstract: Digital pills, sometimes referred to as swallowable electronics, are a new class of smart medical devices that combine medications with biosensors and tiny electronics to improve patient care. Poor drug adherence and restricted access to non-invasive diagnostic techniques are two significant issues facing the healthcare industry that these solutions are intended to address. The first FDA-approved digital pill, Abilify MyCite, paired aripiprazole with a wearable patch and an ingestible event marker to track ingestion in real time. Despite being novel, it was eventually dropped because of safety and technological issues. Capsule endoscopy tools like CapsoCam Plus offer a panoramic view of the gastrointestinal tract for diagnostic purposes. They have shown promise in treating unexplained gastrointestinal hemorrhage, Crohn's disease, celiac disease, ulcerative colitis, and colonic polyps. More recently, the creation of PillTrek, a "lab-in-a-pill," has broadened the use of digital pills by facilitating real-time monitoring of gut biomarkers such as temperature, pH, glucose, and serotonin, thus connecting biochemical analysis and diagnoses. Even while these technologies show great promise for increasing adherence, improving diagnostic precision, and facilitating individualized therapy, issues with patient acceptance, cost, energy constraints, and device dependability still exist. These obstacles should be removed by ongoing research in biodegradable materials, wireless connectivity, biosensor miniaturization, and artificial intelligence. All things considered, swallowable electronics represent a paradigm shift in the provision of healthcare by providing safer, more accurate, and more patient-friendly options for non-invasive diagnostics and adherence monitoring.
authors: Rashmi Rajeghorpade, Satyajit Sahoo*, Sapna Desai, Archana Kaushik, Sarankhawala Aadil S.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: When Imaging is Negative: Endoscopic Diagnosis of a Secondary Aortoduodenal Fistula
abstract: Aortoenteric fistula is a life-threatening aortic graft complication with a narrow opportunity for treatment. We present a patient with aortobifemoral bypass who developed recurrent anemia and melena. Despite previous upper endoscopy and colonoscopy, computed tomography angiogram, and tagged red blood cell scan, his symptoms were persistent. Capsule endoscopy showed blood in the duodenum. Push enteroscopy revealed graft erosion in the duodenum, confirming aortoduodenal fistula. He underwent aortobifemoral graft excision, and resection of the third portion of the duodenum with end-to-side duodenojejunostomy, highlighting the importance of endoscopy in timely diagnosis of aortoenteric fistulae.
authors: Avneet Kaur; Ayushi Shah; Anand Gupta; Muhammad Nauman Jhandier

title: Deep Learning Based Classification Of Gastrointestinal Lesions Using Wireless Capsule Endoscopic Images
abstract: Although wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) has proven as an important minimally invasive diagnostic tool in the field of gastrointestinal (GI) diseases, it presents enormous difficulties when examining these images and the variety of lesions encountered. The deep ensemble learning model for gastrointestinal lesion segmentation and detection are involved image preprocessing, lesion segmentation using deep learning, feature learning, and ensemble classification, which are designed to enhance the localization of lesions and diagnostic accuracy. For experimental evaluation we used the Kvasir-SEG dataset comprising of 1000 gastrointestinal polyp images, each accompanied by a segmentation mask. Three different types of CNN architectures (SegNet, U-Net and DeepLab) were trained to learn complementary spatial and contextual features independently. The segmentation results were then stacked to combine them together to improve the prediction accuracy with the help of a Random Forest Classifier (RFC). The individual models exhibited competitive segmentation performance with U-Net performing the highest validation accuracy (92.96%) and SegNet performing best with Dice coefficient (0.7210) and IoU (0.5654). The proposed ensemble framework showed a significant improvement in performance with 99.95% accuracy, 99.91% F1-score, 99.85% ROC-AUC, 99.99% precision, and 99.70% recall. Confusion Matrix analysis also substantiated good lesion identification with only a few false-positive and false-negative predictions. The results show the effectiveness of heterogeneous ensemble learning that merges the different strengths of various segmentation architectures and offers an effective method for automated analysis of gastrointestinal lesions. The proposed framework can be applied to decrease diagnostic burden and to aid computer-aided diagnosis systems for clinical applications of WCE.
authors: Pakistan Journal of Medical & Cardiological Review
venue: Pakistan Journal of Medical & Cardiological Review

title: Advances in the Diagnosis of Barrett’s Esophagus
abstract: Barrett's esophagus (BE), the intestinal metaplasia arising from chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease, is the principal identifiable precursor of esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC), whose incidence rose from 0.4 to 2.8/100,000 person-years between 1975 and 2017 and whose prognosis, once symptomatic, remains poor. Because outcomes depend on intercepting the metaplasia-dysplasia-carcinoma sequence, diagnostic accuracy is decisive. White-light endoscopy with Seattle-protocol biopsy remains the reference standard, yet it is constrained by the following three interrelated weaknesses: sampling error, as random forceps biopsies interrogate only about 3.5% of the Barrett's mucosa; poor reproducibility of dysplasia grading, with interobserver agreement of only κ 0.24-0.27 for the pivotal distinction of low-grade dysplasia; and a substantial burden of missed disease, with roughly one-quarter of EACs diagnosed within a year of an index endoscopy reported as nondysplastic. This review synthesizes the technologies converging to address these gaps. Advanced imaging, encompassing high-definition endoscopy, narrow-band imaging, acetic acid chromoendoscopy, and the optical-biopsy platforms confocal laser and volumetric laser endomicroscopy, raises dysplasia yield by approximately 34% over standard white-light examination. Image-enhanced endoscopy improves targeted detection while remaining complementary to structured biopsy sampling. Molecular, genetic, and epigenetic biomarkers, notably DNA-content abnormalities, p53 immunohistochemistry, and multi-gene methylation panels, add an objective read on progression risk. Their pairing with non-endoscopic sampling, including Cytosponge-TFF3, capsule endoscopy, exhaled volatile organic compounds, and circulating microRNA liquid biopsy, is reshaping screening at population scale, while artificial intelligence standardizes interpretation and narrows the expert-nonexpert gap. Together these advances point toward a risk-stratified, multimodal paradigm, though prospective validation and cost-effectiveness evidence remain prerequisites for guideline adoption.
authors: Ravi Patel; Ali Ghazanfar; Rida Fatima; Rushin Shah; Aman Patel; Vikash Kumar Karmani; Devanshi Bhatt; Muhammad Bilal; Zarak H. Khan; Haider Ghazanfar

title: Herbal and Natural Products for NSAID-Induced Small Intestinal Injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
abstract: Objectives: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), including aspirin, are widely used medications that frequently cause small intestinal injury (enteropathy). Conventional proton pump inhibitors do not prevent this injury and may exacerbate it through dysbiosis. Herbal medicines and natural products offer potential therapeutic benefits, but synthesized clinical evidence remains limited. Thus, this study will systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of herbal medicines and natural products for preventing NSAID-induced small intestinal injury. Methods: MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure will be searched to identify articles published since inception, without restrictions on publication date or language. Randomized controlled trials involving adults aged ≥ 18 years receiving NSAIDs will be included. Two reviewers will independently perform study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment using the RoB 2 tool. If appropriate, a meta-analysis will be conducted. The primary outcome will be mucosal injury, objectively assessed using video capsule endoscopy or measures of intestinal permeability. Secondary outcomes will include symptoms and adverse events. Results: This study will synthesize the current clinical evidence on natural interventions for NSAID-induced enteropathy. Conclusion: The findings will inform the management of small intestinal injury and guide future research.
authors: Ji Hye Hwang; You-Kyung Choi

title: Artificial intelligence in gastrointestinal endoscopy: From technical performance to clinical translation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being increasingly used in gastrointestinal endoscopy for lesion detection, optical characterization, procedural quality monitoring, multimodal assessment, clinical decision support, and documentation. The strongest clinical evidence supports computer-aided detection during colonoscopy and selected applications for upper gastrointestinal neoplasia. Randomized trials have shown that AI can increase adenoma detection and assist in real-time lesion recognition. However, the benefits observed in controlled studies are not always reproduced in routine practice. Evidence for optical diagnosis, invasion depth assessment, inflammatory bowel disease, capsule endoscopy, pancreatobiliary endoscopy, and endoscopic ultrasonography remains heterogeneous, and many systems have been evaluated, mainly using retrospective or selected datasets. However, technical performance alone does not establish clinical value. Higher sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic accuracy may not lead to safer decisions, more efficient workflows, or better patient outcomes. False-positive alerts, automation bias, correction burden, geographic and platform dependence, limited external validation, and poor workflow integration can affect real-world performance. Vision-foundation models, multimodal systems, and large-language models extend AI beyond single-task image analysis to reusable representations, automated reporting, and well-defined clinical support. Their clinical transferability remains uncertain because of domain shifts, data leakage, unsupported generation, and variable performance across settings. This review examined the evidence from gastrointestinal endoscopy using two complementary dimensions: clinical function and stage of evaluation. The clinical function describes the role of AI in the endoscopic pathway. Stage of evaluation distinguishes among retrospective internal testing, independent external validation, prospective clinical evaluation, interventional evaluation, and real-world or post-deployment assessment. We also use reasoning-aligned AI to describe systems whose tasks, intermediate representations, evidence integration, and outputs are organized around clinically meaningful observations and decisions, without implying human-like cognition or causal reasoning. Wider adoption should depend on independent validation, prospective evaluation of complete human–AI workflows, appropriate clinical oversight, operational reliability, governance, economic value, and reproducible benefits in routine care.
authors: Wenxin Xue; Xueying Wang; Tongrui Yang; Honggang Yu

title: Artificial intelligence assisted colon capsule endoscopy : evaluating its role in enhancing diagnostic performance
abstract: The global burden of colorectal cancer (CRC) continues to rise, increasing demand for effective lower gastrointestinal (GI) diagnostics. Colon Capsule Endoscopy (CCE) is a minimally invasive alternative to colonoscopy, yet adoption has been limited by variable diagnostic accuracy, lengthy reading times, and high capsule-to-colonoscopy conversion (CCC) rates. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer potential to improve detection and efficiency. This thesis addresses the key barriers to the scalable implementation of CCE. A meta-review and umbrella meta-analysis confirmed the high diagnostic accuracy of second-generation CCE (CCE2), with pooled per-patient sensitivities of 0.90 for polyps of any size and 0.96 for CRC. CCE2 reliably detects polyps ≥6 mm and ≥10 mm with high specificity and low heterogeneity. The CESCAIL (Capsule Endoscopy at Scale through Enhanced AI Analysis) study, involving 14 NHS centres, evaluated the AI-assisted platform AiSPEED™ in 720 patients. In per-patient analysis comparing colonoscopy vs no follow up, AI-assisted readings improved the diagnostic yield (70.6% vs 63.6%) and reduced the mean reading time by more than fivefold (8.7 vs 47.3 minutes). Specificity declined slightly from 99% to 96% (p=0.058), this reflected a higher false-positive rate inherent to AI-assisted CCE interpretation. Per-polyp analysis showed higher sensitivity for smaller and left-sided polyps, with strong performance for hyperplastic lesions, supporting its potential as a triage tool for invasive colonoscopy. A parallel substudy examined inter- and intra-observer variability in bowel cleansing assessment using Leighton-Rex and CC-CLEAR scores. Interobserver agreement was poor with Leighton-Rex scale but improved with CC-CLEAR among experienced readers. AI-assisted scoring did not consistently improve agreement and could reduce it among less experienced readers, indicating a need for refinement and better integration. Further work explored CCC drivers, including excretion rates, bowel preparation, and diagnostic yield. A national audit and meta-analysis that were conducted by the author reported CCC rates of 42–50%, higher with CCE2 due to greater sensitivity. Another multicentre audit demonstrated that FIT-based triage achieved optimal cost-effectiveness at thresholds ranging between 10 and 17.6 μg/g. These findings support a scalable, AI-enabled CCE service integrating cloud platforms, telemedicine, and home capsule delivery to reduce endoscopy backlogs while preserving diagnostic accuracy.
authors: Ian Io Lei
venue: Warwick Research Archive Portal (University of Warwick)

title: PREFERENDO: a preference for the full picture in pediatric capsule endoscopy
abstract: The PREFERENDO consensus provides a valuable framework for pediatric endoscopy reporting [1]. Its capsule domain already includes preparation quality, completeness, lesion description and interpretation. The opportunity for refinement lies in connecting these fields to the endorsed scores. We suggest an implementation principle: each reported score should include the information needed to understand what it measures and how examination quality constrains its interpretation.
authors: Anastasios Koulaouzidis; Ervin Tóth; Wojciech M. Marlicz

title: MultiAttenGastro: Multi-Dimensional Attention Augmentation for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy Classification
abstract: Automated gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy classification requires models that generalize across diverse modalities and class distributions, often far from natural-image pretraining. We propose MultiAttenGastro, a plug-and-play attention framework with parallel 1-D channel, 2-D spatial, and 3-D contextual heads, and present the first systematic cross-dataset evaluation across eight CNN and transformer backbones on five public GI datasets (80 backbone--dataset runs). We find that attention effectiveness is not universal but tracks the representational gap between ImageNet features and the target distribution: MultiAttenGastro improves 6 of 8 backbones on Kvasir-Capsule (14-class WCE, large gap; best macro F1 98.33\%), is uniformly negative on the small-gap Kvasir-v2 benchmark (0/8), and shows mixed outcomes on datasets with intermediate gap. Five-seed ablation on the strongest case (Kvasir-Capsule, ConvNeXt-Tiny) shows this improvement is directionally consistent, but not statistically decisive (paired $t$: $p=0.47$; Wilcoxon: $p=0.63$), and that individual attention heads are not uniformly beneficial in isolation only their combination yields a positive mean effect. Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) analysis links this pattern to representational redundancy: low inter-head CKA under large domain gaps coincides with the framework's only consistent gains, while high redundancy under small gaps coincides with its losses. We report these results, including the non-significant margins, as evidence for when and why multi-dimensional attention helps GI endoscopy classification, rather than as a claim that MultiAttenGastro is a strictly superior architectural choice.
authors: Sadhana Devarajan; Praveen Kumar Chandaliya; Dhruvin Jashvant Kumar Shah; Kishor P. Upla; Kiran Raja

title: Constipation Not So Vibrant: A Case Report of Colonic Obstruction From Capsule Retention
abstract: Vibrating capsules represent a novel, nonpharmacologic approach for chronic idiopathic constipation, with favorable safety profiles in clinical trials, showing no reported retention events. Although generally well tolerated, patients with severe motility disorders and use of narcotics pose risk of retention of capsules. We report a case of a 73-year-old woman with a history of gastroparesis and slow-transit constipation, who developed colonic retention of multiple vibrating capsules, requiring colonoscopic retrieval. Careful patient selection, monitoring, and timely imaging may prevent complications when treating patients with vibrating capsules.
authors: Merve Ertem; Aaron Rampersad; Angel Rochester; Monia Elisa Werlang
venue: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians Open

title: System design and performance analysis of wireless body area networks
abstract: One key solution to provide affordable and proactive healthcare facilities to overcome the fast world population growth and a shortage of medical professionals is through health monitoring systems capable of early disease detection and real-time data transmission leading to considerable improvements in the quality of human life. Wireless body area networks (WBANs) are proposed as promising approaches to providing better mobility and flexibility experience than traditional wired medical systems by using low-power, miniaturised sensors inside, around, or off the human body and are employed to monitor physiological signals. However, the design of reliable and energy efficient in-body communication systems is still a major research challenge since implant devices are characterised by strict requirements on size, energy consumption and safety. Moreover, there is still no agreement regarding QoS support in WBANs. The first part of this work concentrates on the design and performance evaluation of WBAN communication systems involving the ‘in-body to in-body’ and ‘in-body to on-body’ scenarios. The essential step is to derive the statistical WBAN path loss (PL) models, which characterise the signal propagation energy loss transmitting via intra-body region. Moreover, from the point of view of human body safety evaluation, the obtained specific absorption rate (SAR) values are compared with the latest Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 802.15.6 Task Group technical standard and the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) safety guidelines. Link budget analysis is then presented using a range of energy-efficient modulation schemes, and the results are given including the transmission distance, data rate and transmitting power in individual sections. On the other hand, major quality of service (QoS) support challenges in WBANs are discussed and investigated. To achieve higher lifetime and lower network energy consumption, different data routing protocol methods, including incremental relaying and the two-relay based routing technique are taken into account. A set of key QoS metrics for linear mathematical models is given along with the related subjective functions. The incremental relaying routing protocol promises significant enhancements in in-body WBAN network lifetime by minimising the overall communication distance while the two-relay based routing method achieves better performance in terms of emergency data transmission and high traffic condition, QoS-aware WBANs design. Moreover, to handle real-time high data transmission applications such as capsule endoscope image transmission, a flexible QoS-aware wireless body area sensor networks (WBASNs) model is proposed and evaluated that can bring novel solutions for a realistic multi-user hospital environment regarding information packet collision probability, manageable numbers of sensor nodes and a wide range of data rates.
authors: Yangzhe Liao
venue: Warwick Research Archive Portal (University of Warwick)

title: Letter to the Editor: Reconsidering water based boosters for small bowel capsule endoscopy
abstract: Ferreira et al's in the World Journal of Gastrointestinal Endoscopyconducted a prospective, multicenter, quasi-randomized trial comparing three intraprocedural booster regimens for small bowel capsule endoscopy: Polyethylene glycol, polyethylene glycol with ascorbic acid, and still water.The study has several strengths including the prospective, multicenter design with efforts to minimize confounding, use of the validated Small Bowel Cleansing Assessment and Report scoring system with excellent interobserver agreement, and assessment of patient tolerability.Key limitations include quasi-randomization, unequal group allocation, a wide non-inferiority margin, and the lack of formal confidence interval-based analysis.In agreement with recent studies such as the PrepRICE trial, the CROHN PREP trial, and a recent umbrella meta-analysis, the findings suggest that booster timing may matter more than the agent used, though reduced cleansing in the distal small bowel with water remains a concern.Future noninferiority trials are needed before water-based boosters can be adopted as standard practice.
authors: Sriya Baru; Anokhi Amara; Micheal Tadros

title: Colon capsule endoscopy and cost-effectiveness across colorectal care: a valuable filter, but a poor universal substitute
abstract: Colon capsule endoscopy (CCE) is a patient-friendly, minimally invasive alternative to conventional colonoscopy, but its value depends on pathway performance rather than diagnostic accuracy alone. This narrative review examines the cost-effectiveness of CCE across colorectal cancer screening, symptomatic investigation, incomplete colonoscopy, post-polypectomy surveillance, inflammatory bowel disease monitoring, and AI-supported implementation. Targeted literature searches were performed in PubMed and official guidance sources through 6 July 2026. Across broad screening populations, CCE is not yet cost-effective compared with biennial faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) or 10-yearly colonoscopy; contemporary Dutch MISCAN modelling found all CCE screening strategies dominated at full adherence, largely because unit cost and follow-up colonoscopy burden remained high. The dominant economic problem is pathway duplication: a 2025 meta-analysis found a pooled follow-up endoscopy rate of 42%, and contemporary UK/Scottish service data showed that about half of patients required further optical endoscopy or sigmoidoscopy. CCE may offer conditional value after incomplete colonoscopy, in lower-risk symptomatic triage, and in carefully selected surveillance pathways where a negative or low-risk capsule result may avoid, defer, or focus colonoscopy. Evidence from Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis monitoring is encouraging but should not be extrapolated uncritically to colorectal cancer screening or dysplasia surveillance, where biopsy and therapy remain decisive. AI-assisted CCE may reduce reading time and improve polyp detection, but robust lifetime cost-effectiveness models are still needed. The current evidence supports CCE as a pathway-dependent filter, not a universal substitute for colonoscopy.
authors: Anastasios Koulaouzidis; Ian Io Lei; Ramesh Pulendran Arasaradnam; Rami Eliakim

title: ColoACT: Multi-Cue Action Chunking for Smooth Autonomous Colon Navigation on a Self-Propelled Endoscopic Robot
abstract: Autonomous colonoscopic navigation can reduce operator burden and the risk of loop formation or tissue trauma, but remains challenging due to deformable anatomy, weak-texture and specular endoscopic visuals, and contact-rich viscoelastic interactions. Existing methods either rely on geometry-driven pipelines, which are efficient and interpretable yet brittle due to manually engineered features and switching logic, or adopt learning-based policies, whose inferred depth/geometry can become temporally inconsistent or overly smooth under weak texture and specular highlights while simulation-trained variants (e.g., deep reinforcement learning) may further suffer from a sim-to-real gap. We propose ColoACT, an autonomous navigation system that integrates an RGB-D-E based Action Chunking Transformer policy (ColoACT policy) for a compact self-propelled Bevel-Gear-Based Endoscopic Robot (BGER). The ColoACT policy augments RGB with estimated relative depth and a gradient-based pseudo-elevation map to enhance fold-ridge saliency and other high-frequency geometric cues, and enables smooth continuous control of the BGER by predicting overlapping action chunks and fusing them via temporal ensembling. In different \textit{ex-vivo} porcine colons (approximately 60 cm), our system achieves success rates of 85.4\% and 72.5\% in straight and curved segments, respectively, and achieves 70\% success in 90-degree turns and 60\% in double-bend sequences, with feasibility further demonstrated in challenging triple-bend segments. The project page is available at: https://Adamhu1.github.io/ColoACT/.
authors: Jian Hu; Shujing He; Leixin Chang; Zongze Li; Ding Huang; Chaoyang Shi; Chengzhi Hu

title: Image-enhanced autonomous navigation in intestinal robotics: a threshold-triggered approach combining dark-area localization and morphological contour guidance short title: enhancing visibility and navigation precision in confined spaces
abstract: on the triangular path. Highlight suppression increased the proportion of frames with normalized center error below 0.1 from 65% to 71%, below 0.2 from 95% to 97%, and below 0.3 from 98% to 100%. The adaptive mechanism decreased runtime by approximately 2% compared to continuous contour processing. Although this absolute reduction was modest, it recovered approximately 89% of the runtime difference between the contour-only and dark-area-only baselines. These phantom-based results support conditional perception allocation while keeping average processing time close to that of lightweight navigation.
authors: Shiwei Wang; Junying Yuan; Haoran Deng; Hanyu Deng; Xiuquan Yue; Tianshi Zhang; Shenjin Chen; Haishan Chen

title: StenoVLA-3D: 3D-Aware Reasoning VLA for Navigation Through Gastrointestinal Stenoses
abstract: Autonomous endoscopic navigation requires the policy model to predict actions from texture-poor monocular observations, make safe control decisions, and retain evidence of lesions after they leave the field of view. Existing vision-language-action (VLA) models primarily rely on visual appearance and short-term context, limiting geometric grounding and episode-level reporting. We introduce StenoVLA-3D, a 3D-aware VLA framework for navigating through stenotic regions. We integrate point-maps into the Cosmos-Reason 2 backbone through learned geometry-gated fusion, and also propose a temporal state branch to model traversal progress. Our reasoning-and-action backbone predicts grounded reasoning with actions, while dedicated heads estimate stenosis shape and generate the final lesion report. We further introduce EndoCausal, an episode-level dataset with lesion annotations, actions, and temporally grounded reasoning. On 40 held-out recorded test episodes, StenoVLA-3D reaches 95.2\% semantic accuracy and 83.4\% action accuracy. On the physical 3-DoF endoscope, it attains 88.9\% and 77.8\% task success in esophageal and colonic phantoms (36 trials each), substantially outperforming the evaluated baselines.
authors: Tamima Tabassum; Yiming Huang; Tianchun Wu; Changjing Liu; Zhiqing Tang; Chi Kit Ng; Beilei Cui; Liangjing Shao; Jiewen Lai; Hongliang Ren

title: Recurrent Bleeding Due to Ileal Angiodysplasia: Clinical Case
abstract: Small bowel bleeding is a rare clinical condition that remains difficult to diagnose and manage. Due to its recurrent nature and limited accessibility, identifying the bleeding source may require complementary diagnostic investigations [1,2]. This study aimed to present a challenging case of recurrent small bowel bleeding and highlight the role of repeated multimodal diagnostic evaluation. A literature review using the PubMed database and analysis of a clinical case were performed. We included English-language articles published in the last decade. A 72-year-old woman with recurrent severe anaemia and suspected gastrointestinal bleeding underwent repeated endoscopic, radiological, and surgical investigations. Capsule endoscopy and SPECT/CT indicated a possible bleeding site in the ileum, however, angiography and diagnostic laparotomy failed to identify the source. A loop ileostomy was created to facilitate further localization and endoscopic access in case of recurrent bleeding. When bleeding recurred, enteroscopy via the ileostomy identified a bleeding ileal angiodysplasia, and successful endoscopic haemostasis was achieved with clips. In conclusion, recurrent small bowel bleeding may remain undetected despite repeated diagnostic investigations. When clinical suspicion persists or bleeding recurs, repeated and multimodal evaluation is necessary [3,4]. In this case, enteroscopy through the ileostomy enabled identification and treatment of the previously unconfirmed bleeding source.
authors: Ąžuolas Rudnickas; Justė Daratytė; Justas Žilinskas

title: 5G succeeds (setting up CCE home delivery service) : pilot study of developing 5G connected CCE home delivery service
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cancer and the second leading cause of cancer-related mortality. The COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted endoscopy services, leading to prolonged waiting times and an increased risk of delayed CRC diagnoses. To address these issues, the 5G SUCCEEDS pilot study explored the feasibility of delivering Colon Capsule Endoscopy (CCE) directly to patients' homes using advanced 5G technology. This study aimed to determine if CCE could be effectively performed at home, thus eliminating the need for hospital visits. It also assessed patient acceptability of the home-based CCE service, compared its diagnostic efficiency to traditional colonoscopy and evaluated the carbon footprint of different diagnostic pathways. The study was conducted at University Hospital Coventry and Warwickshire, in collaboration with WM5G, NHS Arden& GEM CSU, and Corporate Health International UK. Patients referred from primary care with low to intermediate risk for CRC were invited to participate. A 5G-enabled CCE Smartbox was delivered to their homes, facilitating remote procedure management and communication. The study aimed to recruit 25 patients, and with enhanced connectivity, participants benefited from virtual assistance, real-time equipment monitoring, and faster identification of irregularities. The results indicated that home-based CCE is a feasible and effective alternative to traditional hospital-based procedures. The use of advanced technology improved patient satisfaction and supported a patient-centred approach to CRC diagnostics. This innovative method aligns with the NHS X digital strategy, offering a viable solution to reduce delays in CRC diagnosis while promoting more sustainable and efficient healthcare delivery.
authors: Gohar Jalayeri Nia

title: Efficient Monocular Depth Estimation on Embedded Systems with Neural Cellular Automata
abstract: Real-time monocular depth estimation is an essential task for autonomous drone navigation, yet existing models require hundreds of billions of floating-point operations per in-ference, rendering them impractical for deployment on resource-constrained embedded systems. On the MidAir aerial imagery dataset, a mean absolute error of 5.05 m is obtained with mea-sured CPU inference latency of 3.66 ms and 40,832 parameters—2.9–6.1× faster and 5.4–16.3× fewer parameters than com-parable lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) base-lines (FastDepth, MiniDepth, RT-MonoDepth-S, MiDaS-Lite). A depth-augmented semantic segmentation variant performs simultaneous depth estimation and semantic segmentation in a single forward pass with approximately 59,000 parameters, enabling holistic computer vision for autonomous flight. Diverse image and video processing tasks are supported by the same design, providing a practical foundation for efficient real-time computer vision in edge computing applications.
authors: Kurt Nunn; Tooraj Nikoubin

title: Changing Colorectal Cancer Epidemiology Demands a Risk-Adapted European Screening Strategy
abstract: European colorectal cancer screening remains largely age-defined despite changing epidemiology, heterogeneous risk, non-participation and finite colonoscopy capacity. European guidance already anticipates risk-based thresholds, intervals and test allocation; how to test these across heterogeneous health systems remains unresolved. We propose a four-decision policy and research framework, not a validated clinical protocol, addressing when screening should begin or recur, which first-line test should be offered, what result or risk trajectory should trigger escalation, and how diagnosis and treatment should be completed. Quantitative faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) should remain a principal population-based strategy and high-quality colonoscopy the confirmatory and therapeutic standard, while national programmes may differ. Previous quantitative FIT results, age, sex, family history, comorbidity and screening behaviour can be prospectively evaluated as modifiers of interval and threshold. Multitarget stool tests, blood-based cell-free DNA, microbiome or volatile-organic-compound classifiers, colon capsule endoscopy and CT colonography should address defined pathway failures rather than act as interchangeable competitors. Because evidence for risk adaptation remains modelled or observational, implementation should proceed only through prospectively governed pilots. Evaluation should prioritise sustained participation, advanced neoplasia removed, interval cancer, colonoscopy use, equity and societal cost. Risk adaptation should optimise existing workflows through prospectively validated programmatic rules, not unvetted diagnostic layers.
authors: Anastasios Koulaouzidis; Ramesh Pulendran Arasaradnam; Pablo Cortegoso Valdivia; George Koulaouzidis; Ervin Tóth; Wojciech M. Marlicz

title: A diagnostic cascade from cholecystitis to Meckel's diverticulum rupture: a case report.
abstract: Background: Meckel's diverticulum (MD) is the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract, yet it rarely becomes symptomatic in adults. Perforation is an uncommon and often overlooked complication that may mimic more frequent abdominal conditions, particularly in the postoperative setting. MD presenting shortly after unrelated laparoscopic surgery is exceptionally rare and can pose a significant diagnostic challenge. Case presentation: A 36-year-old woman presented with acute right upper quadrant pain and was diagnosed with calculous cholecystitis. She underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy and was discharged after an uncomplicated recovery. On postoperative day 3, she returned with abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, and persistent pain. Imaging revealed a port-site hematoma but no clear source of obstruction or leak. Due to sustained leukocytosis and clinical deterioration, diagnostic laparoscopy was performed, revealing bilious peritonitis and a necrotic, perforated MD with terminal ileal herniation. Diverticulectomy was completed, and the patient recovered fully. Discussion: Perforated MD can closely mimic postoperative ileus, small bowel obstruction, or biliary pathology, leading to delayed diagnosis. Imaging modalities frequently fail to detect this condition, underscoring the limitations of relying solely on radiologic evaluation when symptoms persist. Although a direct causal link to recent laparoscopic surgery cannot be confirmed, postoperative mechanical and perfusion-related changes may contribute to diverticular compromise in susceptible individuals. Conclusion: This case highlights the need to consider MD complications in patients who deteriorate unexpectedly after abdominal surgery. When clinical findings are discordant with imaging, early diagnostic laparoscopy remains essential for accurate diagnosis and timely intervention.
authors: Lotfollah Abedini; Taha Negahdari; Sepehr Moradi; Reza Hosseinpour

title: Improved diagnostic model for gastrointestinal disorders through novel masking and semantic segmentation
abstract: The integration of advanced computing techniques, such as computational intelligence, in disease classification and prediction through medical imaging has become a prominent practice within the field of computer vision. A critical aspect of this process is precise image segmentation, which helps identify and isolate relevant areas in medical images, thereby streamlining the analysis and enhancing the accuracy of predictions. Among various segmentation methods, semantic segmentation, which assigns class labels to each pixel, has proven particularly effective. In this study, we introduce the U+EfficientB0 Net model, specifically designed to segment gastro-intestinal images, including dyed-lifted polyps, polyps, and ulcerative colitis. The proposed work is different from traditional EffeicientNetB0 encoder as it utilizes Decoder-guided Adaptive Skip Refinement (DASR) module for feature refinement before combining the features obtained from encoder with the features obtained through decoder. Utilizing advanced computing techniques like computational intelligence for disease classification and prediction through medical imaging is a prominent practice in computer vision. Precise image segmentation is crucial as it identifies relevant areas, streamlining analysis, and bolstering prediction accuracy. Semantic segmentation, assigning class labels to each pixel, proves especially effective. This study introduces the (U+EfficientB0) Net model specialized in segmenting gastro-intestinal images, notably dyed-lifted-polyps, polyps and ulcerative colitis leveraging the Kvasir-Seg dataset for polyps and while corresponding masks for dyed-lifted polyps and ulcerative colitis are generated using pixel-based annotation approach. Trained on a thousand images supervised by medical experts, proposed model achieved remarkable accuracy (92.89%) and dice coefficient (80%). Additionally, the study presents a classification approach using DenseNet-121 that uses the predicted segmented images as input and its performance is compared with similar model’s using non-segmented image and achieved better results (Accuracy 99.63) over segmented images in earlier epochs.
authors: Rohit Srivastava; Manish Madhava Tripathi
venue: East African Journal of Science Technology and Innovation

title: Multidisciplinary Perspectives in Colorectal Polyps and Polyposis Syndromes : Integrating Pharmacotherapy, Laboratory Biomarkers, Diagnostic Imaging, Rehabilitation, and Genetic Profiling
abstract: Background: Colorectal polyps are common gastrointestinal lesions with heterogeneous histological, molecular, and malignant potential. Although many polyps are benign, adenomatous and serrated lesions may represent important precursors of colorectal cancer. Hereditary polyposis syndromes further increase cancer risk and require early recognition, genetic assessment, and structured surveillance. Aim: This review aimed to provide an integrated overview of colorectal polyps, focusing on their classification, etiology, epidemiology, pathophysiology, histopathology, clinical presentation, diagnostic evaluation, differential diagnosis, and contemporary management strategies. Methods: Relevant clinical and scientific literature addressing colorectal polyps and hereditary polyposis syndromes was reviewed. Evidence concerning genetic mechanisms, environmental risk factors, endoscopic and radiological diagnosis, histopathological classification, colonoscopic polypectomy, advanced endoscopic techniques, surgical interventions, and multidisciplinary management was synthesized. Results: Colorectal polyps comprise hyperplastic, inflammatory, hamartomatous, adenomatous, and serrated lesions with substantially different biological behaviors. Molecular abnormalities involving APC, KRAS, TP53, mismatch-repair genes, BRAF, STK11, SMAD4, MUTYH, and PTEN contribute to distinct hereditary and sporadic pathways. Colonoscopy remains central to diagnosis and treatment, allowing simultaneous detection, characterization, biopsy, and removal. Cold and hot snare polypectomy, endoscopic mucosal resection, and endoscopic submucosal dissection provide increasingly tailored approaches for different lesions. Surgical and transanal procedures are reserved for selected advanced, unresectable, malignant, or hereditary disease. Conclusion: Accurate characterization and complete management of colorectal polyps are essential for colorectal cancer prevention. Integration of endoscopy, pathology, laboratory and molecular testing, radiology, genetics, pharmacy, surgery, and rehabilitation supports individualized treatment and long-term surveillance.
