title: Prevalence of Pathological Lesions and Normal Variations in the Oral Mucosa among Geriatric Patients at the University Veracruzana
abstract: Objective: To determine the prevalence of pathological lesions and variants of normalcy in the oral mucosa among geriatric patients who visited the University of Veracruz. Materials and Methods: A descriptive study was conducted by analyzing clinical records of 34 patients treated in two groups of the Geriatric Dentistry Educational Experience during the period from August to December 2024; To evaluate the association between variables (age, presence of chronic degenerative diseases, and sex), Fisher's exact test was used, with a statistical significance level of p < 0.05. Results: 32.4% had at least one pathological lesion, and 85.3% had at least one variant of normal. No statistically significant association was identified between the variables and the presence of lesions and/or variants. Conclusions: The study characterized the oral lesions present in the geriatric population. The findings highlight the importance of a systematic intraoral examination in geriatric dentistry.
authors: Claudia Citlalli Yanez Cedillo; Claudia Olguín Yobal; Dra Mercedes Soledad Briceno Ancona; Jacinto Izquierdo Jacome
venue: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)

title: Development of software for use of dental mannequins in virtual environments or virtual reality and the metaverse
abstract: This research aims to present an interactive tool called OdontoSim 3D, which simulates dental procedures, providing an immersive educational experience, allowing risk-free practice for patients, and improving clinical skills. The use of detailed 3D models and features such as zoom and rotation enabled accurate analysis. The virtual system offers advantages over the use of physical mannequins, such as the elimination of clinical risks and cost reduction. The repetition of procedures and real-time interaction with three-dimensional models improved student learning. The software also showed scalability, allowing expansion to more complex procedures.
authors: Raissa Costa Silva; Nadja Maria da Silva Oliveira; Marcelo da Costa Borba

title: Tribology of dental materials: from laboratory metrics to clinical durability: review and translational roadmap
abstract: The functional integrity of dental restorations is known by their resilience within the dynamic and hostile tribological ecosystem of the oral cavity. Despite significant advancements in material science, the premature failure of restorations due to wear remains a critical clinical challenge, rooted in a persistent disconnect between controlled laboratory metrics and unpredictable clinical realities. This review provides a comprehensive critical appraisal of dental tribology, delineating the complex interplay of wear mechanisms, attrition, abrasion, erosion, and abfraction, and evaluating the spectrum of current assessment methodologies, from fundamental in vitro simulations to advanced clinical quantification. We identified the primary limitations hindering accurate material prediction, specifically the lack of protocol standardization, the inability to replicate synergistic degradation processes such as tribo-corrosion, and the exclusion of patient-specific variables. To bridge this translational gap, we proposed a strategic roadmap integrating multi-tiered testing standardization, finite element analysis, and machine learning to enhance predictive capabilities. Furthermore, we advocated for the development of clinically relevant in vitro models that incorporate patient-specific parameters, such as occlusal loading profiles and salivary properties. By shifting the paradigm from descriptive testing to predictive, patient-centric material science, this review outlined a transformative pathway for the development of next-generation restorative materials, ultimately optimizing clinical longevity and treatment outcomes.
authors: Naif H. Al-Qahtani; Shahad Alqahtani; Shorooq K. Almajhad; Amjaad M. Almarzoogi; Noha Taymour

title: An Efficient Out-of-Core Tomographic Imaging Framework for Edge Devices
abstract: Computed Tomography (CT) is an essential 3D imaging technology widely used in medical diagnostics and scientific research. However, performing CT imaging on edge devices is challenging due to limitations in computational power, memory capacity, and energy budget. This paper presents an efficient CT reconstruction framework, called edgeFBP, designed for Nvidia Jetson System-on-Chip (SoC) devices. edgeFBP adopts an end-to-end pipeline design for efficient out-of-core image reconstruction under tight power and memory constraints. edgeFBP utilizes a mixed-precision strategy leveraging half-precision Tensor Cores (TCs) to accelerate the bottleneck back-projection (BP) kernel. edgeFBP achieves a 1.83x speedup over the widely used RTK library on Jetson Nano and a 2.56x speedup on Jetson AGX. Under a strict 25-Watt power budget, edgeFBP on Jetson Nano achieves up to 5-48x higher energy efficiency than an Nvidia DGX A100, enabling datacenter-scale imaging on constrained edge devices.
authors: Xuetao Chen; Cong Ma; Xiangyu Meng; Du Wu; Zhengyang Bai; Tao Luo; Zhaorui Zhang; Emmanuel Jeannot; Edgar Josafat Martinez‐Noriega; Xun Wang; Peng Chen; Amelie Chi Zhou; Mohamed Wahib

title: Biodigital Transformation in Dentistry: From Diagnosis and Biological Preservation to Multidisciplinary Rehabilitation
abstract: Advances in digital technologies have expanded diagnostic and treatment possibilities in dentistry while making the preservation of biological tissues and collaboration among specialties increasingly important. This book, *Biodigital Transformation in Dentistry: From Diagnosis and Biological Preservation to Multidisciplinary Rehabilitation*, was prepared to address these developments from an integrated perspective. It follows a scientific progression from biodigital diagnosis and clinical decision-making to preventive care in pediatric dentistry; from the preservation of the pulp and natural dentition to periodontal and orthodontic treatment; and from digital prosthetic planning to implant-supported rehabilitation. Written by contributors from different dental specialties, the chapters examine both the clinical applications and the limitations of current technologies. We hope this book will serve as a valuable resource for dental students, residents, academics, and clinicians, and we thank all the authors for their knowledge, time, and contributions.
authors: Gizem Yazdan Özen; Nebiha Hilal Bilge; Feride Aktaş; Bekir Haseki; Yücel Aydemir; Nur Sima Eken; Kübra Aslantaş Akar; Sevgi Yaşar; Ceren Yeniay; Berk Kaya; Nedim Güneş; Ladise Ceylin Has; Mevlüt Furkan Sadeler; Ali Kağan Özen; Nesli Damla Deniz; Muhammed Mustafa Akar; Alptuğ Kendirci; Zehranur Kızıldağ

title: Digital twin technology in dentistry: Applications, challenges, and future perspectives in precision oral healthcare
abstract: Background Digital twin technology creates virtual replicas enabling real-time monitoring, simulation, and predictive analysis. Whilst extensively explored in medical disciplines, its integration in dentistry remains emerging. Complex anatomical structures, individualised treatment requirements, and precision demands position digital twin technology as promising for enhancing clinical outcomes and patient care. Aim This review examines current applications of digital twin technology in dentistry, identifies associated benefits and challenges, and explores future directions for research and practice. Method A comprehensive narrative review searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore for articles published between 2015 and 2026. Search terms included combinations of "digital twin", "virtual twin", "virtual patient model", "digital replica", "dentistry", "oral health", and related dental specialty terms, combined using Boolean operators. Articles focusing on digital twin applications, implementation strategies, technological frameworks, and clinical outcomes were included. Results Digital twin technology demonstrates diverse applications across orthodontics, prosthodontics, oral surgery, endodontics, and periodontics. Key applications include treatment planning, surgical simulation, prosthesis design, outcome prediction, and patient education. The technology integrates three-dimensional imaging, intraoral scanning, electronic health records, and biomechanical simulations to create comprehensive virtual representations. Where genuine bidirectional digital twin frameworks are implemented, benefits include enhanced precision, reduced treatment time, improved outcomes, and personalised care. However, challenges related to data integration, computational requirements, costs, and standardisation persist. Conclusion Digital twin technology holds substantial promise for advancing dental practice through improved treatment planning, enhanced precision, and personalised care. As technological infrastructure develops and integration challenges are addressed, applications are expected to expand significantly, transforming clinical workflows and elevating standards. However, the current evidence base remains largely preliminary, and large-scale clinical validation is needed before definitive conclusions can be drawn.
authors: David B. Olawade; Priscillia C. Fidelis; Olabanke Florence Olawuyi; Rosemary Olasilola; Babajide David Makanjuola; John Oluwatosin Alabi

title: Overview of Persistent Inter-Professional Rivalry Within the Laboratory Medicine Practice Domain of Tertiary Healthcare Institutions in Nigeria: A Narrative Review
abstract: The persistent inter-professional rivalry within the laboratory medicine practice domain of Nigerian tertiary healthcare institutions constitutes a systemic crisis that undermines diagnostic accuracy, jeopardizes patient safety, and disrupts healthcare delivery. This longstanding conflict between the Medical Laboratory Scientists (MLS) and the laboratory-based physicians (Clinical Pathologists) centers mainly on operational independence, leadership in clinical laboratories, and statutory boundaries. This review examines the historical, legal, educational, and socio-political causes of this rivalry in Nigerian tertiary healthcare settings. Historically, laboratory medicine practice functions shifted from physician-led to specialized, autonomous scientific roles, leading to overlapping claims over laboratory and clinical consultation domains. Conflicting laws—such as the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria (MDCN) Practitioners Act and the Medical Laboratory Science Council of Nigeria (MLSCN) Act—have created parallel regulatory frameworks, resulting in ongoing legal disputes at the National Industrial Court. These dynamics foster operational silos, strikes, and diagnostic errors, often causing preventable misdiagnoses. To transform this rivalry into collaborative clinical efforts, the article recommends a comprehensive approach that includes legislative reforms, separation of administrative and clinical roles, formal interprofessional education in training, and joint governance boards in tertiary healthcare settings. Ultimately, resolving this conflict is vital to achieving international standards and protecting Nigerian patient care from interprofessional conflicts.
authors: Collins Amadi; Roy Amadi; Sasha Amadi; Elena Amadi; Comfort John

title: Patients’ Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation in Dental Practice: A Cross-Sectional Study from Romania
abstract: Background/Objectives: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies into dental practice is reshaping clinical workflows, administrative processes, and, increasingly, the patient experience and the doctor–patient relationship. While prior research has documented the attitudes of clinicians and practice managers, the perspective of the patient remains comparatively underexplored. This study examined how dental patients perceive AI integration and digital tools across the dental care pathway, together with the associated implications for data security, cost, and the human dimension of care. Methods: A cross-sectional, questionnaire-based study was conducted among 200 dental patients in Bucharest, Romania, and the surrounding region. The instrument assessed perceived difficulty and availability regarding digital technology, current use of digital tools, demographic and educational characteristics (age, gender, practice environment, educational level), and two attitudinal dimensions, namely digital prudence and concern for technological sustainability, across five subdomains of the dental care pathway: scheduling, diagnosis, treatment planning, feedback, and follow-up (dispensarization). Responses were analyzed using non-parametric tests and exploratory principal component analysis with internal-consistency validation. Results: Patients expressed moderate-to-high interest in AI support during the diagnostic (median = 3.3, IQR = 2.7–3.9) and feedback (median = 3.11, IQR = 2.78–3.67) stages and the lowest interest in scheduling (median = 2.7, IQR = 2.0–3.3). A marked level of digital prudence was observed (median = 3.24, IQR = 2.82–3.61), reflecting concerns about data security, automation, and a possible weakening of the clinician–patient bond. Younger and academically educated patients reported lower perceived difficulty, higher availability, and greater current use of digital tools (all p ≤ 0.001); counterintuitively, the same patients scored significantly higher on digital prudence (Spearman’s ρ = −0.260, p < 0.001). Greater familiarity with digital tools was therefore accompanied by a more critical awareness of their informational risks rather than by uncritical acceptance. Conclusions: Dental patients approach AI through a dual lens of openness and informed caution, welcoming efficiency gains in the clinical and continuity-of-care stages while voicing measured concerns about data security, affordability, and the preservation of human contact. To interpret this profile, we propose two conceptual contributions: a mapping of patient needs onto Maslow’s hierarchy in the context of AI-mediated care and the Informational VUCA framework, which characterizes the volatility, uncertainty, complexity, and ambiguity that patients face when navigating AI-generated information. The findings point to a clear practical agenda of transparent communication, robust data governance, and education strategies adapted to patients’ educational and demographic profiles, so that AI-enhanced workflows strengthen rather than erode the doctor–patient relationship.
authors: Alin Flavius Cozmescu; Ana Cernega; Andreea Cristiana Didilescu; Marina Meleșcanu Imre; Cristian Funieru; Silviu-Mirel Pițuru

title: Perception of Special Needs Dentistry Amongst Allied Dental Professionals in Australia
abstract: OBJECTIVE: In Australia, Dental Therapists (DTs), Dental Hygienists (DHs) and Oral Health Therapists (OHTs) encounter Special Needs (SN) patients in their clinical practice. This study investigates their perception, training, working experience and referral patterns within Special Needs Dentistry (SND). MATERIALS AND METHODS: Paper-based questionnaire was distributed to a systematically selected sample of 1000 registered DHs, DTs and OHTs who were members of professional bodies in Australia. Respondents were included irrespective of age, gender, length of working experience and country of graduation. Data analysis consisted of Chi-squared regression analysis (p < 0.05) using IBM SPSS Windows Version 29.0 (Melbourne, Victoria, Australia). RESULTS: A response rate of 49.8% (215 DTs, 107 DHs and 163 OHTs) was obtained. A significantly larger proportion of OHTs (59.5%) was aware of SND as a specialty compared to DHs (45%) and DTs (41.9%) (p < 0.05) and hence OHTs referred to SND specialists more often than other groups. In addition, 73.6% of OHTs, 63.6% of DHs and 40% of DTs had both didactic and clinical training in SND (p < 0.05). All the categories stated lack of training and continuing professional development (CPD) in SND as the main reasons for not treating SN patients. They therefore expressed interest in attending related CPD training (OHTs: 90.2%, DHs: 88.8% and DTs: 88.3%). CONCLUSIONS: OHTs demonstrated greater awareness, training, working experience and referral in SND than DHs and DTs; however, training gaps across all groups highlight the need for strengthened undergraduate education and accessible CPD in SND. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Understanding the perception of allied dental professionals regarding SND is crucial for improving access to and the quality of care for patients with special needs. Prior research has highlighted gaps in training and confidence levels amongst general practitioners; however, little is known about the perspectives of allied professionals. This study provides valuable insights into their awareness, perceived roles and educational needs, emphasizing the importance of inclusive team-based care.
authors: Jessica Francis; Gelsomina L. Borromeo

title: Next-generation microneedle patches for transdermal therapeutics and diagnostics
abstract: Microneedle patches (MNPs) have emerged as versatile platforms for minimally invasive transdermal drug delivery, biosensing, and point-of-care diagnostics by transiently breaching the stratum corneum while minimizing pain and tissue damage. Recent advances in biomaterials, microfabrication, additive manufacturing, and bioelectronics have expanded MNP functionality beyond drug delivery to include controlled therapeutic release, interstitial fluid sampling, wearable biosensing, and closed-loop therapeutic systems. However, despite substantial technological progress, clinical translation remains constrained by challenges related to manufacturing scalability, device reproducibility, standardized characterization, quality assurance, regulatory approval, and commercialization. Unlike previous reviews that primarily emphasize microneedle classifications or material platforms, this review provides a critical translational perspective by integrating materials science, engineering, manufacturing, biosensing, and regulatory considerations into a unified framework. Major fabrication strategies, material platforms, and characterization methods are systematically compared with respect to mechanical performance, manufacturability, reproducibility, and clinical applicability. Current therapeutic and diagnostic applications are critically evaluated alongside the key barriers to industrial production and regulatory implementation. Emerging opportunities, including smart biosensing, stimuli-responsive materials, additive manufacturing, and closed-loop therapeutic systems, are also discussed. By highlighting the factors that govern technology readiness and clinical implementation, this review provides practical insights for accelerating the development and commercialization of next-generation microneedle platforms for drug delivery, biosensing, vaccination, and precision medicine.
authors: Tsung‐Hsien Chen; Ming‐Tse Hsu; Kun-Hua Lee; Riya Karmakar; Arvind Mukundan; Sangamithirai Sridharan Kuzhali; Chu‐Kuang Chou; Wen-Shou Lin; Hsiang‐Chen Wang

title: SurgiCLAW: An Interpretable Atomic-Skill Agent for Precision Robotic Micromanipulation
abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and vision--language--action models have provided robots with new capabilities for long-horizon task understanding and planning. In surgical robotics, however, end-to-end prediction of low-level actions remains limited by insufficient precision, opaque decisions, and scarce data. This paper presents SurgiCLAW, a hierarchical skill-based framework for precision surgical manipulation. SurgiCLAW confines an MLLM to intraoperative visual understanding, structured explanation, and atomic surgical-skill selection, while delegating physical execution to verifiable deterministic control programs. For brain--machine-interface implantation, a representative high-precision surgical task, we construct a state-to-skill invocation dataset and expand it through visual and state perturbations. The model first learns structured skill invocation through supervised fine-tuning and is then optimized using three rewards for action correctness, operation prerequisites, and format validity, improving action selection, operational safety, and output parseability. We evaluate subtask success, offline model comparison, real-robot performance, and ablations. On a fixed test set, SurgiCLAW achieves 94.6% skill-selection accuracy and 93.0% macro-averaged F1 (Macro-F1). Across 50 closed-loop real-robot implantation trials, it achieves an 88.0% task success rate.
authors: Angen Ye; junjie xie; Yujia Song; Junkai Huang; Dapeng Zhang

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AS A DECISION-SUPPORT TOOL FOR MATERIAL SELECTION IN PROSTHODONTICS: AN ANALYTICAL REVIEW OF THE LITERATURE
abstract: Background. The rapid development of digital dentistry and artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding the range of technologies available for diagnosis, treatment planning, prosthetic design, and outcome prediction. Material selection remains a clinically important component of prosthodontic treatment because the choice of restorative material must account for mechanical, functional, biological, and esthetic requirements. Aim. To analyze recent literature on the application of AI in prosthodontics, with particular attention to its potential role in supporting restorative material selection, integrating clinical and digital parameters, predicting prosthetic outcomes, and personalizing treatment planning. Materials and methods. A narrative analytical review was developed from literature published during seven completed calendar years (January 2019–December 2025). Relevant publications were identified in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and NCBI resources using combinations of terms related to artificial intelligence, machine learning, prosthodontics, dental materials, CAD/CAM, crowns, dental prostheses, occlusion, and treatment outcomes. Publications were thematically analyzed according to AI application, type of prosthodontic task, data source, clinical purpose, reported outcomes, and limitations. Results. The reviewed literature demonstrates that AI is increasingly applied in prosthodontic diagnostics, treatment planning, automated crown design, finish-line detection, occlusal assessment, prediction of prosthetic outcomes, and digital workflows. AI-assisted CAD systems have shown potential to improve design efficiency and, in selected studies, achieve clinically acceptable crown fit. However, the evidence remains heterogeneous with substantial differences in datasets, algorithms, validation procedures, and outcome measures. Direct evidence supporting independently validated AI systems for individualized restorative material selection remains limited. Current evidence therefore supports the use of AI primarily as a clinical decision-support tool rather than as an autonomous system for material selection. Conclusions. AI has considerable potential to support individualized material selection and prosthodontic treatment planning by integrating multiple clinical and digital parameters. At the same time, current evidence does not support treating AI as an autonomous replacement for professional clinical judgment. Direct validation of AI systems specifically designed to select restorative materials remains limited, and many predictive models require stronger external validation and prospective clinical evaluation. The most appropriate current framework is therefore a human-in-the-loop decision-support model in which AI augments, rather than replaces, clinical expertise
authors: Tetiana I. Dzetsiukh

title: DentalGEN: a large-scale controllable generative AI framework for automated dental crown restoration
abstract: Dental crown restoration addresses a global public health burden, yet is constrained by a slow, variable, and labor-intensive manual design process that limits access to high-quality treatment. Here we introduce DentalGEN, a large-scale controllable generative artificial intelligence framework for automated dental crown restoration. DentalGEN is the first framework capable of designing a patient-specific crown while simultaneously satisfying morphological, functional, and aesthetic criteria. Its core is a novel multi-view diffusion model that leverages explicit control mechanisms to incorporate clinical constraints directly within the generative process. This approach enables the integrated synthesis of view-consistent geometry and texture, achieving a level of precision and integration unattainable with prior automated methods. Evaluated on the largest reported multi-center dataset, DentalGEN’s designs achieved clinical scores statistically equivalent to those of human experts in blinded assessments, while outperforming state-of-the-art methods by 70% in Hausdorff Distance. Furthermore, a clinical proof-of-concept study demonstrated the feasibility of integrating DentalGEN into a supervised scan-design-manufacture paradigm, reducing active design time by over 90%. DentalGEN represents a crucial step in bridging the translational gap for generative AI in dental restoration, paving the way for more accessible, accurate, and efficient dental care.
authors: Jiamin Wu; Ying Liu; Yanning Chen; Yuqiang Zhang; Jiaying Gu; Yuan Liu; Mengxun Li; Wenping Wang; Yuanfei Fu; Zhiming Cui; James Kit Hon Tsoi; Dinggang G. Shen

title: The use of Artificial Intelligence in Dentistry: Applications, challenges, and future perspectives
abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence [AI] has enhanced contemporary dental practice by providing advanced tools for diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient management. Objective: This narrative review examines the current applications of AI in dentistry, evaluates its diagnostic efficacy, identifies challenges for clinical implementation, and discusses future perspectives. Methods: A narrative literature review was conducted by searching PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, SciELO, and LILACS for studies published between 2020 and 2026. Observational studies randomized clinical trials, systematic reviews, and methodological studies were included. DeCS/MeSH descriptors were combined using the Boolean operators AND and OR. Study selection was purposive, prioritizing recent publications with higher methodological quality and scientific relevance. Results: AI demonstrated high accuracy in detecting dental caries, periapical lesions, periodontal diseases, and other oral conditions. Applications span all dental specialties, including radiology, endodontics, orthodontics, periodontics, and oral and maxillofacial surgery. Despite these advancements, significant barriers persist, including ethical concerns regarding patient privacy, the need for rigorous clinical validation, and integration into existing clinical workflows. AI should be considered a complementary tool that enhances clinician capabilities rather than a substitute for clinical judgment. The future of dentistry will involve the integration of explainable AI systems, federated learning for data protection, and digital education for the dental workforce. Conclusion: AI holds transformative potential to improve access, quality, and efficiency in dental care, provided it is implemented with methodological rigor, continuous human oversight, and appropriate ethical considerations.
authors: Glayson Pereira Vitor

title: Effects of Dental Noise on Dentists’ Performance and Stress Responses: A Randomized Crossover Trial
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To investigate the effect of continuous noise generated during dental treatment on dentists' performance and stress responses. METHODS: This study involved a questionnaire survey and an experimental investigation. The questionnaire survey was conducted with 44 dentists to assess dental noise-related subjective burden and noise sources perceived as the most uncomfortable. In the experimental phase, a randomized crossover trial was performed with 11 participants under silent and noisy conditions. Work performance was evaluated using the total number of calculations (work volume) and error rates in the Uchida-Kraepelin test. Saliva samples were collected before, during, and after the test, and salivary alpha-amylase (sAA), chromogranin A (CgA), and secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) levels were measured to assess stress responses. RESULTS: In the questionnaire survey, clinical noise was perceived as uncomfortable by 93.2% of dentists, with the extraoral suction unit being identified as the most unpleasant device (equivalent continuous noise level: 91.7 ± 0.6 dBA). In the randomized crossover trial, work volume in the Uchida-Kraepelin test significantly decreased, and the error rates significantly increased, under the noisy condition. With respect to salivary stress markers, sAA levels were significantly higher under the noisy condition, and sIgA levels were significantly increased. By contrast, CgA levels did not significantly differ between the conditions. Furthermore, sAA levels were significantly correlated with work performance. CONCLUSIONS: Dental noise reduced dentists' performance and elicited stress responses. These findings highlight the need for noise mitigation and occupational stress management strategies in dental practice.
authors: Daisuke Kido; Sayaka Katagiri; Ayako Tanaka; Sachi Umemori; Koji Mizutani; Hiroshi Nitta

title: Clinical Reasoning: A 60-Year-Old Woman With Fever, Headache, Diplopia, and Unilateral Periorbital Swelling
abstract: Evaluating delayed vascular complications after a focal cranial infection can be diagnostically challenging. In this case, a 60-year-old woman with approximately 1 month of recurrent gingival swelling and pain later developed fever and headache, followed by horizontal diplopia and progressive unilateral periorbital swelling. Examination showed a left abduction deficit and conjunctival chemosis. Cerebral angiography obtained during evaluation demonstrated severe narrowing of the cavernous segment of the internal carotid artery. Although the patient improved clinically after antimicrobial therapy, routine follow-up imaging 1 year later revealed a new vascular lesion at the site of the prior arterial abnormality. This case highlights the importance of interval neurovascular follow-up imaging when cavernous internal carotid artery abnormalities are identified during the initial presentation of febrile ophthalmoplegia.
authors: Naijimiding Rexiati; Naijimiding Rexiati; Shihao Jiang; Aximujiang Axier; Nizhamidingjiang Rexiati; Nizhamidingjiang Rexiati; Riqing Su; Zengliang Wang; Pahaerding Balatiniyazi; Aisha Maimaitili

title: Terahertz Antenna Design for Biomedical Sensing and Imaging
abstract: Background/objectives: Research in terahertz (THz) frequency range has accelerated, bridging the gap between microwave and infrared technologies, in response to the increasing demand for quicker data transmission, improved image resolution, and effective biomedical diagnostics. The non-ionizing nature of the THz band makes it highly suitable for high-resolution imaging and noninvasive biomedical sensing. The choice of substrate, however, significantly impacts on THz antenna performance, affecting radiation efficiency, bandwidth, and biocompatibility. This study aims to construct and optimize microstrip patch antennas operating at 1 THz to determine which substrate is best suited for biological sensing and imaging applications. This study also aims to develop a comparative understanding of the impact of substrate dielectric characteristics on antenna performance and their suitability for integration into sixth-generation (6G)-enabled healthcare systems. Methods: CST Microwave Studio was used to model and simulate several THz microstrip patch antennas. A 50-Ω waveguide port was used to excite each antenna, and open boundary conditions were used to simulate free-space propagation. Several substrate materials, such as polyimide, FR4, Rogers RT/Duroid 5880, gallium arsenide (GaAs), and silicon arsenide (SiAs), were selected for comparative analysis of THz antenna performance. To assess return loss, gain, directivity, bandwidth, and radiation efficiency, frequency sweeps were conducted over 0.5–1.5 THz. Finding the substrate material with the best trade-offs between electrical and biological compatibility was the primary goal of the comparative investigation. Results: According to simulation data, polyimide and Rogers RT/Duroid 5880 substrates outperformed FR4, GaAs, and SiAs in terms of antenna performance. With gain values of approximately 5 dBi at 1 THz, these materials demonstrated improved radiation efficiency, a wider impedance bandwidth, and minimum return loss (<−30 dB). In on-body designs, polyimide offers additional benefits, such as flexibility, low dielectric loss, and consistent responsiveness, making it particularly suitable for wearable biomedical devices. The investigation confirmed that impedance matching and the overall radiation behavior are significantly influenced by the substrate’s dielectric constant and loss tangent. The findings indicate the promise of THz antennas for high-speed wireless communication, noninvasive diagnosis, and real-time biological sensing in healthcare settings. Conclusions: This study offers a methodical comparison of THz patch antennas made of various substrate materials for biomedical imaging and sensing. According to the results, polyimide and Rogers RT/Duroid 5880 are the most effective substrates because they provide the best possible balance of biocompatibility, wide bandwidth, and high gain. The integration of these materials into future implantable and wearable medical systems based on THz shows excellent promise. For 6G communication-enabled healthcare networks and next-generation biomedical equipment, the study advances the creation of high-performance antennas. Future work includes exploring flexible and miniature antenna topologies, experimental validation of the proposed designs, and evaluating real-time performance in biological environments.
authors: Mandeep Singh; Simranjit Singh; Simarpreet Kaur

title: Internal Validation of a YOLOv8 Model for Classifying Temporomandibular Joint Disc Displacement With Versus Without Reduction on Open‐Mouth Proton‐Density‐Weighted MRI
abstract: BACKGROUND: The temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disc plays an important role in maintaining normal joint function. However, disc displacement is a common condition that can lead to pain, restricted jaw movement and chronic TMJ dysfunction. OBJECTIVE: To develop and evaluate a deep learning model capable of autonomously localizing the TMJ region from magnetic resonance (MR) images during mouth opening using the You Only Look Once (YOLO) v8 framework, and to discriminate between TMJ disc displacement with reduction (DDwR) and disc displacement without reduction (DDwoR). METHODS: This study included 237 patients (48 males, 189 females; age range, 19-83 [mean, 44.73 ± 18.3] years) who underwent MRI examination at our hospital for suspected TMJ disorders and were diagnosed with disc displacement based on imaging findings. After exclusion, 439 proton density-weighted MR images during mouth opening were preprocessed and divided on a patient basis into training (280 images), validation (71 images) and test (88 images) datasets. The TMJ region was manually annotated using LabelImg, including the condyles, articular disc and articular tubercle. The YOLOv8 deep learning model was trained for 200 epochs to localize the TMJ region and classify DDwR or DDwoR. RESULTS: The YOLOv8 model achieved promising results for the detection and classification of TMJ disc displacements. The performance metrics were a precision, recall and F1 score of 0.983, 0.988 and 0.987, respectively, indicating a high accuracy in detecting and identifying disc displacement patterns. CONCLUSION: The YOLOv8 deep learning model demonstrated promising performance in automatically localizing and classifying TMJ disc displacement from MR images.
authors: Kotaro Ito; Hirotaka Muraoka; Satoshi Tokunaga; Kohei Otsuka; Tomohiro Komatsu; Yuta Kohinata; Shoya Hirohata

title: Transoral robotic surgery in otorhinolaryngology: patient perspectives and determinants of outcomes
abstract: A retrospective study in the North of the Netherlands Simple SummaryTransoral Robotic Surgery (TORS) is increasingly used for various conditions, yet its success and failure remain underexplored.In this multicenter study, we assessed 220 TORS interventions across 211 patients.Success criteria differed by condition, including tumor identification for CUP, resection margins for malignancies, and symptom improvement for benign cases like OSA and chronic lingual tonsillitis.Predictors of success varied, with factors such as patient comorbidity, tumor characteristics, and demographics playing roles.Conversely, failure predictors encompassed postoperative complications and pain, linked to patient health and demographics.These insights into TORS outcomes may aid in patient selection and counseling across different conditions, informing clinical practice and enhancing patient care.
authors: Alexandra G. L. Toppenberg

title: Digital planning and static guided surgery in a limited prosthetic space: a clinical case report
abstract: Dimensional reduction of the alveolar ridge after tooth extraction in the posterior mandible may limit available bone volume and prosthetic space, increasing the risk of improper implant positioning. Digital technologies (CBCT, intraoral scanning, virtual planning, and guided surgery) have enhanced three-dimensional control of the procedure and reduced clinical subjectivity. Objective: To report a clinical case in which digital planning and static guided surgery improved the predictability of a single-tooth rehabilitation in a posterior region with limited bone availability. Case report: A 51-year-old female patient with a root fracture and mobility of tooth 36 underwent extraction. After 12 months, a new CBCT scan and intraoral scan were obtained and superimposed for reverse planning and fabrication of a 3D-printed surgical guide. A 3.75 × 8.5 mm implant was placed using a guided protocol, with an insertion torque of 60 Ncm and an initial ISQ of 75. After five months, the ISQ increased to 80; an intraoral scan with a scan body was performed, and a zirconia crown cemented on a TiBase was fabricated and delivered without the need for occlusal adjustment. Results: Progressive implant stability was observed throughout clinical follow-up, with a functional definitive restoration and no reported complications. Conclusions: This case suggests that integrating digital planning with static guided surgery may support accurate three-dimensional implant positioning and increase the predictability of single-tooth rehabilitations in posterior regions with limited bone availability.
authors: Beatriz Cristina DE PAULO; Leandro César da Silva SIMÕES; Tatiana Cursino Pereira; Diana Pereira CUNHA; Guilherme de Siqueira Ferreira Anzaloni Saavedra

title: The Nano-Dental Complex: Clinical Breakthroughs, Structural Advancements and Global Horizons in Nanodentistry
abstract: Background: Nanobiotechnology is rapidly transforming modern healthcare, with its integration into dentistry opening novel pathways for advanced clinical outcomes.This review provides a comprehensive overview of the practical applications of the nano-dental complex (nanodentistry) and explores how recent innovations are revolutionizing oral healthcare.Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted across major electronic databases, including PubMed, Google Scholar, and Scopus, alongside official health repositories such as the World Health Organization (WHO), to synthesize recent data on nanotechnology in dental science.Results: Nanodentistry leverages nanomaterials, nanorobotics, and molecular engineering to optimize the diagnosis, management, and prevention of oral pathologies.The descriptive analysis categorizes these advancements across diverse dental specialties, including orthodontics, preventive dentistry, prosthodontics, restorative dentistry, periodontics, and oral surgery.Additionally, the evolution of dental restoration technologies through nanomaterial integration is detailed.Conclusion: While nanodentistry holds immense potential to enhance treatment planning, patient care, and regulatory frameworks in healthcare, widespread adoption faces significant hurdles.High production costs and limited accessibility remain primary barriers, particularly in resource-constrained regions.This review maps the historical trajectory, current clinical landscape, and future horizons of nanotechnology to guide subsequent research and development in oral healthcare.
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: Comparing Diagnostic Ability of Two Off-the-Shelf Large Language Models with That of Endodontists for Teeth Requiring Initial Root Canal Treatment: A Multicenter Retrospective Investigation
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Despite growing interest in large language models (LLMs) for endodontic diagnosis, prior studies have used simulated cases, examination formats, or small selected series. This multicenter retrospective study compared the diagnostic accuracy of ChatGPT-5.2 and Gemini 3.0 with that of calibrated endodontists across 645 teeth requiring initial root canal treatment. METHODS: Cases were evaluated across four endpoints: pulpal diagnosis, periapical diagnosis, treatment planning, and case difficulty. Standardized clinical summaries and radiographs were submitted to endodontists and both LLMs using a fixed single-pass protocol. Exact-match accuracy, Cohen's κ, Gwet's AC1, macro-averaged F1 score, McNemar tests, and generalized estimating equations were used for statistical comparison. RESULTS: Endpoint accuracies ranged from 74% to 88%. Macro F1 was highest for periapical diagnosis (ChatGPT-5.2, 0.724; Gemini 3.0, 0.719) and lowest for treatment planning (0.385; 0.550), where both models showed lower observed performance in minority categories, interpreted as suggestive given small subgroup sizes. Composite accuracy across the three clinical endpoints was 61.1% (95% CI, 57.4%-64.8%) and 59.4% (95% CI, 55.3%-63.3%), and four-endpoint accuracy was 47.3% (95% CI, 43.3%-51.2%) and 46.2% (95% CI, 42.3%-49.8%), indicating at least one clinically relevant error in about half of cases. Treatment planning was the only endpoint differing between models after Holm-Bonferroni correction, favoring Gemini 3.0 (OR, 1.457; adjusted p = .003). CONCLUSIONS: Both models performed acceptably on individual endpoints and common presentations, but performance was endpoint-specific and substantially reduced on integrated assessment and low-prevalence categories. These findings support use of LLMs in endodontic diagnosis and treatment planning as adjunctive tools, but not without expert supervision.
authors: Mahmoud Torabinejad; Patricia A. Tordik; Mona Alenezi; Masoud Parirokh A; Omid Dianat; Mohammad Reza Foroughi; Zegar Zegar; Udochukwu E. Oyoyo

title: Prospects for respiratory training with immersive technologies and biofeedback in patients of outpatient dental practice
abstract: This study evaluates the effectiveness of structured respiratory training using virtual reality (VR) and biofeedback for reducing psychophysiological tension in patients of outpatient dental practice. Thirty-four patients were enrolled in this pilot randomised study and allocated to a main group (training with VR and biofeedback, n=17) and a comparison group (n=17). In the main group, breathing awareness increased from 35.8±7.5 to 41.4±9.0 points (p=0.052 by the sign test and p=0.011 by the Wilcoxon signed-rank test) and relaxation self-efficacy increased from 4.8±3.6 to 7.0±3.5 points (p=0.043 by the sign test and p=0.006 by the Wilcoxon signed-rank test). Between-group comparison of changes showed a statistically significant advantage of VR-assisted training for the gain in breathing awareness (p=0.038 by the Mann–Whitney U-test); no between-group difference was found for relaxation self-efficacy (p=0.092). The findings suggest that a single session of respiratory training with immersive technologies and biofeedback promotes the development of breathing self-regulation skills. Given the sample size, the single-session design and the use of non-validated scales, these data are preliminary and require confirmation in larger studies assessing anxiety, autonomic measures and treatment adherence.
authors: И.Р. Ганжа; Nikolay V. Popov; A.A. Blazhnova; Alexander Vladimirovich Zakharov; Igor V. Shirolapov; Elena Khivintseva

title: Accuracy of Free-Hand Versus Various Computer-Assisted Techniques in Dental Implant Surgery: a Systematic Review

authors: Reina Fayad; Julius Maminskas; Dalius Sakavičius; Dainius Razukevičius; Povilas Daugėla

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Quadrant-Level Treatment-Site Estimation for Patient Safety
abstract: Introduction and aims Safety interventions in dentistry, including checklists, have been reported; however, it remains difficult to demonstrate sufficient effectiveness in preventing treatment site misidentification, including wrong tooth extraction. This study aimed to establish a foundation for an artificial intelligence (AI)-based patient-safety measure by developing a system that estimates the dental treatment site at the quadrant level from images captured during dental procedures. Methods Single-frame still images (n = 2,446; training 1,780, validation 445, test 221) were extracted from clinical videos recorded during treatment performed by a single dentist between 27 July 2022 and 21 December 2023. Treatment-site estimation models were developed using VGG16, a convolutional neural network-based image-classification model, and YOLOv9, an object-detection model. Performance was compared using three metrics: quadrant accuracy (correct upper/lower and left/right), vertical accuracy (correct upper/lower only), and lateral accuracy (correct left/right only). Results Among five approaches (four VGG16 conditions and one YOLOv9 condition), YOLOv9 achieved the highest performance across all metrics, with quadrant accuracy of 88.7%, vertical accuracy of 96.8%, and lateral accuracy of 91.9%. For VGG16-based approaches, performance across these metrics varied according to image pre-processing. Conclusion This system may support detection and prevention of quadrant-level errors, which are reported to be the second most common type of wrong tooth extraction following adjacent-tooth errors. Clinical relevance AI-based treatment-site estimation may provide an additional preventive safety layer in dentistry by supporting clinicians’ judgement and enabling detection of quadrant-level site misidentification during dental procedures.
authors: Shintaro Nishimoto; Shintaro Oka; Kazunori Nozaki; Harumi Kitamura; Kyota Nakamura; Kazue Nakajima; Mikako Hayashi

title: Role of Generative AI in Personalized Smile Design: A Clinical Evaluation of Esthetic Outcomes
abstract: Background Digital Smile Design (DSD) has become an important component of contemporary esthetic dentistry because it permits visualization of proposed dental changes before irreversible treatment. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may further enhance this process by rapidly producing individualized smile simulations. However, the esthetic value of AI-generated designs compared with conventional clinician-designed and clinician-refined designs remains incompletely established. Aim To evaluate the esthetic acceptability of generative-AI-assisted personalized smile designs and compare conventional Digital Smile Design, AI-generated smile design, and clinician-refined AI-assisted smile design. Materials and Methods A prospective comparative study was designed involving 60 adult participants seeking esthetic dental treatment. Standardized facial and intraoral photographs were obtained. Three smile-design conditions were produced: conventional clinician-generated DSD, AI-generated DSD, and AI-generated DSD subsequently refined by an experienced clinician. Patients and dental professionals independently evaluated the designs using a 10-point visual analogue scale (VAS), satisfaction assessment, and paired-preference testing. Objective digital parameters and design-generation time were also recorded. Repeated-measures data were analyzed using the Friedman test with pairwise comparisons. Results Illustrative simulated results: Mean patient VAS scores were 7.39 ± 0.64 for conventional DSD, 7.74 ± 0.76 for AI-generated DSD, and 8.37 ± 0.71 for AI-refined DSD. The overall difference was statistically significant (Friedman test, P < 0.001). Professional ratings were 7.89 ± 0.68, 7.35 ± 0.77, and 8.64 ± 0.76, respectively (P < 0.001). Mean design times were 62.4 ± 11.6, 24.8 ± 6.4, and 35.6 ± 7.8 minutes, respectively. Conclusion The illustrative findings suggest that generative AI may improve smile-design efficiency, while clinician refinement may further improve esthetic acceptance. The findings support an AI-assisted rather than AI-replacement model of personalized smile design. Actual patient data must replace the simulated dataset before scientific submission.
authors: Anand Awadhesh Tripathi; Anandadevi Chinnasamy; Dr. Vritti Aggarwal; Dr. Sunny Sharma; Dr. Nalumino Sayela; Imran Iqbal Patel

title: Transoral Robotic Surgery in the Treatment of Head and Neck Cancer: Application and Prospect
abstract: Transoral robotic surgery (TORS) has reshaped the surgical management of head and neck neoplasms since its introduction in the mid-2000s, offering a minimally invasive transoral route to lesions of the oropharynx, larynx, hypopharynx, and nasopharynx. This narrative review synthesizes the technical foundations, current clinical evidence, and emerging directions of TORS, with explicit attention to study rigor and evidentiary hierarchy. Powered by the da Vinci platform, TORS provides magnified three-dimensional visualization and wristed instrumentation that enable en bloc resection with reduced external morbidity, shorter hospitalization, and the potential to spare or de-intensify adjuvant radiotherapy in selected human papillomavirus (HPV)-driven oropharyngeal cancers. For early-stage oropharyngeal disease, local control rates of 90–95% and disease-specific survival above 90% are consistently reported, and recent systematic reviews and large multicenter cohorts, including the international Recurrent Tumors of the Upper Aerodigestive Tract (RECUT) experience, confirm durable oncologic and functional outcomes in both primary and salvage settings, although randomized trials have yielded nuanced, sometimes divergent quality-of-life results. We appraise outcomes by anatomical subsite, the de-escalation trial landscape, complications and their mitigation, learning-curve dynamics, health economics, and the rapidly evolving integration of artificial intelligence in segmentation, augmented-reality navigation, intraoperative margin assessment, and outcome prediction. Recent evidence confirms that TORS is a valuable but expertise-dependent option whose benefit is greatest in carefully selected patients managed within multidisciplinary, high-volume pathways. We conclude by defining the principal unresolved questions and the evidence required to position TORS appropriately within contemporary multidisciplinary care.
authors: Qiang Huang; Chi‐Yao Hsueh; Jian Biao Zhou; Chengzhi Xu; Lei Tao

title: Association between socioeconomic status and dental caries in adolescents – a systematic review of cohort studies
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Early adolescence is a critical period for caries initiation, underlining the need for updated knowledge on effective caries indicators. This systematic review of cohort studies aimed to assess the association between socioeconomic status (SES), involving a wide range of indicators, and dental caries in adolescents aged 12-19. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Four databases (MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science) were systematically searched for relevant publications from January 1, 2000, through December 5, 2025. SES and SES proxy indicators were parental education, income, and occupation, and adolescents' school type, their social capital, and immigrant background. Composite SES indicators combined the aforementioned variables. The risk of bias was evaluated using a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. RESULTS: Studies (n = 21) from 11 countries across five continents were included, covering approximately 66,000 adolescents. An inverse relationship was documented between caries and mothers' education (six of seven studies), fathers' education (three of four studies), and parental income (three of six studies). School type (three studies), social capital (two studies), immigrant background (four studies), and composite SES indicators (five of six studies) were also linked to caries. However, the effect measures and definitions of exposures and outcomes were not consistent. CONCLUSIONS: An inverse association was observed between maternal education and caries, while corresponding associations with fathers' education and parental income were weaker and less consistent. This type of association was also observed for adolescents' school types, their social capital, and composite SES indicators. Immigrant background served as a caries predictor. However, the substantial heterogeneity in the included studies did not allow for meta-analyses and limited definite conclusions. The findings underscore the need to develop and validate robust composite SES measures applicable across diverse global contexts.
authors: Marit Slåttelid Skeie; Kristin Solveig Klock; Göran Dahllöf; Hedda Høvik; Ida Sofie Karlsen Sletten; Tone Natland Fagerhaug; Abhijit Sen

title: From algorithm performance to clinical value in AI-assisted skin cancer diagnostics
abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) has demonstrated high diagnostic performance in skin cancer detection and is increasingly being integrated into clinical workflows. However, whether these advances translate into meaningful patient-relevant and healthcare system outcomes remains unclear. Evidence on value-oriented outcomes has not been systematically synthesized. Methods We conducted a PRISMA-ScR–guided scoping review of studies published between January 2015 and October 2025 identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science. Studies evaluating AI-based technologies for skin cancer diagnosis, triage, risk stratification, or management were included if they reported outcomes beyond technical performance metrics. Reported outcomes were mapped to three value-oriented domains: clinical and prognostic, process and experiential, and system-level and economic outcomes. Results Of 4,021 records identified, 33 studies met the inclusion criteria, whereas 389 publications were excluded because they reported only technical performance metrics without value-oriented outcomes. Reported outcomes were predominantly process and experiential (28/33 studies), including diagnostic confidence, workflow efficiency, and user acceptance. Clinical and prognostic outcomes were reported in only five studies, with four studies focussing on prognostic utility and one study focussing on patient management, while system-level and economic outcomes were identified in three studies. Most evaluations were conducted in controlled experimental settings, whereas prospective real-world implementation studies were less common. Overall, the available evidence predominantly focused on process-level benefits, with limited evidence for clinical and prognostic or system-level and economic outcomes. Discussion Current evaluation strategies for AI-based skin cancer diagnostics remain predominantly performance-oriented and are largely focused on process and experiential outcomes. From a value-based healthcare perspective, current evidence remains largely confined to intermediate stages of the diagnostic value chain: although AI-assisted systems may improve diagnostic workflows, clinician confidence, and clinical decision making, few studies have evaluated their impact on downstream patient-relevant clinical and prognostic, or system-level and economic outcomes. Future research should prioritize prospective real-world studies, outcome-driven evaluation frameworks, and economic assessments that examine the impact of AI-supported decision-making on clinical outcomes and healthcare systems. Conclusion Despite promising effects on diagnostic processes, evidence for the clinical and system-level value of AI-based skin cancer diagnostics remains limited. Outcome-driven evaluation frameworks are needed to bridge the gap between algorithmic performance and meaningful healthcare impact.
authors: Lennart Ocker; Elisabeth Livingstone; Georg Christian Lodde; Eggert Stockfleth; Nessr Abu Rached; Dirk Schadendorf; Stephan Nüesch

title: CHALLENGES AND MEDICAL-SOCIAL RATIONALE FOR DENTAL CARE IN THE CONTEXT OF SOCIO-ECONOMIC TRANSFORMATIONS IN UKRAINE
abstract: Introduction. The article analyzes problematic aspects of the organization of dental care for the population of Ukraine in the context of socio-economic transformations. Medical and social approaches to improving the accessibility and effectiveness of dental care are substantiated, taking into account the current challenges facing the healthcare system.Aim. The aim of the study is to substantiate the medical and social aspects of the organization of dental care in Ukraine in the context of socio-economic transformations, identify systemic gaps in financing mechanisms and access to services within the framework of the Medical Guarantees Program, and determine strategic directions for optimizing the sector through the integration of dental prevention into the primary health care system.Materials and methods. To achieve the stated aim, a comprehensive approach was applied using the following methods: bibliographic-semantic and analytical methods, system analysis, and comparative analysis.Results. Dental care in Ukraine operates under a mixed model with limited public coverage, which, for adults, is largely limited to emergency interventions, while children and eligible groups are provided with a broader range of services. Insufficient funding, regional inequalities in access, and fragmentation of the system were identified. The integration of dentistry into primary health care remains limited, and the preventive role of family physicians is only partially implemented, reducing the effectiveness of early detection and population-level prevention.Conclusions. The role of family physicians in the provision of dental care remains only partially implemented due to insufficient training, a lack of integrated clinical protocols, limited financial incentives for preventive activities, and fragmentation of the healthcare system. Improving the effectiveness of dental care requires expanding NHSU service packages, integrating dental prevention into primary health care, enhancing the training of family physicians, and implementing interdisciplinary collaboration.
authors: Viktor Y. Yelenskyi

title: Artificial intelligence in orthodontics: clinical maturity, evidence gaps, and emerging applications—a narrative review
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming orthodontics by enhancing diagnostic accuracy, supporting clinical decision-making, and facilitating digital workflows. This narrative review provides a comprehensive overview of current AI technologies and their applications in orthodontics, including diagnostic imaging, treatment planning, treatment monitoring, patient communication, education, and emerging generative AI tools. The available evidence indicates that automated cephalometric landmark detection and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) segmentation have among the most advanced technical and external-validation evidence bases in orthodontic AI, whereas digital-model analysis has demonstrated high technical performance but more limited independent validation. However, no application met the predefined criteria for higher clinical maturity because prospective clinical effectiveness remained insufficiently established. Other emerging or experimental applications include AI-assisted treatment planning, remote monitoring, large language models (LLMs), and robotic systems, for which evidence remains predominantly retrospective, technical, feasibility-based, or early clinical. However, much of the current evidence is derived from retrospective studies, technical validation investigations, and proof-of-concept reports, with limited prospective clinical data demonstrating improvements in treatment quality, efficiency, or long-term patient outcomes. Important challenges remain regarding data quality, algorithmic bias, external validation, explainability, patient privacy, and regulatory oversight. Overall, AI should currently be regarded as a clinician-supervised decision-support tool rather than a replacement for professional expertise. Future progress is likely to depend on robust prospective clinical trials, transparent reporting, and responsible integration of AI into evidence-based orthodontic practice and the broader digital transformation of dentistry.
authors: Kanza Ahmed Chandio; Laiba Iftikhar; Anum Shehzad; Ifrah Rao; Minahil Waseem; Muhammad Anas; Muhammad Farrukh; Ammar Al Shalabi; Sameh Talaat; Sinan Şen; Fatma E. A. Hassanein; Tarek M. Elshazly

title: Periodontal Phenotype and Soft Tissue Management in Multidisciplinary Treatments
abstract: In contemporary dentistry, achieving successful, aesthetic, and sustainable treatment outcomes relies heavily on the accurate analysis of soft tissue dynamics and the periodontal phenotype by clinicians. This book chapter comprehensively examines the strategic role of periodontal phenotype and soft tissue management at the intersection of various dental disciplines, including orthodontics, implantology, and prosthodontics. Within the scope of the study, the historical evolution of the periodontal phenotype concept is first addressed, defining its position in modern dental practice. Subsequently, current clinical evaluation and diagnostic methods are detailed to ensure precise treatment planning. The core body of the chapter optimizes the most critical components of multidisciplinary approaches: maintaining tissue stability before and after tooth movement in orthodontic-periodontal relationships, enhancing long-term implant success through peri-implant soft tissue management and phenotype modification techniques in implantology, and preserving gingival health by ensuring the biological compatibility of restorative margins at the prosthetic interface. The final section provides comprehensive decision trees to guide clinicians swiftly in daily practice and discusses future horizons in the field. Consecutively, this study offers an evidence-based framework aimed at preventing tissue recession, optimizing aesthetics, and achieving biologically compatible, predictable results in complex multidisciplinary cases.
authors: Mevlüt Furkan Sadeler

title: The Diagnostic Frontier of Artificial Intelligence in Orthodontics: Accuracy, Clinical Pitfalls, and Interdisciplinary Boundaries in Complex Malocclusions. A narrative review
abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into orthodontic practice marks a paradigm shift from a purely analogue or traditional "occlusion-driven" specialty to an objective, "face-driven," data-dense medical discipline.Encompassing machine learning (ML), artificial neural networks (ANNs), and deep learning (DL), these technologies have transitioned from theoretical laboratory frameworks into clinically validated diagnostics.Bibliometric analyses reveal that nearly 83% of the existing peer-reviewed literature on orthodontic AI has emerged since 2021, focusing heavily on automated cephalometric landmarking and three-dimensional (3D) automated segmentation.[1,8] Though AI-driven architectures optimize routine tasks, shorten processing times, and enhances the diagnostic reproducibility, a critical performance gap persists regarding absolute geometric accuracy in severe skeletal deformities, non-linear growth forecasting, and material behaviour predictions [8,9].This narrative review considers recent high-impact literature from 2024 to evaluate the mechanical limitations, structural blind spots, and systemic pitfalls of automated tools, advocating for an ethically sound, semi-automated orthodontic workflow.
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: Automated Localization and Identification of Recurrent (Secondary) Caries Around Dental Restorations Using a Hybrid CNN–Vision Transformer Framework with Grad-CAM Explainability
abstract: Recurrent caries, also termed secondary caries, is a carious lesion that develops at the margin of an existing dental restoration and is widely reported as the leading cause of restoration failure and re-treatment. Diagnosing recurrent caries from two-dimensional radiographs is difficult because restorative materials such as amalgam, composite resin, and cast metal produce radiopaque or radiolucent artifacts that overlap, mask, or mimic the radiographic appearance of a carious lesion, and because inter-observer agreement among clinicians for this task is known to be inconsistent. Most existing deep-learning studies on dental caries treat the problem as an imagelevel or tooth-level classification task, which reports whether caries is present but does not explain where the lesion lies relative to the restoration margin. This paper proposes an end-to-end, restoration-aware deep learning framework that reframes recurrent-caries diagnosis as a localization-first problem rather than a classification-only problem. The proposed pipeline is organized into six stages: radiographic pre-processing (contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization and denoising), automatic restoration localization using a one-stage object detector, peri-restoration lesion segmentation using an attention-gated U-Net, feature extraction and classification using a hybrid convolutional neural network–Vision Transformer (CNN–ViT) encoder, a recurrent-caries decision head, and a Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) explainability layer that visually justifies each prediction. Seventeen governing mathematical formulations, covering pre-processing, segmentation losses, attention computation, classification losses, the Grad-CAM formulation, and evaluation metrics, are presented to make the framework fully reproducible. A literature review of twenty representative studies is used to position the proposed framework against existing caries-detection, restorationsegmentation, and explainable-AI approaches, and a comparative summary of previously reported performance figures is provided as a benchmark reference. This work is presented as a proposed framework rather than a completed clinical trial, no fabricated experimental outcomes are reported; instead, a rigorous evaluation protocol, including dataset design, crossvalidation strategy, and expected-metric templates, is defined so that the framework can be trained and validated on institutional or public bitewing, periapical, and panoramic radiograph datasets. The principal contribution of this work is the shift from image-level caries classification toward automated restoration localization coupled with pixel-level lesion segmentation and visually interpretable decision support, which is intended to narrow the gap between algorithmic output and clinical usability in restorative and cariology practice.
authors: Dr Anushree Raj; Dr Lokesh C K; Dr Pallavi M O; K. Annapoorneshwari Shetty; Anusha N
venue: European Journal of Prosthodontics and Restorative Dentistry

title: Digital Impressions and Virtual Patient Applications in Prosthodontics
abstract: Digital impressions and virtual patient technologies have become integral components of prosthodontic workflows linking clinical data acquisition, diagnosis, treatment planning, and restoration fabrication. This chapter aims to evaluate the technical foundations, clinical applications, accuracy, and limitations of intraoral scanning and virtual patient technologies in the context of the current literature. The optical principles of intraoral scanners, three-dimensional data acquisition, and file formats such as STL, PLY, and OBJ are outlined. Accuracy, trueness, and precision are distinguished, and the effects of scanning extent, scanning strategy, operator experience, preparation geometry, moisture control, and implant scan body characteristics on impression outcomes are considered. Indication-dependent applications of digital impressions in tooth-supported fixed restorations, implant-supported prostheses, and removable prosthodontics are compared with conventional techniques. Virtual patient construction is examined through the integration of intraoral scans, three-dimensional facial scans, cone-beam computed tomography, digital photographs, and mandibular motion records. Data registration, virtual articulators, digital facebows, and the transition from static three-dimensional models to dynamic four-dimensional representations are discussed. Although digital workflows may facilitate data exchange, visualization, and patient communication, full-arch and completely edentulous cases remain challenging because of recording accuracy, soft-tissue dynamics, interoperability, and costs. The potential of artificial intelligence-assisted design and individualized planning is considered alongside limitations in the available clinical evidence. Overall, digital impressions and virtual patient technologies should not be regarded as universal replacements for conventional procedures. Instead, they represent complementary tools whose use should be guided by clinical indication, required accuracy, patient-specific conditions, and available resources. The chapter emphasizes that technical feasibility alone does not establish clinical superiority and that careful validation is needed before emerging dynamic and artificial intelligence-based approaches are routinely implemented.
authors: Nesli Damla Deniz

title: Advances in hydrogels with biomimetic mechanical properties for dental and periodontal tissue engineering and organoid applications
abstract: Mechanically biomimetic hydrogels have emerged as promising extracellular matrix-mimicking platforms for dental and periodontal tissue engineering because of their capacity to reproduce the mechanical, structural, and biochemical characteristics of native tissue microenvironments. By providing controllable matrix stiffness, viscoelasticity, stress relaxation, fluid shear stress, and three-dimensional topographical cues, these materials can regulate stem cell fate, coordinate epithelial–mesenchymal interactions, guide tissue morphogenesis, and promote the functional maturation and mineralization of regenerating tissues. This review summarizes recent advances in the design and application of mechanically biomimetic hydrogels for the regeneration of dentin–pulp complexes, tooth germs, periodontal ligament, alveolar bone, and other craniofacial tissues, with particular emphasis on their emerging applications in dental and periodontal organoid engineering. Key material and design parameters, including biomimetic mineralization, mechanical tunability, three-dimensional architectural organization, and dynamic crosslinking, are systematically discussed. The mechanotransductive mechanisms by which hydrogel-derived cues regulate odontogenic, osteogenic, and periodontal differentiation are further examined. In addition, advanced fabrication strategies, including microfluidics, photocrosslinking, three-dimensional bioprinting, and decellularized extracellular matrix-based composites, are reviewed in relation to multicellular organization, vascular network formation, and reconstruction of tissue-specific interfaces. Despite substantial progress, challenges remain, including the attenuation of mechanical signals during long-term culture, insufficient spatiotemporal control of multicellular organization, limited vascularization and innervation, and discrepancies between engineered mineralized tissues and native dental hard tissues. Future developments in intelligent mechanoresponsive hydrogels, high-resolution developmental mechanobiological atlases, organoid-based multiscale validation systems, and automated biomanufacturing may facilitate the transition from empirical tissue repair toward mechanically programmed dental and periodontal regeneration.
authors: Wenting Lu; Sucheol Shin; Ao Zheng; Shuaiting Wu; Jinling Liu; Zhuoyuan Li; Xiao Wang; Lingyan Cao

title: Proposal and elucidation of a novel coding classification for maxillary impacted canines from an orthodontic perspective
abstract: Objectives: Impacted maxillary canines are a challenge in the field of orthodontics, which requires an accurate diagnosis and treatment approach. Various factors are considered in determining the complexity of the treatment, which are patient age, position of the impacted tooth, presence of any dental malocclusion, and the presence of teeth surrounding the impacted tooth. This paper will seek to offer a new classification of maxillary impacted canines based on a number of diagnostic factors. Material and Methods: This system was created from the retrospective study of maxillary canine cases with the help of diagnostic parameters synthesized from existing literature with the objective of integrating ten diagnostic parameters such as age, mesiodistal space, positional relationship, angular relationship, root structure, and buccopalatinal position, among others, with values attributed to each variable using a color-coded system for better applicability. This would help overcome the limitations of single-factor assessments. Results: The proposed system of classification allows for a comprehensive approach in determining the complexity of MIC. This allows orthodontists to evaluate the severity of impaction, approximate the time required in treatment, as well as the approach to be taken. This is because it takes various diagnostic elements into account. Conclusion: This novel classification system offers a structured, multidimensional approach for organizing the diagnostic features of MIC. By integrating multiple parameters, it provides a standardized framework that may support clinicians in assessing case complexity and planning orthodontic management. Further studies are required to validate its diagnostic performance and its potential impact on clinical outcomes.
authors: Mohammad Khursheed Alam; Suliman Alsaeed; Kiran Kumar Ganji; Mohammad Younis Hajeer; Huda M. Abutayyem; Afnan Alayyash; Hande Uzunçıbuk; Gabriele Cervino; Maria Maddalena Marrapodi; Giuseppe Minervini

title: A tongue-controlled FES-robotic exoskeleton restores hand function in users with cervical spinal cord injury
abstract: Abstract Hand exoskeletons and functional electrical stimulation (FES) have shown promise in restoring hand function after stroke or cervical spinal cord injury. However, major challenges remain in providing reliable user command input in individuals with severe paralysis and in enabling safe and effective control of hand closing and opening. Here, we present a non-invasive tongue-based control strategy for a hybrid soft hand exoskeleton system combining tongue-controlled independent tendon-driven flexion of five fingers with tongue-triggered FES-induced finger extension. This user-intent-driven hybrid approach supports multiple activities of daily living, such as grasping a bottle or toothbrush, and enables hand opening while mitigating muscle fatigue and reducing system complexity. The system was evaluated in five users with cervical spinal cord injury, demonstrating high task success rates in daily living tasks and user preference due to its wearability and ease of use, as well as consistently low reported levels of discomfort, pain, and fatigue. These findings show that the proposed hybrid system can restore activities of daily living in individuals with cervical tetraplegia, including those with long-term injuries.
authors: Oğuzhan Kırtaş; Petrus H. Veltink; Rasmus Leck Kæseler; Alexander L. Ammitzbøll; Ellen Merete Hagen; Mostafa Mohammadi; Lotte N. S. Andreasen Struijk

title: Beyond Behavioral Observation: Digital Biomarkers and Precision Sedation for Non-Verbal Dental Patients: Narrative Review
abstract: Behavioral assessment scales are widely used to evaluate dental anxiety in clinical practice; however, they have important limitations because they rely on subjective interpretation and may not accurately identify anxiety in non-verbal dental patients, including individuals with developmental disabilities and anxious pediatric patients with limited communication abilities. Recent advances in objective physiological monitoring and digital technologies offer promising alternatives for individualized anxiety assessment and precision sedation in this vulnerable population. This review examines whether objective digital biomarkers can overcome the limitations of behavioral assessment in non-verbal dental patients and how close these technologies are to clinical application in precision sedation. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on physiological biomarkers, including heart rate variability, electrodermal activity, pupillometry and respiratory variability, as well as computer vision, multimodal biosensing and closed-loop monitoring systems. We retrieved relevant literature from PubMed, Scopus and Google Scholar, prioritizing studies published from 2019 onward. Current evidence indicates that objective physiological biomarkers, computer vision and multimodal wearable biosensing provide complementary information for anxiety assessment in non-verbal dental patients. Integrating these digital biomarkers with artificial intelligence enables individualized monitoring and establishes the foundation for precision, closed-loop sedation; however, further clinical validation and standardization remain necessary. No single technique is sufficient on its own; rather, a multimodal, patient-specific approach is needed to improve the accuracy and safety of anxiety management in special care dentistry, particularly in populations for whom conventional behavioral observation is limited or unreliable.
authors: Raquel Del Giudice; Yohana Rodriguez-Perez; Arlen Blanco-Rodriguez; Lucia Argüello-Lacayo; Alyssa Alvarez-Campa

title: Eye-in-hand vision based PID control of a Dobot Magician with online homography calibration for precision manipulation
abstract: This study evaluates a vision-guided robotic pick-and-place system integrating an eye-in-hand camera with a proportional integral derivative (PID) controller and an adaptive online homography calibration algorithm. To mitigate environmental disturbances, the framework utilizes hue, saturation, and value (HSV)-based object detection and a RANSAC-refined homography method that continuously updates the mapping between image pixels and the robot workspace. The system’s precision was tested under varying lighting conditions by comparing a non-PID baseline against the PID-integrated framework using mean execution time, standard deviation (SD), and t-tests.
