title: EXPRESS: Detection of Mycoplasma species and respiratory pathogens in cats with rhinitis and healthy cats
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To investigate the prevalence of Mycoplasma spp. in cats with rhinitis compared to healthy cats and to evaluate factors associated with detection. METHODS: A total of 46 cats with rhinitis and 37 asymptomatic controls were prospectively enrolled. Nasal swabs were collected, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays for Mycoplasma spp., Mycoplasma felis, feline herpesvirus (FHV), feline calicivirus (FCV), Bordetella bronchiseptica (B. bronchiseptica) and Chlamydia spp. were performed. All Mycoplasma spp.-positive samples underwent sequencing for species identification. RESULTS: PCR analysis revealed a significantly higher prevalence of Mycoplasma spp. in cats with rhinitis compared to healthy controls (28.3% vs 5.4%; p = 0.037). Mycoplasma felis was detected in 21.7% of rhinitis cases but in none of the controls (p = 0.017).FHV was significantly more prevalent in cats with rhinitis (39.1% vs 8.1%; p = 0.027). In addition, detection of FHV was significantly associated with detection of Mycoplasma spp. and M. felis within the rhinitis group. FCV (17.4% vs 5.4%; p = 0.352) and Chlamydia spp. (4.3% vs 0%; p = 0.481) did not differ between groups. B. bronchiseptica was not detected in either group. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: The findings support an association between Mycoplasma detection, particularly M. felis, and feline rhinitis, suggesting clinical relevance of these organisms in feline upper respiratory tract disease. The observed association between Mycoplasma detection and FHV suggests potential viral-bacterial interactions in the pathogenesis of feline upper respiratory tract disease.
authors: Julia Deveci; Katharina Kerner; Elisabeth Müller; Yury Zablotski; Bianka S. Schulz
venue: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery

title: Physiotherapy for Urinary Incontinence After Radical Prostatectomy: Current Evidence and Therapeutic Challenges
abstract: Urinary incontinence remains one of the most frequent and distressing complications after radical prostatectomy and can substantially affect quality of life. Physiotherapy, particularly pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT), is widely used as part of conservative postoperative management; however, substantial variation exists in patient populations, surgical and perioperative factors, intervention protocols, timing of initiation, adjunctive modalities, outcome definitions, and follow-up. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on pelvic floor rehabilitation after radical prostatectomy, focusing on prehabilitation, PFMT, biofeedback, electrical stimulation, neuromodulation, and emerging modalities such as transfer energy capacitive and resistive (TECAR) therapy. PFMT is the most widely studied conservative physiotherapy intervention and may accelerate early recovery of continence in some patients, although its effects on longer-term continence rates are less certain. The role of biofeedback and electrical stimulation remains unclear because of heterogeneous protocols and inconsistent outcome reporting. Evidence for neuromodulation is limited and should be interpreted according to the specific intervention and study population. TECAR therapy currently lacks direct clinical evidence supporting its efficacy in post-prostatectomy urinary incontinence. Across the literature, differences in continence definitions, intervention content and dose, baseline symptom severity, surgical techniques, timing of treatment, and follow-up complicate direct comparison and may confound observed improvements because spontaneous recovery is common after surgery. Current evidence supports PFMT as a reasonable core component of conservative management after radical prostatectomy, particularly for accelerating early continence recovery, whereas long-term superiority and the added value of adjunctive modalities remain uncertain.
authors: Izabela Mastej-Stawarska; Edyta Łuszczki; Maciej Tomasz Kochman

title: Towards Robust Prehensile Manipulation in Open-Ended Environments
abstract: We propose to use Quality-Diversity (QD) algorithms to solve robotic prehensile manipulation tasks in open-ended environments. Our approach enables the efficient discovery of a wide range robust grasp configurations, which serve as reliable starting points for generating diverse prehensile manipulation trajectories on articulated objects. The resulting diversity in manipulation behaviors enhances generalization and adaptability, enabling effective deployment continuously evolving open-world settings.
authors: Mathilde Kappel; Mahdi Khoramshahi; Louis Annabi; Faïz Ben Amar; Stéphane Doncieux

title: SLAMSqueezeBench: Comparing SLAM Systems under Resource Constraints
abstract: Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is one of the services running on an autonomous robot. It is typically run to assist other tasks such as planning, manipulation, etc. All these tasks are run on edge hardware and are subject to severe resource constraints. However, most SLAM systems are built and tested in isolation, and their performance is reported as if they are the only task running on a system. We observe that existing benchmarks lack a common mechanism for comparing SLAM systems under realistic resource constraints. To address this limitation, we have developed SLAMSqueezeBench, a framework that allows testing of SLAM systems under realistic workloads on edge hardware. It does so by imposing constraints on compute and memory resources available for the SLAM system during execution. It also simulates realistic camera frame acquisition with frame drops when a finite buffer is full. Using SLAMSqueezeBench, we compare nine SLAM systems spanning classical systems, learning-based systems, and approaches for Gaussian splatting. Our testing framework will be available for use by the community upon publication.
authors: Mohamed Muslim Hefny; Karthik Dantu; Steven Y. Ko

title: Tendon-Driven Continuum Robot with Modular Stiffness and In-Situ Self Pose Estimation
abstract: Continuum robots enable smooth shape morphing and safe interaction in confined environments. However, most existing systems are task-specific and depend on external sensing infrastructure, limiting their adaptability and real-world deployment. This paper presents a self-contained modular continuum robotic platform that combines mechanical reconfigurability with onboard pose estimation. The robot is constructed from interchangeable continuum joints with analytically precomputed stiffness, allowing rapid assembly and direct programming of the robot shape. Proprioceptive sensing is achieved using magnetic sensors and a modular learning-based framework, where a single model is trained per joint and reused across configurations. The system is experimentally validated in real world, demonstrating self-sensing capabilities and adaptation without external tracking.
authors: Guo Ning Sue; Sue; Junzhe Hu; Junzhe Hu; David Quinn; Tiancheng Wu; Zackory Erickson; Carmel Majidi

title: Magnetic based In-situ Self 3D Pose Estimation for a Modular Soft Tendon-Driven Continuum Robot via IMU-Fusion
abstract: Continuum robots are well suited for gentle manipulation because of their inherent compliance and ability to adapt to complex environments. However, their continuously deformable structure makes accurate configuration estimation challenging, particularly when external vision systems are unavailable or obstructed. In this work, we present an embedded pose sensing framework that combines inertial measurement units (IMUs) and active magnetic fields to estimate the robot configuration without relying on external cameras. The angular measurements from the IMU and magnetic-field references are fused to improve local orientation estimation and reduce accumulated orientation error during operation. This pose sensing scheme achieves an update rate of 16.7~Hz, allowing real-time feedback. The proposed system is experimentally validated through closed-loop control, where the estimated robot configuration is used to maintain the end-effector at a desired position while interacting with an object. These results demonstrate the potential of distributed magnetic--inertial sensing for real-time pose estimation and closed-loop control of continuum robots.
authors: Sue; Guo Ning Sue; Xiangyun Bu; David Quinn; Junzhe Hu; Carmel Majidi

title: Reorienting TMS treatments for fear memories and posttraumatic stress disorder. The emerging potential of the anterior prefrontal cortex.
abstract: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterized by re-experiencing trauma through vivid and involuntary intrusions, avoidance of cues that could trigger traumatic memories, and alterations in mood and cognition. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) offers a promising approach to modulating activity and functional coupling within neural circuits underlying these processes. To date, TMS studies in fear-conditioning research and PTSD have mainly focused on dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and ventromedial (vmPFC)-connected or broader medial-prefrontal (mPFC) targets, yielding encouraging but heterogeneous effects on posttraumatic symptoms. In parallel, emerging evidence has implicated the anterior prefrontal cortex (aPFC; Brodmann area 10) in threat- and trauma-related processes, including memory retrieval, higher-order control of defensive responding, adaptive strategy selection, and resilience. Whereas the dlPFC and vmPFC have been incorporated into mechanistic models of fear regulation, the aPFC has received limited attention in theoretical frameworks of fear and PTSD. Here, we review TMS studies organized around dlPFC, vmPFC-connected or mPFC, and aPFC neuroanatomical targets, integrating evidence from experimental and clinical research. Based on the hierarchical model of prefrontal organization, we argue that these regions represent potential TMS targets or circuit nodes, but likely act on partially distinct mechanisms. The vmPFC appears primarily involved in early automatic downregulation of defensive responses; the dlPFC may support cognitive control strategies such as reappraisal; and the aPFC may enable a supraordinate influence over higher-order representations and avoidance-related circuitry, as well as flexible selection of emotion-regulation strategies. We conclude that integrating the aPFC into this framework may guide next-generation, mechanistically-informed TMS treatments for PTSD.
authors: Alba Chiara La Pastina; Eugenio Manassero; Benedetto Sacchetti

title: From Oscillations to Brain States: Real-Time EEG-TMS for Adaptive Neuromodulation.
abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) enables non-invasive, focal modulation of cortical circuits by inducing electric currents in the brain through electromagnetic induction, thereby influencing neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity. High inter- and intra-individual variability has led, however, to moderate efficacy and reproducibility of stimulation and treatment protocols, motivating a shift toward brain-state-dependent stimulation. Over the past decade, real-time phase-triggered EEG-TMS has established the oscillatory phase-particularly focusing on the sensorimotor mu rhythm-as a key determinant of cortical excitability and plasticity modulation. The field, however, remains largely confined to univariate, sensor-space analyses of local mu-rhythm phase, missing large-scale network dynamics. Recent advances in online EEG source reconstruction and multivariate machine and deep learning (ML/DL) approaches have begun to move beyond local phase toward whole-brain, network-level state estimation, achieving encouraging preliminary accuracies in predicting trial-by-trial cortical excitability, with promising applications in network-dysregulation conditions such as chronic pain. Integrating source-space reconstruction and individual biological variability, and adaptive ML/DL pipelines into closed-loop frameworks promises to move beyond generic stimulation protocols toward selective, network-targeted neuromodulation tailored to the individual's dynamic brain state. Against this background, this review provides a critical overview of current achievements and limitations, while highlighting emerging methodological directions toward fully brain-state-adaptive and network-targeted EEG-TMS. We further present an illustrative use case of adaptive EEG-TMS for pain modulation, where treatment responses remain heterogeneous and the relevant dynamics are distributed across networks, and which therefore stands to gain most from individualized, network-targeted protocols.
authors: Melissa Null; Elena Mongiardini; Chiara Leu; Giulia Liberati; Paolo Belardinelli

title: A transdiagnostic framework for neurological intervention in maladaptive repetitive behaviors.
abstract: From daily rituals to pathological patterns of behavior and thought, a wide spectrum of habitual behaviors emerges through repeated reinforcement learning and becomes embedded in cortico-basal ganglia circuits. Once established, these behaviors operate automatically and resist conscious control. This review summarizes neurological intervention strategies for correcting pathological habits (e.g., addiction, obsessive-compulsive disorder) and restoring adaptive behavioral patterns. Pharmacological approaches target the plasticity of habit circuits via modulation of dopamine, serotonin, and glutamate systems. Non-invasive brain stimulation techniques-such as repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), and deep TMS-can modulate cortical control networks and indirectly influence connected subcortical circuitry. Behavioral interventions include extinction learning, reinforcement of alternative actions, contextual modification, cognitive strategies, and memory reconsolidation-based techniques. Recently, hybrid approaches combining AI-based digital therapeutics (DTx) with neuromodulatory devices have gained attention. Invasive techniques such as optogenetics and deep brain stimulation (DBS) enable direct modulation of specific neural circuits, allowing suppression of habitual responses or facilitation of alternative learning. Beyond clinical applications, these approaches elucidate the neural mechanisms underlying habitual behavior. Modulation of habits is most effective when employing multi-level, combinatorial interventions rather than a single technique. Integrating these strategies, this paper proposes a staged framework-habit circuit suppression → alternative learning → consolidation → sustained management-and a neuroscience-based, personalized model for behavioral treatment with implications for future clinical and research applications.
authors: Se Jin Jeon; Darine Froy Mabunga; Chan Young Shin

title: A first realization of reinforcement learning-based closed-loop EEG-TMS.
abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a powerful tool to investigate neurophysiology of the human brain and treat brain disorders. Traditionally, therapeutic TMS has been applied in a one-size-fits-all approach, disregarding inter- and intraindividual differences. Brain state-dependent EEG-TMS, such as coupling TMS with a pre-specified phase of the sensorimotor μ-rhythm, enables the induction of differential neuroplastic effects depending on the targeted phase. But this approach is still user-dependent as it requires defining an a-priori target phase. Here, we present a first realization of a machine-learning-based, closed-loop real-time EEG-TMS setup to identify user-independently the individual μ-rhythm phase associated with high- vs. low-corticospinal excitability states. We applied EEG-TMS to 25 participants targeting the supplementary motor area- primary motor cortex network and used a reinforcement learning algorithm to identify the μ- rhythm phase associated with high- vs. low corticospinal excitability. We employed linear mixed effects models and Bayesian analysis to assess effects of reinforced learning on corticospinal excitability indexed by motor evoked potential amplitude, and functional connectivity indexed by the imaginary part of resting-state EEG coherence. Our results show that reinforcement learning identified the μ-rhythm phase associated with high- vs. low-excitability states, and their repetitive stimulation resulted in long-term increases vs. decreases in functional connectivity in the stimulated sensorimotor network. Our work demonstrated the feasibility of a reinforcement learning-based adaptive closed-loop EEG-TMS approach in a full experimental cohort, enabling user-independent identification of μ-rhythm phases associated with corticospinal excitability states.
authors: Dania Humaidan; Jiahua Xu; Jing Chen; Christoph Zrenner; David Emanuel Vetter; Laura Marzetti; Paolo Belardinelli; Timo Roine; Risto J Ilmoniemi; Gian Luca Romani; Ulf Ziemann

title: Brief Trains of Closed-loop TMS Induce Controllable Power in FM-theta Oscillations
abstract:
Objective

Frontal-midline theta (FM-theta; 4–8 Hz) oscillations are thought to support cognition. Brief trains of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can probe these oscillations with high temporal precision but have rarely changed theta power. One possible reason is that prior studies ignored the instantaneous phase of the oscillation, which strongly shapes the cortical response to TMS. We tested whether brief TMS trains triggered at specific FM-theta phases in real time directionally modulate post-train FM-theta power.

Approach

Six healthy adults received TMS over dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (Fz) with concurrent electroencephalography during a whole-report working memory task. A beamformer and real-time phase-estimation pipeline triggered four-pulse 6 Hz trains (110% of resting motor threshold) at FM-theta peaks (0°) or troughs (180°), randomized trial by trial. Post-train spectral power was decomposed into total, induced (non-phase-locked) and evoked (phase-locked) components.

Main results

Trough-triggered trains transiently increased post-train FM-theta power relative to peak-triggered trains; task performance did not differ. Cluster-based permutation tests showed trough−peak differences in total (4.6–7.1 Hz) and induced (5.0–7.8 Hz) power ∼50–440 ms after the train, suggesting amplification of the oscillation . No evoked effect was detected. The total-power effect was robust at the subject level (Cohen’s dz = 1.32, p = 0.023). Within-train theta power did not differ between conditions, suggesting a cortical origin.

Significance

To our knowledge, this is the first study to lock brief rhythmic TMS trains to the real-time phase of an ongoing oscillation, and to show phase-dependent modulation of FM-theta power after individual trains on timescales relevant to behavior. Open-loop brief-train protocols may have missed such effects by mixing facilitatory and suppressive phases. Phase-locked brief trains offer a precise tool for testing the causal role of oscillations in cognition.
authors: Erickson B, Kim B, Degenhart A, Stenroos M, Rich R, Medaglia J.

title: Causal evidence for the role of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in the implementation of cognitive control adjustments
abstract: Cognitive control processes enable us to use recent contextual information to flexibly adapt to current task demands. This ability to adapt control processes is exhibited in response conflict tasks. In these tasks, participants must respond to a relevant piece of information while overcoming the tendency to respond to task-irrelevant information that cues an automatic or habitual response. Control demands can be updated in these tasks via two separate routes. Both errors and conflict between task-irrelevant and task-relevant information affect performance on subsequent trials. A body of work has implicated dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) in implementing these control adjustments. However, this work has primarily relied on correlational techniques or focused on a single index of control adaptation. Here, we combine inhibitory transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over DLPFC with computational modeling of behavior to test the causal role of DLPFC in control adaptation. We show that inhibitory TMS to DLPFC reduces the effect of previous trial conflict, and committing an error on the previous trial further reduces adaptive effects. This result provides causal evidence for DLPFC playing a general role in implementing trial-to-trial control adjustments.

title: PSYCHIATRY The Case for Starting Over
abstract: AbstractPsychiatry is the only branch of medicine that still diagnoses without reference to the organ it treats. Psychiatry: The Case for Starting Over argues that this is a structural failure rather than a temporary gap. The descriptive nosology inherited from Kraepelin and formalized in the DSM achieved diagnostic reliability at the cost of validity. Its categories were assembled by committee consensus rather than grounded in mechanism, and so it cannot guide the circuit-targeted therapies now reshaping the field.The book traces this problem historically and then builds an alternative from three converging lines of work. The first is computational neural-network modeling of psychopathology, from Hopfield and Hinton through Hoffman's simulations of schizophrenia and the author's own work. The second is systems neuroscience, including large-scale networks, global workspace and integrated information theories, attractor dynamics, and small-world connectivity. The third is Friston's Free Energy Principle and predictive processing.From this synthesis the book introduces Neuroanalysis and its clinical instrument, Clinical Brain Profiling (CBP). CBP treats mental disorders as disturbances of dynamic brain-network organization and organizes them across four timescales of plasticity:•Cognizance plasticity (milliseconds) is centered on the central executive network and linked to psychosis and negative signs.•Reactive plasticity (minutes to hours) is centered on the salience network and linked to anxiety.•Adaptive plasticity (days to weeks) sits at the salience–default mode interface and is linked to depression and mania.•Developmental plasticity (lifetime) is centered on the default mode network and linked to personality disorder patterns.The book reviews the neuromodulation toolkit: ECT, DBS, TMS, tDCS/tACS, psychedelic-assisted therapy, and focused ultrasound. It then proposes an entity-matched "grammar of plasticity" for selecting, combining, and sequencing these interventions. Guiding principles include strengthening prefrontal regulation before driving motivation, opening plasticity windows before directing them, and continuous biomarker monitoring.Throughout, the author separates established science from theoretical proposal and untested hypothesis. He outlines what validation would require: prospective outcome trials, clinically feasible network measures, and a cultural shift from single-label diagnosis to multidimensional profiling. The result is a case for rebuilding psychiatry as a measurement-based, mechanism-guided clinical neuroscience.
authors: Peled A.

title: Perturbational signature of the somato-cognitive action network in human primary motor cortex
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Functional-MRI evidence recently identified inter-effector regions in the primary motor cortex that show preferential connectivity with the action mode network (AMN), constituting the somato-cognitive action network (SCAN). Direct causal evidence for the functional engagement of these regions remains limited. AIM: Here, we investigated the perturbational neural response of one inter-effector region using transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG). METHODS: Sixteen healthy participants underwent recording of transcranial evoked potentials from the first dorsal interosseus, tibialis anterior, and the inter-effector region between them, which was identified with TMS motor mapping. RESULTS: Differences between conditions were assessed using cluster-based permutation testing and general linear modeling. Inter-effector-specific TMS-EEG activity was observed at approximately 42 ms post-stimulation, partially involving regions of the AMN. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION: Our findings provide the first perturbational characterization of inter-effector regions in human M1 and identify TMS-EEG markers that enable probing of SCAN functional organization.
authors: Marco Mancuso; Davide Maccarrone; Giulia Ruocco; Angelo Collura; Stefano Pellegrini; Danny Adrian Spampinato; Daniele Belvisi; Alfredo Berardelli; Antonella Conte; Giorgio Leodori

The field, however, remains largely confined to univariate, sensor-space analyses of local mu-rhythm phase, missing large-scale network dynamics. Integrating source-space reconstruction and individual biological variability, and adaptive ML/DL pipelines into closed-loop frameworks promises to move beyond generic stimulation protocols toward selective, network-targeted neuromodulation tailored to the individual's dynamic brain state. Against this background, this review provides a critical overview of current achievements and limitations, while highlighting emerging methodological directions toward fully brain-state-adaptive and network-targeted EEG-TMS. We further present an illustrative use case of adaptive EEG-TMS for pain modulation, where treatment responses remain heterogeneous and the relevant dynamics are distributed across networks, and which therefore stands to gain most from individualized, network-targeted protocols.
authors: Melissa Null; Elena Mongiardini; Chiara Leu; Giulia Liberati; Paolo Belardinelli

title: TMS timed to interictal epileptiform discharges
abstract: Abstract Interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs) are pathological hypersynchronous bursts of electrical brain activity that occur between seizures in patients with epilepsy. IEDs are caused by transient brain states that are difficult to predict, making them a challenging neurophysiological and technological case for brain-state-dependent stimulation. Administering stimulation at IED onset may provide insight into the epileptic network and optimize neurostimulation therapies. Here, we assessed the feasibility of IED-triggered transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) in two children with self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (SeLECTS), a common pediatric epilepsy in which IEDs emerge from the motor cortex. A convolutional neural network (CNN) was trained on the participants’ pre-recorded electroencephalography (EEG) data with IEDs annotated by an epileptologist. The CNN was integrated into an EEG-processing pipeline that classified EEG segments as “IED” or “non-IED” in real time. With this pipeline, TMS pulses were administered during IED or non-IED periods in an interleaved, randomized design. We stimulated both the motor cortex generating the IEDs and the contralateral motor cortex and tested the impact of IEDs on TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs). Our study demonstrated that TMS can be timed to IEDs and that there is a site-specific increase in TEP amplitude when stimulating during IEDs. Out of the TMS pulses aimed at an IED, 19% and 39% were successfully delivered during an IED for the two participants, respectively. For future research, we propose ways to address the methodological challenges of IED-timed TMS, enabling brain-state-dependent TMS for epilepsy research and treatment.
authors: Matilda Makkonen; Olli‐Pekka Kahilakoski; Miguel Menchaca; Ivan Zubarev; Oula Siljamo; Umair Hassan; Xiwei Shé; Wendy Qi; Tuomas P. Mutanen; Risto Juhani Ilmoniemi; Pantelis Lioumis; Fiona Mitchell Baumer

title: Bayesian adaptive design for neural recruitment curves
abstract: Nonlinear response models remain ubiquitous across disciplines with recruitment curves describing muscle response to neural stimulation. Conventional acquisition methods typically rely on static uniform sampling, requiring many stimuli, while adaptive threshold-hunting designs such as ML-PEST forfeit accurate characterization of the overall curve. We present a Bayesian adaptive design that uses posterior uncertainty over curve parameters to propose stimuli that maximize information gain across the full recruitment curve. We additionally implement a focused acquisition method that can target arbitrary subset of curve parameters, which we use to evaluate and interpret our design. In simulations, our design outperforms uniform sampling in recovering threshold while matching ML-PEST, and outperforms ML-PEST in predictive curve accuracy while matching uniform. It likewise matches our threshold-focused acquisition, suggesting our design doesn't trade off threshold estimation for recovering the curve. We further show data collected using our design yields greater power when detecting a change in threshold in intervention studies. Our design proposes the next stimulus within 5 seconds, making it feasible for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) experiments. Finally, we validate our design in TMS experiments and provide a library for Python, called onMEP, for online acquisition of neural recruitment curves.
authors: Vishweshwar Tyagi; Saihari S. Dukkipati; Daniel Twili; Jonas M. Mikhaeil; Andrew Gelman; Jason B. Carmel; James R. McIntosh

title: Invariant-Governed Adaptive Systems: Delayed-Commit Stability and Return Without Erasure
abstract: Abstract This research record presents two related proposed frameworks for invariant-governed adaptive systems: the Morrison Delayed-Commit Stability Principle and RETURN WITHOUT ERASURE — Causal Correction Under Invariant Preservation. The first studies the separation between proposal dynamics and committed-state dynamics. A candidate-generating process may remain exploratory, oscillatory, drifting, or nonconvergent while a distinct governance layer determines which proposed transitions are permitted to enter committed history. Under explicit Lyapunov-descent, admissibility, and invariant-preservation assumptions, the committed trajectory remains non-increasing in the chosen Lyapunov functional, preserves its protected invariant component, and has square-summable accepted increments even when convergence of the proposal process itself is not assumed. This formalizes the distinction PROPOSAL ≠ PERMISSION ≠ COMMIT. The second framework addresses retrospective invalidation. When later evidence establishes that an earlier committed transition was invalid, conventional rollback may discard valid subsequent evolution simply because it occurred later in time. RETURN WITHOUT ERASURE instead introduces a causal dependency relation between commits, removes the invalid commit and its dependency cone, preserves independent surviving commits, and reconstructs a minimally disturbed admissible state subject to exact preservation of a protected invariant. A central open problem is repair confluence: determining conditions under which independent retrospective corrections produce the same repaired state regardless of correction order. Disjoint causal dependency alone may be insufficient where admissibility geometry, invariant constraints, or reconstruction operators couple otherwise independent repairs. Characterising the sufficient and necessary conditions for confluence—and constructing minimal counterexamples where those conditions fail—is therefore identified as a primary research target. Together, the papers investigate a common principle: exploration, authorization, commitment, correction, and invariant preservation can be treated as mathematically distinct operations. The results are presented as proposed mathematical frameworks under active investigation; broader novelty and relationships to supervisory control, runtime assurance, truth-maintenance systems, belief revision, event sourcing, CRDTs, viability theory, and related fields remain subjects for formal comparative review. title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation(TMS) for Autism Spectrum Disorder
abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental condition characterized by impairments in social communication, repetitive behaviors, sensory processing abnormalities, and variable cognitive deficits. Despite significant advances in behavioral therapies and pharmacological interventions, effective treatments capable of directly modulating dysfunctional neural networks remain limited. Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) has emerged as a promising non-invasive neuromodulation technique that can alter cortical excitability, enhance neuroplasticity, and potentially improve cognitive and behavioral outcomes. Simultaneously, recent developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), Reinforcement Learning (RL), and Digital Twin technologies have created new opportunities to personalize TMS protocols using multimodal patient data, including structural and functional neuroimaging, electroencephalography (EEG), behavioral assessments, genetic information, and longitudinal clinical outcomes.

title: MRI-guided navigated TMS protocol for language production lateralization in right- and left-handed individuals
abstract: Hemispheric language lateralization has been assessed using various neuroimaging techniques in both basic research and clinical settings. The use of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) for this purpose, however, has shown low to moderate concordance with other neuroimaging techniques, particularly in cases of atypical lateralization and when studying the right hemisphere. The present study aimed to develop an MRI-guided navigated TMS protocol based on a verb-generation task to identify optimal conditions for determining language lateralization. Thirty healthy participants were classified into three groups according to hemispheric dominance during the verb-generation task: right-handers with left-hemisphere dominance, left-handers with left-hemisphere dominance, and left-handers with right-hemisphere dominance. TMS was applied at four predetermined locations within the inferior frontal gyrus while participants performed a picture-based verb generation task outside the scanner. Results showed a larger proportion of error responses when TMS was applied to the dominant language hemisphere, as defined by fMRI, across all groups. Concordance values between fMRI and TMS language lateralization ranged from 89 % to 100 %. Naming times were slower when the dominant hemisphere was stimulated, but only in the left-handed group. Trials more likely to induce TMS-related errors were characterized by longer reaction times, a greater number of response options, lower word frequency, and the absence of a clearly dominant response. These findings support the reliability of the proposed navigated TMS protocol for individual-level assessment of language lateralization during verb generation task as well as identify task-related conditions that increase the likelihood of verbal errors following TMS interference.
authors: Cristina Cano-Melle; Miriam Lluesma-Martín; Cristina Narganes-Pineda; Joaquín J. Ramírez-Guerrero; Ana B. Chica; César Ávila

title: Excitation-Inhibition Balance and Fronto-Limbic Connectivity Distinguish TMS Treatment Outcomes in Refractory Depression
abstract: BACKGROUND: Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is effective for treatment-resistant depression, but outcomes remain variable. The neurophysiological mechanisms underlying response remain poorly understood, limiting precision neuromodulation. METHODS: We combined transcranial magnetic stimulation with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and connectome-based Jansen-Rit neural mass modeling to investigate the mechanistic basis of treatment efficacy in 90 patients with treatment-resistant depression. Individualized whole-brain models were fitted to pre- and post-iTBS TMS-evoked potentials, yielding subject-specific estimates of synaptic connectivity, excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance, and cortical dynamics. Brain states were defined by singular value decomposition of the model's population activity, and partial least squares analysis with nested cross-validation identified the brain-state pattern distinguishing responders from non-responders. RESULTS: We identified two neurophysiological signatures associated with treatment response. First, responders showed greater post-treatment reductions in 3-10 Hz oscillatory power, driven by shifts in E/I balance toward greater inhibitory control through reduced excitatory drive and increased inhibitory-to-pyramidal connectivity. Second, a pre-treatment brain state characterized by opposite-polarity dynamics between subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) and left DLPFC distinguished responders from non-responders, consistent with prior fMRI findings on frontolimbic anticorrelation. Neural trajectory analysis further revealed greater dynamical reorganization and increased attractor stability in responders following treatment. CONCLUSIONS: These findings provide a neurophysiologically-informed framework linking iTBS treatment efficacy to specific changes in cortical E/I balance and frontolimbic circuit dynamics, pointing toward candidate markers that, with subject-specific structural connectivity and independent validation, may inform personalized neuromodulation approaches in treatment-resistant depression.
