title: Accelerated, augmented, and precision-targeted: The emerging landscape of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) in psychiatry and neurology
abstract: The landscape of neuromodulation therapy is changing rapidly.Accelerated transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) protocols now compress 6-week depression treatment courses into as little as 5 days.Exploratory studies of a single-day regimen have reported remission rates of 49-72% in treatment-resistant depression (TRD).Three converging principles define this shift: acceleration (compressing treatment from weeks to hours); augmentation (pharmacologically enhancing synaptic plasticity); and precision targeting (connectomeinformed, individualized site selection).This narrative review synthesizes evidence across all 3 domains, with an emphasis on studies published from 2022 to 2026.Key milestones include a second sham-controlled RCT confirming the efficacy of the SAINT/SNT (Stanford Accelerated Intelligent Neuromodulation Therapy) protocol and the first clinical description of a single-day TMS regimen (ONE-D (Optimized, Neuroplasticity-Enhanced techniques in Depression)) that leverages pharmacological augmentation with D-cycloserine (DCS) to enhance neuroplasticity.Precision strategies, including resting-state functional connectivity magnetic resonance imaging (fcMRI)-guided targeting, closedloop electroencephalography (EEG) systems, and emerging biomarkers, are increasingly complementing anatomical landmark-based methods.We devote particular attention to Parkinson's disease (PD), where the identification of the somato-cognitive action network (SCAN) as a key dysfunctional circuit illustrates how these principles translate into clinical efficacy.SCAN-targeted TMS approximately doubled the magnitude of motor improvement compared with conventional motor cortex stimulation.Finally, we review comparative effectiveness data positioning TMS alongside pharmacotherapy and esketamine, emerging health-economic evidence supporting its cost-effectiveness, and the challenges of scaling precision approaches for routine clinical care.This is a narrative review without a formal risk-of-bias assessment or meta-analytic pooling; limitations of this approach are discussed in the section "Limitations and translational challenges".
authors: Dawid Wiener; Mikołaj Pawlak; Filip Rybakowski

title: Financial Reporting Quality: The Mediating Role of Accounting Information Systems in Indonesia's Religious Affairs Ministry
abstract: Purpose: This study aims to examine the effects of Human Resource Competence (HRC) and Top Management Support (TMS) on Financial Reporting Quality (FRQ), while investigating the mediating role of Accounting Information Systems (AIS) in the public sector context.Research Methodology: This study employed a quantitative approach using a survey method at the Ministry of Religious Affairs of Jambi Province, Indonesia. Primary data were collected through structured questionnaires distributed to financial management personnel. A total of 320 respondents were selected using purposive sampling, and the data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS.Results: The findings show that HRC (β = 0.418) and TMS (β = 0.465) positively influence AIS. Furthermore, HRC (β = 0.283), TMS (β = 0.258), and AIS (β = 0.444) significantly improve FRQ, with AIS demonstrating the strongest direct effect. AIS also mediates the relationship between HRC and FRQ (β = 0.186) and between TMS and FRQ (β = 0.207).Conclusions: FRQ is enhanced when competent human resources and strong managerial support are integrated with effective AIS.Limitations: This study was limited to one public institution and focused only on four variables, restricting broader generalization.Contributions: This study extends FRQ literature by integrating Institutional Theory and Stakeholder Theory to explain AIS mediation and provides practical insights for strengthening public sector financial management.
authors: Puspa Riza; Sri Eko Puji Rahayu; Enggar Diah Puspa Arum; Yudi Yudi

title: Probing the role of left inferior frontal gyrus in vocal motor control: Evidence from TMS and causal inference analysis
abstract: Beyond an established role in speech initiation and planning, the left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) may contribute to sensorimotor control of speech production. We applied continuous theta burst stimulation (cTBS) over the anterior (aIFG) and posterior (pIFG) regions to investigate their roles in vocal motor control. A causal inference analysis (CIA) framework was developed to characterize source-space network organization. cTBS over both left aIFG and pIFG reduced vocal responses and enhanced P2 responses to pitch feedback perturbations, with no significant differences between two active stimulations. However, global dissimilarity analysis revealed greater P2-related topographic deviation from sham stimulation following aIFG stimulation than following pIFG stimulation. CIA further identified different source-space network patterns associated with aIFG and pIFG stimulation. These findings demonstrate the causal involvement of the left IFG in auditory-vocal integration and highlight the potential of CIA for characterizing distributed network organization underlying vocal motor control.
authors: Yichen Chang; Qifan Guo; Shuzhi Zhao; Tingni Li; Xiuqin Wu; Dongxu Liu; 戴光艳; Xiaoxia Zhu; Xi Chen; Lan Wang; Peng Liu; Nan Yan; Hanjun Liu

title: Implementation of RFID Technologies in Logistics and Supply Chain Management
abstract: RFID technology is increasingly used to automate object identification and improve the visibility of warehouse and transportation operations. However, existing studies provide limited sector-specific guidance on selecting appropriate tagging objects, configuring RFID control points, integrating RFID data with warehouse and transportation management systems, and evaluating implementation outcomes in agricultural logistics. This study addresses this gap by developing a phased RFID implementation framework designed for agricultural and warehouse logistics. The research combines an analysis of 20 standards, implementation guidelines, and prior academic studies with an illustrative before-and-after warehouse scenario. The framework covers product-batch and logistics-unit identification, RFID read-zone configuration, integration with WMS, ERP, TMS, and GPS records, employee training, performance measurement, data security, and implementation-cost assessment. The examined scenario compares warehouse inventory operations before and after the introduction of RFID-based identification and automated WMS event recording. In the illustrative scenario, the duration of a warehouse inventory count decreased from 16 hours to 4 hours, representing a 75% reduction. RFID-supported event recording also reduced the need for delayed manual entry of receiving, movement, and shipping data and enabled the automatic verification of tagged logistics units at configured control points. The economic assessment demonstrates that RFID feasibility depends on the selected tagging level, transaction volume, infrastructure and integration costs, tag-replacement requirements, maintenance, exception handling, and the value of measurable operational savings. The study shows that RFID performance depends on the level at which objects are identified, the configuration of read zones, the quality of master data, and the integration of RFID events with warehouse and transportation records. The proposed framework contributes a sector-specific approach that links physical cargo identification, warehouse events, transportation data, documentation, performance measurement, economic assessment, and implementation-risk control.
authors: Krystyna Hulyda
venue: International Journal of Economics and Management Studies

title: System Quality, Information Quality and Support/Training: Effects on Logistics Process Performance
abstract: In a context of accelerating digitalization of logistics and supply chains, organizations expect information systems (ERP, WMS, TMS) to deliver tangible efficiency gains (shorter lead times, higher productivity, fewer errors). However, such benefits depend less on the mere presence of tools than on perceived system quality, perceived information quality, and the level of support/training provided to users. Drawing on the information systems success literature (DeLone & McLean, 2003; Petter et al., 2008), this study examines the effects of system quality (QS), information quality (QI), and support/training (SF) on process performance (EP). Based on a 5-point Likert survey administered to N = 227 professionals, we estimate hierarchical multiple regression models with HC3 robust standard errors (MacKinnon & White, 1985). Results show positive and significant effects of QS (B = 0.339, p < 0.001), QI (B = 0.402, p < 0.001), and SF (B = 0.204, p = 0.002) on EP in the full model (R2 = 0.506), while tested moderation effects are not significant. Common method bias checks and diagnostic tests (VIF, Breusch-Pagan, Shapiro-Wilk, influential observations) complement the analysis and support the robustness of conclusions.
authors: Mohammed RIAD

title: Transcranial magnetic stimulation in autism spectrum disorder: a narrative review of neurobiological mechanisms, clinical efficacy, and future directions
abstract: Abstract Background Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a complicated neuropsychological disorder associated with social communicational problems, stereotypical interests, and behavior patterns. Though ASD has many causes, there are no treatment modalities today that have an overall impact on the condition itself, leaving room for improvement in existing approaches. Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) is one of the innovative approaches to treat such disorders by means of a noninvasive method of neuron activation using a strong magnetic field. Body The TMS could have an influence on the interconnection of the brain networks, synaptic plasticity, and the brain cortex excitability, which are associated with the alleviation of the symptoms of ASD. Although some randomized and open-label studies have reported improvement, the evidence is weakened by small samples, inconsistent protocols, and the large proportion of uncontrolled studies. This would mean that the process of selecting patients as well as administering TMS would need careful attention. There are no documented long-term impacts of TMS. For future studies, there should be incorporation of the principles from neuroimaging and electrophysiology. TMS is performed using different techniques depending on its objectives, which include single-pulse TMS that assesses brain topography; paired-pulse TMS in evaluating the inhibitory or facilitating nature of the brain cortex; repetitive TMS (rTMS). Conclusion It can be concluded from all the information presented above that TMS might have immense potential as an add-on treatment for ASDs based on the data we have accumulated. However, more studies are needed to assess the efficacy of this treatment method in addressing ASDs.To summarize, TMS is a relatively novel neuromodulation therapy that can benefit individuals with ASDs based on the neurobiological aspects of their disorders.
authors: Abdur Rehman; Md. Tosaddeque Hossain Siddiqui; Maryam Asghar Jamal; Awais Ahmad; Syeda Hamna; Zain Ul Abedeen; Zahoor Ullah; Anousheh Malak; Maliha Said; Asma Gulshan; Waheed Khan
venue: The Egyptian Journal of Neurosurgery : the official publication of the Egyptian Society of Neurological Surgeons/Egyptian journal of neurosurgery

title: Governance of talent management systems and national innovativeness: The moderating role of culture
abstract: This study conceptualizes talent management (TM) systems as a governance mechanism influencing national innovation performance. Building on contextual talent-management research and the Hofstede (1984) cultural framework, the paper examines the association between country-level talent competitiveness and national innovativeness and assesses whether individualism/collectivism changes this relationship (Gallardo-Gallardo et al., 2020; Hofstede, 2011). Using 2022 Global Talent Competitiveness Index (GTCI) and Global Innovation Index (GII) ranking data, together with The Culture Factor Group (2023) (formerly Hofstede Insights) cultural indicators, the study applies simple regression, moderated regression, independent-samples t-tests, and group-specific regression models for 70 countries. The results show a strong positive association between talent-management rankings and innovation rankings, meaning that countries with stronger talent systems tend to occupy better innovation positions. Cultural context differentiates the level and pattern of this relationship: individualist and collectivist groups show statistically significant differences in GTCI, GII, and related components, although interaction effects require cautious interpretation. The study contributes to governance and regulation literature by positioning TM as an institutional and policy-driven system and by highlighting the need for culturally adaptive human-capital and innovation policies.
authors: Д. Б. Жуламанова; Azamat Zhanseitov; Saule Iskendirova; Aliya Daueshova; Ulagat Yussupov

title: Financial Reporting Quality Determinants in Indonesia's Religious Affairs Ministry: The Moderating Role of Organizational Culture
abstract: Purpose: This study examines the effects of Human Resource Competence (HRC) and Top Management Support (TMS) on Financial Reporting Quality (FRQ), with the moderating role of Organizational Culture (OC) within the Regional Office of the Religious Affairs Ministry of Jambi Province, Indonesia. Methodology: The study involved data collected through a structured questionnaire distributed to 320 financial management officers at the Religious Affairs Ministry of Jambi Province. The data were analyzed using PLS-SEM with SmartPLS software. Results: Empirical evidence demonstrates that HRC and TMS have positive and significant effects on FRQ. Furthermore, OC significantly strengthened the relationship between HRC and FRQ and between TMS and FRQ. Conclusions: The results demonstrate that improving employee competence and strengthening managerial commitment are essential for enhancing the quality of financial reporting. A supportive organizational culture further reinforces the effectiveness of these factors in producing transparent, reliable, and credible financial statements. Limitations: This study is limited to the Religious Affairs Ministry of Jambi Province and examines only two antecedents of financial reporting quality, namely human resource competence and top management support, with organizational culture as the moderating variable. Contributions: Theoretically, this study extends Institutional Theory by positioning organizational culture as an institutional mechanism that strengthens the effects of human resource competence and top management support on financial reporting quality. Practically, the findings suggest that the Religious Affairs Ministry should integrate competency development and managerial support with its five cultural work values to strengthen the quality of financial reporting.
authors: Puspa Riza; Sri Eko Puji Rahayu; Enggar Diah Puspa Arum; Yudi Yudi
venue: Annals of Human Resource Management Research

title: Immediate cortical responses to transcranial magnetic stimulation of the human motor leg area
abstract: Abstract Background Immediate transcranial evoked potentials (iTEPs) are ultra-early electroencephalographic responses elicited by single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of the primary motor cortical hand area (M1-HAND). Their characteristic latency, waveform, and sensitivity to short-interval intracortical inhibition suggest a close relationship to the cortical generators of indirect corticospinal volleys (I-waves). Here, we tested the hypothesis that iTEPs constitute a fundamental physiological response of human motor cortex and therefore generalize across motor representations, including the leg representation (M1-LEG). Methods Single-pulse TMS was delivered over the motor cortical representation of the right tibialis anterior (TA) in 16 healthy volunteers. In a subset of participants (n=10), stimulus–response curves and paired-pulse short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI) measures were obtained. Results TMS of M1-LEG elicited reproducible iTEPs consisting of a slow positive deflection with superimposed high-frequency peaks with topographic maxima in electrodes adjacent to the stimulation site. M1-LEG iTEPs emerged close to active motor threshold and increased in prevalence and amplitude with increasing stimulation intensity. Paired-pulse stimulation produced consistent SICI of the second and third iTEP peaks. M1-LEG stimulation also evoked conventional later TEPs with latencies and polarities closely resembling those recorded after M1-HAND stimulation. Conclusions TMS of the human M1-LEG elicits robust iTEPs that closely resemble those recorded from M1-HAND in their timing, intensity dependence, and sensitivity to intracortical inhibition. These findings indicate that iTEPs are not specific to M1-HAND but reflect a general physiological response of human motor cortex closely linked to corticospinal I-wave generation. This broadens their utility as a non-invasive probe of excitatory and inhibitory circuit dynamics throughout the human motor system. Highlights Single-pulse TMS of the leg motor cortex (M1-LEG) elicits reproducible immediate TMS-evoked potentials (iTEPs). M1-LEG iTEPs emerge near active motor threshold, increase with stimulation intensity, and display selective short-interval intracortical inhibition of late iTEP peaks with paired-pulse TMS. Immediate and later TMS-evoked responses show striking resemblance in leg and hand motor cortex. The shared properties of M1-LEG and M1-HAND iTEPs support iTEPs as a general motor cortex response linked to corticospinal I-wave generation and intracortical inhibition.
authors: Mikkel Malling Beck; Marten Nuyts; Laura Sakalauskaitė; John C. Rothwell; Hartwig Roman Siebner; Lasse Christiansen

title: Multi-omics characterization of anoikis-related hub genes and macrophage-centered immune persistence with validation of HAVCR2 in atherosclerosis
abstract: Background Atherosclerosis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory vascular disease characterized by immune dysregulation, metabolic disturbance, and progressive vascular remodeling. Although anoikis resistance has been extensively investigated in cancer biology, its involvement in immune-cell persistence and plaque progression in AS remains poorly understood. Methods We integrated two publicly available bulk transcriptomic datasets (GSE100927 and GSE28829) to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and performed weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) to determine disease-associated gene modules. Anoikis-related candidate genes were obtained by intersecting DEGs, WGCNA-derived module genes, and a curated anoikis-related gene set, and were further prioritized using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression and random forest algorithms. Immune infiltration and cell type–specific expression patterns were evaluated using CIBERSORT and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analyses. The expression of the leading candidate was validated using both in vitro and in vivo experiments. Results We identified eight core anoikis-related hub genes—HAVCR2, CD36, PLAU, TNF, PYCARD, SERPINA1, BLNK, and CHI3L1—that were closely associated with AS. These genes were enriched in inflammatory and metabolic pathways and showed strong diagnostic performance across validation analyses, with AUC values greater than 0.83. Immune deconvolution and single-cell transcriptomic analyses revealed that the anoikis-related signature was predominantly localized to macrophage and T-cell compartments within atherosclerotic lesions. Among the identified candidates, HAVCR2 showed the most consistent disease-associated pattern. HAVCR2 expression was markedly increased in oxLDL-stimulated THP-1-derived macrophages and was enriched in macrophage-rich atherosclerotic lesions in high-fat diet–fed ApoE −/− mice, supporting its association with lipid-induced macrophage activation and vascular inflammation. Conclusion This study defines a macrophage-centered anoikis-related immune signature in atherosclerosis and identifies HAVCR2, together with CD36, PLAU, TNF, PYCARD, SERPINA1, BLNK, and CHI3L1, as potential biomarkers and candidate targets for future diagnostic and therapeutic investigation.
authors: Qiang Shen; Zhengfeng Fan; Jincheng Hou; Fei Li; Yixuan Wang; Zongtao Liu; Chen Jiang; Nianguo Dong

title: Physics-informed neural operators for rapid electric field prediction in transcranial magnetic stimulation of healthy and tumor subjects
abstract: Accurate and rapid prediction of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)-induced electric fields is essential for personalized clinical applications, from individualized therapy in major depressive disorder to presurgical functional mapping in neuro-oncology. Yet conventional finite element methods are often too computationally expensive for interactive use. Existing deep learning surrogate models partly address this limitation but are largely constrained to fixed voxel-grid representations that cannot naturally accommodate the irregular geometry of subject-specific head meshes. We present the first physics-informed neural operator (PINO) for subject-specific prediction of vector TMS electric fields, built on a mesh-native dual-encoder architecture that jointly encodes head anatomy and coil configuration. By incorporating a curl-based regularization term aligned with the curl-free nature of the TMS secondary field, the PINO model promotes physical consistency as a soft regularizer alongside data-driven supervision. Trained on 75 subjects from the IXI dataset, the framework was evaluated across four independent held-out test datasets, including healthy subjects from two additional MRI cohorts and, for the first time in learning-based TMS electric-field prediction, tumor patients. The resolution-agnostic formulation generalizes across subjects, coil types, and spatial resolutions without retraining, predicting vector electric fields on approximately 300,000 gray matter volume nodes in under 100 ms on a consumer-grade GPU. Across all test datasets within the focality-50% region, the PINO model achieved median center-of-gravity errors of 0.39–0.43 mm, RMSE of 0.12–0.16 V/m, and mean angular deviations of 6.7°–7.3°, with performance within or below the error ranges reported by recent deep-learning approaches. At the selected 5% physics-loss weighting, curl loss decreased by 9.1% relative to the data-only model, while RMSE and MAD increased by only 1.6% and 1.3%, respectively. These results suggest that physics-informed neural operators provide a scalable technical foundation for rapid gray-matter electric-field approximation, supporting future studies on real-time electric-field-guided TMS workflows
authors: Philipp Moser; Fabian Greifeneder; Dominik Freinberger; Gernot Reishofer; Pia Ritter; Louis Frank; Stefan Thumfart; Sascha Freigang; K Mahdy Ali

title: Brain state-contingent stimulation to probe task-dependent functional networks
abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a fundamental tool for causal inference, but identical stimulation produces different outcomes depending on the instantaneous brain state, undermining interpretation and reproducibility. EEG-guided TMS studies to date have primarily addressed this by timing stimulation to local oscillatory features over circumscribed regions during the resting state. However, because these approaches do not control concurrent large-scale state dynamics, each stimulus is delivered within unconstrained and highly variable network regimes. We provide a theoretical and methodological framework for real-time control of large-scale functional networks, enabling stimulation to be delivered when a predefined network pattern, modulated by task demands, is expressed. By framing this neural variability as an informative resource, our approach aims to strengthen conditional causal inference through the real-time estimation of task-relevant connectivity. We define a workflow, from offline operationalisation and validation to real-time state-contingent stimulation, to promote shared standards and reproducibility in the study of human behaviour and to inform its clinical translation, from TMS-EEG biomarkers of network dysfunction to individualised, network-targeted neuromodulation.
authors: Arianna Brancaccio; Carlo Miniussi

title: Real-time noise cancellation for EEG monitoring and brain–computer interfaces
abstract: Raw electroencephalography (EEG) data suffer from a low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Effective real-time cleaning of EEG would improve the robustness of EEG monitoring, brain–computer interfaces, and brain-state-dependent stimulation applications in both laboratory and real-life environments. Here, we present a real-time source-estimate-utilizing noise-discarding algorithm (rtSOUND) for EEG noise suppression. We adapted the established offline SOUND algorithm for real-time use and implemented it into an open-source EEG-processing software. Instead of using conventional temporal filtering, SOUND operates the data with a spatial filter. This makes it particularly suitable for real-time applications, since each streamed data sample can be cleaned separately in near real-time. Unlike temporal filtering methods, SOUND does not make assumptions about the frequency content of noise and brain signals but assumes that the noise topographies differ from those generated by brain activity. With an EEG forward model, rtSOUND cross-validates the EEG time series and estimates the spatial distribution of noise, resulting in a data-cleaning linear spatial filter. Each streamed EEG sample is processed synchronously, and the filter is periodically updated in an asynchronous parallel process. The algorithm rapidly updates the spatial filter in response to changes in the data, ensuring that noise reduction is both immediate and accurately adapted to the current EEG state. rtSOUND was validated with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)–EEG and resting-state EEG datasets measured from 25 healthy subjects. SNR of both TMS-evoked potentials and resting-state data consistently improved across various metrics. rtSOUND particularly benefitted channels with poor SNR, while retaining the waveforms in high-quality channels. The algorithm was fast enough to process data streamed at 5 kHz. rtSOUND improves the SNR of EEG in real time, providing a robust method to improve signal quality for brain-state-monitoring applications.
authors: Matilda Makkonen; Olli‐Pekka Kahilakoski; Johanna Metsomaa; Pantelis Lioumis; Risto Juhani Ilmoniemi; Tuomas P. Mutanen

title: Induction of interhemispheric visual plasticity by paired associative stimulation
abstract: ABSTRACT Unveiling the plastic mechanisms of the primary visual cortex (V1) is crucial for understanding how visual processing can change and adapt, ultimately informing interventions to promote functional recovery following visual system damage. Paired associative stimulation (PAS) protocols can induce associative plasticity within the human V1. However, previous paradigms used full-field visual stimulation, engaging both hemispheres simultaneously, leaving unclear whether plasticity can be selectively targeted to a single visual pathway and whether it can modulate the non-stimulated hemisphere. Across three experiments in healthy participants, we investigated the neurophysiological, behavioural, and interhemispheric outcomes of a novel lateralized visual PAS protocol (vPAS). Pattern-reversal checkerboards were presented in a single visual hemifield and time-locked to transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) pulses delivered over the contralateral V1. Experiment 1 assessed neurophysiological effects by recording hemifield-lateralized visual-evoked potentials (VEPs) and testing three inter-stimulus intervals (ISIs: 75, 100, and 125 ms) between vPAS-paired stimuli. Experiment 2 evaluated perceptual changes in contrast detection, while Experiment 3 examined vPAS hemispheric specificity and aftereffects on interhemispheric visuomotor transfer. Only the 75-ms ISI consistently modulated visual processing in the non-conditioned hemisphere, reducing N75 amplitude and improving contrast detection for visual stimuli presented contralateral to the TMS side. Longer ISIs were not effective. Furthermore, this protocol altered interhemispheric transfer exclusively when the left, but not the right, V1 was targeted during vPAS. In conclusion, lateralized vPAS induces timing-dependent changes beyond the stimulated cortex, suggesting that associative plasticity can engage contralateral visual circuits and modulate visual processing.
authors: Francesca Crespi; Giacomo Guidali; Eleonora Arrigoni; Nadia Bolognini

title: Fear learning–induced brain dynamics predict individual extinction memory expression following transcranial magnetic stimulation
abstract: Abstract Fear learning and extinction unfold as time-dependent processes. Herein, we examined whether fear learning dynamically reorganizes brain activity and whether such reorganization predicts subsequent extinction-memory expression under transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)-modulated extinction. Eighty-seven healthy adults completed a three-day Pavlovian threat-learning protocol with resting-state fMRI, TMS-modulated extinction, and extinction-memory fMRI. Using coactivation pattern analysis with a hidden Markov model, we identified a fear-learning–induced brain state characterized by increased engagement and transition uncertainty after conditioning. Functional connectivity reorganization within this state predicted individual differences in extinction recall- and renewal-related brain activation under TMS-modulated extinction (cross-validated; recall r = 0.47, p = 0.001; renewal r = 0.37, p = 0.01; permutation-tested), but not natural extinction. In separate brain–behavior correlation analyses, the neural variates identified in the TMS-modulated extinction were associated with behavioral expression. These findings demonstrate that fear learning reshapes brain-state dynamics and identifies a candidate biomarker of neuromodulation-linked extinction-memory expression.
authors: Kai Zhang; Lihan Cui; B Isabel Moallem; Hani Meelad; Zakiya Atiyah; Muhammad Badarnee; Isabella Mason; Zhenfu Wen; Mark S. George; Mohammed R. Milad

title: Disrupting the Right Inferior Frontal Gyrus Increases ‘Social Brain’ Activity During Emotion Recognition
abstract: Abstract Neuroimaging studies have identified a specialised social brain network that supports emotion recognition and social cognition. This network performs a range of functions that include facial expression recognition and inferring the mental states of others. Studies of neuropsychological patients report that damage to the right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), the top-down control area in this network, impairs facial expression recognition. To investigate how transient disruption of the right IFG affects the wider social brain we combined transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Participants ( n =20) were scanned across two sessions while performing a delayed match-to-sample emotion recognition task in which happy or fearful expressions were preceded by a congruent or incongruent word cue. Prior to each scan, thetaburst TMS was delivered over the right IFG or over the vertex control site (session order was balanced across participants). A group whole-brain analysis revealed that TMS to the IFG increased neural activity in multiple regions of the social brain network. These included the bilateral temporal pole, precuneus and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). This pattern of results shows that the disruption of top-down control mechanisms localised in the IFG alters the neural processing in remote nodes of the social brain network. Our findings are discussed within the wider context of how we recognise and understand the emotions of other people.
authors: Emel Küçük; Hannah Gofton; Cameron Smith; DANIEL H. KAISER; David Pitcher

title: When humans and agents form a collective: a framework for collective intelligence in persistent organizational human-AI teams
abstract: Artificial systems increasingly participate in organizational work as recurrent contributors to interdependent activity, yet research remains fragmented across system capabilities, individual responses, episodic interactions, and constructs derived from human-only teams. This article develops Organismic Human-Artificial Intelligence (OHAI) as a bounded integrative theoretical framework for studying collective intelligence in persistent organizational human-AI teams. Its focal unit is a bounded collective of distinguishable human and artificial contributors whose interdependent activity extends across successive cycles and whose prior collective activity can affect later artificial participation. The framework distinguishes system configuration, collective functioning, and collective intelligence (CI) as analytical objects, with CI as its primary theoretical target. CI denotes a general group-level capacity manifested across diverse tasks within a specified and empirically qualified task universe. Task performances may provide indicators for estimating CI or serve as external criteria, while the framework separately examines broader employee, team, and organizational consequences, including changes in human working relationships and employee wellbeing. Its central inferential rule is that a property implemented in an artificial component does not by itself establish a corresponding team-level phenomenon. Collective functioning must instead be demonstrated in the enacted organization and use of distributed contributions. Partner modeling, transactive-memory-system-related coordination, and shared-mental-model-related representational alignment provide selective lenses on such functioning. Persistence makes collective history consequential, bringing recursive updating, overlapping timescales, reconfiguration, and collective-intelligence trajectories into view without presuming adaptation or improvement. Human-only teams serve as secondary epistemic references for bounded tests of observable-pattern and functional correspondence, while relational-pattern correspondence remains a limited future methodological possibility. The empirical program distinguishes four nonmandatory stages of research maturity: configuration and measurement qualification, local relations, longitudinal team-level phenomena, and integrated multilevel studies. The framework thereby provides a disciplined basis for cumulative research on how heterogeneous contributions become collectively consequential and change over time.
authors: Alessandro Rovetta; Alessandro Bortolotti; Claudio Di Berardino

title: Investigating Neuropharmacological Features of the Cortical Activity of Cannabidiol GWP42003 P—A Phase 1 Clinical Trial
abstract: Background/Objectives: Despite the clinical efficacy of cannabidiol (CBD) in treating certain epilepsies, its in vivo neuropharmacological mechanisms remain incompletely understood. This Phase 1 clinical trial aimed to evaluate the acute effects of a single oral dose of highly purified CBD (GWP42003-P) on cortical excitability. Transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and electromyography (TMS-EMG) were utilized as assessment tools. Methods: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial, 15 healthy male participants received a single 1500 mg dose of GWP42003-P or placebo. Cortical activity metrics, including resting and active motor thresholds (RMT, AMT), short intracortical inhibition (SICI), TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs), TMS-related spectral perturbations (TRSP), and inter-trial phase clustering (ITPC), were recorded pre-dose and at 1, 4, and 6 h post-dose. Results: RMT and AMT significantly decreased over time following CBD administration, though without a significant Condition × Time interaction. While primary analyses showed no condition-driven alterations for SICI, TEPs, or TRSP, secondary longitudinal modeling revealed a transient reduction in beta-band desynchronization 1 h post-dose, aligning with peak plasma concentration. The drug condition also exhibited a qualitative, non-significant trend toward increased alpha ITPC and decreased delta ITPC at 4 and 6 h post-dose compared to placebo. Conclusions: A single acute 1500 mg dose of GWP42003-P did not produce statistically significant alterations in widespread cortical excitability in healthy adult males. However, the transient blunting of beta desynchronization at peak concentration may reflect CBD’s distinct, non-classical neuromodulatory profile. Overall, these largely null findings suggest that acute CBD administration lacks a robust, direct modulatory effect on cortical networks. Capturing its precise neuropharmacological mechanisms will likely require future investigations utilizing chronic dosing paradigms or clinical patient populations.
authors: Viviana Santoro; Po‐Yu Fong; Andrea Biondi; Isabella Premoli; Harry Clark; Lorenzo Rocchi; Mark Philip Richardson

title: Stimulus predictability rather than inter-trial interval itself affects motor evoked potential amplitudes
abstract: Abstract The inter-trial interval (ITI) of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can modulate motor-evoked potential (MEP) amplitude and may thus confound assessments of corticospinal excitability. We tested whether this effect depends on the ITI duration per se or the associated temporal predictability and whether intracortical inhibitory processes mediate these effects on. In 26 healthy participants, we recorded single-pulse MEPs and paired-pulse measures of short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI; 2-ms interstimulus interval) and long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI; 100-ms interstimulus interval) at ITIs of 2, 5, and 10 s. ITIs were presented in different Patterns, i.e., separate fixed blocks (FXD), randomly intermingled within blocks (RND), or randomly intermingled but auditorily cued at 950 ms pre-TMS (RNDC). MEPs showed significant effects of ITI, Pattern, and their interaction, being smaller at 2 s than at longer ITIs in FXD but not in RND and RNDC. However, RNDC produced marked MEP suppression across all ITI. SICI showed a Pattern × ITI interaction but no main effect of Pattern or between-pattern differences per ITI, whereas LICI showed complex Pattern × ITI interaction and both main effects. Notably, ITI affected SICI and LICI oppositely. While GABA-A-receptor mediated inhibition (SICI) showed an ITI dependency compatible with the ITI effects on single-pulse MEPs, it was unlikely mediating the predictability effects but may rather relate to an independent ITI driven suppression. In contrast, GABA-B-receptor mediated inhibition (LICI), was clearly modulated by predictability, but incompatible with the observed ITI effects on MEP amplitude. In summary, the effect of ITI duration on MEP amplitude seems to be largely explained by anticipatory suppression of corticospinal excitability based on the predictability of TMS pulses as derived from their temporal context, being easier for shorter and more regular ITIs and maximal for explicit cues immediately preceding the TMS pulse. SICI and LICI are modulated by ITI as well, with the latter affected by predictability, but neither can explain the observed predictability effects on single-pulse MEP amplitudes.
authors: Saman Seifpour; Nele Haferkorn; S. Vijayakumar; Til Ole Bergmann

title: The motor component of pain anticipation: corticospinal excitability as a conditioned response
abstract: Pain is an adaptive and predictive experience, serving not only as a reaction to injury but also as a mechanism for anticipating and preventing harm. The human brain continuously generates predictions about potential bodily threats, preparing the motor system for defensive responses before nociceptive input occurs. Despite extensive evidence of sensory, affective, and cognitive modulation during pain anticipation, the motor component of this process remains poorly understood. To address this gap, the studies reported in this thesis aim to investigate how predictive learning of painful stimulation engages the motor system. Specifically, we examined how corticospinal excitability encodes the intensity, spatial location, and timing of anticipated acute pain. By combining Pavlovian conditioning with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and autonomic recordings, results revealed sensory-tuned, topographically organized in both hemispheres, and sustained motor inhibition, characterized by muscle-specific reductions in corticospinal excitability in the upper limbs that reflect the predicted features of pain. This motor modulation occurs alongside global autonomic adjustments, indicating parallel recruiting of complementary systems. Together, these findings highlight how the brain integrates motor and autonomic responses to optimize anticipatory defense, while also revealing mechanisms that may contribute to maladaptive conditions when persistent or altered.
authors: Daniela <1997> Dalbagno
venue: AMS Dottorato Institutional Doctoral Theses Repository (University of Bologna)

title: Left-DLPFC theta-burst stimulation produces delayed effects on musical pleasure without affecting piano-melody learning
abstract: Abstract Reward operates as a cycle in which a stimulus produces a pleasure response, and the degree of pleasure experienced reinforces the behaviours that lead back to it. Music provides a useful model for examining this cycle because it is intrinsically pleasurable, can be learned, and engages reward-related frontostriatal circuitry that overlaps with circuitry involved in primary and secondary rewards, such as food, sex, and money. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), a non-invasive stimulation method, has been shown to produce bidirectional effects on music-evoked pleasure by increasing or decreasing activity in cortical regions, such as the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), that are functionally connected to subcortical regions, including the striatum. Here, we further characterize the reward cycle by incorporating TMS into a paradigm that combines musical pleasure ratings with an early musical skill acquisition task. In a within-subjects, counterbalanced crossover design, 23 participants with 2-10 years of musical experience received intermittent TBS (iTBS; excitatory) and continuous TBS (cTBS; inhibitory) over the left DLPFC in separate sessions. Participants rated the pleasantness of short piano melodies before stimulation (T0), immediately afterwards (T1), and 24 hours later (T2). After stimulation, they learned to play the melodies, and pitch and rhythm accuracy were assessed during three performance phases, namely acquisition, immediately after acquisition, and 24 hours later. Liking did not differ between conditions at T1; however, the increase in liking from baseline (T0) to T2 was significantly larger following iTBS than cTBS, a divergence that emerged across the 24-hour interval spanning both learning and sleep. Pitch and rhythm accuracy did not differ between conditions at any phase, despite improvement across trials in both. These results indicate that TMS to the left DLPFC can produce delayed, condition-dependent shifts in musical liking without a parallel change in early skill acquisition.
authors: Sofia Simonetto-Rizk; Yang Liu; Jérémie Ginzburg; Robert J. Zatorre; Emily B. J. Coffey

title: Neuroimaging-Guided Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: Rates of response to repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) vary widely. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated whether neuroimaging-guided targeting personalization, from fixed-coordinate neuronavigation to individually connectivity-personalized targeting, moderates clinical response, safety, and neural mechanisms in OCD. Following PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines, PubMed, the Cochrane Library, and ScienceDirect were searched through July 2026 for randomized and non-randomized studies of neuroimaging-guided transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) in OCD. Risk of bias (RoB) was assessed using Cochrane RoB2 for RCTs (randomized controlled trials) and ROBINS-I (Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions) for non-randomized studies. Random-effects inverse-variance and risk-ratio models pooled Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) scores and responder rates; non-poolable data were synthesized narratively. Nine study cohorts across eight publications met inclusion criteria (five RCTs and four open-label/single-arm). Pooled analysis of four sham-controlled RCTs showed no significant benefit of neuroimaging-guided TMS on Y-BOCS total score (MD = −0.64, 95% CI = −3.60, 2.32) or responder rate (RR = 1.46, 95% CI = 0.68, 3.15), with moderate heterogeneity. However, trials using individually connectivity-personalized pre-supplementary motor area (pre-SMA) targeting consistently trended toward benefit, while fixed-coordinate neuronavigated trials trended toward null or sham-favoring results. A narrative synthesis of non-poolable and non-randomized studies showed larger, mostly positive within-group reductions in Y-BOCS scores (25%-48%), particularly among patients with moderate disease severity, alongside mechanistic evidence linking individualized connectivity-based targets to symptom improvement. TMS was well tolerated overall, with mild, transient headache being the most common adverse event and no serious safety concerns identified. Overall, neuroimaging-guided TMS showed no pooled benefit in OCD; however, individually connectivity-personalized targeting may be more beneficial than fixed-coordinate approaches, warranting adequately powered trials that directly compare targeting-personalization strategies.
authors: Maria Alejandra Rodriguez Gaviria; Paula Andrea Cuenca Cuevas; Rodrigo Nava Muñoz; Angie Coraline Moreno Báez; Andrés Felipe Cardenas Gamboa; Natalia Vanegas Arias; Christopher Alejandro Jiménez Beltrán; Leidy Catherine Guerrero Pasijojoa

title: Editorial: Non-invasive brain stimulation: from basic science to clinical application
abstract: Non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) techniques are used both as causal probes of brain function and as clinically established or investigational interventions for neurological and psychiatric disorders. Transcranial electrical stimulation (tES), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) differ in their physical principles, spatial resolution, and biological effects, yet share a central translational challenge: stimulation must engage the right neural system, in the right patient, at an appropriate dose, and ultimately produce clinically meaningful benefit. title: Beyond technological readiness: How financial benefit and top management support drive public electric vehicle charging station investment in Indonesia
abstract: This study investigates what drives potential business partners in Indonesia to invest in public electric vehicle charging stations (PEVCS). Using the TOE framework and TPB, this study examines key determinants of investment decisions in a B2B context. Survey data from 242 organizational respondents were analyzed using PLS-SEM. Results indicate that Perceived Financial Benefit (PFB) is the strongest driver of investment intention, consistent with the economic logic that business decision-makers prioritize profitability and anticipated returns over other considerations. Top Management Support (TMS) also emerges as influential, directly affecting investment intention and reinforcing financial confidence among organizational stakeholders. A notable characteristic of the sample dominated by national private firms with highly centralized structures appears to meaningfully shape how decisions are made within organizations. One of the more striking outcomes of this study is that Government Support (GSP) showed no direct bearing on investment intention. Government incentives only drive investment when perceived as tangible financial gains via cost reduction or revenue growth confirming that policy instruments must translate into firm-level economic value to influence decisions. Perceived complexity, meanwhile, did not register as a meaningful obstacle within this sample, suggesting that surveyed organizations possess formalized capabilities to manage technical and integration challenges. On the other hand, perceived compatibility proved consistently relevant, particularly when the technology slots naturally into pre-existing systems such as parking facilities or customer loyalty programs, thereby amplifying perceived financial returns. From a practical standpoint, these findings carry important implications for policymakers, specifically the need to sharpen messaging on return on investment when engaging top management and to design incentive structures that speak directly to financial attractiveness. While contributing to the sustainable energy infrastructure literature, the cross-sectional design limits causal inference; future studies should examine how ownership type and competitive dynamics moderate investment decisions.
authors: sudianto d; Heronimus Yudhanto; Achmad Meidiansyah; Evi Rinawati Simanjuntak

title: สมรรถนะดานการสอสารของผนำทสงผลตอการสรางวฒนธรรมความยงยนในธรกจรานอาหารเครอขายของไทย
abstract: This study aimed (1) to examine the leadership communication competencies present in Thailand’s chain restaurant businesses and (2)to analyze the roles and communication-related factors of leaders influencing the formation of sustainability culture within these businesses. A qualitative research design was employed. In-depth interviews were conducted with nine executives from large chain restaurant businesses in Thailand that operated multiple branches nationwide and formally declared sustainability policies. The participants were selected through purposive sampling. Data were analyzed using thematic content analysis. The findings revealed that leader’s communication competencies for fostering a culture of sustainability comprised four key dimensions: (1) message design competency, emphasizing clarity, conciseness, and the translation of policies into actionable practices; (2) relational communication competency, encompassing active learning, trust building, and positive reinforcement: (3) communication technology utilization competency, facilitating accessibility and continuity of communication across multiple business branches; and (4) shared meaning creation and persuasive communication competency, enabling employees to recognize the value of sustainability and translate this understanding into sustainable practices. Key factors that facilitated or hindered effective communication included top management support, internal communication structures, employee workload and technological readiness. The findings suggest that strengthening leaders’ communication competencies across all four dimensions can facilitate the effective implementation of sustainability initiatives in Thai chain restaurant business and foster an organizational culture that balances economic, social, and environmental responsibilities.
authors: Kittika Sapwetamornkul; Chatmongkol Naenna; Somsak Wanitchayaporn; Surawong Wannapak
venue: Journal of Administration and Social Science Review

title: Hydration status and repetitive head impacts: neurophysiological responses and functional implications
abstract: Combat sport athletes frequently experience two distinct yet potentially interacting physiological stressors: repetitive head impacts (RHIs) and rapid weight loss through hypo-hydration. While each has been studied independently, limited research has examined their combined neurophysiological consequences. This thesis aimed to investigate how RHIs and hypo-hydration influence neuromuscular and cortical function, using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and motor nerve stimulation (MNS) as assessment tools. An initial survey of over 100 combat sport athletes highlighted widespread engagement in rapid weight loss practices, with many reporting overlapping symptoms of hypo-hydration and concussion. In addition, some athletes reported exacerbation of concussion symptoms after undergoing a weight-cut. A reliability study confirmed that TMS and MNS measures could be used with sufficient precision in ensuring robustness for subsequent investigations. In the first experimental study, exercise and heat-induced hypo-hydration impaired maximal strength and voluntary activation but did not significantly alter corticospinal excitability or inhibition, suggesting preserved central drive under fluid-restricted conditions. In contrast, the following study examined responses to a single sparring session and found significant increases in cortical inhibition and motor thresholds, along with reduced maximal strength and voluntary activation, all of which resolved within 48 hours. A follow-up longitudinal study using instrumented mouthguards revealed that impact magnitude e.g., cumulative angular acceleration predicted the degree of increased cortical inhibition. Finally, a 10-week case series tracked three fighters through their fight camps. Voluntary activation and strength showed the most frequent meaningful changes, and over 200 RHIs were recorded in approximately 35% of their monitored sparring sessions. In summary, repeated head impacts elevated cortical inhibitory activity and central fatigue, while heat-induced hypo-hydration produced a contrasting neurophysiological response. These opposing effects may suggest a complex physiological interplay if they occur concurrently, whereby head-impact-related neural inhibition could disrupt or override compensatory mechanisms associated with fluid loss, potentially increasing vulnerability to injury and impairing athletic performance.
authors: Nasir Uddin
