Methods We searched the PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP and other databases from inception to 8 January 2026. Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data and assessed the risk of bias using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool. Because of substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity and inconsistent outcome-data types, we did not pool effect estimates; instead, we performed a structured synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM) and graded the certainty of evidence using GRADE. Results Ten randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 537 participants were included. All 10 studies reported a favorable direction of effect for EMG-BF, but the evidence for every outcome was of low or very low certainty. Across the five RCTs reporting surface electromyography (sEMG), all reported larger signal amplitudes in the EMG-BF arm, although the outcome data types varied (means vs. medians) and the muscle sites and comparators differed. Two RCTs reported greater lower-limb muscle strength with EMG-BF. One RCT reported a higher functional independence measure score, and two reported higher ASIA motor scores with the use of the EMG-BF. Four RCTs reported reduced spasticity (modified Ashworth scale, MAS), but MAS was reported inconsistently as ordinal grade distributions or as grade-derived scores, precluding any pooled estimate. Three RCTs reported higher Berg balance scale scores with the use of the EMG-BF. Only one pilot RCT reported pain, and it permitted only within-group comparisons. Conclusion Low- to very-low-certainty evidence suggests that EMG-BF may improve sEMG signals, lower-limb muscle strength, functional independence, ASIA motor scores, spasticity and balance in patients with SCI, but these findings are preliminary. Large, well-designed RCTs with allocation concealment, blinding of outcome assessors, standardized comparators and prospective registration are needed. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261282923 , Identifier: [CRD420261282923].
authors: Mingwei Liu; Zhong-yuan Liu; Bing-can Zhang; Shu-ji Gao; Hui-de Peng

title: Evaluating the rehabilitative and assistive impact of the Agilik exoskeleton: a pre–post single-group study in children with cerebral palsy
abstract: Introduction Cerebral palsy (CP) is a common childhood-onset neurological condition often associated with crouch gait, a pathological walking pattern impairing mobility. Wearable robotic devices are emerging as promising tools for paediatric gait rehabilitation, but evidence on their rehabilitative and assistive effects remains limited. This exploratory study evaluated the rehabilitative and assistive effects of a 10-session training programme using Agilik, a paediatric knee exoskeleton, in children with CP and crouch gait, during level-ground, uphill, and downhill walking. Methods Eight children with CP completed the intervention. Assessments were performed at baseline (T0) and post-intervention (T1), including walking endurance, speed, balance, spasticity, and clinical joint and muscle length assessments. Three-dimensional gait analysis (GRAIL system) quantified sagittal-plane hip, knee, and ankle range of motion during level-ground, uphill, and downhill walking. At T1, joint range of motion was analysed with and without Agilik to assess its assistive effect. User satisfaction was evaluated using the child-adapted QUEST 2.1 questionnaire. Results Given the exploratory nature of this study, results were interpreted primarily at the individual level using predefined minimal clinically important difference (MCID) thresholds. When clinically relevant changes occurred, improvements were more frequently observed than deteriorations in walking endurance (MCID > 15 m), speed (MCID > 0.1 m/s), muscle lengths (>5°), and joint range of motion (>5°). No significant group-level rehabilitative changes were observed (all p > 0.05). In contrast, the assistive evaluation showed statistically significant increases in knee and hip range of motion across all walking conditions ( p < 0.05), with all participants improving at the knee in every condition. Satisfaction scores (7-point scale) were high for size, appearance, usability, and set-up time (median ≥ 4/7), while weight, reliability, and timely performance received lower ratings (median 3.5/7). Conclusions This exploratory study demonstrates a clear assistive biomechanical benefit of Agilik, particularly at the knee and hip. Individual-level analyses suggest that some participants may experience clinically meaningful improvements following training; however, these observations are hypothesis-generating and cannot be interpreted as evidence of a rehabilitative effect. Larger randomised controlled studies are needed to determine whether repeated exposure to assisted gait translates into sustained functional gains.
authors: Roberta Nossa; Giorgia Malerba; Anna Falivene; Eleonora Diella; Riccardo Riboni; Valentina Grasso; Luca Emanuele Molteni; Mattia Chiappini; Fabio Alexander Storm; Cristina Maghini; Emilia Biffi

title: Gait disorders in neurological diseases: clinical significance, assessment methods, and rehabilitation potential
abstract: Gait disturbances are a common manifestation of neurological disorders and a major contributor to functional limitations, increased fall risk, and reduced quality of life. Nevertheless, gait impairment often remains underrecognized in routine neurological practice, and its evaluation is frequently confined to basic spatiotemporal parameters, such as gait speed, without sufficient consideration of the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms. The aim of this review was to summarize current evidence regarding the types and mechanisms of gait disorders in neurological diseases, clinical approaches to gait pattern analysis, and contemporary therapeutic strategies. A literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, EMBASE, and The Cochrane Library, focusing on studies examining the clinical characteristics of pathological gait, methods of gait assessment, rehabilitation interventions, and medication-based management of gait disturbances in patients with neurological conditions. The available evidence indicates that different neurological pathologies can result in comparable alterations in fundamental gait parameters, including decreased walking speed and reduced step length. However, detailed gait pattern analysis enables determination of the specific locomotor pattern and facilitates identification of the predominant mechanisms underlying gait impairment, including muscle weakness, spasticity, sensory deficits, impaired motor control, limited joint mobility, and pain. Furthermore, distinguishing primary gait abnormalities from compensatory adaptations is essential for selecting targeted and effective interventions. Optimal functional outcomes are achieved through comprehensive, mechanism-oriented approaches that integrate physical therapy, orthotic management, and oral medication-based or injection-based therapies.
authors: Yuriy Flomin; Anastasiia Orlovska; A.V. Tsyhanii; M.V. Guliaieva; Mykola Romanyshyn; Anastasiia Honchar; I.R. Havryliv; Maksym H. Tsariapkin

title: Electrotherapy in Pediatric Rehabilitation: A Structured Narrative Review of Clinical Applications, Treatment Parameters, Safety, and Evidence Gaps
abstract: Background/Objectives: Electrotherapy encompasses diverse therapeutic modalities used in Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine, but pediatric evidence varies substantially across modality–indication pairs. This structured narrative review critically synthesized evidence on clinical applications, treatment parameters, efficacy, safety, and evidence gaps in pediatric rehabilitation. Methods: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for publications from 1 January 2000 to 17 July 2026. Evidence was synthesized by electrotherapy modality and clinical indication and classified using Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine (OCEBM) Levels of Evidence. Results: The strongest evidence was identified for rESWT in cerebral palsy-related spasticity; TENS and IFC in bladder and bowel dysfunction; and NMES/FES, rTMS, and tDCS for selected motor rehabilitation outcomes. PBM/LLLT, PEMF, and HILT showed promising but indication-specific evidence, whereas TECAR had preliminary adjunctive evidence. Therapeutic ultrasound and Deep Oscillation Therapy remain insufficiently supported, and several modalities lack pediatric clinical evidence. Short-term tolerability was generally favorable, but long-term safety data remain limited. Conclusions: Electrotherapy has an adjunctive role in selected pediatric rehabilitation indications, but prescription should be based on specific modality–indication pairs. Standardized multicenter trials and long-term safety studies are required.
authors: Andreea Veronica Stavăr; Cristina Octaviana Daia; Brînduşa Ilinca Mitoiu; Madalina Codruta Verenca

title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation paired with a 3D-printed ankle-foot orthosis for ankle-foot dysfunction among older adults following subacute stroke: clinical findings and exploratory neurophysiological analyses
abstract: Objective This work evaluated clinical effects of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) plus custom-made 3D-printed ankle-foot orthosis (AFO) for older adults living with post-stroke ankle-foot impairment. Neurophysiological assessments were also carried out for exploratory purposes, drawing exclusively on indirect physiological readouts. Materials and methods Sixty older participants with ankle-foot dysfunction after subacute stroke were randomized into three parallel groups: conventional-only rehabilitation, 3D-printed AFO therapy, and combined rTMS-AFO intervention ( n = 20 per group). Evaluations including ankle active range-of-motion (AROM), resting motor threshold (RMT), integrated surface electromyography (iEMG), Clinical Spasticity Index (CSI), Fugl-Meyer Assessment of the Lower Extremity (FMA-LE), Berg Balance Scale (BBS), and 10-Metre Walking Test (10MWT) were performed at baseline and four-week post-intervention time-point. Results Noticeable within-group functional improvements emerged in all three study arms upon completion of treatment ( p < 0.001). Participants assigned to combined therapy achieved greater functional improvements compared with those receiving standalone 3D-printed-AFO or conventional rehabilitation ( p < 0.05). The conventional rehabilitation group produced the weakest magnitude of functional recovery across measured endpoints. Conclusion Compared with single-modality rehabilitation approaches, adding rTMS to 3D-printed AFO therapy brought measurable improvements in ankle mobility, muscle recruitment, balance and walking performance. These clinical benefits occurred alongside elevated excitability within the ipsilesional corticospinal tract. Explanations regarding sensorimotor integration and afferent-efferent circuit regulation should be regarded as exploratory hypotheses because direct neural measurements were not obtained in this investigation. Further independent research is needed to test these mechanistic assumptions.
authors: Yuting Zhang; Hehe Chen; Rui Xu; Lingyu Zhu; Siyuan Song; Weixin Zhu

title: Lower limb orthotics in cerebral palsy
abstract: Uvod: Cerebralna paraliza je neprogresivna nevrološka motnja, ki nastane kot posledica okvare osrednjega živčnega sistema v obdobju razvoja. Zanjo so značilne trajne motnje v nadzoru gibanja, koordinacije in telesne drže, ki lahko pomembno vplivajo na posameznikovo samostojnost in funkcionalnost v vsakdanjem življenju. Pri osebah s cerebralno paralizo so najpogosteje prizadeti spodnji udi, kjer se pojavlja spastičnost, zmanjšana stabilnost, slabša kontrola gibov in patološki vzorci hoje, ki lahko sčasoma vodijo v razvoj deformacij in drugih sekundarnih mišično-skeletnih sprememb. Pomemben del obravnave predstavlja ortotična oskrba, katere cilj je izboljšanje biomehanike gibanja, stabilizacija sklepov in preprečevanje napredovanja deformacij. Namen: Namen diplomskega dela je predstaviti ortotično obravnavo spodnjih udov pri osebah s cerebralno paralizo in prikazati vpliv različnih ortotičnih rešitev na biomehaniko hoje in funkcionalno mobilnost. Metode dela: V diplomskem delu je bila uporabljena deskriptivna metoda dela s pregledom domače in tuje znanstvene ter strokovne literature. Za iskanje literature smo uporabili bibliografske podatkovne baze: ScienceDirect, PubMed, ResearchGate, Journal of Prosthetics and Orthotics in Google Scholar. Rezultati: V pregled literature je bilo vključenih šest raziskav, ki so obravnavale uporabo ortoz za spodnje ude pri osebah s cerebralno paralizo. Analizirane raziskave poročajo o izboljšanju parametrov hoje, predvsem hitrosti hoje, dolžine koraka, stabilnosti in poravnave sklepov. Stopnja izboljšanja se je med raziskavami razlikovala glede na klinične značilnosti preiskovancev, vrsto uporabljene ortoze in cilje ortotične obravnave. Razprava in zaključek: Uporaba ortoz za spodnje ude pri osebah s cerebralno paralizo pomaga omiliti patološke gibalne vzorce in preprečuje dolgoročni razvoj deformacij. Z ustrezno ortotično oskrbo osebi omogočimo učinkovitejše gibanje, ki je bolj varno in energijsko učinkovito. Uspešnost zdravljenja je odvisna od individualnih značilnosti uporabnika, vrste patologije ter izbire ustrezne ortoze, njenih komponent in materialov. Za doseganje optimalnih rezultatov je potrebno dobro poznavanje biomehanike gibanja, klinične slike cerebralne paralize in principov delovanja ortotičnih pripomočkov.
authors: Taris Vaš
venue: Repository of the University of Ljubljana (University of Ljubljana)

title: Improving undergraduate clinical skills through Generative AI virtual assistants: A pilot study of history taking and physical examination
abstract: Beyond the AI Hype: Evaluating GenAI Virtual Assistants for Undergraduate Clinical Skills Across Kirkpatrick Levels 1 to 3 1. Background & The Educational Problem History-taking and physical examination remain the bedrock of clinical diagnosis, skills developed primarily through experiential practice rather than didactic learning. However, preclinical curricula face chronic structural bottlenecks: students have minimal supervised patient exposure prior to clinical clerkships, while simulated and standardized-patient (SP) encounters demand substantial institutional resources, rooms, trained actors, and faculty time that cannot scale indefinitely. While Generative AI (GenAI) offers scalable, asynchronous simulation, the literature remains saturated with perception-based studies and short-term knowledge recall. Critical questions remain unanswered: Can custom GenAI assistants safely facilitate structured clinical practice? Does performance transfer to authentic human encounters? And crucially, is GenAI truly the active ingredient, or simply an auxiliary tool within structured assessment? 2. The Intervention: Purpose-Built GenAI Assistants We engineered and deployed two specialized, prompt-standardized conversational AI assistants built on Google Gemini (custom Gems) to eliminate instructional variability: Anamnesio : A virtual patient simulating outpatient consultations via free-text dialogue. It remains strictly in character, reveals clinical information only upon structured inquiry, and concludes with automated feedback targeting communication, consultation structure, and diagnostic reasoning. ExplorIA : A Socratic clinical tutor focusing on physical examination. Rather than passively presenting solutions, it introduces diagnostic scenarios where physical findings are pivotal, prompting learners to justify selected maneuvers, interpret signs, and correct procedural reasoning. 3. Study Design & Evaluation Framework We conducted a four-week, multi-phase proof-of-concept study mapped systematically across Kirkpatrick Levels 1 to 3. Participants : Twenty-two third-year medical students (68% women; median age 20) were randomized 1:1, stratified by sex, into sequential training tracks: Group A used Anamnesio only during Weeks 1–2; Group B used ExplorIA only. In Weeks 3–4, all participants accessed both tools concurrently. Assessment Protocol : Students underwent three standardized clinical encounters (Weeks 0, 2, and 4) featuring unseen clinical cases enacted by specialist registrars serving as standardized patients. Objective performance was scored by blinded, trained senior evaluators using validated analytic rubrics (History: 0–9; Physical Examination: 0–7). To isolate independent learning, no human faculty feedback was provided during the intervention period; students received only AI-generated feedback between formal checkpoints. No participants were lost to follow-up) Eight months post-intervention, participants' objective performance was assessed in an authentic hospital clinical practice rotation involving real inpatients, evaluated by clinical faculty entirely blinded to study participation (n=19 vs. n=201 historical/peer controls). 4. Key Findings Kirkpatrick Level 1 (Reaction): Usability and educational acceptability were high: 95.5% found Anamnesio easy to use (81.8% for ExplorIA), and 86.4% reported subjective skill improvement. Crucially, students demonstrated sophisticated pedagogical discernment: 90.9% viewed GenAI as complementary to existing curricular resources, and only 22.7% believed AI could replace real human interactions (63.6% actively disagreed). Kirkpatrick Level 2 (Learning): Objective standardized scores demonstrated statistically significant, large effect-size gains from Week 0 to Week 4: History Taking: Mean baseline increased from 3.0 to 7.0/9 (+4.0 points [95% CI 3.3–4.7], p < 0.001, Hedges' g = 1.5). Physical Examination: Mean baseline increased from 3.3 to 5.5/7 (+2.2 points [95% CI 1.7–2.8], p < 0.001, Hedges' g = 1.3). Kirkpatrick Level 3 (Behavior & Clinical Transfer): In the 8-month follow-up clinical clerkship with real inpatients, participants demonstrated significantly higher median performance than non-participants (9.25 [IQR 9.0–9.5] vs. 9.00 [IQR 8.7–9.5], p = 0.042). Crucially, the primary effect was an elimination of the performance floor: 100% of participants achieved grades > 9.0, whereas non-participant scores ranged widely from 6.0 to 10.0. 5. Critical Nuance: What the Data Actually Reveal In contrast to uncritical portrayals of GenAI in education, our granular analyses challenge AI-centric causation: 1. Absence of Sequence Effect : The initial two-week single-assistant phase yielded no domain-specific advantage; between-group scores did not differ at Week 2 or Week 4. 2. Absence of a Clear Dose-Response Curve: Cumulative usage hours did not correlate with history-taking improvement ($p = 0.729), and physical examination correlated only weakly (\rho = 0.438, p = 0.042), dissolving at subdomain levels. Total platform exposure was remarkably modest (median 3.5 hours for Anamnesio, 2.0 hours for ExplorIA). 3. Rival Explanations :Given the lack of a non-intervention control arm, the observed gains cannot be attributed strictly to GenAI. Instead, the data strongly support programmatic assessment principles: the dominant driver appears to be the *synergistic triad* of autonomous GenAI practice, repeated authentic standardized-patient encounters (testing effect), and rapid-cycle feedback. Furthermore, participant self-selection likely contributed to baseline academic resilience. 6. Curricular Implications: The Tripartite Hybrid Model These findings argue decisively against positioning GenAI as an autonomous replacement for clinical teaching. Instead, we advocate a pragmatic three-tier implementation framework: 1. Asynchronous GenAI Practice: Low-stakes, 24/7 repetitive practice for cognitive framing, communication structure, and procedural justification without patient burden. 2. Standardized Patient Encounters : High-fidelity simulation introducing social realism, non-verbal nuance, and emotional pressure that digital interfaces cannot replicate. 3. Faculty-Led Debriefing : Expert human calibration to contextualize AI feedback, model professional behavior, and prevent diagnostic ossification. Open Science Note: Anonymized participant-level dataset available at DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21207512.
authors: Luís Corral-Gudino; Candela Campo-Martínez; Isabel Herrera Montano; Cecilia Bombin-Escribano; José Pablo Miramontes‐González; Isabel DE LA TORRE-DÍEZ

title: Effectiveness of the SEFT teaching model on the clinical practice competence of surgical residents: a retrospective cohort study
abstract: Background This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of the SEFT teaching model in improving surgical residents’ clinical practice competencies, so as to provide a basis for optimizing training strategies.Methods This single-center, non-randomized retrospective cohort study included 38 residents. The 2019 cohort (n = 19) was the control group, receiving traditional demonstration and practice-based training, while the 2020 cohort (n = 19) was the intervention group, trained via the SEFT teaching model. Scores across five core competencies were compared using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test.Results The intervention group scored significantly higher than the control group across all five assessment domains (all p < 0.05): medical history taking (90.43 ± 3.83 vs. 84.29 ± 10.63, p = 0.039), physical examination (91.20 ± 4.88 vs. 83.76 ± 11.51, p = 0.017), initial medical record documentation (90.61 ± 4.98 vs. 84.20 ± 4.97, p < 0.001), and clinical reasoning and decision-making (87.00 ± 3.64 vs. 80.76 ± 9.24, p = 0.039).Discussion The SEFT teaching model, with its closed-loop structure and targeted feedback, showed promising potential to enhance surgical residents’ clinical practice competencies.
authors: Xiang Jin; Weihong Zhao; Xinye Lin; Xiaomei Xie; Xinli Mao; 李卫林

title: Siliconvs. Stethoscopes: Why Healthcareis Resistingthe Ai Revolution
abstract: The present study attempts to assess if modern artificial intelligence (AI), consisting of CNNs in medical imaging and LLMs in language processing, would replace the physicians in the near future and find the most significant barriers to this process. The narrative review of the scientific literature about AI performance and reproducibility in medical imaging, LLM's competence in assessing medical knowledge and communicating with patients, lack of generalization beyond the distribution, lack of physical examination and sensory input, and the existing regulatory and legal environment, especially the one in the European Union is performed. AI is highly accurate and reproducible in narrowly defined tasks of image interpretation, lesion measurement, triage, documentation assistance, and written communication. These abilities diminish the interobserver variation and improve the workflow efficiency. Physicians are here to stay, and that is for a reason. While the AI is impressively accurate in many tasks, it fails miserably the moment the case is out of the training set distribution, cannot do physical examination and surgery, and still invents some answers with full confidence. Apart from technical problems, the most significant issue here is the one of accountability: who will be sued once an algorithm makes a wrong decision? For a foreseeable future, the AI will remain a valuable assistant, but never a physician. It will be able to handle repetitive and well-defined tasks in the background, but the high-stakes part of medicine – physical examination, complex ethical decisions, bedside care, and overall legal responsibility – will remain a doctor's duty.
authors: Satya Prakash Behera; Manjuta Khadia; Sanatan Pujari; Satwik Kumar Mohanty
venue: International Research Journal on Advanced Engineering Hub (IRJAEH)

title: A FOCUS-PDCA quality improvement model involving unlicensed assistive personnel for improving clinical effectiveness and efficiency in inpatient physical examination: a quasi-experimental, historical-control study
abstract: The accuracy and efficiency of inpatient examinations depend on a well-collaborated working team that involves doctors, nurses, and unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP). This study aimed to evaluate the clinical effectiveness and efficiency of a FOCUS-PDCA quality improvement model involving UAP in improving inpatient physical examinations. A quasi-experimental, historical-control before-and-after study was conducted among 372 patients who received the FOCUS-PDCA quality improvement examination management (the observation group) and another 385 patients under normal management (the control group). Clinical effectiveness and efficiency were compared between the two groups. Compared to the control group, the FOCUS-PDCA group had significantly lower rates of defect examinations (19.6% vs. 44.7%, p < 0.01), nursing interruption events (14.5% vs. 26.4%, p < 0.01), and nurse referral events (6.1% vs. 24.7%, p < 0.01). Furthermore, the FOCUS-PDCA group had higher patient satisfaction (9.04 ± 0.82 vs. 8.45 ± 0.96, p <0.01) lower hospital cost [Median: 29,434.70 RMB (IQR: 9,705.00–52,451.40) vs. 34,537.60 RMB (IQR: 14,689.98–64,222.12), p < 0.001], and shorter length of hospital stay [Median: 4.00 days (IQR: 3.00, 5.00) vs. 5.00 days (IQR: 4.00, 6.00), p < 0.001]. The FOCUS-PDCA model involving UAP was associated with improved clinical effectiveness and efficiency of inpatient physical examination, which may be applied in hospital management to enhance the quality of care and patient outcomes. Further validation in other clinical settings is needed to test its broader application.
authors: Jing Li; Yixia Zhao; Shi Zhou; Guangyan Lv; Weihong Huang; Jianzhong Hu; Jing Chong; Fang Li

title: In Vivo Validation of Automated Knee Arthrometry: What Do These Measurements Really Represent?
abstract: Background: Objective assessment of anterior knee laxity (AKL) is important for evaluating graft integrity after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. Automated arthrometers, such as the GNRB, provide reproducible measurements; however, the in vivo biomechanical meaning and validity of these measurements remain unclear. Hypothesis/Purpose: The primary purpose was to validate GNRB-derived AKL measurements against biplanar videoradiography (BVR)–derived metrics under in vivo postoperative conditions. It was hypothesized that GNRB measurements would differ significantly from BVR-derived measures of tibiofemoral translation and ACL graft elongation. A secondary, exploratory purpose was to examine the relationships between GNRB- and BVR-derived laxity measures. Study Design: Cohort study (Diagnosis); Level of evidence, 2. Methods: Twenty patients (6 months post-ACL reconstruction) underwent simultaneous AKL testing using a GNRB arthrometer and BVR. Six BVR-derived laxity metrics were calculated, including tibiofemoral translation, tibial tuberosity displacement, and ACL graft elongation. Arthrometer accuracy was assessed using a repeated-measures analysis of covariance, and linear regression analyses were used to evaluate relationships between GNRB- and BVR-derived measures. Results: GNRB-derived laxity differed significantly from all BVR-derived measures ( P < .001). Compared with BVR-defined tibiofemoral and graft-based metrics, the GNRB consistently overestimated AKL (bias: 3.4-6.1 mm). The strongest relationship to GNRB was observed in BVR-derived tibial tuberosity displacement expressed in the world coordinate system ( r = 0.93), whereas associations with ACL graft elongation were weakest ( r = 0.51-0.66). Differences between tibial tuberosity displacement expressed relative to the femur versus the world coordinate system indicated a substantial contribution of femoral motion during arthrometric testing. Conclusion: This study provides the first in vivo validation of GNRB-derived AKL measurements following ACL reconstruction. Using BVR as the reference standard, the GNRB consistently overestimated AKL and showed the weakest correlation with ACL graft elongation. These findings highlight the need to better understand how arthrometry relates to knee motion and ACL graft elongation to improve the reliability and clinical interpretation of postoperative AKL assessments.
authors: Tomasz Bugajski; Alonso Figueroa; Bonnie P. Gregory; Walter Richard Lowe; Payam Zandiyeh

title: Prevalence of Bovine Spastic Syndrome in Sweden
abstract: Bovine Spastic Syndrome (BOSS) is a chronic, progressive neuromuscular disorder that affects adult cattle. The disorder causes intermittent episodes of painful cramps in the hindlimbs that impair movement. Little is known about its presence in Sweden. This study aimed to explore the occurrence of clinical signs compatible with BOSS in Swedish cattle herds and to identify herd-level factors associated with farmer-reported cases. An online survey aimed at Swedish cattle owners was conducted between June and September 2025, yielding 201 responses from all 21 counties and a range of production systems. Approximately one-third of respondents reported having observed animals over three years of age showing clinical signs consistent with BOSS. Reports were geographically widespread but varied by county. Observations were substantially more common in dairy herds: 60% of dairy respon-dents had observed signs, and dairy producers accounted for 80% of all positive reports. In contrast, only 6% of beef producers reported observing signs. Although the study relied on self-reported observations and cannot confirm clinical diagnoses, the results indicate that clinical signs compatible with BOSS are present in many parts of Sweden and may be more frequently recognized in dairy systems. These findings highlight the need for improved diagnostic awareness, targeted epidemiological surveillance, and further investigation into risk factors and potential genetic components of the syndrome.
authors: Teodora Linton Fischer
venue: Epsilon Archive for Student Projects (University of Southampton)

title: RADIOLOGICAL JOINT SPACE WIDENING OF THE UNAFFECTED COMPARTMENT IN VARUS OR VALGUS KNEES IS ASSOCIATED WITH ABNORMAL INTRAOPERATIVE LIGAMENTOUS LAXITY
abstract: Introduction Krackow Type II valgus deformity is defined by attenuation of the medial collateral ligament (MCL). However, little quantitative information exists about associated intra-operative MCL laxity. Furthermore, a corollary may exist in varus deformity with associated lateral ligament laxity but is poorly described. Robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (raTKA) includes quantitative assessment of intraoperative ligament function. This study evaluated whether increased preoperative medial or lateral radiographic joint space width (JSW) in valgus or varus knees, was associated with increased intraoperative soft tissue laxity of the respective compartment. Methodology Intraoperative data from 348 consecutive raTKAs with 270 varus knees (hip-knee-ankle angle [HKA]<-2°), and 78 valgus knees, (HKA>2°) were retrospectively reviewed. For varus knees, lateral JSW was measured on preoperative, standing anteroposterior radiographs to determine lateral widening (threshold 8.0mm). For valgus knees, medial JSW was evaluated to determine medial widening (threshold 7.0mm). Intraoperative medial and lateral gaps at 0° and 90° had been recorded during manual stress testing. Linear regression was performed to determine associations between intra-operative gaps, radiographic JSW, and HKA. Results 51 varus knees demonstrated lateral widening and 15 valgus knees had medial widening. In varus knees, lateral JSW was positively associated with the lateral extension (β=0.76, P <0.001) and flexion (β=0.74, P <0.001) gaps. Similarly, for valgus knees, medial JSW was positively associated with the medial extension (β=0.75, P <0.001) and flexion (β=0.77, P <0.001) gaps. Conclusion Increased preoperative radiographic JSW of the medial and lateral compartment in valgus and varus knees, predicted increased intraoperative gaps of that compartment, consistent with ligament attenuation.
authors: Austin E. Wininger; Jose M. Iturregui; Zachary K. Christopher; Joshua S. Bingham; Henry D. Clarke

title: Optimasi Penjadwalan Proses Produksi Berbasis Laxity dengan Algoritma ELLF untuk SmartEdu Station
abstract: Penjadwalan urutan eksekusi job pada mesin produksi merupakan keputusan operasional krusial yang memengaruhi throughput dan pemenuhan tenggat waktu. Di antara algoritma penjadwalan dinamis, pendekatan berbasis laxity dengan Least Laxity First (LLF) secara teoretis optimal namun mengalami laxity thrashing, yaitu peralihan konteks berlebihan ketika beberapa job memiliki nilai laxity yang sama. Penelitian ini mengimplementasikan Enhanced Least Laxity First (ELLF) sebagai perluasan LLF dengan mekanisme exclusion shield untuk menghilangkan thrashing, yang diadaptasi dari penjadwalan prosesor berskala tick mikrodetik ke skala waktu manufaktur berbasis tick detik. Algoritma diterapkan pada arsitektur IoT empat lapis berbiaya rendah menggunakan Raspberry Pi dengan tumpukan pemantauan InfluxDB dan Grafana, pada studi kasus mesin induction-forging baut. Pengujian mencakup dua skenario beban (underload dan overload) dengan delapan job periodik selama lima kali pengulangan independen. Hasil menunjukkan ELLF mencapai nol preemption pada kondisi overload (penurunan 100% dari 1,28 preemption/job pada LLF), dengan trade-off berupa kenaikan waktu tunggu sekitar 15% dan tardiness rata-rata 232 ms. Arsitektur IoT mendistribusikan telemetri penjadwal ke InfluxDB dengan latensi sub-detik tanpa mengganggu kinerja. Melalui pengujian simulasi perangkat lunak, penelitian ini membuktikan secara empiris bahwa pendekatan berbasis laxity, khususnya ELLF, efektif untuk penjadwalan produksi soft real-time pada arsitektur IoT berbiaya rendah. Sistem penjadwalan ini ditujukan untuk diintegrasikan pada SmartEdu Station.
authors: Noer Fajrin; Yuliadi Erdani; Muhammad Avila Thirafi; Suharyadi Pancono; Cyndi Odilia Sumantri; Natasya Nareswari

title: Knee proprioception in children with spastic cerebral palsy: an observational study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Proprioception, the sense of body position and movement, is vital for motor control but has been sparsely explored in children with cerebral palsy (CP), particularly in the lower extremities. This study explored proprioception as the capacity to reproduce and maintain a knee flexion angle in children with CP. METHODS: Fifty-seven children aged 6-18 years with spastic CP; 20 unilateral (USCP), and 37 bilateral (BSCP), at Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) I-IV, and 42 typically developing (TD) children participated. Three-dimensional motion analysis was used to capture knee movements during a joint position sense test performed in sitting with occluded vision. The test consisted of (i) the criterion angle (CA) trial; the leg was passively elevated to a knee flexion angle of 45 degrees (CA) by an examiner and the position was maintained by the child, and (ii) the reproduced angle (RA) trial; the angle was actively reproduced (RA) and maintained by the child. Joint position sense errors were evaluated as the difference between CA and RA. The children's capacity to maintain the leg position was measured as the difference in knee angles, fluctuations (root mean square error) and drift (linear regression). Data were analysed with non-parametric statistics. RESULTS: Joint position sense errors were greater in the USCP-group than the BSCP-group (p = 0.037), with a more extended knee in the USCP-group (p = 0.012). When maintaining the passively positioned knee angle for 2.5 s, the CP-group compared to the TD-group, showed increased knee flexion and greater movement fluctuations (p = 0.006). Within-group analysis showed increased knee flexion at the passively assumed position (CA vs. maintained for 2.5 s) compared to at the actively assumed position (RA vs. maintained for 2.5 s) in the BSCP-group (p = 0.015) and the GMFCS II-group (p = 0.028). The BSCP-group also showed increased drift over time towards knee flexion when the leg was passively compared to actively positioned (p = 0.040). CONCLUSIONS: The results reveal a divergence in proprioceptive function: while the USCP-group had greater difficulty than the BSCP-group in reproducing a knee angle, the BSCP-group demonstrated greater difficulty in maintaining the knee position during passive positioning of the lower limb. TRIAL REGISTRATION: This study was observational and was therefore not registered as a clinical trial.
authors: Annika Ericson; Åsa Bartonek; Israel Luis; Marie Eriksson; Cecilia M. Lidbeck

title: Joint line obliquity change was associated with femoral and tibial resection patterns and smaller final flexion imbalance after robot‐assisted total knee arthroplasty
abstract: Abstract Purpose Associations between preoperative‐to‐post‐operative changes in arithmetic hip–knee–ankle angle (aHKA) and joint line obliquity (JLO) and final balance after robot‐assisted total knee arthroplasty (TKA) were evaluated. Relationships with resection redistribution and tibial‐varus reduction were also examined. Methods A retrospective single‐surgeon series of 402 primary robot‐assisted TKAs was analysed. Preoperative and post‐operative aHKA, JLO and coronal plane alignment of the knee (CPAK) type were determined from full‐length radiographs. Final extension and flexion imbalance and laxity ranges after trial implantation were the primary outcomes. Signed and absolute changes were assessed in multivariable models; resection redistribution and a varus‐only tibial‐boundary subgroup were examined in supportive analyses. Results A change in CPAK type was observed in 300 knees (74.6%), including a JLO‐zone change in 221 (55.0%). Greater ΔJLO was associated with smaller final flexion imbalance (β = −0.060; p < 0.001) and a narrower final extension laxity range ( β = −0.055; p = 0.002). Corresponding associations were found for |ΔJLO| ( β = −0.046; p = 0.018 and β = −0.070; p = 0.004). Neither signed nor absolute aHKA change was associated with final extension or flexion imbalance. In varus knees, tibial‐varus reduction was associated with greater JLO and aHKA changes, coronal femoral adjustment and smaller final flexion imbalance. Neither |ΔaHKA| nor |ΔJLO| was associated with improvement in the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement. Conclusions Greater JLO change was associated with smaller final flexion imbalance and a narrower extension laxity range rather than impaired balance. In varus knees, JLO change accompanied tibial‐varus reduction and coordinated femoral adjustment. JLO change may therefore reflect specific aspects of the final balancing state rather than an unintended deviation from the native phenotype. Level of Evidence Level III, retrospective cohort study.
authors: Yugo Morita; Jonggu Shin; Mohammed El-Hassan; Ittai Shichman; William John Long; Peter Keyes Sculco

title: Robotic exoskeleton Remotion in outpatient gait rehabilitation for young adult patients with cerebral palsy
abstract: Background. Although a significant number of studies have focused on the rehabilitation of children patients with cerebral palsy (CP), the use of restorative treatment in the adult population with this pathology remains understudied. High-technology robot-assisted rehabilitation using exoskeleton systems for gait restoration has proven effective in various neurological disorders, including the rehabilitation of children with CP. However, questions concerning the application of these methods in adult patients require further clarification. Aim. To investigate the effect of robot-assisted gait training in an exoskeleton in an outpatient setting on mobility, gait speed, and gait biomechanics in adult patients with CP (students of an inclusive university), and to determine the feasibility and effectiveness (i.e., the appropriateness) of outpatient motor rehabilitation using such training for this patient population. Materials and methods. The study included 11 patients with spastic CP (spastic diplegia), classified as Gross Motor Function Classification System levels II–III. All patients underwent 10 training sessions on the Remotion robotic exoskeleton system (JSC "Volzhsky Electromechanical Plant", Russian Federation) once a day, 5 days a week. Clinical assessment included the timed up and go test and the 10-meter walk test. To objectify the clinical assessment data, biomechanical analysis of cyclic walking was performed using the Biomekhanika Nevrokor system (LLC Nevrokor, Russian Federation). Results. The study demonstrated a clinically significant improvement in mobility as assessed by the timed up and go test (p 0.05) and in fast walking speed measured by the 10-meter walk test (p 0.05). Based on the gait biomechanics analysis, the patients were divided into two groups: a symmetric gait group (n = 5) and an asymmetric gait group (n = 5). In the asymmetric gait group, a statistically significant improvement in step phase symmetry was observed after the rehabilitation course using the Remotion exoskeleton system. These changes occurred due to a reduction in compensatory movements at the hip joint and normalization of the phase characteristics of the flexion/extension angles of the lower limb joints. Conclusion. The present study confirmed that outpatient motor rehabilitation using robot-assisted therapy with an exoskeleton system is feasible, appropriate, and effective in adult patients with a previously established diagnosis of CP who are continuing their higher education.
authors: Anastasia E. Khizhnikova; A. S. Glukhov; А. Н. Островский; K. A. Sargsyan; L.A. Savin; Иконникова Екатерина Сергеевна; Олена Анатоліївна Кириченко; Sergey Nikolaevich Illarioshkin; V.I. Mikhalev; Natalia A. Suponeva

title: FUNCTIONAL ALIGNMENT REDUCES RESIDUAL LATERAL LAXITY AND IMPROVES PATIENT SATISFACTION COMPARED WITH MECHANICAL ALIGNMENT USING A 3° MEDIALLY INCLINED JOINT LINE IMPLANT IN CONSTITUTIONAL VARUS KNEES
abstract: Purpose This study compared postoperative laxity and clinical outcomes between mechanically aligned total knee arthroplasty (MA-TKA) and functional alignment TKA (FA-TKA) using a 3° medially inclined joint line implant in patients with Coronal Plane Alignment of the Knee (CPAK) type 1. Methods This retrospective cohort study included patients with preoperative CPAK type 1 who underwent primary unilateral TKA for osteoarthritis with ≥12 months follow-up. All procedure used an implant with a 3° medially inclined joint line and a bi-cruciate substituting design, performed using manual MA-TKA (2017–2021) or robotic-assisted FA-TKA (2022–2024). Among 155 eligible patients, 44 matched pairs were generated using propensity matching for age, sex, follow-up duration and preoperative Forgotten Joint Score-12 (FJS-12). Radiographic parameters including the arithmetic hip–knee–ankle angle (aHKA) and joint line obliquity (JLO), were measured pre- and postoperatively. Varus–valgus stress radiographs at 1 year quantified medial and lateral joint opening. Patient-reported outcomes included FJS-12, Knee Society Score (KSS), and Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Scores (KOOS). Results At 1 year, lateral opening under varus stress was smaller after FA-TKA (4.8 ± 1.9 vs 6.0 ± 2.1; p =0.03), whereas medial opening under valgus stress did not differ. FA-TKA produced a more varus postoperative aHKA (−2.4 ± 1.8 vs −1.4 ± 2.6; p = 0.03) and required less coronal correction (ΔaHKA: 3.0 ± 2.8 vs 4.6 ± 3.3; p = 0.01). Greater coronal correction correlated with larger lateral opening (r = 0.39; p = 0.0006). FA-TKA demonstrated greater improvement in KSS satisfaction scores (18.9 ± 8.2 vs 15.2 ± 8.3; p = 0.04). FJS-12 scores were higher after FA-TKA; however, not statisticaly significant. Conclusion In CPAK type 1 knees, robotic-assisted FA-TKA better preserved coronal alignment and reduced postoperative lateral laxity compared with manual MA-TKA, resulting in higher patient satisfaction at 1 year.
authors: Ken Okazaki; Shunya Otani; Masafumi Itoh; Umito Kuwashima; Junya Itou

title: Preoperative coronal phenotype is associated with the initial balance state but only weakly with final balance in robot‐assisted TKA
abstract: Abstract Purpose To determine how preoperative coronal phenotype and structural remodelling relate to initial and final intraoperative balance in robot‐assisted total knee arthroplasty. Methods Initial analyses included 429 knees; final/change analyses included 389. Preoperative phenotype was characterised by hip‐knee‐ankle angle (HKA), arithmetic HKA (aHKA), functional knee phenotype (FKP), and categorical aHKA–joint‐line obliquity (JLO) components. Structural factors included medial and lateral osteophyte burden and coronal tibiofemoral subluxation. Medial and lateral gaps and coronal laxity ranges were recorded in extension and flexion before and after balancing. Signed mediolateral gap difference was defined as lateral minus medial, and change as final minus initial. Initial extension signed gap difference was the primary outcome; corresponding initial flexion, final, and change outcomes were secondary. Compartment‐specific gaps, laxity ranges, and varus–valgus analyses were exploratory. Multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index, with patient‐level cluster‐robust standard errors and Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction. Results The FKP model incorporating all structural factors yielded adjusted R 2 values of 0.201 for the primary outcome and 0.125 for initial flexion, leaving approximately 80% of primary‐outcome variability unexplained. In the overall cohort, the maximum adjusted R 2 across final outcomes was 0.064. For extension and flexion changes, FKP alone and HKA alone yielded adjusted R 2 values of 0.234 and 0.122, respectively. In exploratory comparisons, valgus knees had greater initial extension and flexion signed gap differences than varus knees (adjusted mean differences, 3.10 mm [95% confidence interval, 2.39–3.81] and 2.98 mm [2.23–3.74], respectively; both false discovery rate‐adjusted p values were < 0.001). Conclusions Preoperative coronal phenotype and structural remodelling explained only modest variability in the initial intraoperative balance state and changes between assessments, and little variability in final balance, particularly in flexion. These findings support direct intraoperative assessment. Level of Evidence Level III, retrospective cohort study.
authors: Yugo Morita; Nikolaos Mylonakis; Jonggu Shin; Mohammed El-Hassan; Ittai Shichman; Eustathios Kenanidis; Eleftherios Tsiridis; Peter Keyes Sculco

title: The impact of intensive treatment on gait in an adult with spastic cerebral palsy - a case study
abstract: Uvod: Cerebralna paraliza je neprogresivna motnja, ki nastane zaradi okvare nerazvitih možganov. Povzroči motorične motnje, ki so pogosto združene s kognitivnimi motnjami. Hoja je ena najpogosteje prizadetih funkcij oseb s CP. Večina raziskav o učinkovitosti intenzivnih terapevtskih intervencij za izboljšanje hoje obravnava otroke in mladostnike, medtem ko so spremembe, dosegljive v odrasli dobi, slabo raziskane. Namen: Namen raziskave je bil ovrednotiti spremembe hoje pri odrasli osebi s cerebralno paralizo po obdobju intenzivne terapevtske obravnave. Metode dela: Izvedli smo študijo primera. Vključen je bil 22-letni moški preiskovanec s spastično diplegijo, razvrščen v prvo stopnjo po sistemu GMFCS. Meritve smo izvedli pred in po fizioterapevtski obravnavi. Uporabili smo vprašalnik RAND-36, modificirano Ashworthovo lestvico, test hoje na 10 metrov (hitrost, kadenca), meritve dolžinskih spremenljivk hoje, časovno merjeni test vstani in pojdi ter šestminutni test hoje. Fizioterapevtska obravnava je potekala trikrat tedensko in je obsegala 50 enot, ki so vključevale funkcijsko vadbo hoje, učenje hoje, vadbo za povečanje mišične sile, hojo na prostem in igro z loparjem (padel). Rezultati: Po fizioterapevtski obravnavi smo zabeležili klinično pomembne izboljšave. Hitrost sproščene hoje se je povečala za 11,6 % (0,16 m/s), hitrost hitre hoje pa za 28,6 % (0,54 m/s). Kadenca se je pri sproščeni hoji povečala za 11 korakov na minuto, pri hitri hoji za 32 korakov na minuto. Prehojena razdalja pri šestminutnem testu hoje se je podaljšala za 179 metrov (31,1 %), čas pri testu vstani in pojdi pa se je skrajšal za 0,99 sekunde (19,6 %). V domeni telesnega delovanja vprašalnika RAND-36 smo zabeležili izboljšanje za 25 točk. Spastičnost po modificirani Ashworthovi lestvici je ostala nespremenjena. Zmanjšala se je tudi variabilnost dolžine in širine desnega koraka med hitro hojo. Razprava in zaključek: Rezultati kažejo, da je intenzivna, v funkcijo usmerjena terapevtska obravnava pri odraslem s spastično obliko CP privedla do klinično pomembnih izboljšav v hitrosti hoje, vzdržljivosti hoje, funkcijski premičnosti in kakovosti življenja, in sicer brez sprememb v spastičnosti. Ugotovitve podpirajo smiselnost izvajanja intenzivnih programov tudi v odrasli dobi in dopolnjujejo še razmeroma omejeno literaturo na tem področju. Zaradi narave študije primera rezultatov ni mogoče posploševati, zato so za posplošitev ugotovitev potrebne nadaljnje raziskave z večjim vzorcem in dolgoročnim spremljanjem.
authors: Žan Vrhovnik
venue: Repository of the University of Ljubljana (University of Ljubljana)

title: THE REPRODUCTION OF THE NATIVE LAXITY PHENOTYPE GUARANTEES A MORE NATURAL KNEE KINEMATICS COMPARED TO THE RESTORATION OF THE STATIC MORPHOTYPE: A GAIT ANALYSIS EVALUATION FOLLOWING TOTAL KNEE ARTHROPLASTY
abstract: Introduction Alternative alignments in total knee arthroplasty (TKA) are gaining popularity over mechanical alignment because they aim to replicate patients’ natural alignment and restore the original joint line position and obliquity as measured on preoperative weight-bearing X-rays. Supporters of these alternative methods also argue that their approach more accurately replicates natural knee motion. This study presents gait analysis data from patients who underwent TKA, comparing objective outcomes after restoring their preoperative bony morphotype with those after achieving ideal native ligament laxity. Materials and Methods This gait analysis study included 41 patients who underwent TKA. Inclusion criteria were a minimum 9-month follow-up after successful primary medial-pivot or medially congruent TKA for isolated degenerative knee disease. Patients were randomly assigned to three surgical groups, matched by age, sex, and BMI: A) Unrestricted Kinematic Alignment (uKA) (#12); B) Robot-assisted (#12) restricted-KA (rKA: ±3° from the neutral hip-knee-ankle axis) with a slight asymmetry in the intercompartmental gap (maximum 2 mm lateral opening); C) Augmented reality-assisted (#17) TKA (AR) with the medial collateral ligament (MCL) exhibiting nearly isometric intraoperative behavior throughout the range of motion. In groups B and C, intraoperative soft-tissue balancing was recorded at 30° of knee flexion using the included classification (Figure 1) based on ideal native ligament laxity. Gait analysis was performed on instrumented treadmills equipped with 3D cameras, and both spatiotemporal and kinematic parameters were recorded. Results Sagittal knee kinematic data: During the early-stance phase of gait, the uKA group exhibited less consistent weight acceptance and a less efficient transition from the first knee-flexion peak to the mid-stance extension plateau than the rKA and AR groups. Analysis of the flexion peak during gait showed a statistically significant difference between the uKA group (38º±6.0º) and the rKA (45º±10.0º) and AR (49.0º± 9.34º) groups. Spatiotemporal and gait quality data: No statistically significant differences were found among the three groups in walking speed and step length, though the rKA and AR groups showed a trend toward better performance. Conclusion This study presents objective data indicating that newer alignment techniques, which aim to restore patients’ static phenotype and native joint line obliquity as determined on preoperative long, weight-bearing films, do not reproduce near-normal native knee kinematics; better performance was achieved by targeting a slight intercompartmental asymmetry.
authors: Pier Francesco Indelli; Fjorela Qordja; Pieralberto Valpiana; Andrea Giordano Salvi; Michele Paolo Festini Capello; Stefano Ghirardelli

title: Evaluation of high-dose alerts in computed tomography using an automated dose monitoring system: a retrospective institutional study
abstract: Radiation dose monitoring software (DMS) tools are increasingly used to support automated monitoring of radiation dose in medical imaging. This study evaluated the frequency and causes of high-dose events detected by a DMS in computed tomography (CT). All CT examinations performed at one hospital across three CT scanners over a one-year period were retrospectively analysed to establish the frequency and causes of high-dose alerts. Descriptive statistics summarized alert frequency and distribution, and multivariable logistic regression identified factors independently associated with high-dose alerts. Of 11,865 CT examinations, 851 (7%) exceeded predefined dose thresholds. High-dose alerts occurred most frequently in spine (17%), musculoskeletal joint (14%), abdomen/pelvis (8%), vascular angiography (8%), chest/lung (5%), and head/face (4%) examinations. Reasons for high-dose alerts included high body mass index (29%), scan repetition (25%), additional scans (15%), patient malpositioning (12%), excess scan range (11%), and orthopaedic hardware (6%). Multivariable analysis showed that overweight status, scanner model, spine and joint examinations, and patients aged 45-74 years were independently associated with high-dose alert occurrence (P < .05). DMS is an effective tool that enables imaging facilities to automatically identify high-dose events, facilitating investigation of their causes, protocol review, and identification of opportunities for dose optimisation.
authors: Mohammed Sadon Alanazi; Peter L. Kench; Seyedamir Tavakoli-Taba; Matthew Russell; Ernest Usang Ekpo

title: Physical Ergonomics in Robotics
abstract: With the emergence of embodied intelligent systems like collaborative robots (cobots), the landscape of physically demanding work is changing. Indeed, robotic devices can augment human strength, optimize performance, and minimize the physical demands associated with a job or a task. These achievements of human-robot interaction (HRI) surely match the objectives of physical ergonomics: making physical interactions between humans and other elements of a system more efficient, more gratifying, and safer. One of the key goals of physical ergonomics certainly is to prevent work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs). Therefore, a cobot must have insight into the effect of physical stress on the human body. One of the most common ways to provide that is to use the established ergonomics look-up tables that indicate which working configurations and conditions may cause WMSDs based on experience. Another approach is to use musculoskeletal models to get real-time estimates of key internal body parameters, such as joint torques, muscle forces, and muscle fatigue. A cobotic or, in general, robotic system can then use these ergonomic indexes and variables to guide a human co-worker to more favourable configurations and conditions. In this chapter, we examine physical human-robot interactions (pHRIs) to have an introductory overview of possible scenarios and constraints. We then look into the fundamentals of physical ergonomics such as anthropometry, biomechanics, and environmental factors, including important ergonomic assessment tools and innovative indicators developed in robotics. Subsequently, concrete examples of methods that address physical ergonomics with collaborative robotics are examined in terms of design and control methods.
authors: Pauline Maurice; Luka Peternel; WanSoo Kim; Simona Crea; Vineet Vashista; Giacinto Barresi; Alberto Ranavolo; Anna Bucchieri; Giulia A. Albanese; Michael Holmes; Jacopo Zenzeri

title: Optimal Admittance Control of Human–Robot Interaction for Robotic Rehabilitation Under Uncertainties
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper presents a human–robot interaction (HRI) scheme by using an adaptive admittance control, which helps stroke patients perform rehabilitation training tasks and optimizes their performance. Considering the impact of human factors, the control structure is designed to have two control loops. In the inner loop design, a model‐free adaptive control (MFAC) method is proposed to handle the unmodeled dynamics and unknown disturbances for the desired trajectory tracking, and the convergence and boundedness of this method are strictly proved by using the compression mapping principle. Then, a task‐specific outer loop is developed to find the optimal parameters of the admittance model and transformed into an LQR problem, and a learning algorithm is utilized to solve the given problem without requiring knowledge of the human arm model. Considering the safety of HRI, the constraint of the end‐effector orientation is designed. Simulation studies indicate that the proposed strategy effectively enables stroke patients to execute active training tasks on the robotic exoskeleton.
authors: Xinglong Pei; Liqun Wen; Jianhui Wang
venue: International Journal of Robust and Nonlinear Control

title: Volitional control of wearable robots
abstract: This Comment motivates the development of human–machine interfaces that decode spinal motor neuron activity and resulting muscle force information in moving humans. Such interfaces could enable users across the neuromuscular functional spectrum to volitionally control wearable robots with muscle-like behaviour.
authors: Massimo Sartori; Gregory S. Sawicki

title: Botulinum toxin type a within function-oriented management of post-stroke spasticity: a narrative review
abstract: Post-stroke spasticity (PSS) is a heterogeneous complication of stroke that affects motor recovery, care needs, pain, positioning, and participation in daily life. Current management frameworks commonly stratify patients by time since stroke, but disease duration alone does not capture differences in neural mechanisms, residual voluntary control, functional priorities, or response to intervention. This narrative review searched PubMed, the Cochrane Library, and Wanfang databases from inception to May 2026, prioritizing randomized controlled trials, prospective cohort studies, systematic reviews, real-world studies, Goal Attainment Scaling research, the Upper Limb International Spasticity cohort series, best-practice guidance, and clinical trials including BEST and InTENSE. We synthesize evidence that PSS heterogeneity can be understood across central and peripheral mechanisms, temporal trajectories, and active versus passive functional consequences. Available studies suggest that active and passive functional goals differ in baseline functional profiles, outcome assessment, treatment response, and intervention requirements. However, patients sharing a functional goal type may still differ in residual voluntary control, neural and non-neural contributors to movement restriction, pain, mobility, and care dependency. Botulinum toxin type A is well aligned with focal tone reduction and passive goals, including pain relief, hygiene, and limb positioning. It may also support contracture-prevention strategies when modifiable neural muscle overactivity remains, whereas active functional gains usually require preserved motor potential and integration with task-oriented training, rehabilitation, and adjunctive modalities. We propose that functional goal type should complement time-based staging as a decision dimension rather than serve as a complete clinical phenotype. This combined framework may better align patient selection, intervention matching, outcome assessment, and longitudinal treatment planning. Prospective goal-stratified studies and standardized assessment tools are needed to test its clinical utility.
authors: Baoling Su; Yating Huang; Xiaotong Li; Kun Wang; Bing Bao

title: PROSPECTIVE DOUBLE-BLINDED RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL ON ROBOTIC ARM-ASSISTED VERSUS CONVENTIONAL ONE-STAGE BILATERAL TOTAL KNEE ARTHROPLASTY WITH TWO-YEAR FOLLOW-UP
abstract: Introduction Robotic arm assisted total knee arthroplasty(RA-TKA) has gained popularity. Yet for postoperative pain and patient reported outcomes, high quality evidence is lacking. We hypothesize that RA-TKA would provide better postoperative pain control and patient reported outcomes in Chinese patients. Methods This is a double blinded randomized controlled trial(RCT) with 2-year follow-up in patients undergoing one stage bilateral total knee arthroplasty at a tertiary institution. All patients were randomized to receive one conventional TKA(C-TKA) targeting mechanical alignment while the other received RA-TKA targeting restricted kinematic alignment. Triathlon cruciate retaining cementless TKA were used exclusively. Primary outcome measure was numeric pain score(10). Secondary outcome included patient's preferred side, Oxford knee score(OKS), Knee injury and osteoarthritis outcome score(KOOS), mediolateral laxity, range of motion(ROM), alignment and complications. Measurements were recorded preoperatively, daily during inpatient stay, 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year and 2 years. Results 59 patients(118 TKAs) completed the study. RA-TKA group showed statistically significant better pain score than C-TKA on postop Day 3 (RA-TKA: 4.6, C-TKA: 4.2, p =0.014) up to 6 weeks (RA-TKA: 3, C-TKA: 2.6, p =0.04). There was no difference in patient's preferred side at 6 weeks, 1 year and 2 years with 29% favouring conventional side, 36% favouring robotic side and 35% felt no difference between two sides (p=0.36). Oxford knee scores, KOOS scores were comparable. Operating times were longer for RA-TKA(97 min) compared to C-TKA(81min)(p<0.001). Medial-lateral laxity at both 0° and 90° were significantly more in C-TKA(6° and 6°) compared to RA-TKA(4.1° and 3.7°) respectively(both p<0.001). Postoperative alignment showed significantly more alignment outliers(>3°deviation) with C-TKA(16) compared to RA-TKA(10). Discussion and Conclusion This double blinded RCT demonstrated small but significant reduction in pain for RA-TKA compared with C-TKA before 6 weeks but similar patient reported outcomes. There was no clear preference of robotic or conventional side surgery.
authors: Henry FU; Vincent Wai Kwan Chan; Amy Cheung; Man Hong Cheung; Michelle Hilda Luk; Kwong Yuen Chiu

title: ROBOTIC QUANTIFICATION AND CLINICAL VALIDATION OF SURGICAL STRATEGIES FOR INTRAOPERATIVE EXTENSION DEFICIENCY IN TOTAL KNEE ARTHROPLASTY: DEVELOPMENT OF A PREDICTIVE ALGORITHM
abstract: Purpose Intraoperative extension deficiency (IED) following trial implantation in total knee arthroplasty (TKA) must be distinguished from preoperative fixed flexion contracture (FFC). Its optimal management remains poorly quantified and likely depends on patient-specific biomechanical and geometric factors. This study aimed to quantify the mechanical contribution of posterior capsule release (PCR), posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) excision, and incremental distal femoral resection using robotic-assisted measurement, and to develop a predictive model incorporating deformity and femoral geometry. Materials and Methods A two-phase study was performed. A cadaveric robotic-assisted TKA model (29 knees) assessed sequential effects of PCR, PCL excision, and distal femoral resection on extension and laxity. A prospective clinical cohort of 195 robotic-assisted TKAs with IED was then analyzed to validate biomechanical relationships in vivo. A multivariable regression model was constructed to estimate the effect of distal femoral resection on extension correction, incorporating flexion contracture coronal alignment, implant positioning, and femoral size as a geometric scaling factor. Results In the cadaveric model, PCR corrected IED in 36.8% of cases (1.68° ± 1.11°). Distal femoral resection produced 4.3°/mm with an intact PCL and 2.8°/mm after PCL excision. PCL excision alone provided minimal correction (1.1° ± 1.3°). Larger femoral morphology reduced angular gain per millimeter of resection, consistent with geometric scaling effects. In the clinical cohort, distal femoral resection showed a mean effect of 5.8°/mm but demonstrated marked inter-patient variability. Correction sensitivity increased with native flexion contracture (+0.72°/mm per degree) and varus alignment (+0.1°/mm per degree), while femoral size reduced angular response. PCL status was not significant. Conclusions Distal femoral resection is the dominant factor in correcting IED, but its effect is not fixed. It is modulated by deformity severity and femoral geometry, particularly size-dependent scaling of the femorotibial radius. These findings support a nonlinear, patient-specific mechanical model of extension correction and provide a basis for predictive intraoperative decision-making in TKA.
authors: Joan Leal‐Blanquet; Oriol Pujol; Erquicia Ji; Novillos M; Albert Pons; Pedro Hinarejos

title: Medial expected gap (mEG): a quantitative, biology-guided predictor of coronal plane correction and knee balance in robotic functionally aligned total knee arthroplasty
authors: Harish Kumar Murugesan; Rex Chandrabose; Avinash TP; C. Premanand

title: Mediolateral Joint Balance Assessment Is Reproducible Between Surgeons, Under No Standardized Varus–Valgus Stress, During Robot-Assisted Total Knee Arthroplasty
abstract: Objective: To evaluate inter-surgeon variability in mediolateral joint balance assessment during robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (TKA) using the robotic surgical assistant (ROSA) Knee System, and to determine whether such variability influences the surgical planning generated by this system. Methods: An observational study was conducted including 101 patients undergoing primary robotic-assisted TKA. Two experienced surgeons independently assessed intraoperative mediolateral laxity by manually applying varus–valgus stress across six predefined flexion angles (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, and 120°). Measurements of medial and lateral gaps (mm) and varus–valgus alignment (°) were recorded using the ROSA Knee System. Inter-observer differences were analysed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and reliability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). The impact of inter-surgeon variability on surgical planning, including bone resection and compartmental space measurement parameters, was also evaluated. Results: No statistically significant inter-observer differences were observed in mediolateral gap measurements or varus–valgus alignment across all flexion angles (p > 0.05). Inter-observer reliability for varus–valgus measurements was good to excellent in extension and early flexion (ICC 0.86–0.91), decreased to moderate at 90° (ICC 0.68–0.74) and was poor for varus assessment at 120° (ICC 0.46, 95% CI 0.29–0.60). For gap measurements, reliability was excellent for the medial gap and good for the lateral gap in extension (ICC 0.93 and 0.89, respectively), and moderate for both gaps at 90° (ICC 0.71–0.74). No significant inter-observer differences were found in cut or space measurements, with excellent agreement for cut parameters (ICC > 0.95). Conclusions: Inter-surgeon assessment of mediolateral joint balance during robot-assisted TKA showed good-to-excellent reproducibility in extension and early flexion, with reduced reproducibility in deep flexion. Statistically significant inter-observer differences were not observed in the resulting cut and space measurements.
authors: Graciela Grillo; Alexandre Coelho; David Martí; Marçal Pineda Tortajada; Sergi Gil-González; Juan Manuel Peñalver; X. Pelfort López

title: Postoperative Quadriceps Symmetry, Knee Laxity, and Single-Leg Hop Performance in Association with 24-Month Ipsilateral Graft Retear After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Cohort Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Ipsilateral graft retear after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) remains a major concern in athletes, while the relationship between postoperative mechanical and functional measures and retear remains uncertain. METHODS: This cohort study included 48 athletes after primary unilateral ACLR with hamstring-tendon autograft. Follow-up was scheduled at 6, 9, and 12 months (184 ± 13, 276 ± 17, and 368 ± 22 days), and the analytic export retained one postoperative value per athlete for GNRB side-to-side laxity at 250 N, concentric isokinetic quadriceps limb symmetry index (LSI) at 60°/s, single-leg hop-for-distance LSI, and patient-reported outcomes, without preserving the originating visit. MRI-confirmed ipsilateral graft retear was recorded within 24 months after clinically suspected reinjury; retear dates were not retained. RESULTS: = 0.011), and each 1-SD higher quadriceps LSI was associated with lower retear odds (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.21-0.89). In an exploratory threshold analysis, quadriceps LSI < 85% was associated with a higher retear proportion (RR 3.21, 95% CI 1.17-8.82). Associations for knee laxity, hop performance, and patient-reported outcomes were not statistically robust. CONCLUSIONS: Postoperative quadriceps symmetry showed the clearest association with 24-month graft-retear status. However, because the originating measurement visit and retear dates were unavailable, temporal precedence could not be established, and the exploratory <85% LSI finding should not be interpreted as a validated return-to-sport threshold.
authors: Georgios Kakavas; Nikos Malliaropoulos; Florian Forelli

title: Active Function Improvement with Repeated Injections of Botulinum Toxin A in Upper Limb Spasticity: A Longitudinal Analysis from the ULIS-III Study
abstract: Improvement in active function (making it easier to use the limb) is a common goal following treatment of upper limb spasticity with botulinum toxin (BoNT-A). ULIS-III was a large international, observational, longitudinal study (N = 953) conducted in the context of usual clinical practice over two years. In this secondary post hoc analysis, we examine whether goals for improvement in active function were met over repeated injection cycles. Patients were selected if improved active function (AF) was a primary/secondary goal for at least one cycle of treatment (n = 286/953). They were assessed at the start and end of each cycle using the Goal Attainment T-score alongside the Arm Activity measure (ArmA). Serial changes and predictors of improvement were explored. Across eight cycles, there were 1167 injections for active function, 875/1998 (44%) AF goals were set and 493 (57%) of those goals were achieved. Patients continued to show significant improvement in AF (p < 0.001) for each injection at least up to three cycles, which is likely to be clinically significant, especially in patients with milder spasticity who were naïve to BoNT-A. No statistically significant predictors were confirmed on mixed effects modeling. Conclusions: Repeated BoNT-A continued to produce significant improvement in active function for at least three cycles, regardless of patient- or treatment-related factors in this cohort, but type II errors due to small numbers cannot be excluded.
authors: Stephen A. Ashford; Mark Weatherall; Klemens Fheodoroff; Jorge Jacinto; Richard John Siegert; Christian Hannes; Lynne F. Turner‐Stokes

title: A Retensionable Inlay/Onlay Hybrid Double-Bundle Medial Collateral Ligament Reconstruction Produces Superior Restoration of the Uninjured State When Compared to a Single-Bundle Inlay Reconstruction
abstract: Background: Traditional superficial medial collateral ligament (sMCL) reconstruction techniques have not consistently restored native laxity. Purpose/Hypothesis: The purpose of this study was to develop a retensionable inlay/onlay hybrid medial collateral ligament (MCL) reconstruction through comparison to a biomechanically and clinically validated reconstruction. It was hypothesized that increasing the distal footprint on the tibia through a double-bundle construct and a retensionable construct would better restore native laxity. Study Design: Controlled laboratory study. Methods: A total of 27 cadaveric knees were tested on a 6 degrees of freedom robot system. Knees were tested with valgus and external rotation (ER). Each knee was tested in a native state and an injured state after sectioning of the sMCL. One of 3 reconstructions using an anterior tibialis allograft was then performed: (1) single-bundle inlay reconstruction, (2) double-bundle inlay/onlay hybrid reconstruction with tibial fixation at both the proximal and distal (PD) tibial insertions of the sMCL footprint, or (3) double-bundle inlay/onlay hybrid reconstruction with tibial fixation at the anterior and posterior (AP) aspects of the distal sMCL tibial insertion. The constructs used retensionable variable-loop devices, allowing for retensioning after knee cycling. The constructs were tested after cycling and retensioning. Results: Sectioning of the sMCL resulted in significantly increased laxity compared to the native state for both valgus and ER laxity testing ( P < .001). After flexion cycling and subsequent retensioning, both AP and PD double-bundle reconstructions demonstrated significantly higher restoration of stability compared to cycled single-bundle reconstructions ( P < .001). Both double-bundle reconstructions were significantly closer to the native state than the single-bundle reconstruction for valgus rotation ( P < .001) and ER ( P < .05). For valgus testing, there was no difference between retensioned double-bundle constructs and the native state, with a pooled valgus difference of 0.56° (95% CI, 0.05°-1.06°; P = .032). For ER testing, no differences were found between the retensioned AP double-bundle and the native state ( P = .836), suggesting more complete restoration was achieved by AP double-bundle restoration. Conclusion: A retensionable inlay/onlay hybrid double-bundle MCL reconstruction with a larger femoral footprint and 2 distal anterior-posterior tibial footprints produced superior restoration of the uninjured state when compared to a traditional single-bundle inlay reconstruction. For double-bundle reconstructions, an anterior-posterior tibial fixation achieved mean values closer to the native state than proximal-distal fixation. Clinical Relevance: A double-bundle retensionable inlay/onlay hybrid reconstruction is an effective alternative to a single-bundle inlay reconstruction technique. The double-bundle reconstruction may better withstand early unrestricted range of motion during postoperative phases.
authors: Adam William Anz; Garrett Waller; Jeremy D. Carroll; Gabe Colbrunn; Aiden Cole Magoolaghan; Jessi Truett; Achraf Cohen; Mangesh M. Kulkarni; Mark C. Callanan
venue: The American Journal of Sports Medicine

title: Smartphone-Based 3D Ocular Reconstruction for Automated Quantitative Blepharoptosis Evaluation
abstract: Importance: External ocular examination is central to ptosis evaluation, yet it often relies on manual, experience-dependent measurements with variable accuracy and reproducibility. Objective: To develop and prospectively evaluate the Digital Rulers of Ptosis (DRP), a smartphone-based 3-dimensional (3D) reconstruction system for automated quantitative external ocular assessment in blepharoptosis, including marginal reflex distance 1 (MRD1) and levator muscle function (LF), and clinical classification. Design, Setting, and Participants: This diagnostic/prognostic study was conducted prospectively across 5 hospitals in 2025. Participants 3 years and older underwent smartphone video capture and same-day oculoplastic specialist assessment as the reference standard. Participants undergoing surgery received repeat specialist measurements of MRD1 and LF at 3 months postoperatively to assess recurrence. Exposure: DRP uses a 10-second smartphone video for 3D reconstruction with metric unit conversion and real-time quality control. Main Outcomes and Measures: Agreement between DRP and specialist measurements was assessed by mean absolute error (MAE) and intraclass correlation coefficient. Diagnostic performance was assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value. For patients who underwent surgery, 3-month postoperative recurrence was assessed. Results: Among 952 participants (1904 eyes), the mean age was 27.9 years (range, 3-86 years); 493 participants were female (51.8%) and 459 were male (48.2%). A total of 1862 eyes were included in MRD1 analysis and 1830 eyes in LF analysis after quality control. DRP demonstrated high agreement with specialist measurements for MRD1 (MAE, 0.52 mm; 95% CI, 0.50-0.54 mm) and LF (MAE, 0.95 mm; 95% CI, 0.91-0.98 mm). For diagnosing ptosis, DRP achieved an AUC of 0.97 (95% CI, 0.96-0.97). For identifying surgical approach, DRP achieved an AUC of 0.98 (95% CI, 0.97-0.98). Performance remained consistent across sex, age, and geographic region. Among 206 surgical participants (248 eyes), the 3-month postoperative recurrence rate was 7.3% (95% CI, 4.4%-11.2%; 18/248 eyes), within the lower range of previously reported rates. Conclusions and Relevance: This study found that accurate, standardized quantitative blepharoptosis assessment might be supported by commercially available smartphones, demonstrating the potential of smartphone-based 3D reconstruction for external ocular assessment and clinical decision-making. Further studies are needed to evaluate its clinical impact.
authors: Yahan Yang; Yuxuan Han; Ruixin Wang; Sinting Ling; Junfeng Lyu; Chengkai Li; Lanqin Zhao; Qianni Wu; Jingyi Wen; Tingxin Cui; You Li; Yunxi Lai; Danqi Zeng; Xinwei Chen; Yongxin Zhang; Lin Ye; Weihua Yang; Xiuyun Gao; Jianmin Hu; Can Gong; Jiemin Zou; Jie Meng; Xingyi Li; Xuanwei Liang; Danping Huang; Patrick Yu‐Wai‐Man; Feng Xu; Haotian Lin

title: Rotational perturbation training improves muscle coordination during reactive standing balance in trained and untrained conditions in children with spastic cerebral palsy
abstract: ABSTRACT Perturbation training seems a promising tool to improve reactive balance in children with cerebral palsy. However, experimental evidence remains limited. In particular, little is known about how perturbation training alters muscle coordination, limiting insight into the mechanisms underlying training-induced improvements in balance control. Furthermore, it is unclear whether adaptations in balance control generalize to untrained balance tasks. Here, we investigated the effect of rotational perturbation training on reactive balance performance and reactive muscle activity during trained and untrained perturbation conditions in children with cerebral palsy and typically developing children. We performed a longitudinal intervention study in fourteen children with cerebral palsy and ten typically developing children. Reactive balance was assessed before and after the intervention using toe-up rotational and backward translational perturbations of standing balance. The training intervention consisted of nine sessions over three weeks, with each session including 96 rotational perturbations. Perturbation intensity was adapted to the participant’s performance level. Reactive balance performance was quantified as the ability to stay upright without stepping.
