title: Toward the Use of Centrifugation for Point-of-Care Plasma Separation: Evaluation of a Compact Battery-Powered Centrifuge
abstract: Background/Objectives: Despite advances in point-of-care (POC) blood test development, the lack of a simple, low-cost approach to the separation of capillary blood to generate liquid plasma remains a barrier to POC measurement of many analytes. The battery-operated, internally balanced Labcorp TrueSpin® centrifuge offers a potential POC solution for blood collected into a BDMicrotainer®. We compared the quality of plasma generated by TrueSpin centrifugation versus conventional centrifugation. Methods: Venipuncture was performed on 10 volunteers. After collection of blood into Sarstedt Monovettes® (Lithium Heparin with gel (LiHep/Gel), EDTA), blood from the same tubing was collected into three Microtainers (LiHep/gel, LiHep without gel (LiHep), EDTA). Microtainer and Monovette samples received TrueSpin and conventional centrifugation, respectively. Hemolysis index and plasma amino acids (n = 24) were measured for all Monovette and Microtainer plasma samples. For 3 additional volunteers, capillary blood was collected from the arm into LiHep/Gel and EDTA Microtainers using the Labcorp Comfort DrawTM device with a gentleheel® lancet and centrifuged (TrueSpin) to generate plasma. Results: TrueSpin centrifugation took approximately 10 min; batteries supported 8–11 runs. Microtainer plasma H-indices (including blood from Comfort Draw) were ≤10. For all 24 amino acids combined, measurements for TrueSpin Microtainer samples had excellent Pearson’s correlation (r > 0.99) with paired conventional Monovette plasma. Conclusions: Plasma quality after TrueSpin centrifugation of Microtainer blood samples is comparable to plasma quality after conventional Monovette centrifugation, including for capillary blood collected using the Comfort Draw. The TrueSpin was reliable and easy to use. The TrueSpin centrifuge has potential future use for POC plasma separation.
authors: Adam S. Ptolemy; Alexander Kolb; Ayse Mehmke; Sami Rifai; Nira R. Pollock

title: A-390 Method comparison of a novel capillary blood collection device for clinical chemistry testing: comparison with venous blood on two automated platforms
abstract: Abstract Background Venipuncture remains the standard for blood collection but presents barriers including patient anxiety, need for trained phlebotomists, and limited accessibility for remote testing. Capillary blood collection offers a less invasive alternative that could expand access to laboratory testing. The Tasso+ lancet paired with BD SST microtainer is a novel, push-button solution designed for easy capillary blood collection without fingerstick lancets. This study evaluated the performance of 23 clinical chemistry analytes in Tasso+ capillary serum samples compared to matched venous samples. Methods A prospective, multi-site clinical study was conducted at five US sites with 163 evaluable participants. The study population included adults with diverse demographics and health conditions to promote adequate analyte distribution across clinically relevant ranges. Participants provided paired capillary blood samples collected by healthcare professionals (HCPs) along with venous reference samples obtained via standard venipuncture. Testing was performed within 48 hours of collection (transported under ambient conditions) on Abbott Alinity ci-series and Roche cobas c 503/e 801 analyzers. Twenty-three clinical chemistry analytes were evaluated: albumin, alkaline phosphatase (ALP), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), calcium, chloride, total cholesterol, creatinine, cystatin C, GGT, glucose, HDL, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), potassium, LDL, lipoprotein(a), sodium, NT-proBNP, total bilirubin, total protein, triglycerides, and bicarbonate (CO2). Method comparison utilized Deming or Passing-Bablok regression assessment with estimated bias at medical decision points (MDPs). Acceptance criteria were applied to slope (0.95 - 1.05) and R values (at least 0.95) in addition to bias at each MDP (within 50% CLIA 2025). Results for analytes with range limitations which met one out of two regression criteria were considered preliminary. Results Nine analytes met acceptance criteria on both platforms: ALP, ALT, BUN, cholesterol, hsCRP, and lipoprotein(a). GGT and NT-proBNP were only tested on one platform and also met acceptance criteria. AST, and glucose met criteria on one platform with provisional acceptance on the other. Several electrolytes as well as albumin, bilirubin, and triglycerides did not meet acceptance criteria, likely due to sample matrix effects and/or pre-analytical variables (transport/storage time). The safety profile was favorable with a 3.1% adverse event rate (5/163 participants): 4 events were mild and 1 was moderate intensity. All AEs were pre-determined expected reactions that included discomfort, itchiness, or skin marks at the collection site. Conclusion Upper arm capillary collection using Tasso+ devices demonstrates acceptable analytical performance for multiple clinically important analytes when compared to venous blood reference samples. Analytes suitable for capillary testing include liver enzymes, lipids, cardiac biomarkers, renal function markers, and inflammatory biomarkers. The device shows promise for expanding access to laboratory testing through simplified collection, particularly for wellness screening, chronic disease monitoring, and remote healthcare applications. Further optimization may improve performance for electrolytes and other biomarkers. These findings support continued development of capillary blood collection as a viable alternative to traditional venipuncture for select clinical chemistry testing.
authors: Kaylan Olds; J Poppa; Spencer Stowell; Brian Massie; Evgenia Macke; Erwin Berthier; Timothy Bauer

title: Skin Swabbing as a Noninvasive Alternative to Fin Clipping for Commercial Automated Genotyping
abstract: Fin clipping remains the most common sampling method for genotyping zebrafish, yet it requires anesthesia and tissue removal, raising animal welfare concerns and potentially impacting behavior in the short term. To address this, we have validated a non-invasive skin swabbing technique that eliminates the need for fin clipping adults while maintaining genotyping accuracy during automated genotyping. This method involves gently swabbing the fish's skin to collect mucus and epidermal cells for DNA extraction. This approach avoids anesthesia, reduces handling stress, and is much less invasive than traditional fin clipping with limited tissue injury. We conducted a comparative analysis of swab-derived DNA against traditional fin clip samples sent for automated genotyping. Swab and fin clips samples taken from the same animal matched genotype results, demonstrating substantial promise as a refinement for automated genotyping under the 3Rs framework. Further testing of the swabbing technique, transport, and sample processing was optimized across nine sessions. Key aspects of the collection technique include focusing on consistent swabbing pressure and sample dry time. Proper technique is critical to ensuring robust and reproducible genotyping outcomes. Our findings indicate that skin swabbing offers a welfare-improving alternative to fin clipping for automated genotyping. Broad adoption of this technique has the potential to enhance animal welfare standards while maintaining scientific rigor, aligning with the principles of the 3Rs and advancing non-invasive research practices in zebrafish facilities worldwide. While the current success rate indicates some limitations relative to fin clip genotyping results with automated genotyping, swabbing remains a promising refinement that can substantially improve welfare in zebrafish facilities.
authors: Mollie E. Millington; Ceinwen A. Tilley; Nathan Nowak

title: Clinical evaluation of an intelligent venipuncture robotic system: performance, patient acceptance, and pre-analytical outcomes
abstract: OBJECTIVES: In high-throughput outpatient settings, manual venipuncture is frequently constrained by extreme time pressure and inherent human operator variability, which collectively exacerbate pre-analytical errors and diminish operational efficiency. To address these clinical challenges, we conducted a retrospective study of an intelligent venipuncture robot using 13,803 clinical encounters collected over 18 months in a high-volume outpatient clinic. METHODS: We analyzed performance metrics and patient feedback across three consecutive phases to evaluate both the system's technical maturation and patient acceptance. Furthermore, we validated its clinical utility by comparing procedural success, failure causes, and specimen rejection rates against historical manual practice records. RESULTS: The results demonstrated that the robotic success rate increased steadily over time (from 95.02 % to 97.57 %) alongside sustained high patient acceptance (up to 96.70 %). Most crucially, the robotic system demonstrated a remarkable full-period zero specimen rejection advantage, effectively eliminating the pre-analytical sample rejections that typically compromise manual phlebotomy. During the same observation window, the primary cause of failure shifted chronologically from device puncture errors (47.58 % in Phase I) to patient movement (57.14 % in Phase III). CONCLUSIONS: This study provides robust real-world data supporting the integration of intelligent venipuncture robotics. Given the evident shift in failure mechanisms toward human factors, future advancements must prioritize optimizing human-machine interaction design and implementing targeted pre-procedure psychological interventions to mitigate involuntary patient movements.
authors: Bo Wang; Yao Yao; 叶良平; Dan Wu; Hong Zhao; Meijuan Zheng; Yuanhong Xu; Min Zhang; Jinxing Xia; Anyong Wang

title: B-046 Automated De-Capping Compatibility of V-PRO® Blood Collection Tubes in a Total Laboratory Automation System
abstract: Abstract Background V-PRO® blood collection tubes are designed to meet the operational requirements of Total Laboratory Automation (TLA) systems in medical laboratory. Their precise dimensional specifications, consistent stopper performance, and robust medical-high grade polymer construction facilitate reliable automated de-capping, accurate sample handling, and efficient high-throughput laboratory workflows. Accordingly, this study aimed to confirm the compatibility and operational efficiency of V-PRO® blood collection tubes within a fully automated laboratory environment. Material & Methods A total of 510 V-PRO® blood collection tubes representing different tube types, sizes, and manufacturing batches were evaluated for automated de-capping compatibility within a TLA system. The study was conducted using the GLP System automated de-capping unit (Abbott) under standardized operating conditions. De-capping performance was assessed as a binary outcome (success or failure), and the primary endpoint was the de-capping success rate. Exact binomial analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism software to calculate the success proportion and corresponding 95% confidence intervals. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. Results Automated de-capping was successfully achieved for all 510 V-PRO® blood collection tubes, resulting in a 100% success rate with no observed failures. Exact binomial analysis demonstrated that the observed success rate was 100% (510/510), with a 95% confidence interval ranging from 99.25% to 100%. No de-capping failures were recorded (0/510), corresponding to an estimated failure rate of 0% (95% CI: 0.00%–0.75%). The binomial test showed no statistically significant discrepancy between observed and expected outcomes (p > 0.9999), confirming suitability and reliable performance of V-PRO® tubes within the TLA system. Conclusion V-PRO® blood collection tubes demonstrated excellent compatibility with TLA, achieving a 100% automated de-capping success rate with no observed failures. Exact binomial analysis confirmed a high level of performance reliability, with narrow confidence intervals supporting the robustness and consistency of tube design under automated conditions. These findings indicate that V-PRO® blood collection tubes are well suited for high-throughput automated laboratory workflows and can be reliably integrated into TLA-based pre-analytical processes.
authors: Somaya Qattan; Safiah Almushawwah; Maryam Aldammas; Muzan Ismail; جمال یوسف

title: Alzheimer's Disease Biomarkers Measured by Capillary Blood Collection Versus Venous Plasma and Cerebrospinal Fluid
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Blood biomarkers are increasingly critical for non-invasive Alzheimer's Disease (AD) diagnostics and research but typically require on-site processing. Remote point-of-care collection methods could enhance biomarker testing in clinical and research settings. We evaluated the safety and accuracy of blood collection via venous blood and two capillary blood collection devices (Tasso+ and TAPII) for measurements of amyloid-beta 42/40 ratio (Aβ42/40), phosphorylated-tau-217 (pTau217), neurofilament-light (NfL), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) from capillary plasma to simultaneously collected venous plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). METHODS: Patients seen at the Johns Hopkins Center for CSF Disorders (N = 192) underwent diagnostic lumbar punctures and venipuncture. Warming packs were held to the skin for 5 min before collecting capillary blood (via TAPII or Tasso+ device) and numeric pain scores. CSF, venous, and capillary plasma were analyzed using Quanterix SIMOA immunoassays. Statistical analysis included Pearson/Spearman correlations, Lasso regression, and quantitative comparisons using Bland-Altman plots. RESULTS: 86 TAPII and 126 Tasso+ plasma samples were collected (77 M, 115 F; mean age 61 ± 18.3 years, range 16-91). Tasso+ devices were 90.3% successful in collecting > 50 μL whole blood, and TAPII devices were 86% successful. Mean pain scores were significantly higher in venous than capillary collections (Venous 2.24/10, TAPII 0.73/10, Tasso+ 0.2/10, p < 0.001). Capillary Aβ42/40, NfL, and GFAP strongly correlated with venous plasma analytes (Tasso+: Aβ42/40 r = 0.75, NfL r = 0.91, GFAP r = 0.80, all p < 0.001; TAPII: Aβ42/40 r = 0.74, NfL r = 0.86, GFAP r = 0.84, all p < 0.001). Tasso+ capillary pTau217 weakly correlated with venous (r = 0.23, p = 0.04). Capillary NfL and GFAP correlated modestly with CSF NfL and GFAP (TAPII NfL r = 0.74, GFAP r = 0.6, all p < 0.0001; Tasso+ NfL r = 0.69, GFAP r = 0.59, all p < 0.0001). Capillary Aβ42/40 and pTau217 did not significantly correlate with CSF measures. Lasso regression identified age and GFAP as significant predictors of AD across capillary and venous samples (Tasso+ AUC = 0.87, TAPII AUC = 0.75, Venous AUC = 0.83). INTERPRETATION: Neurodegeneration biomarkers Aβ42/40, NfL, and GFAP in capillary plasma (Tasso+, TAPII) strongly correlated with venous plasma measures. Capillary and venous pTau217 correlated weakly, indicating further assay refinement is needed. Tasso+ collection was less painful and caused less hemolysis compared to TAPII.
authors: Sara Grace Ho; Ziling Shen; Alexandria Lewis; Megha Patel; Anny Zheng; Gianna Proscino; Thaovy Ho; Jiangxia Wang; Marilyn Albert; Abhay Moghekar
venue: Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology

title: Impact of Nasopharyngeal Swab Freezing Storage on the De-tection of Common Respiratory Viral Molecular Targets
abstract: Archived respiratory specimens are valuable for retrospective diagnostic studies, although long-term storage may affect viral RNA detection. This study evaluated nasopharyngeal swabs (NPS) stored at −80 °C for at least one year and retested using automated molecular assays with different multiplexing formats. Qualitative agreement with initial results and changes in cycle threshold (Ct) values were assessed, with discordant results investigated using an independent assay. SARS-CoV-2 showed the highest stability (positive percent agreement, PPA: 97.1–98.6%; mean Ct increase: 2.8–3.4), followed by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV; PPA: 88.4–97.1%; mean Ct increase: 1.75–4.50) and influenza virus (PPA: 80.0–92.9%; mean Ct increase: 5.48–7.92). Ct increases were significant for all viral targets. Differences across assay configurations suggested that assay formulation and target characteristics may influence post-storage detection. NPS aliquots stored at −80 °C remain useful for retrospective molecular testing, although target- and assay-dependent signal loss should be considered when interpreting results from archived specimens. title: The impact of blood collection method (capillary or yenous) on erythrocyte sedimentation using the mini-cube analyzer
abstract: Hitrost sedimentacija eritrocitov (ESR) predstavlja eno izmed osnovnih laboratorijskih preiskav za oceno prisotnosti in intenzitete vnetnih procesov ter drugih patoloških stanj v organizmu. Na rezultat preiskave lahko vplivajo številni predanalitični, analitični in biološki dejavniki, med katerimi je pomembna tudi vrsta odvzema krvi. Namen magistrske naloge je bil raziskati vpliv vrste odvzema krvi - kapilarnega in venskega - na vrednosti ESR z uporabo analizatorja Mini-Cube. V raziskavo so bili vključeni preiskovanci, pri katerih sta bila izvedena oba načina odvzema krvi. Določitve ES so bile opravljene pod standardiziranimi laboratorijskimi pogoji z uporabo analizatorja Mini-Cube, ki omogoča avtomatizirano določanje sedimentacije iz manjšega volumna vzorca. Zbrane rezultate smo statistično analizirali z namenom ugotavljanja morebitnih razlik med kapilarnimi in venskimi vzorci ter ocene stopnje ujemanja med metodama. Rezultati raziskave so pokazali, da lahko vrsta odvzema krvi vpliva na določene vrednosti SE. Ugotovljene razlike med kapilarnimi in venskimi vzorci so bile ovrednotene z vidika klinične pomembnosti in uporabnosti metode v rutinski laboratorijski diagnostiki. Analiza je omogočila presojo zanesljivosti kapilarnega odvzema kot možne alternative venskemu odvzemu, predvsem v primerih, kjer je odvzem venske krvi otežen ali manj primeren. Ugotovili smo, da kapilarni odvzem krvi na analizatorju Mini-Cube zaradi reoloških omejitev, značilnosti mikrocirkulacije in tveganja za hemodilucijo s tkivno tekočino ne more predstavljati splošne alternative venskemu odvzemu. Metoda je primerna zgolj za presejalno testiranje zdrave populacije s pričakovanimi normalnimi vrednostmi, medtem ko venski odvzem za diagnostiko in spremljanje vnetnih stanj ostaja edina metodološko varna izbira.

title: A Passive AI System for Verifying Physical State on Automated Liquid Handlers
abstract: Automated liquid handlers execute digital protocols, but operators must assemble the deck and confirm that the physical setup matches the intended experiment. We present the Labware Setup Checker, a passive vision system that verifies deck preparation on an Opentrons Flex without modifying its hardware or firmware. A consumer webcam mounted outside the robot supplies images to a browser application. The checker segments the deck into slots, corrects slot assignments using the known deck geometry, classifies the labware, and compares the observed setup with a reference protocol library to report missing, misplaced, or unexpected labware. It operates independently of the robot controller and does not interrupt or gate a run. During SwabSeq Respiratory Viral Panel (RVP) pre-PCR deck preparation, the checker tracked a slot from empty to a base and then to the completed plate-and-base assembly, identifying the completed assembly in all 29 frames before robot motion. Across these frames, 95.1% of the 348 labware classifications for slots requiring exact matches agreed with the protocol reference. In 480 frames with partially occluded reservoirs, all 6,720 slot assignments were correct. Across three camera positions and two lighting conditions, slot assignment was 100% correct, and 97.73% of labware classifications matched the protocol reference. Median verification time was 2.10 s on a laptop using only its CPU and 4.24 s from frame capture to receipt of results during AWS deployment in the laboratory. These results show that an external camera and independent software can provide verification of deck setup against protocol requirements within seconds, allowing operators to review the physical setup before starting a run.
authors: Junqiong Joanne Qiu; Zeckria Kamrany; Anand, Ananya; Emma Vidal; Yunjia Johanna Bai; Nathan S Chen; Sean Son; Varada Abhyankar; Taryn E. Jakub; Eleazar Eskin

title: Measles ( rubeola) virus qualitative real-time reverse transcription–polymerase chain reaction assay: development and clinical validation on an automated workflow
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Detection of Measles virus (MeV) RNA is an important method for confirming infection. This study described the clinical validation of a qualitative real-time reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) assay for MeV detection. METHODS: A real-time RT-PCR assay was developed and validated using primers and probes previously reported in the literature. The assay was evaluated using reference materials, cultured virus, and previously tested clinical throat swab samples. An automated workflow was established for RNA extraction, RT-PCR amplification, and result reporting using robotic platforms and a real-time PCR instrument. The assay targets the measles nucleoprotein (N) and hemagglutinin (H) genes, with human RNase P gene used as an internal control. RESULTS: The MeV RT-PCR assay has a limit of detection of 500 genome copies per milliliter. The assay was tested against 85 different samples: 50 positive clinical samples and reference materials and 35 negative clinical samples or reference materials. All expected results were correctly identified, giving 100% sensitivity (50/50) and specificity (35/35). The assay showed 100% interassay and intra-assay reproducibility. No cross-reactivity was observed with other respiratory viruses or common bacterial and fungal pathogens. DISCUSSION: This automated measles RT-PCR assay demonstrated high accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility.
authors: Lan Yu; Li Chen; Kevin Dumas; Nickolas Weyandt; Michael Meyers; Pei Irwin; Jennifer L. Eitson; John W. Schoggins; Jason Y. Park

title: Isolation and Identification of Microorganisms Associated with Automated Teller Machines in Calabar Metropolis
abstract: The metallic keyboards of automated teller machines situated within Calabar metropolis were investigated for microbial contamination due to their vast dermal contact by multiple users. Swab sticks soaked with normal sterile saline were used to collect specimens from the keypads. Isolation was done on nutrient agar and eosine methylene blue (EMB) for bacteria and Sabouraud dextrose agar for fungi using standard microbiological procedures. Identification of microorganisms was done using colonial, microscopic and biochemical characteristics. The results reveal that these machines that serve as cash dispensing device can be a potential disease dispensing machines as samples analyzed revealed bacterial isolates such as Staphylococcus spp (32%)), Bacillus spp (24%), Escherichia spp (20%), Pseudomonas spp (18%) and Salmonella spp (6%) while fungal isolates of the samples analyzed include microorganisms such as Rhizopus spp (56%), Aspergillus spp, (25%) and Penicillium spp (19%). These findings necessitate the need for adequate personal hygiene by users and frequent routine cleaning of these machines by the bank’s authorities is highly recommended.
authors: Chinyere Osondu-Anyanwu

title: Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra on nasopharyngeal swabs has lower sensitivity for pulmonary tuberculosis than tongue swabs: a nested case-control study in South African primary care
abstract: BACKGROUND: Non-sputum alternatives for tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis are a priority. Nasopharyngeal swabs (NPSs), routinely used for viral testing, may have promise. Comparative performance to tongue swabs (TSs), which are recommended for TB detection but have suboptimal sensitivity, is unknown. METHODS: We evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra (Ultra; Cepheid, USA) on stored wet or dry NPSs (NPSU) from adults with presumptive TB consecutively presenting to primary care in Cape Town, South Africa. Using a nested case-control design, all TB-positive participants had NPSU (n=148) and random selection of TB-negative participants frequency-matched by HIV-status (n=117). We used a microbiological reference standard (MRS) and extended MRS (eMRS). A consecutive subset participant (n=130) also had TSs collected and of these, 62 TB-positive and 68 TB-negative people had TS Ultra (TSU) done. RESULTS: NPSU sensitivity was 35% (95% CI 27, 43) and specificity 88% (80, 93). Wet swabs had higher sensitivity than dry swabs [45% (34, 57) vs 21% (12, 34)]. Overall sensitivity was lower in HIV-positive participants [24% (14, 36) vs 44% (32, 56)]. TSU had higher sensitivity [67% (53, 79); p<0.001] than NPSU in head-to-head comparisons. Specificities were comparable. CONCLUSION: NPSU sensitivity was lower than TSU, especially among dry NP swabs, and neither NPSU sensitivity nor specificity met WHO benchmarks for non-sputum confirmatory tests. NPSs do not appear useful for TB diagnosis without further optimisation.
authors: Robinah Nakawunde; Jay Achar; Brian Allwood; Suventha Moodley; Loren Rockman; Welile V. Dube-Nwamba; Anna O. Okunola; D P Naidoo; Niaz Banaei; Charissa C. Marsh; Grant Theron

title: Distribution and Age Dynamics of Respiratory Mycoplasmosis in Birds on Farms of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic
abstract: Experiments revealed that 1- to 60-day-old chickens are more susceptible to respiratory mycoplasmosis. Those chickens that contracted the disease experienced developmental delays. Serological studies revealed that the serum droplet agglutination test (SDR) in chickens testing positive for mycoplasmosis resulted in high infection rates in 1- and 20-day-old chickens, amounting to 57.5% and 62.5%, respectively. Respiratory mycoplasmosis infection was recorded in 35.5% of 40-day-old chickens and 6.6% of 60-day-old chickens. Thus, during the study, the percentage of infected chickens did not fall below 50.0% in the RSPN, with the infection peaking at 7 and 10 months of age, amounting to 91.6% and 80.0%, respectively. According to the hemagglutination test, 100% antibodies to mycoplasma were detected at all age periods. At the same time, the maximum average titer (5286±932) was also recorded during the period of intensive egg production. With age, a decrease in the average titer to 3171±428 was recorded. Bacteriological examination of throat swabs taken from healthy laying hens revealed M. gallisepticum cultures in 26.6%–53.3% of all age groups. Detection of the causative agent of respiratory mycoplasmosis in embryos and one-day-old chicks indicates that the infection is transmitted transovarially. The highest mycoplasma carriage rate (53.3%) was detected in 10-month-old hens. Among 12-month-old roosters, the mycoplasma carriage rate was 64.0%.
authors: A. Ibragimov; M. Maharramov; G. Mammadova

title: Drill with Confidence: Real-Time Automated Drilling Fluid Testing and Dynamic Hydraulic Modeling for Drilling Optimization
abstract: Abstract Manual drilling fluid measurements typically conducted 2–4 times per day, lack the resolution required for precise hydraulic calculations and management in high-performance wells. This paper details the implementation of a closed-loop workflow involving an inline automated fluid testing device and real-time hydraulics simulation and monitoring across two wells in the field. The primary objective was to replace intermittent manual sampling with high-frequency data integrated into a live hydraulic and hole-cleaning simulator to monitor and optimize drilling performance parameters such as Rate of Penetration (ROP), tripping speeds, and circulation times. The technology utilized an inline dual-sampling drilling fluid characterization device to continuously analyze mud properties in the circulating system. The automated system achieved a significant increase in data density, providing 46 rheology tests and 1,920 density readings per day, a massive improvement over the conventional 2–4 rheology tests and 48 density readings. These real-time parameters (Density, PV, YP, and 6-speed readings) and drilling parameters were streamed to a Real-Time Center where a hydraulics modelling software was used for real-time monitoring and optimization. This allowed for the continuous monitoring of the Hole-Cleaning Index (HCI), Cuttings Bed Height (CBH), and Equivalent Circulating Density (ECD) against planned pressure and fracture gradients and identify opportunities for drilling parameter optimization. The integration of real-time data into predictive simulations yielded substantial operational efficiencies as follows: Drilling Performance: The system enabled a maximum ROP of 400 ft/hr while maintaining good hole cleaning. A field-best 24-hour footage of 3,945.68 feet was achieved in the 6-inch section at this time.Circulation Optimization: While the original plan was six bottom-up cycles, predictive simulations suggested optimizing this sequence to just two (a potential saving in circulation time of 67% whilst ensuring a clean wellbore)Tripping Efficiency: Real-time surge/swab monitoring enabled potential tripping speed increases of nearly 100% over previous rig KPIs, offering 15–25% time savings compared to the best-performing rigs in the region.Data Accuracy: Comparative analysis showed a high correlation between simulated ECD and actual annular pressure while drilling (APWD) data, confirming the reliability of automated fluid inputs for pressure management. This work demonstrates that automating the fluid-data-to-simulation loop moves the industry from reactive monitoring to proactive drilling management. It quantifies the specific "time-savings" value of high-frequency rheology data, proving that automated testing is a critical precursor to fully autonomous drilling systems.

title: The comparison of excision, swabbing, tape-lifting, and scraping as techniques for DNA evidence recovery: A preliminary study
abstract: In the Final Report of the Commission of Inquiry into Forensic DNA Testing in Queensland , Recommendation 28 recommended that alternative procedures to the scraping method should be investigated for the recovery of biological material from crime scene exhibits for downstream DNA testing. This study forms the first phase of a larger project comparing swabbing, tape-lifting, scraping and excision of biological fluids from a fabric substrate to determine the most effective recovery procedure. Calico cotton swatches were seeded with two concentrations (neat and 1:1000) of blood, semen and saliva, samples commonly encountered in forensic casework. Each sample type was collected using the four evidence recovery methods, extracted, quantified, and the 1/1000 dilution samples were short tandem repeat (STR) profiled to assess the practical limits of each method. Excision had the greatest DNA yield with a large effect size and best STR profile quality compared to all other recovery methods for blood ( p < 0.0001, ŋ 2 > 0.95), semen ( p < 0.0001, ŋ 2 = 0.96) and saliva ( p < 0.0001, ŋ 2 = 0.82). There were no statistical differences found between the MWE Sterile Tubed Dryswab™ Rayon swab 1028, the Puritan® 6” Standard Rayon Swab w/Polystyrene Handle – 806-PR, HazPak tape-lift or scraping for neat blood and semen. Tape-lifting had a statistically higher efficiency than scraping ( p = 0.0012), the Puritan ( p = 0.0046) and the MWE swabs ( p = 0.0145). Results suggest that excision is the most effective biological material recovery technique for blood, semen, and saliva from 100 % white cotton.

title: Development, validation and clinical implementation of cellular swab materials for quality assurance of pharmacogenomic point-of-care testing
abstract: Abstract Background Pharmacogenomic point-of-care testing (PGx POCT) enables genotype-informed prescribing at the bedside, but implementation is limited by the lack of suitable reference materials for clinical verification and standardised external quality assessment (EQA). Methods Fixed lymphoblastoid cell lines were formulated as swab-based materials at defined cellular inputs for MT-RNR1 POCT. Materials were evaluated using Genedrive® assays, quantitative PCR, acceptance quality limit batch release, workflow-perturbation testing and stability studies, then deployed for clinical verification and in an international EQA programme. Results Materials were homogeneous, workflow compatible and reproducible, with 100% correct genotype calls at the lowest intended manufacturing cell load. Clinical verification of 11 Genedrive® systems across five neonatal units demonstrated 99% concordance with expected genotype classifications (232/234 results). Seven EQA surveys yielded 253 participant results, with full-mark rates of 87.5–100%, and six test failures. Most failures occurred with low cell-input materials near the assay limit of detection. The materials supported genotype concordance, performance monitoring and identification of workflow and sample-related variability. Conclusions Workflow-compatible cell-based reference materials combined with EQA provide a scalable framework for quality-assured PGx POCT beyond specialist laboratories. Clinical verification of Genedrive® systems within neonatal units using the cell-based swab materials, together with deployment of an International MT-RNR1 PGx POCT EQA programme, demonstrated their suitability for supporting both pre-implementation testing and ongoing quality assurance in decentralised healthcare settings. The framework may provide a model for the implementation, clinical verification and ongoing quality assessment of PGx POCT services. Further evaluation across platforms, analytes, settings and participant groups is required to establish broader applicability.
authors: Henry Thomas; John Henry McDermott; William G. Newman; Shaun Ainsworth; Gino Miele; Simon J. Patton; Rosa Morra

title: Mitigating lateral sensing blind spots: A dual-segment bronchoscopic robot with a bioinspired skin
abstract: Lateral force blind spots frequently trigger airway injuries during robotic bronchoscopy. Traditional sensing approaches lack fine spatial resolution, and single-segment robots suffer poor posture adjustment flexibility, worsening unmonitored tissue contact. We integrate a snake-scale-inspired 64-channel gradient piezoelectric film with a dual-segment manipulator to resolve lateral blind spots for secure bronchial navigation. The conformally wrapped sensor delivers fast (<10 ms), precise force detection ( R 2 > 0.98, RMSE < 0.145 N, CV < 2%) and filters bending pseudo-forces. The dual-segment design enables coordinated proximal-distal motion to avoid overcontact in tortuous lumens. Phantom and ex vivo porcine lung tests confirm real-time force localization, 5.0 N safety alarms, and autonomous tuning to keep contact forces below 3.0 N. This synergistic robot-sensor design supplies a translatable safety control strategy for flexible surgical manipulators.
authors: Qiqi Pan; Wenke Duan; Jingjing Luo; Lei Wang; Shijie Guo; Yongfei Feng; Hongbo Wang

title: Olfactory Swab-Derived Human Neuroepithelium Cell Culture as a Novel Model to Study Neurodegeneration-Related Proteins
abstract: The olfactory neuroepithelium (ON) collected with nasal swabs (NS) is a valuable source for studying brain processes in physiological and pathological conditions, due to its anatomical proximity to the brain and heterogeneous neural cell population. In this proof-of-concept study, we developed a protocol for co-culturing distinct cellular populations from ON, establishing a human olfactory neuroepithelium cell culture (hON) model from healthy individuals (HIs) without differentiation factors. We characterized the cellular composition of ON samples at harvesting, identifying sustentacular cells (Pan-CK+), neuronal cells (PGP9.5+), and ciliated respiratory cells (βIV-tubulin+) by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry. We assessed the expression and distribution of TDP-43, Tau, and α-synuclein, together with their phosphorylated isoforms, to establish a physiological reference profile. Furthermore, Seeding Amplification Assay (SAA) analysis, including disease-positive and healthy control cohorts, confirmed the absence of aggregated protein species in HIs. While p-Tau and p-α-syn localization was preserved between collection and culture, p-TDP-43 displayed neuron-specific nuclear redistribution upon culture, suggesting distinct regulatory dynamics. Longitudinal monitoring revealed that hON cultures maintain a stable neuronal population for up to 21 days, after which cells transition toward a fibroblast-like phenotype. This study establishes NS-derived hON as a feasible model for investigating neurodegenerative mechanisms, providing a baseline for disease comparisons.
authors: Francesco Silvestri; Erika Bronzato; Ilaria Scambi; Valerio Arietti; Luca Sacchetto; Raffaella Mariotti; Gianluigi Zanusso; Matilde Bongianni; Ermanna Turano

title: Cotton‐Swab‐Anchored Suspension Technique for Hands‐Free Lower Extremity Limb Sterilization During Surgical Preparation
abstract: Manual limb suspension during surgical preparation is labor-intensive, requires additional personnel, and may increase the risk of musculoskeletal injuries among surgical staff. We describe a cotton-swab-anchored suspension technique that uses a sterile bandage (Kerlix) looped around the ankle, secured with 2 cotton swabs inserted into the knot, and suspended from a heavy-duty intravenous pole. This method enables hands-free limb elevation, allowing efficient preoperative preparation. After completion of preparation, the limb is released by simply removing the cotton swab. This technique eliminates the need for manual limb holding, reduces occupational strain, provides stable mechanical support, and enables quick, controlled limb release without instruments. It is cost-effective, reproducible, and suitable for various lower extremity procedures.
authors: Chen Zhou; Zhouzhou Hu; Lather Sagar; Shengwu Yang; Zhenhan Deng

title: The transformative power of artificial intelligence and machine learning in blood banking/transfusion medicine: A vein‐to‐vein approach from blood collection to transfusion services: On behalf of the AABB Foundation
abstract: BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence (AI)/machine learning (ML) are poised to transform transfusion medicine across the vein-to-vein continuum, from donor recruitment to recipient outcomes. Large datasets generated from millions of donations and transfusions create opportunities for predictive modeling, precision medicine, improved safety, and operational efficiency. This review outlines key applications of AI in blood banking and transfusion medicine using a comprehensive vein-to-vein framework. METHODS: The review synthesizes perspectives from blood services and hospital-based transfusion practices. Applications are discussed across donor recruitment, collections, testing, inventory management, hospital transfusion services, and education. Finally, AI safety, including ethical, regulatory, privacy, and implementation challenges, is addressed. This is a narrative, non-exhaustive review; given the rapidly evolving pace of AI/ML capabilities, this synthesis should be interpreted as a framework for ongoing surveillance rather than a fixed inventory of applications. RESULTS: Donor-focused applications include personalized recruitment, individualized iron management, and fairness auditing to reduce inequities. In supply chain operations, ML can improve demand forecasting, minimize waste, and optimize inventory. Federated learning may support multi-institutional collaboration without sharing raw data. Omics and genomic applications can enable high-throughput analysis, phenotype prediction, and precision transfusion support for rare blood types and alloimmunized patients. In hospitals, AI can augment hemovigilance by identifying/predicting adverse transfusion reactions, while large language models and retrieval-augmented generation may enhance decision support, patient blood management, and education through adaptive learning. CONCLUSION: AI holds substantial promise to improve transfusion safety, efficiency, equity, and sustainability. Realizing this potential will require robust governance, model validation across diverse populations, privacy safeguards, bias mitigation, reproducibility, regulatory oversight, and human-in-the-loop implementation.
authors: Ruchika Goel; Sheharyar Raza; W. Alton Russell; Jansen N. Seheult; Tho D. Pham; Angelo D’Alessandro; Rounak Dubey; Celina Montemayor; David B. Daniel; Cliff Numark; Brian Custer; Jason Sapia; Tony Casina; Jerry A. Holmberg; Aaron A.R. Tobian; Na Li

title: Effects of a low dose of 3-nitrooxypropanol and a combination of direct-fed microbials on methane emission, oral swab bacterial community, and performance in dairy cows
abstract: Abstract Background 3-Nitrooxypropanol (3-NOP) can inhibit ruminal methane production by inactivating the key enzyme during methanogenesis. Combining 3-NOP and direct-fed microbials (DFM) can potentially provide a dual-action approach to reduce ruminal methane production. The objective of this study was to investigate the effects of supplementation of a low dose of 3-NOP and a mixture of DFM, on methane emissions, performance, and rumen microbial community of dairy cows. Results Forty-eight Danish Holstein dairy cows were used in a 14-week randomized complete block design. Due to a mixing error, 3-NOP was included at an unexpected low dose (6.0 mg/kg DM). Cows were fed with one of four experimental diets: (1) control diet, and other treatment diets were control diet supplemented with (2) 3-NOP, or with (3) DFM (12 mg/kg P. acidipropionici strain P169 and 120 mg/kg Bacillus subtilis and B. licheniformis mixture), or with (4) a combination of 3-NOP and DFM. 3-NOP inclusion did not affect DMI, feed efficiency, or milk yield and composition. DFM supplementation reduced partial mixed ration intake and total DMI. 3-NOP supplementation significantly reduced CH 4 production (g/d) (8%) and CH 4 intensity (g/kg ECM) (9%) but did not affect CH 4 yield (g/kg DMI). Furthermore, 3-NOP supplementation increased H 2 production, yield, and intensity. DFM supplementation reduced milk yield from weeks 3 to 8 and ECM yield from weeks 3 to 7, but these effects diminished over time. 3-NOP alone or in combination with DFM resulted in higher abundance of Megasphaera and Prevotella genera in oral swab samples. DFM supplementation had no effect on gas emissions, and it only tended to improve feed efficiency (ECM/DMI, kg/kg) during the later stage of the experiment. DFM supplementation led to higher abundance of certain species within the Lactobacillaceae family particularly at later stages of the experiment. Conclusions An unforeseen reduced dose of 3-NOP supplementation still can effectively mitigate methane emissions (both production and intensity) and increase H 2 emissions without affecting DMI or performance. DFM supplementation reduced DMI and milk yield at the onset of the experiment, but the effects subsided over time, resulting in an increased feed efficiency by the end of the experiment.
authors: Wenji Wang; Sadjad Danesh Mesgaran; Ruth Gómez Expósito; A. Rytz; N. Walker; Elodie Soussan; S. Pruvost; D Yáñez-Ruiz; P. Lund

title: Comparative Evaluation of Conventional, Chromogenic, and Automated Methods for Identification of Candida Species
abstract: Background: Accurate identification of Candida species is essential for timely antifungal therapy, particularly in the context of the rising prevalence of Non-Candida albicans species with variable antifungal susceptibility. Advances in diagnostic methods have expanded laboratory options beyond conventional phenotypic techniques, necessitating systematic evaluation of their diagnostic performance. Aim: The present study was therefore undertaken to comparatively assess conventional phenotypic methods, chromogenic media, and automated identification systems for the identification of Candida species isolated from clinical specimens. By evaluating their diagnostic performance in a tertiary care setting, this study aims to provide practical insights to guide laboratory workflows and optimize the diagnosis of Candida infections in diverse healthcare environments. Materials & methods: A prospective laboratory-based comparative study was conducted in a tertiary care teaching hospital in eastern India from November 2013 to September 2015. A total of 400 clinical specimens were processed, yielding 150 Candida isolates. Species identification was performed using conventional phenotypic methods, chromogenic media (CHROMagar Candida), biochemical sugar assimilation tests, and an automated identification system (VITEK). The sensitivity and specificity of Sabouraud’s dextrose agar, CHROMagar Candida, and corn meal agar were calculated using automated identification as the reference standard. Results: Non-Candida albicans species predominated among isolates. CHROMagar Candida demonstrated the highest diagnostic performance, with a sensitivity of 98.6% and specificity of 99%, enabling rapid and reliable presumptive species identification within 24–48 hours. Sabouraud’s dextrose agar showed comparable sensitivity (98%) but lower specificity (97%), while corn meal agar exhibited high specificity (98%) with reduced sensitivity (96.6%). Sugar assimilation tests provided supportive biochemical confirmation but required longer turnaround times. Conventional methods such as germ tube testing remained useful for presumptive identification of Candida albicans but lacked discriminatory power for non-albicans species. Conclusion: CHROMagar Candida offers superior accuracy and speed for routine identification of Candida species and, when integrated with conventional morphology and automated systems, forms an effective tiered diagnostic approach. Adoption of such strategies can enhance laboratory efficiency and support antifungal stewardship, particularly in resource-limited settings. Keywords: Candida species; Chromogenic media; CHROMagar Candida; Automated identification systems; Diagnostic accuracy; Clinical mycology

title: The effects of anticoagulant and sample storage time on hematologic values in Humboldt penguins (Spheniscus humboldti )
abstract: Preanalytical variation in hematologic values due to factors including anticoagulant and sample storage time have been documented in several avian taxa. This study evaluated differences in PCV, total solids, WBC count, and leukocyte differential in Humboldt penguin (Spheniscus humboldti) blood samples exposed to different anticoagulants and storage durations. Blood was collected from eleven individuals and anticoagulated with either lithium heparin (LH) EDTA. Hematologic values were compared at the time of blood collection (0 h) and after refrigeration at 8 h and 24 h. Leukocyte differential values were also compared to fresh, non-anticoagulated blood films created immediately after venipuncture (0 h). On immediate evaluation (0 h), there were no statistically significant differences in total WBC count or leukocyte differentials between LH, EDTA, and non-anticoagulated whole blood. Statistically and clinically relevant shifts in differential counts occurred within 8 h of sample storage, including a reduction in absolute monocytes (p = 0.001), and altered heterophil:lymphocyte ratio (p = 0.0016). Increased relative (proportion of) lymphocytes and decreased relative heterophils were documented in samples anticoagulated in LH within as little as 8 hours of storage in the refrigerator. Conversely, samples anticoagulated in EDTA (p < 0.0001) showed increased relative heterophils and decreased relative lymphocytes within 8 hours of storage (p < 0.0001). These findings indicate that rapid sample processing is key to limiting artifactual changes in leukogram evaluation. Furthermore, anticoagulant and sample storage time should be considered during interpretation of Humboldt penguin hematology.

title: Advances In NLP-Driven Analytics for Automated Detection of Regulatory Liabilities in High-Volume Contracts
abstract: Contract portfolios at large enterprises now routinely exceed tens of thousands of active agreements, and the regulatory obligations attaching to those agreements have multiplied faster than legal review capacity. In 2025 this gap became acute: the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) became applicable on 17 January without a transition period, forcing thousands of financial entities into large-scale contract remediation, while the general-purpose AI obligations of the EU AI Act took effect on 2 August. Both events created demand for systems that can read an entire contract portfolio and flag, with evidence, where regulatory liability exists. This paper reviews the state of natural language processing for automated regulatory liability detection as of the end of 2025 and sets out a layered architecture for production deployment. Regulatory liability detection is distinguished here from the better-studied task of clause extraction, on the argument that the former is a normative verification problem requiring a rule base, an evidence retrieval mechanism, and an adjudication step, rather than a span-labelling problem. Four technical shifts that reshaped the field during 2025 are surveyed: the maturation of long-context models beyond the length of most commercial contracts, the emergence of legal-specific retrieval evaluation, the arrival of explicit reasoning models capable of rule-grounded justification, and the closing but still material gap between proprietary and open-weight models on clause-level risk identification. Evidence is also drawn from compliance analytics research in financial audit, cybersecurity governance, critical infrastructure protection, procurement, supply chain assurance, payments, pharmaceutical regulation, aviation safety oversight, and enterprise systems engineering, on the argument that the design problems in regulatory liability detection are not confined to legal NLP and that adjacent literatures have already resolved several of them. A metric suite appropriate to the asymmetric cost structure of compliance work is then set out, in which a missed mandatory clause is not commensurate with a false alarm, and the F1 scores dominant in the literature are argued to be a poor proxy for deployment value. The paper closes on a reflexive governance question specific to this application: a system that classifies legal risk may itself fall within the scope of the regulation it is deployed to manage.
authors: Uchechi Ngonadi

title: Developmental validation of the Maxwell® DE System – a semi-automated differential extraction method
abstract: Differential extraction is widely used to recover male DNA from sexual assault evidence, but manual workflows can introduce variability and contamination risk. This validation evaluated the Maxwell® DE System, a semi-automated approach to differential extraction, through multi-laboratory studies conducted in accordance with SWGDAM guidelines at three forensic laboratories. Analytical performance was assessed across sensitivity, reproducibility, stability, workflow flexibility, post-coital interval, and case-type studies. Sperm fraction (Fraction 2) male DNA recovery increased with semen input and reflected the availability of intact sperm cells, with informative autosomal STR profiles obtained at low input levels. At lower inputs tested and extended post-coital intervals, autosomal results were limited; however, partial Y-STR profiles were recovered, supporting their use when male DNA is minimal. Intra-run variability within sites was low less than 30%. Under the conditions evaluated, the system reduced the impact of tested inhibitors and produced comparable results across lysis durations and Fraction 1 processing approaches. Performance was assessed across a range of sample types and reagent blanks. All reagent blanks were below the PowerQuant® System analytical threshold, with no exogenous human DNA detected. Performance was assessed across a range of sample types, and no evidence of exogenous human DNA introduced by the workflow was identified. These findings support the use of the Maxwell® DE System as a semi-automated approach for differential extraction in forensic workflows.

title: Validation of an automated method for DNA isolation from samples derived from sexual assault cases
abstract: In recent decades, the automation of forensic sample processing has significantly increased the efficiency of forensic genetics laboratories. Traditional manual DNA extraction, based on the separation of sperm cells from epithelial cells through multiple washing and centrifugation steps, is associated with the loss of biological material and limitations in throughput. The Differex™ system (Promega, USA) enables automated DNA extraction and rapid separation of sperm cells from epithelial cells through selective digestion of epithelial cells with proteinase K, followed by differential centrifugation and fraction isolation. The application of Differex™ in combination with DNA IQ™ technology and the automated Maxwell® FSC platform allows the integration of DNA extraction into a fully automated workflow. The aim of this study was to validate the Differex™ kit (Promega, USA) using reference samples (semen and epithelial cells), mixed samples simulating forensic evidence, as well as challenging samples of low quality and low cellular content. The results demonstrate that the Differex™-based method enables the isolation of DNA of sufficient quality for downstream STR-PCR analysis. The system exhibits good efficiency and reproducibility, and its integration with the automated Maxwell® FSC platform significantly improves laboratory throughput while reducing the risk of cross-contamination. The applied method represents a valuable tool for the routine analysis of biological evidence in cases involving sexual offences.

title: Repurposing a commercial artificial intelligence vision platform for automated surgical instrument identification: a proof-of-concept study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Retained surgical items are classified as never events but continue to occur, and the count meant to prevent them is often recorded as correct even when an item is retained. Computer vision could provide an independent check on what is on the instrument table, but purpose-built surgical systems are scarce. Industrial vision platforms offer a faster route, although their surgical performance is unknown. METHODS: In a prospective experimental study, a commercial artificial intelligence vision platform developed for industrial inspection was applied to 19 surgical instruments and 3 suture items, each presented once in 100 runs (2,200 experiments). No software redesign was required, but the classifier had been trained on this item set, making this a supervised rather than a zero-shot setting. Two outcomes were recorded: whether the platform assigned the exact item identity, and whether it registered an item as present at the packing step irrespective of type, termed count-presence detection. Because experiments are clustered within items and runs, the primary estimate is the mean per-item accuracy with cluster-adjusted intervals. RESULTS: The correct instruments were identified in 2,036 of 2,200 experiments (92.5%). The mean per-item accuracy was 92.5% (95% confidence interval 88.4 to 96.7; cluster-adjusted 87.7 to 95.6). Count-presence detection was 99.1% (98.7 to 99.4). Performance was reproducible across runs (intraclass correlation 0.02), whereas variance clustered by item (0.12). Accuracy ranged from 64% (suture needle 6-0) to 100% (six items). Errors were directional and almost always within visually near-identical sub-types. CONCLUSIONS: An industrial vision platform detected item presence with high reliability and identified item type with high accuracy, however, with a residual error rate of 7.5%. The errors were predictable and confined to visually similar classes, pointing to correctable mitigations rather than a fundamental limit. These figures represent an upper bound under highly controlled conditions rather than expected intraoperative performance. Such a system is intended to support rather than replace the perioperative team. This study establishes feasibility rather than clinical benefit; a prospective intraoperative study is the necessary next step.
authors: Simon Stoerzer; Klinto Xhemo; Felix Gronau; Linda Feldbruegge; Philipp Felgendreff; Maximilian Kaltenecker; Jacques Hahn; Gerrit Grannas; Moritz Schmelzle

title: Abstract A123: AI-PACED: A prospective feasibility study of automated risk stratification, AI-augmented serial imaging, and biobanking for early detection of sporadic pancreatic cancer
abstract: Abstract Purpose: Sporadic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) is diagnosed almost exclusively after symptom onset, often when curative resection is no longer feasible. Glycemically-defined new-onset diabetes (gNOD) with an ENDPAC score ≥3 identifies a population at markedly elevated short-term risk, and radiomics-based AI models have identified sub-visual, pre-diagnostic imaging signatures of PDA that precede symptomatic presentation. Translating these signatures into a prospective early detection pathway requires establishing recruitment yield, imaging and biospecimen adherence, and integration of a radiomics-based AI into real-world workflows. We designed the AI-Augmented Pancreas Cancer Early Detection (AI-PACED) study, a prospective, dual-cohort feasibility trial (NCT07324096) evaluating serial AI-analysis of CT and longitudinal blood biobanking in a gNOD, ENDPAC-enriched high-risk population. Methods: Individuals with gNOD, identified through weekly semi-automated EMR-based risk stratification and confirmed by manual chart review, self-select into Cohort A1 (serial CT and blood biobanking), Cohort A2 (blood biobanking alone), or passive EMR surveillance (Cohort B). Target enrollment is 100 (70 in A1/A2, 30 in Group B). Cohorts A1 and A2 undergo blood collection at baseline, 6, and 12 months. Cohort A1 additionally undergoes paired portal venous phase contrast-enhanced CT, concentrated during the first year after gNOD onset, when PDA risk is highest, to prioritize detection while limiting incremental radiation exposure. All CTs are interpreted by non-study radiologists per standard institutional protocol. The AI analyses is applied post-hoc, firewalled from clinical care. Feasibility endpoints include gNOD identification yield, recruitment, and cohort self-selection among eligible high-risk individuals. The protocol is IRB-approved and open to accrual at Mayo Clinic, Rochester, Minnesota since March 2026. Results: Semi-automated EMR screening identified 253 candidate individuals, of whom manual chart review confirmed 175 (mean age: 66.6 years, range 50-84; 50.9% females) as true gNOD, comprising 16 with ENDPAC ≥3, 139 with ENDPAC <3, and 20 in whom ENDPAC could not be calculated. The remaining 78 were excluded as false positives (e.g., active malignancy, inaccurate glycemic values). This confirmation step distinguishes true, actionable gNOD from EMR artifact prior to outreach. Conclusions: AI-PACED supports the feasibility of a two-stage algorithmic and manual workflow for distinguishing true gNOD from EMR artifact, while quantifying the false-positive burden that will inform refinement of a fully automated pipeline. Recruitment into asymptomatic, imaging-intensive surveillance is likely to remain the principal constraint, particularly because most glycemic elevation is managed outside quaternary centers. These constraints motivate extending enrollment infrastructure beyond a single center to inform a multi-institutional trial evaluating lead-time advantage of an AI-driven strategy for earlier, potentially curative detection of sporadic PDA. AI-PACED: A prospective feasibility study of automated risk stratification, AI-augmented serial imaging, and biobanking for early detection of sporadic pancreatic cancer [abstract]. title: Ultrasound‐Guided Peripheral Venous Catheter for Automated Erythrocytapheresis in a Paediatric Population Affected by Sickle Cell Disease
abstract: Introduction: Automated erythrocytapheresis (aEEX) is an effective therapy for severe sickle cell disease (SCD). Its use in paediatrics can be limited by challenges in obtaining reliable venous access. Methods: We conducted a retrospective, single-centre study to evaluate the safety and feasibility of ultrasound (US)-guided peripheral venous catheter (PVC) placement for aEEX compared with central venous catheter (CVC) use in children and adolescents with SCD. Results: Between May 2018 and July 2025, 99 aEEX procedures using PVC were compared with 44 using CVC in 23 patients (median age: 16.4 years). The most frequent indication was severe disease phenotype (62.9%), defined as recurrent vaso-occlusive crises and/or splenic sequestration and/or acute chest syndrome despite optimal hydroxyurea therapy. The procedure success rate was 99.0% for PVC and 97.7% for CVC, with median post-apheresis HbS of 26.5% and 24.0%, respectively. Complications, mostly transient and without clinical impact, occurred in 9.1% of PVC procedures and 6.8% of CVC procedures. No infectious or and thrombotic events were reported. Conclusions: These findings indicate that aEEX under light sedation with US-guided PVC placement is a safe, well-tolerated and effective alternative to CVC in selected paediatric patients with SCD. This approach may expand access to aEEX reducing reliance on CVC and manual exchange procedures. Trial Registration: The authors have confirmed clinical trial registration is not needed for this submission.
authors: Laura Ocello; Fabio Pavan; Giulia Maria Ferrari; Fabiola Guerra; Alessandra Moretto; Elena Tassistro; Maria G. Valsecchi; Irene Lepri; Linda Gregorio; Alice Passoni; Adriana Balduzzi; Valentina Baldini; Paola Corti

title: Designing a Functional Social Robot for Blood Test Procedures in the Emergency Department: A Human-Centered Approach
abstract: Blood tests are a common initial procedure in the emergency department (ED) and are often experienced as highly stressful, particularly in acute care areas. Robots’ social capabilities may help address patients’ emotional needs, yet their integration into such a complex environment requires clear alignment with existing clinical workflows. We present a human-centered design process for a robotic platform intended to support blood test procedures in the acute care area of the ED. A need study indicated two central guidelines: practical assistance with blood test equipment and emotional support for patients and nurses. The informed iterative design process resulted in a robotic platform that provides a mobile work surface for blood test equipment, with a small robotic arm that performs social gestures intended to provide emotional support. An initial field-validation deployment of the robot across four blood test procedures suggested that patients and nurses perceived the robot as a positive assistant capable of supporting emotional needs. We highlight the potential of integrating social features into functional robots in challenging environments such as the acute care ED.

title: B-313 Validation of the MGISP-100 Automation Platform for Pre-Capture NGS Library Preparation in Clinical Workflows
abstract: Abstract Background Automation of next-generation sequencing (NGS) library preparation can improve efficiency, reproducibility, and contamination control by standardizing pipetting-intensive steps and reducing operator-dependent variability. In clinical laboratories, these gains may translate into more predictable turnaround times, reduced hands-on labor, and tighter control of process critical quality attributes (CQAs) that impact downstream sequencing performance. Here, we evaluated the MGISP-100 Automated Sample Preparation System (MGI Tech) for pre-capture library preparation in a routine-like clinical setting, using CQAs and sample-integrity indicators relevant to day-to-day laboratory release criteria. Methods Fifty-three routine-like specimens (29 whole-blood EDTA and 24 oral swabs; 24 males and 29 females) were processed. Genomic DNA was extracted using Maxwell (Promega). Pre-capture library preparation (DNA fragmentation, end-repair/A-tailing, adapter ligation, SPRI-based cleanups, and library PCR amplification) was performed either by an established manual workflow or on the MGISP-100 Automated Sample Preparation System using the xGen DNA Library Prep kit and xGen UDI Primer Plate 1 (Integrated DNA Technologies). Libraries were quantified by Qubit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and sized by TapeStation 4200 (Agilent). Capture/enrichment was held constant (manual, identical conditions in both arms) and was not evaluated as an outcome; analyses focused on pre-capture library preparation. Sequencing was performed on DNBSEQ-G400 (paired-end 300-cycle). A reference control sample was prepared under both conditions for head-to-head variant calling comparison using DRAGEN v4.3.17 (Illumina), summarized by F-measure across SNVs, INDELs, and CNVs. To assess sample integrity and potential mixture/cross-contamination, IDR_BAF (inter-decile range of B-allele frequency across variant sites) was extracted from validation-run samples and compared between workflows. Comparisons were reported overall and stratified by specimen type (whole blood EDTA vs swab). Results No MGISP-100–specific failures occurred, and QC pass rates were consistent across specimen types. Libraries met sequencing QC targets with appropriate fragmentation and yield (mean fragment size: MGISP-100 342.76 ± 13.19 bp vs manual 334.20 ± 20.80 bp; mean concentration: MGISP-100 70.97 ± 12.81 ng/µL vs manual 64.33 ± 13.97 ng/µL). In the control sample, variant calling performance was comparable between workflows (F-measure: SNVs > 0.97, INDELs > 0.77, CNVs > 0.50). IDR_BAF values remained below the laboratory alert threshold (<0.20) in both groups, supporting preserved sample integrity. Overall mean IDR_BAF was higher with MGISP-100 (0.12328 ± 0.01096; n=25) than manual preparation (0.11464 ± 0.00776; n=28) (p=0.00210; 95% CI 0.00332–0.01396), while remaining below the threshold. Conclusion In both whole-blood EDTA and swab specimens, the MGISP-100 Automated Sample Preparation System produced pre-capture libraries with QC metrics and downstream variant calling performance comparable to the manual workflow. The small shift in IDR_BAF observed with MGISP-100—although statistically significant—remained below the established alert threshold and is consistent with minor process effects (e.g., subtle differences in pipetting dynamics, bead mixing, or cleanup stringency) rather than actionable cross-contamination. Overall, MGISP-100 supports standardized, scalable pre-capture library preparation suitable for routine clinical NGS implementation without compromising key QC or sample-integrity indicators.
authors: Gustavo Barcelos Barra; Pedro Góes Mesquita; Milena Torres; Anderson Santos; Nara Pessoa; Ilária Cristina Sgardioli; Amanda Lamas; Lorena Gama; Rosenelle Benício; Rafael Jacomo; Lídia Nery

title: COWFISH2A+ as a versatile and accessible platform for digital bioanalysis
abstract: Digital bioanalysis enables single-molecule detection of biomolecules and holds transformative potential across the life sciences and clinical diagnostics. However, its broader translation remains limited by accessibility and versatility. Here, we present COWFISH2A+, a compact, fully automated device integrating wide-field imaging with a custom dispensing module. Using an open-type microchip, COWFISH2A+ enables diverse assays at low cost through direct liquid deposition. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate two types of digital bioanalysis: a digital enzyme assay and an amplification-free digital genetic assay, SATORI. The digital enzyme assay discriminates alkaline phosphatase, a blood biomarker, at the single-isozyme level with sub-femtomolar sensitivity, while SATORI achieves attomolar-level detection of multiple pathogen-derived genetic targets. Furthermore, to demonstrate the translational potential of SATORI, we directly test 159 clinical specimens, detecting SARS-CoV-2 from nasopharyngeal swabs within ∼20 min with 92% sensitivity and 85% specificity. COWFISH2A+ thus provides an accessible and versatile platform for digital bioanalysis.
authors: Tatsuya Iida; Hajime Shinoda; Mami Yoshimura; Asami Makino; Taichi Yoshimura; Masaharu Nakazawa; Hiroshi Hayakawa; Yasushi Kogo; Kosuke Miyauchi; Takeshi Noda; Toshiaki Ban; Hiroaki Takeuchi; Masashi Toyoda; Rikiya Watanabe

title: LC−MS-Based Chlorine-Signature Query Engine Strategy for Automated Discovery of Phosphate-Containing Metabolites
abstract: Abstract Comprehensive profiling of phosphate-containing compounds (PCCs) in untargeted metabolomics remains challenging due to their high hydrophilicity, poor separation, and low stability, which hampers high-throughput screening from large-scale liquid chromatography−mass spectrometry (LC−MS) datasets. Herein, an LC-MS-based chlorine-tagging strategy integrated with a Chlorine Signature Query Engine (Cl-SQE) was established for the rapid identification of potential PCCs in complex matrices. The novel derivatization reagent, [5-(2-chlorophenyl)isoxazol-3-yl]methyl amine (ClXIMA), can react with phosphate groups on PCCs, such as nucleotides, sugar phosphates, glycerophosphates, and nucleotide sugars under mild conditions, thereby markedly enhancing reversed-phase retention and separation resolution. More importantly, the incorporation of chlorine, identifiable by its characteristic isotopic peak pattern, provides a unique digital signature in the mass spectra. Leveraging these features, Cl-SQE, a data mining program, was developed to systematically and automatically extract candidate PCCs from large-scale datasets. By applying this strategy to liver tissues from a mouse model of cholestasis, 318 potential ClXIMA derivatives were screened out, and 189 metabolites were identified or tentatively assigned. Statistical analysis revealed significant disturbances in nucleotide metabolism, addressing a critical gap in phospho-metabolomic profiling for cholestatic disease and revealing dysregulated nucleotide homeostasis as a potential feature of cholestasis-associated metabolic remodeling. Overall, this platform facilitates the discovery of PCCs in complex matrices and provides new insights into the pathogenesis of cholestasis and other clinical diseases.
authors: Xiaolin Chen; Yujie Li; Lanjia Ao; Xiqing Bian; H.K. Zeng; Na Li; Jian‐Lin Wu

title: Integrated Microfluidic CRISPR-Based Diagnostic Device for Rapid Testing of HPVs
abstract: Screening for high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) is a pivotal strategy for the prevention of invasive cervical cancer, particularly in resource-constrained settings. In this study, we developed a CRISPR-based compact automated real-time detection system, termed Ccard, for rapid testing of HPV16, HPV18, and the internal reference gene GAPDH through a streamlined workflow. A simple room-temperature treatment efficiently releases nucleic acids directly from swab samples, bypassing the need for extraction. The mixture was driven through the channels and loaded into the reaction chambers on the microfluidic chip by a vacuum pump. The lyophilized reagents in the reaction zone of the microfluidic chip were redissolved. The system subsequently performs a single-step RPA-CRISPR/Cas13a reaction, with real-time detection enabled by an Internet of Things device. The assay achieved detection within 30 min, with a limit of detection (LOD) of 5 copies/µL for both HPV16 and HPV18. Validation with clinical samples demonstrated high sensitivity (96.8% for HPV16 and 100% for HPV18) and 100% specificity. These results highlight the reliability, precision, and strong potential of the Ccard system for rapid testing of HR-HPVs.
authors: Tianci Wang; Lingyun Li; Yunxiang Wang; Yongjun Han; Teng Li; Chaoran Yu; Yufeng Lou; Zhen Rong; Kai Lin; Shengqi Wang

title: DNA metabarcoding samples from nest soil and beaks outperform samples from talons and faeces when identifying diversity of white-tailed eagle diet in South Greenland
abstract: DNA metabarcoding is an emerging approach to study diets across a broad range of species but requires careful optimisation of the sample collection method and substrate used. The suitability of different sample types to identify the diet of the target species remains under investigated. Here, we address these knowledge gaps by collecting four different sample types - faeces, beak swabs, talon swabs, and soil samples - during nest visits of white-tailed eagles (Haliaeetus albicilla) during the 2025 breeding season in South Greenland. We further investigated whether some eagle dietary taxa could act as vectors for microplastic pollution. Our analyses revealed a broad diet, with 25 dietary taxa for white-tailed eagles. Lumpfish (Cyclopterus lumpus) was the most frequently detected dietary taxon in the diet, which was composed of 75 % fish, 19 % birds, and 7 % mammals. Our findings indicate that diets varied strongly between nesting sites. Although each sample type was efficient in capturing diet, soil and beak swabs were most promising for eagles and gave comparable results. On the other hand, faeces provided a distinct dietary profile with a reduced detection of fish, while requiring an increased sample size, and talon swabs missed rare food items. Finally, we recovered microplastic contamination in 33 % of our samples, but no dietary taxon was associated with microplastic pollution. Taken together our results underline the overlooked value of soil from nests to provide dietary information and highlight the necessity to deepen our knowledge of Arctic food webs and their microplastic contamination.
authors: Mael Perroud; Kay Lucek; Knud Falk; Nicholas Per Huffeldt

title: Molecular detection of respiratory viruses from breath samples: Evaluation of nucleic acid extraction systems and PCR panels
abstract: Background Reliable and scalable molecular testing is essential for risk assessment and monitoring of respiratory viruses with epidemic or pandemic potential. The AveloMask Kit (Avelo) is a non-invasive sampling device that collects exhaled breath aerosols (XBA) using a high-performance filter, which can be released into a stabilizing buffer for nucleic acid preservation. Detection of viral nucleic acids in breath samples remains challenging, as viral loads are typically lower than in conventional upper-respiratory swabs. Therefore, optimizing extraction and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) workflows is critical to maximizing analytical sensitivity. Methods In this proof-of-concept study, we compared the nucleic acid extraction efficiency of ELITe InGenius® (ELITech) and QIAsymphony (Qiagen) automated platforms in combination with an in-house real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) panel and a commercial PCR panel (RespiFinder® 2Smart, Pathofinder). Using synthetic ribonucleic acid (RNA) standards, we determined the limit of detection (LOD) for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), influenza A, influenza B, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) as a performance indicator for both extraction platforms and PCR panels. As proof-of-concept, we analyzed seven XBA samples from infected individuals, eight from healthy controls, and one from a person recovering from a cold. Results Our results demonstrate that ELITe InGenius and QIAsymphony provide comparable extraction efficiencies without negatively impacting downstream RT-qPCR. The combination of QIAsymphony and RespiFinder 2Smart achieved LODs below 100 viral copies/mL and detected all pathogens in clinical XBA samples (7/7) that were also detected in matched swabs. Conclusions These initial findings suggest the compatibility of high-throughput extraction systems and PCR panels with XBA samples collected using AveloMask and warrant further investigation of XBA sampling as a non-invasive method for respiratory virus detection.
