title: Microbiological surveillance after automated reprocessing of gastrointestinal endoscopes in routine clinical practice: A prospective randomized microbiological surveillance study
abstract: Microbiological surveillance is used to monitor the quality of gastrointestinal endoscope reprocessing, but prospective data comparing automated endoscope reprocessor systems under routine workflow conditions remain limited. We conducted an exploratory, single-center, prospective randomized surveillance study of 222 endoscope-use episodes involving patient-used forward-viewing upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopes. Endoscope-use episodes were allocated 1:1:1 to strongly acidic electrolyzed water, ozonated water, or peracetic acid using an Excel-generated random-number procedure (n = 74 each). Assigned reprocessing was performed after standardized bedside pre-cleaning and manual cleaning. Post-reprocessing samples were obtained from predefined external and internal sites. Surveillance success was defined as ≤20 colony-forming units per sample at all sampled sites and absence of predefined indicator organisms. Success was achieved in 67/74 (90.5%) strongly acidic electrolyzed-water episodes, 71/74 (95.9%) ozonated-water episodes, and 71/74 (95.9%) peracetic-acid episodes. Risk differences in surveillance success versus peracetic acid were -5.4 percentage points (95% confidence interval, -14.6 to 3.2) and 0.0 percentage points (95% confidence interval, -7.7 to 7.7), respectively. In exploratory post hoc non-inferiority analyses using a -5 percentage-point margin, non-inferiority was not demonstrated for either functional-water system. A -10 percentage-point margin supported ozonated water but not strongly acidic electrolyzed water. Post hoc scope-level sensitivity analyses were directionally consistent with the primary analysis and highlighted the influence of repeated failures in an individual physical endoscope. These findings should be interpreted as exploratory microbiological quality-assurance data, not as evidence of clinical infection risk or comparative clinical effectiveness. Study registration: University Hospital Medical Information Network Clinical Trials Registry (UMIN-CTR), UMIN000061627 (registered May 19, 2026; enrollment began November 8, 2024).
authors: Masayuki Kato; Hideki Hayashi; Nobuharu Hironaka; Masafumi Chiba; Takahiro Abe; Nana Shimamoto; Mamoru Ito; Masakuni Kobayashi; Kazuki Sumiyama

title: Robotic Beyond Total Mesorectal Excision With Synchronous Perineal Flap Reconstruction: Feasibility and Early Outcomes
abstract: BACKGROUND: Advanced rectal and anal malignancies often require dissections beyond total mesorectal planes for improved oncological outcomes. While minimally invasive techniques facilitate this approach, they result in larger perineal defects, creating reconstructive challenges. Robotic-assisted surgery enhances precision, visualisation, and ergonomics, potentially optimising outcomes. However, data on robotics beyond total mesorectal excision (bTME) remain limited. This study evaluated robotic bTME and synchronous gracilis or PAP (profunda artery perforator) flap reconstruction. METHODS: This retrospective case series reviewed 10 patients with locally advanced or recurrent anorectal cancer who underwent elective robotic bTME with synchronous perineal gracilis or PAP flap reconstruction. RESULTS: Median operative time was 465 minutes. Gracilis flap harvest was concurrent. No major flap-related complications or reoperations. R0 resection was achieved in 80%. At 1-year, local recurrence was 0%, distant metastases 30%, and disease-free survival 70%. CONCLUSION: Robotics bTME with synchronous gracilis or PAP flap reconstruction is feasible, efficient, and oncologically safe.
authors: Ahlam Alharbi; Muhammad Rafaih Iqbal; Dolly M. Dowsett; Eleanor J. M. Rudge; Hassan I. Shah; Sandeep Kapur; Richard Matthew Haywood; Anais Rosich‐Medina; Irshad Shaikh

title: Prediction of moderate-to-severe postoperative thirst in general anesthesia patients based on automated machine learning and clinical nursing translation
abstract: Objective: To develop an Automated Machine Learning (AutoML)-based model for screening Moderate-to-Severe Postoperative Thirst (MSPOT) risk at surgery-to-PACU handover and a prototype clinical decision support system. Methods: = 278). An Improved Wave Optics Optimizer (IWOO) framework integrated feature selection and hyperparameter optimization using demographic, preoperative, and intraoperative variables. Prediction was performed at anesthesia-to-PACU handover, after final intraoperative data became available and before routine postoperative NRS thirst assessment. Performance was evaluated using ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, calibration analysis, Brier score, and decision curve analysis (DCA). SHAP was used to summarize feature contributions. Results: In the held-out internal test set, the AutoML model achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.9053, PR-AUC of 0.9080, and Brier score of 0.129, outperforming conventional models. DCA showed greater net benefit across thresholds of 1%-95%. In same-center temporal validation, discrimination remained acceptable (ROC-AUC: 0.8807; PR-AUC: 0.8778), but calibration deteriorated (Brier score: 0.1924; intercept: -1.2250; slope: 0.5811), indicating average risk overestimation and overly extreme probabilities. Six predictors were identified: esmolol use, intraoperative blood loss, operation time, ASA classification, ERAS, and intraoperative fluid volume. Conclusions: The AutoML model showed strong discrimination and transparent feature attribution. The prototype illustrates its potential use at PACU handover to prioritize early assessment and comfort-oriented thirst management. However, temporal miscalibration indicates that individualized probabilities are not ready for clinical decision-making without recalibration and subsequent prospective validation.
authors: Yi Zhan; Siting Yang; Haoran Wang

title: Detection of Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa among Diabetic Foot Ulcer Patients in Wasit Province
abstract: Diabetic foot ulcer infection is a severe clinical complication that is determined by neuropathy, vascular impairment, tissue injury and successful bacterial invasion. Diabetic foot infections are the most common complication affecting people with diabetes, and bacterial pathogens play a key role. In this study, 90 subjects including 35 patients with diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) as well as 35 diabetic patients without ulcers and 20 healthy controls were enrolled. Methods: Wound swabs from ulcer group were processed through conventional culture, selective media, VITEK 2 identification and PCR. Univariate analysis identified isolation of P. aeruginosa (17/35;48.6%) being the most frequent isolate followed by S.aureus (13/35;37.1%) while other bacteria represented only 14.3%. Molecular confirmation using 16S rRNA, nuc and oprL genes showed complete concordance with phenotypic identification. Identification probabilities of both species on the VITEK 2 were greater than 90%. P. aeruginosa and S. aureus are clinically significant in diabetic foot ulcers due to their persistence, biofilm-forming ability and antimicrobial resistance; study results highlight concurrent use of culture, automated identification and PCR for accurate diagnosis/management
authors: Zaman Sami Kareem; Alaa Ali Matrood

title: Robotic Palpation for Spatiotemporal Arterial Pulse Quantification and Mapping Using Multilevel Microdome‐Based Soft Pressure Sensors
abstract: ABSTRACT Humanoid robots have advanced capabilities through physical and physiological examinations, but their reliance on visual information limits biological‐object assessment, underscoring the need for tactile perception. Current tactile systems primarily detect basic contact using a limited number of sensors, hindering accurate soft‐object localization and physiological signal acquisition. This study introduces a robotic palpation strategy by utilizing a fully soft‐tactile‐sensor‐integrated humanoid hand for real‐time spatiotemporal arterial pulse diagnosis. A facile fabrication technique produces an artificial pressure‐sensitive layer with multilevel microscale dome‐on‐dome (DoD) structures using eutectic gallium‐indium, achieving high‐density (>72 500 ea/cm 2 ) and large‐area (wafer‐scale >98% yield) fabrication. The DoD‐integrated pressure sensor exhibits a 7.5 × enhanced dynamic response compared with a single‐level sensing layer, enabling the simultaneous detection of subtle vibrations under high‐pressure conditions. The artificial skin is integrated into a humanoid hand, featuring 81 sensors on the fingertip and a total of 801 sensors on the hand, allowing real‐time spatiotemporal arterial pulse quantification and mapping.

title: Utility of nano-impregnated surface coating to achieve continuous active disinfection in ICU of a tertiary trauma center
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Implementing continuous active disinfection presents challenges as conventional cleaning methods may not fully mitigate risks. Hence, evaluating innovative technologies becomes imperative. This study assessed a nanoparticle-based surface coating containing titanium dioxide engineered into nano-molecules that is activated by normal light and provides ongoing disinfection. METHODOLOGY: The research took place in two intensive care units (ICUs): ICU A (coated) and ICU B (control). Data on healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and environmental factors were collected pre- and post-coating application to gauge its impact. The change in percentage of positive swabs/HAI cases in ICU A was compared to ICU B and statistically analyzed using a 2-sample test for equality of proportions. RESULTS: ICU A witnessed a 26.5% decrease in positive environment swabs post-coating, while ICU B saw a 160.9% increase. This disparity was statistically significant (p = 0.000). Both ICUs experienced decreased ventilator associated pneumonia (VAP) cases, though central line associated-blood steam infection (CLA-BSI) and catheter associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) cases increased in ICU A post application. Following coating, positive environmental swabs and VAP decreased by 71.8%, and 72.5%, while CLA-BSI and CAUTI increased by 198% and 43.5%. CONCLUSIONS: The evaluation showed that the coating may serve to supplement traditional cleaning and disinfection methods. Further research into the efficacy and cost-effectiveness of such antimicrobial coating is needed for overall improvement in patient care.

title: Behavioural and hormonal correlates of virtuality during autobiographical memory retrieval
abstract: Virtual reality (VR) is increasingly permeating medical practice, facilitating new health interventions and diagnostic tools to delay or alleviate cognitive aging. However, it remains unclear whether fully automated virtual memory tasks match the efficacy and physiological safety of traditional interventions administered by human providers. To address this, we evaluated an odour-triggered autobiographical memory task across four discrete conditions. Selected as strategic points along the latent „virtuality continuum”, these conditions model the step-by-step translation of clinical memory tasks—from reality human-facilitated real-world care (VR0), augmented care using multisensory VR (VR1) to fully autonomous, text-guided VR (VR2) and virtual agent-mediated interactions (VR3). Subjective sense of presence was equivalent across all VR environments (VR1–VR3), confirming a controlled baseline of visual immersion. Subjects recalled comparable numbers of autobiographical memories in all conditions, but the virtual social environment (VR3) triggered the longest recall durations. All VR environments elicited memories with more positive emotional valence than real-person delivery. Critically, salivary levels of the social hormone oxytocin were significantly decreased after tasks performed in automated environments (VR2 and VR3) compared to the human-guided VR1. These findings confirm VR’s high potential for memory training while highlighting a possible reduction in physiological social activation when replacing human providers with virtual agents. As virtual agents expand in daily healthcare, our data underscore the importance of assessing physiological social responses, particularly for prolonged interventions.

title: Haematological alterations in dogs with canine distemper virus-associated respiratory tract infection in Guwahati, Assam
abstract: Canine distemper is a multisystemic viral disease of dogs in which the blood picture changes with the stage of infection and with secondary complications. This study evaluated the haematological alterations in dogs with respiratory tract infection associated with canine distemper virus (CDV) under field conditions in Guwahati, Assam, India. Twelve dogs formed two groups of six: dogs with respiratory signs that were positive for CDV antigen in a rapid immunochromatographic test of nasal and conjunctival swabs (CDV group) and apparently healthy dogs (control group). Haemoglobin (Hb), total erythrocyte count (TEC), packed cell volume (PCV), thrombocyte count, total leukocyte count (TLC), and differential leukocyte percentages were measured with an automated haematology analyser. Groups were compared by the independent samples t-test, with P < 0.05 considered significant. Dogs in the CDV group had significantly (P < 0.01) lower Hb (42.3%), TEC (32.3%), PCV (25.5%), and thrombocyte count (40.3%) than the control group, and all four values were below the canine reference limits. The TLC was significantly (P < 0.01) higher (46.2%), with higher percentages of granulocytes and monocytes and a lower percentage of lymphocytes. The absolute granulocyte (14.45 × 103/µL) and monocyte (1.68 × 103/µL) counts estimated from the group means exceeded the upper reference limits, whereas the estimated lymphocyte count (1.77 × 103/µL) remained within the reference interval. The results indicate anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and granulocytic leukocytosis with monocytosis in CDV-infected dogs and suggest that the fall in lymphocytes was relative and not absolute.
authors: Shveta Singh; Deepa Lahkar; Arabinda Phukan; Ditul Barman; Durlav Prasad Bora; Lukumoni Buragohain; Archana Hazarika

title: Machine learning-based early detection of abnormal heart rate in critically ill patients: a real-world clinical dataset study with automated alert system integration
abstract: Introduction: Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) are a leading global health challenge, particularly in resource-constrained settings where delayed diagnosis worsens outcomes. Abnormal heart rate (tachycardia/bradycardia) is a modifiable, independent risk factor that benefits from early, automated detection. Methods: We used a large real-world dataset from Hospital Santa Maria, Lisbon (23,122 patients, January 2019-November 2021, spanning the COVID-19 period). Two operational outcome definitions were evaluated: (i) an interquartile-range (IQR)-based, patient-specific definition, used to compare four classifiers (Logistic Regression, K-Nearest Neighbors, Random Forest, Naive Bayes), and (ii) standard clinical thresholds for tachycardia/bradycardia, applied to the best-performing model. Following CRISP-DM, models were trained and evaluated with patient-grouped, walk-forward time-series cross-validation to prevent patient-level data leakage. Results: Logistic Regression was the best-performing model. Under the IQR-based definition: AUROC 0.78, recall 85.4%, precision 66.1%, F1-score 74.5%. Under the clinically standard threshold-based definition: AUROC 0.81, recall 91.7%, precision 68.8%, F1-score 78.6%. Expanded metrics (event prevalence, false-positive rate, alert burden, calibration, confidence intervals) are reported. A prototype real-time e-mail alert system was demonstrated as a feasibility proof-of-concept and reviewed informally by two cardiovascular specialists. Discussion: Recall and AUROC alone do not establish clinical utility. Key limitations include the single-centre design, substantial missingness in ethnicity/diagnosis variables, the small clinician-evaluation sample (n = 2), and pandemic-period data collection. This work is presented as a methodologically strengthened proof-of-concept, with prospective, multi-site, multi-clinician external validation identified as the necessary next step.
authors: João C. Ferreira; Luís B. Elvas

title: Statistical quality control practices in a sample of Spanish Blood Establishments: a mixed-methods exploratory study: Statistical QC practices in Spanish Blood Establishments
abstract: Background - The European Directorate for the Quality of Medicines & HealthCare (EDQM) provides guidance for statistical quality control in blood component manufacturing, including recommendations for sampling and statistical process control. However, the extent to which these recommendations are implemented in routine practice remains unclear. Materials and methods - We conducted a sequential explanatory mixed-methods study among professionals working in blood establishments, recruited through the Spanish Society of Blood Transfusion blood processing working group. Phase 1 was a cross-sectional survey (10 responding centers across 10 autonomous communities; response rate 77%). Phase 2 comprised semi-structured interviews with a purposive sample of survey respondents (No.=7). Survey findings informed the interview topic guide. Thematic analysis followed the Braun and Clarke approach. Findings from both phases were integrated using a joint display. Results - Respondents represented centers with varied production volumes, and most had more than 6 years of experience (80%). Use of statistical quality control methods was limited: 90% reported using descriptive statistics only and 10% used control charts. For sample size determination, 80% applied fixed production percentages without formal statistical justification. Spreadsheet-based workflows with custom formulas predominated (90%). Key challenges included determining sample size and laborious report generation (both 80%). Interviews highlighted uncertainty about sampling adequacy, potential for earlier trend detection, perceived complexity of guidance, and the need for interpretive decision support. All participants expressed interest in automated approaches. Discussion - Among participating centers, variation in the implementation of statistical quality control practices relative to EDQM recommendations suggests opportunities for improved harmonization. Automated tools that embed recommended sampling and monitoring methods may support implementation, although larger studies are needed to estimate prevalence at national level.
authors: Héctor Sarmiento; María Isabel Ortiz de Salazar Martín; Luis Roberto Larrea González; Ana M Arruga Manzano; María Luisa Ayape; Aida Isabel Azcarate Gonzalez; Teresa Díaz Rueda; Marta López Melchor; Pascual Marco Vera; María del Carmen Martín Alonso; María Mercadillo González; Ana Isabel Pérez Aliaga; Magdalena Prohens‐Batle

title: Integrity Detection and Characterization of Malicious Injections in RAVEN II
abstract: The increasing adoption of robotic systems in surgery, together with the expanding range of procedures they can support and the growing level of autonomy they provide, has substantially increased the complexity of surgical robots. As these systems integrate more sensors, controllers, communication interfaces, and model-driven control components, their attack surface continues to expand. A compromise of the integrity of a surgical robot can therefore cause unintended robot behavior and potentially threaten patient safety. In this paper, we characterize the detection boundary of malicious injections on RAVEN II using a public dataset that pairs the platform's telemetry with external high-resolution encoder ground truth. We identify three injection points spanning the command and observation paths and evaluate three injection patterns with increasing temporal dispersion. To capture different detection behaviors, we perform detection at two timescales: the window scale and the session scale. Rather than reporting detection rates at an arbitrarily chosen threshold, we quantify, for each injection point and injection pattern, the smallest end-effector deviation that can be resolved while maintaining an alarm rate acceptable for surgical operation. Our results show that detectability is strongly influenced by how the injected deviation is distributed over time. An abrupt step can be detected at deviations well below the 1 mm clinical tolerance, whereas the same overall deviation spread across a window or a session can remain hidden from single-window statistics. The open source code can be found at http://github.com/RAVENIIROS/RAVENIIIntegrity.
authors: Xingli Zhang; Diba Afroze; Fei Hu; Xiali Hei

title: Association Between COVID-19 Vaccine Doses and Neurosensory Symptoms Among COVID-19-Positive Patients: A Retrospective Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Ageusia and anosmia are common manifestations of COVID-19. This study examined whether their frequency among infected patients was associated with the recorded number of Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine doses; it was not designed to estimate causality or vaccine effectiveness. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional analysis of 5,348 COVID-19-positive patients over five years of age followed by the San Miguelito Health Region, Panama, from July 7, 2021, through November 2, 2022. Unvaccinated patients and vaccinated patients whose recorded doses were exclusively Pfizer-BioNTech were included. Separate logistic regression models estimated associations between vaccine dose category (zero, one, two, or three to four doses) and self-reported ageusia and anosmia, with two doses as the reference. A post hoc sensitivity analysis additionally adjusted for swab month. RESULTS: Ageusia was reported by 507 patients (9.48%), and anosmia by 584 patients (10.92%). In the primary adjusted models, compared with two doses, adjusted odds ratios (aORs) for zero, one, and three to four doses were 1.87 (95% confidence interval (CI) 1.48-2.38), 2.68 (95% CI 1.99-3.60), and 0.26 (95% CI 0.18-0.36), respectively, for ageusia, and 1.82 (95% CI 1.46-2.27), 2.53 (95% CI 1.91-3.35), and 0.18 (95% CI 0.12-0.25), respectively, for anosmia. After categorical adjustment for swab month, all six dose-category estimates were attenuated, and none remained statistically significant. CONCLUSIONS: Primary models identified strong associations between recorded vaccine dose category and self-reported ageusia and anosmia among infected patients, but these associations did not persist after adjustment for swab month. The results are compatible with substantial confounding by epidemic period and should not be interpreted as causal effects or estimates of vaccine effectiveness.
authors: Jaime Ricardo Sevillano Giráldez; Grace Thompson; Luis Escobar; Isaac Fernández Carmago; Luis Alberto Flores

title: Improved metabolic profiles, body condition score and body weight as positive modulators of conception rate of nondescript pre-partum does fed concentrates
abstract: Does fed with roughage and concentrate had higher average body weight (p<0.01) and body condition score (p<0.05) from the second month until the end of the feeding period. Mean serum cholesterol concentrations were higher (p<0.05) in does fed roughage and concentrate compared to those fed roughage alone except during the first blood collection, while no significant differences (p>0.05) were found in mean serum triglyceride and glucose levels. Does fed with roughage and concentrate showed 100% estrus, 80% conception rate, shorter estrus cycle length (29.4 days vs. 32.6 days), and higher conception rate (80% compared to 37.5%) than does fed with roughage only.
authors: C. F. Olo; M. L. Autriz; I. D. L. Matel; G. A. Pareja; D. D. Olarve; K. J. P. Dawis; K. L. D. C. Obispo

title: Closed-loop artificial intelligence agents for animal epidemic prediction and decision support in livestock farming: a review
abstract: Animal diseases continuously threaten livestock production and public health, yet current surveillance approaches remain largely passive and fragmented. Conventional artificial intelligence models typically function as open-loop predictors, delivering static outputs that fail to accommodate the dynamic operational needs of veterinarians in real-world farm settings. This review explores an emerging paradigm of AI agents for animal disease monitoring, emphasizing how such agents can transition from passive observation to active intervention through a closed-loop perception-decision-feedback architecture. We first classify multi-scale sensing technologies: at the micro-scale, automated molecular diagnostics and biosensors; at the macro-scale, computer-vision-based phenotyping. These technologies collectively provide the data streams required for continuous surveillance. The review then discusses how multi-modal inputs, time-series forecasting, resource-aware decision-making, and reinforcement learning can be integrated into an agent-based workflow. Importantly, most current veterinary research evidence supports only the individual components of this framework, rather than the deployment of fully autonomous, iteratively evolving closed-loop agents in actual field environments. Translating closed-loop AI from a conceptual framework into a reliable veterinary decision-support tool will therefore require further advances in validation, standardization, governance, and human oversight.
authors: Yuzhi Wang; Yingtong Zhou; Liyu Li; Huiling Xu; Wangze Ni; Xiaoliang Li

title: Association Between Ferritin Levels and Hemoglobin Concentration Among Adolescent Girls in Indonesia
abstract: Background: Anemia remains a critical global public health concern, particularly among adolescent girls who face heightened vulnerability due to rapid physical growth spurts and periodic menstrual blood loss. Iron deficiency is recognized as the leading etiological factor, clinically culminating in iron deficiency anemia (IDA). Standard public health screenings routinely rely on standalone hemoglobin (Hb) measurements; however, a decline in Hb represents a late-stage manifestation of chronic iron depletion, which risks masking individuals suffering from latent iron deficiency. Methods: A cross-sectional school-based study was conducted in April 2026, involving 126 adolescent female students aged 12–18 years in Padang City who met the rigorous inclusion criteria. Whole blood samples were collected via venipuncture; hemoglobin concentrations were determined using an automated hematology analyzer, and serum ferritin levels were quantified via Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA). Statistical evaluations were performed using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient (r_s) and Fisher's Exact test. Results: The majority of the respondents were non-anemic (84.9%) and presented with normal ferritin levels (77%). Spearman's Rho correlation test revealed a statistically significant, weak positive relationship between serum ferritin and hemoglobin levels (r_s=0.398, p=0.000). The scatter plot model illustrated a non-linear trajectory, characterized by a steep increase in Hb within the lower ferritin range (<30" ng/mL" ) before flattening into a plateau at higher ferritin values. Cross-tabulation indicated a highly significant association between anemia and iron deficiency status (p=0.000), showing that 68.4% of anemic participants were iron deficient. Notably, within the non-anemic cohort, 15% of the adolescent girls had already developed latent iron deficiency. Conclusion: There is a significant positive correlation between serum ferritin and hemoglobin concentrations, governed by a non-linear homeostatic threshold. Relying solely on isolated hemoglobin screenings risks misclassifying and omitting adolescent girls with latent iron deficiency, emphasizing the urgent need for comprehensive, universal preventive iron supplementation strategies.
authors: Annisa Lidra Maribeth; Rosfita Rasyid; Nur Indrawaty Lipoeto; Rahma Yulia Putri; Fatimah Khairiyah; Dewi Marhaeni Diah Herawati
venue: Nutrición clínica y dietética hospitalaria/Nutrición clínica, dietética hospitalaria

title: Diagnostic testing for pulmonary tuberculosis in low and middle-income countries: innovations to achieve universal access—a narrative review
abstract: Though rapid molecular diagnostics for tuberculosis (TB) have substantially improved diagnostic accuracy and turnaround times, implementation and impact has been constrained by cost, infrastructure requirements, and continued reliance on sputum. This review examines advances in diagnostic technologies and sampling strategies that could overcome these barriers and accelerate universal access to TB diagnostics. We conducted a narrative review of studies published between Jan 1, 2020, and April 30, 2026, focusing on near-point-of-care molecular (NPOC) platforms, next-generation lipoarabinomannan (LAM) assays, and non-sputum sampling approaches. Emerging NPOC molecular platforms, demonstrate high sensitivity using both sputum and tongue-swab specimens while substantially reducing equipment and testing costs compared with existing nucleic acid amplification test platforms. Next-generation urine LAM assays offer improved sensitivity and potential for use beyond people living with HIV. In addition, parallel testing approaches with multiple sample types, including sputum, tongue swab, stool for children, and urine testing, can substantially increase diagnostic yield in specific populations. Integrating low-cost technologies with non-sputum sampling strategies could provide a scalable pathway towards universal access to TB diagnostics. Realizing this potential will require streamlined regulatory pathways, sustainable financing, and integration of these tools into primary healthcare systems. Funding: None.
authors: Nazir Ahmed Ismail; Rebecca H. Berhanu; Nina von Knorring; Marguerite Massinga Loembé; Mikashmi Kohli; Rumina Hasan; Siva K. Shanmugam; Surbhi Sheokand; Achilles Katamba; Madhukar Pai; Shaheed V. Omar

title: Genomic tracking of Campylobacter jejuni along poultry and pig value chains in Northeast India: Implications for food safety
abstract: Campylobacter jejuni is the predominant causative agent of human campylobacteriosis. A total of 864 samples (poultry cloacal swabs, chicken intestine, chicken meat, pig rectal swab, pig intestine, pork) were screened for the presence of C. jejuni using standard methods. A total of 27 isolates were confirmed with PCR with an overall occurrence rate of 3.13%. Highest isolation rates were from chicken intestine samples (9.72%), followed by pork (7.64%) and chicken meat (1.39%). Resistance levels were high towards nalidixic acid, tetracycline, ampicillin and ciprofloxacin. Multidrug-resistance and biofilm formation featured in 30.77% and 53.84% isolates, respectively. Genomic characterization identified the highest presence of T86I mutation in gyrA and cmeABC system. The isolates were abundant with important virulence genes such as cdtABC, wlan, neuABC and cstIII . The isolates belonged to diverse Penner serotypes and MLST types with ST 353 complex being the predominant clonal complex. Phylogenetic analysis indicated tendency of the genomes with similar ST/CC to cluster together and indicated wide genetic diversity . To the best of our knowledge, this serves as the first genome submission of C. jejuni from porcine sources of India. Further, this study underscores the need for exploiting modern technologies, including genomics, to study various food-borne pathogens.
authors: Arockiasamy Arun Prince Milton; Kandhan Srinivas; Heiborkie Shilla; Balusamy Dhayananth; Samir Das; G Bhuvana Priya; Sandeep Ghatak

title: Terra Firma-Forme Dermatosis or Dermatosis Neglecta: A Diagnostic Continuum Illustrated by a Pediatric Case of Post-circumcision Penile Allodynia
abstract: Terra firma-forme dermatosis (TFFD) and dermatosis neglecta (DN) can look identical on the skin, both presenting as dirt-like, verrucous plaques that clear with 70% alcohol swabbing. In both conditions, the plaque consists of retained, loosely adherent keratin and debris overlying otherwise normal skin, rather than a true structural epidermal lesion, which is why alcohol removes it. Classically, TFFD persists despite proper washing, whereas DN clears once hygiene resumes; alcohol swabbing does not distinguish between the two. We report a 13-year-old boy with probable autism spectrum disorder who developed a dirt-like, verrucous plaque on the penile shaft after circumcision, where persistent hyperesthesia (increased cutaneous sensitivity) and allodynia (pain provoked by a stimulus that would not normally be painful) made washing painful. Biopsy showed orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis with a normal dermis, ruling out a verrucous epidermal hamartoma. Rubbing the plaque with 70% alcohol produced complete clearance, ruling out a fixed lesion. No findings suggestive of caregiver neglect were identified; the avoidance was localized and self-directed. Hygiene was subsequently discussed with the patient and his caregiver in light of his pain threshold and sensory sensitivities, and he was referred for neuropsychiatric follow-up. This case highlights an underrecognized cutaneous complication of pediatric circumcision, where pain avoidance combined with neurodevelopmental vulnerability can mimic a primary keratinization disorder.
authors: Jules Roullée; Guillaume Chaby; Christophe Attencourt; Florian Lombart

title: Selective Laser Sintering and Graphitization for Mono‐Matrix Unibody Fabrication of Integrated Stereo‐Circuit and Stereo‐Fluidic Wearable Electronics
abstract: Wearable integrated electronic devices for biomedical, robotics, and sensing applications require greater compactness and functional complexity while maintaining wearability. However, seamlessly integrating electronic and microfluidic components remain challenging due to fabrication heterogeneity, material mismatches, and complex assembly requirements. In this study, we present an innovative selective laser sintering and graphitization (SLSG) 3D printing technology that enables seamless integration of 3D circuits (stereo-circuits) and 3D fluidic channels (stereo-fluidics). SLSG achieves unibody, autonomous mono-matrix fabrication through adaptive photonic modulation of carbon-rich precursors (e.g., polyetheretherketone (PEEK) powder), simultaneously creating insulating sintered structures and conductive graphitized patterns with conductivity up to 1,895 S/m, yielding 7.64-fold higher electrochemical performance than classic glassy carbon electrodes (GCEs). Using SLSG, we fabricated a watch-type wearable unibody multimodal microfluidic biosensor (UMMB) with integrated electrochemical biosensors for on-body sweat metabolite monitoring. UMMB incorporates stereo-circuits for sensing and signal routing, plus stereo-fluidic channels for sweat respiration, achieving effective lactate and glucose sensing. The device demonstrates excellent sensitivities of 29.43 and 16.86 µA/mM for detecting lactate and glucose, respectively, while exhibiting nondetectable interference or circuit-fluidic crosstalk. This novel SLSG 3D printing technology introduces a transformative unibody approach to fabricate multifunctional bioelectronic-fluidic platform for integrated point-of-care devices, wearable sensors/biosensors, actuators, advanced theranostics, and personalized biomedical devices.
authors: Li Zhang; Wing Cheung Mak

title: Stage-Specific Associations of Automated RPR With Treponema pallidum qPCR Positivity and Cycle Threshold in Early Symptomatic Syphilis: A Multicenter Study Using Specimens Collected During Routine Care
abstract: Background: Treponema pallidum quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) positivity and cycle threshold (Ct) by rapid plasma reagin (RPR), disease stage, and other characteristics are poorly characterized in routine-care specimens, leaving it unclear when qPCR of such specimens is informative for diagnosis. Methods: This Japanese multicenter cross-sectional study explored qPCR positivity and Ct by these characteristics. Nonblood specimens collected during routine care underwent qPCR at a central laboratory for this study. Bayesian logistic and normal regressions modeled positivity and mean Ct of TP0574 and polA with stage-specific continuous automated RPR terms, patient characteristics, collection site, and facility random intercepts. Estimates were standardized over the analyzed specimens. Population-group predictions were instead averaged within each group. Results: Among 154 nonblood specimens from 145 patients (71.7% non-MSM men and women) at 14 facilities, 109 (70.8%) were qPCR positive. At RPR 1, adjusted positivity was 72.2% (95% credible interval, 60.9%—82.9%) in primary and 43.8% (16.7%—69.9%) in secondary syphilis. Positivity showed a modest downward trend with RPR in primary but increased in secondary syphilis, reflecting a stage-by-RPR interaction (secondary-to-primary ratio of odds ratios, 1.78; 1.25—2.65). Predicted positivity showed an upward trend with RPR values among MSM; adjusted positivity was relatively high for genital/urethral/urinary and anal/perianal/rectal specimens. Adjusted mean Ct increased with RPR in primary and followed an inverted-U pattern in secondary syphilis. Conclusions: In primary syphilis, nonblood qPCR positivity was high even at low RPR. When serologic findings remain inconclusive in this stage, qPCR is highly recommended for securing an early diagnosis.
authors: Ayu Kasamatsu; Yuki Ohama; Yui Tomo; Kazuo Imai; Shu‐ichi Nakayama; Ryosuke Omori; Takuya Yamagishi; Mitsuru Yasuda; Yukihiro Akeda

title: Differences in microbiota profiles of simple and complicated pediatric appendicitis cases
abstract: This study aimed to identify the differences in microbial composition between simple appendicitis (SA) and complicated appendicitis (CA) in a limited sample size using culture and microbiota analysis. Appendix tissues and rectal swabs for microbiota analysis and conventional cultures were collected from patients. 16S rRNA regions were amplified using a DNA preparation kit with primers designed to target the V3-V4 region. Sixteen (41%) of the patients were classified as CA based on the histopathological analysis, and the rest as SA. The effect size was slightly greater in rectal swab samples than in appendiceal tissue samples. Based on the conventional culture, the most common aerobic bacteria were Escherichia , Klebsiella spp., and Enterococcus spp. A decrease in both Pseudomonadota and Bacteriodota phyla was observed in tissue samples, while a decrease in Bacteriodota and an increase in Pseudomonadota were observed in rectal samples. Differences in the relative abundance of Coprobacter and Hungatella were observed between CAT and SAT samples; however, no genus-level difference remained significant after ANCOM-BC2 multiple-testing correction. The most notable feature of the CAT group was the relatively higher presence of potential pathobionts. Bacteriodes and Roseburia showed higher relative abundance in the SA rectal (SAR) group. The genera Eubacterium and Clostridioides showed a significant increase in both the SAR and CA rectal (CAR) groups. Lower relative abundances of Parvimonas, Prevotella , and Dialister and a higher relative abundance of Tyzzerella were observed in CAR compared with controls, although these differences did not remain significant after multiple-testing correction. In the ANCOM-BC2 pairwise analysis, an unclassified genus within Enterobacteriaceae was significantly enriched in CAR compared with healthy controls (LFC = 3.56, q = 0.003). No statistically significant distinction was shown at the alpha and beta diversity levels between SA and CA cases. Our findings support previous studies on increased density and diversity at the phylum level in the CA group. The main limitations were the limited sample size and the use of pre-operative antibiotics. Microbiota profiling of appendiceal tissue and rectal swab samples may provide complementary information for understanding microbiota-associated patterns in appendicitis; however, the diagnostic or predictive utility of these microbial profiles requires validation in larger, independent cohorts using dedicated predictive modeling and diagnostic performance analyses.
authors: Lütfiye Öksüz; Evrim Özdemіr; İdil Tuncer; Secil Yüksel; Tayyip Karaman; Başak Erginel
venue: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology

title: Molecular Detection and Expression of the blaZ Gene in Clinical Staphylococcus aureus Isolated from Hospital Patients
abstract: This study aimed to investigate the presence and expression of the blaZ gene in clinical Staphylococcus aureus isolates obtained from patients attending hospitals in Iraq. A total of 140 clinical specimens were collected, including wound swabs (71), vaginal swabs (35), urine samples (20), and sputum samples (14). Bacterial isolation was performed using Mannitol Salt Agar (MSA), followed by morphological and biochemical identification and confirmation using the VITEK-2 Compact system. Among the collected specimens, 25 S. aureus isolates were identified. β-Lactamase production was assessed using the Nitrocefin disk test, with 20 isolates showing positive results. These β-lactamase-positive isolates were selected for molecular analysis. PCR was performed for detection of the blaZ, mecA and 16S rRNA genes, and the blaZ gene was detected in all 20 examined isolates. The mecA gene was also detected in all selected isolates. The expression of blaZ was subsequently analyzed by real-time quantitative PCR using 16S rRNA as the reference gene. The results revealed considerable variation in blaZ expression among the examined isolates, with fold-change values ranging from 0.001953 to 128 and an overall mean of 17.90. Overall, the study demonstrated the presence of blaZ among the selected β-lactamase-positive clinical S. aureus isolates and showed considerable variation in its expression between isolates. These findings provide molecular characterization of blaZ expression among the clinical isolates examined in this study. Keywords: Staphylococcus aureus; blaZ; β-Lactamase; Antimicrobial resistance; mecA; 16S rRNA.
authors: Manal Dheyaa Mohammad

title: FORENSIC CLASSIFICATION OF GUNSHOT RESIDUE PARTICLES USING SEM-EDX AND MACHINE LEARNING
abstract: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly shaping forensic science by enabling more accurate and objective evidence analysis. This study applies ML algorithms to classify gunshot residue (GSR) particles using spectral data obtained through scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDX). Conventional GSR identification relies on detecting characteristic inorganic particles containing lead (Pb), barium (Ba), and antimony (Sb), which point to firearm discharge residue. Twelve spectra were collected from four hand swabs taken during a simulated shooting scenario, alongside control samples that yielded no residue signal. The particles were analysed for elemental distribution and subjected to ML-assisted classification. A statistical framework combining probabilistic modelling with likelihood ratios (LRs) was then used to weigh the evidential strength of competing hypotheses. Results revealed marked differences in elemental composition across samples, underscoring the importance of rigorous statistical treatment rather than relying solely on visual or qualitative assessment. Three of the four swab classes offered strong support for GSR presence, yielding high LRs favouring the prosecution hypothesis. One sample, however, deviated from the model's underlying assumptions, illustrating how elemental signatures alone can be misleading if interpreted without appropriate methodological safeguards. Overall, integrating ML with probabilistic modelling offers a robust framework for forensic GSR analysis. Nonetheless, the findings highlight that methodological rigor cannot be sacrificed for computational convenience, and analysts should remain attentive to cases where statistical assumptions break down.
authors: Tolulope Bayode Abejide; Graham Souch; David Olayemi Alebiosu

title: Tissue-specific virome variation and diversity of the Himalayan marmot on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau

title: Phenotypic and Molecular Characterization of Heme Release in Selected Clinical Isolates of Staphylococcus aureus: Expression Analysis of PSMA and HLD Genes by RT-PCR and Quantification by HPLC.
abstract: This study evaluated whether the expression of psmα and hld is associated with HPLC-detected heme release from human erythrocytes after exposure to clinical S. aureus isolates. A total of 90 human clinical samples were examined, including wound swabs, pus aspirates, blood-culture isolates and catheter-tip isolates. S. aureus was identified using culture, Gram staining, catalase, coagulase, mannitol fermentation and automated biochemical confirmation. Thirty confirmed S. aureus isolates were selected for the erythrocyte-exposure experiment. Bacterial isolates were incubated with washed human erythrocytes for 2 h at 37°C. Total RNA was extracted from bacterial pellets, converted into cDNA and analyzed by RT-qPCR for psmα and hld, using gyrB as the housekeeping gene. Free heme released into the supernatant was quantified by reverse-phase HPLC using a hemin chloride calibration curve. S. aureus was recovered from 42/90 samples, giving an isolation rate of 46.7%. Among the 30 selected isolates, 15 were classified as high heme-release isolates and 15 as low heme-release isolates. High heme-release isolates showed significantly higher psmα expression than low heme-release isolates, with mean fold expression of 3.41±1.02 versus 1.48±0.51, respectively. The hld gene was also significantly upregulated in high heme-release isolates, with mean fold expression of 2.87±0.94 versus 1.26±0.42. HPLC analysis showed significantly higher free heme concentration in the high heme-release group than in the low heme-release group, 38.6±9.4 µM versus 12.4±5.1 µM. psmα expression correlated positively with HPLC-detected heme concentration, while hld expression also showed a significant positive correlation. Clinical S. aureus isolates with increased psmα and hld expression showed greater HPLC-detected erythrocyte heme release.
authors: S Ismael; Hiba Ali Hilal; Ruaa Hussein NADA

title: Multicentre Evaluation of Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) for Environmental Monitoring of Nosocomial Pathogens in Italian Hospitals
abstract: Background: Environmental contamination of hospital surfaces, especially in high-risk clinical areas, partly sustains healthcare-associated infections. The detection of microbiological contamination in hospital settings using culture-based methods remains fundamental, even though these methods are not rapid, show moderate sensitivity in areas with low microbial loads, and are unsuitable for some microbial species. This multicentre study evaluated the performance of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) for the rapid detection of major nosocomial pathogens on hospital surfaces. Methods: A multicentre observational method–comparison study was conducted in three Italian hospital centres. Overall, 298 environmental surface samples were collected from clinical areas included in local infection-prevention monitoring plans. For each sampling point, LAMP swab sampling was paired with an adjacent contact plate culture. LAMP assays targeted Staphylococcus aureus, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Manual and automated nucleic acid extraction workflows were analysed separately. Diagnostic performance, agreement metrics, and discordant paired results were assessed using a contact plate culture as the microbiological comparator. Results: No LAMP-negative/RODAC-positive pairs were observed. Positive percent agreement (PPA) relative to contact plate culture was therefore 100% in the subgroups evaluated. Relative specificity ranged from 90.9% to 98.6%, while overall accuracy ranged from 93.8% to 98.6%. Discordant results were exclusively LAMP-positive/contact plate-negative and were more frequent for S. aureus and P. aeruginosa. Selective culture verification supported several LAMP-positive findings not recovered by routine contact plates. Conclusions: LAMP showed high negative agreement, high specificity, and rapid target-specific detection of selected nosocomial pathogens on hospital surfaces. It may complement conventional cultures in environmental surveillance, particularly when timely feedback is needed to guide infection-prevention and sanitation-monitoring strategies.
authors: Biagio Santella; Antonio Donato; Vittoria Satriani; Laura Grumiro; Stefano Stracquadanio; Emanuela Santoro; Luigi Fortino; Claudia Colosimo; Alice Nicolosi; Maddalena Calvo; Graziella Manciagli; Zirone Nunziata; Agata Silvana Trifilò; Maria Giuseppina Pecora; Giuseppe Arcoleo; Monica Cricca; Stefania Stefani; Vittorio Sambri; Giovanni Boccia

title: Single-Tube Six-Channel Ultrafast PCR with Melting-Curve Discrimination for Seven Respiratory Pathogens
abstract: Abstract Expanding single-tube multiplexing beyond the number of fluorescence channels on a real-time PCR instrument is a persistent challenge for point-of-care testing (POCT). Here, we break this barrier by leveraging melting temperature (Tm) as an extra information dimension. By employing a probe-cleavage-mediated reporter-duplex strategy, we circumvent the conventional limitation that hydrolyzed TaqMan probes cannot participate in postamplification melting analysis. Two FAM-labeled probes, each containing an engineered 5′-terminal nontarget extension, generate cleavage-dependent reporter amplicons with distinctly different melting temperatures (ΔTm = 10.3 °C), enabling precise differentiation between BV (72.5 °C) and BY (82.8 °C) within a single optical channel. Combined with a lyophilized-bead cartridge that automates nucleic acid release (4 min) and an ultrafast PCR run (16 min), the platform detects eight targets─seven respiratory pathogens (SARS-CoV-2, influenza A H1N1/H3N2/H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, influenza B Victoria/Yamagata, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae) plus one internal control (B2M)─using only six optical channels. The assay achieves a limit of detection of 5 copies per reaction (R2 > 0.97, amplification efficiency 96–104%) with no cross-reactivity against 55 nontarget microorganisms, and intra/inter-assay CVs < 5%. The lyophilized beads remain stable for 12 months at 25 °C (ΔCt < 1.5). In 272 clinical throat swabs, the system shows 100% agreement with single-plex qPCR. Mixed BV/BY infections produce two distinct melting peaks, with the low-abundance peak detectable down to a 400:1 ratio under the tested conditions. This six-channel ultrafast PCR system reliably detects eight targets in one tube within 20 min without extra hardware, providing a generic strategy for higher-order multiplexing in point-of-care settings.
authors: Yang Li; Yi-Nuo Zhao; Xiang Li; Ting Sun; Lin-wei Zhu; Miao-jin Zhu; L. Liang; Hangping Yao

title: Mosaicism for Cohen–Gibson Syndrome in a Female Individual With Overgrowth and Neurodevelopmental Delay
abstract: BACKGROUND: The Embryonic Ectoderm Development (EED) gene encodes a core component of the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2), which regulates chromatin structure and plays a key role in embryonic development and cell differentiation. Pathogenic variants in EED are associated with overgrowth-intellectual disability syndrome (Cohen-Gibson syndrome, OMIM #617561), though reported cases are rare and typically involve heterozygous germline variants. This study presents an individual with confirmed postzygotic mosaicism in EED, contributing to diagnostic complexity. METHODS: A 12-year-old girl with tall stature, dysmorphic features, developmental delay, and congenital anomalies underwent clinical and genetic evaluation. Exome sequencing and targeted deep sequencing were used to identify and validate the genetic variant across multiple tissues. RESULTS: A likely pathogenic mosaic EED variant c.1091G > T; p.(Trp364Leu) was identified in the patient with a 31% variant allele fraction in peripheral blood. Deep sequencing confirmed the variant and its de novo origin in the parents' samples. Mosaicism was also detected in two independently collected buccal mucosa samples (dry swab and buccal swab collection kit; 11% and 17%) and in saliva (30%), indicating somatic mosaicism in multiple tissues. DNA methylation profiling revealed a high-confidence epigenetic signature consistent with a PRC2 complex-associated disorder, further supporting the likely pathogenic classification of the identified variant. CONCLUSION: This case broadens the molecular understanding of EED-related disorders and highlights the clinical significance of mosaicism. Deep sequencing and multi-tissue analysis are crucial for accurate diagnosis, management, and genetic counseling in overgrowth syndromes.
authors: Fei Song; Manuel Michels; Beate Betz; Walburga Vorhoff; Teresa Neuhann; Lisa Senninger; Dagmar Wieczorek

title: Nanopore metagenomic sequencing links clinically relevant resistance determinants to pathogens
abstract: Abstract Culture-independent metagenomics enables the detection of plasmid-encoded antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes directly from clinical samples; however, the clinical significance of these genes depends on their bacterial host and genomic context, which metagenomics cannot fully infer. Nanopore sequencing technology intrinsically encodes epigenetic modifications such as methylation, which can be leveraged for plasmid-host associations from metagenomic data. Existing methods rely on the recovery of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), which can introduce bias toward abundant taxa and leave clinically relevant, low-abundance pathogens unassociated. To address this limitation, we extended methylation-based plasmid-host association from the MAG level to individual assembly contigs and sequencing reads. The CUPID pipeline implements the calculation of contig and read similarity scores, which compare weighted mean methylation rates across motifs genetically shared between any contig or read pair. We validated this approach on a mock metagenomic community composed of ten carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales isolates, where we achieved 93.8% accuracy at the contig level and 100% at the read level for carbapenemase plasmid-host associations. When applied to metagenomic and quasimetagenomic data of sixteen patient rectal swabs collected during routine hospital surveillance, our approach assigned every detected plasmid-encoded carbapenemase to its correct bacterial host at the contig level, using matched culture-based diagnostics and whole-genome sequencing as a ground truth. Read-level analysis identified additional associations that were missed at the contig level, including a multi-host plasmid confirmed by established diagnostics. These findings demonstrate a pathway from rapid AMR gene detection using metagenomics to actionable surveillance for infection prevention, transmission tracing, and outbreak investigation. Impact statement Culture-independent metagenomics can detect antimicrobial resistance genes, but their clinical significance depends on the bacterial host and genomic context. Here, we show that nanopore-derived bacterial DNA methylation patterns can link carbapenemase genes to pathogenic hosts and plasmid context directly from patient samples. This provides a route from rapid antimicrobial resistance gene detection to actionable public health surveillance. Data summary All sequencing data after human content filtering have been deposited at the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA, BioProject accession PRJEB108076, with all isolate sequencing data for mock community generation available under the sample accession numbers SAMEA121375149-58, all isolate sequencing data from the rectal swabs available at SAMEA121334008-24, all metagenomic data from the rectal swabs available at SAMEA121325220-27, and all quasimetagenomic data available at SAMEA122914816-23, SAMEA122920068-74). All code is available at GitHub: https://github.com/harikaurel/cupid . All other supporting data are provided in the article and supplementary tables.

title: A-076 Evaluation of the Sysmex UF-5000 WBC parameter to detect urethral inflammation in remnant male urine specimens: Implications for ruling-in urethritis
abstract: Abstract Background The most common disease associated with Neisseria gonorrhoeae (GC), Chlamydia trachomatis (CT), and Trichomonas vaginalis (TV) infection in men is urethritis (inflammation of the urethra). To diagnose urethritis, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidelines recommend that objective evidence of urethral inflammation be documented based on (1) the presence of urethral discharge; (2) increased numbers of white blood cells (WBCs) on Gram stain microscopy of urethral secretions or spun first-catch urine; or (3) the presence of leukocyte esterase (LE) in first-catch urine. Existing recommended tests have limitations: The urethral swab procedure is painful, the Gram stain and microscopy process is time consuming, and the LE assay has poor sensitivity and specificity. Novel sensitive and specific assays that can detect urethritis at the point of care are needed. We evaluated the performance of the Sysmex UF-5000(TM) Fully Automated Urine Particle Analyzer’s- White Blood Cell (WBC) parameter to detect urethral inflammation and urethritis in men. Methods Remnant urine and urethral swab specimens were collected from men attending the Bell Flower STI clinic in Indianapolis, Indiana. Urine aliquots were used to measure LE by urinalysis and WBC count per microliter urine using the UF-5000. Clinical data was abstracted from the Electronic Medical Record, including age, race/ethnicity, prior history of STIs, presence of symptoms and a discharge on physical exam, urethral Gram stain microscopy results and GC, CT, and TV Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT) results. Statistical significance was evaluated by Mann-Whitney using GraphPad Prism (v10.6.1). Associations were considered significant if P < 0.05. Results One thousand men were enrolled in this study and 144 men had a urethral Gram stain performed for a clinical indication. The median age of study participants was 31 (range 18–80), 33% were White, 47% were Black, and 20% were Hispanic. A prior STI was reported in 57% and 21% reported urethral symptoms. GC and CT were detected by NAAT+ in 3.3% and 6.5%, respectively; TV was detected in 20 men (7.9%) with an indication for testing. Urethritis was defined if any of the following were present: (1) urethral discharge on exam; (2) LE+ by urinalysis; or (3) urethral Gram stain with >2 WBC per high power field. Comparing men with and without urethral symptoms, the UF-5000 WBC count was significantly elevated in men with urethral symptoms (3.9 vs 22 WBC/µl, P < 0.0001). In symptomatic men (N=209), the UF-5000 WBC count was significantly elevated in men with a positive LE (9.2 vs 360 WBC/µl, P < 0.0001), a diagnosis of urethritis (4.6 vs 164 WBC/µl, and increased WBCs on urethral Gram stain (8.1 vs 176 WBC/µl, P < 0.0001, Figure). Conclusion Using the Sysmex UF-5000 WBC parameter, increased urinary WBCs were significantly associated with markers of inflammation (urethral symptoms, positive LE, increased Gram stained-WBCs) and a urethritis diagnosis, suggesting it may be a powerful tool to diagnose urethritis in clinical settings. Future studies are needed testing clinical specimens at the point-of-care to establish the appropriate WBC cutoff to rule-in or rule-out urethritis, which may aid clinicians in optimizing antibiotic stewardship practices.

title: Multicenter evaluation of Coyote FlashDetect LyocartE multiplex assays for six respiratory pathogens: a comparative analysis with Sansure and Cepheid assays
abstract: (MP), share many of the same symptoms and may progress to severe complications in some cases. Multiplex molecular point-of-care testing (mPOCT) enables automated and rapid differential diagnosis for timely intervention. This study independently evaluated the clinical performance of Coyote FlashDetect LyocartE SARS-CoV-2/FluA/FluB and FlashDetect LyocartE RSV/MP/ADV multiplex mPOCT assays using the Sansure as the primary comparator, followed by a subset-based, target-specific paired comparison with Cepheid mPOCT assay for selected respiratory pathogens (FluA, FluB, and RSV). Specifically, 642 and 427 throat swab specimens were used to evaluate the Coyote SARS-CoV-2/FluA/FluB and Coyote RSV/MP/ADV multiplex mPOCT assays against Sansure assays, respectively. Coyote assays demonstrated high concordance with Sansure assays, with overall percent agreement (OPA) values ranging from 93.8% to 100.0% for six pathogens covered by two Coyote assays. Most discrepancies with Sansure assays occurred in samples with cycle threshold (Ct) values ≥35, especially among FluA samples. Moreover, 414, 414, and 215 specimens were allocated for FluA, FluB, and RSV, respectively, to conduct target-specific paired comparison between Coyote and Cepheid. Each Coyote assay also demonstrated high concordance with the Cepheid assays, with PPA values of 96.0%, 100.0%, and 98.3% for FluA, FluB, and RSV, respectively. These results support the use of Coyote mPOCT assays in specific settings. Coyote assays demonstrated a high degree of concordance for shared targets with comparator methods, supporting their use as a rapid and user-friendly diagnostic approach for multiplex respiratory pathogen detection.IMPORTANCEThis study highlights the value of multiplex molecular point-of-care tests. The POCT assays demonstrate high concordance with the laboratory-based lab tests in this retrospective specimen cohort, offering a viable, rapid, and user-friendly alternative for multiplex respiratory pathogen detection and hold the promise to be used in primary healthcare settings and public health surveillance.

title: Quality control of blood components: A Six-Year Multicentre Retrospective Study in Tertiary Care Hospitals in Bangladesh
abstract: Background Before prescribing blood components physicians must know the quality of blood that actually fulfil the requirements of patients. In the field of transfusion medicine, blood components therapy is also a standard care therapy globally. In this study we evaluated three hospital data related to quality control of blood components that we prepare and issue. Objectives To evaluate compliance of blood components with AABB quality standards. Materials and Methods A multicentre retrospective study with 95% confidence interval, the study were done in three tertiary care hospitals in Dhaka, Bangladesh. In which total number of Whole Blood (WB) were 55650, RCC were 45420, SDP were 20124, RDP were 25264 and FFP were 48530. Sampling method was simple random sampling technique. Four of each blood components were analyzed every monthly throughout the study period. All blood units (RBCs, RCCs, RDPs, SDPs and FFP) from donors in Ibn Sina Medical College, Delta hospital and Green Life Hospital blood bank were included in the study with the exclusion of blood units which were not processed in these hospital (Outside Blood), leucocyte depleted blood products and washed blood products. Automated cell counter Sysmex XN-1000, and XN -2000, Stago auto analyser were used to obtain desired parameters. Results In our study, 91% of WB, 91% of RCC, 92% of RDP, 95% of SDP and 80% of FFP met the quality compliance with international standard. Conclusion The quality control (QC) data generated in this study provides essential insights into the performance of modern blood collection and processing systems. More than 90% studied blood components like WB, RCC, RDP, SDP strictly complied with international standards. However, FFP analysis could not be done according to AABB and international guideline due to financial constrain rather it was surrogate study. Ultimately, establishing a comprehensive QC program, alongside strict adherence to departmental protocols and manufacturer instructions is vital for blood centers to ensure effective and reliable operational outcomes. title: SWINE VIRAL INFECTIONS IN KAZAKHSTAN
abstract: The article presents the results of molecular diagnostics of 156 biological samples (105 nasopharyngeal swabs and 51 blood serum samples) collected from small and large pig farms in Central, Eastern, and Northern Kazakhstan. PCR results determined the presence of genetic material of type 2 circovirus in 2.56% of the samples out of the total (156 samples) from the nasopharyngeal swabs of pigs, and these results were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Positive results were also obtained (3.21%) in RT-PCR for hepatitis E from blood plasma, as well as for reproductive-respiratory syndrome in pigs (0.64%). The obtained results indicate the circulation of the second type of circovirus in the pig population of Central Kazakhstan, and possibly the hepatitis E virus in pigs of the Northern region. The results of molecular epizootiology of pig viruses are important for veterinary authorities in interpreting outbreaks of disease and controlling imported breeding herds, which are a source of virus introduction into the local population. В статье представлены результаты молекулярной диагностики 156 биологических образцов (105 носоглоточных смывов и 51 сыворотки крови), собранных в мелких и крупных свинофермах Центрального, Восточного и Северного Казахстана. Результаты ПЦР определили наличие генетического материала цирковируса второго типа в 2,56% проб от общего количества образцов (156 проб) в назофарингеальных смывах свиней, что подтверждено результатами секвенирования по Сенгеру. Также были получены положительные результаты (3,21%) в ОТ-ПЦР на гепатит Е из плазмы крови и репродуктивно-респираторного синдрома свиней (0,64%). Полученные результаты свидетельствуют о циркуляции цирковируса второго типа в популяции свиней Центрального Казахстана, и возможно, вируса гепатита Е у свиней Северного региона. Результаты молекулярной эпизоотологии вирусов свиней важны для ветеринарных структур при расшифровке вспышек заболеваемости и контроле за импортируемыми племенными стадами, являющимися источником заноса вируса в местную популяцию.

abstract: in plasma and serum, even in the presence of many RNases. The analytical signal is, however, a composite result of blood collection, clotting or anticoagulation, platelet and erythrocyte carryover, storage, RNA recovery, reverse-transcription chemistry, amplification efficiency, and normalisation. This comprehensive evaluation assesses the whole analytical process from the management of whole blood/plasma/serum to RNA extraction, reverse transcription, and quantitative PCR. Contemporary data supports the use of matrix-specific standard operating procedures, clear quality control for haemolysis and platelet contamination, validated low-input extraction with stage-specific spike-ins, assay-specific reverse transcription validation, and normalisation utilising validated endogenous controls, global mean methods, or absolute quantification when suitable. U6 and RNU48 must not be regarded as universal extracellular reference standards. Digital PCR enhances precise quantification at minimal copy numbers; yet, it does not eradicate pre-analytical or reverse transcription biases. MIQE 2.0 (2025) enhances the reporting standards for assay design, efficacy, dynamic range, limits of detection/quantification, controls, and normalisation. Clinical translation requires a finalised Standard Operating Procedure, calibration particular to the matrix, orthogonal validation, and prospective external validation.

title: AI for rural healthcare: Transforming villages of India through intelligent and predictive systems
abstract: Rural healthcare systems face persistent shortages of trained personnel, diagnostic infrastructure, continuous monitoring capability and rapid referral pathways. This paper extends a Python-based artificial-intelligence framework for rural healthcare into a portable multimodal screening architecture termed the Quantum Suitcase. The name denotes a compact field-deployable health-monitoring platform; it does not imply that unvalidated “quantum resonance” measurements can diagnose disease. The system prioritizes non-invasive, needle-free first-line screening using physiological signals that can be measured through established physical principles: photoplethysmography and pulse oximetry, electrocardiography, oscillometric blood pressure, infrared thermometry, respiratory monitoring, digital auscultation and camera-based observation. Optional point-of-care laboratory tests may be added when clinically required, but the initial screening workflow is designed to operate without routine venipuncture. The paper develops a mathematical representation of the patient as a time-varying physiological state, a sensor observation model, signal-quality estimation, multimodal feature fusion, probabilistic risk estimation, temporal deterioration detection and uncertainty-aware referral. Physics-based equations are provided for optical absorption, bioelectric potential measurement, pressure sensing, acoustic signals and signal-to-noise behavior. A hierarchical AI architecture combines local edge inference with explainable models and optional cloud or telemedicine support. The system is intended for village health camps, community health workers and Primary Health Centers where internet connectivity, power and specialist access may be intermittent. Rather than replacing laboratory diagnosis or clinicians, the platform is designed to identify abnormal patterns, estimate screening risk, prioritize referrals and preserve a longitudinal record for subsequent care. A validation protocol is defined for device-level accuracy, algorithm discrimination, calibration, subgroup performance, clinical workflow and field usability. This framework converts a broad AI-for-rural-healthcare concept into a testable engineering and clinical research program suitable for prototype development and prospective evaluation.

title: Surveillance of zoonotic respiratory viral infections in animal farms: a model project with a focus on One Health approach–A study protocol
abstract: Background: The One Health approach recognizes the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health in addressing the growing threat of zoonotic diseases. This study aims to establish an integrated One Health surveillance system for the early detection and monitoring of zoonotic respiratory viral infections at the human-animal-environment interface in Tiruvallur District, Tamil Nadu, India. Objectives: The study aims to establish a longitudinal surveillance system for the early detection of emerging and re-emerging zoonotic respiratory viral infections across livestock animals, animal handlers, and the farm environment interface; and ii) determine the occurrence and distribution of selected zoonotic respiratory viruses, and assess the influence of seasonal and climatic factors on their occurrence and transmission. Methods: Following sensitization of farm owners and animal handlers through the Animal Husbandry Department, 40 livestock farms from four selected blocks of Tiruvallur District, rearing cattle, buffalo, goats, sheep, swine, and poultry, will be enrolled in each surveillance round. Animal nasal swabs, respiratory samples from animal handlers, and environmental samples (air and wastewater) will be collected. Field surveillance will be carried out by a study team comprising a veterinarian and field investigators. Sixteen surveillance rounds (eight rounds annually) will be conducted over 2 years, covering two complete climatic cycles. Approximately 7,360 animal swab samples, 960 samples from animal handlers, and 960 environmental samples will be collected in each study phase. Animal samples will be screened using a pooled testing strategy followed by real-time RT-PCR for the detection of selected zoonotic respiratory viruses, while human samples will be tested individually. Expected outcomes: The study is expected to establish a robust One Health surveillance framework and generate baseline epidemiological data on zoonotic respiratory viruses circulating among livestock, animal handlers, and the farm environment in Tamil Nadu. The findings will strengthen integrated surveillance, support early warning systems, facilitate timely veterinary and public health responses, and provide evidence to inform future One Health policies and preparedness strategies for emerging zoonotic respiratory viral infections.

title: Salivary ferning as a diagnostic window: Bridging hormonal dynamics and oral health
abstract: Recent advancements in digital health and point-of-care testing have revitalised interest in non-invasive salivary diagnostics. This review evaluates the clinical utility of salivary arborization, commonly known as ferning, as a cost-effective and accessible biomarker. By bridging reproductive endocrinology and oral-systemic health, we propose that salivary ferning offers a unique, chair-side diagnostic window for monitoring hormone-mediated periodontal reactivity. Salivary ferning patterns occur due to the crystallization of sodium and potassium chloride on a dried mucous slide, a process heavily influenced by fluctuating systemic estragon and electrolyte levels. Throughout the menstrual cycle, ascending estragon peaks trigger distinct crystalline structures that mirror systemic fertility windows. Beyond reproductive tracking, these hormonal shifts profoundly alter oral tissue physiology. Elevated estragon receptors in the periodontium heighten inflammatory responses to dental plaque, predisposing individuals to gingival inflammation and exacerbated periodontal reactivity during specific hormonal phases. Integrating this diagnostic approach into routine dental practices provides significant clinical advantages without relying on complex laboratory infrastructure. Salivary collection eliminates the patient discomfort and anxiety typically associated with traditional venipuncture while delivering rapid, visual feedback suitable for dynamic chair-side evaluations. Furthermore, the inherent cost-effectiveness of this method reduces overall overhead, making preventative screening widely accessible in diverse healthcare settings. By leveraging these insights, clinicians can personalize periodontal maintenance schedules based on real-time endocrine profiles, ultimately optimizing both oral and systemic health outcomes for patients.

title: Toward uncertainty-aware clinical decision support for treatment response prediction in metastatic NSCLC: integrating FDG-PET, T-cell repertoire, and cytokines with conformal prediction
abstract: Background: Variable response to chemoimmunotherapy in metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (mNSCLC), together with the limited discriminative accuracy of PD-L1 tumor proportion score, highlights the need for reliable, uncertainty-aware early response prediction using multimodal biomarkers. We developed and prototyped a multimodal clinical decision support (CDS) framework integrating longitudinal FDG-PET, T-cell receptor (TCR), and cytokine biomarkers with conformal prediction to deliver uncertainty-quantified, patient-level response predictions. Methods: Thirty-five patients with mNSCLC receiving first-line carboplatin-pemetrexed-pembrolizumab on the PET-BRIGHT trial (NCT04151940) underwent FDG-PET/CT and blood collection at baseline and week 3. Multimodal biomarkers included FDG-PET metrics (standardized uptake value/total lesion glycolysis), TCR diversity metrics, and inflammatory cytokines. Nested leave-one-out cross-validation with automated feature selection identified a single biomarker per modality. Class-balanced logistic regression was used for classification, with discrimination assessed by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and calibration by the Brier score. Conformal prediction (targeting 80% reliability) quantified patient-level uncertainty via prediction sets and singleton rate. Unimodal and multimodal early- and late-fusion models were evaluated using baseline-only and combined baseline plus mid-treatment biomarkers. Models were benchmarked against PD-L1 tumor proportion score, and statistical significance was assessed by permutation testing against an empirical null. Results: PD-L1 tumor proportion score, the current clinical standard, discriminated poorly (AUROC 0.58, 95% CI 0.39-0.78). At PreTx, unimodal TCR was the strongest single modality (AUROC 0.80), followed by PET (0.76) and cytokines (0.54). Late fusion of PET and TCR achieved the highest PreTx discrimination (0.85) and increased singleton predictions from 78% to 89%. After incorporating mid-treatment biomarkers, cytokines became the strongest single modality (0.78) while TCR was attenuated (0.66); late fusion of PET and cytokines achieved the highest discrimination overall (0.86). Thirteen of 22 model and timepoint combinations exceeded a permutation null at p < 0.05, and empirical coverage was 78% and 82% against an 80% target. Conclusions: A multimodal framework combining longitudinal biomarkers with conformal prediction substantially outperformed the current clinical standard while identifying patients for whom a confident prediction could not be made. A prototype CDS interface demonstrates feasibility for clinical translation. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04151940, registered 26 September 2019.
