The removal of serum may also facilitate shipping, where country-specific guidelines for animal-based serum prevent import/export as well as reducing costs.
authors: Ilie A, Bissoyi A, Tang Q, Oral CB, Grover O, Gibson MI.

title: Reframing decentralized diagnostics with a programmable multi-dimensional microfluidic system
abstract: Decentralized diagnostics are vital for infectious disease control, yet current point-of-care tools remain largely one-dimensional, failing to capture the multidimensional profiles required for precision management. Here, we show SID-WAVES (Smartphone-Integrated Diagnostics with Wax-encoded Amplified and Versatile Evaluation System), an intelligent, multimodal microfluidic platform. Integrating low-melting-point phase-change and dual-siphon valves with RPA–CRISPR/Cas12a nucleic acid detection and protein immunoassays, the platform enables automated, one-step, sample-to-answer operation via an AI-assisted smartphone readout that reduces operator-dependent variability. Spatial-temporal-signal encoding supports multiplexed, multi-sample, and multimodal analysis, achieving attomolar-level sensitivity (10−18 M) and >95% diagnostic accuracy across 225 clinical and self-collected molecular assays, demonstrating robust usability. For proteins, a triple-amplification strategy and hierarchical capture enhance sensitivity 125-fold, improving accuracy from 87.6% to 100% in 54 simulated samples. Functioning as a reconfigurable analytical framework where panels are changed by swapping targets and probes, this work helps mitigate the Sensitivity–Multiplexing–Accessibility trade-off, reframing decentralized diagnostics from single-target screening to multi-dimensional health profiling. Decentralized diagnostics has the potential to improve health equity as well as support a more rapid response to disease outbreaks. Here authors present SID-WAVES, a multimodal microfluidic platform which allows ‘sample-in, results-out’ detection of both nucleic acid and protein biomarkers.
authors: Tao Xu; Ying Zhang; Xin Tang; Hongguo Wei; Lingyan Kang; Qize Zhou; Shunji Li; Xudong Zhao; Jiashuo Li; Zimeng Zhang; Chao Wan; Yufei Zhang; Dongjuan Chen; Ye Tian; Bi-Feng Liu; Peng Chen

title: Cure-induced viscoelastic effects in in-air photopolymerized droplets for microfluidic droplet-based 3D printing
abstract: Motivated by droplet-based additive manufacturing processes, this work presents a multiphysics numerical framework for in-air photopolymerization of resin droplets and their subsequent impact, spreading, and recoil on a solid substrate. The model couples two-phase incompressible flow with energy and species transport, incorporating radiative transport through the Beer–Lambert law to describe free-radical photopolymerization. This formulation enables prediction of core–shell droplet morphologies, in which a partially or fully cured outer shell encapsulates an uncured liquid core prior to impact. The key novelty of the proposed framework lies in the introduction of a cure-induced viscoelastic shell model, described using an Oldroyd-B-type constitutive formulation. The evolving stress response during photocuring is decomposed into equilibrium (elastic, spring-like) and non-equilibrium (viscous, Maxwell-type) contributions. The viscoelastic properties of the shell – including relaxation time as well as equilibrium and non-equilibrium moduli – are explicitly linked to the local degree of cure, allowing the progressive evolution of material stiffness and elasticity to be captured. Using this approach, we systematically quantify how cure-dependent viscoelasticity governs droplet-substrate interaction for micro-scale droplets across various UV intensity exposures with a specific impact velocity. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of viscoelasticity in post-impact recoil and rebound suppression. The proposed model provides a predictive tool for understanding and controlling droplet dynamics in UV-curable, droplet-based additive manufacturing processes.
authors: Saquib Rouf; Johnny Moughames; Arnaud Bertsch; Hang Jerry Qi; Frédéric Demoly

title: Blood test on a chip: Sample-to-answer immunoassay on a structurally programmed microfluidic chip
abstract: During COVID-19, rapid antigen tests (RATs) have demonstrated their enormous potential to relax and decentralize the healthcare system for timely results. However, disease diagnosis mostly requires blood tests with quantitative readouts, which are hardly achieved by conventional lateral flow strips. Here, we report a concept of “Blood Test on a Chip” (BTOC) that streamlines the entire sample-to-answer immunoassay process on a single microfluidic chip. Without any external processes, the BTOC can operate independently based on a series of structurally programmed capillary events, including automated blood plasma separation, on-chip reaction, and a length-based quantitative result displayed on the chip. This platform demonstrated a limit of detection (LOD) of 3.78 ng/mL of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) in whole blood, which is below the clinical threshold of 4 ng/mL for PSA abnormality. Clinical validation involving 77 volunteer samples showed strong agreement between the BTOC and standard hospital tests (Lin's concordance correlation coefficient ρ ̂ c = 0.932 ). This all-in-one, self-contained chip eliminates the need for peripheral laboratory settings, offering a simple, affordable, and quantitative at-home test for telemedicine, large-scale screening in primary care and disease self-management.
authors: Jiaheng Li; Zhuoting Han; Hogi Hartanto; Lin Pang; Jianpeng Wu; Zhibing Chen; Lok Ting Chu; Ting-Hsuan Chen

title: Plasmonic metasurface microfluidic accelerates redox reactions for rapid phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing
abstract: Electron-accepting chain reactions play crucial roles in diagnostics for bacterial infections, from nucleic acid amplification for bacterial identification to metabolic assays for phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing. When coupled with redox mediators, these reactions can be interrogated using an electroanalytical method. We demonstrate kinetic acceleration of loop-mediated isothermal amplification-based identification and resazurin-based phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility profiling through enhanced electromagnetic fields and modulated hot electron injection at the multilayered plasmonic metasurface-fluidic interface. We systematically investigate rounded versus sharp-apex plasmonic architectures, quantifying near-field magnitude and decay to identify geometries that maximize kinetic amplification under electrochemical readout. This approach is further combined with machine learning-assisted Gaussian fitting to improve data quantification and interpretation. Across diverse bacterial species, we achieved rapid identification with no cross-reactivity and phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing without overnight culture. In a prospective pilot clinical study of urine specimens directly from patients with suspected urinary tract infections, we observe high accuracy and strong essential and categorical agreement with standard clinical microbiology assays for bacterial identification and antibiotic susceptibility testing.
authors: Roozbeh Siavash Moakhar; Mahsa Jalali; Tamer AbdElFatah; Sripadh Guptha Yedire; Max Petkun; Carolina del Real Mata; Ziwei He; Hamed Shieh; Geoffrey A. McKay; Rachel Corsini; Grace Reszetnik; Seyed Vahid Hamidi; Sahar Sadat Mahshid; Sahar Sadat Mahshid; Cédric P. Yansouni; Dao M. Nguyen; Sara Mahshid; Sara Mahshid

title: Autonomous Droplet Navigation via Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Precise manipulation of liquid droplets underpins lab-on-a-chip platforms for diagnostics, chemical synthesis, and biological assays. Yet autonomous droplet transport through confined geometries of varying complexity remains an open challenge. Droplets exhibit contact-angle hysteresis, deformability, and capillary pinning, which make their response to actuation nonlinear and history dependent, that classical controllers and pre-programmed trajectories cannot cope in multi-turn environments. Here we demonstrate autonomous navigation of a liquid droplet through geometries of increasing complexity on a gravity driven (Labyrinth) platform using model-based reinforcement learning. A thin silicone oil film reduces contact-line pinning while two-axis tilt supplies the gravitational driving force, and an overhead camera tracks the droplet in real time. An offline-trained policy discovers effective tilt strategies from limited physical interaction data, without simulation or analytical droplet models. The system operates under partial observability, as oil-film thickness, instantaneous contact angle, and droplet deformation state remain hidden from the controller. Despite these challenges, the learned policy achieves reliable navigation across straight, right-angle, and curved-arc paths, including outside-corner geometries. We further demonstrate that a policy trained on a simpler geometry transfers to complex ones, succeeding zero-shot on right-angle and staircase paths and reaching full success on a curved arc with a fifth of the training data. The findings suggest promising avenues for enabling droplet based microfluidic systems to serve as intelligent chemical laboratories.
authors: Rajneesh Anand; Mayuresh V. Kothare

title: Micro/Nanostructured Materials and Microfluidic Diagnostic Platforms Enable Multimodal Detection of Circulating Tumor Cells
abstract: Circulating tumor cells (CTCs), as pivotal targets in liquid biopsy, offer dynamic, multidimensional insights into tumor heterogeneity and metastatic progression. However, their extreme rarity, pronounced heterogeneity, and the complexity of the blood microenvironment severely constrain detection accuracy. Advances in micro/nanomaterials and functional device engineering have enabled substantial improvements in CTC enrichment efficiency by refining the topographical and chemical properties of capture interfaces. These innovations also provide a compatible foundation for multimodal molecular profiling. This review systematically outlines the structure-function relationships of functionalized nanomaterials, microfiltration substrates, and biomimetic microfluidic devices, highlighting how material parameters-such as nanoscale architectures and membrane pore sizes-govern CTC capture performance. We further explore the integration of micro/nanomaterials with functional platforms for multidimensional molecular analyses across DNA, RNA, and protein levels. Coupled with emerging digital PCR technologies, these systems show promise in overcoming the sensitivity barriers associated with rare mutation detection and protein quantification, enabling multi-omics data fusion. We also discuss how artificial intelligence (AI)-driven feature selection, clustering, and prediction integrate multidimensional data to decode tumor heterogeneity and guide disease monitoring. Despite rapid progress, key challenges remain-including the lack of standardization, limited integration of multi-omic datasets, and the need for robust clinical validation. Future directions may lie in the convergence of microfluidic-integrated materials, single-cell multi-omics, and AI-driven analytics to establish dynamic, high-resolution monitoring platforms that bridge the gap between fundamental research and clinical precision oncology.
authors: Hao Li; Jiaojiao Sun; Kunguo Liu; Shijie Wang; Bowen Fu; Hong Zhu; Peng Cao; Xin Han

title: Microfluidic technology: from historical development to modern applications
abstract: Microfluidics is a rapidly evolving interdisciplinary field focused on the precise manipulation and control of fluids at the micrometre scale. The kingdom of microfluidics is ruled by tiny fluid volumes through the development of novel applications that benefit from the use of these small samples. Typical manipulations involve small volumes of fluid (microliters or sub-microliters) leading to improved capability to manipulate fluids, increased accuracy over traditional methodologies, and many successful implementations in diverse domains including health care, environmental capabilities, and chemical processing. Examples of microfluidic implementation that have significantly improved testing efficiency, effectiveness, and portability include lab on chip & point of care testing appliances. The primary advantages of microfluidics include lower sample use, faster analysis times, improved sensitivity, and the ability to combine with other systems for automated operation and control. This review highlights the historical development and fundamental principles of microfluidics along with its growing importance in modern science and engineering. Various applications of microfluidic systems in healthcare diagnostics, environmental monitoring, chemical synthesis, and biological analysis are comprehensively discussed. In addition, the review outlines the current limitations and challenges associated with microfluidic technologies, including fabrication complexity and scalability issues. Overall, this review offers a comprehensive understanding of both possible opportunities and existing limitations of microfluidics. Therefore, it is concluded that further development and improvement of this area are of significant importance, as it may become the basis for future scientific and engineering breakthroughs. Finally, future perspectives and trends in microfluidics are discussed, highlighting its potential to enable revolutionary approaches in subsequent analytical and biomedical technologies.
authors: Sourav Ghosh; Jit Chakraborty; Avishek Saha; Arijit Das; Kalachand Mahali; Sanjay Roy

title: Soft bioelectronics for wireless drug delivery: programmable, minimally invasive and closed-loop therapeutics
abstract: Soft bioelectronics is reshaping drug delivery from passive dosing to programmable, tissue-interfaced therapeutics. This Review examines the co-design of soft materials, wireless power, drug reservoirs, release mechanisms and feedback control for wearable and minimally invasive implantable therapeutic systems. We organize the field around key constraints including controllability, reversibility, payload capacity, dosing precision, drug stability and feedback latency, guiding the development of adaptive closed-loop drug delivery platforms for clinical translation.
authors: Feng Zhang; 孙富昌; Zheng Yan

title: Microfluidics to assess the impact of transfused blood components
abstract: Assessing the function of transfused blood components within the dynamic environment of the vascular system remains challenging, as conventional assays are largely static and poorly represent the dynamic mechanical and biochemical interactions between blood cells and the vessel wall. Microfluidic approaches, which study blood flow within small-scale channels, provide an opportunity to bridge this gap by introducing physiologically relevant flow and shear rates into experimental models. This review synthesises the current literature describing the application of microfluidic technologies to the assessment of transfused blood components, with particular emphasis on platelet concentrates, red cell concentrates and plasma-derived products. Across existing studies, microfluidic models have demonstrated differences in component function related to storage conditions, manufacturing methods and emerging transfusion products that are not always detected using conventional bulk assays. These approaches have provided new insights into platelet haemostasis at defined shear rates, red cell deformability and gas exchange, and plasma-mediated coagulation in trauma and critical illness. However, substantial diversity in device design, experimental conditions and analytical endpoints limits direct comparison between studies and constrains translation into routine practice. The development of more standardised platforms, alongside integration with endothelialised and organ-on-a-chip models, may help to overcome these challenges. Overall, microfluidics represents a promising tool for improving functional assessment of blood components and supporting future advances in transfusion medicine research and personalised transfusion strategies.
authors: Edward John Sayers; Jamie Nash; E. M. Davies; Christine V. Saunders; Chloë E. George

title: Next-generation point-of-care diagnostics for urinary tract infections: a systematic review of rapid pathogen detection methods
abstract: Background: Urinary tract infections are among the most prevalent bacterial infections worldwide, with Escherichia coli as the leading pathogen. Conventional diagnostic methods, including urine culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, require 48–72 hours, often delaying targeted therapy and promoting empirical antibiotic use, thereby exacerbating antimicrobial resistance. Objective: This review summarizes advances in point-of-care diagnostic technologies for rapid detection and antimicrobial susceptibility testing in localized or uncomplicated urinary tract infections. Methods: A comprehensive literature review of studies published between 2008 and 2025 was conducted using MeSH and free-text searches for “point-of-care testing”, “urinary tract infection”, “rapid diagnostics”, and related terms. Included studies described the mechanisms, performance, and clinical applicability of emerging point-of-care systems. Results: Thirty-four studies met inclusion criteria. Paper-based assays, lateral-flow tests, microfluidic devices, and hydrogel biosensors demonstrated rapid bacterial detection (from <5 min to 6 h) with variable sensitivities (10–106 CFU/mL). Among commercial devices, the Sysmex PA-100 antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) system provided phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing within 30–45 minutes and achieved over 95% specificity compared with standard microbiology, while the Lodestar DX (LAMP-based) and Bosch Vivalytic (PCR-based) systems enabled molecular identification of uropathogens and resistance genes within 40–146 minutes. Conclusions: Point-of-care diagnostic platforms substantially reduce diagnostic turnaround, improve antibiotic stewardship, and offer cost-effective alternatives to conventional culture. The Sysmex PA-100 system currently represents the most clinically validated phenotypic point-of-care tool for uncomplicated urinary infections management. Future research should focus on expanding diagnostic panels, validating clinical outcomes, and facilitating integration into primary care and antimicrobial stewardship programs.
authors: Silvia Juste-Álvarez; José Medina‐Polo

title: Self-buoyant cell-spheroid culture programming multi-spheroid assembly
abstract: Tempo-spatially controlled culture and assembly of cellular spheroids are fundamental in engineering tissue-like assembloids for scalable application, yet remain a technical challenge. Here, we show self-buoyant culture of cell spheroids and programmable assembly of multi-spheroid by microbubbles in a high-throughput, external field-free and miniaturized format. This approach allows one-step engineering of biocompatible cell-adhesive buoyancy interface that lifts the self-adaptive levitation growth of reliable one-drop-one-spheroid in an array without requiring any external fields. Using this self-floating spheroidal microarray, we find that a facile droplet 'kiss' facilitates the buoyancy-driven ultrafast transfer (∼1 s) of spheroids between top-down adjacent droplets, thus achieving rapid spheroid relocation, media exchange, and drug administration in parallel. Such a self-buoyant approach allows programmable horizontal/vertical bioassembly and enhanced fusion of homo/heterogeneous multi-spheroids into different "buoyantoid" patterns via sequential flash transfer along droplet array. This self-powered design provides a promising tool to enable mass production and smart manipulation of encoded assembloids for precision medicine, tissue engineering and high-throughput drug screening.
authors: Yuanhang Xiang; Binqi Wei; Yueyang Sun; Weifeng Liu; Hui Zhao; Xiaojie Qin; Changfeng Zhu; Xinchun Li; Fan Yang

title: Organ-on-a-chip platforms for disease modeling and in vitro diagnostic applications
abstract: Organ-on-a-Chip (OoC) systems, as microphysiological models integrating microfluidic engineering, 3D tissue construction, and sensing technologies, can faithfully recapitulate the barrier functions, dynamic microenvironments, and inter-tissue crosstalk of human organs. They effectively address the inherent limitations of traditional 2D cell cultures and animal models in in vitro diagnostics (IVD), offering a novel avenue to tackle the high failure rate of candidate drugs and biomarkers in clinical translation. This review systematically summarizes the technological advances and application practices of OoC in the IVD field, covering core construction technologies (microfluidic regulation, cell and tissue engineering, material innovation), the integrated optimization of the "online real-time monitoring-offline in-depth analysis" dual-detection system, and typical applications in disease modeling, biomarker screening, drug toxicity evaluation, and personalized diagnosis. It further explores Multi-Organ-Chip (MOC) systems and Artificial Intelligence (AI) empowerment, analyzes core bottlenecks including insufficient physiological complexity, lack of standardization, and barriers to clinical translation and industrialization, and prospects future directions from technological optimization, standardization establishment, and regulatory pathway exploration. By focusing on the IVD-oriented perspective, this review aims to provide theoretical references and practical guidance for the transformation of OoC from laboratory research to clinical IVD tools.
authors: Po Hao; Deng Jingrong; Jian Xu

title: Microfluidics-Integrated Spectroscopic Technologies for Food Safety and Quality Assessment: From Complex-Matrix Processing to On-Site Decision-Making
abstract: Food safety and quality analysis is shifting from laboratory-based end-point testing toward faster, lower-volume and matrix-adapted on-site decision-making. Near-infrared (NIR), visible-near-infrared (Vis-NIR), hyperspectral, Raman, surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS), fluorescence, colorimetric and terahertz approaches, together with impedance time-series readout, provide complementary information on composition, molecular vibrations, spatial distribution, reaction outputs, or electrical responses. In real foods, however, lipids, proteins, sugars, salts, pigments, particles and native fluorescence can alter spectral baselines, mass transfer and model stability. The value of microfluidics is therefore not limited to miniaturization but lies in organizing filtration, homogenization, splitting, mixing, extraction, enrichment, reaction, and readout positions into a controllable sample-to-signal workflow. This review first distinguishes chemical hazards, biological hazards, authenticity issues, and quality changes according to target and matrix characteristics, and then compares the functional boundaries of continuous-flow, paper-based, droplet, digital-hybrid and enrichment-oriented chips. It further analyses how microfluidics affects detection time, sample and reagent consumption, sensitivity, selectivity, repeatability, portability and cross-matrix applicability through spectral interfaces, signal enhancement, labelled and label-free detection, chemometrics, and machine learning. Representative applications involving pesticides, mycotoxins, pathogens, antibiotics, heavy metals, adulterants, oxidation products, and freshness indicators in real foods are discussed within a unified chain linking chip architecture, spectral signal generation and decision models. Finally, requirements for translation are proposed in terms of standard and real samples, chip-to-chip variation, external model validation, data traceability and scalable manufacturing, providing an operational framework for the joint design of broad-spectrum spectroscopic technologies and microfluidic systems.
authors: Jingwen Zhu; Xianjun Sun; Yu Guo; Zhenghao Zhang; Xiaoyan Geng; Hui Jiang

title: Development of an immersion-type hydrogel-integrated microfluidic glass fiber-based analytical device and its application to smartphone-assisted glucose colorimetric assay
abstract: Microfluidic paper-based analytical devices (μPADs) are attractive platforms for on-site analysis; however, quantitative analysis remains challenging because sampling strongly influences analytical performance. Existing sampling methods often require precise volumetric sampling or operator-dependent handling, which involves an inherent trade-off between analytical simplicity and quantitative reliability. To overcome this limitation, herein, we propose the concept of a quantitative assay using an immersion-type hydrogel-integrated microfluidics glass fiber-based analytical device (IHμGFAD). The IHμGFAD consisted of a reagent-encapsulated hydrogel for reaction/detection with a glass fiber channel for sampling. The combination of the hydrogel with the glass fiber channel was realized by exploiting the self-adhesive property of hydrophobic patterns fabricated using a liquid crystal display 3D printer. The immersion-based quantitative assay using the IHμGFAD was demonstrated with a glucose oxidase/horseradish peroxidase-based glucose colorimetric assay as a model system. The limit of glucose detection (3σ) was estimated to be 68 μM. The immersion-based assay was also applied to the quantification of glucose in human serum controls and pooled human serum, demonstrating its potential applicability to real-sample analysis. The immersion-based assay provides a μGFAD-based analytical method that achieves both practical user-friendliness and reliable quantitative performance, and it contributes to the advancement of on-site quantitative analysis in a wide range of fields, including healthcare, environmental monitoring, and food safety.
authors: Hayate Kitazume; 高広 石川; Konoka Nakamura; Akira Seyama; Yukiko Moriiwa; Atsushi Shoji; Akio Yanagida; Kazuhiro Morioka

title: Scale‐Down Platforms for Process‐Oriented Enzyme Screening Using Microfluidics
abstract: Enzyme screening platforms are typically evaluated based on their throughput and analytical performance rather than their ability to mimic the conditions encountered at large scale. In bioreactors, enzymes experience gradients in substrate concentration, oxygen availability, pH, temperature, and interfacial exposure, caused by imperfect mixing and multiphase operation. These gradients affect both enzyme activity and stability, yet they are rarely incorporated into the assays used to select biocatalysts. Traditionally, a variant is chosen based on its performance under static, well-mixed laboratory conditions, yet those conditions do not necessarily represent the process conditions it must eventually perform under. Microfluidic devices can in principle recreate process-relevant conditions at a small scale since these devices offer precise control over the flow, residence time, and multiphase contact. Yet most current platforms are not built to mimic the scale-down process-derived conditions. Here, we assess current microfluidic tools against this process-relevant conditions and outline how modular designs can be combined into sequential screening platforms that generate the conditions in a bioreactor, for early-stage biocatalyst selection.

title: Microfluidic Devices for Imaging and Biochemistry Analysis of Microbes Under Mechanical Pressure
abstract: ABSTRACT Growth-induced pressure arises when proliferating cell populations are confined within rigid microenvironments and is increasingly recognized as a determinant of microbial physiology in soils, biofilms, and host tissues. We present two complementary microfluidic devices that confine microbes within polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) chambers and apply defined, optically read-out growth-induced pressure of up to 1.5 MPa. The first, the self-closing (SC) chip, confines cells in multiple small chambers accommodating hundreds of cells; it provides excellent nutrient supply and rapid medium exchange, supports single-cell imaging, and allows multiplexing of cellular or chemical conditions. The second, the pressure-recovery (PR) chip, confines cells in a single 5 cm- long chamber accommodating hundreds of thousands of cells; a scalpel-cut step recovers live cells from the channel within minutes for bulk biochemical assays. The two devices share a single two-layer soft-lithography fabrication process and a common brightfield wall-displacement pressure readout. Together, they enable single-cell imaging and bulk biochemical analysis under matched, defined pressure conditions. We illustrate the protocol with two representative validations: rapid β-estradiol-induced transcription in the SC chip, in which nascent transcription foci appear within 5 min independently of the applied pressure, and the PR chip, which produces uniform growth-induced pressure along the entire 5 cm channel and recovers between 0.1 × 10 6 and 1 × 10 6 cells per device in a pressure-tunable manner. SUMMARY This protocol describes two complementary polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) microfluidic devices that apply defined growth-induced pressure to microbial populations while maintaining uniform nutrient supply. The self-closing chip supports single-cell imaging under multiplexed pressure conditions; the pressure-recovery chip yields up to approximately 1 × 10 6 cells per device for downstream biochemical analysis.
authors: Hyo-Jun Kim; Nicolas Nguyen; Baptiste Alric; Lucie Albert; Morgan Delarue

title: A critical review of microfluidic dielectrophoresis technology in microparticle separation chips
abstract: Abstract In recent years, dielectrophoresis (DEP) technology based on microfluidic chips has become a key method for the efficient manipulation of particles, owing to its advantages of being non-contact, highly precise and highly controllable. This paper reviews the latest advancements, fundamental principles, mixing mechanisms, application fields, and future challenges associated with DEP particle separation technology. It provides a detailed overview of the structural design, separation efficiency, voltage, frequency and other parameters of electrode-based and insulatorbased DEP, and discusses the challenges currently facing this technology. Furthermore, the paper proposes a novel classification scheme for synergistic strategies combining DEP with other separation mechanisms. These are categorized into sequential separation, collaborative separation, and multi-stage separation, with a discussion of the respective advantages and limitations of each approach. Finally, the paper summarizes recent progress in the application of DEP particle separation across fields such as biological cell identification, environmental particle monitoring, and chemical particle analysis. It concludes by outlining future directions for the development of DEP and hybrid separation technologies, thereby offering theoretical and technical references for achieving high-precision, high-throughput, and multifunctional capabilities within the field of microfluidic separation.
authors: Yu Liu; Wenbo Han; Haoyu Yue; Xinran Wang; Siqi Zhang; Guo Wenxuan; Xiaotong Mu; Wei Li; H.O.N.G.P.E.N.G. Zhang

title: Microfluidic Technologies for Seminal Fluid Analysis: from Sperm Selection to Liquid Biopsy in Prostate Cancer
abstract: Microfluidic technologies, which enable precise manipulation of cells and biological fluids at the microscale, represent a promising platform for reproductive medicine and urologic oncology. This review examines the operating principles, engineering features, and clinical potential of microfluidic systems for seminal fluid analysis, sperm selection, and liquid biopsy in prostate cancer. The reviewed domestic and international literature addresses microfluidic sperm selection, sperm DNA fragmentation, rheotaxis, inertial microfluidics, circulating tumor cells, and molecular biomarkers in seminal fluid. Microfluidic devices can facilitate gentle processing of spermatozoa, enrichment of samples with progressively motile cells, and isolation of tumor cells, extracellular vesicles, and cell-free DNA. Particular attention is paid to the potential for standardized processing of viscous and heterogeneous samples prior to molecular analysis and cytological evaluation in specialized laboratories. A particularly promising area is the development of integrated platforms suitable for clinical validation and subsequent incorporation into diagnostic pathways for patients with prostate diseases.
authors: S. P. Sametov; R. F. Gizatullin; R. I. Tukhvatullin

title: A review on monitoring orthodontic treatment: from traditional approaches to innovative point-of-care tools
abstract: Orthodontic treatment is performed to treat malocclusions by improving oral functions, tooth alignment, and facial esthetics that impact the quality of life of patients significantly. Nevertheless, various factors like complexity of malocclusions, patient compliance, and dental hygiene can influence treatment outcomes. Traditional diagnostic methods such as clinical evaluation, radiography techniques, and dental casts have played a major role in orthodontics and have remained a standard diagnostic method in dentistry to date. On the other hand, these methods are associated with major disadvantages like radiation exposure and invasive procedures. To address these limitations, recent diagnostic methods have identified various biomarkers in gingival crevicular fluid and saliva as non-invasive diagnostic methods. These biomarkers can help clinicians in planning orthodontic treatment at the optimal time and determine the appropriate initiation of the treatment. Point-of-care diagnostic tools such as lateral flow assays, Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats and microfluidic devices, and wearable technologies are emerging as promising alternatives for orthodontic treatment monitoring by offering rapid, cost-effective, and non-invasive alternatives to traditional methods. Recent developments such as incorporation of artificial intelligence and machine learning into orthodontic software attempt to improve the overall monitoring of orthodontic treatment. This review aims to present various traditional and innovative methods that have shown promising outcomes in research, along with insights into emerging areas that serve as potential game changers in orthodontic treatment monitoring.
authors: Ananya Nair; Prajwal Shetty; M.S. Ravi

title: Harnessing microfluidics for microbiology: from bacteria-host interactions to emerging cancer therapies
abstract: Microfluidics has emerged as a powerful technology for precisely controlling mechanical and chemical environments across a wide range of biological systems, from single cells to complex co-cultures. In microbiology, the microscale dimensions of bacteria pose experimental challenges that microfluidic systems have effectively addressed, offering compatibility with live imaging and enabling quantitative investigations of bacterial behaviors and host-bacteria interactions. Historical microfluidic designs are now routinely used to quantify bacterial growth and lineage with unprecedented temporal-spatial resolution and precise control of external conditions. In parallel, organ-on-chip technologies are increasingly applied in microbiology to study host-bacteria interactions within physiologically relevant and well-controlled microenvironments. Recently, cancer tissues have been recognized as unexpected hosts for bacteria, with mounting impactful evidence showing that intratumoral microbes can influence cancer progression and response to therapy. Despite growing interest, the application of microfluidics to cancer-bacteria interactions remains limited. Addressing this gap requires the development of appropriate methodological tools that replicate the relevant tumor microenvironment features and allow the quantification of both cellular responses and bacterial colonization dynamics upon the bacterial-host interaction. In this review, we first outline the foundational applications of microfluidics in microbiology from single-cell to collective behavior studies. We then describe how organ-on-chip technology enables the fine-tuned formation of organ-specific conditions, which are critical for modeling the complex tumor microenvironment. We further examine recent findings on intratumoral bacteria across cancer types and discuss how microfluidics, especially tumor-on-chip approaches, can advance this emerging field, from mechanistic insights to therapeutic development.
authors: Léa Pinon; Auriane Debache; Alexandre Thuaud; Luca Tiraboschi; Gerlanda Vella; Jessica Riou-Ramon; Céline Cordier; Clara Helal; Pascal Hersen; María Rescigno; Maria Carla Parrini; Stéphanie Descroix

title: Multiscale mechanobiology of circulating tumor cells: microfluidics and atomic force microscopy
abstract: Cancer progression is shaped by coupled molecular, biochemical, and mechanical changes across multiple scales, from altered signaling and cytoskeletal organization to cellular deformation, adhesion, and metastatic dissemination. Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) are rare and heterogeneous in blood, occurring as single cells and multicellular clusters that provide access to evolving tumor phenotypes through liquid biopsy. Their apparent elasticity, deformability, adhesion, and viscoelastic behavior may reflect invasive potential, treatment response, and phenotypic state, while cytoskeletal proteins, membrane lipids, cell surface glycans, and receptors provide molecular context for these mechanical signatures. This review examines the complementary roles of microfluidics and atomic force microscopy (AFM) in multiscale CTC mechanobiology. Microfluidic platforms support label-free and affinity-based enrichment, capture, positioning, and recovery of viable cells. AFM provides localized measurements of apparent elasticity, deformation, adhesion, viscoelastic response, and nanoscale surface architecture in liquid, while functionalized probes enable molecular recognition and molecule-specific force measurements. We evaluate physical, affinity-based, cluster-preserving, open-space, and artificial intelligence-assisted microfluidic strategies together with reversible device assembly, automated AFM targeting, fluidic probes, advanced mapping modes, and treatment-response applications. Existing studies establish feasibility, including direct AFM measurements of individual patient-derived CTCs and automated analysis following microfluidic enrichment in model rare-cell mixtures. Clinical evidence remains limited, many integrated workflows rely on cultured cells or spiked samples, and within the literature identified in this review, direct AFM characterization of intact patient-derived CTC clusters was not found. Clinical translation will require confirmation of tumor identity, standardized acquisition, analysis, and reporting, increased throughput, statistical analysis that preserves the hierarchy of patients, cells, and force curves, and validation in independent patient cohorts. Integrated AFM-microfluidic platforms could extend CTC liquid biopsy beyond enumeration toward functional mechanobiological analysis relevant to metastasis, therapeutic response, and biomarker development.
authors: Ayoub Glia; Muhammedin Deliorman; Mohammad Ameen Qasaimeh

title: Index
State-of-the-art microfluidics technology for CO₂-foam flooding and geological CO₂ storage: A review
abstract: Microfluidic technology has been a powerful tool for exploring CO₂-foam flooding and CO₂ sequestration at the microscale. Traditional methods, e.g., core flooding experiments, are prone to facing challenges in simulating fluid dynamics in porous media accurately; however, microfluidic platforms allow for direct observation and real-time evaluation of multiphase flow dynamics. This review evaluates cutting-edge microfluidic techniques, such as rock-on-a-chip and high-temperature high-pressure (HTHP) chips, with enhanced functionalities in simulating reservoir conditions. Additionally, advances in image processing and machine learning greatly promoted data analysis in microfluidics-driven experiments. The integration of microfluidics with digital rock physics and reservoir simulations offers a platform for the translation of laboratory findings into field-applicable operations. Besides advances in technology, this review considers the economic feasibility and environmental benefits of microfluidic operations in enhanced oil recovery (EOR) and carbon capture and storage (CCS). The results show that microfluidics can play a key role in optimizing CO₂ injection strategies, enhancing oil recovery, and ensuring the security of long-term CO₂ storage, and thus promoting energy efficiency as well as climate change mitigation.
authors: Muhammad Raees Khan

title: Molecular point-of-care: technological evolution, clinical applications, and future perspectives
abstract: The landscape of clinical diagnostics is undergoing a fundamental shift from centralized laboratories toward decentralized point-of-care testing (POCT) models. Conventional molecular diagnostics often suffer from prolonged turnaround times, high operational costs, and a strict reliance on sophisticated infrastructure. To overcome these limitations, modern POCT platforms have deeply integrated advanced molecular techniques. These include diverse isothermal nucleic acid amplification methods (such as LAMP, RPA, and RCA) and highly specific CRISPR/Cas recognition systems. Furthermore, coupling these biochemical reactions with microfluidic chips and smartphone-based digital platforms has enabled fully automated, "sample-in, answer-out" diagnostic capabilities. This review systematically summarizes the technological evolution of these molecular POCT platforms. It highlights their transformative clinical applications across diverse fields, including infectious disease containment, early oncology screening, cardiovascular emergency triage, and metabolic disease management. Despite remarkable progress, several critical bottlenecks still prevent the widespread clinical translation of molecular POCT. These challenges include cross-interference in multiplexed detection, enzyme stability outside strict cold chains, high costs of core components, and the lack of tailored regulatory frameworks. Addressing these barriers via synthetic biology, robust system integration, and artificial intelligence is critical to advancing the core vision of delivering rapid, accessible, and precise healthcare solutions in resource-limited settings.
authors: Danfeng Zhang; Xin Cui; Ruijie Zhang; Wenlong Cai; Wang Li; Jichun Yang

title: Fungal hyphae through the lens of microfluidic devices: From biological properties to novel therapeutic opportunities
abstract: Fungal diseases are increasingly being recognized as a major health problem worldwide. Advancing therapeutic approaches against fungal pathogens require comprehensive knowledge of their biological properties, which enable fungi to explore host environments, interact with host cells and coinhabiting microorganisms, adopt colonization and infective strategies. Thus, fungus intrinsic as well as extrinsic mechanisms functionally cooperate for successful host infection and disease development. In this regard, fungal hyphae, i.e. long, filamentous structures with polarized tip growth, represent a unique feature of multicellular fungi and play critical roles during the infectious process, calling for in-depth characterization of their functional and structural properties. In this context, reproducing hyphal growth in physiological conditions represents a fundamental prerequisite for disease modeling and therapeutic development. For their potential to accommodate and interconnect cells and miniature tissues, microfluidic devices stand as unique opportunities in this direction by overcoming acknowledged limits of animal models and traditional cell cultures. Based on these premises, we herein provide an overview of the use of microfluidic devices in the study of fungal hyphae, from the investigation of their biological properties to the analysis of inter-organismal networking, including the interaction between fungal hyphae and host cells. By dissecting hyphal strategies of environmental navigation as well as modalities of cell-cell interactions, resorting to microfluidics devices may provide novel opportunities for therapeutic targeting of fungal pathogens, in line with the objectives of the World Health Organization.
authors: Angela Di Battista; Lassi Sukki; Consuelo Fabi; Sarah Balucchi; Marilena Pariano; Pasi J. Kallio; Claudio Costantini

title: A Highly Efficient DLD Microfluidic Chip With Two‐Stage Inclined Elliptical Pillars for Particle Separation and Purification
abstract: Deterministic lateral displacement (DLD), a hydrodynamic particle manipulation technology, has been extensively studied for the development of fast and efficient microfluidic chips for particle manipulation and detection. However, particles are prone to clogging in DLD chips with closely spaced pillars, which can reduce sorting efficiency. Previous studies have shown that elliptical pillars provide better separation performance than equilateral triangular pillars. In elliptical-pillar DLD, a negative angle of inclination (Aoi) reduces the particle period and facilitates efficient isolation of large particles, whereas a positive Aoi decreases the critical diameter, thereby improving the sorting of smaller particles. On the basis of these findings, we designed a two-stage DLD microfluidic chip with inclined elliptical-pillar arrays, using an Aoi of -45° in the first stage and 45° in the second stage. The combination of negative and positive Aoi values enhanced the isolation of large particles, improved the purification of medium- and small-sized particles, and reduced the risk of clogging. This design provides a practical approach for improving the separation and purification performance of DLD devices and offers potential for efficient multi-size particle separation.
authors: Di Jiang; Yujiang Li; Jiawen Guo; Pengcheng Zhao; Bin Wu

title: PK-Informed Microphysiological Systems: From Dynamic Dosing to Quantitative In Vitro–In Vivo Translation
abstract: Conventional in vitro drug evaluation relies largely on static concentration-response assays that fail to reproduce the dynamic pharmacokinetic (PK) profiles observed in vivo, contributing to the gap between preclinical findings and clinical outcomes. Recent advances in microphysiological systems (MPSs), particularly microfluidic organ-on-chip platforms, enable programmable concentration-time profiles that more closely mimic physiological drug exposure. These PK-informed platforms allow systematic investigation of schedule dependency, time-dependent pharmacodynamics (PD), and exposure-driven efficacy under controlled flow conditions. Spatially resolved analytical approaches further reveal heterogeneous drug penetration and metabolic responses within tissues, emphasizing the importance of spatiotemporal PK-PD coupling. Integration of multi-organ and vascularized chip systems with physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling increasingly supports quantitative in vitro-in vivo translation. This review outlines how PK-informed MPSs can generate dynamic in vitro exposure and response data that inform PBPK modeling, thereby supporting quantitative in vitro-in vivo translation of drug disposition and response.
authors: Su Jeong Kang; Seok Ho Bong; Min Jeong Jo; Jae Min Lee; Moon Sup Yoon; Seonmin Park; Yeseung Lee; Yuseon Shin; Hye Jin Lee; Chun‐Woong Park; Dae Hwan Shin

title: Droplet microfluidics for energy and bioelectrochemical applications
abstract: Droplet microfluidics has become a modern technology for chemical, biological, electrochemical and energy applications, which helps in the manipulation of a discrete droplet in a size range from 10 pL to 100 nL. Compared to conventional techniques, the droplet-based platform provides a 10–100-fold faster mass-transfer rate, reduces reagent usage by up to 95%, decreases reaction time from hours to minutes, and enables ultra-efficient screening of 10 3 –10 4 droplets s -1 . The capabilities have greatly advanced the discovery and optimization of advanced materials, catalysts, and bioelectrochemical systems. This review covers all aspects of droplet generation, manipulation, detection methods and the latest progress in device manufacturing for energy and bioelectrochemical applications. Representative studies show that the droplet-assisted microfluidic platforms can be used to screen electrocatalysts within minutes, can be used for membrane-less electrochemical systems with current densities over 100–500 mA cm -2 , and can be used to reduce material consumption by over 80% with enhanced catalyst utilization. Droplet microfluidics has enabled rapid microbial screening, improved control of biofilms, removal of up to 95% chemical oxygen demand (COD), and microbial electrolysis system with hydrogen production rates up to 314 ± 17 m 3 H 2 m -3 reactor per day with optimized electrode configuration in bioelectrochemical applications. The review also emphasizes the use of AI, machine learning, digital microfluidics and automation for autonomous experimentation and optimization based on data. Finally, the current challenges regarding scalability and standardization of devices, long-term operational stability and commercialization of devices are critically discussed. Overall, droplet microfluidics is a versatile and scalable platform that has the potential to speed up the next-generation of sustainable energy technologies and to bioelectrochemical systems by providing more precise control of reactions, high throughput experimentation, and more efficient use of resources.
authors: Amir Ibrahim Madaje; Pritam Shinde; Sanket Goel
venue: Frontiers in Lab on a Chip Technologies

title: Determinants of Phase-Separation Propensities, Material States, and Material Properties of Biomolecular Condensates
abstract: Conspectus Phase separation of various materials has been studied for one and a half centuries, laying foundational principles in materials science. In the last two decades, phase separation of proteins and nucleic acids has received enormous attention, due to its relevance to cellular functions. Despite this explosion of empirical data, many observations on the resulting biomolecular condensates lack a rigorous theoretical underpinning. The first goal of this Account is to put forward theoretical frameworks for the phase-separation propensities, material states, and material properties of biomolecular condensates. Using these frameworks, I rationalize mechanistic interpretations in our recent experimental and computational studies, and synthesize these studies with prior literature to draw novel, unifying conclusions. To evaluate phase-separation propensities, I establish a direct relationship between the threshold (or saturation) concentration (Cth) and the excess chemical potential in the dense phase (μexII). μexII is fundamentally dictated by the collective strength and valency of intermolecular interactions. The relationship between Cth and μexII readily rationalizes the effects of amino-acid composition and solvent conditions like temperature, pH, and salt on phase-separation propensities. Regarding material states, I posit that liquid droplets represent the completion of phase separation, whereas other states─including amorphous dense liquids, reversible aggregates, and gels─arise from premature termination of spinodal decomposition. Specifically, amorphous dense liquids occur near the critical point and early during spinodal decomposition, kinetically trapped as overly weak interactions prevent further condensation. Gels and aggregates are different forms of dynamically arrested states, one driven by directional interactions that favor tip growth, extending outward into system-spanning networks, the other driven by monomer addition at interior sites to maximize valency, producing densely packed, amorphous particles. For material properties, I highlight the crucial roles of the stress relaxation time (τ1), which is determined by the mean lifetime of intermolecular bonds in a condensate. This relaxation time dictates how the condensate manifests viscoelasticity, including shear thickening and shear thinning, and accounts for the wide variation in zero-shear viscosity (ηz) among different condensates. Indeed, I propose a correlation between ηz and τ1, which is supported by available data. I also devise a theoretical model to explain the relative constancy of surface tension. Given this constancy, the inverse fusion speed can be used as an indicator of viscosity. Validating and expanding these conclusions will further strengthen the theoretical foundations of the biomolecular condensate field. Looking forward, several high-impact opportunities emerge. First, it may be possible to bridge the persistent gap between all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and in-vitro experiments, by extending the size and time limits of MD simulations via taking advantage of deep learning. Second, expanding the experimental toolkit, by borrowing techniques from materials research, will further push the study of biomolecular condensates from mesoscales to molecular scales. Finally, testing mechanistic hypotheses inside cells will connect the physics of phase separation to cellular functions.
authors: Huan‐Xiang Zhou

title: Surface‐Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy Aptasensors for Nucleic‐Acid Detection: Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
abstract: Nucleic-acid biomarkers play pivotal roles in disease diagnosis, therapeutic monitoring, and precision medicine, creating an urgent demand for analytical platforms combining high sensitivity, molecular specificity, and rapid detection. Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) integrated with aptamers, short single-stranded DNA or RNA oligonucleotides, has attracted considerable attention by coupling programmable molecular recognition with ultrasensitive plasmon-enhanced Raman detection. This review evaluates recent advances in aptamer-based SERS biosensors for nucleic-acid analysis, systematically examining sensing mechanisms, plasmonic substrate engineering, aptamer immobilization, signal-transduction pathways, and amplification approaches, including catalytic hairpin assembly, hybridization chain reaction, rolling circle amplification, and CRISPR-assisted systems. Recent developments in microfluidics, artificial intelligence-assisted spectral analysis, portable Raman instrumentation, and point-of-care platforms are assessed while distinguishing true aptamer-mediated sensing from conventional hybridization-based DNA detection. Rational hotspot engineering, deterministic nanogap architectures, and advanced amplification strategies have enabled detection from femtomolar to attomolar levels with improved selectivity, multiplexing, and reproducibility. Challenges including substrate variability, quantitative standardization, aptamer stability, biosafety, and clinical translation are discussed. Future directions toward standardized, intelligent, clinically deployable SERS platforms for next-generation molecular diagnostics and precision healthcare are proposed.
authors: MK Alam; Kazi Mohammed Mehedi Hassan; Monika Tarafdar; Mohammad Imran Hossain; Mohammad Anwar Parvez; Mostafizur Rahaman; Mohammad A. Hasnat

title: Recent Advances in Nanofabrication Strategies for Biosensors: From Precision Nanopatterning to Scalable, Flexible, and AI-Assisted Manufacturing
abstract: Nanofabrication has become central to the development of high-performance biosensors by enabling precise control over sensing interfaces, enhanced signal transduction, and integration across optical, electrochemical, microfluidic, and wearable platforms. This review examines the evolution of biosensor nanofabrication from deterministic top-down patterning toward scalable and integrated manufacturing strategies. Top-down approaches, including electron-beam lithography, focused ion beam milling, nanoimprint lithography, reactive ion etching, and laser-based fabrication, are discussed alongside replication and transfer processes, soft lithography, lithography-free plasmonic structuring, and additive three-dimensional fabrication. Bottom-up strategies based on nanoparticle assembly, DNA nanotechnology, block-copolymer and nanoporous templating, and stimuli-responsive materials are further considered as routes to programmable nanoscale organization and functional biointerfaces. Particular attention is given to flexible and wearable biosensors, where substrate mechanics, conductive-interface fabrication, textile integration, epidermal microfluidics, packaging, power management, and wireless communication introduce manufacturing requirements beyond conventional rigid devices. Across these approaches, the review emphasizes that analytical sensitivity alone is insufficient for translation; nanoscale precision must be accompanied by reproducibility, scalable processing, stable biofunctionalization, antifouling performance, packaging, storage stability, and device-level quality control. Emerging AI-assisted fabrication and process optimization strategies are also discussed as tools for linking manufacturing parameters with structural and analytical performance. Overall, the review provides a manufacturing-oriented perspective on how hybrid nanofabrication strategies can bridge high-performance laboratory biosensors with reproducible, scalable, and application-ready sensing systems.
authors: Meryem Beyza Avci; Furkan Kocer; Seda Nur Topkaya; Konstantinos Papatryfonos; Arif E. Çetin

title: All-optical closed-loop control of human cardiomyocyte networks exploiting holographic optogenetics
abstract: Heart diseases can trigger life-threatening arrhythmias by disrupting cardiac contraction wavefront propagation. In contrast to conventional treatments like electrical pacemakers, optogenetics offers high spatial and temporal resolution for non-invasive interrogation and modulation of cellular activity. However, combining sensing and actuation into a real-time control loop remains challenging. A major obstacle is the data load associated with dense sensor arrays typically required for spatially resolved wavefront monitoring. To overcome this, we present an all-optical, closed-loop control strategy using adaptive holographic stimulation and sparsely sampled, label-free imaging data, enabling robust classification and quantitative characterization of spatial wavefront properties in real time. We successfully demonstrate spatiotemporal optogenetic closed-loop control of wavefront dynamics in functional syncytia of human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes in at least 107 out of 109 evaluated cases across all experiments. This framework establishes a foundation for advanced feedback control strategies aimed at mimicking, detecting and terminating abnormal propagation patterns.
authors: Robert Wendland; Felix Schmieder; Muhammad Atif Sikandar; Frithjof Knüppel; Wolfram‐Hubertus Zimmermann; Olaf Bergmann; Lars Büttner; Jürgen W. Czarske

title: New Era of Biosensors - Integration of Artificial Intelligence and Technology in Healthcare
abstract: The connection between biological systems and electronic devices has developed beyond simple glucose tests or pregnancy checks. It is now a transformative area in modern science. This chapter looks at the “New Era of Biosensors,” where molecular biology, materials science, and information technology come together to provide a clear view of our integration of Artificial intelligence in biosensors. We follow the transition from large, lab-based equipment to decentralized, patient-focused diagnostics. By moving the process from hospital beds to homes, these technologies change healthcare from a reactive approach to a proactive approach. Three advances enable this shift. Microfluidics and nanotechnology bring lab-grade sensitivity to chip-scale devices. Epidermal electronics maintain signal quality on flexible, skin-conformable substrates. Artificial intelligence removes noise from real-world recordings, identifies patterns that precede clinical symptoms, and tunes predictions to individual baselines. Translation from prototype to clinical deployment remains difficult. This chapter examines the technical, regulatory, and ethical barriers to implementation, including data privacy under Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) and General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), algorithmic bias arising from non-representative training data, and power constraints in implantable and energy-harvesting devices. Drawing on clinical applications such as smart bandages and remote cardiac monitoring, the chapter outlines how continuous, AI-supported sensing can shift healthcare from episodic consultation toward sustained physiological monitoring and earlier intervention.
authors: Sagar Pralhad Kanekar; Sahil Vaghole; Aarya Kamat; Anirjit Kartha

title: Programmable Axial–Radial Multichannel Nickel Microtubes Fabricated by Core-Filament Jet Electrodeposition
abstract: Programmable hollow metallic microdevices with lateral outlets are attractive for distributed fluid handling, but integrating an axial lumen, side channels, and a sealed distal tip remains fabrication-intensive. Here, a core-filament jet electrodeposition (CF-JED) strategy combines segmented electrolyte-jet operation with sacrificial nylon-fiber templating to fabricate multichannel nickel microtubes. An 80 μm nylon core defines the axial lumen, whereas 50 μm transverse and helical fibers prescribe lateral channels. Interrupting the jet creates the in situ assembly interval for template placement; resumed localized electrodeposition encapsulates the fibers and can close the distal tip, and physical pull-out releases the channels without chemical dissolution or drilling. Stable growth was obtained at 2.5 mA with an axial growth rate of approximately 15 μm·min−1. Micro-computed tomography revealed a 50 ± 5 μm radial channel and a 76 ± 6 μm axial lumen interconnected within the sealed-tip structure. SEM/EDS confirmed open lateral apertures and nickel-rich walls, while water-immersion gas testing provided qualitative evidence of channel interconnectivity. CF-JED therefore provides a template-defined route to programmable multichannel hollow-metal microstructures; direct liquid-flow, mechanical, and biological validation remain necessary for application-specific use.
authors: Wei Wang; Hongtao Qian; Pengju Liu; Zhonghe Li; Yulong Li; Xiaohong Yang

title: Silicon Photonics and Optically Controlled Microrobotics at the Limit English Introduction and Research Abstract This monograph asks whether silicon-photonic chips can create, observe, communicate, and close control around microscale agents with lower total burden than magnetic, wired, mechanical, microfluidic, or external-optical alternatives. It replaces impressive motion with a complete evidence chain from the commanded chip field to terminal task quality, thermal and photochemical exposure, recovery, and independent replay. Scientific position The candidate objective is O_ctrl = B_control P_track - L_couple - Delta T_abs - C_align. Optical control is valuable only when usable control bandwidth and tracking success remain meaningful after coupling loss, absorbed heat, alignment, compute, calibration, packaging, missed agents, and failed recovery are counted. Unsafe exposure, runaway motion, lost identity, irreversible material change, corrupted command ancestry, or missing evidence are hard vetoes. Research architecture The PDF contains thirty gold derivations, eighty-two chapters with five single-page sections each, and two hundred detailed one-page Research Gates. Every derivation links to chapter, experiment, and Gate corridors. Every chapter opens with its governing formula. Fixed quotas for Easter-Egg Equations and Phoenix Answer Embryos are not used. Five research layers Function and burden contract: Define terminal tasks control bandwidth eligible agents external infrastructure strong baselines and hard vetoes. Photonic field and sensing plane: Calibrate power phase polarization spatial fields pose information and coordinate ancestry. Mechanism-resolved actuation: Separate optical momentum electrokinetic thermal fluidic acoustic chemical adhesion and surface effects. Closed-loop multi-agent qualification: Join estimation latency constrained control identity occlusion collision recovery and independent task readout. Reliability portability and succession: Count exposure aging packaging foundry variation economics security transfer redesign safe stop and retirement. Minimum demonstrator A silicon-photonic test chip generates calibrated fields over an inert microfluidic workspace. Randomized agents carry independent visual or spectral references. The experiment compares integrated optical, external optical, magnetic, and wired control on identical path following, sensing, transport, and safe-stop tasks. Hidden phase, alignment, occlusion, latency, and absorption faults test the controller. Independent thermometry and post-mission surface assays challenge the claimed mechanism and safety. Central deliverable The Photonic Microrobot Control Plane binds circuit genealogy, source-to-agent power, phase and polarization commands, field maps, agent identity and material history, mechanism evidence, raw observations, state estimates, control actions, thermal and photochemical exposure, task outcomes, failures, recoveries, cost, and successor authority. Another team must be able to reproduce, refute, simplify, fork, repair, or retire the claim.
