title: Transforming Brain Organoids Into Functional Platforms: Convergence of Engineering, Imaging, AI, and Ethics
abstract: Brain organoids are self-organizing 3D aggregates derived from pluripotent stem cells and thus mirror many aspects of human brain development, including gene expression programs, spatial organization, and neuron subtype specification. As a result, these organoids have been used to emulate neurodevelopmental, neuropsychiatric, and neurodegenerative diseases. Yet, their maturation remains fundamentally constrained by diffusion-limited necrosis, incomplete vascularization, limited visualization, and the absence of large-scale circuit integration, which collectively prevent progression beyond the fetal stage. These intrinsic limitations have catalyzed a convergence across microfluidics, biofabrication, imaging, and ethical frameworks, giving rise to a multidisciplinary movement aimed at enhancing organoid viability, reproducibility, and physiological relevance. This perspective examines how these technologies are transforming brain organoids from developmental models into experimentally robust, functional platforms.
authors: Aishwarya Pantula; Kaustubh G. Joshi; Swarangi Samant; Greta Babakhanova; Annie Kathuria

title: The fabrication and application of diamond sensors for electrochemical analysis in single and multiple phase systems
abstract: Polycrystalline boron-doped diamond (pBDD) has acquired great interest as a electrode material exhibiting low background currents, wide potential windows and a host of extreme physical properties such as mechanical hardness, chemical inertness and a high resistance to harsh environments. pBDD’s exceptional electrochemical characteristics have made its application as a material for high performance electrochemical sensors the basis of a hugh amount of research over the last decade. Work in this thesis describes the fabrication and application of pBDD sensors in both stationary and fluid flow environments where conventional electrode materials would be unsuitable or problematic. pBDD electrodes functionalised with catalytic metal nano-particles are demonstrated as a means of detecting hydrazine, a genotoxic impurity of interest in pharmaceutical analysis, even in the presence of potentially interfering pharmaceutical matrix. This same sensor is then employed as a means of detecting the presence of non-polar oils on an electrode surface in dual-phase, aqueous/oil systems. An investigation of electrochemical techniques for detecting and characterising phase changes in the form of microdroplets moving under flow in microfluidic systems is detailed. Limitations to the use of conventional materials used to fabricate such microfluidic devices are discussed. In an effort to address these issues as well as those expected in extreme environments, with aggressive media, a fabrication route for realising all-diamond microfluidic devices with integrated, high-quality pBDD electrodes is outlined.
authors: Jonathan C. Newland
venue: Warwick Research Archive Portal (University of Warwick)

title: Pendant drop microtraps for signal enhancement of microbead-based bioassays
abstract: Reliable fluorescence-based biosensing often requires efficient preconcentration of analytes, but existing preconcentration methods are highly prone to clogging and biofouling. Active methods, on the other hand, demand complex tools and operational steps. In this study, we present a pendant drop microtrap that uses a wall-free and pump-free configuration to preconcentrate microbeads before fluorescence readout. Droplets (0.5–4 μL) containing microbeads were dispensed onto hydrophobic polystyrene substrates and inverted to form stable hemispherical pendant drops. Target non-magnetic microbeads accumulated at the drop apex under gravity alone, whereas magnetic beads were concentrated by gravity and magnetic force. We studied the effects of droplet volume on bead distribution and fluorescence signal intensity. The platform was evaluated with fluorescently labeled magnetic Dynabeads and non-magnetic polystyrene beads, and demonstrated up to a 5.7-fold signal enhancement with 4 μL droplets. The pendant drop microtraps concentrated Dynabeads and non-magnetic polystyrene beads functionalized with various labels and antibodies, specifically streptavidin-Cy5, an anti-TNF-α antibody, and a FITC-conjugated rabbit anti-goat IgG (H + L) antibody. The pendant drop microtrap therefore offers a simple, wall-free, pump-free, and cheap preconcentration platform that can be readily integrated into existing fluorescence-based bioassay workflows.
authors: Amin Ghaffarzadeh Bakhshayesh; Isabella Walker; Huiyan Li

title: Towards rapid 3D direct manufacture of biomechanical microstructures
abstract: The field of stereolithography has developed rapidly over the last 20 years, and commercially available systems currently have sufficient resolution for use in microengineering applications. However, they have not as yet been fully exploited in this field. This thesis investigates the possible microengineering applications of microstereolithography systems, specifically in the areas of active microfluidic devices and microneedles. The fields of micropumps and microvalves, stereolithography and microneedles are reviewed, and a variety of test builds were fabricated using the EnvisionTEC Perfactory Mini Multi-Lens stereolithography system in order to define its capabilities. A number of microneedle geometries were considered. This number was narrowed down using finite element modelling, before another simulation was used to optimise these structures. 9 × 9 arrays of 400 μm tall, 300 μm base diameter microneedles were subjected to mechanical testing. Per needle failure forces of 0.263 and 0.243 N were recorded for the selected geometries, stepped cone and inverted trumpet. The 90 μm needle tips were subjected to between 30 and 32 MPa of pressure at their failure point - more than 10 times the required pressure to puncture average human skin. A range of monolithic micropumps were produced with integrated 4 mm diameter single-layer 70 μm-thick membranes used as the basis for a reciprocating displacement operating principle. The membranes were tested using an oscillating pneumatic actuation, and were found reliable (>1,000,000 cycles) up to 2.0 PSIG. Pneumatic single-membrane nozzle/diffuser rectified devices produced flow rates of up to 1,000 μl/min with backpressures of up to 375 Pa. Another device rectified using active membrane valves was found to self-prime, and produced backpressures of up to 4.9 kPa. These devices and structures show great promise for inclusion in complex, fully integrated and active microfluidic systems fabricated using microstereolithography alone, with implications for both cost of manufacture and lead time.
authors: Philip Huw King
venue: Warwick Research Archive Portal (University of Warwick)

title: Smart materials for biosensing of infectious diseases: Mechanisms, materials, platforms, and translational opportunities
abstract: Rapid and decentralized detection of infectious diseases remains a critical challenge for global healthcare systems. Conventional diagnostic methods such as polymerase chain reaction and immunoassays provide high analytical accuracy but often require centralized laboratories, complex workflows, and trained personnel, limiting their accessibility in point-of-care and resource-limited settings. Smart materials—materials capable of dynamically responding to external physical, chemical, or biological stimuli—have emerged as powerful platforms for next-generation biosensors due to their tunable physicochemical properties, signal amplification capabilities, and compatibility with miniaturized sensing architectures. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in smart-material-enabled biosensors for infectious disease detection. Key material classes including graphene-based nanomaterials, piezoelectric materials, light-responsive nanostructures, magnetic materials, Prussian blue derivatives, metal–organic and covalent–organic frameworks (MOFs/COFs), and conductive polymer–hydrogel systems are discussed in terms of their sensing mechanisms, transduction strategies, and analytical performance. We highlight how these materials enable diverse detection modalities—including electrochemical, optical, piezoelectric, and magnetically mediated sensing—allowing rapid and highly sensitive detection of viral and bacterial pathogens. Emerging fabrication approaches, integration with microfluidic systems, wearable devices, and data-driven diagnostics are also examined. Finally, we discuss key challenges for clinical translation, including stability, biocompatibility, antifouling performance, large-scale manufacturing, and regulatory considerations. Smart materials provide a versatile foundation for developing next-generation biosensing technologies capable of enabling rapid, decentralized, and continuous infectious disease monitoring.
authors: Seyed Mojtaba Sajjadi; Zahra Abooalizadeh; Mohammad Mehdi Banoei; Bahareh Babamiri; Ahmad Rezaei Kolahchi; Mehdi Mohammadi Ashani; Amir Sanati‐Nezhad

title: Controlling water-in-water droplets and extracellular environments in microfluidics
abstract: Many biological and soft-matter processes take place in water-rich environments. In cells, biological fluids, and polymer-rich materials, molecules do not always remain evenly mixed. Under suitable conditions, a homogeneous aqueous solution can separate into two liquid phases through liquid–liquid phase separation. In aqueous two-phase systems, this process can produce water-in-water droplets, in which both phases are water-rich but differ in polymer or salt composition. These droplets are attractive for biological studies because they provide mild, fully aqueous, and cell-compatible microenvironments. They can also serve as simple models for membraneless compartments, artificial cells, and extracellular microenvironments. However, water-in-water droplets are difficult to control. Their aqueous–aqueous interface has an extremely low interfacial tension, which makes droplet formation and stabilization much more difficult than in water-in-oil systems. Conventional droplet microfluidics often relies on interfacial breakup under controlled flow, but this method becomes less effective when the interface is very weak. As a result, water-in-water droplets are often hard to generate reproducibly, trap stably, and observe over long periods. Their size, composition, and surrounding chemical environment are also difficult to adjust in real time. These limitations restrict their use in biological studies that require stable and tunable aqueous microenvironments. This thesis addresses this challenge by developing a microfluidic platform for the controlled formation, trapping, and manipulation of water-in-water droplets. The central idea is to shift water-in-water droplet control from a flow-breakup problem to a diffusion-and-confinement problem. Instead of generating droplets upstream by shear, active perturbation, or oil-assisted emulsification, the platform forms droplets directly inside dead-end microchambers connected to a main channel. The main channel provides a controlled aqueous solution, while diffusion between the main channel and the chambers changes the local polymer composition and induces liquid–liquid phase separation. In this way, droplets form in place, remain physically confined, and stay chemically connected to the surrounding aqueous phase. This allows the droplet microenvironment to be changed during the experiment without oil, surfactants, or complex flow control. Chapter 1 introduces the background and motivation of the thesis. It explains liquid–liquid phase separation, aqueous two-phase systems, and water-in-water droplets, and places them in the context of soft matter and biological studies. Compared with water-in-oil droplets, water-in-water droplets avoid oil and surfactants and are therefore better suited for cells and biomolecules. At the same time, their weak aqueous–aqueous interface makes them difficult to produce and control. Chapter 1 identifies a key gap in the field: many existing platforms can generate water-in-water droplets, but fewer can combine droplet formation, stable trapping, long-term observation, and dynamic environmental control in one system. The chapter also introduces the biological motivation of the thesis. Cells are not only regulated by biochemical signals, but also by physical properties of their surroundings, such as viscosity, confinement, and the material state of the extracellular environment. Chapter 2 develops the core microfluidic platform. A fused-silica device is fabricated using femtosecond laser micromachining. The device contains a main channel connected to multiple dead-end microchambers. When aqueous polymer solutions are supplied through the main channel, solute diffusion into the chambers changes the local composition and induces liquid–liquid phase separation. As a result, water-in-water droplets form directly inside the chambers and remain trapped at the same location. Using the PEG/dextran aqueous two-phase system, Chapter 2 shows that droplet size and composition can be controlled in a stable and reproducible way through solute diffusion, phase equilibrium, and chamber geometry. The same platform is then extended to associative phase-separating systems, including coacervate droplets with internal structures. The main technical conclusion of Chapter 2 is that weakly interfacial aqueous droplets can be controlled without oil, surfactants, or complex flow breakup, by using diffusion-driven phase separation and geometric confinement instead. Chapter 3 extends the platform from droplet control to cell manipulation. For cell studies, cells first need to be positioned inside the dead-end chambers. This is achieved by using a dextran concentration gradient to drive cell capture. In this process, dextran mainly acts as a neutral macromolecular solute that creates a concentration gradient and an osmotic pressure imbalance near the cell surface. The interaction between dextran and cells is mainly physical and non-specific, rather than biochemical. Because dextran molecules are partly excluded from the thin interfacial region around the cell surface, the polymer gradient can generate a driving force that moves cells into the chambers. This method allows cells to be captured without direct mechanical pushing or strong flow through the chambers. By adjusting the gradient, the initial cell density, and the chamber geometry, the number of cells in each chamber can be controlled. The method is demonstrated with both fission yeast and leukemia cells. After capture, cells can be enclosed inside PEG/dextran water-in-water droplets. This creates a controllable three-dimensional extracellular environment around the cells and integrates cell capture, droplet formation, and extracellular-environment control in one microfluidic system. Chapter 4 uses this integrated platform to study how cells respond to changes in extracellular fluid viscosity. This question is relevant because many biological environments, such as tissues, mucus, and biofilms, are not simple dilute liquids but crowded and physically complex materials. In conventional cell-culture systems, it is difficult to isolate the effect of extracellular viscosity from other factors, such as osmotic pressure, nutrient transport, and biochemical composition. In Chapter 4, the PEG/dextran aqueous two-phase system is used as a reductionist physical model to tune extracellular fluid viscosity under controlled microfluidic conditions. It should not be understood as a chemical mimic of a specific extracellular matrix or biological fluid. Instead, it provides a defined system for testing how cells respond to extracellular viscous resistance. Using fission yeast as a model organism, Chapter 4 examines how extracellular fluid viscosity affects cell-division progression, glucose uptake, plasma membrane tension, and cytosolic viscosity. The results show that extracellular viscosity can strongly influence cell growth and division. When the surrounding fluid becomes too viscous, cells can no longer divide normally. Below this threshold, however, cells can adapt. The central adaptive response is an increase in cytosolic viscosity. This internal material-state change links the physical condition outside the cell to the cell-cycle outcome. It is also associated with preserved glucose-transporter activity and continued growth. Further experiments show that β-1,3-glucan and trehalose contribute to this adaptation. When these components are disrupted, cells lose part of their ability to tolerate high extracellular viscosity. These findings suggest that cytosolic viscosity is not only a passive physical property of the cell interior. Instead, it can behave as a regulated material state that helps cells maintain function under physical stress. At the same time, the biological interpretation must remain specific. The quantitative viscosity threshold measured in the PEG/dextran system is system-dependent and should not be treated as a universal threshold for all cells or extracellular environments. The broader conclusion is that cells can respond to physical changes outside the cell by tuning their own internal material properties. Chapter 5 brings together the technical and biological findings of the thesis. At the technical level, this thesis provides a fully aqueous microfluidic platform for generating, trapping, observing, and controlling water-in-water droplets over time. The platform differs from conventional droplet methods because it does not rely on flow breakup, oil phases, or surfactants. Instead, it uses diffusion-driven phase separation and geometric confinement. At the biological level, the thesis shows that the same platform can be used to create controlled extracellular microenvironments for cell studies. It also shows that extracellular viscosity is not merely a passive background condition, but a physical factor that can affect cell growth, division, and intracellular material state. Overall, this thesis connects water-in-water droplet microfluidics with the study of cellular adaptation to physical environments. It provides a technical strategy for controlling weakly interfacial aqueous droplets and a biological strategy for studying how cells respond to extracellular physical constraints. By bringing together soft matter physics, microfluidic engineering, and cell biology, this work offers a new experimental framework for studying aqueous microenvironments and the adaptive behavior of living cells.
authors: Chi Li

title: Bioinspired Surface Enabled by Anisotropic Pyramid Structure Arrays for Directional Liquid Self‐Transport
abstract: ABSTRACT Inspired by the phenomenon of directional liquid transport in natural organisms, various bionic surfaces with customized topological structures have been designed and fabricated, contributing to advances in such fields as microfluidics, microreactors, energy harvesting, biomedicine, etc. Despite extensive progress, bionic surfaces with directional liquid self‐transport capabilities still suffer from high technical thresholds, cumbersome fabrication processes, and contamination‐induced failure, limiting their widespread applications. In this work, a bioinspired surface with anisotropic inverted pyramid groove arrays was developed to achieve directional self‐transport of diverse liquids, from water to blood. Bioinspired by the nepenthes alata peristome, a discretely anisotropic inverted pyramid model was theoretically constructed, and then the surface with inverted pyramid groove arrays was efficiently and simply prepared via three‐dimensional (3D) printing and cast molding. This bioinspired surface exhibited rapid, long‐distance, and continuous liquid self‐transport with high unidirectionality under the optimal structural parameters. Moreover, this bioinspired surface was innovatively applied to achieve efficient removal of blood cells from diluted blood without complex operations, providing a proof‐of‐concept foundation for future applications of bioinspired surfaces in microfluidics, plasma separation, and biomedical detection.
authors: Yi‐Ke Wang; Chaowei Sun; Pin Lv; Shengjun An; Zhao Meng-qian; Hu‐Chen Zhang; Si‐Yu Tian; Yan‐Yan Sun; Jun‐Yue Chen; Yu‐Yin Xu; Fan Zhang; Li‐Yun Zheng; Shegan Gao; Hong‐Xing Xu

title: Microchemical Strategies and AI-Enabled Biosensing for Non-Invasive Liquid Biopsy in Precision Oncology
abstract: Traditional blood-based liquid biopsy platforms have established crucial paradigms in precision oncology by enabling the longitudinal tracking of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs). However, blood sampling remains minimally invasive, requires dedicated clinical infrastructure, and is restricted by physiological boundaries such as the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Non-Invasive Liquid Biopsy (NILB) addresses these limitations by utilizing painlessly collected alternative biological matrices, including saliva, urine, breath, stool, sweat, sputum, tears, and cervical secretions. From a microchemical and analytical perspective, these biofluids present extreme analytical challenges: target biomarkers exist at attomolar-to-picomolar concentrations within dense, highly variable chemical matrices containing high background noise and interference. This review outlines the microchemical, physical, and bio-sensing strategies developed to overcome these pre-analytical and analytical barriers. We evaluate advanced microfluidic architectures, nanoscale deterministic lateral displacement, functionalized surface chemistry, isothermal signal amplification, and label-free optical spectroscopy. Furthermore, we evaluate how Artificial Intelligence (AI) and chemometric algorithms—such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and multivariate spectral extraction—decode low-abundance, fragmented multi-omic signatures from complex noise. Finally, we propose a standardized analytical framework to bridge point-of-care microchemical devices with routine clinical diagnostic pipelines.
authors: Samuel Long; Abigail Long

title: Laser-induced local wetting on self-assembled monolayers for microscale fluid control
abstract: Precise spatial control of surface wettability is central to emerging technologies in microfluidics, biosensing, and medical applications. However, current methods for wetting control can be limited by low spatial resolution, a narrow range of achievable wettability modulation, or reliance on masks that are time-consuming to fabricate. Here, we introduce Laser-Induced Local Wetting (LILoW), a maskless technique that uses nanosecond ultraviolet laser pulses to selectively change the wettability of self-assembled monolayer (SAM) coated surfaces. By locally irradiating the SAM coating near its ablation threshold to expose selected regions of the underlying substrate, LILoW combines the broad wetting tunability of coating-based approaches with the high-resolution patterning capabilities of laser systems. We describe the principle of the technique and analyze the contrast in wettability—up to nearly 90 ° —as a function of laser parameters, including laser pulse energy and irradiation pitch, all without inducing damage to the substrate. As a proof of concept, we fabricated an open-air, pumpless Y-shaped microfluidic guide that facilitates capillary-driven laminar co-flow, with high interfacial stability in the absence of physical wall confinement. The rapid and cost-effective platform represented by LILoW can pave the way to democratizing high-resolution wettability patterning for bioanalytical sensing and surface-guided chemical applications.
authors: Lidia Lozano‐Martín; Olga Bantysh; José María Gómez; Jordi Ignés‐Mullol; Martí Duocastella

title: CRISPR‐Scan: Cas13a Mismatch Tolerance Enabled Ultra‐Multiplexed Detection of Same‐Site Indels in Acute Myeloid Leukemia
abstract: Detection of gene mutations related to acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is crucial for its early diagnosis, personalized treatment, and recurrence monitoring. However, accurate detection of diverse mutations occurring at the same locus remains technically challenging. The CRISPR/Cas system, with its unique programmable nucleic acid recognition capabilities, provides a promising solution. Here, we elucidated that CRISPR/LwaCas13a is tolerant to consecutive substitutions but highly sensitive to insertions or deletions (indels) at specific positions of the spacer sequence, enabling rational CRISPR RNA (crRNA) design for multiplex detection of same-site indels. Guided by these principles, we achieved effective detection of ultra-multiplex nucleophosmin 1 (NPM1) c.863_864 4-bp insertions with a single crRNA, while maintaining specificity against the wild-type transcripts. We further established a one-pot CRISPR system, CRISPR-Scan, by integrating recombinase polymerase amplification with LwaCas13a cleavage. CRISPR-Scan enabled detection of mutations in backgrounds as low as 0.01%. In clinical validation, it identified NPM1 mutations in 43 of 120 AML patients, consistent with next-generation sequencing (NGS). Continuous monitoring of four AML patients indicated early recurrence with higher sensitivity than first-generation sequencing (FGS) and full concordance with NGS. A microfluidic chip and portable device further facilitate accurate AML mutation detection. This platform offers an efficient and convenient approach for early AML diagnosis and measurable residual disease (MRD) monitoring.

title: Soil-on-chip for bioremediation studies in PAH-polluted soils: new insights into fungi-bacteria interactions and pollutant dynamics
abstract: Bioremediation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) by fungi and bacteria is a sustainable and cost-effective approach for the depollution of soils. However, considering the complexity of soil matrix involving a wide range of parameters, the mechanisms by which microorganisms take up contaminants may vary depending on its composition and endogenous microbial communities. We used a compartmentalized microfluidic device in a soil-on-chip approach to study the bioremediation mechanisms of benzo[a]pyrene (B[a]P) adsorbed on soil-mimicking matrices and real soil particles. These microsystems were observed using confocal microscopy to investigate, at a cellular level, the desorption of B[a]P from soil and its internalization by fungi, either alone or in co-culture with bacteria. Rapidly after the fungal hyphae came in contact with the polluted particles, cellular labelling corresponding to B[a]P was observed, implying that the contaminant was taken up by the fungus. Cellular labelling enabled the localization of pollutant storage sites within model bacteria. Observations about mycelium influence on B[a]P transport and bacterial mobility at microscale were considered alongside macroscopic experiments. Results of this study demonstrate the ability of microorganisms to desorb hydrophobic organic pollutants adsorbed onto soil particles and highlight the potential of microfluidic devices to investigate PAH biodegradation in soils.
authors: Salomé Bertone; Léna Rasse; Fabrice Alliot; Sylvie Collin; Anne Le Goff; Antoine Fayeulle

title: An automated endpoint control platform for a cyclone concentration pipette
abstract: In the point-of-care, microfluidic, and biochemistry areas, the sample volume is becoming as small as µL order. In this study, we introduce a cyclone concentration pipette that integrates quantitative concentration and sample ejection functions for liquid volume conversion (mL to µL). The concentration pipette is a three-scale polypropylene (PP) tube comprising a cm-scale cyclone concentration chamber, a mm-scale channel for keeping the 10 µL liquid, and a µm-scale orifice (105 µm ± 6 µm) for ejecting liquid. The cyclone concentration system requires continuous observation to determine the endpoint (10 µL). This work introduces an automated control system designed for precise control of a 10 µL volume. The system is built on a Raspberry Pi platform with a Logitech C920 USB camera (1920 × 1080). It monitors the tube in real-time using three parallel detection methods: a convolutional neural network (CNN) for liquid state classification, a MOG2 background subtractor for droplet movement detection, and temporal pixel variance analysis across a 40-frame rolling window for flow state monitoring. When no activity is detected by any method for 30 consecutive seconds, the Raspberry Pi automatically closes a KOGANEI proportional pneumatic valve via a PWM-to-voltage converter (0-10 V). The system automatically terminated concentration without manual intervention. For the water concentration, the mean final volume was 10.6 μL with a standard deviation of 1.65 μL, corresponding to a coefficient of variation (CV) of 15.6% and a bias of + 6.0% relative to the target volume of 10 μL (n = 10). The optimized imaging conditions improved the stability of endpoint detection and volume control, resulting in a final volume of 10.4 μL (CV = 8.2%) with a bias of + 4.0% relative to the 10 μL target, demonstrating acceptable endpoint control accuracy. For the Sunset Yellow solution, a recovery of > 90% and a concentration factor of approximately 90-fold were achieved, indicating that the automated control strategy maintained high sample recovery while achieving efficient concentration.
authors: Ruying Wang; Chenyu Zhou; Ryoichi Ohta; Kazuma Mawatari

title: Mathematical analysis of electromagnetically driven squeezing flow in confined microchannels
abstract: Abstract Nanofluids flowing through confined channels are widely used in micro-cooling systems, miniature pumps, and other microfluidic technologies, where the combined effects of electromagnetic forces and variable fluid properties play an important role in transport phenomena. This study explores the squeezing flow of a nanofluid between two parallel plates, specifically focusing on a stretching, porous lower plate. We examine how external electric and magnetic fields influence flow transport. Temperature-dependent viscosity and thermal conductivity are included in the model to obtain a realistic thermophysical behaviour of the nanofluid flow. The novelty of the study lies in simultaneously considering electro-magnetohydrodynamic effects together with variable fluid properties within the Buongiorno nanofluid model. The governing equations are transformed using similarity transformations and solved by the Optimal Homotopy Analysis Method (OHAM). The results reveal that squeezing, electroosmotic, and electric field parameters enhance the forward flow, whereas suction and magnetic field intensity oppose the fluid motion. Brownian motion and thermophoresis increase the fluid temperature, while increasing the thermophoresis and Lewis number leads to a reduction in the nanoparticle concentration. The combined influence of electromagnetic effects and variable fluid properties demonstrates their importance in controlling flow and heat transfer in confined microfluidic systems.
authors: Mahantesh Chandaragi; Tripathi Dharmendra; Shruthi Karanth; Rajashekhar Choudhari; Hanumesh Vaidya; K. V. Prasad

title: Optoelectronically Enabled Simultaneous and Decoupled Navigation and Selective Pairing of Electrically Driven Janus Particles for Multi-Agent Microrobotics
abstract: Self-propelled Janus particles are promising active agents for microscale manipulation and microrobotic applications. However, when powered by a global external energy source, such as an electric, magnetic, or optical field, all particles respond simultaneously, preventing their independent and concurrent control. Achieving parallel, decoupled control without continuous particle-specific feedback, while preserving intrinsic self-propulsion, remains a significant challenge. Here, we present an optoelectronic (OE) strategy for simultaneously and independently controlling electrically driven, self-propelled metallo-dielectric Janus particles (JPs) using spatially programmable virtual electrodes. These electrodes are generated by projecting a single predefined illumination pattern from a digital micromirror device onto a photoconductive surface. The resulting confinement landscape enables multiple JPs to follow distinct trajectories without continuous monitoring, feedback, or pattern reconfiguration. We demonstrate controlled pairing of JPs with passive polystyrene particles and biological cells. For automated multi-agent operation, an image-based assignment framework identifies optimal agent-target pairs, excludes intersecting trajectories, and generates a single composite pattern for simultaneous, selective pair formation without real-time updating. Finally, we demonstrate independent manipulation of multiple magnetically rolling JPs under a globally applied magnetic field. Overall, this programmable open-loop strategy provides a versatile framework for multi-agent microrobotic manipulation, with potential applications in in-vitro micromanipulation and microfluidic systems.
authors: Srikanta Debata; Ido Rachbuch; Gilad Yossifon

title: Current Translational 3D In Vitro Models of Human Placental Tissue
abstract: Cellular models of placental tissue have the potential to recapitulate normal physiology, model disease, and facilitate therapeutic drug testing. In vivo or two-dimensional (2D) in vitro models of placental conditions have not been sufficiently representative of whole human tissue, thus have limited physiological relevance. This can be attributed to interspecies differences in placental physiology or a lack of structural complexity. In comparison, three-dimensional (3D) multicellular model systems provide a more sophisticated analogue of human placental tissue. Newer models of human placenta include 3D organoids, placenta-on-a-chip and organoid-on-a-chip, employing a range of materials and methods including pluripotent or trophoblast stem cells, microfluidics and 3D bioprinting. Accurately mimicking in vivo human tissue is crucial to the success of these translational 3D models of the placenta.In turn, a reliable representation of placental tissue architecture will allow discovery of the mechanisms underlying abnormal placental development and inform the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of pregnancy-related disorders such as preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction. Here, we provide a comprehensive critical appraisal of recent advances in 3D placental models, which aim to elucidate placental physiology, development and dysfunction. Additionally, we discuss how these platforms can accelerate the development of better monitoring and treatment strategies for pregnancy complications induced by a dysfunctional placenta.
authors: A.S. Raman; Niamh E. P. Mills; Louise Cole; Claire Richards; Lana McClements

title: From Cell Clusters to Complexity: Testicular Organoids as Emerging Platforms in Male Reproductive Research and Biotechnological Innovation
abstract: BACKGROUND: Conventional 2D cultures and animal models incompletely recapitulate the human testicular niche, limiting translation for male infertility, toxicology, and endocrine research. Limited and highly variable access to human testicular tissue restricts translational research. Testicular organoids (TOs), self-organizing assemblies of germ and somatic cells within biomimetic scaffolds, microfluidic chips, or bioprinted constructs, can reproduce seminiferous cord/tubule-like organization, elements of the blood-testis barrier and steroidogenic function, and increasingly support germ-cell progression. By integrating defined media, matrix cues, and controlled microenvironments, TO platforms enable mechanism-driven studies and human-relevant new approach methodologies for toxicology, disease modeling, and fertility-preservation research. This, in turn, supports endocrine and reprotoxicology testing, disease modeling, and prepubertal fertility-preservation strategies. Broad and responsible adoption will require clinically concordant read-outs, stable long-term cultures, reproducible and complete human spermatogenesis, and a robust ethical framework. This review aims to comprehensively evaluate TO systems, spanning cell sources, biomaterials, and microenvironmental control to functional read-outs of morphogenesis, steroidogenesis, and germ-cell progression. By synthesizing recent advances, we clarify mechanistic determinants of organoid performance and outline their translational implications for male infertility research, toxicology, and fertility-preservation strategies.
authors: Merve Görgülü; Leyla Satı

title: Bioelectronics beyond proof-of-concept demonstration
abstract: Biomedical electronic devices are developed to monitor physiological activity and deliver interventions at specific sites in the body. Their operation requires stable biological interfaces, suitable power delivery and reliable interpretation of electrical signals. These requirements become particularly important during movement and prolonged use, when changes in the interface can affect device performance. Developing clinically useful systems therefore requires an understanding of how materials and device architectures preserve the intended function under these conditions. Recent contributions to APL Electronic Devices address these requirements through advances in wearable sensors, biomolecular detection, soft actuators and power sources. We argue that the next stage of development requires closer integration of these capabilities around defined clinical needs. This Editorial examines the resulting design priorities for biological interfaces, feedback control, functional lifetime and reproducible fabrication.
authors: Yeon Sik Choi

title: Miniaturized biosensor platforms for early detection of neurodegenerative diseases and their potential for clinical translation
abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders (NDs), such as Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), and prion diseases, are defined by the gradual deterioration of neurons that frequently occurs prior to the onset of clinically observable symptoms. The early diagnosis of these conditions relies on analytical systems that are capable in detecting disease-related biomarkers at low concentrations within complex biological fluids. This analysis extensively evaluates miniaturized biosensor systems aimed at disease-specific biomarkers, such as amyloid-β and tau for Alzheimer’s disease, α-synuclein (α-syn) and DJ-1 for Parkinson’s disease, and prion protein isoforms for prion disorders. Electrochemical, optical, surface plasmon resonance, field-effect transistor, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy, microfluidic lab-on-a-chip, portable, and wearable systems are assessed concerning their biorecognition methodologies, signal-transduction processes, linear ranges, detection thresholds, selectivity, sample matrices, and suitability for point-of-care applications. Recent research indicates that nanostructured sensing interfaces and microfluidic integration can improve analytical sensitivity, minimize sample needs, and facilitate biomarker identification in blood, plasma, cerebrospinal fluid, saliva, and other therapeutically pertinent matrices. However, remarkably low detection thresholds alone do not establish clinical significance. Biofouling, matrix influences, intricate production, prolonged stability, insufficient clinical validation, and the absence of standardized multicenter research persist in limiting clinical application. This review evaluates the development of biosensors for the diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases towards miniaturized and portable systems based on current studies. It also comprehensively addresses the key limitations in the clinical validation, standardization, scalable production, and commercialization processes. Graphical abstract
authors: İnci Uludağ Anıl; Buse Sancakli; Nicole J. Jaffrezic-Renault; Hamdi Ben Halima; Mustafa Kemal Sezgintürk

title: Liquid Metal Resistive Sensing Architectures for Measuring Diaphragm Strain Responses on Obstructed Surfaces
abstract: ABSTRACT The mechanical response of diaphragm actuators for microfluidics and soft robotics is typically characterized on flat surfaces rather than the obstructed interfaces encountered in practical devices. Upon diaphragm actuation on textured or obstructed interfaces, geometric constraints redirect the strain from uniform bending to a constrained draping mode, which is not transduced by standard strain sensing. We formulate a liquid metal‐based strain sensing architecture integrated on a circular diaphragm to measure and control diaphragm deformation on even and uneven surfaces, using a rigid bead to create an obstructed diaphragm interface. Using finite element simulations, the electrical readouts from the strain sensor on the actuated diaphragm are correlated to its progression from symmetric diaphragm deformation to constrained geometry‐induced nonlinear diaphragm deformation and eventually to saturated diaphragm deformation at the bead center, with the predicted bead‐constrained deformation showing close agreement to the cross‐sectional confocal measurements across the diaphragm. The electrical readouts from the strain sensor reflecting the deformation regimes under geometric interruptions are utilized to control diaphragm‐induced confinement on an array of beads, which is validated based on its biomolecular immobilization level. This electromechanical basis for transducing diaphragm displacement on obstructed surfaces provides a roadmap to control actuation in microfluidic and soft‐robotic systems.
authors: Abdullah‐Bin Siddique; Jui‐Hong Weng; Deng‐Kai Yang; Chia‐Fu Chou; Nathan S. Swami

title: Programmable Porosity in Polymers via Microfluidic Templating and 3D Printing
abstract: Polymeric functionally graded porous materials (pFGPMs) enable spatial control over transport and mechanical response in a continuous solid in which porosity is strategically placed rather than uniformly distributed. Early research on the production of pFGPMs has demonstrated that graded architectures can be induced as indirect outcomes of time-evolving temperature, pressure, or concentration fields. Because these gradients emerge from process-driven kinetics, reproducibility and spatiotemporal control remain limited. Fluid templating offers a more direct route: the transient structure of polymerizable/crosslinkable foams or high internal phase emulsions (HIPEs) can be transferred into a solid matrix while controlling compartment size, packing, and film stability during solidification. Microfluidics enhance fluid management by confining interfacial breakup to produce monodisperse bubbles or droplets whose size, volume fraction, and interconnectivity can be tuned independently, transforming liquid templates into programmable solid architectures. This review follows the evolution of microfluidic templating toward its integration with additive manufacturing, with an emphasis on platforms that embed in-line bubble or droplet generation at the printhead. We conclude with an outlook on the opportunity to expand the palette of available materials and discuss the emerging role of data-driven approaches in managing the coupled dynamics of formulation, breakup, and solidification, enabling truly programmable polymeric FGPMs.
authors: Federico Serpe; Roberta Angelini; Andrea Barbetta; Vanessa Rosciardi

title: Reconfigurable acoustic tweezers based on a programmable droplet array
abstract: Conventional acoustic manipulation relies on either direct acoustic radiation force acting on particles or indirect methods using acoustic streaming generated by acoustic pressure fields to manipulate particles. While acoustic devices generating standing waves can create patterned arrangements of particles and cells, these methods are typically limited to producing regular arrays in static configurations. This study introduces a dynamic acoustic field modulation method to overcome these limitations, significantly enhancing manipulation flexibility. Crucially, the propagation of acoustic energy varies substantially at liquid-solid interfaces or gas-solid interfaces due to differences in acoustic impedance matching. To exploit this, we use a digital microfluidic chip (DMF) to manipulate droplets and generate a programmable droplet array via the electrowetting-on-dielectric effect. By utilizing the programmable droplet array, we dynamically alter the spatial distribution of the acoustic field from a bulk acoustic wave (BAW) device in real time and demonstrate this technique's capability for capturing and manipulating particles on demand. We believe this is a unique method to create acoustic tweezers with great flexibility and reconfigurability, which holds promising potential for advanced applications in micromanipulation, micro-assembly, and beyond.
authors: Zhen Wang; Menglei Zhao; Kangfu Chen; Yao Lu; Haopu Wang; Zongliang Guo; Zonghao Li; Meiyi Zhou; Huiliang Cao; Kaiqiang Cao; Xiaoyi Wang; Rongxin Fu; Hang Li; Zhichao Ma; Jiafang Li; Huikai Xie; Xicheng Zhang

title: Advances in hydrogels with biomimetic mechanical properties for dental and periodontal tissue engineering and organoid applications
abstract: Mechanically biomimetic hydrogels have emerged as promising extracellular matrix-mimicking platforms for dental and periodontal tissue engineering because of their capacity to reproduce the mechanical, structural, and biochemical characteristics of native tissue microenvironments. By providing controllable matrix stiffness, viscoelasticity, stress relaxation, fluid shear stress, and three-dimensional topographical cues, these materials can regulate stem cell fate, coordinate epithelial–mesenchymal interactions, guide tissue morphogenesis, and promote the functional maturation and mineralization of regenerating tissues. This review summarizes recent advances in the design and application of mechanically biomimetic hydrogels for the regeneration of dentin–pulp complexes, tooth germs, periodontal ligament, alveolar bone, and other craniofacial tissues, with particular emphasis on their emerging applications in dental and periodontal organoid engineering. Key material and design parameters, including biomimetic mineralization, mechanical tunability, three-dimensional architectural organization, and dynamic crosslinking, are systematically discussed. The mechanotransductive mechanisms by which hydrogel-derived cues regulate odontogenic, osteogenic, and periodontal differentiation are further examined. In addition, advanced fabrication strategies, including microfluidics, photocrosslinking, three-dimensional bioprinting, and decellularized extracellular matrix-based composites, are reviewed in relation to multicellular organization, vascular network formation, and reconstruction of tissue-specific interfaces. Despite substantial progress, challenges remain, including the attenuation of mechanical signals during long-term culture, insufficient spatiotemporal control of multicellular organization, limited vascularization and innervation, and discrepancies between engineered mineralized tissues and native dental hard tissues. Future developments in intelligent mechanoresponsive hydrogels, high-resolution developmental mechanobiological atlases, organoid-based multiscale validation systems, and automated biomanufacturing may facilitate the transition from empirical tissue repair toward mechanically programmed dental and periodontal regeneration.
authors: Wenting Lu; Sucheol Shin; Ao Zheng; Shuaiting Wu; Jinling Liu; Zhuoyuan Li; Xiao Wang; Lingyan Cao

title: Colloidal shadows reveal hidden solute transport
abstract: An object releasing a chemical into a surrounding flow leaves behind a plume that encodes the rate of release, but for most solutes, that plume is invisible. Classical transport theory describes this configuration through a self-similar concentration boundary layer whose structure has never been resolved experimentally in forced flow at low Reynolds number: a century of measurements at these conditions has returned integrated transfer rates rather than the field itself. Here we show that both the field and the information it carries are experimentally accessible. Around hydrogel posts photopatterned inside a microfluidic channel, a released solute drives suspended colloidal particles away by diffusiophoresis, i.e., their drift along chemical gradients, carving a particle-free ``shadow'' downstream. Using a fluorescent solute, we resolve the concentration field around the post and recover the classical self-similar structure of convective mass transfer. For an invisible surfactant, the width of the shadow, benchmarked against a directly imaged solute on the same platform, then serves as a proxy for the dimensionless rate of mass transfer from the post. Finally, comparing two orientations of a triangular post tests a classical prediction by Brenner: the local concentration fields rearrange, yet no orientation dependence of the integrated transfer rate is resolved. For solute--tracer pairs whose diffusiophoretic response is known, colloidal shadows thus turn ordinary tracer particles into quantitative reporters of chemical exchange that cannot be observed directly.
authors: Haoyu Liu; Zehao Chen; Amir A. Pahlavan

title: Machine Learning–Assisted Fluorescent Eu@ZnMOF for the Enoxacin and Glyphosate Detection in Food by Suppressing Sensitization and Ligand–Metal Charge Transfer
abstract: ABSTRACT The antibiotics and pesticides in the ecosystem environment, owing to their extensive application in veterinary medicine and insecticides, present a significant hazard to public health. Herein, we developed a novel bimetallic metal‐organic framework (MOF) as a ratiometric fluorescent sensor for the simultaneous monitoring of enoxacin (ENX) and glyphosate (GLY). To fabricate a dual‐responsive probe, we synthesized the ZnMOF by reacting Zn 2+ ions with the ligands (2,2′‐bipyridine‐5,5′‐dicarboxylic acid, 8‐hydroxyquinoline, and 2‐aminoterephthalic acid). Subsequently, the bimetallic Eu@ZnMOF was synthesized by loading europium (Eu 3+ ) ions into the ZnMOF based on the coordination with the 2,2′‐bipyridine‐5,5′‐dicarboxylic acid sites. The Eu@ZnMOF‐based detection system exhibits a distinct green emission due to the suppression of excited‐state intramolecular proton transfer in 8‐hydroxyquinoline by Zn 2+ ions. In the detection system, ENX enhances the red emission of Eu@ZnMOF by sensitizing Eu 3+ ions. Accordingly, the ENX fluorescent sensing system was fabricated. Moreover, ENX‐modified Eu@ZnMOF was fabricated. Upon the addition of GLY, suppression of sensitization and ligand‐to‐metal charge transfer (LMCT) occurs, which quenches the red emission of Eu 3+ and boosts the blue emission, resulting in a distinct color transition from red to blue. The ratiometric fluorescent sensor allows detection limits of 0.05 and 0.10 mg/L for ENX and GLY, respectively. Moreover, we integrated this material into a microfluidic chip. By combining this platform with smartphone imaging and machine learning algorithms, we constructed a rapid detection protocol capable of simultaneous multi‐sample analysis. These results demonstrate the promising application potential of Eu@ZnMOF for advanced environmental and food‐safety testing.
authors: Ze Li; Yan Man; Qingju Liu; Jilong Han; Zhikun Zhang

title: A Wheatstone Bridge-Inspired Microfluidic Trap For Precise Tuning of the Content of an Immobilized Droplet
