title: Digital transformation of clinical trials with remote patient monitoring solutions
abstract: Remote patient monitoring (RPM) is becoming increasingly feasible to implement in clinical trials. A framework is presented for developing RPM digital solutions incorporating the needs and perspectives of patients and healthcare professionals, and regulatory requirements/guidance. This framework is illustrated with recent examples of RPM deployments in the context of skin toxicities and stomatitis. Strategies to overcome challenges in the adoption of RPM solutions in clinical trials are discussed.
authors: Elisabeth Piault; Ramya Sita Palacholla; SIMON PULMAN‐JONES; Emmett Alton Sartor; Sergio Simön; Jill Bell

title: Rapid‐Forming Conductive Antifouling Hydrogel Coating Enables Magnetically Guided Electrochemical POCT for Direct at‑Home Blood Testing
abstract: Electrochemical point-of-care testing for complex clinical samples is frequently hampered by matrix interference, signal instability, and laborious electrode modification procedures. Herein, we report a magnetic portable electrochemical immunosensor utilizing a conductive, anti-fouling hydrogel coating composed of sodium alginate, polyethylene glycol, and graphene (SPG). Upon calcium-ion triggering, the SPG solution forms a stable electrode hydrogel coating within 1 min, effectively resisting nonspecific adsorption while maintaining low‑impedance electron transfer. Guided by a 3D-printed magnetic apparatus, the MpECis directly captures target-bound magnetic complexes, enabling rapid enrichment and electrical readout within 25 min. By implementing time‑domain averaging over the enzymatic reaction plateau, the coefficient of variation of electrical signals generated by nanoenzyme catalysis was reduced to 3.4%, markedly improving measurement reproducibility. The clinical practicality of the SPG MpECis platform was validated through three independent cohorts, including detection of cardiac troponin I in 59 serum samples, quantification of extracellular vesicles in 47 plasma samples, and detection of C-reactive protein in 17 fingertip blood samples. Compared with the reference method, the area under the curve of this method are 0.99, 0.93, and 1.00, respectively. This platform offers a practical route for stable electrochemical diagnostics in complex biological matrices and home-based precision medicine.
authors: Menghan Li; Kai Su; Ruiwei Hu; Ke Gao; Yuanjie Liu; Lu Zhang; Ningke Fan; Yirong Chen; Wei Cheng; Shijia Ding; Haiping Wu

title: Systematic process for design and manufacturing of ergonomic handles for para-table tennis: a case study
abstract: Abstract Wheelchair table tennis serves as an affordable and accessible means of enhancing the physical and psychological well-being of individuals with tetraplegia; however, limited hand mobility and grip strength continue to constrain performance. To address these issues, this study presents a systematic, end-to-end workflow for designing and manufacturing customized, competition-legal table tennis handles tailored to tetraplegic athletes, evaluated through a single-athlete feasibility case study rather than a clinical or sports-performance validation. The process integrates hand geometry capture, computer-aided design (CAD) refinement through iterative additive prototyping, and final fabrication using optimized materials and surface finishing. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, a case study was conducted comparing an athlete’s performance using the old and new handles in terms of accuracy, control, and overall playing performance. In this single-athlete case study, successful shots showed roughly $$2.4\times$$ the odds of success with the new handle across drills. As a proof-of-concept evaluation, these findings are preliminary and indicate an association observed in one athlete, not a demonstrated causal effect, and are not intended to generalise to tetraplegic players more broadly. The customized handle was also reported by the athlete to be more comfortable and easier to use.
authors: Sachintha Alwis Weerasinghe; Mojtaba Mohammadalizadeh; Marko Kasurinen; Grzegorz Orzechowski; Aki Mikkola

title: Fluorescence-enhanced isothermal amplification for multiplex pathogen detection: Emerging strategies and persistent challenges
abstract: Multiplex pathogen detection is essential for addressing the increasing complexity of infectious diseases and co-infections, yet conventional polymerase chain reaction-based methods remain hindered by the requirement for sophisticated laboratory infrastructure. Isothermal amplification offers a robust alternative for point-of-care testing, though high-order multiplexing in these systems has historically been limited by signal discrimination challenges. In this review, we synthesize recent breakthroughs in fluorescence-enhanced isothermal amplification, which have transformed multiplex diagnostics through advanced signal encoding and intelligent processing. We illustrate how the convergence of diverse molecular engines, ranging from sequence-specific probes to orthogonal clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats-associated effectors and programmable DNA logic circuits, enables precise, multi-target identification in a single reaction. Beyond the biochemical framework, we further discuss the integration of these molecular strategies with microfluidic platforms, portable optical detection systems, and deep learning-based signal analysis, which collectively facilitate the transition from laboratory prototypes to automated diagnostic platforms. Finally, we examine persistent challenges, including assay crosstalk and amplification bias, and outline future directions toward accessible and scalable multiplex diagnostic systems.
authors: Yuanshou Zhu; Xitian Xu; Yuxin Chen; Mengyuan Huang; Shoulong Wang; Haoyu Li; Zhigang Zhu

title: Your Programming Students' Cognition with ChatGPT: Higher Performance, Lower Retention, and Reduced Ownership
abstract: Generative AI can improve students' programming performance, but successful task completion may not reflect what they retain. We examined performance, retention, cognitive load, and ownership in a controlled between-subjects experiment with 59 undergraduate computer science students, 55 were retained for analysis. Participants completed three introductory C programming tasks with access to ChatGPT-4.5 or conventional web search without generative AI. We measured task performance, self-reported mental effort and difficulty, pupillary responses, heart rate variability, and ownership, and assessed cued recall immediately and 48 hours later. ChatGPT-assisted students achieved higher coding scores (89% vs. 69%) but lower recall scores immediately (41% vs. 53%) and after 48 hours (39% vs. 52%). There was no significant difference in the loss of recall information over 48 hours between the groups. Self-reported mental effort increased less across tasks in the ChatGPT condition (Holm-adjusted p = .047), and students attributed less of the submitted code to themselves (45% vs. 81%). Confirmatory physiological tests did not detect significant differences in trajectories between conditions; substantial data loss limits their interpretation. These findings reveal a gap between assisted task performance and subsequent recall and sense of ownership in this setting. They motivate the need for assessment practices and AI learning tools that require students to explain, retrieve, and contribute to the work they submit as active participants in their education.
authors: Christian Henrik Bergh; Benjamin Tag; Alexandra Vassar; J. Renzella

title: Development and clinical translation of smartphone-based digital biomarkers for Parkinson’s disease: a structured review
abstract: Diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) remains a major clinical challenge, particularly in the prodromal and early clinically evident stages, when symptoms are subtle and phenotypically overlap with other mimicking disorders. The widespread availability of smartphones equipped with inertial, acoustic, touchscreen, and geolocation sensors has enabled the emergence of smartphone-based digital biomarkers that capture continuous, real-world motor and non-motor manifestations of PD. To critically review the validation state, construct validity, clinical applications, and potential for longitudinal monitoring of smartphone-derived digital biomarkers for early PD detection and for differential diagnosis from mimicking disorders, while addressing methodological, regulatory, and implementation challenges. This manuscript reviews the current evidence on smartphone-based active and passive digital assessments for the early diagnosis and screening of PD. We examine clinical validation and implementation, as well as advances in technological processing, multimodal digital phenotyping, and machine learning models, for the early detection and screening of PD. Smartphone-derived digital markers demonstrate promising capability for detecting several symptoms and support early diagnosis of PD. A total of 30 studies showed significant correlations of such markers with established clinical scales and suggested utility in differentiating PD from other Parkinsonian syndromes and prodromal PD patients. Six major categories based on the clinical assessment were identified: 8 studies with voice-based assessment, 6 with touchscreen-based assessment, 4 with video-recording assessment, 4 with inertial measurement unit-based assessment, 7 with multimodal assessment approaches, and 1 with questionnaire-based smartphone assessment. However, substantial limitations persist, including device and protocol heterogeneity, limited external validation, small datasets, algorithmic bias, inadequate explainability, and inconsistent reporting standards. Smartphone-based digital biomarkers offer a promising approach to improving diagnostic accuracy in PD and are emerging as a frontier in precision neurology and scalable PD care. However, these findings have several limitations and should be interpreted with caution. Future research should prioritise multicentre longitudinal validation, multimodal integration, explainable AI, and real-world deployment to establish clinically actionable digital biomarkers for early PD detection and differential diagnosis.
authors: Onanong Phokaewvarangkul; Suppakorn Yamutai; Roongroj Bhidayasiri; Peerapon Vateekul; Decho Surangsrirat; Walter Maetzler; Andrea Pilotto; Chaewon Shin; Genko Oyama

title: Emergent blink rate in early childhood is associated with neural origins of executive function
abstract: Abstract Executive function develops rapidly in early childhood and predicts later success in life, yet its neurobiological correlates during this period remain poorly understood. In adults, executive function is supported by prefrontal–striatal circuits under neuromodulatory control, including dopamine. Here, we show that spontaneous eye-blink rate (sEBR), a physiological output influenced by neuromodulatory systems, is associated with the developmental trajectory of executive function and prefrontal functional differentiation. We used fNIRS to monitor prefrontal cortex (PFC) activation in 113 children (35–80 months) during a cognitive flexibility task. With increasing age, the children’s task performance improved, and their PFC activation showed greater right-hemisphere and dorsal bias, reflecting functional differentiation. Importantly, higher sEBR was also associated with this right-dorsal PFC activation and with better task performance. The current findings demonstrate that emergent sEBR is associated with the neural origins of executive function development in young children. This highlights the potential of sEBR to serve as a unique and previously unrecognised indicator of this critical developmental neural mechanism.
authors: Ryuta Kuwamizu; Nozomi Yamamoto; Kota Otani; Yusuke Moriguchi

title: From Speed and Sensitivity to Robust Reliability: Addressing the Detection Bias of Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) in Food Authentication
abstract: Food adulteration poses severe threats to the integrity and safety of global food supply chains. Innovations in analytical techniques, especially the rapid development of LAMP-based detection methods, are indispensable for addressing these risks. However, the dominant research paradigm, which has long prioritized accelerated amplification kinetics and ultralow detection limits, largely obscures a critical limitation: insufficient detection reliability when deployed in complex field environments. This review consolidates state-of-the-art advances targeting reliability optimization and delineates key technical strategies to construct robust, improved-reliability LAMP platforms for real-food testing. Specifically, we summarize critical factors at the reaction and readout levels that compromise the reliability of LAMP under realistic scenarios, such as inexperienced operators, degraded samples, matrices containing inhibitory substances, and uncontrolled environments. We further elaborate on effective solutions to bridge the reliability gap between laboratory validation and on-site deployment, which requires coordinated technical improvements throughout the full LAMP testing pipeline. Ultimately, we propose a forward-looking developmental principle for next-generation LAMP assays: analytical reliability and operational robustness should be elevated to equal priority alongside the traditionally pursued ultra-rapid amplification and high sensitivity. This balanced technical framework may help pave the way toward large-scale standardization of LAMP-enabled food authentication, although its presumptive results must be confirmed by an independent validated method before they can support regulatory enforcement or other formal decisions.
authors: Xiong Xiong; Yahui Zhang; Mengxuan Liu; Yan Guo; Ying Yang

title: Adeno‐associated virus ‐mediated restoration of Na V 1.1 in targeted brain regions ameliorates epilepsy in symptomatic Dravet syndrome mice
abstract: Abstract Objective Dravet syndrome (DS) is a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy primarily caused by haploinsufficiency of the SCN1A gene, which encodes the alpha subunit of Na V 1.1 voltage‐gated sodium channel. The disease manifests with febrile and spontaneous seizures, developmental delay, cognitive impairment, and increased risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. Most preclinical therapeutic strategies aim to enhance endogenous Scn1a gene expression or deliver a functional copy via perinatal interventions. Although promising, these approaches face challenges in achieving efficient brain‐wide delivery, targeting all interested brain areas. Methods In this study, we used a conditional DS reversible mouse model ( Scn1a Stop/+ ) to assess the therapeutic potential of postsymptomatic restoration (postnatal day 30) of Na V 1.1 physiological levels in all neuronal populations but restricted to minimal brain regions. Results We found that hippocampal correction alone reduces seizure susceptibility, whereas simultaneous restoration in the hippocampus, thalamus, and overlying somatosensory and visual cortex was associated with a trend toward further reduction in seizure burden and improved survival. Significance These findings indicate that hippocampal restoration accounts for a substantial component of the therapeutic benefit, and broader network correction may confer additional advantages.
authors: Martina Mainardi; Simone Brusco; Serena Gea Giannelli; Vania Broccoli; Gaia Colasante

title: Machine Learning for Noninvasive Diagnosis of Neurodegenerative Diseases Using Retinal and Optic Nerve Imaging: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis, encompass a wide range of chronic conditions with irreversible damage to the central nervous system. Current diagnostic workups of these disorders rely on invasive, time-consuming, and costly tests, such as magnetic resonance imaging and cerebrospinal fluid analysis, preventing accurate decision-making and timely therapeutic interventions. The retina is an extension of the central nervous system; thus, retinal imaging, which is a noninvasive and easily accessible tool, provides a unique window to study brain pathologies. There is a great body of evidence suggesting that neurodegenerative disorders are associated with various structural and vascular problems within the retina. Notably, training machine learning models with retinal images has yielded high levels of accuracy in classifying neurodegenerative diseases, encouraging a new era for early and automated diagnosis of these disorders. This article reviews studies that use such models for classifying these disorders.
authors: Ali Aghababaei; Masoud Etemadifar; Amir Atapour-Abarghouei; William Innes; Masoud Aghsaei Fard; Friedemann Paul; Hossein Rabbani; Rahele Kafieh

title: Quick fabrication of 3D-printed prosthetic sockets with embedded sensors to track limb motion
abstract: Introduction A simple time-efficient method to fabricate prosthetic sockets with embedded sensors to track limb motion may facilitate the clinical application of continuously collected quantitative data in prosthetics practice. Methods A 3D-printed inner structure of the socket shape with debosses on the outside surface to hold sensors was fabricated, the sensors were affixed in place, and the socket was laminated and trimmed. Results The time to fabricate an embedded sensor socket was 12% less than that required to fabricate a traditional carbon-fiber socket with sensors. The investigational sockets increased in volume slightly, <0.2%, over the course of 4 weeks of take-home use, likely because of compression of the inner structure material during ambulation. Sockets with a vapor-smoothed finish had a significantly lower coefficient of friction (COF) with the liner fabric backing than sockets with a normal surface finish ( P < 0.01), though participant preference for the lower COF socket was mixed. Discussion The speed, quality, and durability of the investigational sockets warrant clinical studies to determine which quantitative limb motion metrics (e.g., pistoning, volume, anterior distal motion) help prosthetists meaningfully enhance their patient care.
authors: Joan E. Sanders; Amy P. Culter; Mathew J. Weissinger; Paul Fallon; Joseph C. Mertens; Katheryn J. Allyn; Benjamin N. Sanders; Joseph L. Garbini

title: Microfluidic technology: from historical development to modern applications
abstract: Microfluidics is a rapidly evolving interdisciplinary field focused on the precise manipulation and control of fluids at the micrometre scale. The kingdom of microfluidics is ruled by tiny fluid volumes through the development of novel applications that benefit from the use of these small samples. Typical manipulations involve small volumes of fluid (microliters or sub-microliters) leading to improved capability to manipulate fluids, increased accuracy over traditional methodologies, and many successful implementations in diverse domains including health care, environmental capabilities, and chemical processing. Examples of microfluidic implementation that have significantly improved testing efficiency, effectiveness, and portability include lab on chip & point of care testing appliances. The primary advantages of microfluidics include lower sample use, faster analysis times, improved sensitivity, and the ability to combine with other systems for automated operation and control. This review highlights the historical development and fundamental principles of microfluidics along with its growing importance in modern science and engineering. Various applications of microfluidic systems in healthcare diagnostics, environmental monitoring, chemical synthesis, and biological analysis are comprehensively discussed. In addition, the review outlines the current limitations and challenges associated with microfluidic technologies, including fabrication complexity and scalability issues. Overall, this review offers a comprehensive understanding of both possible opportunities and existing limitations of microfluidics. Therefore, it is concluded that further development and improvement of this area are of significant importance, as it may become the basis for future scientific and engineering breakthroughs. Finally, future perspectives and trends in microfluidics are discussed, highlighting its potential to enable revolutionary approaches in subsequent analytical and biomedical technologies.
authors: Sourav Ghosh; Jit Chakraborty; Avishek Saha; Arijit Das; Kalachand Mahali; Sanjay Roy

title: Infectious skin diseases in athletes, with particular reference to contact and combat sports: a narrative review of epidemiology, prevention and treatment
abstract: Introduction and purpose. The skin is the body's largest organ and its principal barrier against the external environment. In athletes—especially those in contact and combat sports—continuous mechanical, thermal and microbial stress predisposes to cutaneous infection and to team-wide transmission. This review synthesises current evidence on the epidemiology, clinical features, diagnosis, prevention and treatment of infectious skin diseases in athletes, with emphasis on wrestling, judo, boxing and mixed martial arts. Material and methods. A narrative review of peer-reviewed reviews, epidemiological and microbiological studies, outbreak investigations and case reports addressing bacterial, viral, fungal and parasitic skin infections in athletes. Results. Bacterial infections—chiefly Staphylococcus aureus, including community-associated methicillin-resistant strains, and Streptococcus pyogenes—together with herpes gladiatorum (herpes simplex virus type 1) and dermatophytoses (tinea gladiatorum, predominantly Trichophyton tonsurans) dominate the clinical picture. Transmission occurs mainly through direct skin-to-skin contact, with fomites playing a secondary role. Diagnosis is largely clinical but is strengthened by potassium hydroxide microscopy, culture and polymerase chain reaction. Management combines targeted antimicrobial therapy, incision and drainage of purulent lesions, isolation and, for herpes gladiatorum and tinea gladiatorum, chemoprophylaxis; return to competition is governed by defined criteria. Conclusions. Early recognition, accurate diagnosis, prompt treatment and isolation, rigorous hygiene, environmental disinfection and evidence-based prophylaxis are the cornerstones of minimising morbidity and interrupting transmission of skin infections in athletes.
authors: Jakub Palian; Szymon Kurzyński; Katarzyna Czernecka; Igor Smędowski; Kacper Kazimierczuk; Natalia Mordko; Mateusz Góras; Łukasz Mazelanik; Wojciech Tokarczyk; Julia Pawlak

title: Neural encoding of auditory processing in schizophrenia
abstract: Introduction: Auditory processing abnormalities are a core feature of schizophrenia and are linked to deficits in speech perception, cognitive function, and everyday communication. It remains unclear which stages of auditory processing are most disrupted and how these disruptions relate to symptoms at the level of population-wide neural representations. Methods: We used fMRI recordings acquired while individuals with schizophrenia and matched healthy controls completed a controlled block-design speech-perception task. Voxel-wise encoding models mapped self-supervised speech-model representations, together with complementary acoustic and linguistic features, to neural responses. Results: Across cross-validated evaluations, individuals with schizophrenia showed numerically higher encoding alignment than matched controls across all evaluated regions of interest, although no effect survived false discovery rate correction in this small sample. The largest numerical group differences occurred in frontal language regions, including the middle frontal gyrus and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, and in early auditory cortex. Subgroup analyses suggested that patients without auditory verbal hallucinations drove much of this numerical separation. Discussion: These descriptive, hypothesis-generating findings suggest that model-based encoding can reveal a frontal-auditory signature in schizophrenia, but they do not establish a clinically actionable biomarker or preserved or enhanced speech encoding. Larger, adequately powered studies with richer feature spaces are needed for confirmatory inference and to test whether encoding-based measures can serve as clinically meaningful biomarkers.
authors: Lakshma Reddy Vuyyuru; Anitha Raju

title: Towards Next-Generation Artificial Intelligence Models for Integrated Diagnostics Embedding Eye-Brain Connections
abstract: Abstract The brain and eye share profound and homologous relationships in terms of development, anatomy, and microcirculatory structures, yet current analyses typically examine them in isolation, limiting cross-organ insights and the development of integrated artificial intelligence (AI) models. Such a fragmented paradigm also constrains clinical understanding despite growing evidence of shared, anatomically connected, and predictive relationships between ocular and cerebral phenotypes in both brain and eye diseases. In this context, this review introduces an Eye-Brain Connection Pyramid, a multiscale organizational framework for examining eye-brain relationships at three complementary biological levels: genetic and genomic susceptibility, molecular and protein processes, and neurovascular and tissue phenotypes. The pyramid does not represent a serial causal pathway. Across these levels, the framework distinguishes shared vulnerability and parallel pathology, direct brain-to-eye effects, retinal correlates and predictors of cerebral or systemic disease, and putative eye-to-brain causal contributions, which remain insufficiently established in humans. This framework may inform future clinical research and the development of AI models integrating multimodal cross-organ data, whose incremental diagnostic value over existing single-organ and clinical approaches requires prospective validation. Furthermore, this review presents a comprehensive AI research roadmap, spanning longitudinal prognostic models, explainable algorithms for clinical adoption, validation of incremental clinical value, fundus-based brain health screening setups, and multi-site collaboration. By outlining these priorities, the proposed Eye-Brain Connection Pyramid provides an organizational framework for investigating integrated eye-brain diagnostics and for evaluating the potential clinical value of cross-organ AI in risk stratification, longitudinal monitoring, and healthcare delivery.
authors: Zhen Chen; Cheng Wang; Tianliang Yao; Jianwen Liang; Yijin Huang; Jianfeng Feng; Dongfeng Gu; Pearse A. Keane; Xiaoying Tang; Yixuan Yuan

title: Acceptability of a Peer‐Led Faith‐Based Intervention to Improve Breast, Bowel and Cervical Cancer Screening Uptake Among UK Muslim Women: A Qualitative Evaluation
abstract: BACKGROUND: Early cancer detection through screening can improve treatment outcomes. However, screening uptake remains lower among some communities, including Muslim women, which puts them at risk of late diagnosis and poor outcomes. In 2020, we worked with 10 Scottish Muslim women to co-design a peer-led, faith-based and culturally tailored intervention to encourage uptake of breast, bowel and cervical cancer screening. The intervention was delivered twice online and qualitatively evaluated. The study was subsequently funded as a feasibility trial, and the intervention was delivered a further 16 times, both online and face-to-face. This paper reports findings from a qualitative evaluation exploring participants' perspectives on the acceptability and implementation of the intervention. METHODS: The intervention is a 2-h workshop comprising four components: (1) a peer-led cancer screening discussion, (2) a doctor-led health education session, (3) testimonials from Muslim women, and (4) an Islamic perspective delivered by a female religious scholar. In 2024, women participated in online or in-person workshops in North-East England and Scotland. After each workshop, women were invited to participate in focus groups or interviews to provide feedback on the workshop. Qualitative data collection and analysis were guided by the Theoretical Framework of Acceptability. Data were analysed using the Framework Analysis method. RESULTS: A convenience sample of 36 women was recruited. Participants described the workshop's content as comprehensive and providing new information. The workshop's informal atmosphere and use of different delivery methods enhanced information attainment. They appreciated the use of interpreters, who assisted non-English speakers. Bringing a medical and Islamic perspective together was novel to participants and made the workshop more impactful. Participants expressed more positive attitudes towards screening after the intervention. CONCLUSION: A peer-led, culturally-tailored and faith-based intervention for improving cancer screening uptake for Muslim women was deemed acceptable. However, more work is needed to assess the intervention's effectiveness and impact. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: The intervention was co-designed with 10 Muslim women. A public involvement group worked with the research team throughout the study; they provided their views on the intervention, recruitment, data collection and interpretation of findings. Some were trained as peer educators to help deliver the intervention. Two members of the community (FH and CS, who are also listed as authors) were also employed on the project as Community Recruitment Leads, facilitating participant recruitment and contributing to all stages of the research as valued members of the research team, ensuring the community's voice was embedded throughout.
authors: Rawand Jarrar; Kathryn A. Robb; Marie K. Murphy; Cerysh Sadiq; Anna Matthews; Fozia Haider; Alex McConnachie; Aasim Ilyas Padela; Floor Christie-de Jong

title: HIV prevention and care in the afterlife of the HIV/AIDS crisis
abstract: Introduction Queer and trans individuals face stark inequities in HIV prevention and care. Existing theories and models explain how individual- and interpersonal-level stressors shape health among queer and trans populations, but less theoretical attention has been paid to how histories of structural violence continue to shape contemporary HIV-related inequities.Theory Drawing on Saidiya Hartman’s conceptualization of the “afterlife of slavery,” we conceptualize contemporary HIV-related inequities among queer and trans populations within an “afterlife of the HIV/AIDS crisis.” This framework considers how normative logics surrounding gender and sexuality that structured responses to the HIV/AIDS crisis persist within contemporary institutions, policies, and practices.Method We conducted an interdisciplinary critical narrative review examining historical and contemporary scholarship on the HIV/AIDS crisis and the health of queer and trans populations. We synthesized literature across disciplines to identify recurring conceptual frameworks and cross-disciplinary themes through which historical responses to HIV/AIDS continue to shape contemporary conditions.Results Three dominant themes emerged: (1) pathologization contributed to the stigmatization of queerness and transness; (2) rhetoric employed by the media, political actors, and the scientific community demoralized and dehumanized queer and trans people; and (3) the codification of homophobia and transphobia in laws and policies contributed to the criminalization of queerness and transness. Across these themes, historical responses to the HIV/AIDS crisis established and reinforced structural conditions that continue to shape HIV prevention and care.Discussion Contemporary HIV inequities among queer and trans populations cannot be fully understood without attention to the historical processes through which they were produced and sustained. Situating present-day HIV prevention and care through the framework of the afterlife of the HIV/AIDS crisis highlights the persistence of structural violence and provides a framework for identifying and addressing its contemporary manifestations.
authors: Tyler D. Harvey; Bryce Puesta Takenaka

title: Environmental Scan of Public Health Directives During COVID-19: A View Through the Lens of Children With Complex Care Needs and Their Families
abstract: Background: The COVID-19 pandemic shaped childhood globally. The experiences of vulnerable children in Canada’s Maritime provinces reveal important lessons about equity, resilience, and the unintended consequences of public health directives. Public health restrictions were enacted in the early days of COVID-19. At-risk populations such as children with complex care needs (CCN) were among those most impacted by health system changes due to COVID-19. To better understand how COVID-19 public health measures impacted children with CCN who were highly susceptible to the virus and associated disruptions, we conducted an environmental scan to map changes in COVID-19 public health directives and services impacting children with CCN. Methods: We systematically retrieved government news releases communicating new or changing COVID-19 public health directives published March 1, 2020-March 31, 2022. All directives and service changes in the health and education sectors were included. Directives were divided into 13 categories co-developed with parent and decision-maker partners, and we identified whether directives included support measures relevant to children with CCN. Results: The environmental scan revealed that children with CCN were largely overlooked in COVID-19 directives across the Maritime provinces. We identified 699 public health directives and services changes. Fewer than 2.2% of COVID-19 directives explicitly referenced children with CCN, with most guidance focusing on general social restrictions, vaccinations, and education/daycare. Mental health and well-being were also rarely addressed (13 directives). Conclusion: The Maritimes’ predominately rural and geographically dispersed population exacerbates the inequities experienced by children with CCN, offering insights relevant to other regions about the unintended consequences of broad public health policies delivered to heterogeneous populations. Examining this data through the lens of children with CCN and their families can inform recommendations to better support this vulnerable population in future public health emergencies.
authors: Janet Curran; Holly McCulloch; Catie Johnson; Jennifer Lane; Leah Boulos; Lisa Keeping‐Burke; Mary-Ann Standing; Julie Clegg; Robyn M. Kydd; Helen W. L. Wong; Kristy Hancock; Margie Lamb
venue: International Journal of Health Policy and Management

title: From Promise to Practice A HEALinc Global Summit White Paper
abstract: This paper, developed by HEALinc CEO and Founder Dr. Desirée Cox, translates a day of multidisciplinary discussion at the 2026 HEALinc Global Summit, New York City (NYC) Day Conclave into a coherent systems framework and action agenda. It is not a transcript, clinical guideline, regulatory opinion, or endorsement of every intervention or claim discussed at the Summit. The source material captures perspectives from scientists, physicians, biotechnology leaders, lawyers, investors, former regulators, patient advocates, educators, architects, and other participants. Sponsors, speakers, and key opinion leaders represented at the HEALinc New York City (NYC) Day Conclave are identified in the Appendices. The proceedings ranged from late-stage clinical development and international regulatory pathways to whole-person health, patient experience, digital monitoring, medical education, and the design of healing environments. The purpose of this paper is to identify the recurring system-level insights, clarify where genuine convergence occurred, and convert those insights into a practical architecture for translation. Some interventions and outcomes described during the discussions were preliminary, anecdotal, contested, or outside established standards of evidence. They are treated here as signals of emerging questions and unmet needs – not as validated clinical conclusions. Any therapy must be evaluated according to its own evidence, manufacturing quality, ethical acceptability, regulatory status, and risk profile. Interpretive StanceThe field should neither equate regulatory caution with obstruction nor equate permissive access with progress. The task is to create controlled velocity: faster, more coherent learning and access under stronger evidence, ethics, quality, and accountability.
authors: Desiree C. T. Cox

title: Recent advances in dielectric and two-dimensional material-based surface plasmon resonance biosensors for ultrasensitive refractive index sensing and diverse applications
abstract: Advanced biosensors utilizing Surface Plasmon Resonance (SPR) are becoming powerful label-free optical sensing platforms for the real-time detection of biochemical interactions owing to their incredibly high sensitivity toward refractive index (RI) changes. Conventional metal-based SPR sensors typically suffer from optical losses, large resonance curves, and degraded detection sensitivity. The combination of widespread advances in high-RI dielectric materials and two-dimensional (2D) nanomaterials has greatly contributed to the improvement of SPR sensor performance, as a result of improved electromagnetic field confinement, enhanced biomolecular interactions, and higher overall sensing efficiency. This review summarizes the progress in dielectric- and 2D material-based SPR biosensors for both applications: ultrasensitive RI sensing and diverse biomedical, environmental, and chemical sensing. The basic concept of SPR, sensing performance indicators, and the nature of dielectric and 2D materials, multilayer devices, and theoretical modelling strategies are reviewed in detail. Moreover, the enhancement of RI sensing and biomarker detection is presented recently to analyze their benefits and obstacles experienced by different material platforms. Lastly, we gather the ongoing challenges in material stability, fabrication complexity, and clinical translation, along with the advent of new opportunities such as artificial intelligence-assisted sensor optimization, portable sensing systems, and next-generation hybrid plasmonic platforms. A holistic overview through this review will motivate researchers to develop cutting-edge SPR biosensors in the near future for advanced label-free detection applications.
authors: M. Jagadeeswar Goud; Yesudasu Vasimalla; Bhishma Karki; Santosh Kumar

title: Multiobjective Optimization of Performance and Emission Profiles in a WCO–Butanol‐Fueled RCCI Engine: An RSM‐Based Investigation of EGR and Injection Duration Interactions
abstract: ABSTRACT This investigation develops a multiobjective optimization framework for Reactivity Controlled Compression Ignition (RCCI) engines utilizing a butanol, waste cooking oils–biodiesel, and diesel ternary blend. Moving beyond traditional parametric sweeps, the study employs Response Surface Methodology in conjunction with a Face‐Centered Central Composite Design to systematically decode the coupled influences of Injection Duration (ID), exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) rates, and engine load on combustion dynamics. Statistical validation via analysis of variance ensures high predictive fidelity, offering a robust mapping of the dual‐fuel reactivity landscape. Experimental results initially identified a peak brake thermal efficiency (BTE) of 32.0% at high‐load conditions (16 kg); however, this point exhibited significant NO x penalties. To reconcile the performance‐emission trade‐off, a multiobjective optimization was executed using desirability functions. The global optimum was identified at 5.68°CA ID, 13.58% EGR, and 6.66 kg load, yielding a predicted BTE of 23.73% and NO x emissions of 809.2 ppm. At this Pareto‐optimal point, NO x was reduced by 35% compared with baseline diesel through thermal dilution and reactivity stratification. The model was validated through confirmatory experiments, with a maximum error of 1.89%, confirming that the RCCI strategy offers superior environmental‐performance trade‐offs at midload conditions for sustainable, low‐carbon propulsion.
authors: Naresh Ajmeera; Ravi Kumar Puli

title: Reframing decentralized diagnostics with a programmable multi-dimensional microfluidic system
abstract: Decentralized diagnostics are vital for infectious disease control, yet current point-of-care tools remain largely one-dimensional, failing to capture the multidimensional profiles required for precision management. Here, we show SID-WAVES (Smartphone-Integrated Diagnostics with Wax-encoded Amplified and Versatile Evaluation System), an intelligent, multimodal microfluidic platform. Integrating low-melting-point phase-change and dual-siphon valves with RPA–CRISPR/Cas12a nucleic acid detection and protein immunoassays, the platform enables automated, one-step, sample-to-answer operation via an AI-assisted smartphone readout that reduces operator-dependent variability. Spatial-temporal-signal encoding supports multiplexed, multi-sample, and multimodal analysis, achieving attomolar-level sensitivity (10−18 M) and >95% diagnostic accuracy across 225 clinical and self-collected molecular assays, demonstrating robust usability. For proteins, a triple-amplification strategy and hierarchical capture enhance sensitivity 125-fold, improving accuracy from 87.6% to 100% in 54 simulated samples. Functioning as a reconfigurable analytical framework where panels are changed by swapping targets and probes, this work helps mitigate the Sensitivity–Multiplexing–Accessibility trade-off, reframing decentralized diagnostics from single-target screening to multi-dimensional health profiling. Decentralized diagnostics has the potential to improve health equity as well as support a more rapid response to disease outbreaks. Here authors present SID-WAVES, a multimodal microfluidic platform which allows ‘sample-in, results-out’ detection of both nucleic acid and protein biomarkers.
authors: Tao Xu; Ying Zhang; Xin Tang; Hongguo Wei; Lingyan Kang; Qize Zhou; Shunji Li; Xudong Zhao; Jiashuo Li; Zimeng Zhang; Chao Wan; Yufei Zhang; Dongjuan Chen; Ye Tian; Bi-Feng Liu; Peng Chen

title: Noninvasive diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease: a review of emerging biomarkers and multimodal approaches
abstract: Noninvasive biomarkers are expanding access to biological assessment of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). This review evaluates blood-based, neuroimaging, retinal, electrophysiological, digital, and behavioral measures alongside structured cognitive and functional assessment, and examines multimodal and machine-learning approaches for detection, differential diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment monitoring. Plasma phosphorylated tau, particularly p-tau217, currently offers the strongest scalable evidence for identifying amyloid and advanced tau pathology, whereas PET and MRI retain complementary roles in pathological confirmation, regional staging, exclusion of alternative causes, and characterization of atypical phenotypes. Retinal, electrophysiological, speech, sleep, and eye-tracking measures remain promising but require greater standardization and external validation. Across modalities, biomarker trajectories are temporally staggered, assay and platform differences affect interpretation, and pathology–phenotype mapping is modified by disease stage, cognitive reserve, copathology, vascular factors, and population characteristics. We therefore propose a phenotype-anchored, stepped pathway that begins with patient and informant history, objective cognitive and functional assessment, structural imaging, and routine laboratory evaluation; adds validated blood biomarkers when they resolve a defined uncertainty; and reserves CSF or PET for unresolved, atypical, or treatment-relevant cases. Discordant findings should prompt reassessment rather than automatic reclassification. We describe the literature-search and descriptive evidence-categorization approach used to select and categorize the evidence reviewed, and we place the findings within the emerging regulatory context of blood-based testing. Clinical translation will depend on harmonized thresholds, representative prospective cohorts, calibration, independent validation, and evidence that multimodal systems improve decisions and patient outcomes rather than benchmark accuracy alone.
authors: Junsheng Zhao; Chenqi Nie; Rong Gao; Zekai Hu; Yajie Lin

title: Ideas and Perspectives: Value and efficiency of ocean sample return and laboratory analysis: Key analytes are orders of magnitude rarer than a needle in a haystack
abstract: Abstract. There is a pressing need to understand how the oceans are responding to human perturbations, yet their vastness poses a considerable challenge. The development and deployment of biologically and ecologically relevant in situ sensors are frequently invoked as a means to improve this understanding; however, there are still relatively few sensors for these parameters due to the analytical challenges involved in their measurement. Specifically, many analytes of interest are orders of magnitude rarer by mass than a needle in a haystack (e.g., dissolved iron and eDNA are 104 to 108 times rarer), and this scarcity creates challenges involving preconcentration, interfering elements or compounds, and analytical methods difficult to perform underwater. While sensor development is important, the role of sample collection and return is also an important, yet oft overlooked, complement for studying ocean change and is ripe for additional development. Laboratory analyses of returned samples can be high throughput for challenging analytes like micronutrients and omics parameters, and these techniques are operational now. Moreover, sample return allows parallel analyses and archiving through splitting of sample material. Similar to human health diagnostics, laboratory analyses can provide ocean health diagnostic capabilities showing how ecosystems are responding, complementing sensor-based vital sign measurements indicating environmental change. Together, these properties make sample collection and return a critical component for achieving the global ocean coverage needed to capture the environmental changes well underway today, and this approach should continue to be factored into ocean observing strategies.
authors: Mak A. Saito; Matthew R. McIlvin; Annette F. Govindarajan; J. A. Breier

title: Theory framework and application for coiled acoustic metastructure in contactless passive state sensing enhancement
abstract: Acoustic contactless sensing technology is becoming a promising but challenging technology because of features in cheap cost, convenient sensor deployment but strong signal propagation attenuation. Acoustic metastructure based sensing scheme is proposed for improving signal strength, focusing acoustic energy, and overcoming propagation attenuation. Theory framework for providing bridge of mainstream gradient acoustic metastructures conversion is established, and acoustic features difference are comparatively studied. Inspired by the superiority of sonic black hole (SBH) in low frequency wave manipulation, coiled conical metastructure (CCM) is proposed by introducing the strategy of exchanging bandwidth with space, and better acoustic performance is realized by compacter structure and much smaller volume compared with classical SBH. The applications of proposed metastructure in drone detection and condition monitoring of rotating machinery are widely studied, and extraordinary performance is realized in acoustic energy focusing, signal strength enhancement and feature extraction. This work provides a comprehensive view in comparing differences of mainstream gradient acoustic metastructures and verifies the promising prospects of proposed method in long-distance contactless sensing enhancement based on acoustic signals.
authors: Zuanbo Zhou; Niaoqing Hu; Yi Yang; Liu Wenjie; Zhengyang Yin; Xiaosong Lin

title: Ambient intelligence-based framework for quantitative evaluation of cell culture operations to support standardization and training
abstract: Introduction: The widespread implementation of cell therapy has increased the demand for stable and reproducible cell manufacturing methods. However, many cell manufacturing processes rely heavily on manual cell culture operations, and operator training remains largely dependent on subjective assessment and tacit knowledge. This limits the establishment of training targets and hinders operational standardization. Recent advances in ambient intelligence have created new opportunities for digitizing human work processes and supporting their quantitative evaluation. In this study, we developed an ambient intelligence-based framework for digitizing, visualizing, and quantitatively comparing manual cell culture operations. Methods: A defined mock seeding operation was performed by one expert with 10 years of cell culture experience and three trainees with approximately two years of experience. Videos of the operation were recorded inside a biosafety cabinet, and the dominant-hand motion was extracted using an artificial intelligence (AI)-based skeleton estimation. The resulting time-series data were converted into quantitative speed-based temporal profiles for each operation, termed Operation Profiles. To compare operations with different execution times, the similarity between each Operation Profile and the target Operation Profile derived from the expert was evaluated using fast derivative dynamic time warping (fastDDTW). Distance and gap index were used as complementary metrics to assess the waveform deviation and temporal misalignment, respectively. Results: Skeleton estimation AI, combined with visual quality control, interpolation, and manual correction, extracted the dominant-hand motion from the operation videos and enabled the construction of interpretable Operation Profiles that reflect the internal temporal structure of the defined cell culture operation. Although all operators performed the same operation, their Operation Profiles differed, indicating operator-dependent variations in the operation patterns. Iterative feedback based on phase-specific differences from the target expert operation was associated with progressive improvement in the trainees' similarity to the target Operation Profile. Conclusions: This study established a framework for recording, digitizing, and quantitatively evaluating cell culture operations using ambient intelligence. These findings demonstrate that the alignment of cell culture operations toward a target expert operation can be quantitatively evaluated through an Operation Profile analysis. By enabling objective comparison of operator behavior and quantitative evaluation of alignment toward a facility-defined target operation, this approach may provide a basis for operational standardization and training support in cell manufacturing.
authors: Kengo Momose; Takeru Shiina; Yuto Takemoto; Mai Okada; Kakeru Koide; Tomohiro Yokoi; Ayako Sugimoto; Kei Kanie; Kenjiro Tanaka; Ryuji Kato

title: A Knowledge Management System for University Public Music Education Based on Ambient Intelligence and Data Steganography
abstract: Digital transformation brings new challenges to cultural knowledge management in higher music education. This paper develops an integrated system combining ambient computing and steganography technology to manage explicit and implicit music knowledge. The system protects knowledge assets, tracks resource sources, and facilitates the fusion of different types of music culture. Comparative experiments prove its reliability and practicality. The findings expand the application of intelligent technologies in educational knowledge management and contribute to the digital inheritance and innovative development of traditional music culture.
authors: ShiChu Qin

title: A Conceptual Framework for Intelligent IoT and AI-Driven Neurocognitive Healthcare Assistive Systems
abstract: Intelligent Internet of Things (IoT) and assistive technologies are revolutionizing neurocognitive healthcare, with the ability to continuously monitor, use early diagnostics, assess disease progression and deliver personalized interventions. In this chapter, a conceptual framework concerning the integration of wearable sensing technologies, ambient intelligence, edge–cloud computing, multimodal artificial intelligence, explainable deep learning, and assistive technologies for rehabilitation to support proactive personalized care is introduced. The framework covers the neurocognitive disorders such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, dementia, autism spectrum disorders, attention-related disorders and post-stroke cognitive rehabilitation. Future directions for precision neurocognitive healthcare are presented for emerging technologies including federated learning, digital twins and brain–computer interfaces. The chapter serves as a handy guide for researchers, clinicians, and health care technology developers.
authors: Berlin Magthalin R; Mizpah Queeny R

title: Healing cascades and infections in wounds monitored using a wearable sensor of gaseous flux
abstract: Abstract Capabilities for quantitative monitoring of chronic wounds remain an unmet clinical need, as existing diagnostic approaches rely on semiquantitative evaluation of symptoms that lack sensitivity especially during early stages of infection. Here we present a scheme for tracking wound physiology that leverages a miniature, wireless skin-interfaced device for non-contact, transient measurements of the flux of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and water vapor from the wound microenvironment. Unlike emerging smart bandage platforms that rely on physical contact with the fragile wound bed to interrogate liquid-phase biomarkers, this strategy uses an engineered microclimate and suspended suite of sensors to measure the diffusive transport of wound-derived gases across the wound surface but separated from it. The result enables quantitative evaluation of metabolic activity and healing progression without perturbing the healing tissues. In biofilm growth models of Staphylococcus aureus , measurements demonstrate that trends in VOC flux correlate strongly with bacterial growth kinetics and precede any visible biofilm formation. Longitudinal monitoring in infected murine wound healing models shows that concurrent measurements of water vapor and VOC flux provide complementary physiological insights, capturing both the trajectory of barrier restoration and the dynamics of bacterial burden. The findings establish this non-contact sensing scheme as a distinct and clinically translatable paradigm for wound monitoring, with broad implications for non-invasive surveillance of disease states in which tissue metabolic activity and skin barrier integrity serve as actionable physiological readouts. Significance Statement Limited capabilities in continuous, quantitative assessment of a wound make early diagnosis and effective management challenging, particularly in cases of infection that rapidly progress before symptoms appear. Non-contact approaches for wound monitoring that preserve fragile tissue can transform wound care. In this context, gaseous flux from the wound bed provides an integrative measure of microbial activity and barrier restoration. This study establishes a wearable sensing platform that quantifies these fluxes in real time, enabling early infection detection and temporal tracking of wound healing. These results highlight a path toward personalized treatment strategies and reduced reliance on episodic clinical evaluation.

title: Air-Coupled Acoustic Emission Detection Using a Multifrequency MEMS Sensor
abstract: Acoustic emission (AE) monitoring is widely used for structural health monitoring (SHM) and nondestructive evaluation (NDE), yet most conventional sensors require direct mechanical contact with the monitored structure. Air-coupled sensing offers a non-contact alternative, but only a small fraction of elastic wave energy radiates from solids into air due to severe acoustic impedance mismatch, producing extremely weak airborne signals. This work presents an experimental demonstration of air-coupled acoustic emission detection using a compact multifrequency microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) sensor. The sensor consists of an array of sixteen diaphragm-type resonators with resonance frequencies distributed between 100 kHz and 700 kHz and microfabricated using the PiezoMUMPs process. Airborne acoustic signals generated by pencil lead break excitation on an aluminum plate were recorded with the MEMS sensor positioned in air without mechanical contact. The sensor successfully detected leaky acoustic emission signals, exhibiting clear transient responses and distinct spectral peaks aligned with its designed resonance frequencies while also capturing low-frequency components. The results demonstrate that multifrequency MEMS sensors provide sufficient sensitivity and frequency-selective response for detecting weak airborne AE signals, highlighting their potential for compact and scalable non-contact acoustic emission monitoring in structural health monitoring applications.

title: DCG-Fixer: A deep learning method for radar heartbeat signal imputation, anomaly detection and restoration
abstract: Doppler Cardiogram (DCG) signals, obtained through radar technology, provide a non-invasive method for vital sign monitoring. However, these signals are often compromised by missing data and anomalies that affect their reliability. This paper presents DCG-Fixer, a novel self-supervised deep learning framework designed to address these challenges. DCG-Fixer employs a two-stage quality assessment, Q V I and Q H E R , to ensure the selection of high-quality segments for training. DCG-Fixer’s architecture, DCG-Fix-Net, combines temporal and frequency-domain processing streams for signal restoration. The temporal stream utilizes a pre-trained transformer encoder to learn time-series patterns, while the frequency-domain stream employs a spectral attention module to restore corrupted spectral components. Evaluations on two FMCW radar datasets (IWR1642-RVSD-36 and MMWCAS-RVSD-21) demonstrate that DCG-Fixer outperforms existing methods. Under 30% missing data, DCG-Fix-Net achieved an imputation MAE of 0.43, a Pearson correlation of 0.86, and an IBI-estimation MAE of 21.77 ms. Across six anomaly settings, detection rates ranged from 83.5% to 99.8%, with restoration PCC values of 0.90–0.95. The complete model also produced the lowest SDNN, RMSSD, and HF errors, supporting short-term HRV preservation. These findings support its potential for contactless vital-sign monitoring.

title: Touch-Free Vital Signs Monitoring for Burn Victims Using Radar System
abstract: Touch-free vital sign monitoring is particularly useful for burn victims and critically ill patients, for whom conventional sensor attachment can cause pain, irritation, or infection. This paper presents a contactless system for real-time monitoring of respiration rate, heartbeat activity, and body temperature using non-invasive sensing techniques integrated with an embedded processing unit. The acquired signals are processed using signal conditioning and filtering techniques to reduce noise and improve measurement reliability. The proposed system is designed to be low-cost, portable, and suitable for real-time operation in burn care units, intensive care, emergency, and remote healthcare environments. By minimizing physical contact, the system provides a practical alternative to conventional monitoring methods while improving patient comfort and supporting timely medical attention. Keywords— Touch-free vital sign monitoring, burn victims, contactless system, respiration rate, heartbeat activity, body temperature, non-invasive sensing, signal processing.

title: 24-Hour Radar-Based Activity Monitoring Dataset for a Simulated Nursing Home Environment
abstract: This dataset contains multi-session radar recordings collected during two pilot studies in which each participant simulated a patient, a nurse, or visitors with the aim of replicating a real nursing home environment. The experiments took place in a Living Lab environment at the Health Lab of VSB – Technical University of Ostrava (more information about the laboratory is available at https://healthlab.vsb.cz/en/). The data collection aimed to study whether a privacy-preserving, contactless mmWave radar sensor can recognize daily-care activities (sleeping, relaxing, eating, caregiver visits, etc.) of an older adult over long, realistic time periods, 24 hours, without cameras or wearable devices. In addition to radar, the dataset includes environmental air-quality/context information used for room-dynamics analysis: CO₂ concentration, temperature, relative humidity, and door opening information. Sensor and data format. Radar data are acquired using InvisiAngel (https://invisiangel.vsb.cz/en/), a 60 GHz radar device, for privacy preserving monitoring of movement, activity and falls. The device is based on Texas Instruments (TI) IWR6843 60 GHz FMCW mmWave sensor (IWR6843ISK-ODS/AOP module). The device is mounted on the ceiling at approximately 2.8–3 m and runs TI's “Overhead 3D People Tracking” demo firmware. Instead of storing raw radar signals, the sensor performs on-board detection and tracking and provides two processed outputs: TLV type 1020: a 3D point cloud of detections in spherical coordinates (elevation, azimuth, Doppler velocity, range, SNR); TLV types 1010/1021: a list of tracked people with 3D position, velocity, acceleration, tracking-error covariance and a binary presence indicator. Environmental data are collected with wireless CO₂ monitoring based on the IQRF indoor air-quality system documented by Velička, Pies and Hájovský (2018), with data collected every 5 minutes. In this dataset, the exported environmental streams include CO₂ concentration, relative humidity, and temperature. The exported CSV file is structured in the following way: Timestamp (Time) CO₂ values (ppm) Temperature (°C) Humidity (RH). Door opening and closing are recorded using a Tuya Wi-Fi/Zigbee magnetic contact sensor. For both pilots, the door-contact stream was processed into a three-column event table (Date, Time, Door Status), with the Open/Closed states already harmonized from the raw Boolean values. No magnetic sensor was installed on the window in either pilot: window opening and closing were instead inferred from the time-stamped "Room ventilation" and "Window closed" events recorded in the activity log. Ground truth. Each recording session is paired with an activity log (CSV/XLSX file) automatically generated by a custom Python application we developed. The log file is organized as: Date Start and end time Type of activity performed Number of people present in the room Who performed it (patient, nurse, visitor) The application also allows users to write notes and, for example, to annotate changes in the activity. It was used to log activities in real time during each session, allowing radar timestamps to be precisely aligned with the corresponding activity and occupancy. The activities performed are: Patient relaxing: the patient is on the bed relaxing or doing light activity Patient sleeping: the patient is sleeping on the bed Patient hygiene: the nurse is assisting the patient with personal hygiene Meal service: the nurse is serving the meal to the patient Eating: the patient is eating his meal while sitting on the bed or sometimes at the table. The nurse stays there to assist the patient Meal collection: the dishes are collected Patient checks: the nurse checks the patient to see if he needs something, trying to measure vital signs or simply assess his health status Nurse cleaning: the nurse is cleaning the room or making the bed Visiting hours: relatives or friends of the patient come to visit Patient out of the room: the patient is not in the room Room ventilation: the nurse is opening the window Window closed: the nurse is closing the window. Known data-quality note. A small number of rows in radar_data_1021_1010_Pilot1.xlsx contain a corrupted posY value (a logging artifact), which should be filtered or clipped by downstream users. title: Real-Time Fall Detection in Indoor Environments Using FMCW Radar and Lightweight Ensemble CNN on Edge Devices
abstract: Falls are a leading cause of injury and mortality among the elderly, particularly indoors where privacy concerns limit real-time monitoring. This study developed a privacy-preserving, real-time fall detection system using a frequency-modulated continuous wave radar sensor and a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture deployed on an edge device. To address the limitations of wearable and vision-based methods, the system leverages contactless radar sensing and an ensemble of two independent CNN models, namely, a base model designed to capture the entire fall sequence for high recall and a sub-model aimed at pinpointing the fall moment with high precision. The final decision is executed through a voting mechanism that triggers a fall alert only when both models agree, significantly reducing false positives. On 14 recording sessions withheld from the training of both models, the ensemble detected 13 of 14 falls (recall 92.9%, 95% CI 68.5-98.7%) without false alarms, and in a 24-trial on-device test comprising 4 falls and 20 non-fall activities it detected every fall with no false alarm. Running on a low-power microcontroller, the system indicates the feasibility of privacy-preserving on-device fall detection, while validation with older adults and in real living environments remains necessary.

title: DuBCG: Unlocking In-Home, Clinically Comparable mmWave Cardiac Monitoring for Co-Sleepers via Physics-Informed Spatial Sensing
abstract: Continuous, fine-grained cardiac monitoring during sleep is vital for cardiovascular health. Emerging as a promising alternative to cumbersome wearables, mmWave radar offers a contactless, privacy-preserving modality capable of capturing minute skin vibrations. However, transitioning mmWave radar from labs to real-world bedrooms remains challenging. Our rigorous empirical evaluation of state-of-the-art systems reveals a severe reliability gap: valid Inter-Beat Intervals (IBI) are captured for only 24%-42% of the night within an error threshold of 50 ms. Since clinical HRV analysis requires millisecond-level precision (e.g., RMSSD changes), such coarse and intermittent tracking renders existing methods medically insufficient. We attribute this failure to two fundamental hurdles: (i) instability driven by overwhelming respiratory interference and postural diversity, and (ii) signal entanglement in co-sleeping scenarios where angular separation defies hardware resolution. To bridge this gap, we present DuBCG. First, to tackle instability, we introduce a Head-Facing configuration to capture the Radar Ballistocardiogram (R-BCG). By leveraging the body's longitudinal recoil, this approach achieves orthogonal respiratory suppression and posture-invariant robustness. Second, to resolve entanglement, we propose the Multi-point Scattering Spatial Selectivity Model, theoretically proving that signal separability is achievable beyond physical resolution limits. Extensive real-world benchmarks demonstrate that DuBCG achieves a median IBI error of 8.4 ms—an 8× improvement over existing methods. This precision bridges the gap from existing intermittent monitoring to long-term, clinically comparable continuous HRV assessment.
