title: Sensitive detection of chloroplast movements through changes in leaf cross-polarized reflectance
abstract: Abstract We show that the positioning of chloroplasts in plant cells affects the ability of photosynthetic organs to depolarize linearly polarized light through diffuse reflection. We apply this phenomenon for the detection of blue-light-induced chloroplast movements using light reflected from leaves and green stems. High-light-induced chloroplast avoidance leads to an increase in reflectance, while chloroplast accumulation in low light has the opposite effect. The changes in reflectance are correlated with an increase in the leaf’s ability to depolarize linearly polarized light. Inclusion of polarization information in the detection procedure allows for the mitigation of the effects of sample orientation and for an increase in the specificity of detection. We applied this approach to examine chloroplast movements in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana and four flowering plant species collected in the field. Despite the importance of chloroplast movements for the optimization of photosynthetic efficiency and biomass production, high-throughput reflectance-based methods are not routinely employed. Our approach opens the possibility of non-invasive, non-contact detection of chloroplast movements in a manner insensitive to the orientation of the leaf.
authors: Paweł Hermanowicz; Aleksandra Giza; Katarzyna Sowa; Paweł Korecki; Justyna Łabuz

title: Sistem Pemantauan Aktivitas Manusia Menggunakan Sensor Human Presence Radar HLK-LD2410C Dan ESP32
abstract: Indoor human activity monitoring is essential for Internet of Things (IoT) security and automation. However, Passive Infrared (PIR) sensors and cameras face limitations regarding low-movement detection and privacy issues. This study implements an HLK-LD2410C Human Presence Radar using 24 GHz mmWave and ESP32 to classify real-time activities. Parameters including Presence, Distance, P_Energy, and M_Energy from UART communication are categorized via thresholding into No Presence, Static, Light Movement, and Heavy Movement. Testing reveals detection ranges up to 5.2 m for Static, 5.3 m for Light Movement, and 3.8 m for Heavy Movement. Confusion matrix evaluation yields 97.50% accuracy, 97.73% precision, 97.50% recall, and a 97.49% F1-score. M_Energy values depend on distance and movement intensity, while multi-object scenarios reflect the dominant activity within the detection zone. Consequently, the proposed system provides a non-contact, responsive, and privacy-preserving solution for indoor human activity monitoring.
authors: Mikha Viyo Nugroho; Gogor Christmass Setyawan; Yo’el Pieter Sumihar

title: Non-contact Cardiorespiratory Monitoring in a Smart Triage Chair using Laser Speckle Pattern Dynamics
abstract: Emergency triage requires rapid, simultaneous vital-sign acquisition, yet contact-based sensors create throughput bottlenecks during surge events. We present a triage chair that measures heart rate (HR) and respiration rate (RR) simultaneously without patient contact, using time-varying laser speckle patterns projected onto the posterior thorax. We conducted our experiments in a cohort of 34 volunteers (19 males, 15 females, age 39.6 ± 11.4 years). RR estimation showed good agreement with an MAE of 1.9 br/min and an RMSE of 3.4 br/min (95% CI: [0.9, 2.9] br/min). For HR estimation, an MAE of 10.68 BPM and an RMSE of 19.0 BPM were obtained (95% CI: [5.2, 16.2] BPM).
authors: Yevgeny Beiderman; Ayuushi Dutta; Yael Mordechay; Matan Hod
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Mapping Conventional and Emerging Sensors for Neonatal Physiological Monitoring: A Scoping Review of the Technological Transition and Validation Gaps
abstract: Continuous physiological monitoring is a cornerstone of neonatal intensive care. Yet, current NICU sensing technologies- adhesive electrodes, contact pulse oximeters, and wired thermistors- carry well-documented clinical limitations, including adhesive-related skin injury, restricted mobility, and interference with family-centered developmental care protocols. Although the past decade has witnessed a proliferation of alternative sensing proposals spanning flexible electronics, wireless wearable platforms, and fully contactless approaches, this body of research remains fragmented across distinct technical communities, and no comprehensive mapping of the conventional and emerging sensor ecosystem has been published to date. To address this gap, this scoping review followed the PRISMA-ScR guidelines and was structured around a Population, Concept, and Context (PCC) framework: Population, neonates admitted to the NICU; Concept, sensors used in physiological monitoring equipment; Context, the hospital neonatal intensive care setting. Searches in PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore retrieved 197 records, reduced to 166 unique records after deduplication; 40 studies published between 2016 and 2026 were included following a two-stage screening process. The synthesized evidence reveals that emerging technologies predominate (26 of 40, 65%), with optical transduction as the leading physical principle (15 of 40) and flexible or wearable form factors already outnumbering rigid designs (23 of 40 versus 9 of 40). Research activity concentrates heavily on respiratory rate (20 of 40) and heart rate (18 of 40), while electroencephalography and transcutaneous bilirubin each appear in only 1 of 40 studies and blood pressure exclusively as a secondary channel in multiparameter platforms (3 of 40), gaps independently corroborated by contemporaneous systematic reviews of the same domain. Regulatory transparency is markedly absent, with 85% of included studies making no mention of regulatory status, reflecting the field's predominantly proof-of-concept readiness. These findings delineate the current technological frontier of neonatal sensing, identify priority targets for future complementary searches, and underscore the urgent need for standardized validation frameworks to enable direct cross-technology comparisons in subsequent reviews.
authors: Gabriela Cianciarullo; Salvador Pinillos Gimenes; Carlos Eduardo Thomaz
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Mechatronic Platform Driven by Thoracic Impedance Signals for the Experimental Evaluation of a Radar-Based Respiratory Monitoring System
abstract: Short-range FMCW radar has emerged as a promising contactless technology for respiratory monitoring. However, the experimental evaluation of radar-based respiratory monitoring systems using human subjects is often affected by inter-subject variability, involuntary body movements, and the limited repeatability of respiratory patterns. This work presents a mechatronic platform that reproduces respiratory motion using thoracic impedance signals from the publicly available BIDMC dataset to enable controlled evaluation of the Acconeer XM132 radar. The respiratory signals were resampled, normalized, and converted into motion commands for MG90S servo motors, reproducing physiological breathing patterns through a movable PLA and acrylic structure. A total of 12 recordings, each lasting 240 s, were analyzed. The filtered radar signal was used as the primary source for respiratory rate (RR) estimation, while an MPU6050 inertial sensor provided an auxiliary measurement of the platform motion. Different analysis window lengths and RR estimation methods were investigated. FFT-based estimation using 60 s windows achieved a mean error of 1.94 breathing per minute (bpm) and a median error of 0.09 bpm, whereas analysis of the complete 240 s recordings yielded a median error of 0.03 bpm. The proposed platform contributes to the development of biomedical instrumentation for radar-based respiratory monitoring by providing a controlled and repeatable environment for evaluating radar acquisition parameters, signal filtering techniques, and RR estimation algorithms, representing an intermediate step between laboratory characterization and clinical validation.
authors: Júlio Cardoso Scorpion; João Lucas Pereira dos Santos de Paula; Feres A. Salem; Elço João dos Santos; Flávio Gabriel Oliveira Barbosa; Paulo Alberto Macedo Vieira Violada
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Non-invasive monitoring of human vital signs under dynamic conditions: A review of acoustic, optical and ballistocardiographic methods
abstract: Introduction: Modern healthcare systems face a critical shortage of personnel, which in the traditional model leads to dangerous “time windows” (reaching up to 22 h per day) during which the patient remains unsupervised. The response to this challenge is the dynamic development of contactless monitoring technologies, enabling continuous assessment of vital parameters without the discomfort associated with cabling. However, the implementation of these solutions in real-world environments encounters a fundamental barrier in the form of motion artifacts, variable environmental conditions, and demographic heterogeneity. Aim: This article provides a review of non-invasive monitoring methods under dynamic conditions, with a particular emphasis on interference compensation techniques. The aim of the work is a comparative analysis of three leading modalities: optical and guided-wave photonic (rPPG, thermography, LiDAR, FBG, FPI), vibrational-mechanical (BCG, SCG), and acoustic (passive and active), in the context of their clinical reliability, privacy protection, and motion robustness. Methodology: The review includes a literature analysis from the years 1947–2025, with a special emphasis on the “digital era” after 2010. The effectiveness of modern signal processing algorithms was analyzed, including bounded Kalman filters, Tile and Aggregation (T&A) methods for diverse skin pigmentation, and deep learning architectures (UNet, Bi-LSTM) used for the reconstruction of biomedical signals, alongside targeted strategies evaluated for specific vulnerable demographics (high BMI, preterm infants, and elderly populations). Results: The analysis shows a clear specialization of individual technologies. Optical methods (rPPG) offer the highest precision in measuring heart rate and saturation, particularly in neonatology (SIDS prevention), but are limited by lighting conditions and privacy issues, whereas guided-wave photonics offer complete electromagnetic immunity. Vibrational methods (BCG/SCG) provide discrete “zero-effort” measurement and unique hemodynamic data (PEP, LVET), yet they exhibit critical sensitivity to patient motor activity. Acoustic technologies, especially active ultrasonic sonars, represent a compromise that allows for respiratory monitoring in the dark and through obstacles. Conclusions: There is currently no single, universal measurement method robust to all environmental interferences. The future of non-invasive monitoring lies in hybrid systems (sensor fusion), combining the advantages of different modalities (e.g., optics and vibration), and in edge processing (Edge AI). Addressing the strict trade-offs between computational overhead in matrix-inversion algorithms and hardware power constraints will be key. Only the integration of multi-source data will allow for the effective elimination of motion artifacts and the implementation of medical safety-critical systems in home and mobile conditions.
authors: Marek Ostrysz

title: Contactless Upper-Limb Bradykinesia Monitoring for Parkinson's Disease via Semantic-Aware mmWave Sensing in Daily Life
abstract: Upper-limb bradykinesia, a cardinal symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD), significantly disrupts daily activities with slowness and reduced amplitude of voluntary movement. Current clinical assessments are episodic and subjective, and fail to capture real-world symptom fluctuations, while wearable systems suffer from low long-term adherence and vision-based solutions raise privacy concerns. We introduce mmBrady, the first contactless system that enables continuous, privacy-preserving estimation of upper-limb bradykinesia in daily environments using mmWave radar. To address core challenges including coarse clinical supervision, noisy superimposed signals, and heterogeneous daily activities, we propose three key modules: (1) a decoupled strategy using cross-modal dense supervision for kinematic extractors; (2) a hierarchical framework modeling spatial joint synergy to disentangle overlapping reflections; and (3) a semantic-aware multi-instance regressor that aggregates motion-stage-specific observations to distinguish pathological slowness from normal pauses. Evaluated on 42 PD patients across 8 real-world environments (clinic, nursing home, and homes), mmBrady achieves a high correlation of 0.73 and a low MAE of 1.59 with clinician-anchored MDS-UPDRS bradykinesia scores, which is even better than state-of-the-art single-wearable solutions but with no user burden. We will release the first contactless bradykinesia dataset to advance in-home neurological healthcare. We envision that mmBrady paves the way for longitudinal, low-burden PD monitoring to support timely medication adjustments and improve patient quality of life.
authors: J. Wang; Qingyong Hu; Yizhen Zhang; Yuxuan Zhou; Guihua Li; Qian Zhang
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive Mobile Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies

title: Software-defined radio sensing for self-harming behaviour detection using CWT transformation and deep learning
abstract: Self-harming, prevalent among youths and adolescents, is highly linked to coping difficulties, emotional distress, trauma, and low self-esteem. Such behaviors are a serious problem as regards social well-being, mental health and emotional stability, which are detrimental to individuals, society and healthcare systems. Early detection of self-harming behavior is vital for enabling timely intervention and mitigating long-term psychological risks. In this article, we propose an intelligent human self-harming behavior detection system leveraging Software Defined Radio (SDR) signals-based non-contact platform and deep learning. The proposed system uses a multi-carrier orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) signal to extract wireless channel state information for self-harm detection. It employs the Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) to convert raw one-dimensional (1D) OFDM signals into two-dimensional (2D) spectrogram representations, enriching the feature set for deep learning models. A customised convolutional neural network (CNN) is designed to capture abrupt physical movements associated with self-harm while maintaining low computational complexity for real-time deployment. The customised CNN is rigorously evaluated against benchmark pre-trained deep learning models, including AlexNet, ResNet18, and GoogleNet, to demonstrate competitive sensitivity and specificity. Comprehensive comparisons are conducted based on performance metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and computational efficiency parameters. The proposed customised model achieves competitive accuracy (96%) and F1-score (94%) while being significantly more computationally efficient, requiring only 3,305,801 trainable parameters, 12.61 MB of memory, and 45.09 ms inference time.
authors: Farman Ullah; Shumayla Yaqoob; Ali Mustafa; Ammar; Irfan Hussain; Mobeen Ur Rehman

title: PhySinc-Net: A physics-informed interpretable deep learning architecture for non-contact respiratory rate monitoring in dairy goats
authors: Wenxuan Lu; Rui Mao; Bohan Jiang; Jiayi Tian; Hanrui Li; Xianyao Zhu; Mei Li

title: Machine Learning Augmented Detection of Trace Explosives on Surfaces Using Active Longwave Infrared Imaging
abstract: There is a need for rapid non-contact detection of trace explosives on arbitrary surfaces for applications such as checkpoint screening and post-blast forensics. In this work, active longwave infrared imaging, using a tunable quantum cascade laser light source, is shown to be able to detect three common explosives on typical luggage material substrates at surface concentrations as low as 230 ng/cm 2 . Use of a random forest machine learning algorithm, trained using synthetically produced spectra, allows performance beyond predicted limitations of speckle noise. The random forest algorithm further allows discrimination against ambient dust without specific training. Use of high collection angles reduces the dynamic range requirement of the system without impairing performance. Potential system improvements are discussed to meet the area coverage rate needs of several applications.
authors: William M. Barney; Mitesh Amin; William D. Herzog; Jason M. Jong; Max Kenngott; Keegan Quigley; Patrick Wen; Roderick Russell Kunz

title: New Oxygen Sensor with Polyaniline Spin Probe and Low Frequency EPR (L-Band) Detection System
abstract: Our research demonstrates the potential of certain PANI samples to serve as sensitive and reliable spin probes for oxygen detection, while also highlighting the advantages of the low-frequency EPR technique. Compared to other methods of measuring oxygen concentration, the new sensor—based on a PANI spin probe and a low-frequency EPR detector—offers unique benefits: it ensures high sensitivity to changes in oxygen concentration and does not require direct contact between the EPR detector and the sensor itself (the polyaniline probe). This sensor can be placed in isolated environments, including biological samples (tissues), and - thanks to the use of nanodispersed polyaniline - even inside living cells.
authors: Mikolaj Baranowski; Sebastian Golczak; Jerzy J. Langer

title: Aerial Magnetic Anomaly Target Detection Method Based on Multi-Scale Orthonormal Basis Function Convolution and Convolution-Augmented Gated Attention
abstract: Magnetic anomaly detection from aerial platforms enables passive, non-contact detection of underwater ferromagnetic targets. To address the issues of traditional Orthonormal Basis Function (OBF) detection relying on prior knowledge of the closest contact distance and susceptibility to mismatch with single-scale templates, this paper proposes an aerial magnetic anomaly target detection method that integrates multi-scale OBF with a convolution-augmented gated attention unit (CGAU). Six sets of fixed OBF convolution kernels each output three matching responses, which are concatenated with the original sequence to form 19-channel features. Four layers of one-dimensional (1-D) convolution and two stages of CGAU extract local waveform features and capture long-range dependencies. The precision (PC), detection rate (DR), and F1-score of the proposed network on the simulated test set are 94.70%, 95.11%, and 94.90%, respectively (best-performing seed = 42). On the measured dataset, it detected 11 of 12 overpass events, achieving an event detection rate of 91.67%. The proposed network has approximately 0.43 M trainable parameters and achieves a higher mean F1 across three random seeds than the seven selected baselines, demonstrating its potential for aerial magnetic anomaly target detection.
authors: Haozhe Chen; Ke Zhang; Wanhua Zhu

title: Wearable optical fiber sensor for recognition of nasal and oral breathing patterns
authors: Yaxun Zhang; Wenmi Li; Pingbang Huang; Zhiliang Huang; Xiaoyun Tang; Yu Zhang; Zhihai Liu

title: A Curved Bimodal Hair Sensor for Airflow and Electrostatic Perception in Robotic Control
abstract: ABSTRACT Noncontact environmental perception is crucial for autonomous alerting and behavior control in mobile robots, yet existing artificial sensory systems still fall short in integrating weak‐stimulus detection, interaction‐direction discrimination, and multimodal sensing within a single device. Drawing inspiration from the electroreceptive hair‐like sensilla of treehoppers and the high‐curvature proboscis of butterflies, we report a Curved Bimodal Hair Sensor (CBHS) that achieves dual‐mode noncontact perception of electrostatic and airflow stimuli. The high‐curvature hair architecture enhances mechanical coupling, and a sliding‐rheostat‐based length‐encoded resistance mechanism enables stable detection of compressive and tensile loads down to 10 −4 N. Electrostatic and airflow stimuli are inherently discriminated by their contrasting time scales and signal profiles. Under airflow, hair oscillation induces interfacial contact electrification, dynamically modulating the electrical state to enable wind‐speed detection as low as 0.9 m·s −1 , with a random forest model classifying six speed levels at 98.89% accuracy. When integrated into a robotic platform, CBHS directly maps electrostatic polarity to approach and escape behaviors, while a four‐sensor array enables airflow‐direction‐guided vigilance and closed‐loop directional motion. This work presents a structure‐driven bioinspired strategy for low‐complexity multimodal artificial sensory systems directly coupled to robotic behavior.
authors: Yiwei Zhou; Hengsheng Gao; Qixuan Hao; Weiqi Wang; Xiangtian Ding; Qi Zheng; Jiacheng Cai; Qianru Li; Jianhua Liu; Shiquan Lin

title: Status Quo of Artificial Intelligence- and Machine Learning-Supported Medical and Administrative Processes in Ambulatory Care Practice Management Systems: Systematic Review (Preprint)
abstract: BACKGROUND Electronic health records (EHRs) and practice management systems represent the digital foundation of outpatient care worldwide. Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)-supported medical and administrative processes (AMP) into these platforms offers a profound opportunity to streamline clinical workflows and standardize patient care. However, existing research remains highly fragmented and focused on isolated tools. This creates a critical research gap, as there is currently no comprehensive mapping of how these diverse medical and administrative workflows collectively integrate and perform within the real-world clinical environment of ambulatory care. OBJECTIVE This study aims to address this research gap by comprehensively mapping the global status quo of natively EHR-integrated AMP in ambulatory care. Specifically, we explore the types of digital processes currently available and how physicians and medical assistants interact with these technologies in clinical environments. METHODS We conducted a systematic review of PubMed and Scopus databases (searching from inception to March 24, 2026) following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. We targeted empirical studies evaluating outpatient clinical and administrative processes driven by AI, ML, or AI-enabled decision-support algorithms natively embedded within EHR or practice management systems. To ensure literature saturation, backward citation searching of included studies was conducted (yielding no additional eligible studies). Study selection, data extraction into a standardized matrix, and methodological quality assessment using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal checklists (tailored to RCTs, quasi-experimental, cohort, cross-sectional, and qualitative studies) were conducted by one reviewer and independently verified by a second reviewer. RESULTS A total of 39 empirical studies were included. Methodological quality assessed via JBI tools was moderate to high, with common limitations being a lack of participant and personnel blinding (system-inherent) and selection bias due to reliance on voluntary early adopters. Our synthesis identified 5 primary categories of natively EHR-integrated AMP: point-of-care clinical decision support systems (CDSS) (16/39, 41%), active background screening and triage (9/39, 23%), ambient intelligence for clinical documentation (8/39, 21%), administrative processes and patient communication (4/39, 10%), and remote patient monitoring (RPM) (2/39, 5%). While ambient AI demonstrated success in reducing documentation effort and burnout, point-of-care CDSS was heavily hindered by alert fatigue (with override rates up to 96%), and active background screening was constrained by algorithmic opacity (“black-box” characteristics) and clinician distrust. CONCLUSIONS Rather than achieving full automation, AMP technologies currently function as assistive tools within primary care. Real-world utilization requires a strict human-in-the-loop verification process, where medical professionals actively oversee both AI- and ML-driven outputs. Successful integration depends on addressing critical workflow barriers, particularly minimizing alert fatigue and enhancing algorithmic transparency to foster clinician trust. CLINICALTRIAL PROSPERO [CRD420261327094]
authors: Sandra Steinkasserer; Martin Emmert; Reiner Hofmann

title: Water-cut measurement using a planar microwave resonant sensor under flowing operating conditions
abstract: Accurate monitoring of water content in flowing oil/bitumen pipelines remains a critical challenge in the petroleum industry, as it directly affects production optimization, custody transfer, and reservoir management. In this study, we present a new microwave sensor approach for real-time, noncontact quantification of water content in flowing oil-water mixtures under operating conditions. The sensing approach exploits the strong dielectric contrast between water and oil/bitumen by monitoring the flowing stream over a defined microwave frequency range and tracking resonance frequency shifts associated with changes in effective permittivity. The sensing system consists of a planar battery-less sensing tag electromagnetically coupled to a reader at a specific distance, enabling contactless monitoring. The sensor shows high sensitivity within the 600–850 MHz frequency band and a total resonance frequency shift of about 18 MHz across the full water-cut range. To replicate oilfield-relevant operating conditions, we constructed a laboratory-scale flow loop to circulate two-phase oil-water emulsions. The experiments were conducted at water cuts from 0 to 100 wt% and temperatures from 24 to 110 °C at 150 psig. The sensor shows a continuous, monotonic response across the entire emulsion spectrum ( i.e ., water-in-oil, oil-in-water, and phase-inversion regimes). The proposed technique offers fast, instantaneous response, high sensitivity, and robust performance under elevated temperature and pressure, while remaining low-cost, passive, and easy to integrate with existing pipeline infrastructure.
authors: Shadi Kheirollahi; Nima Karbaschi; Mabkhot S. BinDahbag; Zahra Abbasi; Hassan Hassanzadeh

title: VibraGlot: Contactless Vocal Disorder Screening via mmWave Neck-Surface Vibration Sensing
abstract: Vocal disorders often begin as subtle mechanical irregularities in vocal-fold vibration before speech quality noticeably degrades. Early identification of such abnormalities is valuable because timely intervention may prevent progression to more advanced stages. However, detecting these weak early cues outside clinical settings remains challenging: microphone-based analysis observes an acoustically shaped signal that may only weakly express source-level irregularity, while contact-based vibration sensors suffer from low user compliance. We present VibraGlot, a contactless screening system that leverages millimeter-wave radar to sense neck-surface micro-vibrations during a short, non-linguistic sustained phonation (3-5 s). Rather than adopting generic end-to-end learning, VibraGlot uses a kinematics-first design. It first isolates the laryngeal region through observability-aware locking to suppress static clutter, then performs cycle-synchronous reconstruction in a canonical phase domain. Crucially, this pipeline explicitly preserves template-violating motion as structured residuals, transforming irregular mechanical behavior into diagnostic features rather than smoothing it away as noise. We evaluate VibraGlot on a clinical cohort of 74 subjects spanning five common vocal pathologies and healthy controls, collected in both hospital and home environments. Under a strict minimal-input protocol, the system achieves a macro-F1 score exceeding 0.91. These results demonstrate that radar-based neck-surface kinematics provide a robust, interpretable, and contactless pathway for scalable early vocal disorder screening, particularly when pathology is still expressed as subtle mechanical irregularity.
authors: Yuanhao Feng; Zhi Liu; Takuya Fujihashi; Shunsuke Saruwatari
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive Mobile Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies

title: Millimetre-Wave Radar for Sports Engineering Applications: A Scoping Review of Current Evidence, Validation, and Future Directions
abstract: Millimetre-wave (mmWave) radar has emerged as a promising non-contact sensing technology capable of capturing human movement and physiological information without requiring wearable devices or continuous visual recording. Although mmWave radar has been extensively investigated in general human sensing applications, its current role and potential translation in sports engineering remain unclear. This scoping review aims to systematically map current evidence regarding mmWave radar applications relevant to sports engineering, including localisation and tracking, movement recognition, pose estimation, and physiological monitoring. The review will summarise sensing configurations, experimental designs, validation approaches, performance metrics, and engineering limitations reported in existing studies. The review will follow the methodological framework for scoping reviews and will be reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. The findings will identify current capabilities, evidence gaps, and future directions for translating mmWave radar technologies into practical sports engineering applications.
authors: Rouli Ye; Xu Wen

title: Probing and Sensing Layer-Dependent van der Waals Interaction via Induced Anisotropy
abstract: Abstract Van der Waals (vdW) interaction, a fundamental force, plays an important role in two-dimensional (2D) systems by enabling atomically sharp assemblies and giving rise to many emergent phenomena. However, experimentally probing and sensing the evolution of vdW interaction between 2D layers remains challenging due to its extreme weakness, very short range, and the difficulty of keeping two atomic layers perfectly parallel while finely adjusting the interaction. Here, we demonstrate an optical strategy to indirectly probe vdW interactions by exploiting induced anisotropy in MoS2/NbIrTe4 heterostructures. We construct heterostructures using isotropic MoS2 and anisotropic NbIrTe4 to ensure perfect parallelism. We modulate and probe the vdW interaction by varying the NbIrTe4 thickness and monitor the vdW-interaction-induced anisotropy in MoS2. We find such induced anisotropy to strongly depend on the NbIrTe4 thickness and clearly observe its fast-decaying nature. This work provides a simple, noncontact approach for indirectly probing interlayer vdW interactions.
authors: Ting Wen; Shuang Cai; Ziluo Su; Yalan Wang; Jiaqi Wu; Jiaze Qin; Chenyin Jiao; Zenghui Wang; Zejuan Zhang; Shenghai Pei

title: Shape memory thermoplastic polyurethane for tailoring flexural ultrasonic transducer dynamics
abstract: Air-coupled flexural ultrasonic transducers (FUTs) are widely used for non-contact measurement, but conventional metallic FUTs are narrowband with fixed dynamic characteristics post-fabrication. This restricts how they can be applied in practice, for example in response to changing operational requirements. This work introduces a novel geometrically reconfigurable FUT for adapting sensor dynamics, where the vibrating plate is fabricated from an additively manufactured thermoplastic polyurethane shape memory polymer (SMP), exploiting the shape memory effect to reversibly programme the plate geometry. The plate can be set into a desired shape above the glass transition temperature and then cooled, from where ultrasonic vibrations are generated only in the rigid glassy state, avoiding the viscoelastic damping that would otherwise arise near the transition. Two nominally identical SMP-FUTs were rigorously characterised across electrical impedance analysis, laser Doppler vibrometry, and acoustic microphone measurement in air, with results correlated against finite element simulations, for three programmed geometry cases: flat baseline, concave, and angled. This study shows that a reversible resonance frequency shift of around 6 kHz is possible for the SMP-FUT, in addition to a tuneable −6 dB bandwidth, a directable beam, and a signal-to-noise ratio of up to 33.1 dB across all cases. Measured and simulated resonance frequencies agreed to within 5.5% for every case. The significance of these results is that multiple acoustic operating conditions, otherwise requiring several separate sensing elements, can be realised within a single geometrically reconfigurable sensor. This establishes SMPs as a viable route towards adaptive ultrasound sensors for applications including proximity sensing, industrial process monitoring, and mid-air haptics.
authors: Jason McKenna; Charles Dowling; Katherine M. M. Tant; Andrew Feeney

title: PS2-15. Multimodal Video and Audio Signal Processing for Estimating Cattle Forage Intake.
abstract: Abstract Accurate quantification of forage intake and rumen digesta during grazing is important for nutrition research but remains difficult to measure at scale. This pilot study evaluated whether contactless video and audio recordings collected during grazing contain kinematic and acoustic signatures that can be related to forage disappearance and rumen digesta dry matter measured via cannulation. Two Angus cattle were recorded across three days during controlled feeding trials in which cereal rye was presented in ground-level pots (three pots per animal per day) and consumed while a fixed-position action camera captured video with onboard audio. Jaw and head keypoints were tracked from video using SLEAP, and grazing-associated audio features were extracted from the video soundtrack using standard digital signal processing implemented in librosa. Features linked to biting events were used as inputs to a linear regression model to estimate forage dry matter disappearance and rumen digesta dry matter recovered after each trial. In this pilot dataset, recovered rumen digesta dry matter was highly correlated with forage disappearance (R² = 0.99), supporting the use of disappearance as a closely aligned intake-related endpoint under these controlled conditions. The results motivate expanded validation across more animals, forage types, and grazing conditions to assess model generalizability and the potential for contactless intake-related monitoring using invasive ground truth for calibration.
