abstract: The evaluation of peripheral pulmonary lesions (PPLs) represents a persistent clinical challenge, particularly in the context of rapidly expanding lung cancer screening programs generating unprecedented volumes of screen-detected nodules requiring tissue evaluation. Conventional bronchoscopic techniques and earlier navigation platforms, including electromagnetic navigation bronchoscopy (ENB), improved access to peripheral airways but demonstrated variable and generally suboptimal diagnostic performance—historically plateauing at 60–70%—attributable principally to CT-to-body divergence and the diagnostic drop-off phenomenon. Robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (RAB) has emerged as a significant advancement integrating robotic catheter control, shape-sensing or electromagnetic navigation, and adjunctive intraprocedural imaging—principally cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)—to improve lesion localization and procedural stability. Available evidence suggests that RAB achieves improved diagnostic yields compared with conventional bronchoscopic techniques, particularly when combined with real-time CBCT-guided tool-in-lesion confirmation and multimodal biopsy strategies including transbronchial cryobiopsy. Reported diagnostic yields generally range from 70% to 87% across pooled meta-analytic datasets, with higher yields described in centers employing CBCT and cryobiopsy. A favorable safety profile—with pooled pneumothorax rates of approximately 2%, substantially below the 20–25% associated with CT-guided transthoracic needle biopsy—represents a clinically important differentiator, particularly in patients with emphysema, coagulopathy, or contralateral lung compromise [1,3]. RAB additionally enables procedural capabilities beyond peripheral lesion biopsy, including simultaneous mediastinal lymph node staging, bilateral same-session lesion sampling, fiducial marker placement for stereotactic body radiotherapy, and investigational therapeutic applications. However, current evidence is largely derived from observational studies and single-arm prospective cohorts, with limited randomized data directly comparing RAB with transthoracic biopsy approaches. Outcomes are meaningfully influenced by lesion characteristics, operator experience, institutional volume, and availability of advanced imaging infrastructure. This review summarizes current evidence on RAB platforms, procedural optimization, diagnostic performance, safety, molecular tissue adequacy, and emerging applications, while explicitly addressing limitations, controversies, and areas requiring further investigation. This review was conducted and reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines adapted for narrative reviews (SANRA framework).

title: Radiation-Associated Lung Adenosquamous Carcinoma Diagnosed by Robotic-Assisted Bronchoscopy With Cone-Beam CT Guidance and Treated With Robotic Superior Segmentectomy: A Case Report
abstract: Prior thoracic or chest-wall radiotherapy carries a small but meaningful risk of second primary malignancy after a prolonged latency period. Chronic post-radiation changes may also complicate the evaluation of new pulmonary lesions, particularly when fibrosis, traction bronchiectasis, and architectural distortion are present. Advances in robotic-assisted bronchoscopy combined with radial endobronchial ultrasound (rEBUS), augmented fluoroscopy, and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) may facilitate localization and tissue diagnosis of suspicious peripheral pulmonary lesions in this setting. We report the case of an 82-year-old woman with a remote smoking history and recurrent myxofibrosarcoma of the left upper back. At Year 0, she underwent surgical resection followed by adjuvant radiotherapy to 60 Gy in 30 fractions. At Year 10, she developed a high-grade local recurrence that was managed with radical re-excision followed by electron re-irradiation to an additional 60 Gy in 30 fractions. Whole-body PET/CT performed during evaluation of the recurrence showed no evidence of distant metastatic disease. She did not receive systemic therapy for her myxofibrosarcoma. During surveillance following re-irradiation, imaging identified an enlarging spiculated left lower lobe lesion with associated traction bronchiectasis adjacent to post-treatment changes in the posterior thoracic region. PET/CT demonstrated increased fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake within the lesion, with a maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) of 2.9, increasing suspicion for malignancy, although inflammatory processes may also demonstrate FDG uptake. Robotic-assisted bronchoscopy with rEBUS, CBCT, and augmented fluoroscopic guidance established the diagnosis of primary lung adenocarcinoma. Following multidisciplinary evaluation, the patient underwent robotic-assisted superior segmentectomy with systematic lymph node dissection and additional margin resection. Final pathology demonstrated a 2.2 cm well-differentiated adenosquamous carcinoma confined to the lung parenchyma, with negative sampled lymph nodes and a negative final margin. Surveillance imaging approximately seven months after resection demonstrated no new pulmonary nodules or masses. The temporal and anatomic relationship of the lesion to prior chest-wall radiotherapy raised consideration of a radiation-associated malignancy; however, causality cannot be established from a single case. Available 2024 boost-plan dosimetry demonstrated limited average pulmonary exposure, although cumulative dose at the exact lesion site was not available. This case illustrates the successful use of robotic bronchoscopy, rEBUS, CBCT, and augmented fluoroscopy for lesion localization and tissue diagnosis in complex post-treatment thoracic anatomy without establishing superiority over alternative diagnostic approaches.
authors: B U Etukudoh; Noah Gordon; Raisa Munshi; Mae Leef; Abdul Hamid Alraiyes

title: Robotic-assisted transbronchial biopsy versus computed tomography–guided transthoracic needle biopsy for peripheral pulmonary lesions: a systematic review and meta-analysis of direct comparative studies
abstract: Robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (RAB) and computed tomography-guided transthoracic biopsy (CTTB) are competing strategies for sampling peripheral pulmonary lesions (PPLs). Whether they differ in yield or safety is uncertain. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review restricted to direct comparisons. We searched MEDLINE, Europe PMC, Scopus, Web of Science and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to 7 July 2026 for studies directly comparing RAB with CTTB in adults with PPLs. The primary outcome was strict 2024 American Thoracic Society/American College of Chest Physicians diagnostic yield. Risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I and certainty with GRADE. A cohort-genealogy step identified, per outcome, the largest set of cohorts sharing no patients; only that set was pooled, with Hartung-Knapp and Mantel-Haenszel sensitivity analyses. Five retrospective studies from one US health system were eligible. Four share patients; at most three cohorts are mutually independent. Across those three, diagnostic yield was comparable (risk ratio [RR] 0.99, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.93-1.06; I²=24%; Hartung-Knapp 0.87-1.13), with an identical relative effect under strict and intermediate definitions although absolute yields fell from 88% to 74-84% under strict criteria. Pneumothorax requiring a chest tube and/or admission was about three-quarters less frequent with RAB across all three cohorts (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.14-0.46; I²=0%; Hartung-Knapp 0.07-0.96). Strict yield (RR 0.99) and any pneumothorax (RR 0.06) were reported by two cohorts each and neither survives the few-studies correction. RAB took about 50 min longer than CTTB where same-session staging endobronchial ultrasound was counted in the robotic time, but only about 8 min longer than CTTB where it was not. Only one cohort reported yield by lesion size category and none reported yield by bronchus sign or lung zone, so lesion-level subgroups could not be pooled. Certainty was low for pleural complications and very low elsewhere. Low-certainty evidence indicates that RAB is associated with fewer pleural complications, with no statistically detectable difference in diagnostic yield; equivalence was not formally established. Because all evidence is retrospective, confined to one health system, and almost never stratified by lesion size or accessibility, these findings are hypothesis-generating and require a multicenter randomized trial.

title: Same-day diagnosis and robotic resection of rare primary pulmonary melanoma: a robotic bronchoscopy-guided approach
abstract: This case report describes a rare presentation of pulmonary melanoma of unknown primary managed through a same-day robotic diagnostic and therapeutic approach. A man in his 70s with an incidentally detected lingular pulmonary nodule suspicious for non-small cell lung cancer underwent robotic navigation bronchoscopy for biopsy and dye marking, immediately followed by robotic-assisted thoracic surgery. Intraoperative frozen section revealed a malignant spindle cell neoplasm, prompting definitive surgical resection during the same anaesthetic event. Final histopathology and molecular analysis confirmed melanoma, with no identifiable cutaneous, mucosal or ocular primary. The patient subsequently received adjuvant immunotherapy and remains disease-free at 24 months. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of pulmonary melanoma mimicking lung carcinoma and demonstrates how integration of robotic bronchoscopy and robotic surgery can enable rapid diagnosis, definitive management and streamlined care within a single operative session.

title: BronchoTop: Bronchoscopy Navigation via RGB-Only Topological Localization
abstract: Accurate localization of the bronchoscope within the bronchial tree is essential for clinicians to be able to reach target lesions, perform biopsies and avoid misidentification of airway segments during diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. However, existing navigation systems typically rely on patient-specific CT scans or additional external sensors, increasing cost, setup time and patient radiation exposure. This work presents BronchoTop, a real-time, RGB-only framework for topological bronchoscopy localization that eliminates the need for patient-specific data. BronchoTop estimates scope location relative to a generic airway model through four modules: lumen detection and tracking, lumen-branch label association, probabilistic scope location estimation, and switch verification. By using only standard bronchoscopy video input, BronchoTop provides practical, real-time navigational assistance to physicians. Evaluation on phantom, simulated and real data demonstrates state-of-the-art accuracy, improving existing approaches performance by over 20% on real bronchoscopy sequences. BronchoTop is the first published framework including both the localization algorithms as well as all the real data used, together with code to generate additional simulations, encouraging and facilitating further developments and benchmarking. The results highlight BronchoTop's potential to enhance procedural safety, efficiency and accessibility in clinical and robotic bronchoscopy.
authors: Clara Tomasini; Ana C. Murillo; Luis Riazuelo

title: Mitigating lateral sensing blind spots: A dual-segment bronchoscopic robot with a bioinspired skin
abstract: Lateral force blind spots frequently trigger airway injuries during robotic bronchoscopy. Traditional sensing approaches lack fine spatial resolution, and single-segment robots suffer poor posture adjustment flexibility, worsening unmonitored tissue contact. We integrate a snake-scale-inspired 64-channel gradient piezoelectric film with a dual-segment manipulator to resolve lateral blind spots for secure bronchial navigation. The conformally wrapped sensor delivers fast (<10 ms), precise force detection ( R 2 > 0.98, RMSE < 0.145 N, CV < 2%) and filters bending pseudo-forces. The dual-segment design enables coordinated proximal-distal motion to avoid overcontact in tortuous lumens. Phantom and ex vivo porcine lung tests confirm real-time force localization, 5.0 N safety alarms, and autonomous tuning to keep contact forces below 3.0 N. This synergistic robot-sensor design supplies a translatable safety control strategy for flexible surgical manipulators.
authors: Qiqi Pan; Wenke Duan; Jingjing Luo; Lei Wang; Shijie Guo; Yongfei Feng; Hongbo Wang

title: Global research trends in interventional bronchoscopy: a bibliometric analysis of publications from 2005 to 2025
abstract: Abstract Background The field of interventional bronchoscopy (IB) has experienced rapid advancements over the past two decades, evolving from a predominantly diagnostic modality into a highly technological specialty encompassing use of endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS), electromagnetic navigation bronchoscopy (ENB), robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (RAB), transbronchial cryobiopsy, airway stenting, and image-guided interventions. Although there have been emerging advancements in the practice of IB, no global research studies have comprehensively evaluated trends in the field. Objective To analyze the global scientific output, collaboration patterns, influential contributors, and thematic evolution of IB research from 2005 to 2025. Methods The bibliometric analysis was performed using Scopus database. Studies related to IB published from January 2005 to December 2025 were identified using predefined search strategy. Records were identified using the predefined search terms. The dataset was then cleaned by removing similar but non-relevant terms, and eligibility was restricted to research articles and conference papers, with review articles, book chapters, and other document types excluded. No language restriction was applied. Data were analyzed using the Bibliometrix and Biblioshiny packages in R. Results A total of 18,019 records were identified, of which 652 eligible publications were included, comprising 609 original research articles and 43 conference papers, with no language restriction. Publication output increased markedly after 2020. Zaroulidis P was the most productive author, while the United States, China, Japan, Germany, and the United Kingdom were among the leading contributing countries, with Nagoya University as the most productive institution. Highly cited studies mainly focused on airway stents and tracheal prostheses, bronchoscopic lung volume reduction, diagnostic and image-guided bronchoscopy, and procedural sedation and safety. More recent highly cited studies increasingly addressed robotic, computational, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted bronchoscopy. Randomized and comparative clinical trials are relatively limited but included EBUS-TBNA and ENB for diagnostic strategies, bronchoscopic lung volume reduction, airway stenting, hybrid EBUS, radial EBUS, and AI-assisted bronchoscopy. Research themes progressively shifted from diagnostic and imaging applications toward therapeutic, navigational, robotic, bioengineering, and AI-enabled approaches. Conclusions In conclusion, IB research has transitioned from predominantly diagnostic and imaging-based techniques (EBUS-TBNA and navigational bronchoscopy), toward therapeutic, robotic, image-guided, bioengineering, and AI-assisted interventions. Emerging bioengineering, and AI-assisted technologies hold promise for IB but require clinical validation.
authors: Tawseef Ahmad; Tawseef Ahmad; Tauqeer Ahmad; Tauqeer Ahmad; Fazal Mustaan; Jamil Ur Rahman; Muhammad Esa

title: Artificial intelligence and digital health in bronchoscopy: advances in diagnostic accuracy, real-time navigation and procedural skills training
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and procedure-linked digital health technologies are beginning to transform bronchoscopy across three interconnected domains. In terms of diagnostic accuracy, deep learning models applied to endobronchial ultrasound images and bronchoscopic videos can match or exceed human readers in differentiating benign from malignant lesions, although nearly all evidence remains at the level of test-accuracy metrics rather than clinical outcomes. In real-time navigation, AI-augmented fluoroscopy and tomosynthesis platforms represent the clearest example of clinically deployed AI that improves lesion localisation and diagnostic yield for peripheral pulmonary nodules, while camera-based localisation and shared-control robotic systems remain largely preclinical. In training, multiple randomised controlled trials demonstrate that AI-guided simulators significantly improve performance across experience levels, and that AI-derived metrics can objectively assess competence, although the first attempt to show impact on real-world clinical performance was inconclusive. This review synthesises the current literature across these three domains, distinguishing technologies that are currently used in clinical practice with supportive published evidence from those that remain investigational. It provides practising bronchoscopists and trainees with a balanced appraisal of what AI can realistically offer today, what limitations persist, and what developments are likely over the coming decade.
authors: Zakaria Mohamed Lahmar; Engi Ahmed; Quentin Wynands; Paul Reynaud; ARNAUD AB BOURDIN

title: Feasibility Of a Multi-Modal Sensing Guidewire for Tissue Interaction Awareness in Bronchoscopic Lung Cancer Intervention: A Conceptual Architecture and Validation Roadmap
abstract: Bronchoscopicaccess to peripheral pulmonary lesions has been transformed by navigation, robotic, and imaging-assisted platforms, yet the physical interaction between an instrument tip and airway tissue remains difficult to quantify directly.Conventional guidewires provide push ability, torque transmission, and mechanical steering, but generally do not return a direct quantitative signal describing tissue interaction.This paper presents a literature-grounded feasibility framework that reimagines the guidewire as a multimodal sensing platform rather than a purely mechanical component.Four complementary sensing channelsforce, localized pressure, electrical impedance, and temperature-are proposed within a guidewire-centred architecture.The methodology comprises channel calibration and signal conditioning, temporal synchronization, feature extraction, lightweight edgeassisted sensor fusion, confidence estimation, and human-in-the-loop clinician feedback.Artificial intelligence is deliberately positioned as a supporting interpretation layer for procedural interaction states rather than as an autonomous cancer-diagnosis mechanism.The study analyses the principal mechanical, electrical, miniaturization, packaging, safety, and manufacturing constraints and defines a staged validation pathway from component calibration and bench testing through tissue-mimicking phantom evaluation, AI validation, preclinical feasibility, and eventual clinical feasibility.No prototype measurements or clinical diagnostic performance are claimed in the present work.The principal outcome is a coherent, experimentally testable architecture and validation roadmap that identifies how quantitative instrumenttissue information could complement existing bronchoscopic navigation while preserving clinician control.Advanced technologies are retained as future extensions outside the present scope. Index Terms-bronchoscopic intervention,

title: Diagnostic Performance and Safety Profile of Shape-sensing Robotic-assisted Bronchoscopy in Peripheral Pulmonary Lesions: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Shape-sensing robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (ssRAB) has emerged as a promising modality for diagnosing peripheral pulmonary lesions (PPLs). This meta-analysis evaluated its diagnostic performance and safety profile. METHODS: PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library were searched from inception to December 2025. Study quality was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-3. Random-effects model was used to estimate the pooled diagnostic yield, sensitivity for malignancy, and complication, with rates (%) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) when the I2 index exceeded 50%. Cumulative meta-analysis was performed to assess the temporal stability and evidence saturation of the pooled diagnostic yield. Publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger's test. RESULTS: A total of 3678 lesions from 18 studies were included. Notably, diagnostic yield varied significantly by outcome definition, with pooled diagnostic yield of 82.5% (95% CI: 78.3%-86.0%) under strict definition versus 88.1% (95% CI: 82.8%-92.0%) under intermediate definition (P=0.036). The pooled sensitivity for malignancy of 90.0% (95% CI: 86.4%-92.8%). Cumulative meta-analysis showed stabilized diagnostic performance after approximately 1,500 lesions for the strict definition and 500 lesions for intermediate definition. Moreover, safety profile was favorable, with pooled rates of pneumothorax 1.8% (95% CI:1.3%-2.3%), chest tube placement 1.1% (95% CI: 0.7%-1.5%), and severe bleeding 0.0% (95% CI: 0.0%-0.3%). Subgroup analyses showed consistent performance across study designs, region, and nodule characteristics. Diagnostic yield was significantly influenced by publication year, and lesion size (P<0.05). CONCLUSION: ssRAB was associated with favorable, definition-dependent diagnostic yield (82.5%-88.1%) with exceptional safety, supporting ssRAB as an attractive first-line minimally invasive diagnostic option in appropriately selected patients, especially for small nodules (<2cm) and patients at elevated procedural risk.

title: Safety and Efficacy of Endobronchial Ultrasound
abstract: Abstract Purpose of review The use of bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) to aid in lymph node and lung biopsy is relatively new. This review will summarize the literature surrounding the efficacy of bronchoscopy with EBUS. Safety of bronchoscopy with EBUS is not markedly different that procedure with EBUS and is impacted by patient features including co-morbidities as well as different sedation modalities. This paper reviews the impact on both safety and diagnostic yield. Recent Findings The yield from using EBUS guided biopsy varies with the diagnosis but is high with linear EBUS. Recent data incorporating other technologies (electromagnetic navigation, robotic assistance) with bronchoscopy has potential to increase diagnostic yields, appears to be equivalent to transthoracic needle biopsies performed by radiology. Different sedation modalities are utilized, including the use of dedicated anesthesia providers, for bronchoscopy with EBUS but do not appear to significantly affect the diagnostic yield. Summary Bronchoscopy with EBUS (both linear and radial) is a safe procedure with acceptable yields. The type of sedation does not appear to affect the diagnostic yield or the safety of the procedure. Further research into incorporation of other technologies may provide for higher diagnostic yields.
authors: Travis Yamanaka; Kevin P. Haas

title: Single Anesthetic Approach to Diagnosis, Staging and Treatment of Lung Cancer
abstract: The conventional workup for suspected early-stage lung cancer requires multiple visits, anesthetics, and procedures. Single anesthetic event lung cancer surgery integrates shape-sensing robotic bronchoscopy, cone-beam CT, rapid on-site cytologic evaluation (ROSE), endobronchial ultrasound staging, lesion localization, and minimally invasive resection into one operative encounter. In this narrative review, we describe the technical components of this pathway, summarize the supporting literature, and offer expert, institution-based troubleshooting guidance for common intraoperative dilemmas. Reported diagnostic yields for shape-sensing robotic bronchoscopy range from 80 to 96%, with approximately 90% concordance between ROSE and final pathology. Published single-institution series report reductions in time from detection to resection of 15-51 days, cost savings of approximately $3000-$10,000, and perioperative outcomes (length of stay 1.8-3.6 days; complication rates comparable to traditional pathways) similar to staged care. The supporting evidence is retrospective and derived from small, single-institution, high-volume referral cohorts; no prospective comparative trials or long-term survival data yet exist. Single anesthetic event lung cancer surgery is therefore best regarded as an emerging, resource-intensive care pathway for carefully selected patients at experienced centers rather than an established standard of care, pending prospective, multicenter validation.
authors: Matthew Aizpuru; Jackson Wittenberg; Janani S. Reisenauer

title: Mobile cone-beam computed tomography combined with electromagnetic navigation bronchoscopy for the diagnosis of peripheral pulmonary nodules
abstract: BACKGROUND: Electromagnetic navigation bronchoscopy (ENB) is widely used for diagnosing peripheral pulmonary nodules (PPNs), but its diagnostic yield remains variable. Mobile cone-beam computed tomography (mCBCT) enables intraprocedural assessment of the tool-lesion relationship and navigation correction; however, prospective data on its incremental clinical value remain limited. RESEARCH QUESTION: Clinical value of mCBCT-guided navigation correction on the tool-lesion relationship and diagnostic yield during ENB for PPNs. STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: This prospective, single-centre, single-arm trial evaluated the diagnostic performance of mCBCT-assisted ENB for PPNs and the incremental clinical value of mCBCT-guided navigation correction. Intraoperative mCBCT assessed the tool-lesion relationship and guided correction before sampling. The primary endpoint was overall diagnostic yield after mCBCT assessment and adjustment. The key secondary endpoint was the tool-in-lesion improvement rate. RESULTS: A total of 108 patients were enrolled. Median nodule size was 21.0 (IQR, 17.0-25.0) mm, and a CT 'bronchus sign' was present in 77.8%. Nodules were peripheral (47.2%), intermediate (33.3%), or central (19.4%) and solid (83.3%), mixed ground-glass opacities (13.9%), or pure ground-glass opacities (2.8%). The overall diagnostic yield was 79.6% (86/108). Navigation correction was required in 42.6% (46/108). Following mCBCT-guided navigation correction, the tool-in-lesion rate increased from 54.6% (59/108) to 87.0% (94/108), an absolute improvement of 32.4%. Procedure-related atelectasis was identified by mCBCT in 8 (7.4%) patients. No serious adverse events occurred. CONCLUSION: mCBCT-guided navigation correction improved the tool-lesion relationship and provided incremental clinical value beyond conventional ENB, particularly for smaller lesions and those without a CT bronchus sign, while maintaining an acceptable safety profile.
authors: Lin Ye; Siyuan Hong; Xiaoxuan Zheng; Junxiang Chen; Fangfang Xie; Shuaiyang Liu; Houteng Xi; Jiajia Ge; Xiaoshu Cai; Jiayuan Sun

title: Revolutionizing Lung Cancer Management: AI-Powered Liquid Biopsy–Immunotherapy Synergy For Early Internist-Led Interventions In High-Risk Populations
abstract: Lung cancer continues to be a predominant global cause of death. Clinical outcomes are significantly influenced by the timely identification of high-risk populations, accurate diagnosis, and appropriate therapy selection. Progress in artificial intelligence (AI), liquid biopsy, and immunotherapy has opened new avenues for improving diagnostic accuracy and individualized treatment. Therefore, this review aimed to summarize the current evidence regarding the integration of artificial intelligence, liquid biopsy, and immunotherapy in improving lung cancer diagnosis, treatment selection, and personalized management. structured literature search was conducted in PubMed using keywords related to AI, liquid biopsy, immunotherapy, and lung cancer, with a focus on publications from the past 10 years. Of 18,169 records, 45 studies were selected after screening. AI-driven deep learning and radiomics enhance the precision of early detection, distinguish between benign and malignant nodules, and predict molecular changes, including EGFR, ALK, and PD-L1 expression. Liquid biopsy facilitates the non-invasive identification of biomarkers, such as ctDNA, CTCs, and exosomes, while AI enhances the interpretation of biomarkers and the characterization of cancer. AI models, such as CNN and multiomics methodologies, accurately predict treatment response and prognosis, thereby facilitating informed decision-making for immunotherapy. The combination of AI, liquid biopsy, and immunotherapy has significant potential to improve lung cancer management by enabling earlier diagnosis, personalized treatment, and improved response prediction
authors: Galih Yudo Pranowo; Gilang Prayoga Putra Permana; Dita Ria Selvyana

title: Fully automatic airway segmentation in CT images via dual-stage neural network with topology-constrained centerline completion
abstract: Background: Precise segmentation of airways from computed tomography (CT) images is critical for pre-procedural planning in navigational bronchoscopy; however, existing methods often suffer from distal branch fractures and morphological losses due to slender diameters, low contrast, and noise. To address these limitations and achieve accurate, topologically complete airway segmentation, this study proposed a novel dual-stage neural network with topology-constrained centerline completion. Methods: A two-stage centerline-guided network (TSC-Net) was developed that innovatively combines centerline structural similarity (CSS) loss and centerline overlap rate (COR) loss. CSS loss maintains the continuity of airway tree structures by strengthening centerline morphological constraints, while COR loss enhances global centerline overlap to ensure branch integrity. Additionally, a topology-difference-driven fracture-region completion mechanism was adopted to adaptively repair the fracturedand misclassified areas. The model employs a residual UNet (ResUNet) backbone integrated with an atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASPP) module to capture multi-scale contextual features and adopts a two-stage training strategy in which the encoder is frozen during stage 2 while the decoder is fine-tuned using dynamically adjusted loss weights. This strategy enables targeted optimization of discontinuous regions without compromising globally well-predicted areas. Results: Experiments on the Airway Tree Modeling Challenge 2022 (ATM'22), Lung Image Database Consortium and Image Database Resource Initiative (LIDC-IDRI), Extraction of Airways from CT (EXACT'09), and private datasets showed that TSC-Net achieved a Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 93.2%±2.1%, significantly outperforming SwinUNETR (92.9%±3.6%, P<0.05), nnUNet (91.2%±1.2%, P<0.05), and UNet (75.6%±4.3%, P<0.05). The tree-length detection (TD) rate reached 95.5%±4.2%, and the branch detection (BD) rate reached 92.6%±3.6%, both of which were significantly higher than those of all baseline methods (P<0.01). Moreover, the segmented distal branches exhibited continuous and smooth morphology. Conclusions: Overall, our method significantly enhanced both segmentation accuracy and distal branch integrity in automated CT-based airway segmentation through multi-dimensional feature enhancement, topological constraint optimization, and a dynamic completion mechanism. This method holds great promise for pre-procedural planning in robotic-assisted bronchoscopy by enabling accurate visualization of peripheral airways and facilitating navigation to distant pulmonary targets.
authors: Harmony Yuan; Yuan Cheng; Chengxi Yan; Jiangang Chen; Qian Ding; Ying Zhou; Minglei Yang
venue: Quantitative Imaging in Medicine and Surgery

title: Simultaneous dual cryobiopsy using two bronchoscopes for multiple peripheral lung lesions: a novel case report
abstract: Abstract Introduction Bronchoscopic biopsy of multiple pulmonary lesions is typically performed sequentially, often requiring repeated imaging confirmation during cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)–guided procedures. Case presentation We report a novel technique using simultaneous dual cryobiopsy with two bronchoscopes to sample separate lesions during a single CBCT acquisition. A patient with multiple lesions in the left upper lobe underwent bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia. Two bronchoscopes were inserted simultaneously through a 9 mm endotracheal tube: an Ambu aScope 5 Broncho (4.2 mm outer diameter, 2.2 mm working channel) with a 1.9 mm reusable cryoprobe and an Olympus MP190F bronchoscope with a 1.1 mm cryoprobe. A single CBCT spin confirmed simultaneous tool-in-lesion positioning for both cryoprobes. Cryobiopsies were obtained successfully from both lesions. Histopathological examination revealed squamous cell carcinoma. Conclusion This case demonstrates the technical feasibility of simultaneous dual cryobiopsy and suggests a potential strategy to improve procedural efficiency and reduce imaging requirements during CBCT-guided bronchoscopy.
authors: Sammy Onyancha; Philipp Conzelmann; Ahmad Sajad Soltani; Tanja Dieball; Gernot G. U. Rohde

title: Navigation Bronchoscopy Specific Cone-Beam CT Software Enabling Pre- And Intraprocedural Guidance
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)- guided bronchoscopy is an established technique for diagnosing peripheral pulmonary lesions, offering 3-dimensional imaging for both navigation and confirmation. However, its usability as a stand-alone modality is limited by a substantial learning curve and a lack of integrated planning tools. This study evaluates the feasibility and performance of navigation bronchoscopy-specific CBCT software that enables preprocedural CT-planning fusion with intraprocedural CBCT imaging and provides intraprocedural support algorithms. METHODS: This prospective, single-center clinical feasibility study exploratively assessed the usability of the AirWaze investigational software. Usability was measured using a standardized system usability score, with scores of 70 or higher considered indicative of good usability (range, 0-100). The performance of the individual software components ('planning,' 'image fusion,' and 'guidance') was evaluated. An ultralow-dose CBCT protocol was compared with conventional CBCT scans for accuracy and radiation exposure. RESULTS: The study enrolled 34 patients with 37 lesions. The investigational software achieved a system usability score of 45. The planning component was available in all cases and was unanimously rated by the endoscopists as accurate and intuitive. In contrast, the image fusion and guidance components were rated as insufficient. The ultralow-dose CBCT protocol provided clinically accurate imaging in 84% of cases and reduced the radiation dose by 94%. CONCLUSION: Integrating planning and procedural guidance within stand-alone CBCT-guided navigation bronchoscopy procedures has great potential. Although several components of the investigational software were considered valuable, further development is required to ensure comprehensive procedural guidance.
authors: Inge Nicole Wijma; William van der Sterren; Roel L.J. Verhoeven; Erik H.F.M. van der Heijden

title: Metabolism of the scientific journal on domestic radiology
abstract: The purpose of this article is to present more fundamentally the natural metabolism of science and the scientific journal, partly using examples from radiology. The journal article is the main tool and practice of the researcher in converting personal knowledge into public knowledge for its verification and pragmatic realization. In national medicine and radiology, there is a problem of long-term preservation of knowledge (the work of scientists and state finances) and its accessibility against the backdrop of the emergence of new journals and their disappearance. If earlier there was a problem with the publication of articles due to the shortage of journals and the queue for publication, now there is a problem with the shortage of high-quality content articles. Virtually all significant results in the exact sciences (at least in the English-speaking world) can be found in the pages of just two journals: “Nature” and “Science”. Lotka’s law is mentioned in the aspect of the scientific literature citation system as a means of tracking the development of science. Attention is drawn to the formation of a new subspecialty – medical writers (since 1940). The replication crisis is described (possibly caused by human factors), a methodological crisis in which the results of many scientific studies are difficult or impossible to reproduce. The mobilization of science in the journal “Radiation diagnostics, radiation therapy” during the COVID-19 pandemic is considered using the example of articles “Low-dose radiation therapy for COVID-19 pneumonia”, “COVID-modulated emphysematous pyelonephritis against the background of severe course of oxygen-dependent covid pneumonia” та “Echocardiographic characteristics of complicated course of coronavirus infection in children (COVID-19) (review and portfolio)”. The bibliometrics of the journal “Radiology” (journal of the Radiological Society of North America.) are presented for comparison: the most viewed articles of 2021 and the most cited articles of 2021. It is demonstrated that the topic of the most cited articles of 2023 is artificial intelligence.
authors: Nikolay Kolotilov

title: Towards clinical translation of endobronchial optical ultrasound imaging
abstract: Abstract Optical ultrasound (OpUS) imaging provides an optical alternative to conventional piezoelectric ultrasound, offering miniaturised interventional probes and clinically-relevant image quality at video-rate frame rates. Here, we report advances in the clinical applicability of a linearly actuated OpUS (LiOpUS) imaging system developed for endobronchial applications, incorporating a clinically relevant probe length and dynamic control over the orientation of the image plane. The system comprises a side-viewing OpUS probe exceeding 2 m in length, a motorised platform enabling both linear scanning and controlled probe rotation, and a compact and integrated imaging console supporting real-time data acquisition and real-time, GPU-accelerated image reconstruction. System performance was assessed in a range of clinically relevant scenarios in terms of both actuator dynamics and imaging performance, confirming the rotational mount exhibited minimal impact on linear scanning motion and effective imaging-plane adjustment over clinically relevant probe length. The results demonstrate a significant step of LiOpUS imaging toward future clinical deployment for endobronchial guidance, validating the system’s compact, mobile design and imaging performance in clinically representative scenarios, and motivating progression to preclinical studies.
authors: Shaoyan Zhang; Semyon Bodian; Nyma Nassren; Ksenia Odintsova; Edward Zhang; Paul C. Beard; Richard J. Colchester; Adrien E. Desjardins; Erwin J. Alles

title: Artificial Intelligence-Related Risks in Interventional Pulmonology: An Exploratory Enumeration and Ranking Study Across Five General-Purpose Large Language Models
abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering interventional pulmonology (IP) faster than its potential risks have been systematically catalogued. We explored whether general-purpose large language models (LLMs), now widely consulted informally by patients and clinicians, could provide a rapid and structured means of enumerating and ranking candidate AI-related risks in IP, potentially contributing to risk awareness and hypothesis generation. Methods: Five LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek) were each queried once, in independent, memory-free sessions, with one standardised prompt requesting ten ranked AI-related risks with impact and likelihood scores (1–5); an informal repeat administration was performed, but output stability was not formally assessed. The resulting 50 risk statements were inductively coded, by an AI coder with independent human validation by two reviewers, into 15 constructs nested in 8 higher-order domains. Results: Mean self-assigned impact was 3.92 (SD 0.78) and mean likelihood 3.54 (SD 0.68). The eight domains comprised AI technical/perceptual accuracy (diagnostic, detection and navigational error); automation bias and over-reliance; generalisability, algorithmic bias and health equity; model and system reliability over time; erosion of procedural competence; explainability, transparency and accountability; cybersecurity, privacy and data integrity; and cognitive and workflow burden. Five domains were raised by all five models and the remaining three by four of five. Two domains-AI technical/perceptual accuracy and automation bias-together accounted for every model’s two highest-ranked risks, and no risk statement outside these two domains was ranked first or second by any model. Deskilling (erosion of procedural competence), although listed by all five models, was never ranked above third by any model, whereas practising IP specialists in our prior international survey rated it the single highest research priority. Conclusions: These exploratory and hypothesis-generating findings suggest that general-purpose LLMs may have potential as a rapid, low-burden means of enumerating and ranking candidate AI-related risks and broadening awareness of issues that may warrant further investigation in IP. The lower ranking of deskilling by the LLMs than by domain experts indicates that LLM-generated rankings may under-prioritise risks that clinicians consider most important. Although their outputs are not validated measures of clinical risk and do not replace expert appraisal, we believe they may provide a starting point for subsequent human-led risk assessment and prioritization in an area of research that remains largely unexplored yet is highly relevant to patient safety.
authors: Gianluca Marchi; Lorenzo Corbetta

title: The unified front: a multidisciplinary approach in the Era of uniportal thoracic surgery
abstract: The evolution of thoracic surgery from open thoracotomy to uniportal video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (U-VATS) represents a paradigm shift toward minimizing surgical trauma. However, the changing landscape of thoracic oncology-characterized by an increase in subsolid nodules, multifocal ground-glass opacities, and locally advanced disease requiring neoadjuvant therapy-demands more than surgical innovation alone. This review explores the critical intersection of U-VATS with multidisciplinary collaboration. We examine how the integration of medical oncology, interventional pulmonology, and radiology enhances the capabilities of the single-port approach. This review will discuss specific combinatorial techniques, including uniportal lung resection following neoadjuvant treatment, navigation bronchoscopic-guided localization strategies, and combining U-VATS with concomitant transbronchial ablation. Finally, we address the logistical and economic challenges inherent in maintaining such complex collaborative frameworks.
authors: Aliss Chang; Wei Liu; Joyce Chan; Clarence Chan; Rainbow Lau; Calvin Ng

title: Initial Diagnosis of Hematologic Malignancies Identified Through Thyroid Fine‐Needle Aspiration
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of the thyroid is crucial in diagnosing thyroid malignancies. While secondary malignancies involving the thyroid constitute only a minority of cases, results from thyroid FNA can offer the initial insight into a systemic process. This retrospective study aims to investigate first-time diagnoses of hematologic malignancies diagnosed by thyroid FNA within our institution in the past 4 years. METHODS: We performed a retrospective review of first-time hematologic neoplasm diagnoses in our pathology database at the University of Colorado Hospital. A total number of 3747 thyroid FNAs were performed during the four-year period. Malignant categories with hematologic neoplasms were chosen for a thorough chart review. Cases of thyroidal involvement by previously diagnosed systemic hematologic neoplasms were excluded. For this study cohort, demographic data and clinicopathologic findings such as age, clinical impression, final cytologic diagnosis, presence of rapid on-site evaluation (ROSE), and additional ancillary testing for every case were collected. RESULTS: The study included nine cases (four males and five females) with a mean age of 53 ± 14.46 years (range: 27-75 years). Five cases had a history of prior thyroid FNA with no definitive diagnosis. ROSE was performed in each of the nine cases. Five cases of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), one case of low-grade follicular lymphoma (FL), one case of plasma cell myeloma, one case of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH), and one case of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) were identified on thyroid FNA. Several patients were at a high stage of disease with systemic involvement at presentation. The patients were treated with chemotherapy (DLBCL, FL, and plasma cell myeloma cases) or targeted therapy (LCH and CML cases). CONCLUSIONS: Hematolymphoid malignancies involving the thyroid gland are challenging to diagnose as they are rare and may mimic other primary thyroid malignancies. However, we find that the thyroid can be the initial and sometimes the only site of presentation of a hematologic malignancy. Thorough cytomorphologic assessment, collaboration with hematopathologists, and ROSE are valuable tools for ensuring appropriate initial testing and facilitating timely, accurate diagnoses.
authors: Catherine L. Eschen; Sanjana Mehrotra

title: Single-center experience in combined video-assisted thoracic surgery with transbronchial microwave ablation—a novel approach to multifocal lung nodules
abstract: Background: The management of multifocal lung malignancies presents significant challenges, particularly when extensive resection may not be feasible due to limited pulmonary reserve. Thus, a hybrid management approach combining lung surgery with transbronchial local ablation has been developed to control local disease while minimizing lung parenchymal loss. We evaluated the safety, feasibility, and mid-term clinical outcomes of this hybrid approach in managing multifocal lung lesions. Methods: A retrospective single-center review was conducted of patients who underwent combined video-assisted thoracic surgery (VATS) lung resection and transbronchial microwave ablation (TMWA) in a hybrid operating room (HOR) between November 2019 and April 2026. Patient demographics, tumor characteristics, procedural details, perioperative complications, and mid-term clinical outcomes were reported, including intraoperative technical success, 30-day morbidity, overall survival, and rate of local recurrence. Results: Twenty-two patients (mean age 56.8 ± 11.8 years) with multifocal lung malignancies or suspicious multifocal lung nodules were discussed at a multidisciplinary team meeting. All twenty-two patients underwent 23 combined procedures. A total of 70 lesions were treated: 41 by VATS resection and 29 by TMWA. Technical success was achieved in 100% of procedures, as confirmed by intraoperative cone-beam computed tomography. The 30-day complication rate was 21.7%, with no procedure-related 30-day mortality. 20 patients have follow-up beyond 30 days (two patients were lost to follow-up). At a median follow-up of 24 months, the local control rate for ablated lesions was 96.6%, with local-recurrence-free survival of 95% and overall survival of 85%. Among the 41 resected lung lesions, 17 were multifocal lung adenocarcinoma, 22 were metastatic nodules, and two showed no evidence of malignancy. However, preoperative histopathological confirmation was available for only four ablated lesions, which showed either atypical pneumocytes or lung adenocarcinoma. Conclusions: Hybrid treatment combining VATS and TMWA is a safe and feasible approach for multifocal lung lesions, with reasonable complication rates and acceptable mid-term disease control. This hybrid technique may offer benefits in parenchymal preservation, particularly in patients with borderline lung function, while achieving reasonable local control.
authors: Aliss T. C. Chang; Rainbow W. H. Lau; Joyce W. Y. Chan; Wei Liu; Calvin S.H. Ng

title: Bronchoscope Tip Localization With Learned Airway Constraints and an Open Source Simulator
abstract: Accurate bronchoscope localization is challenging because airway images contain limited texture and similar views across branches. We present BronchoLoc, a learning‐based framework that combines monocular video with a preoperative CT centerline graph to estimate the 3D bronchoscope tip position. Local visual tracking and global sequence context constrain predictions to the airway anatomy. The accompanying open‐source BronchoSim simulator generates synchronized images, depth, and trajectories (Traj) for training and evaluation. Averaged across Traj, localization RMSE was 5.65 mm in simulation with 82.8% branch selection accuracy and 8.72 mm in the physical phantom. Together, BronchoLoc and BronchoSim provide a framework for developing and evaluating image‐based airway localization.
authors: Emanuele Nicotra; James Davies; Bibhu Sharma; Adrienne Ji; Kefan Zhu; Phuoc Thien Phan; Nigel Hamilton Lovell; Thanh Nho Do

title: Cerebral Air Embolism After Navigational Bronchoscopy Treated With Aspiration Thrombectomy: A Case Report
abstract: Systemic arterial air embolism is a rare but potentially devastating complication of bronchoscopic lung biopsy.A 68-year-old man with severe emphysema developed abrupt bradycardia, hypotension, and failure to regain consciousness after navigational bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia.Computed tomography demonstrated air within the left middle cerebral artery, and angiography confirmed proximal large-vessel occlusion.Urgent aspiration thrombectomy achieved complete reperfusion after one pass, with retrieved material compatible with thrombus.Despite technically successful reperfusion, major neurological deficits persisted.This case highlights haemodynamic collapse and delayed emergence as warning signs and supports rapid neuroimaging with selective endovascular treatment when an accessible large-vessel occlusion is present.
authors: Matthew Eardley; Anushka Jayakrishnan; Essam Hashem; Darshana Dhaka; Ashvini Menon

title: Endobronchial Pulmonary Typical Carcinoid Tumors in Young Adults: A Three-Case Series Highlighting Obstructive Complications and Surgical Outcomes
abstract: Background: Typical pulmonary carcinoid tumors are uncommon, well-differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasms that often arise in the central airways and may present with nonspecific obstruction-related respiratory symptoms, resulting in delayed diagnosis. We report a three-case series of endobronchial typical pulmonary carcinoid tumors in young adults, highlighting their variable obstructive complications and surgical outcomes. Methods: This retrospective case series included three consecutive patients managed at a tertiary university hospital in Syria. Clinical presentation, imaging, bronchoscopic findings, operative details, histopathology, and follow-up data were obtained from medical records. All patients had histopathologically confirmed typical pulmonary carcinoid tumors with central/endobronchial involvement and underwent definitive surgical resection. Patient identifiers were removed, and written informed consent for publication and use of accompanying images was obtained. Results: The patients were 23-35 years old and presented with different manifestations of central airway obstruction: chronic productive cough (Case 1), post-obstructive suppuration with lung abscesses (Case 2), and recurrent hemoptysis with atelectatic/post-obstructive changes (Case 3). Bronchoscopy demonstrated obstructing endobronchial lesions in all three cases, and histopathology confirmed typical carcinoid tumors with low mitotic activity and no necrosis. Case 1 underwent right middle and lower bilobectomy with systematic mediastinal lymph node dissection for a large tumor staged T4N1M0. Cases 2 and 3 underwent left lower lobectomy; in Case 3, this included bronchial segment resection with primary closure and mediastinal lymph node dissection. Resection margins were negative in all cases, and mediastinal nodes were negative in Cases 2 and 3. No adjuvant therapy was administered. Follow-up showed no recurrence approximately 4.5 years after surgery in Case 1, clinical stability at one month in Case 2, and stable chest imaging at six months in Case 3. Conclusion: Endobronchial typical pulmonary carcinoid tumors in young adults can produce diverse obstruction-related complications, including chronic cough, post-obstructive suppuration, and hemoptysis with atelectatic changes. Timely airway evaluation and complete surgical resection with appropriate nodal assessment can achieve favorable outcomes, including in locally advanced disease when complete resection is feasible.
authors: Issam Alkhayer; Mohammad Alaa Aldakak; Youssef Abbas

title: The future of surgery
abstract: Abstract Surgery is entering a period of accelerated transformation driven by artificial intelligence, robotics, and emerging postmodern medical technologies. Unlike prior technological shifts, innovation cycles are compressing into years, challenging established models of evidence generation, regulation, training, and professional identity. This Perspective examines plausible trajectories for digital surgery, emphasizing ethical, educational, and institutional adaptation under conditions of continuous technological acceleration rather than offering definitive predictions.

title: Continuum Robots in Surgery: From Engineering Design to Clinical Practice
abstract: Over the past decades, continuum robots have made significant advancements, yet are still minimally used in industry. The medical field has demonstrated growing interest in these robots, particularly in research but clinical translation has been limited. Their hyper‐redundant structures enable infinite degrees of freedom, offering a wide range of benefits. Specifically, continuum robots are able to navigate torturous pathways reaching deep areas of the body with improved dexterity and minimal risk. This review provides a historical overview of continuum robots and highlights key innovations that have shaped their development. The history also traces the emergence of robotic‐assisted surgery, contextualizing the clinical motivation for the rise of continuum robots. It examines the fundamentals of continuum robot design including structural configurations, sensing technology, modeling techniques, and control strategies. Together, these provide an in‐depth understanding of continuum robots and the common underlying principles as a guide for their future design. The review also discusses medical considerations, current clinical applications, and major challenges that continue to limit the widespread adoption of continuum robots. With decades of development in continuum robots, synthesizing this information is crucial to improving accessibility in the field and fostering continued research and innovation in these highly promising medical systems.
authors: Griffin Smith; Kaitlyn Clancy; Siwen Xie; Xiaochen Li; Sarah Khalifé; Benjamin D. van der Woerd; Onaizah Onaizah

title: ColoACT: Multi-Cue Action Chunking for Smooth Autonomous Colon Navigation on a Self-Propelled Endoscopic Robot
abstract: Autonomous colonoscopic navigation can reduce operator burden and the risk of loop formation or tissue trauma, but remains challenging due to deformable anatomy, weak-texture and specular endoscopic visuals, and contact-rich viscoelastic interactions. Existing methods either rely on geometry-driven pipelines, which are efficient and interpretable yet brittle due to manually engineered features and switching logic, or adopt learning-based policies, whose inferred depth/geometry can become temporally inconsistent or overly smooth under weak texture and specular highlights while simulation-trained variants (e.g., deep reinforcement learning) may further suffer from a sim-to-real gap. We propose ColoACT, an autonomous navigation system that integrates an RGB-D-E based Action Chunking Transformer policy (ColoACT policy) for a compact self-propelled Bevel-Gear-Based Endoscopic Robot (BGER). The ColoACT policy augments RGB with estimated relative depth and a gradient-based pseudo-elevation map to enhance fold-ridge saliency and other high-frequency geometric cues, and enables smooth continuous control of the BGER by predicting overlapping action chunks and fusing them via temporal ensembling. In different \textit{ex-vivo} porcine colons (approximately 60 cm), our system achieves success rates of 85.4\% and 72.5\% in straight and curved segments, respectively, and achieves 70\% success in 90-degree turns and 60\% in double-bend sequences, with feasibility further demonstrated in challenging triple-bend segments. The project page is available at: https://Adamhu1.github.io/ColoACT/.

title: Early applications of apple vision pro in clinical medicine and medical education: a scoping review
abstract: The Apple Vision Pro (AVP), a next-generation spatial computing device, has demonstrated potential applications in multidisciplinary clinical diagnosis, treatment, and medical education, by leveraging its unique technical architecture and performance advantages. In clinical practice, its fundamental advantages of three-dimensional (3D) visualization, real-time image integration, and immersive interaction have been preliminarily employed in disease diagnosis and treatment, surgical planning, precise operations, and postoperative rehabilitation across multiple disciplines. In medical education, AVP surpasses the limitations of conventional models, offering a novel methodology for anatomy education, clinical skills development, specialized practical training, and collaboration of distance learning, thereby alleviating persistent challenges such as unequal distribution of teaching resources, low efficiency in skills and specialized training, and the high cost of distance education. However, AVP faces some limitations, including limited hardware portability, insufficient system compatibility, a lack of specialized medical applications, high costs, and incomplete medical certification. Currently, most evidence derives from feasibility studies, case reports, and opinion pieces. Only two Stage 2b confirmatory studies were identified. Thus, high-level evidence for clinical benefit remains scarce. Readers should interpret all reported benefits as preliminary technical demonstrations rather than established clinical outcomes. Future advancements necessitate iterative development of lightweight hardware design, development of specialized medical software, cross-system optimization, and establishment of standardization protocols. Moreover, more randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and multicenter studies are urgently needed to fully explore and validate its intrinsic value in precision medicine and the equitable allocation of medical resources.
authors: Yiwei Hu; Yaqin Wang; Xiaohua Zuo; Haibo Hu; Bo Min; Chengxiang Wang; Chengxiang Wang; Zilong Tang; Ning Xiao; Chenjun Huang; 王储蓄; 王储蓄

title: StenoVLA-3D: 3D-Aware Reasoning VLA for Navigation Through Gastrointestinal Stenoses
abstract: Autonomous endoscopic navigation requires the policy model to predict actions from texture-poor monocular observations, make safe control decisions, and retain evidence of lesions after they leave the field of view. Existing vision-language-action (VLA) models primarily rely on visual appearance and short-term context, limiting geometric grounding and episode-level reporting. We introduce StenoVLA-3D, a 3D-aware VLA framework for navigating through stenotic regions. We integrate point-maps into the Cosmos-Reason 2 backbone through learned geometry-gated fusion, and also propose a temporal state branch to model traversal progress. Our reasoning-and-action backbone predicts grounded reasoning with actions, while dedicated heads estimate stenosis shape and generate the final lesion report. We further introduce EndoCausal, an episode-level dataset with lesion annotations, actions, and temporally grounded reasoning. On 40 held-out recorded test episodes, StenoVLA-3D reaches 95.2\% semantic accuracy and 83.4\% action accuracy. On the physical 3-DoF endoscope, it attains 88.9\% and 77.8\% task success in esophageal and colonic phantoms (36 trials each), substantially outperforming the evaluated baselines.
authors: Tamima Tabassum; Yiming Huang; Tianchun Wu; Changjing Liu; Zhiqing Tang; Chi Kit Ng; Beilei Cui; Liangjing Shao; Jiewen Lai; Hongliang Ren

title: GPU-resident Execution for Timing-predictable Sensor Processing Systems
abstract: Real-time embedded systems increasingly place GPU-accelerated processing of high-bandwidth sensor streams inside closed-loop systems, but the CPU (the host) remains the primary orchestrator of each iteration. The host observes sensor inputs, submits CUDA work, waits for completion, and commits actuation. This host-mediated path exposes the closed-loop end-to-end latency to I/O interrupts, host scheduler decisions, and CUDA API overheads even after common host-side mitigations such as GPU-memory RDMA or CPU core isolation. This paper presents GPU-resident Execution, a new execution model for real-time sensor processing pipelines that keeps I/O and GPU execution in a long-lived device-resident loop. Sensor inputs arrive in GPU memory, trigger GPU-side processing, and reach GPU-visible output endpoints without any host wakeups. We implement the model in the NVIDIA Holoscan C++ framework and provide reference components for building GPU-resident applications. We evaluate our system on NVIDIA GPUs and SoCs with inference, host-contention, multi-loop, and streaming camera workloads. On an industry-grade 1080p, 60 Hz real-time camera-to-display application, GPU-resident Execution reduces photon-to-display jitter from 4.83 ms to 0.66 ms (7.3x) relative to a CPU-driven GPU-memory RDMA baseline and reduces software-processing jitter from 1.70 ms to 0.01 ms (170x).
authors: Soham Sinha; Rahul Choudhury; Shekhar Dwivedi; Gregory Lee; Gigon Bae; Anisha Goel; Elena Agostini; Patrick O'Grady; Yosi Levi; Mahdi Azizian

title: BronchoTop: Bronchoscopy Navigation via RGB-Only Topological Localization
abstract: Accurate localization of the bronchoscope within the bronchial tree is essential for clinicians to be able to reach target lesions, perform biopsies and avoid misidentification of airway segments during diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. However, existing navigation systems typically rely on patient-specific CT scans or additional external sensors, increasing cost, setup time and patient radiation exposure. This work presents BronchoTop, a real-time, RGB-only framework for topological bronchoscopy localization that eliminates the need for patient-specific data. BronchoTop estimates scope location relative to a generic airway model through four modules: lumen detection and tracking, lumen-branch label association, probabilistic scope location estimation, and switch verification. By using only standard bronchoscopy video input, BronchoTop provides practical, real-time navigational assistance to physicians. Evaluation on phantom, simulated and real data demonstrates state-of-the-art accuracy, improving existing approaches performance by over 20% on real bronchoscopy sequences. BronchoTop is the first published framework including both the localization algorithms as well as all the real data used, together with code to generate additional simulations, encouraging and facilitating further developments and benchmarking. The results highlight BronchoTop's potential to enhance procedural safety, efficiency and accessibility in clinical and robotic bronchoscopy.
authors: Clara Tomasini; Ana Cristina Murillo; Luis Riazuelo

title: Recent Advances in Automated Single-Cell Manipulation Platforms: Optical Tweezers, Microfluidics, Microrobots, and Micropipette/Microneedle Systems
abstract: Automated micromanipulation enables precise, repeatable interaction with single cells and subcellular structures. This review examines four platform archetypes defined by their dominant interaction mechanism: field-mediated optical tweezers, flow-mediated automated microfluidics, mobile microrobots, and fixed-probe micropipette/microneedle systems. Rather than treating them as equivalent robot classes, the review compares their working principles, sensing and control architectures, application fit, quantitative performance evidence, and biological trade-offs. Recent advances in closed-loop operation, intelligent perception, multimodal sensing, and hybrid workflows are analyzed, and a standardized set of reporting metrics is proposed to support objective comparison and translation.

title: MICROROBOTIC SAMPLING AND QUANTUM BIOSENSING CO-DESIGN AT THE LIMIT An Exploratory Engineering Monograph on Sample Handling, Reference Control, and Biological Risk Boundaries This research monograph examines whether controlled micromanipulation can improve the positioning, transport, recovery, and reproducibility of biological research samples without increasing sample alteration, cross-contamination, thermal exposure, or misleading biosensor signals. The guiding three-coupling is Sample Handling × Reference Control × Biological Risk Boundary. Its guiding question is not whether an autonomous microrobot can move a sample, but whether the resulting measurement remains traceable to an authentic, independently verifiable sample state. The work synthesizes three mother research architectures: (S) Swarm Manufacturing and Robotic Matter at the Limit, particularly chapters 9–16 and 33–40, for embodied manipulation and collective transport; (QH) Autonomous Quantum Health Infrastructure at the Limit, especially chapters 9–24 and 67–74, for raw-to-result lineage, uncertainty-aware decisions, human authority and recovery; and (QB) Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit, particularly chapters 57–73, for fabrication variation, reference transfer, calibration, drift and measurement integrity. These sources contribute methods rather than evidence that the cross-domain integration is already demonstrated. Across 82 chapters and 12 single-section research studies per chapter, the monograph examines non-clinical microfluidic sample environments, magnetic and acoustic micromanipulation, optical and electrokinetic methods, nanoscale surface chemistry, quantum-enabled and classical biosensing, correlated uncertainty, sample-to-signal provenance, authorized closed-loop control, physical damage and carryover detection, interlaboratory replication, lifecycle burden, and successor reconstruction. Thirty mathematical and physical derivation plates introduce assumptions and validity boundaries. Every chapter presents a distinct candidate engineering relation and a geometric three-dimensional research portrait. The validation approach prioritizes synthetic phantoms and permitted ex-vivo research standards in closed non-clinical environments. It calls for blinded comparison of skilled manual pipetting, passive microfluidics, and robotic operation under matched sample identity, measurement time, contamination constraints, and independent calibration. A perceived improvement in robotic throughput or algorithmic readout quality does not establish improved sample authenticity. Any claim of quantum advantage must be compared against an appropriate, strong classical sensing baseline end to end. The research architecture closes with 200 independently framed Research Gates and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos, each accompanied by one of 233 indexed equation eggs. Gates specify questions, comparators, pass criteria, and veto conditions; answer embryos can be challenged, decomposed, recombined or retired. An accompanying Research Gates spreadsheet maps these questions to chapters, physical relations, evidence packets and future experiments. The study is explicitly exploratory and non-clinical. It does not establish the existence of mature autonomous in-body nanorobotic medicine, grant permission for diagnosis or therapy, or imply that quantum-enabled detection is intrinsically superior. Candidate indices and equations are design hypotheses unless identified as established physical relations; many passages use a recurring structured research grammar and require independent experiments, domain expert review, and peer assessment. The aim is to leave a reproducible and falsifiable research architecture that subsequent investigators are free to revise, reject, or extend.
