title: Beyond Completion Time: A Multimodal Approach to Characterizing Eye-Hand Coordination During the Nine-Hole Peg Test in Multiple Sclerosis
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) can impair upper-extremity function through motor, sensory, cognitive, and visual deficits. Although the Nine-Hole Peg Test (9-HPT) is widely used to assess dexterity, completion time alone provides limited insight into the eye-hand coordination underlying performance. We characterized 9-HPT performance in nine people with MS (PwMS) and nine healthy controls using simultaneous eye tracking, markerless hand tracking, and object detection. Each peg cycle was divided into transport, manipulation and insertion, and return-to-bin phases. PwMS had longer overall completion times. Transport was prolonged with the non-dominant hand, manipulation was prolonged with the dominant hand, and return-to-bin duration was longer with both hands, representing the largest phase difference. PwMS also made approximately one additional fixation per peg and showed greater variability in gaze landing position during dominant-hand performance. Saccadic amplitude and mean placement error did not differ significantly between groups, and gaze generally preceded hand movement in both groups. These exploratory findings suggest that MS-related slowing is concentrated in phases requiring precise manipulation and transition to the next peg. Multimodal assessment of the 9-HPT can reveal coordination deficits not captured by completion time alone.
authors: Mahya Beheshti; Rajvardhan Gadde; Diana Maloku; Danae S Manta; Bethany Lum; Silvana Lopes Costa; Todd E. Hudson; John‐Ross Rizzo

title: Validez y fiabilidad de la Escala del Escritor Frustrado en la educación superior
abstract: La frustración en la escritura académica se identifica como una experiencia en estudiantes de educación superior, asociada a exigencias institucionales, dificultades lingüísticas y procesos formativos. El objetivo del estudio fue diseñar y obtener evidencias de validez y fiabilidad de la Escala del Escritor Frustrado en estudiantes universitarios. Se realizó una investigación instrumental con una muestra no probabilística de 243 estudiantes de educación superior con una media general de edad de 20.87 años, 83.13% fueron mujeres, 15.24% hombres, 0.82% no binario y 0.82% prefirió no decirlo. La versión inicial del instrumento fue sometida a una evaluación de evidencias de validez de contenido mediante juicio de expertos y, posteriormente, a un análisis de componentes principales (ACP) con rotación oblicua Robust Promin. Asimismo, se evaluó la adecuación muestral mediante el índice Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) y la prueba de esfericidad de Bartlett, y se estimó la consistencia interna mediante el coeficiente omega de McDonald. La estructura final quedó integrada por 22 ítems agrupados en tres componentes determinados mediante análisis paralelo. La adecuación muestral fue satisfactoria (KMO = .888; prueba de esfericidad de Bartlett = 2098.1, p < .001). Los componentes explicaron el 48.3% de la varianza acumulada. La escala presentó un coeficiente omega de McDonald de .901, mientras que los tres componentes mostraron valores entre .807 y .826. Se concluyó que la Escala del Escritor Frustrado presentó evidencias preliminares de validez de contenido y estructura interna, así como de fiabilidad para evaluar experiencias de frustración asociadas con la escritura académica en educación superior, con utilidad potencial para el estudio de la dimensión emocional de la escritura académica.
authors: Jesús Alejandro Muñiz Loredo

title: Disrupted bilateral co‐ordination of soleus motor units during early subacute stroke rehabilitation
abstract: Stroke can affect sensorimotor control, impairing balance and locomotion. These impairments increase fall risk, limit patient independence and reduce quality of life. Here, we investigated how stroke affects bilateral co-ordination of soleus motor units during standing in individuals undergoing subacute rehabilitation. Fourteen individuals were recruited after admission for inpatient rehabilitation with sixteen age- and sex-matched controls. Both groups attended two sessions separated by 1 week, during which high-density electromyography (EMG) signals were recorded from soleus muscles when standing on force plates. Patients also performed the Berg Balance Scale (BBS). EMG signals were decomposed into motor unit spike trains, from which peristimulus time histograms and EMG waveform averages were computed in relation to peaks in centre of pressure (COP). The amplitude of motor unit and EMG activity around COP peaks, directional tuning and bilateral synchronization were estimated. Individuals post-stroke improved their BBS score between visits, but COP displacement and speed were still greater than controls. Soleus activity was tuned anteriorly in both control and non-paretic limbs, whereas it was tuned laterally in paretic limbs. Synchronization of soleus activity was also reduced in the paretic limb compared to controls. Furthermore, cross-correlation lag between limbs was greater in individuals post-stroke than in controls at visit 1, whereas it decreased to control levels at visit 2 (P = 0.008). The decrease in lags was strongly correlated with improvement in BBS score (R = -0.94, P < 0.001). These results highlight the importance of bilateral motor unit co-ordination in balance, which is disrupted in both spatial and temporal domains following stroke. KEY POINTS: We examined bilateral motor unit co-ordination during quiet standing in individuals in the early subacute phase following unilateral stroke, whereas previous works have focused on the chronic phase post-stroke. Although the non-paretic limb of patients exhibited a spatial tuning of its activity oriented in the same direction as those of neurologically intact controls, the spatial tuning of the activity of the paretic limb was altered. Bilateral synchronization between soleus motor units was reduced in individuals post-stroke in comparison with neurologically intact controls. The level of bilateral synchronization between soleus motor units was associated with balance function and improved after one week of inpatient rehabilitation.
authors: Jackson T. Levine; Xin S. Yu; Alyssa Jones; Rebecca Munoz; Martin Zaback; Christopher K. Thompson; Dario Farina; Simon Avrillon; Jose L. Pons

title: Coral Grow-out Robotic Assessment System (CGRAS): Scaling Coral Recruit Monitoring Through Robotics and Computer Vision
abstract: Climate change is the largest threat to coral reefs, with increasing global impacts accelerating the need for scalable reef restoration technologies. Large-scale reef restoration depends on the mass production of corals, such as through coral aquaculture. Coral seeding with recruits grown in aquaculture facilities is a feasible restoration approach, but effective production requires consistent, high-frequency monitoring of tens of thousands of macroscopic (0.5-2mm diameter) recruits, making conventional manual assessment prohibitively labor-intensive. To address this monitoring bottleneck, we introduce the Coral Grow-out Robotic Assessment System (CGRAS) which combines robotic imaging and computer vision to automate data acquisition, perform multi-species detection and counting of corals, and evaluate coral health. CGRAS automatically extracts coral growth, survival and spatial distribution metrics, with the aim of providing timely feedback to operators for optimizing production, grow-out and deployment workflow processes. We demonstrate CGRAS in a large aquaculture facility on standardized coral settlement tiles, reducing the time and labor costs by a factor of 9.6 as compared to manual monitoring, whilst achieving 96.4% agreement for Acropora kenti corals relative to expert counts.
authors: Dorian Tsai; Scarlett Raine; Emilio Olivastri; Riki Lamont; Andrew Lui; Timothy Morris; Joshua Esplin; Christopher A. Brunner; F. Mikaela Nordborg; Reginald Wardleworth; Garima Samvedi; Karen Jackel; Matthew Dunbabin; Tobias Fischer; Andrea Severati

title: Beyond symptoms: wearable digital biomarkers for subclinical detection of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy.
abstract: Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) is the most prevalent dose-limiting toxicity of taxane-, platinum-, and proteasome inhibitor-based regimens, yet clinical management has a structural flaw: assessment depends on CTCAE clinician grading that registers symptoms only after axonal degeneration has reached an irreversible stage. Quantitative sensory testing studies demonstrate that vibration perception, thermal detection, and sudomotor function deteriorate before patients report numbness or pain, suggesting a subclinical window of one to two chemotherapy cycles. Whether detection within this window can prevent permanent nerve injury remains biologically plausible but prospectively unestablished. Wearable sensors-inertial measurement units for gait, plantar pressure insoles, electrochemical skin conductance devices, and vibration sensors-have demonstrated proof-of-concept capacity to capture subclinical CIPN signals, but evidence remains largely cross-sectional with limited longitudinal validation. This Perspective distinguishes the conceptual framework for subclinical CIPN surveillance from the currently available clinical validation evidence. I systematically categorize four sensing modalities by neuropathological substrate, provide a cross-modality readiness comparison, and identify translational barriers including absent alert thresholds and confounding factors such as age, diabetes, anemia, and fatigue. I propose a phased prospective validation framework; specific monitoring recommendations should be regarded as hypotheses for testing rather than current clinical guidance. Wearable sensors should not replace patient-reported outcomes but may add an objective neurotoxicity monitoring layer whose capacity to improve clinical outcomes requires prospective validation.
authors: Di Xu

title: Smartwatch-Detected Sinus Tachycardia Unmasking AL Cardiac Amyloidosis in a Young Adult.
abstract: The clinical presentation of immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) can be very heterogenous resulting in delayed diagnosis and treatment. The use of wearable health technology is rapidly expanding. This case explores the important role this technology can play in the diagnosis of cardiac amyloidosis particularly in younger adults. A 36-year-old woman presented with frequent high heart rate alerts on her smartwatch with mild nonspecific symptoms. Further investigations led to cardiac magnetic resonance imaging that raised suspicion for amyloidosis with Mayo Clinic stage III immunoglobulin A lambda AL cardiac amyloidosis confirmed on laboratory and histological testing. The sinus tachycardia was attributed to atrial amyloid infiltration. Plasma cell therapy resulted in an excellent cardiac and hematological response with normalization of resting sinus heart rates. This case highlights an atypical presentation of cardiac AL amyloidosis. Smartwatch monitoring and alerts were central to early diagnosis and treatment. This case demonstrates the potential role that wearable-technology has in early detection of AL cardiac amyloidosis. To achieve a timely diagnosis of AL cardiac amyloidosis, physicians should remain inquisitive; subtle abnormalities in cardiac biomarkers or electrocardiograms should prompt further investigation.
authors: Grace O'Dea; Peter O'Gorman; Gerard T Giblin

title: The implementation of a smart safety protection system using DL and IoT technologies.
abstract: Safety has always been a concern. Thus, employing and utilizing technology is vital to help society address this concern. This paper looks at the design and implementation of a Smart Safety Protection System (SSPS), which employs the Internet of Things (IoT) to solve the issue of real-time monitoring, geolocation tracking, and emergency alert features. The proposed system is a wearable device that uses sensors and GPS to send continuous data to both an application on smartphones and a database on the cloud. The system's features include detecting unauthorized removal of the device as well as falls and abnormal temperature or heart rate. If anything happens as mentioned, the system will send alerts to the linked mobile application. A Deep Learning (DL) model is integrated into the SSPS system using multimodal WESAD sensor data. A trained Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) neural network achieved 93% accuracy when optimized with Adam and Softmax, enabling reliable identification of Monitored Individuals' emotional states. Steps of functional and integration testing of the prototype proved the reliability of sensor accuracy, data transmission speed, and real-time emergency response. Ultimately, this work emphasizes the potential of using DL and the IoT to improve Monitored Individuals' safety.
authors: Kaouther Omri; Hanen Himdi; Manal M Khayyat; Ala' A Eshmawi; Mashael M Khayyat

title: A Lag-1 Autocorrelation Statistic for Early Warning of Illness and Heat Stress in Older Adults From Everyday Wearables, With a Graded Shunt
abstract: Older people often become seriously ill quietly. An infection may build for two or three days before anyone notices that something is wrong, and by then it may already need a hospital. In a heatwave, an older person may not feel thirsty or hot until it is dangerous. Many older people already wear a smartwatch or a fitness band that measures the heart rate and movement every minute. This paper describes an early warning that works on those readings. The body is always making small corrections to the heart rate; in a healthy body, each small wobble settles back quickly. When illness or heat stress begins, the wobbles settle back more slowly. We measure this slowing with one simple number, and when it rises, the person, their family, or a care-home nurse is alerted in three steps, through the link the wearable already has. It is the same general method as in our companion paper on animals; only a small table of numbers, the "profile", changes. In a computer simulation of 30 people of each kind in each situation, for an infection, compared with the moment the person looked ill: our method gave its first notice about 14 to 15 hours before; today's wearables, which watch the day's activity, alerted about 30 hours after. For frail older people, today's high heart-rate alarm never fired at all. In a heatwave, compared with the moment heatstroke signs appeared: our method's first notice came 88 to 103 minutes before, and even earlier with the heat watch rule on forecast-hot days; today's high heart-rate alarm came 41 to 63 minutes before. Healthy people rarely received a false alarm. All results come from simulated data; testing on real wearable data is the necessary next step.

title: ATRIAL FIBRILLATION, WEARABLE TECHNOLOGIES AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: CURRENT EVIDENCE, CLINICAL UTILITY AND LIMITATIONS
abstract: Background: Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia in adults and represents an important clinical and public health problem because of its association with stroke, mortality, disability, and healthcare burden. Its paroxysmal and frequently asymptomatic course limits the effectiveness of conventional diagnostic strategies based on occasional electrocardiographic recordings. Aim: This narrative review aims to summarise current evidence regarding the use of wearable technologies and artificial intelligence for the detection of atrial fibrillation, with particular emphasis on diagnostic accuracy, clinical utility, and principal limitations. Methods: A structured literature search was performed using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Studies published between 2021 and 2026 were primarily considered. Search terms included “atrial fibrillation,” “wearable technologies,” “smartwatch,” “electrocardiography,” “photoplethysmography,” “artificial intelligence,” “machine learning,” and “diagnostics.” Priority was given to original studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and clinically relevant review articles concerning wearable devices, artificial intelligence, and atrial fibrillation detection. Earlier landmark studies were included when they were necessary to explain key evidence discussed in recent reviews and meta-analyses. Results: Wearable devices such as smartwatches, fitness bands, and portable ECG systems allow longer heart rhythm monitoring in daily life and may help detect paroxysmal and clinically silent atrial fibrillation. ECG-based devices are more consistent with current diagnostic standards, whereas photoplethysmography-based systems are more accessible and can provide passive rhythm monitoring. Artificial intelligence, especially machine learning and deep learning, can support signal interpretation, arrhythmia recognition, and risk prediction. However, diagnostic performance reported in controlled studies may not always translate directly into real-world clinical practice. Conclusions: Wearable technologies and artificial intelligence offer a promising way to support atrial fibrillation screening and monitoring. They may improve early detection, especially in asymptomatic individuals, but should not replace standard diagnostic methods. Photoplethysmography-based alerts should be regarded as screening signals, while a final diagnosis of atrial fibrillation should still be confirmed by ECG in an appropriate clinical context. More large-scale studies are needed before these tools can be widely implemented in routine practice.

title: Can Technology Support Healthy Ageing? Feasibility Study of a Wellbeing Management Platform for Self-care and Early Intervention in Older Adults
abstract: Background: Digital tools may support people to develop and maintain lifestyle changes and make “better-informed decisions about their health”.[1] The use of wearable and smart devices may further enable the identification of subclinical fluctuations in health, facilitating early intervention and preventative care at the population level.[1],[2] This study aims to assess the usability, adherence and feasibility of the Tinteán™ wellbeing management platform in supporting self-care and early intervention in community-dwelling adults over 55.[3] Approach:A total of 100 participants with at least one chronic health condition have been recruited on a voluntary basis from volunteer, community and social enterprises including ALONE (Ireland’s national elder support charity), Friends of the Elderly, disease-specific support groups (COPD Support Ireland, Diabetes Ireland, Asthma Society) and retired professionals associations (Garda Retired Members, Retired Teachers’ Association).[4] Inclusion criteria include: being aged 55 years or older, living independently with a fixed address, owning a suitable smartphone, being independently mobile and living in or willing to travel to Dublin for in-person testing days. Prospective clients were contacted by wellbeing team members to complete a screening questionnaire (adapted from the Tilburg Frailty Indicator) to establish suitability, with those scoring five or above excluded from the study.[5] All participants have received a smart watch and scales, and 10% have been supplied with a smart home blood pressure monitor. Devices are linked with the Tinteán mobile app and readings are uploaded to a user dashboard daily. Results are flagged according to a threshold-based system derived from the HSE’s National Early Warning System and made available to healthcare providers via a unique QR code on participants’ apps.[6] At onboarding and subsequent 3-monthly intervals, participants undergo hearing, vision and cognitive assessments, as well as strength, mobility and balance testing under the supervision of a clinical physiotherapist. Participants also complete regular mental health questionnaires and record relevant life events (e.g., falls, GP visits). These measures of physical, mental, and social health are tracked, and participants are connected with local health and/or social support services based on concerning scores or trends in these metrics. Results: Preliminary results (study to end in March 2026) indicate high levels of acceptance and adherence among participants, despite the reportedly low acceptability of digital devices in this age group.[7] Participants have reported increased awareness of their health status, motivation to improve measures e.g., step count, and a sense of confidence in knowing that someone is looking out for them. Some participants have described feeling better able to advocate for themselves in interactions with healthcare professionals. The main alert categories to date are cardiovascular (55%), strength and mobility (15%), pain (9%), and mental health (8%). Preliminary limitations and issues include the deliberate selection of participants, the high numbers of alerts generated in free-living conditions, the corresponding requirement for healthcare professionals to follow-up the alerts and the complexity of refining the model to generate individualised thresholds for clients. Implications: Pending finalisation of results, though likely applicable across different health system contexts and settings.
authors: Ronan Rooney; Tria Rooney; Crona Rooney-Jermyn; Peter Swords; Deirdre Dolan; Jon Harvey

title: Patient Perspectives to Inform Co-creation of Wearable-Derived Digital Biomarkers for Early Flare Detection and Management in IBD: A Survey-Based Study
abstract: PURPOSE: Wearable-derived digital biomarkers represent a new frontier in remote management of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). They may enable continuous disease surveillance and early flare detection while reducing reliance on questionnaire-based remote monitoring. However, successful implementation into clinical practice critically depends on patient acceptance and perceived relevance. To guide patient-centered digital health strategies, we aimed to investigate patient perspectives on digital biomarkers for (early) flare detection. METHODS: A nationwide cross-sectional survey-based study was conducted among patients with IBD (≥ 16 years) in the Netherlands. A study-specific questionnaire was distributed through the Dutch patient organization Crohn & Colitis NL to assess acceptance, preferences, and perspectives on the use of wearable technology for flare detection. RESULTS: 1,080 participants were included: 72.5% women, 53.4% aged >50 years, and 28.7% current wearable users. Overall, 88% considered remote monitoring for flare detection potentially useful, and over 90% believed wearables could support this. Motivations for using wearables included flare detection, better understanding of symptoms, and health monitoring. User-friendliness, clear alerts, and time efficiency were key device preferences, and smartwatches were the preferred wearable device. Shorter disease duration (p<0.001), more frequent flares (p=0.029), younger age (p=0.016), and current wearable use (p<0.001) were identified as predictors for willingness to use wearables. CONCLUSION: Patients with IBD value wearables for flare detection and disease-monitoring. Most participants expressed willingness to use digital biomarkers and believed that wearables could support routine care. Incorporating patient preferences into digital biomarker development will likely improve patient acceptance and adherence to remote monitoring.
authors: E Godecharle; Koen Totté; Willem Johan van den Brink; Zlatan Mujagic; J. Zhang; R. West; D. van der Horst; Menne Scherpenzeel; Torsten P. M. Scheithauer; Tim van den Broek; Tessa E H Römkens; Marieke J. Pierik

title: From digital phenotype to closed-loop therapy: artificial intelligence–enabled wearable and connected technology for allergic diseases
abstract: Background The prevalence of allergic diseases continues to rise, yet episodic outpatient care remains constrained by delayed symptom recognition, the "black box" of medication adherence, and fragmented management. Wearables, the Internet of Things (IoT), and artificial intelligence (AI) now converge in "digital phenotyping." From a pharmaceutical perspective, this review appraises these AI-enabled technologies for allergic diseases along the thread of "from digital phenotype to closed-loop therapy." Methods A narrative review synthesizing recent literature on the technical framework, real-time monitoring, risk early warning, long-term management, therapeutic wearables, psychological digital phenotypes, and equity and safety. Results These technologies span the "sensing–warning–management–treatment" chain. Adaptive baseline learning, time-aware modeling, and multimodal fusion enable individualized early warning from noisy physiological and environmental signals. The strongest evidence concerns long-term management: digital inhalers and smartwatches, validated in randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses, improve adherence and asthma control and reduce exacerbations, with economic value in averting biologic escalation; devices are extending from passive sensing to active interventions—nasal acoustic therapy, "feedback as therapy," and conceptual closed-loop epinephrine injection. However, most applications remain at small-sample, single-center validation; portable quantitative pollen detection is an empty niche; and drug confounding of digital phenotypes (β 2 -agonist contamination of heart rate variability) and closed-loop amplification of skin-tone–related bias challenge clinical translation. Conclusions AI-enabled wearables are shifting allergy care from intermittent, subjective consultation toward continuous, closed-loop management, with evidence most mature for digital inhalers. Future work should develop multimodal digital phenotypes and allergy-specific foundation models and strengthen medication-covariate modeling, hard-endpoint validation, and whole-lifecycle equity governance.
authors: Yuxiang Pei; Yongxia Wu; Ruoyu Hou; Kun Wan

title: EXTENT OF AWARENESS OF WEARABLE TECHNOLOGY DEVICES AND HEALTH BENEFITS AMONG LECTURERS OF EBONYI STATE UNIVERSITY, ABAKALIKI
abstract: The study investigated the extent of awareness of wearable fashion technology devices and their health benefits among lecturers of Ebonyi State University Abakaliki. Specifically, the study determined the extent of awareness of fashion clothing technology devices among lecturers at Ebonyi State University Abakaliki and the extent of health benefits of fashion clothing technology devices in the area of the study. Using a descriptive survey research design, the population of the study comprised nine hundred and sixty lecturers (960) in Ebonyi State University. A cluster sampling technique was adopted to select a sample of 100 lecturers. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire administered by hand to the study respondents. The data collected was analyzed using mean statistics. Findings revealed that the respondents were unaware of seven out of the ten identified fashion clothing devices; these include smart clothing, smart jewellery, smart rings, smart watches, and others. In the same vein, the respondents were unaware of seven out of the ten identified health benefits; these include control of hypertension, monitoring heart health, control of sleep, and reduction of anxiety, among others. Based on the findings, the study recommends that the university management and relevant public health organizations should initiate targeted digital health literacy programmes focused on clearly demonstrating the health benefits of these devices to lecturers. This is essential for converting low awareness into an active intention to utilize and eventual adoption.
authors: OKORO Victoria Ifeyinwa; Tessy EDE-AUGUSTINE; FRED Chidinma Vivian

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI)–ENABLED WEARABLES FOR CARDIAC RHYTHM MONITORING: DIAGNOSTIC PERFORMANCE, REGULATORY TRENDS, AND CLINICAL INTEGRATION.
abstract: Wearable technologies extend cardiac-rhythm monitoring beyond conventional clinical settings. Smartwatches, handheld single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) devices, adhesive ECG patches, chest straps, rings, and remote-monitoring platforms increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning methods to detect atrial fibrillation (AF), classify rhythm abnormalities, assess signal quality, prioritize ambulatory recordings, and estimate arrhythmia burden. This review examined the technological, regulatory, diagnostic, and clinical-integration considerations relevant to AI-enabled wearable cardiac monitoring. This review evaluates evidence concerning wearable ECG and photoplethysmography (PPG)-based rhythm-monitoring technologies, with attention to diagnostic performance, regulatory authorization, algorithmic limitations, and requirements for safe clinical implementation. Wearable ECG devices can identify AF with high sensitivity and specificity in selected and supervised populations. However, diagnostic performance varies according to device modality, recording quality, patient characteristics, AF prevalence, reference standard, software version, and the handling of inconclusive or unclassifiable recordings. PPG-based irregular-rhythm notifications can provide useful screening signals but do not independently establish an AF diagnosis because they detect pulse irregularity rather than cardiac electrical activity. In contrast, interpretable wearable ECG recordings may provide rhythm documentation when incorporated into an appropriate clinical evaluation pathway. Regulatory authorization defines a device’s permitted intended use but does not establish universal diagnostic accuracy, generalizability, clinical-outcome benefit, or suitability for autonomous clinical decision-making. Effective implementation requires external validation; transparent reporting of unclassifiable recordings; clinician-overread and confirmatory ECG pathways; governance of algorithm updates; privacy and cybersecurity protections; and ongoing post-market performance monitoring. AI-enabled wearable rhythm monitoring is most likely to improve care when used to support, rather than replace clinical judgment.
authors: Supreet Kaur
venue: World Journal of Advanced Engineering Technology and Sciences

title: Artificial Intelligence in Wearable ECG and PPG Devices for Arrhythmia Detection: A Narrative Review
abstract: Cardiovascular disease is the world’s top cause of death. Short recording times and a dependence on clinical settings are two practical drawbacks of traditional methods like Holter monitoring and standard 12-lead ECG. Two significant trends have come together in recent years: the broad availability of consumer-grade wearable technology, including smartwatches and adhesive ambulatory ECG patches, and the quick advancement of deep learning and artificial intelligence. Four main themes currently dominate research in this field: diagnostic accuracy under controlled conditions, algorithmic innovation for real-time and on-device analysis, real-world implementation and performance in large prospective studies, and the persistent technical, clinical, and regulatory challenges that limit widespread deployment.AI-based systems have shown consistently high performance in controlled environments and curated datasets, with reported sensitivities and specificities commonly ranging between 92% and 99%.However, performance, especially specificity and generalizability, frequently declines significantly if these algorithms are exposed to the messiness of daily movement, a variety of patient demographics, fluctuating skin contact, and hardware limitations outside of the lab. More advanced transformer architectures and multimodal techniques that combine ECG signals with photoplethysmography (PPG) waveforms, as well as lightweight convolutional neural networks that can operate directly on the device itself and provide true real-time detection, have been the focus of recent algorithmic work. The present status of wearable ECG and PPG technology for AI-enabled arrhythmia detection is examined in this review. It critically evaluates diagnostic performance, translational gaps that still exist and paying attention to the prospective studies that have shaped the field. All things considered, the data indicates that wearables driven by AI have real potential for screening for arrhythmias at the population level and have already shown promising signs of clinical utility. The field will require larger, longer, and more diversified prospective trials that are sufficiently powered to identify significant differences in hard clinical outcomes.
authors: Farid Taghavi; Shirin Alord; Alireza Ghaffari; Somayyeh Mehanfar; Kamran Mohammadi

title: Comparison of Reachable Workspace Capacity to Real-World Arm Use Performance: A Wearable Accelerometry Study on Chronic Stroke
abstract: Reachable workspace (RWS) quantifies the three-dimensional space accessible to the upper limb, but its relationship with real-world arm use after stroke remains unclear. This study examined associations between camera-based RWS and smartwatch-derived movement behavior in 14 individuals with chronic stroke. Relative surface area (RSA) was measured at baseline, after which participants wore a smartwatch on the affected arm. Smartwatch data were summarized using Gross Movement and Activity Count (GMAC), representing the proportion of wear time spent in active arm movement within a functional workspace, and Active and Diverse Exploratory Movement (ADEM), representing the proportion of wear time that was active and diverse. Clinical outcomes included the Box and Block Test (BBT), Upper-Extremity Fugl-Meyer Assessment (UEFM), and Motor Activity Log (MAL). Total RSA and several workspace regions were reduced in the paretic compared with the nonparetic limb. Greater total RSA was significantly associated with ADEM (ρ = 0.66, p = 0.01), while its association with GMAC was numerically weaker and non-significant (ρ = 0.47, p = 0.09). RSA was also significantly associated with BBT, UEFM, and MAL, with correlations ranging from ρ = 0.57 to 0.76. These findings link camera-based RWS with wrist-worn measures of real-world arm performance after stroke.
authors: Guillem Cornella-Barba; Natanya Gunn; Vicky Chan; David J. Reinkensmeyer; Jay J. Han

title: SensorW: Open-Source Wear Operating System Platform for Continuous Global Positioning System and Multimodal Sensor Data Collection in Real-World Settings
abstract: Digital phenotyping requires continuous, real-world collection of multimodal behavioral and physiological data. Although several smartphone-based sensing frameworks have been developed and used, open-source platforms for long-term smartwatch sensor data acquisition remain limited. To bridge this gap, SensorW was developed, an open-source Wear operating system (OS)-based framework for direct lifelog data collection from smartwatches without requiring a paired smartphone or manufacturer cloud service. SensorW includes a front-end Wear OS application for sensor data collection and a back-end server for application initiation, secure data submission, and storage. The front-end application uses battery-management strategies, such as hybrid Global Positioning System sampling and wake-lock management, to continuously collect multimodal sensor outputs, including location data, physical activity-related metrics, barometric pressure, and device wear status, and submit data to the back-end server. A preliminary technical evaluation of SensorW was conducted with seven participants who wore SensorW-enabled devices continuously for at least seven consecutive days. The technical evaluation demonstrated multimodal data collection during 17-42 days of monitoring, with operational data availability ranging from 0.73 to 1.00 across participants. These findings support the technical feasibility of SensorW as a practical and extensible platform for continuous digital phenotyping using consumer-grade smartwatches.

title: Decentralized Epidemic Tracking using Federated Learning and Edge AI on Consumer Wearables
abstract: Early detection of infectious-disease outbreaks depends on how quickly weak, distributed signals can be turned into a public-health decision, yet conventional surveillance relies on clinic visits, laboratory confirmation, and syndromic reporting that lag infection by days. Consumer wearables such as smartwatches, fitness bands, and smart rings continuously record resting heart rate, heart-rate variability, skin temperature, blood-oxygen saturation, respiration, sleep, and activity, and prior studies show that deviations from a person's own baseline can appear before symptoms. Centralizing this data, however, creates serious privacy, security, and regulatory exposure. This paper proposes a decentralized epidemic-tracking framework that combines Federated Learning (FL) and Edge AI on consumer wearables. Personalized anomaly detectors run on the device; only privacy-protected model updates and coarse, thresholded anomaly flags leave the user's phone; and a hierarchical wearable, smartphone, regional-edge, and health-authority architecture converts local signals into population-level outbreak indicators. Building on a recent wearable-centric review of federated AI, the framework adds eight design innovations: personalized baseline-deviation modelling, hierarchical hybrid aggregation, outbreak-risk-adaptive differential privacy, energy-aware client participation, federated analytics with secure aggregation and k-anonymous geo-cells, a permissioned-ledger audit trail kept off the critical path, federated unlearning for erasure rights, and a pathogen-agnostic cold-start strategy. Six learning approaches are compared conceptually, and detection, timeliness, communication, energy, and privacy metrics are defined. As no field deployment or labelled dataset was collected for this study, the work is presented as a proposed framework and illustrative experimental design rather than a report of empirical results, and all performance figures shown are clearly marked as illustrative placeholders. The discussion covers practical significance for public-health agencies, limitations such as sensor noise, non-IID data, client dropout, dataset shift, and regulatory classification, and the future directions needed to move from prototype to field-ready deployment.
authors: Hariharan. N; Abikayil Aarthi. S; Ajav. V; Gurudev. N; Deerga Tharsan A V; Chandra Mukilan. V; Aravinth. R

title: Privacy Trade-Offs and User Acceptance of Biometric Health Data Collection Via Smart Watches in Workplace Wellness Programs
abstract: Smartwatch-based workplace wellness programs offer significant potential to improve employee health and reduce organizational healthcare costs, they also create substantial privacy risks through continuous biometric data collection. Understanding how to balance these health promotion benefits with privacy protection is critical for developing ethical and effective wellness initiatives. However, research on the privacy trade-offs employees face when participating in workplace biometric monitoring programs remains limited. Current frameworks inadequately address the tension between voluntary participation and economic coercion, the complexities of informed consent, and the effectiveness of different privacy protection models in workplace contexts. The main objective of this qualitative study was to explore the privacy implications of smartwatch-based workplace wellness programs by examining employee acceptance factors, evaluating alternative privacy protection frameworks, and analyzing regulatory and ethical considerations across different jurisdictions. Data were generated from comprehensive literature review and framework analysis, examining empirical studies on employee perceptions, technology acceptance models, regulatory comparisons, and ethical assessments. The analysis was conducted through the lens of the Privacy-Enhanced Technology Acceptance Model and self determination theory. Four distinct privacy frameworks were systematically evaluated: Minimal Collection, Consent and Control, Privacy by Design, and Federated Data models. The analysis revealed several critical insights. First, employees recognized the health benefits of biometric monitoring (62% viewed it positively) but simultaneously expressed strong privacy concerns (78% worried about data misuse). Second, the concept of "manufactured consent" emerged, where financial incentives and social pressure undermined truly voluntary participation. Third, no single privacy framework provided optimal protection; hybrid approaches combining multiple models were most effective. Fourth, trust in employers and vendors significantly moderated the relationship between privacy concerns and program acceptance. The findings suggest that organizations should implement hybrid privacy protection strategies, establish robust governance structures with clear accountability, provide genuine non-monitoring alternatives for earning incentives, and strictly limit biometric data use to wellness purposes. Furthermore, policymakers should develop comprehensive biometric privacy legislation that recognizes workplace power dynamics and mandates equivalent non-monitoring pathways. Employees should remain informed about their rights under applicable privacy laws and carefully evaluate the voluntariness of participation given financial and social pressures.
authors: Obunda Wosa

title: Let there be music: Prompt, command, and cultural capital in the AI music generator Suno
abstract: This paper examines the role of language in prompt-based music production through the case of the AI music generator Suno and questions the widespread claim that such systems democratize music production. Building on Agamben’s (2022) concept of command, the paper conceptualizes the prompt as a command that initiates production. Drawing on Bourdieu’s (1986) concept of cultural capital, the paper considers how linguistic competence may shape prompt construction. The paper adopts an interpretive case study approach. For Suno, the paper tested one minimal and one elaborated text-based prompt in the platform’s freely accessible v4.5 Simple mode and compared the first musical output presented for each prompt. The minimal prompt consisted of a brief, general description, whereas the elaborated prompt included linguistic detail and musical terminology specific to the selected genre. The analysis focused on rock music because its well-established terminology – such as riff, distortion, power chord, pre-chorus, and guitar solo – enabled a clearer comparison of how linguistic and musical specifications were reflected in the musical outputs. The findings indicate that, in these two examples, the minimal prompt is accompanied by a more detailed style description displayed by the platform, whereas the description associated with the elaborated prompt selectively retains, renames, and restructures elements of the original prompt. Thus, algorithmic interpretation is defined as a theoretical account of how the platform maps the user’s command to the resulting musical decisions. The paper concludes that the musical output can be understood as the asymmetrical co-production of the user’s command, shaped by cultural capital, and the platform’s algorithmic interpretation, with the latter occupying a structurally dominant position in this relationship. These findings suggest that the widespread discourse presenting AI music generators as democratizing music production may overlook the distinction between access to production and control over the production process.
authors: Selim Tan

title: DARE to wear: digital health promotion and disease prevention using wearable devices
abstract: Abstract Global healthcare systems are under increasing strain to ensure long-term sustainability, necessitating a fundamental transition towards proactive, preventive healthcare strategies. Wearable sensor technologies are uniquely positioned to facilitate this paradigm shift by enabling continuous physiological and behavioral monitoring, facilitating early risk stratification, and enabling timely interventions. DigitAl lifelong pREvention (DARE) is a nationwide initiative conceived in Italy to develop and evaluate novel digital tools and services aimed at fostering innovative health promotion and disease prevention pathways, with wearable devices identified as a critical enabling technology. Herein, we present a comprehensive overview of 16 pilot investigations designed in DARE to rigorously assess the utility of wearable devices in the continuous monitoring of physical activity, joint mobility, sleep architecture, heart rate variability, nutrition, and glucose homeostasis across diverse health domains, including healthy aging, chronic disease prevention, and lifestyle modification programs targeting over 20000 participants. We meticulously detail the methodological characteristics of these study protocols, explicitly outlining the technical specifications, functional capabilities, and inherent limitations of the 18 distinct wearable devices (sourced from 12 different manufacturers) employed across these clinical trials. The breadth of applications and the heterogeneity of the target populations underscore the significant potential of wearable devices as an integral component of future digital health prevention strategies.

title: ONLINE JOB PORTAL
abstract: The Online Job Portal is a web-based application designed to simplify and improve the process of job searching and recruitment. Traditional job-search methods require candidates to manually search through newspapers, company websites, and multiple recruitment platforms, which can be time-consuming and inefficient. The proposed system provides a centralized platform where job seekers and recruiters can interact and manage the recruitment process online. Job seekers can register, create profiles, upload resumes, search and filter job opportunities, view job details, and apply for suitable positions. They can search for jobs based on job title, skills, location, experience, salary, and employment type. Candidates can also track their application status and receive notifications about job updates. Recruiters can register on the platform, create and manage job postings, specify required qualifications and skills, view candidate applications, and shortlist suitable applicants. The system maintains job postings, candidate profiles, applications, and recruitment information in a centralized database. An administrator module allows authorized administrators to manage users, recruiters, job categories, job postings, applications, and system activities. The system can also provide notifications and basic recruitment reports to improve communication and management.

title: Wearable abdominal acoustic biofeedback for dietary self-regulation among Taiwanese university students: an exploratory randomized pilot study
abstract: Background Manual dietary self-monitoring can impose a burden on university students, limiting sustained engagement with digital nutrition tools. AbSound was developed as a wearable abdominal-acoustic biofeedback system that converts candidate gastrointestinal sound events into uncertainty-aware reflective prompts, rather than validated diagnoses of hunger, satiety, dietary intake, diet quality, or eating speed. This exploratory, randomized pilot study assessed feasibility, acceptability, user experience, preliminary self-reported behavioral signals, and agreement in acoustic event detection among Taiwanese university students. Method Sixty first- and second-year university students in Taipei were randomized 1:1 to AbSound plus a companion app or to an active app-based dietary-tracking comparator for 4 weeks. Primary feasibility outcomes included retention, daily wear time, days worn, prompt exposure, prompt acknowledgment, reported burden, and adverse events. Exploratory behavioral outcomes included self-reported late-night eating, perceived eating speed, a brief dietary-quality score, self-regulation of eating behavior, weight, and waist circumference. TAM ratings, Kano feature classifications, brief interviews, and descriptive acceptance-path analyses characterized adoption and design priorities. Acoustic performance was evaluated post hoc against selected manually reviewed event segments. Results All participants completed follow-up. AbSound users wore the device for 9.2 ± 2.2 h per day on 25.7 ± 2.0 of 28 study days, corresponding to approximately 91.8% of possible study days. Prompt acknowledgment averaged 78% ± 9%. Selected, manually reviewed segments showed approximately 88% agreement in event detection, but this estimate does not establish physiological-state validation. Compared with the active comparator, AbSound users showed larger exploratory reductions in self-reported late-night eating. They reported lower perceived eating-speed scores, higher brief dietary-quality scores, and a marginally greater increase in eating self-regulation. Weight and waist circumference showed no clinically interpretable between-group differences. Acceptance ratings were high; comfort and privacy emerged as must-be design attributes, while feedback agreement and timeliness were performance attributes. Conclusion AbSound demonstrated short-term feasibility and acceptability as a reflective abdominal-acoustic biofeedback tool for non-clinical Taiwanese university students. The findings support further user-centered development but do not establish clinical efficacy or validated detection of nutritional or physiological states. Larger preregistered trials require independent acoustic validation, objective or repeated dietary reference measures, longer follow-up, and explicit psychological-safety monitoring.
authors: Chen Han; Sheng-Ming Wang; Chuan-Chia Wang; Jwo-Shiun Sun; Tung-Jing Fang

title: A scoping review of artificial intelligence-enabled wearables for medication adherence
abstract: Abstract Medication non-adherence remains a major global public health challenge with substantial clinical and economic burden. Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled wearables may offer new opportunities to support medication adherence management. This scoping review assesses the current evidence on AI-enabled wearables for medication adherence, focusing on their applications, performance, and clinical translation. We screened three databases for literature published up to September 18, 2025. A total of 6102 records were identified, and 17 studies met the inclusion criteria. Current applications were concentrated on medication-taking behavior and ingestion event recognition, with fewer studies addressing longitudinal medication adherence assessment or non-adherence risk prediction. No included study evaluated AI-enabled wearables for personalized intervention. Most studies focused on technology development and internal validation. Although reported performance was generally favorable in controlled settings, evidence remains limited for external validation, real-world effectiveness, clinical outcomes, and integration into routine care. These findings suggest that AI-enabled wearables are technically feasible for medication adherence monitoring, but their clinical value remains insufficiently established. Future research should move beyond recognition toward prospective risk prediction, personalized intervention, and clinically integrated decision support.
authors: Ying Chen; He Zhao; Run Xu; Yiyang Li; Shuang Cai; Yingying Hu

title: Theorizing future phenomena: Metaverse, wearables, and humanoids
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We propose that entrepreneurship and strategy research can develop theory about phenomena of the future rather than only explain those of the past. Research has potential for practical relevance when researchers make claims towards applications to decisions practitioners have yet to make. Theory grounded in a world that may differ from the observed world can be built through a process of extrapolation from technological trends, a practice utilized by entrepreneurs and science fiction authors alike. Assuming advances in artificial intelligence, we apply this process to three emerging phenomena: governing scarcity in metaverse virtual worlds, redesigning organizations around pervasive monitoring via wearable devices, and allocating the intellectual property rights of humanoid robots. We argue that embracing theory that speaks to the future can enhance the practical and educational relevance of management research. Managerial Summary Assuming artificial intelligence continues to improve, we highlight three impending phenomena poised to transform conventional approaches to entrepreneurship and strategy. First, in metaverse virtual worlds, managers must manage resources governed by artificial scarcity. Second, with wearable devices allowing continuous monitoring, managers must consider alternative structures for vertical hierarchy and horizontal collaboration. Third, deployment of humanoid robots will complicate intellectual property rights and asset ownership. We propose that scholarship towards developing theoretical frameworks addressing these and other phenomena of the future will be relevant to both managers and students.
authors: Andy Wu; Ronald Wang

title: IOT- BASED WOMEN SECURITY SYSTEM
abstract: The safety of women in public places, workplaces, and while travelling remains a serious social concern. Incidents of harassment, stalking, and assault often take place in situations where the victim cannot reach a phone, unlock it, and dial for help in time. Even when a call is made, the person receiving it may not know the exact location of the victim. This paper presents an IoT-based women security system in the form of a small wearable device that can raise an emergency alert with a single action and share the live location of the wearer with trusted contacts and the nearest police control room. The device is built around an ESP32 microcontroller connected to a GPS receiver, a GSM module, a pulse sensor, a three-axis accelerometer, a small microphone, and a concealed push button. When the button is pressed, or when the device detects a combination of an abnormally high heart rate and sudden violent movement, it enters the emergency mode. In this mode it obtains the current coordinates from the GPS receiver and sends SMS messages containing a map link to preconfigured contacts. At the same time it places an automatic voice call to the first contact so that someone is alerted even if messages are not read immediately. Where Wi-Fi or mobile data is available, the device also publishes its location and sensor readings to a cloud platform using the MQTT protocol. A companion mobile application and a web dashboard display the live track of the wearer, the time of the alert, and the recorded audio clip captured by the microphone during the first seconds of the emergency. The location is updated every few seconds until the alert is cancelled by the wearer with a secret button sequence or closed by a responder, so that contacts can follow the movement of the victim if she is being taken away. The system also includes deterrent features. A loud buzzer can be activated to attract the attention of people nearby, and an optional shock circuit provides a means of selfdefence. A fake call feature on the mobile application allows the user to leave an uncomfortable situation without confrontation. All alerts are logged in the cloud with time, place, and sensor data, which can later assist police investigation and help authorities identify locations where incidents occur repeatedly.
authors: Mrs.V.Harshitha,Kanakam Akhila Bhavani,Masku Hasitha,Redapaka Tharun,Myadarapu Sathwik,Madire Bharath Kumar

title: LMS/ONLINE LEARNING SYSTEM
abstract: The Learning Management System (LMS) / Online Learning System is a web-based application designed to provide an efficient and flexible platform for delivering, managing, and accessing educational content online. Traditional learning methods often require students and teachers to be physically present in classrooms, which can limit accessibility and make it difficult to manage learning materials and academic activities. The proposed system provides a centralized digital platform where students and instructors can interact and manage learning activities. The system allows students to register, log in, enroll in courses, access study materials, watch video lectures, download resources, complete assignments, and attend online quizzes. Instructors can create and manage courses, upload learning materials, prepare assignments and quizzes, and monitor student performance. Students can also track their course progress and view their results through a personalized dashboard. The LMS maintains important information such as student details, course information, learning materials, assignments, quiz results, and progress records in a centralized database. Administrators can manage users, courses, instructors, and system settings through an administrative dashboard. The system can also provide notifications regarding new courses, assignments, quizzes, and other academic activities. Overall, the LMS/Online Learning System provides a convenient, organized, and accessible learning environment that supports education beyond the traditional classroom. It reduces manual academic management, improves communication between students and instructors, and allows learners to study at their own pace. Future enhancements can include AI-based personalized learning, intelligent course recommendations, automated assessment, live video classes, discussion forums, learning analytics, chatbot assistance, and adaptive learning paths.
authors: L Mallika, P Deekshitha , B Hindu, M Sai Kumar, T Naresh

title: Development of a Smart Wearable Assistive Device with Object Detection and Text-to-Speech Functionality for Visually Impaired Individuals using Raspberry Pi
abstract: Visually impaired individuals struggle in terms of their mobility, awareness, and overall quality of life. Traditional aids, such as canes, offer only limited assistance. This capstone project aims to develop a smart wearable device to enhance environmental awareness and assistance for visually impaired individuals in Danao City. The smart wearable assistive device is composed of a Raspberry Pi 4, ultrasonic sensors, a web camera, and text-to-speech technology that is used to deliver audio feedback that helps in better comprehension of information for these individuals. Experimental tests were conducted using percent error and paired t-tests to evaluate the overall performance of the wearable device. Survey questionnaires and interviews were also conducted to test the effectiveness of the device based on participants’ experiences. The quantitative results show that the smart wearable device consistently underperformed in its different functions. In distance range detection, the system has an average distance of 2.5 meters from the desired range, with a statistical analysis (t = 6.74, p < 0.05) indicating a significant difference. Object detection accuracy identifies an average of 9 out of 15 objects with a statistical analysis of (t = -8.96, p < 0.001) and has an effect size of 2.31. The system shows an average of 1-2 missed words per trial and a statistical analysis of (t = -5.13, p < 0.001). Overall, the findings of this study confirm that the smart wearable device's potential, specifically in text-to-speech systems, helps to enhance independence and confidence in common environments.
authors: Chona R. Dagatan; Jestoni P. Tan; Joy Stiffany A. Amodia; Lei Jo C. Bacu; Brett H. Callanga; Jeff Niño G. Caparoso; Avril Mae O. Malaga; Jedelou B. Pepito
venue: International Journal of Engineering Trends and Technology

title: The implementation of a smart safety protection system using DL and IoT technologies
abstract: Safety has always been a concern. Thus, employing and utilizing technology is vital to help society address this concern. This paper looks at the design and implementation of a Smart Safety Protection System (SSPS), which employs the Internet of Things (IoT) to solve the issue of real-time monitoring, geolocation tracking, and emergency alert features. The proposed system is a wearable device that uses sensors and GPS to send continuous data to both an application on smartphones and a database on the cloud. The system's features include detecting unauthorized removal of the device as well as falls and abnormal temperature or heart rate. If anything happens as mentioned, the system will send alerts to the linked mobile application. A Deep Learning (DL) model is integrated into the SSPS system using multimodal WESAD sensor data. A trained Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) neural network achieved 93% accuracy when optimized with Adam and Softmax, enabling reliable identification of Monitored Individuals' emotional states. Steps of functional and integration testing of the prototype proved the reliability of sensor accuracy, data transmission speed, and real-time emergency response. Ultimately, this work emphasizes the potential of using DL and the IoT to improve Monitored Individuals' safety.
authors: Kaouther Omri; Hanen Himdi; Manal M. Khayyat; Manal M. Khayyat; Ala’ Abdulmajid Eshmawi; Mashael M. Khayyat; Mashael M. Khayyat

title: Effect of a wearable-based individualised multidomain lifestyle intervention on cognitive and physical function in older adults at risk of decline (INSPIOR): a single-centre, open-label, randomised controlled trial
abstract: Background Multidomain lifestyle programmes are the leading preventive approach to cognitive decline, but they rely on intensive face-to-face delivery that is hard to scale. We assessed whether an automated, wearable-based multidomain programme of activity, sleep, and optional nutrition prompts changed cognitive and physical function in at-risk older adults. Methods INSPIOR was a 6-month, single-centre, open-label, randomised controlled trial in Kashiwa, Japan. Adults aged 65–92 years with low body-mass index, pre-frailty, frailty, or sarcopenia-related decline were randomly assigned 1:1, in permuted blocks of four and without stratification, to the Fitbit-based intervention or an assessment-only control; allocation was not concealed and outcome assessors were not masked. Co-primary outcomes were the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), Trail Making Test (TMT), and skeletal muscle mass index (SMI), with no pre-specified hierarchy or multiplicity adjustment; analyses used intention-to-treat analysis of covariance with multiple imputation. This trial was registered with UMIN-CTR, UMIN000052707, and ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06135740. Findings Between Nov 8, 2023, and Jul 31, 2024, 355 participants were randomly assigned to the intervention group (n = 178) or control group (n = 177); all were analysed. Adjusted between-group differences were 0·58 MoCA points (95% CI 0·03–1·13; p=0·039; Holm-adjusted p=0·12), 0·16 s (−5·07 to 5·40; p=0·95) for TMT-A, 5·59 s (−3·88 to 15·05; p=0·25) for TMT-B, and −0·01 kg/m 2 (−0·09 to 0·07; p=0·88) for SMI. Mild skin irritation and dietary-recording stress occurred; no serious adverse event was intervention-related. Interpretation The intervention was associated with a small difference in a global cognitive screening score that did not survive multiplicity adjustment and is of uncertain clinical significance; the other two showed none. Larger, longer, masked trials are needed. Funding University of Tokyo–NH Foods Collaborative Research Programme, Google, Mitsui Fudosan.

title: The Efficacy of Auditory and Haptic Cues Delivered via a Wearable Device to Guide Walking Intensity
abstract: Walking is one of the most common forms of physical activity in the UK, promoted by the National Health Service (NHS) through guidelines recommending moderate-intensity exercise. However, the subjective interpretation of "moderate" intensity can lead to inconsistent adherence. Cadence-based thresholds, such as at least 100 steps per minute, have been proposed as an objective alternative, but these absolute markers may not reflect individual fitness levels. Wearable technologies offer an opportunity to personalise physical activity intensity using physiological markers like percentage heart rate reserve (%HRR), and to guide behaviour using nudge-based approaches such as cadence cueing. This study investigated whether metronome (auditory) and haptic cadence cues delivered via an Apple Watch app could guide users to criterion moderate-intensity walking (40 - 59% HRR). Seventy-four adults (18–65 years) completed three 10-minute overground walking trials on a ~60 m figure-of-eight track: (1) self-paced walking guided by NHS moderate-intensity guidelines, (2) walking to an auditory cadence cue, and (3) walking to a haptic cadence cue. Cadence and %HRR were recorded in each condition. Bayesian posterior distributions showed the following mean %HRR (95% credible intervals): self-paced = 41% (39–44%), auditory = 45% (42–47%), and haptic = 43% (41–45%). The proportion of participants reaching 40 - 59% HRR was highest in the auditory (76%) and haptic (65%) cueing conditions, compared to self-paced (41%). These findings suggest wearable-guided cadence cueing, particularly auditory cues, more effectively supports individuals in achieving moderate-intensity walking compared to current NHS guidelines.
authors: Ashley Warner; Natalie Vanicek; Amanda Clare Benson; Tony Myers; Grant Abt

title: LLMs as Narrators of Lived Experience: A Study of Generative Hermeneutical Epistemic Injustice in ADHD Sense-Making
abstract: Large language models (LLMs), as non-human actors, do not have access to first-hand experiences. Yet they are increasingly consulted in processes of making sense of them, from mental health chatbots to reflexive journals. As a result, complex lived realities risk being distorted or flattened through second-order representations. In this paper, we expand on conceptual work to empirically examine narrative mechanisms through which LLMs as narrators give rise to hermeneutical epistemic injustice. We foreground narration as a key interpretive process through which experience is made intelligible. Focusing on ADHD as a motivating case, we compare first-person narratives from online ADHD communities with narratives generated by LLMs. Using an interpretive, reflexive analysis, we examine how these forms of narration construct lived experience. We find that generated narratives organise ADHD experience through recurring modes that individualise, standardise, and stabilise interpretation, reducing messiness, complexity and ambiguity present in community narration. More situated and unresolved accounts remained possible when foregrounded through prompting. We argue that the epistemic concern lies not only in what models can represent, but in which interpretations they make readily available and which require prior conceptual and prompting work.
authors: Anne Arzberger; Dongying Zhang
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society

title: CRAFT: Exploring Wearable Creative AI on Smart Glasses for Fiction Writing in Real-World Contexts
abstract: Creative writing increasingly integrates AI assistance, yet current tools miss in-situ moments when writers draw inspiration from real-world experiences. We envision Context-aware Reality-Fiction Transformation ( CRAFT ), an approach for AI glasses that translates daily experiences into fiction narratives. We explored its desirability, feasibility, and potential viability through three studies. Interviews with nine writers yielded desires and three design goals: 1) augmenting in-situ perception to bridge reality-fiction gaps, 2) promoting authenticity grounded in real-world experiences while maintaining fictionalization, and 3) preserving creative agency, enjoyment, and life-art boundaries. Co-design workshops with 16 writers and researchers operationalized these goals into concrete interaction mechanisms using a technology probe. We then conducted supported field trials with eight writers across 24 sessions using a refined probe, revealing writer-perceived benefits (e.g., enriched fictional ideas from serendipitous encounters), emergent practices (e.g., micro-creation), and design considerations for future sustained use. We contribute design explorations for the CRAFT approach, offering design implications and empirical insights on ubiquitous human-AI creative collaboration in everyday life.
authors: Runze Cai; Yuxuan Huang; Lin-Ping Yuan; Kexin Xiang; David Hsu; Collier Nogues; Jussi Pekka Holopainen; Shengdong Zhao

title: Continuous Temperature Monitoring via Wearable Devices for Fever or Infection Management in Acute Care Hospitals: Scoping Review of Clinical Implementation and Data Analytics
abstract: BACKGROUND: Infections are a major health concern in hospitalized patients. Fever is an early sign of infection, making temperature monitoring essential for infection surveillance. Wearable devices are increasingly being explored for continuous temperature monitoring in acute care hospitals, but how temperature data from wearables are monitored, presented, and used to support fever or infection management in clinical practice remains poorly understood. OBJECTIVE: This study aims to map existing evidence on the use of temperature data from wearables for fever or infection management in acute care hospitals, focusing on wearables' characteristics; data transmission, storage, and presentation strategies; data preprocessing and analytic approaches; and the maturity of wearables' clinical integration. METHODS: We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, CINAHL, and IEEE Xplore for publications from January 2013 to July 2026 using the population, concept, context (PCC) framework. Primary research studies using wearables to monitor patients' body temperature in acute care hospitals for fever or infection management, published in English or Chinese, were eligible. Temperature data analyses were classified according to the descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analytics framework. The clinical integration of wearables was assessed using a tailored maturity framework modified from the World Health Organization's stages of maturity for digital health interventions. RESULTS: We included 29 publications from 26 studies, published between 2018 and 2026. Eighteen wearable devices were identified, monitoring temperature at the axilla, chest, wrist, or upper arm. Continuous data streams were predominantly transmitted in real time, while 5 studies used non-real-time batch uploads, periodic synchronization, or device-memory downloads. Only 7 studies presented wearable temperature data in clinical settings, displaying data on mobile devices and/or centralized monitoring stations; only 1 study reported enabling alerts through electronic health records (EHRs). Invalid sensor data filtering methods varied across studies, such as physiological thresholds, firmware quality scores, and statistical outlier detection. Temperature data were most frequently analyzed by descriptive analytics (n=19) to depict the frequency, timing, and duration of fever episodes, followed by diagnostic analytics (n=6) to identify risk factors or distinguish causes of fever, and predictive analytics (n=9) to forecast impending fever or infections. None of the included studies used prescriptive analytics. For clinical integration, most studies were at the clinical validation stage (n=9) or clinical research stage (n=17), corresponding to an early stage of maturity; 3 studies reached the routine clinical practice stage, and none progressed to multicenter implementation or full integration stages. CONCLUSIONS: While promising, the clinical integration of wearables remains at an early stage of maturity. Critical gaps exist in translating temperature data into actionable clinical insights, with limited data presentation, poor EHR interoperability, and underdeveloped analytic approaches. Future research should prioritize standardized data cleaning frameworks, workflow integration, and clinical interpretation to facilitate the active use of wearable data in clinical decision-making. authors: Yuwei Liu; Qimeng Zhao; Ka Li; Dawn Dowding

title: Effectiveness of Apple watch as a diagnostic tool Compared to Polysomnography in detecting Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Adults
abstract: Background:Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common sleep-related breathing disorder associated with significant cardiovascular and metabolic complications. Polysomnography (PSG) remains the gold standard for diagnosis; however, its cost, complexity, and limited accessibility highlight the need for simpler, non-invasive monitoring tools. Consumer-grade wearable devices, such as the Apple Watch Series 6, have emerged as potential alternatives for continuous sleep monitoring. Aim:To evaluate the comparability of Apple Watch–derived physiological parameters with polysomnography in adults and to assess its potential role as an adjunctive screening tool for obstructive sleep apnea. Materials and Methods: A prospective observational study was conducted among 24 adult participants undergoing overnight polysomnography. Simultaneous recordings were obtained using the Apple Watch. Parameters including oxygen saturation (SpO₂), heart rate (HR), snoring index, and sleep duration were analyzed. Statistical analysis included descriptive statistics, paired sample t-tests for comparison, and Pearson correlation to assess relationships between smartwatch and PSG measurements. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results:The mean apnea–hypopnea index (AHI) measured by polysomnography was 14.88 ± 8.81 events/hour. Apple Watch measurements demonstrated strong positive correlations with PSG for SpO₂ (r=0.99), heart rate (r=0.99), snoring index (r=0.99), and sleep duration.(r=0.99). No statistically significant differences were observed between the two methods for any parameter (p > 0.05). Additionally, individuals with OSA showed lower oxygen saturation, higher heart rate, increased snoring index, and reduced sleep duration compared to non-OSA individuals, with similar trends observed in both measurement methods. Conclusion:The Apple Watch provides physiological measurements comparable to polysomnography and reflects differences between OSA and non-OSA individuals. However, it cannot independently diagnose OSA, as it does not measure the apnea–hypopnea index. Therefore, it may serve as a useful non-invasive screening and monitoring tool, while PSG remains the gold standard.
authors: Prasanna Kumar P.S

title: QUANTUM HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE & MOLECULAR OBSERVATORY CIVILIZATION AT THE LIMIT Safety, Privacy, Equity, Nanomedicine, Wearables, Autonomous Care, Molecular Observatories, Longitudinal Health, and Life-Centered Governance
abstract: QUANTUM HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE & MOLECULAR OBSERVATORY CIVILIZATION AT THE LIMITSafety, Privacy, Equity, Nanomedicine, Wearables, Autonomous Care, Molecular Observatories, Longitudinal Health, and Life-Centered Governance Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli How much continuous molecular observability should a health civilization build, and when does measurement burden exceed health benefit? QUANTUM HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE & MOLECULAR OBSERVATORY CIVILIZATION AT THE LIMIT is a large-scale research monograph exploring what happens when quantum-enabled measurement moves beyond isolated devices and becomes longitudinal health infrastructure. Its flagship Three-Coupling is: Longitudinal Insight x Human Rights x Life-Centered Utility The Quantum Health Civilization Index (QHCI) is introduced as a book-defined research heuristic linking longitudinal insight, rights integrity, health gain, and continuity/trust while explicitly accounting for privacy risk, overdiagnosis, and measurement overreach. QHCI is not a natural law, clinical score, diagnostic threshold, regulatory standard, or policy mandate. Across 82 chapters, the volume develops research architectures for exposure safety, nanomaterial fate, molecular privacy, high-dimensional consent, equitable access, nanomedicine, AI-interpreted health, wearables, portable sensing, home calibration, autonomous and remote care, cybersecurity, human override, molecular observatories, personal baselines, longitudinal molecular information, digital twins, missingness, overdiagnosis, incidental findings, intervention thresholds, watchful waiting, measurement restraint, data minimization, health infrastructure, standards, manufacturing readiness, interoperability, health economics, dual-use risk, environmental lifecycle, hype resistance, responsible communication, trust, intergenerational governance, failure science, and successor handoff. Every chapter begins with a Three-Coupling System, a named Core Relation, and an artistic geometric research model. The geometric research grammar includes the Longitudinal Molecular Observatory Helix, Health-Rights Corridor, Personal Molecular-State Manifold, Intervention Threshold Boundary Surface, Wearable-Home-Hospital Lattice, Autonomous Care Oversight Torus, Civilization Health Constellation, and Measurement-Burden Basin. The volume contains 200 Research Gates and 33 Answer Embryos. The Research Gates are designed as falsifiable entrances for safety studies, molecular-rights research, longitudinal validation, threshold experiments, wearable and autonomous-care stress tests, molecular-observatory infrastructure, standards work, governance, negative-result programs, measurement-restraint research, and successor reconstruction. The 33 Answer Embryos remain deliberately provisional. Each provides a working answer structure, evidence that could strengthen it, evidence that could weaken or falsify it, a design consequence, and a question for the next research hand. The central distinction is simple: More measurement does not automatically produce more health. A civilization capable of measuring nearly everything still needs a rigorous science of what not to measure, when not to alert, when not to intervene, how to preserve the right to refuse observation, and how to hand unresolved uncertainty to the next research generation. Better measurement becomes better life only when technical capability remains subordinate to health gain, dignity, access, trust, proportionality, and human agency.
