title: Precision Exercise Support for University Students: A Scoping Review of Assessment, Prescription, Monitoring, Feedback, and Adaptation
abstract: Objective: To map how exercise and physical-education research with university students has implemented assessment, subgroup targeting, individualized prescription, monitoring, feedback, and response-based adjustment, and to identify what is still required for a reproducible closed-loop precision-support system. Methods: This scoping review followed JBI guidance and the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews. PubMed, Scopus, and CINAHL Ultimate were searched on August 21, 2026, for English-language studies, supplemented by an existing 28-report full-text seed set. Eligible studies involved university students and evaluated an exercise, physical-education, fitness-testing, monitoring, or feedback component relevant to tailoring exercise support. A five-level framework was applied: standardized provision (level 0), subgroup targeting (level 1), assessment- or feedback-informed adaptation (level 2), individual prescription (level 3), and response-adaptive closed loop (level 4). Results: The searches and seed set identified 403 records; 358 unique records were screened, 48 reports were assessed in full text, and 30 studies entered the evidence map. Fifteen studies used standardized provision, three targeted a predefined subgroup, six implemented assessment, monitoring, or personalized feedback without a complete individual prescription, and six reported individual exercise prescriptions. No study fully specified a level-4 closed loop with prospective monitoring variables, decision thresholds, and reproducible rules for changing frequency, intensity, time, or type. Exercise programs improved selected fitness, body-composition, physical-activity, and mental-health outcomes, but effects were outcome-specific and heterogeneous. Wearables and mobile platforms made monitoring scalable, yet fixed goals, multicomponent designs, and limited use of monitored data for treatment decisions constrained personalization. Assessment feedback could also reduce competence and intrinsic motivation when interpreted negatively. Conclusions: The literature has progressed beyond uniform exercise delivery, but digital monitoring should not be equated with precision. A defensible university model requires an auditable chain from multidimensional assessment to stratification, FITT prescription, process monitoring, interpretable feedback, and threshold-based adjustment, alongside evaluation of safety, equity, adherence, teacher workload, and operational efficiency.
authors: Wenshan Du; Yingsoon Goh

title: Artificial Intelligence in Supporting Early Intervention for Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: Opportunities and Challenges
abstract: Early identification and intervention are central to improving developmental trajectories for children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet access to specialist assessment and therapy remains uneven. Artificial intelligence (AI) has been proposed as a way to extend the reach and precision of early support. This article reviews the opportunities and challenges of AI in early intervention for children with ASD, using a conceptual-analytical narrative review. It synthesizes peer-reviewed studies and authoritative guidance across three stages of the care pathway: screening, diagnostic decision support, and intervention delivery, and examines the limitations that accompany each. The findings indicate that machine learning applied to parent reports, home videos, eye-gaze and attention measures, and neuroimaging shows promising accuracy for early detection; that social robots and wearable aids can elicit social behavior in structured settings; and that these gains are constrained by small and unrepresentative samples, limited external validation, algorithmic bias, opacity, privacy risks, and uncertain transfer to everyday life. The discussion argues that AI is best positioned as an augmentation of, and not a substitute for, clinical judgment and family-centered care, and it outlines implications for practitioners and research priorities, including validation in culturally and linguistically diverse populations.
authors: Dr. Bourkache Sabiha

title: Multimodal approaches in hazard detection and risk assessment: current methods and future trends
abstract: Hazard detection and risk assessment are important across transportation, healthcare, mining, industry, and environmental monitoring. Advances in sensor technology and deep learning have increased the use of multimodal approaches that combine complementary sensing and data sources. This structured narrative review examines 89 publications and classifies hazard detection methods as visual-based, environmental sensor-based, wearable device-based, or multimodal fusion methods. Risk assessment methods are organized as deterministic and rule-based, probabilistic, statistical and data-driven, or methods under non-statistical uncertainty. Among the 39 original hazard detection studies, 27 (69.2%) used single-modal or non-fusion approaches, whereas 12 (30.8%) used explicit multimodal fusion. Representative within-study comparisons showed that camera–LiDAR fusion increased detection accuracy from 58.3% to 74.7%, while radar- camera fusion reduced the average false-negative rate from 6.46% for the camera and 6.59% for the radar to 0.61% for the fused tracker. These findings indicate that multimodal fusion can improve detection robustness within the same evaluation setting, although the magnitude of improvement depends on the task, dataset, sensors, and fusion architecture. The review also finds that risk assessment method selection depends mainly on data availability, uncertainty type, explainability, computational resources, and response-time requirements. Sensor alignment, data quality, real-time processing, maintenance cost, and limited common evaluation procedures remain major challenges.
authors: Naji Alhusaini; Amar N. Alsheavi; Abdulqawi Alarefi; Shenghui Zhao; Jing Li; Haibao Chen; Pan Lei; Ibrahim Abdulrab Ahmed; Jamil A. M. Saif; Ali Abdo Mohammed Al-kubati; Peng Gao
venue: Journal of King Saud University - Computer and Information Sciences

title: Recommendations for the development, implementation, and evaluation of technology-assisted physical activity interventions to support healthy aging: insights from PhysAgeNet
abstract: Digital health technologies offer substantial potential to support physical activity among older adults, yet their development and implementation often remain driven by technological possibilities rather than clinical evidence and user needs. This position paper, developed within the PhysAgeNet COST Action, synthesizes current evidence and expert consensus to provide recommendations for designing, evaluating, and implementing technology-assisted physical activity interventions for older adults. We first outline key technology categories and functions relevant to physical activity promotion, including wearables, exergames, mobile applications, telehealth platforms, and smart environments, and highlight critical technical requirements such as accuracy, reliability, connectivity, interoperability, and data security. We then emphasize the need to align digital interventions with established clinical guidelines for physical activity, falls prevention, frailty, and sarcopenia, including explicit specification of exercise dose according to FITT-VP principles and robust monitoring of dual adherence to both physical activity and technology use. Building on technology acceptance models and behavior change theories, we describe how user-centered and co-creative design processes can translate theoretical constructs into concrete digital features that enhance motivation, enjoyment, and long-term engagement. Finally, we propose stakeholder-specific guidance for developers, researchers, and clinicians, including recommendations on user assessment, recruitment of vulnerable groups, implementation frameworks, and clinically grounded evaluation of outcomes and usability. Together, these recommendations provide a pragmatic roadmap for moving from a technology-push paradigm toward evidence-based, acceptable, and equitable technology-assisted physical activity interventions that can be sustainably integrated into routine practice for older adults.
authors: Nadja Schott; Jana Pelclová; Eleftheria Giannouli; Antoine Langeard; Christopher L. McCrum; Rosemary Dubbeldam; Rafael A. Bernardes; Arben Boshnjaku; David Beckwée

title: Artificial Intelligence in Infection Prevention: From Prediction to Protection
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), first defined by John McCarthy in 1955, refers to the science of developing intelligent machines capable of performing tasks that traditionally require human reasoning, learning, and decision-making. Since its early development in the 1960s and rapid expansion in the 2000s, AI has evolved substantially, driven by the availability of large digital health datasets, advances in machine learning, and increased computational power. In infection prevention and control (IPC), AI is emerging as a powerful tool for strengthening surveillance, improving diagnostic accuracy, predicting outbreaks, and supporting timely clinical interventions. AI-powered systems can analyze electronic health records (EHRs), laboratory results, antimicrobial prescribing patterns, microbiological data, patient demographics, and real-time hospital surveillance information to identify patients at high risk of infection and detect potential healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) at an early stage. Furthermore, AI can support antimicrobial stewardship by identifying inappropriate prescribing patterns and predicting antimicrobial resistance trends. Integration of data from wearable devices, environmental sensors, imaging systems, and unstructured clinical notes can provide continuous, real-time monitoring of infectious diseases and infection risks. AI-enabled computer vision and sensor-based technologies may also facilitate automated hand hygiene monitoring, helping healthcare facilities improve compliance with infection-control practices. Predictive models can identify emerging clusters of infection and assist public health teams in forecasting potential outbreaks, enabling earlier containment measures. Thus, AI effectively bridges prediction and protection, enhancing patient safety, healthcare quality, and operational efficiency. However, successful implementation requires high-quality data, robust validation, privacy protection, ethical governance, transparency, and recognition of the limitations of correlation-based predictions.
authors: Madhumita Das

title: Sources of Inequity and Fairness Risks in Wellbeing Sensing
abstract: Passive sensing for wellbeing uses smartphones and wearables to continuously collect human behavioral data and applies ML/AI models to infer psychological states and behaviors (e.g., depression, cognitive load). These systems are increasingly adopted in high-stakes settings, yet fairness research remains limited, primarily to post-hoc, identity-based comparisons of model performance. However, passive sensing combines heterogeneous sensing infrastructures, indirect behavioral inference, and longitudinal deployment---characteristics that, while not exclusive to the domain, are jointly pronounced here and raise two underexplored questions: (1) what additional sources of inequity arise from these characteristics, and (2) how do such inequities propagate beyond algorithmic audits across the system lifecycle? To address this gap, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 14 researchers and practitioners across five countries, examining how fairness risks emerge and are negotiated across the full passive sensing lifecycle. Our findings empirically characterize five situated sources of inequity (e.g., comfort with monitoring, behavioral regularity) that systematically shape fairness risks beyond identity-based attributes. We further synthesize 15 fairness risks and corresponding mitigation strategies across the lifecycle, from study design to deployment. Finally, we identify structural barriers that constrain fair practice in reality, and argue that enabling fair passive sensing requires both individual researcher efforts and ecosystem-level governance support from funders, publication venues, and deploying institutions.
authors: Han Zhang; Vedant Das Swain; Koustuv Saha; Anind K. Dey; Jennifer Mankoff
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society

title: Sweat, Sync, and Exposure: A Privacy Analysis of Interoperable Health and Fitness Ecosystems in Android
abstract: Health and fitness services on mobile platforms operate within interconnected ecosystems that aggregate sensitive data across wearable devices, mobile apps, cloud services, and third-party SDKs. Through integrations with services such as Google Fit, Fitbit, Strava, and Garmin Connect via OAuth 2.0, hundreds of apps can gain access to health records provided by other apps and devices, from heart rate to sleep patterns. Two access control mechanisms regulate health data at different levels: Android runtime permissions govern data on the device, while OAuth scopes govern data exposed through integration platforms. However, neither mechanism con strains how data is subsequently shared with third parties. Once accessed, health data and user identifiers can flow to other apps and to dozens of embedded third-party SDKs. This paper presents the first large-scale empirical study of such health-data dissemination across Android health ecosystems. We study 1,548 health apps and 11 integration platforms using an analysis pipeline that combines static and dynamic analysis, BLE device simulation, sensor fuzzing, and network traffic instrumentation to capture cross-app data flows mediated by OAuth. Our analysis shows that 42.6% of analyzed apps integrate with at least one integration platform and that 57.2% transmit sensitive health data alongside persistent IDs to third parties, enabling cross-app profiling and re-identification for secondary purposes. Finally, we uncover structural privacy risks in OAuth-authorized integrations: 32% of integrating apps forward platform-sourced records to third party SDKs, with little or no user awareness.
authors: Aniketh Girish; Johanna Gunawan; Srdjan Matic; Joel Reardon; Juan Tapiador; Narseo Vallina-Rodríguez

title: The Use of Mobile Applications in Health Promotion and Disease Prevention
abstract: Thesis. Mobile health applications can support the prevention of noncommunicable diseases by facilitating self-monitoring, encouraging healthier behaviours, and extending preventive support beyond conventional healthcare settings; however, their public health value depends on sustained engagement, reliable evidence, data protection, and equitable access. Concept. This narrative review synthesizes peer-reviewed studies and reports concerning mobile applications used to address major modifiable risk factors for noncommunicable diseases. It considers applications supporting physical activity, nutrition and weight management, and the monitoring of physiological parameters, while examining their functions, documented benefits, and implementation challenges. Results and conclusion. The reviewed evidence indicates that mHealth applications can improve physical activity, dietary behaviours, weight management, and selected physiological outcomes, particularly when they incorporate goal setting, personalized feedback, reminders, gamification, and integration with wearable devices. Nevertheless, effects vary across interventions and populations, and long-term adherence frequently declines. Concerns regarding measurement accuracy, limited clinical validation, privacy and security, unequal digital access, and the geographical concentration of the evidence restrict broader implementation and generalizability. Mobile applications should therefore complement rather than replace professionally delivered prevention and should be integrated into public health systems using evidence-based, interoperable, secure, and user-centred approaches. Originality. The article provides an integrated public health perspective that connects the preventive functions of mHealth applications with the behavioural, technological, ethical, and equity-related conditions required for their responsible use in noncommunicable disease prevention. Keywords: mHealth, mobile health applications, noncommunicable diseases, disease prevention, health promotion, digital health, lifestyle interventions
authors: Agnieszka Kiedik; Zuzanna Pietruk; Dzianis Dashkevich; Przemysław Siemiątkowski; Kacper Zima; Dominik Ryszard Płaza; Michał Kozicki

title: On‐Skin Wireless Vibratory Interfaces by Stretchable Multilayer Circuits
abstract: ABSTRACT Emerging technologies in soft electronics are facilitating seamless interactions with the human body's neural network. Among various sensory modalities, vibratory stimulation offers distinct advantages as a feedback strategy in wearable and implantable systems. However, existing devices face challenges of limited battery life, noncompliant device architecture, and complicated circuit designs, particularly for devices requiring adaptive fitting to various curved surfaces of the human body. In this study, we present a wireless and stretchable electronic device with multilayer circuits using elastic and printable metallic inks. The wireless vibratory interfaces were designed with a compact and soft circuit, which directly converts electromagnetic power to produce vibrotactile stimulation. Patterns of the mechanical vibration were highly programmable by frequency‐shift keying (FSK) modulation of the input signals. The wireless and soft vibratory interfaces have excellent mechanical compliance, maintaining their functionalities under large deformations. Together with a fabric signal transmitter fabricated from elastic conductive fibers, we demonstrate a smart and interactive on‐skin device, which translates spatial information into perceptible tactile cues to navigate visually impaired users through unstructured environments. The developed device holds significant promise for applications in sensory substitution, human‐machine interfaces, and biomedical treatments.
authors: Jiawei Liu; Yanfeng Hou; Shengkang Fu; Maoxin Yang; Hongbiao Sun; Yi Huang; ZhiBo Wang; Xiqiang Luo; Chengliang Tao; Qing Tang; Jiangxin Wang

title: Mind the (regulatory) gap: can the European regulatory framework govern non-invasive consumer neurotechnology?
abstract: The most recent advances in neurotechnology are starting to blur the boundary between science fiction and reality. From meditation headbands monitoring brain activity to wearable brain-computer interfaces designed to assist drivers, devices once confined to laboratories are now entering the consumer market, promising greater wellbeing and self-optimization, as users are effectively “giving the key” to technologies to interact with their brain. The growing accessibility of non-invasive consumer neurotechnology raises unprecedented legal challenges: brain-derived data may reveal highly sensitive information, while the integration of AI and connected devices creates novel cybersecurity risks. This dissertation critically assesses whether the current European legal framework can adequately address these challenges, focusing on the Medical Devices Regulation, Cybersecurity regulations, GDPR, and AI Act. It also examines the debate on neurorights, considering whether new fundamental rights are necessary or whether existing protections can address emerging risks. Chapter I introduces commercial non-invasive neurotechnology, distinguishing it from medical and invasive applications and identifying the legal interests at stake. Chapter II analyses the existing EU framework, including fundamental rights and the applicability and limitations of the MDR, GDPR, and AI Act. Chapter III focuses on cybersecurity, by exploring neurosecurity and assessing whether EU legislation and industry standards provide adequate protection. Finally, Chapter IV will consider some international approaches in this domain and will propose a final position on the governance of consumer neurotechnology in the EU.
authors: EMILIYA EMILOVA TAUSHANSKA
venue: Electronic Theses and Dissertations Repository (University of Pisa)

title: A review on monitoring orthodontic treatment: from traditional approaches to innovative point-of-care tools
abstract: Orthodontic treatment is performed to treat malocclusions by improving oral functions, tooth alignment, and facial esthetics that impact the quality of life of patients significantly. Nevertheless, various factors like complexity of malocclusions, patient compliance, and dental hygiene can influence treatment outcomes. Traditional diagnostic methods such as clinical evaluation, radiography techniques, and dental casts have played a major role in orthodontics and have remained a standard diagnostic method in dentistry to date. On the other hand, these methods are associated with major disadvantages like radiation exposure and invasive procedures. To address these limitations, recent diagnostic methods have identified various biomarkers in gingival crevicular fluid and saliva as non-invasive diagnostic methods. These biomarkers can help clinicians in planning orthodontic treatment at the optimal time and determine the appropriate initiation of the treatment. Point-of-care diagnostic tools such as lateral flow assays, Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats and microfluidic devices, and wearable technologies are emerging as promising alternatives for orthodontic treatment monitoring by offering rapid, cost-effective, and non-invasive alternatives to traditional methods. Recent developments such as incorporation of artificial intelligence and machine learning into orthodontic software attempt to improve the overall monitoring of orthodontic treatment. This review aims to present various traditional and innovative methods that have shown promising outcomes in research, along with insights into emerging areas that serve as potential game changers in orthodontic treatment monitoring.
authors: Ananya Nair; Prajwal Shetty; M.S. Ravi

title: Sleep Health in Adults with Intellectual Disability: Recent Advances and Persistent Evidence Gaps
abstract: Abstract Purpose of Review Adults with intellectual disability (ID) experience a disproportionate burden of sleep disorders with major impacts on physical, neuropsychiatric and behavioural health, yet evidence to guide practice has lagged behind the general population. This review updates our 2024 narrative synthesis, focusing on clinically actionable advances in sleep health for adults with ID. Recent Findings Recent observational data in adults with Down syndrome indicate that obstructive sleep apnoea is associated with adverse cardiometabolic, mortality and Alzheimer disease outcomes. Positive airway pressure can be feasible with individualised support, while retrospective studies of surgical treatment suggest possible benefits in selected patients, although residual OSA and confounding by treatment selection remain important considerations. Emerging diagnostic technologies, including home-based acoustic sensors, wearables, cardiorespiratory algorithms and three-dimensional facial biomarkers, represent promising developments that require further evaluation against established diagnostic pathways. Meta-analytic and cohort studies describe aetiology-related sleep phenotypes and persistent sleep and circadian disruption in autistic adults; a small uncontrolled case series provides preliminary evidence that daridorexant may be tolerated and associated with improved sleep in selected adults with intellectual disability. Summary Despite recent advances, major inequalities persist, highlighting the need for accessible diagnostics, population‑specific instruments and adult‑focused guidelines embedding sleep management within lifelong care for people with ID.
authors: Naphat Sirinimnualkul; Bhathika Perera; David John O'Regan

title: NOCTURIA AS AN UNDERESTIMATED PUBLIC HEALTH PROBLEM: SLEEP, PSYCHOSOCIAL AND ECONOMIC BURDEN, AND DIGITAL MONITORING
abstract: Nocturia is prevalent among adults, yet it remains frequently overlooked and underestimated. It is one of the most common lower urinary tract symptoms, but its consequences extend well beyond the urinary tract. This critical narrative review examines nocturia as a public-health problem across sleep, psychological well-being, family and social participation, work, safety, economic burden, and digital monitoring. Targeted backward citation checking was undertaken, with priority given to population studies, systematic reviews, qualitative research, trials with patient-relevant endpoints, guidelines, and large observational datasets. Clinically significant nocturia, commonly operationalized as at least two voids per night, becomes more frequent with age but also affects working-age adults. Objective sleep studies show graded deterioration in sleep continuity as nocturnal voiding increases. Longer time to the first void is associated with longer sleep, and improvements in the first uninterrupted sleep period track with better perceived sleep quality. Nocturia is also associated with a broad range of psychological difficulties, although causal direction remains uncertain. Qualitative, workplace, and claims studies show that burden is transferred across households, employers, and health systems; falls add a safety concern in older adults. Electronic bladder diaries and wearables can improve longitudinal characterization, but direct evidence that monitoring itself improves nocturia-specific outcomes remains limited. A holistic approach to nocturia as a public-health problem is therefore needed. Episode count remains necessary and important, but it should be interpreted alongside sleep continuity, bother, and next-day function.
authors: Kamila Zmysłowska; Jan Mateusz Kiersztyn; Anna Szatkowska; Malwina Kwaśniewska; Adam Hajdaniak; Aleksandra Grabowska; Natalia Seńcio; Klaudia Aleksandra Stadnik
venue: International Journal of Innovative Technologies in Social Science

title: Unmet needs in functional neurological disorder related to digital healthcare
abstract: Functional neurological disorder (FND) is a common yet historically neglected condition that presents major unmet needs across diagnosis, treatment and health service delivery. This article examines how digital healthcare could address gaps in several areas: (i) using large biobank and clinic datasets to reveal epidemiology, comorbidity, mechanisms, economic burden and possibly treatment effects; (ii) augmenting complex and time-consuming assessment processes that currently exceed clinical capacity with artificial intelligence; (iii) using digital tools to improve diagnostic precision-for example through automated tremor analysis, quantification of functional motor signs and speech recognition; (iv) improving self-management and access to therapy via online tools and telehealth programmes; (v) improving outcome measurement and existing therapy using wearables and telehealth; and (vi) new therapies such as AI-assisted therapies, biofeedback and virtual or augmented reality interventions. Finally, I discuss the risks of depersonalization, privacy breaches, therapeutic substitution, digital dependence and digital exclusion. In addition, positive therapist effects-variability in outcomes driven by the clinician rather than the intervention-remain difficult to replicate digitally. The challenge for clinicians and researchers is to ensure that technological advances humanize rather than mechanize care, harnessing digital tools to extend expertise, consistency and accessibility without eroding the therapeutic relationship at the heart of effective FND treatment. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'Digital healthcare for the management of functional neurological disorders'.
authors: Jon Stone
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences

title: Digital Health Interventions for Preventing Type 2 Diabetes in Adults Elevated Risk: A Scoping Review of Interventions, Outcomes, and Implementation Determinants
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is preceded by a modifiable period of prediabetes, creating opportunities for scalable prevention through digital health interventions (DHIs). This scoping review mapped intervention types, study characteristics, outcomes, methodological limitations, and research gaps in DHIs for preventing T2DM among at-risk adults. Following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework, Joanna Briggs Institute guidance, and PRISMA-ScR, 52 records were identified through structured searches and citation tracking. After removing 16 duplicates, 36 records were screened using Population–Concept–Context criteria, yielding 13 eligible studies or trial protocols. The interventions comprised mobile application-based diabetes prevention programs, SMS/text messaging, telehealth or telecoaching, wearables and glucose monitoring, artificial intelligence-enabled coaching, and multicomponent hybrid platforms. Commonly assessed outcomes included weight, body mass index, HbA1c, fasting glucose, incident T2DM, behavioral change, and program engagement. Overall, DHIs showed short- to medium-term benefits for weight reduction and glycemic risk markers, while several landmark trials reported reductions in T2DM incidence. However, the evidence was constrained by short follow-up periods, small and homogeneous samples, high attrition, self-reported outcomes, and limited economic evaluation. No eligible Indonesian prevention study was identified. Future research should prioritize long-term, implementation-informed comparative effectiveness trials in underrepresented Southeast Asian populations, particularly Indonesia, while evaluating sustainability, scalability, equity, and cost-effectiveness.
authors: Januarso Setiawan; Bagoes Widjanarko; Ayun Sriatmi
venue: Journal of Educational Health and Community Psychology

title: Informing personalization of technologies for promoting physical activity: bridging the knowledge, attitude and practice model and human-centered design
abstract: Background Although the benefits of physical activity (PA) are well established and inactivity poses substantial risks, encouraging adults to change and sustain PA behaviors remains a challenge. Mobile technologies have emerged as accessible and cost-effective tools to encourage healthier behaviors. Personalization is a key factor for improving user engagement and adherence, but current approaches often rely on surface-level data and overlook cognitive and motivational aspects. Objective This study explores how mobile exercise- and health-related technologies can be personalized to support PA behavior change by integrating the Knowledge, Attitude, and Practice (KAP) model with a human-centered design approach. Methods We conducted semi-structured interviews with 24 adults aged 34–66 years to explore their PA habits and use of exercise- and health-related technology. Interview recordings were transcribed, reviewed, and analyzed using deductive thematic analysis guided by the three domains of the KAP model: knowledge, attitude, and practice. Results Participants demonstrated varied knowledge of PA, ranging from general health benefits to specific exercise practices. General awareness of the benefits of PA was not always accompanied by practical knowledge about planning exercise or interpreting activity data. Attitudes toward PA and mobile exercise- and health-related technology were influenced by motivation, convenience, and emotional responses, with some participants reporting guilt or stress related to use of mobile exercise- and health-related technology. Practices reflected diverse PA routines, from structured exercise to incidental daily movement. These practices were shaped by work, family responsibilities, physical limitations, preferred environments, and differing needs for social or solitary activity. Engagement with mobile exercise- and health-related technology varied widely, with some participants relying on wearables and apps, while others reported irregular or discontinued use. Together, the findings informed a framework of 20 dimensions describing how individual differences in knowledge, attitudes, and practices can guide the personalization of mobile exercise- and health-related technology for PA promotion. Conclusions Personalization of mobile exercise- and health-related technologies for PA promotion should extend beyond surface-level data to include cognitive, emotional, and contextual factors that influence behavior. Applying the KAP model within human-centered design can inform adaptive, empathetic, and context-sensitive solutions that better resonate with users’ lived experiences and support sustainable PA engagement.
authors: Agnieszka Jaff; Mia Folke; Annica Kristoffersson

title: Revolutionising Clinical Trials with Artificial Intelligence: A Paradigm Shift in Drug Development
abstract: AI is revolutionising clinical trials by improving efficiency, accuracy, and decision-making throughout the study process. Traditional clinical trials are frequently time-consuming, expensive, and constrained by factors such as patient recruiting delays, protocol complexity, data management concerns, and high dropout rates. To solve these limitations, AI technologies such as machine learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics, and deep learning are increasingly being integrated into clinical trials. AI-powered solutions offer quick patient identification and recruitment by analysing electronic health records, real-world data, and genomic databases. Predictive modelling enhances trial design by identifying the best outcomes, stratifying patient populations, and projecting potential dangers. During trial execution, AI improves real-time data monitoring, anomaly detection, and adverse event prediction, resulting in improved patient safety and regulatory compliance. Furthermore, decentralised and virtual trials benefit from AI-powered wearable devices and remote monitoring systems, which provide continuous data collection and increased participant involvement. It will be necessary to fully grasp the advantages of AI in clinical research. Despite its benefits, AI deployment in clinical trials poses problems such as data privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, regulatory uncertainties, and the necessity for uniform validation methods. Ethical issues and openness in AI models are essential for preserving confidence and achieving equitable healthcare results. Overall, AI has the potential to significantly accelerate medication development, cut costs, and improve clinical trial success rates. Continued collaboration between researchers, regulatory agencies, technology developers, and healthcare institutions will be required to fully exploit the benefits of AI in clinical research. Keywords: AI, Clinical Trials, Machine Learning, Predictive Analytics, Patient Recruitment, Real-World Data, Deep Learning, Natural Language Processing (NLP), Drug Development, Digital Health, Decentralised Trials, Data Monitoring, Healthcare Innovation
authors: E Nikitha; K Lara Supriya; K Rakesh; Beena Devi Maddi; M V Naga Bhushanam

title: Digital Health Among Educators: A Scoping Review
abstract: Background: Digital health technologies are increasingly used to support health management, monitoring, and health-related practices. Educators face a range of physical and mental health challenges, yet research on educators’ digital health remains fragmented across educational settings, geographical contexts, and forms of digital health management. This scoping review aimed to map and synthesize the literature on educators’ digital health by examining (1) digital health literacy and related competencies; (2) experiences with digital health technologies, and (3) factors influencing educators’ capacity to navigate the digital health ecosystem. Methods: The scoping review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. A systematic search was conducted for English written empirical peer-reviewed articles related to educators’ digital health on 8 June 2026. Results: A total of 31 studies were included. Three themes were identified. First, educators’ digital health literacy varied across demographic groups and educational settings in different geographical contexts and was associated with health behaviors and well-being. Second, educators engaged with mobile applications, wearable devices, AI-driven technologies, telehealth, and online programs. Third, educators’ engagement with these technologies was shaped by individual, technological, organizational, and contextual factors, including leadership support, privacy concerns, time pressure, and workplace culture. Conclusions: This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of educators’ digital health, covering digital health literacy, experiences with digital health technologies, and factors influencing engagement. The findings highlight uneven digital health literacy, varied experiences with digital technologies, and the importance of institutional support. They also underscore the need for targeted capacity-building initiatives, context-sensitive interventions, and further research to strengthen educators’ digital health.
authors: Weiyan Liao; Min Qiu; Dandan Wu; Xianhan Huang; Junjun Chen; Minjuan Wang; Hui Li

title: PREDICTIVE CHRONIC DISEASE SURVEILLANCE FRAMEWORK: INTEGRATING MACHINE LEARNING, REAL-TIME DATA, AND PUBLIC HEALTH RESPONSE
abstract: Chronic disease surveillance is an essential part of public health because it helps governments and health organizations understand the burden of disease, identify risk factors, recognize disparities, and track changes in health outcomes. Most existing surveillance systems, however, are mainly concerned with describing what has already happened. The growing use of electronic health records, wearable devices, environmental sensors, administrative databases, and other continuously generated sources of information creates an opportunity to move surveillance toward a more forward-looking approach. This article presents the Predictive Chronic Disease Surveillance Framework (PCDSF), a framework for using multiple data sources and machine learning to estimate changing population-level risk and to connect those estimates to public health action. The framework treats predictive surveillance as a continuous cycle: data are collected and combined, population risk is estimated, emerging patterns are identified, decisions are made, interventions are implemented, and the resulting outcomes are fed back into the system. This makes surveillance an ongoing learning process rather than a one-way reporting exercise. The framework also makes an important distinction between predicting disease in an individual patient and predicting changes in risk across populations. Its purpose is not simply to identify who is likely to become ill, but to help public health organizations understand where risk is increasing, which groups may be most affected, and where preventive resources could have the greatest impact. Six propositions are developed around multimodal data integration, timely updating, predictive performance, intervention, equity, and continuous learning. The article also discusses privacy, interoperability, data quality, algorithmic bias, transparency, and organizational capacity as conditions that can determine whether predictive surveillance works in practice.
authors: Lord Amoateng Adjei; Franklin Akwasi Adjei; Justice Manu; Kelvin McKeown Antwi Adjei; Augustine Afriyie; Bernard Kwame Frempong
venue: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews

title: Smart materials for biosensing of infectious diseases: Mechanisms, materials, platforms, and translational opportunities
abstract: Rapid and decentralized detection of infectious diseases remains a critical challenge for global healthcare systems. Conventional diagnostic methods such as polymerase chain reaction and immunoassays provide high analytical accuracy but often require centralized laboratories, complex workflows, and trained personnel, limiting their accessibility in point-of-care and resource-limited settings. Smart materials—materials capable of dynamically responding to external physical, chemical, or biological stimuli—have emerged as powerful platforms for next-generation biosensors due to their tunable physicochemical properties, signal amplification capabilities, and compatibility with miniaturized sensing architectures. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in smart-material-enabled biosensors for infectious disease detection. Key material classes including graphene-based nanomaterials, piezoelectric materials, light-responsive nanostructures, magnetic materials, Prussian blue derivatives, metal–organic and covalent–organic frameworks (MOFs/COFs), and conductive polymer–hydrogel systems are discussed in terms of their sensing mechanisms, transduction strategies, and analytical performance. We highlight how these materials enable diverse detection modalities—including electrochemical, optical, piezoelectric, and magnetically mediated sensing—allowing rapid and highly sensitive detection of viral and bacterial pathogens. Emerging fabrication approaches, integration with microfluidic systems, wearable devices, and data-driven diagnostics are also examined. Finally, we discuss key challenges for clinical translation, including stability, biocompatibility, antifouling performance, large-scale manufacturing, and regulatory considerations. Smart materials provide a versatile foundation for developing next-generation biosensing technologies capable of enabling rapid, decentralized, and continuous infectious disease monitoring.
authors: Seyed Mojtaba Sajjadi; Zahra Abooalizadeh; Mohammad Mehdi Banoei; Bahareh Babamiri; Ahmad Rezaei Kolahchi; Mehdi Mohammadi Ashani; Amir Sanati‐Nezhad

title: Telerehabilitation for Motor Recovery in Adults with Neurological Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Across Motor Domains, Delivery Models, and Follow-Up Effects
abstract: Background/Objectives: Telerehabilitation may extend neurorehabilitation beyond conventional settings, but comparative effects across neurological diagnoses and motor domains remain uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized motor outcomes while distinguishing International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health activity domains, delivery models, and comparator questions. Methods: Five databases were searched from inception to 8 June 2026 using two database-specific Boolean search strategies. Comparative studies of adults with neurological disorders receiving active remote, digital, virtual, wearable, or hybrid rehabilitation were eligible. Random-effects models used restricted maximum likelihood estimation; Hartung–Knapp confidence intervals were primary when at least three studies were available, and DerSimonian–Laird models were sensitivity analyses. Results: Eighty-seven studies included stroke, Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, acquired brain injury, or ataxia. For walking and mobility activities versus usual care, no additional therapy, or waitlist, the point estimate favoured telerehabilitation but was imprecise and compatible with no difference (standardized mean difference 1.06, 95% confidence interval −0.23 to 2.35; three studies; 121 participants; I2 = 57.6%). Global motor-functional and activities-of-daily-living outcomes showed similar uncertainty (0.83, −0.35 to 2.00; three studies; 304 participants; I2 = 73.6%). Both findings had very-low-certainty evidence. No pooled comparison included enough studies to assess publication bias. Two-study datasets for balance-related activity/postural control and upper-limb impairment were highly heterogeneous and interpreted descriptively. Conclusions: Comparative evidence for telerehabilitation across neurological diagnoses and motor domains remains uncertain. Programme characteristics are plausible implementation considerations, not established efficacy modifiers. Small evidence sets, wide intervals, clinical heterogeneity, risk of bias, and inconsistent adverse-event ascertainment preclude conclusions about clinical importance or established safety.
authors: Rocco Salvatore Calabrò; Arnold Fredrick D’Souza; Sanaz Pournajaf; Francesca Baglio; Carl Froilan D. Leochico; Alon Kalron

title: Systematic Review of Artificial Intelligence Techniques for Blood Glucose Predicting in Diabetes
abstract: Background/Objectives: The accurate prediction of Blood Glucose Levels (BGLs) is important for the effective management of diabetes. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become an effective tool for forecasting BGLs and offering decision support and therapeutic interventions. In this study, existing AI techniques for predicting BGLs were reviewed systematically to identify their limitations and strengths. Methods: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, a systematic review of relevant studies was performed. Research was identified through a detailed search of several databases including PubMed, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) Explore, and Scholar with a focus on publications ranging from 2010 to 2025. Search terms included “AI for predicting glucose levels in diabetes” and related keywords. Non-English and irrelevant studies were excluded. Results: Fifty-seven studies met the inclusion criteria. They used AI models such as Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), decision trees, and hybrid models like CNN-Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU). Many models demonstrated high accuracy, especially Bi-LSTM and CNN-GRU hybrids, but were often limited by small datasets, lack of generalizability, and low interpretability. Non invasive sensing technologies and real-time systems using Internet of Things (IoT) and wearable devices showed significant promise but require further validation. Conclusions: AI-based glucose prediction systems have advanced significantly, with some models achieving Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) values below 10 mg/dL in short-term forecasting. However, no single approach consistently outperforms others across all prediction horizons and patient scenarios. Future research should focus on integrating multimodal inputs, enhancing model interpretability, and validating systems using diverse, real-world datasets to ensure clinical reliability.
authors: Mohammed Alotaibi
venue: The International Arab Journal of Information Technology

title: Simulation-Based Training in Emergency Skills: A Narrative Review Across Diverse Learner Populations
abstract: Background: Emergency skills are critical competencies for managing sudden medical events, reducing disability, and lowering mortality rates. Traditional training methods are often limited by deficiencies in knowledge retention, skill acquisition, and clinical application. Despite growing evidence on simulation-based training, a comprehensive synthesis across diverse learner populations and training modalities remains lacking. This narrative review aims to provide a comprehensive narrative synthesis of current evidence regarding the implementation of simulation training in emergency skills education. Main Body: A literature search was conducted across PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus (2010-2026) using keywords related to simulation training, emergency skills, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, virtual reality, and medical education. The review is organized around four thematic areas: (1) theoretical foundations and core design elements of simulation training, including feedback, repetition, and scenario fidelity; (2) simulation training for practicing professionals, encompassing layered training models and crisis resource management; (3) simulation training for diverse learner populations, including school-age learners, health profession students, and community participants; and (4) emerging technologies including virtual reality, augmented reality, and wearable devices, which offer immersive and scalable alternatives despite distinct limitations. These modalities demonstrated significant improvements in knowledge acquisition, skill proficiency, and long-term retention, alongside self-reported gains in learner confidence, a subjective outcome that should be distinguished from objectively assessed competence. However, methodological limitations such as small sample sizes, brief follow-up periods, and heterogeneous outcome measures were pervasive. Conclusions: Simulation training enhances emergency skills across diverse populations, but long-term retention and cost-effectiveness require further investigation. Future directions include multicenter randomized controlled trials with extended follow-up, standardized outcome measures, and rigorous cost-effectiveness analyses to strengthen the evidence base for simulation-based emergency skills education.
authors: Baijian Chen; 王心杰; Deyang Li; Haojie Chen; Feng Gao; Jun Li; Fengxian He; Shiyi Liu; Hui Li; Ruifeng Zeng
venue: Advances in Medical Education and Practice

title: Edge AI for Real-Time Facial Emotion Detection: A Raspberry Pi-Based Approach with CNN
abstract: Forecasts and analysis of human behavior and emotions have received a lot of development in the area of artificial intelligence. There are some potentials that edge computing in the field of human behavior and emotion forecasting and analysis. In this research, an autonomous edge computing system utilizing Raspberry Pi for real-time emotion detection, which can detect seven basic emotions, namely, happiness, anger, sadness, surprise, neutral, fear, and disgust, has been developed. The system extracts several feature sets such as edges, shapes, and textures, as well as landmarks of the face and upper body. A convolutional neural network classifier is applied to these feature sets to classify emotions in real time. A classification model has been trained using a manually developed dataset through the Data Collector class. Real-time testing of the system and evaluation of the system based on several criteria such as F-measure, accuracy, precision, and sensitivity have been performed. It has been found that the proposed system has up to 98% accuracy in real-time emotion detection. authors: Muneera Altayeb; Khaled Abu Al Rub; Ahmad Nazzal; Areen M. Arabiat

title: Long-term quality of life, rehospitalization risks, and economic viability of remote cardiac rehabilitation: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background Although remote cardiac rehabilitation (RCR) is a promising alternative to traditional center-based care, evidence regarding its exact impact on health-related quality of life (HRQoL), cardiovascular safety, and economic viability remains fragmented, necessitating a comprehensive synthesis to guide clinical implementation. Objectives This systematic review and meta-analysis aim to evaluate the HRQoL, cardiovascular safety, and economic viability of RCR versus standard center-based care in cardiovascular disease, with subgroup analyses based on follow-up duration and high-risk patient cohorts. Methods Literature searches were conducted across multiple databases, including PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, supplemented by manual screening of relevant references to identify clinical studies on RCR up to July 2026. Two independent review teams performed data extraction and risk of bias assessment using the RevMan software. Meta-analyses were conducted employing random-effects models to calculate pooled effect sizes with corresponding 95% confidence intervals. Heterogeneity was assessed using the Cochrane Q test and I 2 statistic, and potential publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger's test. To evaluate the robustness of the pooled results and explore potential heterogeneity, subgroup and fixed-effects sensitivity analyses were conducted, supplemented by trial sequential analysis (TSA). Results A total of 45 randomized controlled trials were included in this meta-analysis. RCR significantly improved HRQoL across multiple scales (MacNew: MD = 0.17; MLHFQ: MD = −5.38; P < 0.05), while maintaining SF-36 and HADS outcomes comparable to standard care. Exploratory analyses indicated statistically significant improvements in mental health at 6 months (MD = 1.73, P = 0.03) and physical functioning at 12 months (MD = 1.48, P = 0.0002). Regarding cardiovascular safety, RCR was not associated with a statistically significant increase in the risk of MACEs, all-cause mortality, or adverse events ( P > 0.05) compared to conventional care. RCR significantly reduced the risk of cardiac rehospitalization (RR = 0.70, P = 0.01), with exploratory stratified analyses indicating that this favorable association was evident in the hardware-integrated interventions subgroup (RR = 0.59, P = 0.02) and 6-month observation subgroup (RR = 0.38, P < 0.00001), alongside a non-significant numerical protective trend among high-risk patients (RR: 0.59 vs. 0.74, P = 0.15). The economic viability of RCR remains uncertain, critically depending on initial setup outlays, patient scaling, and subsequent healthcare utilization. Conclusions RCR may serve as an effective and safe alternative to conventional care that improves physical and psychological well-being, was associated with a lower risk of cardiac rehospitalization, and may provide economic value in certain healthcare systems. Systematic Review Registration: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261374977 , PROSPERO CRD420261374977.
authors: Hui Pei; Hengrui Li; Miaomiao Hu; Boyan Liu; Dali Hu; Yuanmin Li; Qiang Feng Xiao

title: Machine Learning-Based Prediction Model of Pilgrims’ Tiredness During Hajj Using Smartwatch Physiological and Mobility Indicators
abstract: Pilgrim safety during Hajj is challenged by dense crowds, sustained physical exertion, and demanding environmental conditions that can increase tiredness and compromise well-being. Although wearable sensing enables objective monitoring, the reviewed literature provides limited evidence on how synthetic augmentation affects predictive performance and cross-participant generalization when wearable data are scarce. To address this gap, this study presents an integrated framework that combines correlation- and domain-informed feature screening with statistically constrained synthetic data generation and a complementary assessment of predictive performance and synthetic data fidelity. Using the Hajj 1445 (June 2024) Apple Watch dataset comprising 120 records from three participants, the study compares classical resampling, univariate normal generation, multivariate normal (MVN) sampling, and covariance-aware generation using Cholesky decomposition and Mahalanobis distance filtering under a consistent classifier evaluation protocol. The highest observed record-level test accuracy is 93.33%, achieved by a Decision Tree using MVN sampling with moderate clipping (±1.4). Leave-one-participant-out evaluation of the same configuration yields a mean accuracy of 68.65% (SD = 19.72%), indicating lower cross-participant generalization. The regularized MVN-Cholesky-Mahalanobis configuration attains a composite synthetic-data quality score of 79.27%. These results show that statistically constrained synthetic augmentation can support tiredness prediction when real data are limited, while the participant-grouped results highlight the need for validation using larger and more diverse Hajj cohorts.
authors: Mazin I. Alshamrani; Shema Alhazmi; Tarik Alafif; Thamir M. Qadah; Malak Aljabri; Walla Al-Eidarous; Abdullah Alhawsawi; Majed Farrash

title: Conceptualising pathological self-monitoring of physical activity
abstract: Background: Technologies that facilitate monitoring one’s physical activity are potentially detrimental for people with high levels of eating psychopathology and compulsive exercise. Investigations in this area are complicated by the diverse functionality these technologies offer, and the varied ways in which a person can engage with a device or application. Furthermore, physical activity can be monitored without these technologies. Objective: This thesis aimed to develop a more comprehensive conceptualisation of physical activity self-monitoring in relation to eating psychopathology and compulsive exercise. Methodology: The research programme used diverse data sources (survey, semi-structured interviews, online forums) and analytical methods – both qualitative (thematic analysis) and quantitative (word-counts, network analysis). First, analyses of eating disorder forums investigated interest in, and engagement with physical activity self-monitoring-related technologies. Forms and focuses of physical activity self-monitoring were then captured through a survey, followed by interviews with people indicating high levels of compulsive exercise to investigate the nature of physical activity self-monitoring in greater depth. Last, further thematic analyses of eating disorder forums – conducted separately for people with high or low focuses on recovery – evaluated the comprehensiveness of the previous findings. Findings: The overall findings were grouped into five themes: Engagement and accuracy (the nature of physical activity self-monitoring); Comparisons (how and to what one’s physical activity is compared); Monitoring non-physical activity focuses (e.g., how monitoring one’s physique relates to physical activity); Cognitions, affect and behaviours (how specific psychological factors potentially relate to physical activity self-monitoring); and Interpersonal factors (how physical activity self-monitoring is enacted in relation to others). Implications: Future research is outlined, with the development of a measurement instrument being particularly emphasised. More immediately, the findings can assist clinicians and technology manufacturers in identifying aspects of physical activity self-monitoring that are potentially detrimental to people with high levels of eating psychopathology and compulsive exercise.
authors: Duncan C. McCaig
venue: Warwick Research Archive Portal (University of Warwick)

title: RESULT ON COMPREHENSIVE SMART EYE RELIEF SYSTEM USING HEAT & VIBRATION
abstract: Digital eye strain has become more common because people use computers, smartphones, and other digital screens for a long period of time. This leads to problems like tired eyes, dryness, irritation, blurry vision, and discomfort [6], [12], [13]. Earlier research shows that warming the eyelids can help make the eyes feel more comfortable and improve the quality of tears. Also, massaging the eyes or using vibration can help relax the eyes and reduce discomfort [1], [2], [3]. Especially, studies on eye masks that use both heat and vibration have shown improvements in dry eye symptoms and some eye-related measurements. This supports the idea that combining heat and mechanical stimulation could be a good, non-invasive way to help relax the eyes [3], [8]. Based on this, this paper introduces a Vision Relief Embedded Eye Relaxation System. It's a small, portable, and rechargeable device that looks like an eye mask. It uses controlled heat and vibration to help relax the eyes and ease discomfort from using digital screens too much. By combining both therapies into one device, the system offers a practical, easy-to-use, and affordable solution for students, office workers, and others who use digital devices a lot. This idea builds on existing research and aims to provide a simple, integrated way to help with eye relaxation.
authors: Arati Bhujabal; Diksha Bhingare; Vaishnavi Bhosale -; Prof. A. C. Pise
venue: International Journal of Mechanical Engineering Research and Technology

title: Moda Tasarımı Eğitiminde Yapay Zekâ Destekli Sürdürülebilir ve İnovatif Tasarım Süreçleri
abstract: Bu araştırma, moda tasarımı eğitiminde yapay zekâ destekli sürdürülebilir ve inovatif tasarım uygulamalarının öğrencilerin öğrenme süreçleri ve tasarım yaklaşımları üzerindeki etkilerini incelemeyi amaçlamaktadır. Araştırma, nitel araştırma yaklaşımı doğrultusunda durum çalışması deseni ile yürütülmüştür. Çalışma, 2025–2026 eğitim-öğretim yılı bahar döneminde Sakarya Uygulamalı Bilimler Üniversitesi Ferizli Meslek Yüksekokulu Tasarım Bölümü Moda Tasarımı Programında yürütülen seçmeli İnovasyon ve Moda dersine kayıtlı beş ikinci sınıf öğrencisi (N=5) ile gerçekleştirilmiştir. Uygulama süreci dört hafta boyunca haftada iki ders saati olmak üzere toplam sekiz ders saati sürmüştür. Bu süreçte öğrencilerden sürdürülebilir moda, doğal ve geri dönüştürülebilir tekstil lifleri, akıllı tekstiller ve giyilebilir teknoloji temaları doğrultusunda ChatGPT ile metinden görsele (text-to-image) üretim gerçekleştiren üretken yapay zekâ araçlarından yararlanarak yenilikçi moda tasarımları geliştirmeleri istenmiştir. Araştırmanın veri setini öğrenciler tarafından hazırlanan beş yapay zekâ destekli tasarım görseli, beş teknik eskiz, beş poster çalışması, araştırmacı gözlem formları ve uygulama sonunda gerçekleştirilen beş yarı yapılandırılmış bireysel görüşme oluşturmuştur. Veriler betimsel analiz ve tematik analiz yöntemleriyle değerlendirilmiştir. Analiz sonuçları, öğrencilerin yapay zekâyı tasarım sürecinin yerine geçen bir sistem olarak değil, yaratıcı düşünmeyi destekleyen ve alternatif tasarım fikirleri geliştirmeyi kolaylaştıran bir öğrenme aracı olarak değerlendirdiklerini göstermiştir. Ayrıca öğrencilerin sürdürülebilirliği yalnızca çevre dostu malzeme kullanımıyla sınırlı görmedikleri; ergonomi, kullanıcı odaklı tasarım, işlevsellik, akıllı tekstiller ve çevresel sorumluluk boyutlarıyla birlikte ele aldıkları belirlenmiştir. Bulgular, yapay zekâ destekli tasarım uygulamalarının öğrencilerin yaratıcı düşünme, problem çözme, eleştirel değerlendirme, teknoloji okuryazarlığı ve sürdürülebilir tasarım farkındalıklarını geliştirdiğini ortaya koymaktadır. Sonuç olarak araştırma, üretken yapay zekânın moda tasarımı eğitiminde yalnızca görsel üretim sağlayan dijital bir araç olmadığını; sürdürülebilirlik bilincini, disiplinlerarası düşünmeyi ve kullanıcı odaklı tasarım yaklaşımını destekleyen etkili bir öğrenme ortamı sunduğunu göstermektedir.
authors: Şebnem Noyat

title: Proceedings from the Consortium for Technology & Innovation in Pediatrics (CTIP) 2025 annual pediatric device innovation symposium
abstract: The 2025 CTIP Pediatric Device Innovation Symposium in Chicago, IL, convened a multi‑stakeholder community of clinicians, entrepreneurs, regulators, investors, and families to examine how pediatric medical devices traverse the "last mile" from regulatory clearance to real‑world adoption. The program featured a keynote fireside chat with Kolaleh Eskandanian, PhD, followed by four focused panels: (1) procurement, reimbursement, and clinical adoption barriers within children's hospitals; (2) pathways for licensing, M&A, and corporate accelerator partnerships; (3) lived regulatory experiences of CTIP portfolio companies across FDA programs; and (4) investing in pediatrics beyond traditional venture capital. A portfolio showcase highlighted five CTIP companies (WearableDose, Luminoah, Makani Science, Madison Scientific, Renata Medical), with an Audience Choice Award recognizing standout innovation. Cross‑cutting themes included the need for earlier engagement with supply‑chain and finance stakeholders at hospital systems; clear value propositions that link device benefits to total cost of care; creative coding and payer‑evidence strategies; right‑sized quality systems and evidence generation for small pediatric markets; and diversified, mission‑aligned capital stacks (family offices, foundations, strategic partners, and non‑dilutive funding). This manuscript synthesizes session discussions, draws actionable lessons for innovators and health‑system decision‑makers, and outlines near‑term priorities for accelerating safe, effective pediatric device availability and access.
authors: Juan Espinoza; Grzegorz Zapotoczny; Bianca Riello; Nadine Afari; Madison Christmas; Jordan Cashwell; Melissa Bent; Yaniv Bar‐Cohen

title: Real-time wearable detection of respiratory infections in pediatric transplant households
abstract: ABSTRACT Consumer-grade wearables can continuously and longitudinally measure health signals such as heart rate (HR), activity, and sleep. While changes in these signals have been implicated in the early detection of infection (e.g., influenza, SARS-CoV-2) and real-time alerting systems have been developed, evidence from prospective deployment in pediatric transplant households remains limited. Here, we study the application of a resting heart rate (RHR)-based real-time alerting algorithm to detect respiratory virus infection in a cohort of solid organ transplant recipients and their household members (n=146) in a Phase IV clinical trial ( NCT06161454 ). Reliable and efficient alerting for infection events may be particularly relevant for this population, enabling isolation, clinical management, and/or treatment. Of 31 antigen-test outcomes, nearly all (29/31, 93.5%) correspond to either influenza, COVID, or other patient-reported symptoms. We describe RHR, HR, activity, and sleep/circadian rhythm features around clinical alarm events, identifying candidate features for further investigation and algorithm improvement.
authors: Caleb Mayer; Eric G. Hurwitz; Tanya Bhatia; Annie Chung; Divya Gandla; Bryanna N. Domenick; E. title: Detection is not resistance: frontier prompt-injection receipts
abstract: Preregistered Batch-API tests of prompt-injection resistance across three frontier models (Claude Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, Haiku 4.5). Sonnet 5 detects a blatant injection on every audit probe while obeying it on 16 of 20 tasks (0.80, 95% CI 0.58-0.92). This is an independent replication of detection without resistance, a mode reported first in arXiv:2606.07808; it is not claimed as a discovery. The obey rate replicates across four independent same-prompt batches (0.738, 0.787, 0.825, 0.850; mean 0.800) but is contingent on the injection being the last text in the prompt: on a length ladder with wording held constant, trailing neutral text takes it to 0.263 at 100 characters and 0.000 at 200, and the same position contrast moved nothing on two open-weight models. The contribution beyond replication is the presentation channel: the identical payload moves Sonnet 5 from 0.00 to 0.33 compliance only when it wears a System, tool-output or cited-spec costume (+0.307, 90% CI 0.226-0.390, n=14), while the same model resists a fabricated reasoning technique (powered null). A block-labeling defense drove observed compliance to zero at n=14 (one-sided 95% upper bound about 19%); applied to a reviewing rather than an acting model it degraded discrimination (0.555 to 0.003 on a leak-free re-run), so it is scoped to the actor channel. Version 1.1.0 adds the reviewer side, measured on open-weight monitors (12B-35B, n=337 per cell, most results replicated on a second task pool). A monitor's recorded verdict can be the attacker's appended word. The untrusted-input label makes a monitor obey dictated verdicts it otherwise ignores. Score-mode and verdict-first formats fall to an automated payload search, and monitor diversity stops only attacks aimed at one monitor. The one defense that held, showing the monitor only the extracted integer, fails once an LLM does the extracting. Raw completions and per-item verdicts ship with stdlib-only re-derivation scripts (reproduce.py, joint_table.py, recency.py, monitor_label.py, oversight.py) that need no API key and no network.
authors: Bentley Moon
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: SAGE: Efficient Protected Vision-Language Inference on Smart Glasses
abstract: Smart glasses are a promising platform for vision-language assistants, but private split inference remains expensive: protecting visual representations before transmission does not remove the cost of on-device vision encoding, wide protected tokens, or hardware-unaware execution. We present SAGE (Smart-glasses-Aware Guarded Encoding), a hardware-aware framework for efficient protected VLM inference on smart glasses. SAGE keeps raw images and unprotected visual tokens on the trusted device, reduces visual input cost, executes shape-specialized INT8 graphs, and compresses protected representations into compact 256-dimensional INT8 packets before transmission. Unlike efficiency methods optimized only for nominal model size, SAGE selects its operating point using downstream answer quality together with measured latency, memory, and thermal behavior on real Mentra Live glasses. On a matched Qwen workload, SAGE reduces glasses inference latency by 39.18%, device-sensor temperature rise by 21.91%, and protected packet size by 96.56%, while retaining 85.62% of the protected reference's relaxed utility and comparable prompted containment. Direct glasses-to-phone tests deliver all 192 packets and reduce median packet-plus-acknowledgment time from 71.3 to 10.0 ms. The compact protected interface also transfers across four additional VLM families. These results show that private wearable VLM inference must be optimized jointly across representation protection, communication, and real-device execution rather than through model compression alone.
authors: Zhimin Li; Pan Wang; Jingxian Chen; Yuantao Tang; Qian Lou; Jingtong Hu

title: Acousto-mechanofluidic synergy: A GHz resonator-enhanced rotary valve system for fully automated, efficient point-of-care nucleic acid testing
abstract: The advancement of point-of-care testing (POCT) is critical for decentralized molecular diagnostics, yet current platforms are hindered by inefficient mixing, complex workflows, long turnaround times, and operator dependency. This study presents the acoustofluidic-enhanced integrated system (AEIS), a fully automated platform that integrates a GHz acoustic resonator with a micro-valve control system for nucleic acid testing. The resonator generates intense acoustic streaming vortices, enabling second-scale mixing and reducing nucleic acid extraction time to under 4 min. Coupled with hydroxyl-modified polystyrene microbeads for nucleic acid extraction (98% efficiency) and automated fluidic control via a rotary valve, the system detects EGFR L858R mutations in plasma with a limit of detection of 2.6 copies/μl and completes the sample-to-answer workflow within 30 min. This enclosed, low-cost, and portable platform minimizes contamination and operator intervention, offering a sensitive and efficient solution for on-site testing in infectious disease control and early cancer screening.
authors: Hongtao Shi; Zhiwei Li; Bingnan Wang; Xuexin Duan; Tiechuan Li

title: Self-aggregated photo-heterostructures enhancing fluorescence for cancer diagnosis and treatment monitoring
abstract: Semiconductor zinc oxide (ZnO) nanostructures as classic photonic materials have sparked the development of low-cost, high-performance fluorescence sensors; however, their scalable clinical applications remain hampered by inadequate sensitivity. Here, we engineer a high-curvature photo-heterostructure aggregate-enhanced fluorescence (PAEF) sensor based on bubble-scaffolded ZnO nanorods. Leveraging synergistic evanescent field coupling and self-aggregation of photo-heterostructures, PAEF sensor streamlines efficient isolation (~90%) and ultrasensitive profiling of tumor extracellular vesicles (EVs) in a single assay, achieving sensitivity <10 EVs/μL (104-fold better than ELISA) without additional amplification, outperforming most state-of-the-art EV fluorescence assays. This self-sufficient sensor enables accurate monitoring of targeted therapeutic efficacy in mouse xenograft models via simultaneous dual-marker readout. We further show its clinical utility in hepatocellular carcinoma diagnosis with ≥96% accuracy (≥98% specificity) in two cohorts (n = 146), improving dynamic monitoring of surgical treatment responses, particularly in alpha-fetoprotein-negative patients. This work provides a cost-effective ultrasensitive liquid biopsy tool advancing non-invasive cancer diagnosis. Fluorescent detection approaches often require specialist equipment or have limited sensitivity. Here, the authors develop a bubble-scaffolded zinc oxide nanorod photo heterostructure aggregate for fluoresce enhancement demonstrating application for detection of circulating extracellular vesicles.
authors: Xifeng Mo; Xiaojie Qin; Linfeng Mao; Yuming Tang; You Li; Hao Lü; Binqi Wei; Yu Yang; Yuyuan Zhang; Min Fang; Xinchun Li; Fan Yang

title: In-molecule machine learning with microfluidic integrated DNA neural computing
authors: Chunhai Fan; Mengyao Cao; Xiewei Xiong; Jianing Wang; Na Li; Bowen Li; Yun Zhu; Tong Zhu; Fei Wang; Longqian Xu; Jiajian Ji; Qunyan Yao; Li Li; Hao Pei; Chunyu Chang

title: Biologically motivated magnetic microfluidic rheostats for precise and scalable flow control
abstract: Precise regulation of hydraulic resistance is essential for controlling flow distribution, particle transport, and chemical synthesis in microfluidics. Despite frequent comparisons between microfluidic networks and electronic circuits, components analogous to electronic rheostats for high-precision continuous resistance tuning remain absent, with flow regulation typically relying on microvalves with discrete open/closed states and external flow-control hardware. Inspired by geometry-modulated flow resistance in heart valves, we introduce magnetic microfluidic rheostats composed of soft magnetic cantilever arrays, whose field-controlled bending modulates the hydraulic diameter to achieve stable and continuous resistance tuning with a minimum measured increment of ~1.7%. Using external permanent magnets instead of complex actuation systems, the rheostat enables low-cost, energy-efficient operation while maintaining high precision. Incorporating the rheostat into a Wheatstone fluidic bridge allows sub-10 µm/s flow balancing and precise microparticle manipulation. Moreover, rheostats with tailored magnetic responses enable one-to-many control under a single magnetic field, allowing multiple channels to be regulated synchronously or asynchronously. This approach simplifies system architecture compared with conventional one-to-one actuation, while maintaining 1-2% composition accuracy across multi-component streams. These results establish microfluidic rheostats as dedicated resistance regulators that expand the functional toolkit of microfluidics for scalable, high-precision manipulation and synthesis.
authors: Jiaqi Miao; Chenglin Jiang; Jingxuan Li; Alan Cheng Hou Tsang

title: Magneto-electrochemistry: A tool for sustainability and green chemistry
abstract: Magnetic fields provide a versatile and energy efficient strategy for modulating electrochemical processes without adding chemical reagents, mechanical stirring, or complex reactor designs. By coupling ionic currents with external magnetic fields, the resulting Lorentz-driven magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) convection accelerates mass transport and regulates interfacial kinetics at the micro- and macro-scale. These transport phenomena govern reaction rates, metal nucleation and growth, electrodeposition quality, and the long-term stability of electrochemical systems. This review examines recent advances in magnetic field assisted electrochemistry through the lens of process intensification and the 12 Principles of Green Chemistry. We discuss how magnetic fields influence fundamental processes, including electrodeposition, electrocatalysis, electrochemical energy storage, and emerging applications such as microfluidics, sensing, and dynamic autonomous systems, with a specific emphasis on the use of permanent magnets as zero-operating-energy tools for controlling transport. By evaluating sustainability metrics and life-cycle considerations, we highlight opportunities to enhance turnover frequencies and reduce the industry's reliance on critical minerals, chemical additives, or mechanical agitation. Finally, we identify key challenges that must be addressed to translate magnetic control from laboratory demonstrations to scalable electrochemical technologies. These include the need for quantitative transport models and reactor designs that can be implemented at industrially relevant scales. Overall, magnetic field assisted electrochemistry is positioned as an emerging approach for improving efficiency and circularity in the next generation of electrified chemical manufacturing.
authors: Kaylie Ann McCracken; Pedaballi Sireesha; William T. McLeod; Mohamed K. Abd El-Rahman; Daniel G. Nocera; George M. Whitesides; Haihui Joy Jiang; Jeffrey Gordon Bell
